{"assumptions":["Independent coordinates, arbitrary measurable state spaces; measurable real f and E Z^2 finite","Each resampling copy independent of original coordinates","Coordinate-infimum application requires a real X_{-i}-measurable infimum; additive equality means equality almost surely"],"created_at":"2026-10-13T09:56:14+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_00a8a829ba7b0cabcfb6107b8a3fcda1a7239d151268d11bb0e4036b513850d6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1,...,X_n be independent random variables on arbitrary measurable coordinate spaces, let f be measurable and real valued, and let Z=f(X_1,...,X_n) belong to L^2. For each i let X_i_prime be an independent copy of X_i, independent of all original coordinates, and let Z^{(i)} replace X_i by X_i_prime in f. Write X_{-i} for the other coordinates and m_i=E[Z|X_{-i}]. Then Var(Z)<=v:=sum_i E[(Z-m_i)^2]=(1/2)sum_i E[(Z-Z^{(i)})^2]=sum_i E[((Z-Z^{(i)})_+)^2]. For arbitrary real X_{-i}-measurable Z_i, Var(Z)<=sum_i E[(Z-Z_i)^2], interpreted in the extended nonnegative sense; if the right side is finite, each Z_i is square integrable. In particular v is the minimum over such square-integrable Z_i, attained at Z_i=m_i. A coordinate infimum inf_x f(X_1,...,X_{i-1},x,X_{i+1},...,X_n) may be used as Z_i only when it defines a real X_{-i}-measurable random variable; those properties are additional conditions, not automatic consequences of measurability of f on arbitrary spaces. Equality Var(Z)=v holds exactly when Z=c+sum_i g_i(X_i) almost surely for some square-integrable one-coordinate functions g_i and constant c. Equality in the arbitrary-Z_i bound holds exactly when this almost-sure additive condition holds and Z_i=m_i almost surely for every i. The Efron-Stein bound is Boucheron-Lugosi-Massart, Concentration Inequalities (2013), Theorem3.1, printedpages54-55; the iff equality characterization here is independently derived using the finite orthogonal Hoeffding decomposition, rather than attributed to the theorem text.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["product measure","all the events increasing (the proof uses FKG on the decreasing complements)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542929+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_01ce16ef6218f32c1f9919a8d7c88e3c9ce4ae7ffd8d9803708ef6d53c50695b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let P be a product measure on {0,1}^E and let A_1, ..., A_k be INCREASING events with the same probability. Then max_i P(A_i) = P(A_1) >= 1 - ( 1 - P( union_i A_i ) )^{1/k}. More generally, without assuming equal probabilities, max_i P(A_i) >= 1 - (1 - P(union_i A_i))^{1/k}. The name comes from the case k = 2, where the bound reads P(A_1) >= 1 - sqrt(1 - P(A_1 or A_2)): if the union is very likely then at least one of two increasing events is likely, quantitatively. This is the standard device for turning a statement like 'some crossing of a box occurs' into 'a crossing in a specific direction occurs with probability bounded below', and it is the engine of Zhang's argument that theta(1/2) = 0 for bond percolation on Z^2. The events must be INCREASING, since the proof is Harris-FKG applied to their complements; for arbitrary events the inequality is false. [standard; e.g. Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., proof of Theorem 11.11, and Bollobas-Riordan, Percolation]","status":"unverified"}

Then for every measurable A, E[ exp( d_T(X, A)^2 / 4 ) ] <= 1 / P(A), and consequently P(A) P( d_T(X, A) >= t ) <= exp( - t^2 / 4 ) for every t > 0. Formally, the axiom establishes existence rather than a construction; it states that for every set I and every I-indexed family (S_i)_{i in I} of nonempty sets, there exists an I-indexed set (x_i)_{i in I} of elements of the union of the S_i such that x_i in S_i for every i in I. {"assumptions":["G has independent N(0,1) entries, m >= n","expectations are over the Gaussian matrix; the concentration statements use the 1-Lipschitz property of singular values in the Frobenius norm","the square case m = n is NOT covered by the lower bound (it gives 0); see the smallest-singular-value theorem for square matrices"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T15:17:03.040820+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_052a3d5f610725674865636ab27b13687c810c26f61037934682b44a583a40cc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let G be an m x n matrix (m >= n) with independent standard Gaussian entries, and let s_max(G) >= s_min(G) denote its largest and smallest singular values (the extreme values of |G x| over unit vectors x in R^n). It was introduced by Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson in a paper in 1933. The Neyman–Pearson lemma is part of the Neyman–Pearson theory of statistical testing, which introduced concepts such as errors of the second kind, power function, and inductive behavior. The previous Fisherian theory of significance testing postulated only one hypothesis. By introducing a competing hypothesis, the Neyman–Pearsonian flavor of statistical testing allows investigating the two types of errors. The trivial cases where one always rejects or fails to reject the null hypothesis are of little interest but it does prove that one must not relinquish control over one type of error while calibrating the other. Neyman and Pearson accordingly proceeded to restrict their attention to the class of all $\\alpha$ level tests while subsequently minimizing type II error, traditionally denoted by $\\beta$. Their seminal 1933 paper, which includes the Neyman–Pearson lemma showed not only the existence of tests with the most power that retain a prespecified level of type I error ( $\\alpha$), but also provided a way to construct such tests. The Karlin-Rubin theorem extended the Neyman–Pearson lemma to settings involving composite hypotheses with monotone likelihood ratios.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a real or complex Banach space","A is linear on a subspace D(A)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.769837+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator semigroups","id":"claim_05b342a8dbfbe497827c01268d9e092d3b7a5c5940a131f4d29aa0e10be41ee7","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a Banach space with dual X*. The duality set of x ∈ X is J(x) = {x* ∈ X* : ⟨x, x*⟩ = ‖x‖² = ‖x*‖²}, which is nonempty by the Hahn-Banach theorem. A linear operator A: D(A) ⊂ X → X is dissipative if for every x ∈ D(A) there exists some j ∈ J(x) with Re⟨Ax, j⟩ ≤ 0. Equivalently (Lumer-Phillips lemma), ‖(λ − A)x‖ ≥ λ‖x‖ for all λ > 0 and all x ∈ D(A). In a Hilbert space (J(x) = {x}) this reads Re⟨Ax, x⟩ ≤ 0 for all x ∈ D(A). A is m-dissipative (maximal dissipative) if it is dissipative and Ran(λ − A) = X for some λ > 0 (then for every λ > 0). A is accretive (m-accretive) if −A is dissipative (m-dissipative). For a dissipative A, λ − A is injective for λ > 0 and its inverse on Ran(λ − A) has norm at most 1/λ.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Independent rate-one Poisson offspring displacement processes.","The layer-tail recursion is the one stated in the source paper."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.363857+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_066f8d6d147ffdc831735ab62b26710560d8571ba00afcc1c575fa46962eb6bf","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; tested by direct Monte Carlo simulation of the Poisson-weighted infinite tree (4000 replicates, k=2,5,10,12), agreeing with the recursion within about 1.5 standard errors] This is the campaign's branching-walk identification behind Conjecture 1 of H. Stepanyants, P. L. Krapivsky, H. Hartle and D. Krioukov, The rank and layer distributions in random recursive trees, arXiv:2608.04303. Let the Poisson-weighted infinite tree have root position zero, with children of each vertex at the points of an independent rate-one Poisson process on (0,infinity), translated by their parent's position. Let M_k be the minimum position of generation k, and set M_0=0. Define s_0(y)=1 for y>=0 and s_k(y)=1-exp(-integral_0^y s_{k-1}(z)dz) for k>=1. Put bar_ell_k=integral_0^infinity s_k(y)exp(-y)dy and ell_k=bar_ell_k-bar_ell_{k+1}. In the source, ell_k is the limiting fraction of vertices in layer k of a random recursive tree, formed by joining each new vertex j uniformly to one of vertices 1,...,j-1. Layer zero consists of the initial leaves, and subsequent layers are obtained by successive leaf removals. For every k>=0 and y>=0, s_k(y)=P(M_k<=y). Consequently bar_ell_k=E[exp(-M_k)] and ell_k=E[exp(-M_k)-exp(-M_{k+1})]. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the counterexample is a 2-dimensional real l^p computation (the ratio at (1, 1/2) is 1.7268 and the maximum over x = (1,t) is attained near t = 0.62 at about 1.7320)","complexification bound: ||T_C f||_q <= ||T u||_q + ||T v||_q for f = u + i v"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.553381+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, interpolation of operators","id":"claim_0730394901107dee5537f5da05c6f3480958fb025978d553df02c49ce8dba25d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Two hypotheses of the Riesz-Thorin theorem are load-bearing and are routinely dropped in write-ups. (1) COMPLEX SCALARS. The proof interpolates through an analytic family f_z, so the conclusion ||T||_{p_theta -> q_theta} <= M_0^{1-theta} M_1^{theta} is a theorem about complex L^p spaces. Counterexample for real scalars: on R^2 with the l^p norms let T(x_1, x_2) = (x_1 - x_2, x_1 + x_2). Over the REALS, ||T||_{l^infinity -> l^1} = 2 (the maximum of |x_1-x_2| + |x_1+x_2| = 2 max(|x_1|,|x_2|) over the unit cube) and ||T||_{l^2 -> l^2} = sqrt(2) (T is sqrt(2) times a rotation). Interpolating the endpoints (p_0,q_0) = (infinity,1) and (p_1,q_1) = (2,2) at theta = 1/2 gives (p,q) = (4, 4/3) and the putative bound 2^{1/2} (sqrt 2)^{1/2} = 2^{3/4} = 1.6818...; but the real operator norm from l^4 to l^{4/3} is about 1.7320 (already the vector (1, 1/2) gives the ratio 1.7268 > 1.6818). No contradiction with the complex theorem: over C the norm ||T||_{l^infinity -> l^1} is 2 sqrt 2 (take (1, i)), and the complex bound becomes (2 sqrt 2)^{1/2} (sqrt 2)^{1/2} = 2, which is consistent. Remedy: for a real-linear T, complexification costs at most a factor 2, so the real conclusion holds with constant 2 M_0^{1-theta} M_1^{theta}. (2) LINEARITY. Riesz-Thorin is false as stated for merely sublinear operators, and it also requires STRONG endpoint bounds; an operator with only weak endpoint bounds, or one that is sublinear (such as a maximal operator), must be interpolated with the Marcinkiewicz theorem instead, whose constant is not M_0^{1-theta} M_1^{theta} and blows up at the endpoints.","status":"unverified"}

Result: By Trofimov's theorem a quasi-transitive graph of polynomial growth is quasi-isometric to a Cayley graph of a virtually nilpotent group, and the critical behaviour of percolation is not a quasi-isometry invariant in general, so this does not reduce directly to Z^d; however the known proof for Z^2 (Harris-Kesten) and the high-dimensional proof (lace expansion, d >= 11) do not transfer either. Exponential growth is Hutchcroft's theorem. The remaining cases are (a) polynomial growth of degree 3 to 10 (and all virtually nilpotent non-abelian cases, e.g. the Heisenberg group of growth degree 4), where the problem is at least as hard as C0023, and (b) intermediate growth (Grigorchuk-type groups), where Hutchcroft's argument fails because it uses that the number of vertices at distance n grows exponentially to compare the cluster with a branching structure. For case (b) I checked the two known routes: the nonamenable route (Burton-Keane fails, so uniqueness monotonicity gives theta(p_c)=0 through the Benjamini-Lyons-Peres-Schramm argument) does not apply since intermediate-growth groups are amenable; the exponential-growth route uses a subadditivity argument on the expected number of vertices at distance n reached by the cluster, which requires growth rate > 1 in the exponential sense. Intermediate growth groups have growth exp(n^alpha), alpha < 1, which is superpolynomial, and Hutchcroft's argument actually needs only that the growth is faster than any polynomial? His proof uses the growth to show that the susceptibility is finite at p_c in a spherically-averaged sense via a comparison with a branching random walk with killing at rate given by the growth; I believe the argument requires exponential growth for the comparison to be uniform, so intermediate growth is a genuine gap. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T16:32:48.605658+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_0796610249b652cccd85914ca99400dbdd061610c80af8c60ca939792be91697","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In linear algebra and functional analysis, a spectral theorem is a result about when a linear operator or matrix can be diagonalized. This is extremely useful because computations involving a diagonalizable matrix can often be reduced to much simpler computations involving the corresponding diagonal matrix of eigenvalues. The concept of diagonalization is relatively straightforward for operators on finite-dimensional vector spaces but requires some modification for operators on infinite-dimensional spaces. In general, the spectral theorem identifies a class of linear operators that can be modeled by multiplication operators, which are as simple as one can hope to find. {"assumptions":["g Borel measurable","P(X in D_g) = 0, where D_g is the discontinuity set of g and X is the LIMIT","for the distributional case: a separable metric space, so that Skorokhod representation applies"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752745+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_08bbed66bee85e7a43e037177ad373d4b632f7fc0a234cb4b033a85493a10a9f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_n and X be random elements of a metric space S and let g : S -> S' be a Borel measurable map whose set of discontinuity points D_g is a Borel set with P(X in D_g) = 0. Then: X_n => X in distribution implies g(X_n) => g(X); X_n -> X in probability implies g(X_n) -> g(X) in probability; X_n -> X almost surely implies g(X_n) -> g(X) almost surely. The hypothesis is that the LIMIT avoids the discontinuity set almost surely, not that g is continuous everywhere - which is what makes the theorem usable for maps such as x -> 1/x when the limit is almost surely nonzero, or x -> 1_{(a, infinity)}(x) when P(X = a) = 0. Without that hypothesis the conclusion fails: with X_n = 1/n deterministically, X = 0, and g = 1_{(0, infinity)}, we have g(X_n) = 1 for all n while g(X) = 0. D_g is always Borel for any g between metric spaces, so that part of the hypothesis is automatic. [standard; e.g. Billingsley, Convergence of Probability Measures, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.7]","status":"unverified"}

Let $a: \\Omega\\times\\mathbb{R}\\times\\mathbb{R}^N \\to \\mathbb{R}^N$ be a Caratheodory function (measurable in $x$, continuous in $(s,\\xi)$) satisfying, for a.e. $x$ and all $s, \\xi, \\eta$: growth $|a(x,s,\\xi)| \\leq \\beta\\,(k(x) + |s|^{p-1} + |\\xi|^{p-1})$ with $k \\in L^{p'}(\\Omega)$; coercivity $a(x,s,\\xi)\\cdot\\xi \\geq \\alpha|\\xi|^p$ with $\\alpha > 0$; strict monotonicity $(a(x,s,\\xi) - a(x,s,\\eta))\\cdot(\\xi-\\eta) > 0$ for $\\xi \\neq \\eta$ (a Leray-Lions operator, e.g. the $p$-Laplacian $a = |\\xi|^{p-2}\\xi$). Consider $-\\operatorname{div}\\,a(x,u,\\nabla u) = f$ in $\\Omega$, $u = 0$ on $\\partial\\Omega$, with $f \\in L^1(\\Omega)$. (Boccardo-Gallouet, J. Funct. Anal. 87 (1989); the estimates are the nonlinear form of Stampacchia's truncation estimates.) A PRIORI ESTIMATES. Let $u \\in W_0^{1,p}(\\Omega)$ be a weak solution for a datum $f \\in L^1 \\cap W^{-1,p'}$ (in practice the solutions $u_n$ of approximating problems with $f_n \\in L^\\infty$, $\\|f_n\\|_{L^1} \\leq \\|f\\|_{L^1}$; all constants below depend only on $N, p, \\alpha, \\|f\\|_{L^1}$, never on $n$). Then: (E1) for every $k > 0$, $\\alpha\\int_\\Omega|\\nabla T_k(u)|^p\\,dx \\leq k\\,\\|f\\|_{L^1}$; (E2) for every $k > 0$, $|\\{|u| \\geq k\\}| \\leq (S^p\\|f\\|_{L^1}/\\alpha)^{N/(N-p)}\\,k^{-N(p-1)/(N-p)}$, where $S$ is the Sobolev constant of $W_0^{1,p} \\hookrightarrow L^{p^*}$, $p^* = Np/(N-p)$; i.e. $u$ is bounded in the Marcinkiewicz space $M^{N(p-1)/(N-p)}(\\Omega)$; (E3) for every $h > 0$, $|\\{|\\nabla u| \\geq h\\}| \\leq C\\,h^{-N(p-1)/(N-1)}$, i.e. $|\\nabla u|$ is bounded in $M^{N(p-1)/(N-1)}(\\Omega)$; hence, $\\Omega$ being bounded, $u$ is bounded in $W_0^{1,q}(\\Omega)$ for every $q < N(p-1)/(N-1)$. If moreover $p > 2 - 1/N$ (equivalently $N(p-1)/(N-1) > 1$), there exists $u \\in W_0^{1,q}(\\Omega)$ for every $q < N(p-1)/(N-1)$, with $T_k(u) \\in W_0^{1,p}(\\Omega)$ for every $k$, $a(x,u,\\nabla u) \\in L^{r}(\\Omega)$ for some $r > 1$, and $\\int_\\Omega a(x,u,\\nabla u)\\cdot\\nabla\\varphi\\,dx = \\int_\\Omega f\\varphi\\,dx$ for all $\\varphi \\in C_c^\\infty(\\Omega)$ (a distributional solution). Sharp edges: (a) $q = N(p-1)/(N-1)$ is not attained - the fundamental solution of the $p$-Laplacian with $f = \\delta_0$ has $|\\nabla u| \\sim |x|^{-(N-1)/(p-1)}$, in $L^q$ iff $q < N(p-1)/(N-1)$; (b) for $1 < p \\leq 2 - 1/N$ the gradient of the solution is in general NOT in $L^1$, $u \\notin W^{1,1}$, and the distributional formulation is meaningless - one must use entropy or renormalized solutions defined through the truncations $T_k(u) \\in W_0^{1,p}$ and a generalized gradient; (c) existence is asserted, uniqueness is NOT: distributional $W^{1,q}$ solutions need not be unique (Serrin's pathological solutions of $\\operatorname{div}(A\\nabla u) = 0$ with $u \\in W^{1,q}$, $q < 2$, $u \\notin H^1_{loc}$, already for $p = 2$ and measurable coefficients); uniqueness holds in the entropy-solution class (Benilan, Boccardo, Gallouet, Gariepy, Pierre, Vazquez 1995) for $L^1$ data; (d) the estimates (E1)-(E3) require $T_k(u)$ to be an admissible test function, which is why they are proved on the approximations; (e) for measure data one gets the same $W_0^{1,q}$ bounds, but for a measure concentrated on a set of zero $p$-capacity the entropy uniqueness theory does not apply.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space and T is continuous","the metric is fixed, but the notions defined are independent of the choice of a compatible metric on a compact space","Gamma_eps(x) is taken with forward iterates for a general continuous map and with two-sided iterates for a homeomorphism","Bowen's entropy h(T,Y) is used for arbitrary, possibly non-invariant, subsets Y"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090635+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, entropy","id":"claim_09ce2d5bcd2dcfca590ed7dbdf3202b050716fcf7e9c95e3a6d615cdc80401f0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, d) be a compact metric space and T : X -> X continuous. For a subset Y of X (not assumed invariant or closed) Bowen's entropy of T on Y is h(T, Y) = lim as delta -> 0 of limsup_n (1/n) log r_n(delta, Y), where r_n(delta, Y) is the least cardinality of a set S that (n, delta)-spans Y, that is such that every y in Y admits s in S with d(T^i y, T^i s) <= delta for all 0 <= i < n. For eps > 0 and x in X put Gamma_eps(x) = { y in X : d(T^i x, T^i y) <= eps for all i >= 0 }, the set of points whose forward orbit shadows that of x at scale eps (for a homeomorphism one lets i range over all integers). DEFINITIONS: T is h-EXPANSIVE (Bowen) if there exists eps > 0 with h(T, Gamma_eps(x)) = 0 for every x in X. The TAIL ENTROPY of T is h*(T) = lim as eps -> 0 of sup over x in X of h(T, Gamma_eps(x)); the limit exists because the supremum is nondecreasing in eps. T is ASYMPTOTICALLY h-EXPANSIVE (Misiurewicz) if h*(T) = 0. Relations and cautions: expansive implies h-expansive (for small eps the sets Gamma_eps(x) are singletons, with the one- or two-sided convention matching the map), and h-expansive implies asymptotically h-expansive; neither implication reverses. Subshifts and expanding maps are expansive, hence h-expansive; every C^infinity diffeomorphism of a compact manifold is asymptotically h-expansive (Newhouse), while for finite smoothness this can fail. The quantity h*(T) measures the entropy invisible at any finite scale - the entropy 'in the tail' - and it is zero exactly when the system admits a principal symbolic extension (Boyle-Downarowicz theory); it is not the same as the topological entropy and carries no information about it.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f_n -> f in measure or mu-almost everywhere","uniform integrability of {f_n}","uniform tightness of {f_n}: on an infinite measure space this is an independent hypothesis"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751693+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_0a5d28e3a2f0563534ddca90e6e5c1998a87b5c53300e2cd9dcf829e15f851d8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"On a FINITE measure space, uniform integrability plus convergence in measure gives L^1 convergence. On a general (for instance sigma-finite but infinite) measure space this is FALSE and a third hypothesis is needed. The correct statement: let (Omega, F, mu) be a measure space and f_n in L^1(mu) with f_n -> f in measure (or mu-a.e.). Then f_n -> f in L^1(mu) if and only if (i) {f_n} is uniformly integrable, meaning sup_n integral_{|f_n| > K} |f_n| dmu -> 0 as K -> infinity, AND (ii) {f_n} is uniformly tight, meaning for every eps > 0 there is a set A with mu(A) < infinity and sup_n integral_{Omega \\ A} |f_n| dmu < eps. Counterexample showing (ii) is not implied by (i): on R with Lebesgue measure take f_n = 1_{[n, n+1]}. Then |f_n| <= 1 so the family is uniformly integrable and dominated, f_n -> 0 pointwise everywhere, yet ||f_n||_1 = 1 for every n. Mass escapes to infinity; on a finite measure space it has nowhere to go, which is exactly why the finite-measure statement can omit (ii). [standard; e.g. Bogachev, Measure Theory, Vol. I, Section 4.5]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. rows C^{1/2} z with z having i.i.d. mean-zero unit-variance entries and finite twelfth moment","p/n -> q_0 in (0, infinity)","the population spectral distribution converges to a limit with bounded support","the formula is used inside the bulk; isolated spikes are handled by the BBP correction"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:50:37.943602+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_0a70bf7dec2d4a8e97f8b3a3a903aaf467d73a6d689fe2fb896f6788c775985a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $E = \\frac{1}{n} X^T X$ be the sample covariance of $n$ i.i.d. rows in $\\mathbb{R}^p$ with population covariance $C$ (rows $C^{1/2} z_i$ with $z_i$ having i.i.d. entries of mean zero, variance one and finite twelfth moment), in the regime $p, n \\to \\infty$ with $q = p/n \\to q_0 \\in (0, \\infty)$, and assume the spectral distribution of $C$ converges to a limit with bounded support. Let $\\lambda_k, u_k$ be the sample eigenvalues and eigenvectors and let $g_E(z) = \\frac{1}{p}\\operatorname{tr}(z I - E)^{-1}$ be the Stieltjes transform of the sample spectrum, with $g(\\lambda - i0) := \\lim_{\\eta \\downarrow 0} g_E(\\lambda - i\\eta)$ inside the bulk. THEOREM (Ledoit and Peche, 2011, Theorem 4; in the form of Bun, Bouchaud and Potters 2017). The oracle eigenvalues $\\xi_k^{\\mathrm{or}} = u_k^T C u_k$ converge, uniformly in $k$ inside the bulk, to $$\\xi(\\lambda_k) = \\frac{\\lambda_k}{\\big|\\, 1 - q + q\\, \\lambda_k\\, g_E(\\lambda_k - i0) \\,\\big|^2}.$$ This limit depends on the population covariance $C$ only through the observable sample spectrum, so it is a consistent, computable estimator (the rotationally invariant estimator, RIE, or nonlinear shrinkage): replace each sample eigenvalue by $\\xi(\\lambda_k)$, keep the sample eigenvectors. In practice $g_E$ is evaluated at $\\lambda_k - i\\eta$ with a small $\\eta$ of order $n^{-1/2}$ times the eigenvalue scale, and the result is floored at a small positive fraction of the bulk level. When $C = \\sigma^2 I$ the formula returns $\\sigma^2$ for every eigenvalue (the Marchenko-Pastur spread is entirely removed); for a spike above the bulk it returns approximately the debiased population spike. Applying the formula to a matrix whose largest eigenvalue is a signal one is trying to keep, and flooring relative to that top eigenvalue, destroys the small eigenvalues that the inverse depends on.","status":"unverified"}

Then the set ext K of extreme points of K is a G_delta set, and for every x in K there is a Borel probability measure mu on K, concentrated on ext K, whose barycenter is x: phi(x) = integral phi dmu for every continuous linear functional phi. {"assumptions":["Finite-dimensional Euclidean space; n>=2 components and K>=2 epochs","Convex C1 f_i with globally L_i-Lipschitz gradients, L_i>0","Proper closed convex psi and an attained finite minimum of F=f+psi","x_1 is in dom psi; eta is constant, positive, and satisfies the displayed K-dependent cap","For the expected random-reshuffling bound, use fresh independent uniform permutations","For the optimized-rate corollaries assume D>0; the fixed-step inequalities do not require D>0"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:34:11.132651+00:00","domain":"Liu Zhou; proximal shuffling; random reshuffling; last iterate; convex optimization","id":"claim_0ab04f1d8562a58b42caeb8c92cdff50dfe5a30627a7b67abd496813c58be7c6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let n>=2, K>=2 and d>=1. Let each f_i:R^d->R be convex C1 with globally L_i-Lipschitz gradient, L_i>0. Let psi:R^d->R union {+infinity} be proper closed convex. Set f=(1/n)sum_i f_i, F=f+psi, and suppose x* minimizes F with F(x*) finite. Start at x_1 in dom psi. Write D=||x_1-x*||, Lbar=(1/n)sum_i L_i, Lmax=max_i L_i, s=1+log K, sigma_any^2=(1/n)sum_i ||grad f_i(x*)||^2 and sigma_rand^2=sigma_any^2+n||grad f(x*)||^2. Use a fixed positive step eta<=1/[4n sqrt(2 Lbar Lmax s)]. In epoch k, set z_0=x_k, take z_i=z_(i-1)-eta grad f_(sigma_i)(z_(i-1)) for i=1,...,n along a permutation sigma, and set x_(k+1)=prox_(n eta psi)(z_n), where prox_(n eta psi)(z) minimizes psi(x)+||x-z||^2/(2n eta). There is an absolute constant C such that, for every sequence of permutations, F(x_(K+1))-F(x*)<=C[D^2/(n eta K)+(n eta)^2 Lbar sigma_any^2 s]. If fresh independent uniform permutations are used in each epoch, E[F(x_(K+1))-F(x*)]<=C[D^2/(n eta K)+n eta^2 Lbar sigma_rand^2 s]. These are bounds for the last epoch iterate, with no strong-convexity assumption. For D>0, balancing eta under the stated cap gives respectively O(D^2 sqrt(Lbar Lmax s)/K+D^(4/3)(Lbar sigma_any^2 s)^(1/3)/K^(2/3)) and O(D^2 sqrt(Lbar Lmax s)/K+D^(4/3)(Lbar sigma_rand^2 s)^(1/3)/(n^(1/3) K^(2/3))). The fixed-step bounds also cover D=0. All norms are Euclidean. Source: Zijian Liu and Zhengyuan Zhou, On the Last-Iterate Convergence of Shuffling Gradient Methods, Theorem 4.4 and its full version Theorem C.1.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f is continuous on a closed cylinder around (t_0,y_0)","f is Lipschitz in y, uniformly in t, on that cylinder"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T14:20:41.451641+00:00","domain":"ordinary differential equations","id":"claim_0ad98344cc4c4b7f94070b09639fced6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f: [t_0-a,t_0+a] x B(y_0,b) -> R^n be continuous, where B(y_0,b) subset R^n is the closed ball of radius b around y_0, and suppose f is Lipschitz in its second argument uniformly in the first: there is L >= 0 with |f(t,y_1)-f(t,y_2)| <= L|y_1-y_2| for all t in the interval and y_1,y_2 in B(y_0,b). Let M = max|f(t,y)| over this compact domain and h = min(a, b/M). Then the initial value problem y'(t) = f(t,y(t)), y(t_0)=y_0, has a unique solution y on [t_0-h, t_0+h]. (When M = 0, read b/M as infinity, so h = a.) Continuity alone does not give uniqueness: y' = 2 sqrt(|y|), y(0) = 0 has infinitely many solutions. If f is continuous and locally Lipschitz in y on an open domain D, the local solutions through (t_0, y_0) patch together into a unique maximal solution, which leaves every compact subset of D as t approaches either end of its interval.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["product measure on a finite product of totally ordered two-point spaces (or a measure satisfying the FKG lattice condition)","both functions increasing, or both decreasing","square integrability"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542860+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0bf9a3e418fbc58529078909919960e7533413ef78f5b985e45f4917e302a72f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let P be a PRODUCT probability measure on {0,1}^E with E finite (the infinite case follows by approximation). Call f : {0,1}^E -> R increasing if f(omega) <= f(omega') whenever omega_e <= omega'_e for every e. Then for increasing f and g in L^2(P), E[f g] >= E[f] E[g]. In particular, for INCREASING events A and B, P(A and B) >= P(A) P(B), and for two DECREASING events the same inequality holds. For one increasing and one decreasing event the inequality REVERSES: P(A and B) <= P(A) P(B). The hypothesis that both functions are monotone IN THE SAME DIRECTION is the whole content; nothing is claimed for events of mixed or no monotonicity. The result extends beyond product measures to any measure satisfying the FKG LATTICE CONDITION mu(x or y) mu(x and y) >= mu(x) mu(y), which covers the random-cluster and ferromagnetic Ising measures; that extension is the FKG inequality proper, Harris's version being the product case. [Harris (1960); Fortuin, Kasteleyn and Ginibre (1971); see Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.4]","status":"unverified"}

For every eps > 0 there exists delta > 0 such that integral_A |f| dmu < eps whenever A is measurable with mu(A) < delta. Equivalently, the finite measure nu(A) = integral_A |f| dmu is absolutely continuous with respect to mu in the strong epsilon-delta sense, not merely in the sense that mu(A) = 0 implies nu(A) = 0. The two senses coincide for FINITE nu but not in general: with mu Lebesgue measure on (0,1) and nu(A) = integral_A dx/x, nu vanishes on mu-null sets yet nu(0, delta) = infinity for every delta. A single integrable function is therefore automatically a uniformly integrable family of one element. [standard; e.g. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 3.5]","status":"unverified"}

A probability measure is unimodal if, for some mode m, it is an atom at m plus an absolutely continuous measure whose density is nondecreasing to the left of m and nonincreasing to the right. Write boxplus for additive free convolution. For t>0 let S(0,t) be the centered semicircle law of variance t, with density sqrt(4t-x^2)/(2pi t) on |x|<=2sqrt(t). Let mu be compactly supported with positive diameter D=sup{|x-y|: x,y in supp(mu)}. Then mu boxplus S(0,t) is unimodal for every t>=D^2. Proof route: by the source's Lemma 3.1 (Biane's description), non-unimodality at time t gives some R>0 and a separating local minimum u_0 of xi_R with xi_R(u_0)<=1/t. The stationary-kernel lower bound, rescaled to diameter D, gives xi_R(u_0)>=1/D^2, so t<=D^2. At t=D^2, equality would hold in that lower bound. This forces mu to be the symmetric two-point law with atoms at u_0±D/2 and R^2=3D^2/4, which is unimodal at t=D^2 by the source's Example 2.1. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

CLAIM, in two halves. (i) YES at m = 3, by an example already in the literature: for the cyclic Volterra operator with a = b = c = 1, matrix A = [[0,1,-1],[-1,0,1],[1,-1,0]], whose leading 2x2 minor is 1 so the operator is transversal and whose fixed-point set - the three vertices and the centre - is finite, the itinerary of every non-fixed interior point is periodic, 1 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> ..., with sojourns 12, 51, 1073, ... growing geometrically by the heteroclinic-cycle mechanism of Ganikhodzhaev and Zanin (2004). (ii) OPEN at m = 4: in the proof of Theorem 5 of Ganikhodjaev and Zanin (arXiv:1205.3841) the trajectory passes between the epsilon-neighbourhoods of the vertices along the routes 1-4-3-2-1, 1-4-2-1 or 1-4-3-1, and a simulated cyclic-type m = 4 map produced the mixed finite prefix 1,4,3,2,1,4,2,1. A finite prefix cannot show that an itinerary is not periodic (every finite word extends to a periodic one), and one trajectory cannot answer an existence question in the negative, so the m = 4 case is not settled here. THE SHARP OPEN QUESTION, which is what the source presumably meant: is every itinerary eventually periodic, or which matrices A force it? The 2012 route analysis is the starting point. STATEMENT: let H and K be complex Banach spaces, A a bounded operator on H, B a bounded operator on K, and suppose their spectra are disjoint: sigma(A) intersect sigma(B) is empty. Then for every bounded operator C from K to H the equation A X - X B = C has a UNIQUE bounded solution X from K to H, and it is given by X = (1 / (2 pi i)) times the contour integral over Gamma of (A - z)^(-1) C (B - z)^(-1) dz, where Gamma is a finite union of positively oriented rectifiable Jordan curves lying in the resolvent set of B, encircling sigma(A) once and sigma(B) not at all. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) disjointness of the spectra is what gives both existence and uniqueness. With A = B and C = 0 the equation A X - X A = 0 is solved by every operator commuting with A, so uniqueness fails badly; and with A = B = 0 on a one-dimensional space the equation is unsolvable for nonzero C. (ii) It is the SPECTRA, not the norms, that matter: no smallness of C is assumed, the solution depends linearly on C, and the bound on X is controlled by the length of Gamma and by the size of the two resolvents on Gamma - a bound that blows up as the spectra approach each other, which is the quantitative content usually needed in perturbation arguments. (iii) The theorem as stated is for BOUNDED A and B; for unbounded operators the analogous statement requires separate hypotheses (sectoriality, semigroup generation), and the contour formula must be justified anew. # Target 1: two-cycle exclusion and necessary overshoot for periodic GD

Version 1, proof unaudited. This excludes possible third fates; it does not
classify all factored-GD trajectories or prove convergence.

Consider the factored model of claim 010 with any eta>0. More generally the
argument applies to any real update
 v_+=v+eta F(v,kq),
 k_+=k+delta q, q_+=q+delta k,
 delta=eta v G(v,kq),
where G is strictly positive at every finite point and F(0,s) has a unique
zero p_bar. The softmax logistic model satisfies these conditions.

1. Every orbit of period dividing two with k^2-q^2!=0 is a fixed point.
   It lies on v=0,kq=p_bar. This holds at every fixed step size.
2. Every nonstationary finite periodic orbit with k^2-q^2!=0 at one (hence
   every) iterate must contain an iterate with delta^2>=2. Equivalently,
   any periodic orbit on which |eta vG|<sqrt(2) throughout is stationary.

Neither statement excludes balanced-plane cycles, long cycles with large
overshoot, unbounded nonconvergent orbits, or nonperiodic bounded invariant
sets. This is a special obstruction result, not a scored global classification.

## Proof of two-cycle exclusion

Let U=k+q and D=k-q. Their exact simultaneous updates are
 U_+=(1+delta)U, D_+=(1-delta)D.
The nonzero imbalance is C=UD, so U,D are both nonzero initially.
For a returning two-step orbit, with a=delta_0,b=delta_1,
 (1+a)(1+b)=1, (1-a)(1-b)=1.
Expansion and addition yield 2ab=0; subtraction yields 2(a+b)=0.
Over the reals this forces a=b=0. Since eta>0 and G>0, v_0=v_1=0.
The factors therefore do not move. The head update then forces
F(0,kq)=0, hence kq=p_bar. This is a fixed point, as claimed.

## Proof of the overshoot requirement

The exact imbalance update is C_+=(1-delta^2)C. If an r-step orbit returns
with C_0!=0, no intermediate C can vanish, and
 product_{t=0}^{r-1}(1-delta_t^2)=1.
If every delta_t^2<2, every absolute factor is <=1, strictly less than 1
whenever delta_t!=0. The product can have absolute value 1 only if every
delta_t=0. Then every v_t=0, the factors stay fixed, and F(0,kq)=0.
Thus any nonstationary periodic orbit requires at least one delta_t^2>=2.

## Relation to the remaining gap

The flow's invariant imbalance is unavailable in GD, but its multiplicative
replacement still excludes every nonbalanced two-cycle, including at steps
beyond the normal-stability threshold of claim 013. A loss of an attracting
normal multiplier therefore does not by itself provide a two-cycle witness.
The unresolved step is controlling general, possibly large factor updates
well enough to show eventual entry into one of claim 010's escaping regions,
or finding a third fate that persists off the balanced planes.


# Target 1: exact balanced two-cycle and its transverse multiplier

Version 1, proof unaudited. Boundary check for claim 014, not a positive-volume
counterexample to an almost-everywhere theorem.

Fix any n>=2 and any distinct positive kappa_i. Put
 b_i=2 cosh(kappa_i)^2/kappa_i,
 a_i=b_i tanh(kappa_i).
These satisfy 0<a_i<b_i. In the usual coupled factored model
h_i(s)=a_i+b_i tanh(kappa_i s), all links have
 h_i(-1)=0, h_i'(-1)=2.

For EVERY fixed eta>0, simultaneous Euclidean GD on the average logistic
loss has an exact two-cycle
 (v,k,q)=(2/eta,1,-1) <-> (2/eta,-1,1).
At both points the loss is log 2, the product is -1, and k^2-q^2=0.
The two-step Jacobian has a transverse multiplier 9 normal to k=-q.
Thus the nonzero-imbalance assumption in 014 is necessary. This cycle
does not establish a positive-measure basin or rule out almost-everywhere
endpoint convergence.

## Proof

At either displayed state every h_i(kq)=0, so g_i=1/2, F=0 and
G=mean_i g_i h_i'=1. The head therefore stays fixed and
delta=eta vG=2. The factor update sends
 (k,q)->(k+2q,q+2k).
It exchanges (1,-1) and (-1,1). The cycle is nonstationary and has exact
period two; the loss remains log(1+exp(0))=log 2. The construction uses
different nonlinear scales, rather than requiring repeated identical examples.

The full factor-sum identity is U_+=(1+delta)U, U=k+q. At U=0 its
linearization gives dU_+=(1+delta)dU=3dU; the term U d(delta) vanishes.
After two steps dU_{++}=9dU, an exact normal multiplier even when v and
the product vary in the perturbation. No stability assertion at a unit
multiplier is involved.

The same constructed family has finite stationary points at v=0,kq=-1,
whereas the displayed periodic points have v=2/eta>0. Hence a classification
of every finite initialization by stationary points and escaping selections
alone would be false at any positive constant step. The exceptional balanced
plane must be allowed, as it is in claim 012's flow statement (which is a
different dynamical system).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["rows independent and identically distributed (the pairs bootstrap resamples rows, not residuals, so heteroscedasticity is allowed)","finite fourth moments and a converging empirical second-moment matrix (Freedman 1981); the predictor is a fixed measurable map of the sample, applied identically to every resample"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T12:03:52.456149+00:00","domain":"regression / resampling","id":"claim_0e4e01deefe6a25c51c622bfa99085bafd98403f8cc1a516a140a42803b61b73","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a least-squares predictor yhat(x) = x' beta_hat fitted on n rows, the textbook variance at a new point x is sigma^2 x'(X'SX)^(-1) x (sigma^2 times the leverage), and the hat matrix H = X(X'SX)^(-1)X'S has trace equal to the number of parameters. {"assumptions":["each F_n nondecreasing, right-continuous, with values in [0,1]","no tightness is assumed, and without it the limit can be defective"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752559+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_0fba1416669badf1de8ab735445eeb6c5d50526da69885c6f0c2f43871a867fd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (F_n) be a sequence of distribution functions on R, that is nondecreasing right-continuous functions with values in [0,1]. Then there exist a subsequence (F_{n_k}) and a nondecreasing right-continuous F : R -> [0,1] such that F_{n_k}(x) -> F(x) at every continuity point x of F. The limit F need NOT be a distribution function: mass can escape to plus or minus infinity, and with F_n the distribution function of the point mass at n one gets F identically 0. This is exactly the gap that tightness closes: the family is tight, meaning sup_n (1 - F_n(M) + F_n(-M)) -> 0 as M -> infinity, if and only if every such subsequential limit is a proper distribution function, which is Prokhorov's theorem on R. Nothing is assumed about the F_n beyond monotonicity, right-continuity and the range [0,1] - no continuity, no tightness, no common support. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 3.2.6]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:37:33.910787+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_102666e82e9e76f7e09da78626d9abe77aa7299d69a63249634afccb3ce8a949","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"The spiked covariance model (Johnstone, 2001) is the family of $p \\times p$ population covariance matrices $\\Sigma = \\sigma^2 (I_p + \\sum_{k=1}^{r} \\theta_k u_k u_k^T)$ with orthonormal vectors $u_1, \\dots, u_r$, spike sizes $\\theta_1 \\ge \\dots \\ge \\theta_r > 0$, and a fixed rank $r$ that does not grow with $p$. The data are $n$ independent rows $x_i \\in \\mathbb{R}^p$ with covariance $\\Sigma$ (Gaussian in the sharpest results; finite fourth moments suffice for the eigenvalue statements), and the object studied is the sample covariance $S = \\frac{1}{n} \\sum_i x_i x_i^T$ in the proportional regime $p, n \\to \\infty$ with $p/n \\to \\gamma \\in (0, \\infty)$. All but $r$ population eigenvalues equal the noise level $\\sigma^2$ (the bulk); the model asks which spikes are visible in $S$ and how far the sample eigenvalues and eigenvectors are from the population ones. With $\\theta_k = 0$ for all $k$ the sample spectrum follows the Marchenko-Pastur law with ratio $\\gamma$ and variance $\\sigma^2$, whose support is $[\\sigma^2 (1 - \\sqrt{\\gamma})^2, \\sigma^2 (1 + \\sqrt{\\gamma})^2]$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["U and V are open subsets of R^n of the same dimension n","phi : U -> V is a bijection, continuously differentiable, with continuously differentiable inverse (equivalently injective C^1 with nonvanishing Jacobian determinant and image V)","Lebesgue measure and Lebesgue measurable functions are used on both sides","f is measurable and either nonnegative or integrable"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090563+00:00","domain":"real analysis, measure theory, integration in R^n","id":"claim_1047e7e34c38c2168c64f635d6e025f096e2d64b3ad9dc9fbd5d8a3856bb2cb5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let U and V be open subsets of R^n and let phi : U -> V be a C^1 DIFFEOMORPHISM: phi is a bijection of U onto V, phi is continuously differentiable, and its inverse is continuously differentiable. (By the inverse function theorem it is equivalent to assume phi is injective, C^1, onto V, with det Dphi(x) nonzero for every x in U.) Let Dphi(x) denote the Jacobian matrix. Then for every Lebesgue measurable f : V -> [0, +infinity], the integral of f(y) dy over V equals the integral of f(phi(x)) |det Dphi(x)| dx over U, both sides being simultaneously finite or infinite; the same identity holds for complex-valued f, with f integrable over V if and only if (f composed with phi) times |det Dphi| is integrable over U. Taking f an indicator gives the measure statement: the Lebesgue measure of phi(E) equals the integral of |det Dphi| over E, for every measurable E contained in U. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) the ABSOLUTE VALUE of the determinant is required. The density is |det Dphi|; the sign records orientation and belongs to the theory of differential forms, not to Lebesgue integration. (ii) Injectivity cannot be dropped without paying for multiplicity: for a general C^1 map the correct statement is the area formula, the integral of f(phi(x)) |det Dphi(x)| dx over U equals the integral over V of f(y) N(y) dy, where N(y) is the number of preimages of y in U; N identically 1 is exactly injectivity. (iii) Smoothness cannot be relaxed to 'differentiable almost everywhere'. One needs the Luzin (N) property, that null sets map to null sets, which C^1 and Lipschitz maps have: in dimension one the Cantor function is continuous and nondecreasing with derivative 0 almost everywhere, yet it maps a null set onto a set of measure 1, and the naive substitution formula is false for it. (iv) The hypothesis is a diffeomorphism between OPEN sets; for maps defined on closed or lower-dimensional sets the statement must be routed through the area or coarea formula.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["d>=2 integer; real harmonics orthonormal for probability surface measure","P_l(1)=1; fixed dimension throughout","polynomials have finitely many coefficients"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:42:45.052423+00:00","domain":"Hermite interpolation; positive zonal kernels; spherical universal optimality","id":"claim_109875adfd105aaef59be23afb39e3a4e35c93b1540b5f44db1f9edd648408b7","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Fix an integer d>=2 and normalized uniform surface measure sigma on S^(d-1). Let H_l be the real degree-l spherical harmonics, h_l=dim H_l, and Y_(l,1),...,Y_(l,h_l) any orthonormal basis in L2(sigma). Let P_l be the degree-l polynomial orthogonal to lower-degree polynomials for weight (1-t^2)^((d-3)/2) on [-1,1], normalized by P_l(1)=1. Then sum_(j=1)^(h_l) Y_(l,j)(x)Y_(l,j)(y)=h_l P_l(<x,y>). In particular P_l(<x,y>) is a positive semidefinite kernel: for any finite x_i on the sphere and real c_i, sum_(i,j)c_i c_j P_l(<x_i,x_j>)>=0. For a real polynomial u=sum_l a_l P_l, its zonal kernel u(<x,y>) is positive semidefinite if and only if every a_l>=0. The product of two such polynomials again has nonnegative P_l coefficients. If every coefficient through the respective degrees is strictly positive, the product also has every coefficient through its degree strictly positive. Here d=2 uses the normalized Chebyshev polynomials, and d>=3 the Gegenbauer polynomials rescaled to value 1 at 1. Positive semidefinite kernels allow zero quadratic forms; strictly positive coefficients do not mean strict positivity of every finite Gram matrix.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X_n) a submartingale for a filtration (F_n)","sup_n E[X_n^+] < infinity (for a martingale: sup_n E|X_n| < infinity)","no uniform integrability is assumed, and without it convergence is only almost sure"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627158+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_111070f1050f003220fb4766d3ba4d411602ec9050d0c6e450a5eeb448ccb643","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X_n) be a submartingale with sup_n E[X_n^+] < infinity. Then X_n converges almost surely to a limit X_infinity with E|X_infinity| < infinity. For a MARTINGALE the hypothesis is equivalent to sup_n E|X_n| < infinity, since E[X_n] is constant and E|X_n| = 2E[X_n^+] - E[X_n]. Convergence is ONLY almost sure: it need not hold in L^1, and E[X_infinity] need not equal E[X_0]. Standard failure: let (X_n) be the product of independent nonnegative mean-one factors, for instance X_n = prod_{k <= n} (1 + eps_k) with eps_k = +1 or -1 with probability 1/2 each - equivalently X_n = 2^n on the event that all signs were +1 and 0 otherwise. Then X_n is a nonnegative martingale with E X_n = 1 for every n, so it is L^1-bounded and converges a.s., but the limit is 0 almost surely and E X_infinity = 0 != 1 = E X_0. {"assumptions":["characteristic 0 (over Q or a field containing Q); the criterion needs the field to contain, or to be extended by, roots of unity","'general' means indeterminate coefficients; a particular polynomial of degree >= 5 may well be solvable (x^5 - 2 is)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.626563+00:00","domain":"algebra","id":"claim_115d87a98ec962f9b30fe189acf038bc99ce62e12c2461843b01819a67bf4895","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For n >= 5 the general polynomial equation of degree n, x^n + a_1 x^{n-1} + ... + a_n = 0 with independent indeterminate coefficients over Q (the field Q(a_1, ..., a_n)), is not solvable by radicals: there is no formula for its roots built from the coefficients by field operations and extraction of k-th roots. For n <= 4 the general equation IS solvable by radicals (the quadratic formula; Cardano's formula for cubics, 1545; Ferrari's method for quartics). {"assumptions":["A a square complex matrix; eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity in the refinement","the discs are closed; a point of the union may fail to be an eigenvalue (the theorem localises, it does not characterise)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479038+00:00","domain":"linear algebra","id":"claim_118eb1edbdd586661b78b6b8a406c50d9aa31e793c06b918802f39726a6468d2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A = (a_ij) be a complex n x n matrix and for each i let R_i = sum_{j != i} |a_ij| be the i-th deleted absolute row sum and D_i = { z in C : |z - a_ii| <= R_i } the i-th Gershgorin disc. Then every eigenvalue of A lies in the union of the discs D_1, ..., D_n. Applying the theorem to the transpose, every eigenvalue also lies in the union of the column discs (radii the deleted column sums), so the spectrum lies in the intersection of the two unions. Refinement: if a union of k of the discs is disjoint from the union of the other n - k, then exactly k eigenvalues (counted with algebraic multiplicity) lie in the union of those k discs. Consequences: a strictly diagonally dominant matrix (|a_ii| > R_i for all i) is invertible, since 0 lies in no disc; a Hermitian strictly diagonally dominant matrix with positive diagonal is positive definite; and the discs can be shrunk by a diagonal similarity D^{-1} A D, which changes the radii to sum_{j != i} |a_ij| d_j / d_i.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Discrete Gaussian free field on a two-dimensional lattice domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions","Gibbs-Markov (domain Markov) property and lattice Green function asymptotics","Random-walk-below-a-barrier (ballot) estimates for the scale walk"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.987849+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_11fcc5b0b92d4300329a446dd3a28c80e7535335cb27eaecb364b7fce9c12206","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The concentric decomposition (Biskup-Louidor) describes the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field h in a box of side N as seen from a point x where the field is near its maximum. Around x one takes nested dyadic annuli; conditioning on the values of h on the boundaries of the concentric boxes, the Gibbs-Markov property splits h into (i) a random walk S_k along the scales, whose increments are the Gaussian binding fields' values at x, with variance of order g log 2 per scale, with the maximum constraint acting as a barrier the walk must stay below (entropic repulsion), (ii) independent zero-boundary fields in the annuli, and (iii) explicit bounded error terms from the non-exact scale invariance of the lattice Green function. The maximum-at-x event becomes a ballot-type event for the walk S_k, handled by random-walk-below-a-barrier estimates, which yield tightness of the centred maximum, the local limit law of the maximum, and the description of the cluster of near-maximal points around x (the cluster law nu). It is the tool behind the full extremal process of the DGFF (Biskup-Louidor 2016, 2018) and the intermediate level sets. It does not by itself give universality for other log-correlated fields: the binding-field structure uses the DGFF's exact Gibbs-Markov property. Typical failure: Treating the annulus fields phi_k as exactly independent rather than approximately so, and carrying a multiscale second-moment computation through without tracking the coupling error terms; because the GFF is only log-correlated rather than an exact branching random walk, the independence used in the concentric decomposition is an approximation that must be explicitly controlled, and skipping this step is a common source of unjustified exponent claims for GFF level-set percolation. Canonical reference: Biskup and Louidor, 2016, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Biskup and Louidor, 2018, Advances in Mathematics; Biskup, Extrema of the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field, PIMS-CRM lecture notes, 2020, Springer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["G finite, connected, undirected, without isolated vertices (weighted graphs work verbatim with weighted degrees and volumes)","the spectral gap is that of the NORMALISED Laplacian; for regular graphs it is (d - mu_2)/d, and the unnormalised version scales by d","conductance is measured against volume; the vertex-count edge expansion h(G) is the same quantity only for regular graphs"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:49:11.846189+00:00","domain":"spectral graph theory","id":"claim_123dda5b10ef9e8af280ba37a63254fd3b1973ad6a342a5785086a24af3d21fc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let G = (V, E) be a finite connected graph with vertex degrees d(v), volume vol(S) = sum_{v in S} d(v), and for a vertex set S with 0 < vol(S) <= vol(V)/2 let phi(S) = e(S, V - S) / vol(S) be its conductance, where e(S, V - S) counts the edges leaving S. The conductance (Cheeger constant) of G is phi(G) = min over such S of phi(S). Let 0 = lambda_1 < lambda_2 <= ... <= lambda_n <= 2 be the eigenvalues of the normalised Laplacian L = I - D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}. CHEEGER'S INEQUALITY (Alon-Milman, Sinclair-Jerrum, Dodziuk; the graph form of Cheeger's 1970 Riemannian inequality): lambda_2 / 2 <= phi(G) <= sqrt(2 lambda_2). For a d-regular graph with adjacency eigenvalues d = mu_1 >= mu_2 >= ..., lambda_2 = (d - mu_2)/d and the edge expansion h(G) = min e(S, V-S)/|S| (over |S| <= n/2) satisfies (d - mu_2)/2 <= h(G) <= sqrt(2 d (d - mu_2)). Both sides are sharp up to constants: the cycle C_n has phi of order 1/n and lambda_2 of order 1/n^2 (so the square root is needed), while the hypercube and expanders have phi and lambda_2 of the same order. If A and B are both increasing events, then mu(A and B) >= mu(A) mu(B); equivalently, for increasing functions f and g, E[f g] >= E[f] E[g]. The same holds when both are decreasing. If one event is increasing and the other decreasing, the inequality reverses: mu(A and B) <= mu(A) mu(B). The inequality says nothing about a pair of events that are neither increasing nor decreasing, and it fails for a general (non-FKG) measure.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. observations with finite variance (Andrews states the result under moment conditions for the CLT)","the constraint is active at the true parameter (theta = 0); for theta > 0 the bootstrap is consistent"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T09:23:59.828365+00:00","domain":"resampling / constrained estimation","id":"claim_128317036fe4b38de221748567b9dd5e4b220bf4b14f749dabab4f8dd0bb0ff4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $X_1, \\dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. with mean $\\theta \\ge 0$ and variance $\\sigma^2$, and let the estimator respect the constraint: $\\hat\\theta_n = \\max(0, \\bar X_n)$. When the true parameter is interior ($\\theta > 0$) the nonparametric bootstrap is consistent: the conditional law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n^* - \\hat\\theta_n)$ converges to $N(0, \\sigma^2)$, the law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n - \\theta)$. When the true parameter is on the boundary ($\\theta = 0$) it is not: $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n - \\theta) \\Rightarrow \\max(0, Z)$ with $Z \\sim N(0, \\sigma^2)$, a law with an atom of mass $1/2$ at zero, whereas the bootstrap law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n^* - \\hat\\theta_n)$ converges, conditionally on the data, to the law of $\\max(0, Z + \\zeta) - \\max(0, \\zeta)$ with $\\zeta \\sim N(0, \\sigma^2)$ a random shift that does not vanish - so the bootstrap distribution is random in the limit and does not equal the sampling distribution (Andrews 2000, Theorem 1). The same failure holds for maximum-likelihood and least-squares estimators under inequality constraints whenever the true parameter has an active constraint, in particular for nonnegatively constrained regression and portfolio weights with coordinates at zero: the bootstrap replicates flip the constrained coordinates between zero and positive values, and the spread of the replicates is not the spread of the estimator. Consistent alternatives: the $m$-out-of-$n$ bootstrap with $m \\to \\infty$, $m/n \\to 0$, and subsampling, both of which recover the limit law at the boundary.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:47:41.429782+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory","id":"claim_128a347949b062310df605967ebb97c6f0c93838dbb92f9d1f69184994c7496e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X,Sigma,mu) be a probability space and T: X -> X a measure-preserving transformation. T is ergodic if every T-invariant measurable set has measure 0 or 1: whenever A in Sigma satisfies T^{-1}A = A up to a mu-null set, mu(A) is 0 or 1. Equivalently, T is ergodic iff every T-invariant measurable function f (f(Tx)=f(x) a.e.) is a.e. constant; equivalently, by the Birkhoff ergodic theorem, iff for every f in L^1(X,mu) the time averages (1/N) sum_{n=0}^{N-1} f(T^n x) converge a.e. to the constant integral_X f dmu.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["d-regular graphs on n vertices; tau_2 = the relaxation time (inverse spectral gap) of the natural random walk, maximised over all d-regular graphs on n vertices for fixed n","the d=3 (cubic) enumerations used are COMPLETE for n<=12 (counts 1,2,5,19,85 match the known sequence); the d>=4 enumerations are RANDOM SAMPLES (isomorphism-deduplicated, stopped after 4000 consecutive repeats) and are NOT certified complete, especially at n=12"],"created_at":"2026-09-24T23:46:59.998009+00:00","domain":"probability/Markov chains","id":"claim_13c3a894a23e44b0acdc4d79135f18d9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"The paper proving the Aldous-Fill spectral gap conjecture leaves conditional the claim that for every sufficiently large even order n, the slowest d-regular graph (maximising relaxation time tau_2) is cubic (d=3); the finite crossover point is n=8. The 2-regular cycle has tau_2 = 1/(1-cos(2 pi/n)) ~ n^2/(2 pi^2), one third of the cubic asymptotic 3n^2/(2 pi^2), so cubic graphs must eventually overtake the cycle but do not lead at first: the slowest-known regular graph by order is 2-regular (the cycle) at n=4 (tau_2=1.0000) and n=6 (2.0000), then becomes 3-regular at n=8 (3.9271, versus the cycle's 3.4142), n=10 (13.5414, cycle 5.2361), and n=12 (17.8846, cycle 7.4641). Separately, the extremal cubic maxima (0.75, 1.50, 3.93, 13.54, 17.88 for n=4,6,8,10,12) jump by a factor of 3.5 from n=8 to n=10, out of line with the surrounding steps; this is because the extremal cubic graph acquires a BRIDGE at n=10 and CANNOT do so at any earlier order. Proof that a bridged cubic graph needs n>=10: if a cubic graph has a bridge uv, deleting it leaves a component A containing u where every vertex has degree 3 except u (degree 2), so the degree sum 3|A|-1 must be even, forcing |A| odd; |A|=1 would need a loop and |A|=3 would need four edges among three vertices (both impossible for a simple cubic graph), so both sides of any bridge are odd and at least 5, giving n>=10. This matches exact enumeration: no bridged cubic graph exists at n=4, 6, or 8; at n=10 there is exactly one bridged cubic graph and it IS the extremal one (tau_2=13.5414, versus 6.8423 for the best bridgeless cubic graph on 10 vertices); at n=12 there are four bridged cubic graphs and the extremal one among them is a 5|7 split (17.8846, versus 10.3190 for the best bridgeless cubic graph), a 6|6 split being impossible by the same parity argument. So the crossover at n=8 (cubic first overtakes the cycle, still bridgeless there, via a narrow 2-edge 4|4 cut) and the jump at n=10 (the bridge becomes possible) are two DIFFERENT events. NOT CERTIFIED: whether any regular graph of degree d>=4 ever competes with the cubic extremal graphs at these orders - only suggested: a 4-regular graph would need a second eigenvalue of 0.944 to compete, and the best 4-regular graph seen has 0.890; and a parity fact (a d-regular graph has a cut of size c across a vertex subset A only if c = d|A| mod 2, checked on 8400 random cuts with zero violations) shows a bridge is impossible outright for any EVEN degree d, which is suggestive but not a proof that odd degrees d>=5 cannot compete either.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["S is a finite subset of R^d","for the final claim: N <= d and x_1,...,x_N are linearly independent"],"created_at":"2026-08-20T03:43:30.215738+00:00","domain":"convex geometry","id":"claim_13f960d12d7361f53f8b9649a3a09792dc53550f7d06e91b0c0b658011ff3912","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $S=\\{x_1,\\dots,x_N\\}$ be a finite subset of $\\mathbb{R}^d$. The following are equivalent: (i) there is $y$ with $\\langle y,x_i\\rangle>0$ for every $i$; (ii) $0 \\notin \\operatorname{conv}(S)$. The frequently attempted substitute is FALSE: the condition that $\\operatorname{conv}(S)$ have empty interior does NOT imply (i). Counterexample in $\\mathbb{R}^2$ with $N=2$: take $x_1=e_1$ and $x_2=-e_1$. Their convex hull is a segment, which has empty interior, yet $0$ lies in it and no $y$ satisfies both inequalities. In particular, the observation that $N$ points in $\\mathbb{R}^N$ span an affine hull of dimension at most $N-1$, and so have a hull with empty interior, proves nothing about separation. What does suffice is linear independence: if $N \\le d$ and $x_1,\\dots,x_N$ are linearly independent then (i) holds, and an explicit witness solves $\\langle y,x_i\\rangle = 1$ for every $i$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["sub-Gaussian increments with respect to the metric d","separability of the process, so that the supremum is measurable and the chaining series converges","convergence of the entropy integral"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628694+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_15319d42d2a2e77a7eb628a9a06e56b61b321dba9d4e5dfffbd869a984b61dbb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X_t)_{t in T} be a stochastic process on a metric space (T, d) with SUB-GAUSSIAN INCREMENTS, meaning P( |X_s - X_t| > u ) <= 2 exp( - u^2 / (2 d(s,t)^2) ) for all s, t and u > 0. Then there is an absolute constant C with E sup_{t in T} X_t <= C integral_0^{diam(T)} sqrt( log N(T, d, u) ) du, where N(T, d, u) is the covering number, the smallest number of d-balls of radius u needed to cover T. If the process is not centred one should read the statement for X_t - X_{t_0} with a fixed base point. Two standard cautions: the bound can be LOOSE - for a centred Gaussian process the sharp answer is Talagrand's generic chaining and the majorizing measure theorem, and Dudley's integral can overshoot by an unbounded factor; and the integral must converge, so a class with covering numbers growing faster than exp(u^{-2}) is not handled. Sudakov's minoration provides the matching lower bound E sup_t X_t >= c sup_{u > 0} u sqrt( log N(T, d, u) ) for centred GAUSSIAN processes, so the two differ exactly by the integral versus the supremum. [Dudley (1967); see Vershynin, High-Dimensional Probability, Theorem 8.1.6]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(a) f absolutely continuous with E|f'(Z)| finite","(c) the characterisation quantifies over a rich enough class of test functions","(d) the Gaussian vector must be CENTRED"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543764+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1564c803ed1f4f740d9c5f603549c04916aaed26f09262fdb378ee739b59ba18","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"(a) Let Z be standard Gaussian on R and f absolutely continuous with E|f'(Z)| < infinity. Then E[ Z f(Z) ] = E[ f'(Z) ]. (b) Multivariate: if X is centred Gaussian on R^n with covariance Sigma and f is differentiable with the appropriate integrability, then E[ X_i f(X) ] = sum_j Sigma_{ij} E[ d f / d x_j (X) ]. (c) STEIN'S CHARACTERISATION: a real random variable Z is standard Gaussian IF AND ONLY IF E[ Z f(Z) ] = E[ f'(Z) ] for every bounded, continuously differentiable f with bounded derivative. This is the identity that makes Stein's method work: to show a law is close to Gaussian, one bounds E[ Z f(Z) - f'(Z) ] over a class of test functions f solving Stein's equation. (d) ISSERLIS-WICK FORMULA: for a centred Gaussian vector, E[ X_1 X_2 ... X_{2m} ] = sum over all PERFECT MATCHINGS of {1, ..., 2m} of the product of the covariances of the matched pairs, and any odd moment vanishes. For 2m = 4 this reads E[X_1X_2X_3X_4] = Sigma_{12}Sigma_{34} + Sigma_{13}Sigma_{24} + Sigma_{14}Sigma_{23}, and in particular E[Z^4] = 3 for a standard Gaussian, which is the '3' that the fourth moment theorem tests against. Centring is essential in (d); for a non-centred Gaussian one must first subtract the means. [standard; Isserlis (1918), Stein (1972); see Nourdin and Peccati, Normal Approximations with Malliavin Calculus, Chapter 3]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T is measure-preserving on a probability space; for the one-sided version T need not be invertible","A is measurable with log^+ ||A|| integrable","the splitting version additionally needs T invertible, A(x) invertible a.e., and log^+ ||A^{-1}|| integrable","all statements hold for mu-a.e. x; exponents depend on mu"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438459+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, Lyapunov exponents, smooth dynamics","id":"claim_1676fc5d4bd4204464d67994de31ed5e2340561ded554ac315e0ddd82660b53e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system and $A: X \to M_d(\mathbb{R})$ a measurable cocycle with $\log^+ \|A\| \in L^1(\mu)$; write $A^n(x) = A(T^{n-1}x)\cdots A(x)$.

ONE-SIDED (FILTRATION) VERSION - no invertibility of $T$ or of $A$ needed. For $\mu$-a.e. $x$: (a) the limit $\Lambda(x) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \big(A^n(x)^{\mathsf T} A^n(x)\big)^{1/2n}$ exists (a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix); (b) there are an integer $1 \le k(x) \le d$, exponents $\infty > \lambda_1(x) > \lambda_2(x) > \dots > \lambda_{k(x)}(x) \ge -\infty$ (only the smallest may be $-\infty$; this happens whenever $A$ is singular with positive probability, and can also happen for a.e.-invertible $A$ when $\log^+\|A^{-1}\|$ is not integrable), and a filtration of linear subspaces $\mathbb{R}^d = V_1(x) \supsetneq V_2(x) \supsetneq \dots \supsetneq V_{k(x)}(x) \supsetneq V_{k(x)+1}(x) = \{0\}$, measurable in $x$, such that $A(x) V_i(x) \subset V_i(Tx)$ and
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n \log \|A^n(x) v\| = \lambda_i(x) \quad\text{for every } v \in V_i(x) \setminus V_{i+1}(x);$$
(c) $k$, the $\lambda_i$ and the multiplicities $m_i = \dim V_i - \dim V_{i+1}$ are $T$-invariant functions of $x$ (constants when $T$ is ergodic); (d) $\lim \frac1n \log |\det A^n(x)| = \sum_i m_i \lambda_i(x)$, and more generally $\lim \frac1n \log \|\Lambda^p A^n(x)\|$ (norm on the $p$-th exterior power) equals the sum of the $p$ largest exponents counted with multiplicity; (e) the $\lambda_i$ with multiplicities are exactly the limits $\lim \frac1n \log \sigma_j(A^n(x))$ of the singular values, i.e. the logarithms of the eigenvalues of $\Lambda(x)$.

TWO-SIDED (SPLITTING) VERSION. If moreover $T$ is invertible, $A(x) \in GL_d(\mathbb{R})$ a.e. and $\log^+ \|A^{-1}\| \in L^1(\mu)$, then for a.e. $x$ all exponents are finite and there is a measurable $A$-equivariant splitting $\mathbb{R}^d = E_1(x) \oplus \dots \oplus E_{k(x)}(x)$, $A(x)E_i(x) = E_i(Tx)$, $\dim E_i = m_i$, with $\lim_{n \to \pm\infty} \frac1n \log \|A^n(x) v\| = \lambda_i(x)$ for all $v \in E_i(x) \setminus \{0\}$ (the SAME exponent forwards and backwards), $V_i(x) = \bigoplus_{j \ge i} E_j(x)$, and the angles between the Oseledets subspaces decay subexponentially along orbits: $\lim_{n\to\pm\infty} \frac1n \log \sin\angle\big(E_i(T^n x), \bigoplus_{j\ne i} E_j(T^n x)\big) = 0$.

WHERE IT FAILS. (1) Without $\log^+\|A\| \in L^1$ the limits need not exist: for $d = 1$ the theorem IS Birkhoff's theorem for $\log|a|$, which fails when $\log^+|a| \notin L^1$. (2) Without $\log^+\|A^{-1}\| \in L^1$ (or with $T$ non-invertible) there is in general NO equivariant splitting, only the forward filtration: the subspaces of vectors with exponent exactly $\lambda_i$, $i \ge 2$, are not canonically defined and the 'slow' directions are not invariant under $A$. (3) The exponents depend on the measure $\mu$: different ergodic measures for the same $T$ and $A$ generally have different exponents, and a point outside the full-measure set need not have exponents at all. (4) Convergence is not uniform in $x$, and the Oseledets subspaces are only measurable, in general not continuous, in $x$. (5) The theorem is about $\|A^n(x)v\|$ along ONE orbit; it says nothing about eigenvalues of $A^n(x)$ or about $\|A^n\|$ averaged over $x$.","status":"unverified"}

Then for every t > 0, P(|X - mu| >= t) <= sigma^2 / t^2; equivalently P(|X - mu| >= k sigma) <= 1/k^2 for every k > 0. The inequality is sharp: for t >= sigma the variable taking the values mu - t and mu + t with probability sigma^2 / (2 t^2) each and the value mu otherwise has mean mu, variance sigma^2 and P(|X - mu| >= t) = sigma^2 / t^2 exactly. It gives no information for t <= sigma, and it is the classical route to the weak law of large numbers: for i.i.d. X_i with finite variance, P(|(X_1 + ... + X_n)/n - mu| >= eps) <= sigma^2 / (n eps^2) -> 0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Recurrent symmetric Markov process; base point o; inverse local time at o","GFF with covariance the Green function of the process killed at o, independent of the process","Identity in law, not a pathwise coupling"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.988309+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_178ab0e20429fbcabddf72bded46fbdf579084e30b0d6607f8a57c199cde4f8b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Generalised second Ray-Knight theorem (Eisenbaum, Kaspi, Marcus, Rosen and Shi, 2000): let X be a recurrent symmetric Markov process on a countable state space (for instance continuous-time random walk on a finite connected graph, or on Z^2), started at a base point o, and let tau(u) be the inverse local time at o, the first time the local time at o reaches u. Let (phi_x) be the Gaussian free field on the state space with covariance the Green function of X killed at o, independent of X. Then the field (L^{tau(u)}_x + (1/2) phi_x^2)_x has the same law as ((1/2)(phi_x + sqrt(2u))^2)_x. Dynkin-type isomorphisms exist for transient processes killed at an independent exponential time (there the shift is absent). Uses: transfer of DGFF extremal results to local-time level sets and cover times (Ding-Lee-Peres via the Gaussian free field maximum), thick points of random walk, and the Sabot-Tarres and Lupu loop-soup couplings. Limits: the isomorphism identifies laws, not couplings, of the two sides unless the stronger Lupu coupling is used; the sign of phi is lost in the square, so events about level sets of the local time correspond to two-sided level sets of phi + sqrt(2u). Typical failure: Using the generalized second Ray-Knight isomorphism but omitting or misplacing the additive shift sqrt(2T) term that appears when T is a fixed constant rather than an inverse-local-time stopping time, as in the classical Brownian motion Ray-Knight theorems; dropping or mislocating this shift silently changes which boundary or starting condition the isomorphism is actually describing. Canonical reference: Ray, 1963, Illinois Journal of Mathematics; Knight, 1963, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society; Eisenbaum, Kaspi, Marcus, Rosen and Shi, 2000, Annals of Probability; Lupu, 2016, Annals of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X's law absolutely continuous with respect to Brownian motion (weaker than the problem's equivalence)","theta the unit shift with recentering on two-sided Wiener space, ergodic and invertible"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:11:19.449623+00:00","domain":"probability, Brownian motion, ergodic theory","id":"claim_178be04644b922b0b199a99ca4c2e4d055a2ff13a8ecf4efb01dca25babd8550","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Burdzy and Scheutzow, Forward Brownian motion (arXiv:1302.6958), Problem 7.5 (p. 26) asks: for any process {X_t, t >= 0} whose law is equivalent to Brownian motion, can one find a random piece to put in front of X so that the new process is a Brownian motion? Our result (id P0032, 2026-09-08): YES - and under absolute continuity rather than equivalence, which is weaker than the problem assumes. The mechanism is a filling-scheme lemma: for theta an invertible ergodic measure-preserving transformation of a standard Borel space (E, P) and Q = f P, there is an almost surely finite integer N >= 0 with law(theta^N Z) = Q for Z distributed as P. Apply it with E = C_0(R) under two-sided Wiener measure and (theta w)(t) = w(t+1) - w(1), lifting the one-sided density of X's law to two-sided paths; the lemma returns a finite N for which {Z(N+t) - Z(N)} has X's law while {Z(t) - Z(0)} is a Brownian motion whose first N units are exactly the prefix. Verification as the source words it: the filling construction was implemented on a finite ergodic system (Z/n with the +1 shift) for n = 5, 7, 12, 60 with random densities - total accepted mass 1.000000000000 every time, the law of theta^N Z matching f P to about 1e-16, E[N] finite - and the negative control is the informative one, since with a non-ergodic theta exactly half the mass is ever accepted and half survives forever. The L^1 ergodic-theorem step in the infinite-dimensional setting was not verified, only read; it is standard but checked by eye only. NOVELTY IS THE WEAK POINT and the campaign's own proof file volunteers it: the lemma is a filling construction related to classical work of Chacon-Ornstein, Rost and Thorisson - sound mathematics, very likely a known consequence.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the signs are independent and symmetric; the identity E S^4 = 3 (sum a_i^2)^2 - 2 sum a_i^4 uses E epsilon_i^4 = 1 and E epsilon_i^2 epsilon_j^2 = 1 for i different from j","coefficients are real (the complex and vector-valued versions hold with modified constants; Kahane's inequality is the Banach-space extension)","dependent or asymmetric signs are not covered"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.049237+00:00","domain":"anti-concentration and moment inequalities (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_1796c911ceeffee80cd7700c686eb05fc27456d52abdbb661721b8f2800206a5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let epsilon_1, ..., epsilon_n be independent Rademacher signs (each +1 or -1 with probability 1/2) and a_1, ..., a_n real numbers, and write S = sum a_i epsilon_i and ||a||_2 = (sum a_i^2)^{1/2}. Khintchine's inequality (1923): for every 0 < p < infinity there are constants A_p, B_p depending only on p with A_p ||a||_2 <= (E|S|^p)^{1/p} <= B_p ||a||_2. The second moment is exact, E S^2 = ||a||_2^2. The fourth moment is an identity, not just a bound: E S^4 = 3 (sum a_i^2)^2 - 2 sum a_i^4, so E S^4 <= 3 ||a||_2^4 and B_4 <= 3^{1/4}, with the constant 3 approached as the coefficients spread out (many equal a_i) and never attained; this is the Gaussian fourth moment. Sharp constants: A_p = 1 for p >= 2 and B_p = 1 for p <= 2; A_1 = 1/sqrt 2 (Szarek 1976); for p >= 3, B_p equals the p-th moment of a standard Gaussian to the power 1/p (Haagerup 1981). The lower bound for p < 2 is the nontrivial direction and is what the fourth-moment identity gives via the Paley-Zygmund argument: E|S| >= (E S^2)^{3/2} / (E S^4)^{1/2} >= ||a||_2 / sqrt 3.","status":"unverified"}

The slicing method controls a penalized or weighted supremum of a random process: cut the index set into slices on which the penalty lies between two levels, remove the penalty on each slice, and add the slice bounds with a union bound. Each remaining term is the supremum of a process without penalty, which chaining can control. van Handel, Section 5.4: writing X_t = E[X_t] + Z_t with subgaussian fluctuations Z_t, sup_t X_t = sup_t {Z_t + E[X_t]} is a penalized supremum of a subgaussian process with E[X_t] as the penalty, and chaining is suited to the fluctuations but not to the penalty. In the multiplicative setting (the additive one works the same way), for the weighted supremum of (X_t − X_s)/ρ(t, s), fix α_k ↓ 0 with ρ(s, t) ≤ α_0 for all s, t; on the slice {α_k ≤ ρ(s, t) ≤ α_{k−1}} the weight is bounded above and below, and a union bound gives P[sup_{s,t} (X_t − X_s)/ρ(t, s) ≥ x] ≤ Σ_{k≥1} P[sup_{ρ(s,t) ≤ α_{k−1}} {X_t − X_s} ≥ α_k x]. The sets {ρ ≤ α_{k−1}} shrink as k grows while the levels α_k x fall, so the penalty and the levels must be chosen to make the probabilities summable; that tuning is specific to each application. Worked example, Theorem 5.32 (modulus of continuity): if {X_t} is a separable subgaussian process on (T, d) and N(T, d, ε) ≥ (c/ε)^q for some c, q > 0 and all ε > 0, then ω(δ) = ∫_0^δ sqrt(log N(T, d, ε)) dε is a modulus of continuity for {X_t}, and E[sup_{t,s} (X_t − X_s)/ω(d(t, s))] < ∞. The proof slices with α_k = ω(Δ2^{−k}), Δ = diam(T), bounds each slice by the local chaining inequality (Proposition 5.35: P[sup_{d(t,s) ≤ δ} {X_t − X_s} ≥ C ∫_0^δ sqrt(log N(T, d, ε)) dε + x] ≤ C e^{−x²/(Cδ²)}), and uses ω(2δ) ≤ 2ω(δ). By Remark 5.34 the covering-number condition is technical: ω is still a modulus of continuity without it, by a more delicate tuning of slicing and chaining. {"assumptions":["each f_n differentiable on [a,b], with [a,b] a bounded interval","(f_n(x_0)) converges for at least one point x_0","f_n' -> g uniformly on [a,b]"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751029+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_18620c87505e98d6c532146546254519319c9d12188204bf60601298432ca6cc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f_n : [a,b] -> R be differentiable on [a,b], suppose the numerical sequence (f_n(x_0)) converges for SOME x_0 in [a,b], and suppose f_n' -> g uniformly on [a,b]. Then f_n converges uniformly on [a,b] to a function f, f is differentiable, and f' = g. The hypothesis that must be uniform is on the DERIVATIVES: uniform convergence of f_n itself is neither necessary nor sufficient. Sufficiency fails: f_n(x) = sin(nx)/sqrt(n) converges to 0 uniformly on R while f_n'(x) = sqrt(n) cos(nx) diverges at every x with cos(nx) bounded away from 0. Convergence of f_n at one point cannot be dropped either: f_n = n has f_n' = 0 -> 0 uniformly and f_n converges nowhere. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 7.17]","status":"unverified"}
