{"assumptions":["X is a topological space; no metrisability, compactness or separation axiom is required","each f_i is upper semicontinuous as a map into the extended reals (continuity is the special case used most often)","the family is nonempty; the index set may be uncountable","the infimum is taken pointwise, and values -infinity and +infinity are allowed"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.089930+00:00","domain":"general topology, semicontinuity","id":"claim_18da4caf8dac6a3433a1aa1a053da36b492c033651287018a2b335ad110cf583","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a topological space (no separation or countability axiom is needed) and let (f_i), i in I, be a nonempty family of functions f_i : X -> [-infinity, +infinity], each upper semicontinuous; in particular each f_i may be continuous. The index set I is arbitrary: finite, countable, or uncountable. Put f(x) = inf over i in I of f_i(x). Then f is upper semicontinuous: the set {x : f(x) < c} is open for every real c, equivalently limsup_{y -> x} f(y) <= f(x) at every point x. The standard consequence: an upper semicontinuous function on a nonempty compact space attains its supremum, so a variational problem whose objective is an infimum of continuous quantities always has a maximiser. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) the direction is not symmetric. A SUPREMUM of continuous functions is lower semicontinuous, not upper: on R, sup over n >= 1 of min(1, n|x|) is the indicator of {x nonzero}, which is lower but not upper semicontinuous at 0. Quoting this result for a supremum is the common misuse. (ii) The infimum of an INFINITE family of continuous functions is in general not continuous: on [0,1], inf over n of x^n equals 0 for x < 1 and 1 at x = 1. Only finite infima of continuous functions are continuous, so upper semicontinuity is the most one can claim. (iii) Upper semicontinuity of each member is exactly what is used; an infimum of merely lower semicontinuous functions has no semicontinuity property at all. (iv) The pointwise version localises: if each f_i is merely continuous AT a point x, the same proof gives limsup_{y -> x} f(y) <= f(x), i.e. upper semicontinuity at that one point, which is the form most often needed in practice.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["independent coordinates with finite ranges","f real valued"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T08:50:16.134177+00:00","domain":"Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition on finite product spaces","id":"claim_18de152cd6b3f3dde27fe3acec21197ea05d1c17bca342890c19af231c9bf2ed","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have independent coordinates with finite ranges, f a real function of X, and f = sum over S of f_S its Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition over subsets S of {1, ..., n}: f_S depends only on X_S, f_empty = E f, and E[f_S | X_T] = 0 unless S is inside T. Put w_S = E[f_S^2] and W_k = sum over |S| = k of w_S, the variance at interaction order k. For 0 <= t <= n let A_t f be the average over t-element sets T of E[f | X_T], and for 0 <= k <= n put P_k = binom(n, k) sum_{t=0}^k (-1)^(k - t) binom(k, t) A_t. Then P_k f = sum over |S| = k of f_S: P_k is the orthogonal projector onto the order-k part, so P_j P_k = 0 for j != k, P_k^2 = P_k, sum_k P_k = I and ||P_k f||_2^2 = W_k. If K_r f(x) is the average over |A| = r of E[f(X^(A)) | X = x], with X^(A) redrawing X_A independently, then K_r = A_{n - r}, so the same alternating combination of the K_{n - t} recovers each order.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X, M) is a measurable space","mu is sigma-finite (needed for the Radon-Nikodym density)","nu is sigma-finite (needed for existence of the decomposition); for signed or complex nu, finite total variation","absolute continuity and mutual singularity are with respect to the same sigma-algebra M"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402094+00:00","domain":"measure theory, Radon-Nikodym and decomposition","id":"claim_18fa6795088dd8fb6799c6e0c0ce7eb13ec14601000f98529cdd5659c067baeb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let mu and nu be SIGMA-FINITE positive measures on M. Then nu can be written as nu = nu_a + nu_s with nu_a absolutely continuous with respect to mu (nu_a << mu) and nu_s mutually singular with mu (nu_s perp mu), and this decomposition is unique. Combined with the Radon-Nikodym theorem, nu_a has a density: there is an M-measurable f >= 0, unique up to mu-null sets, with nu_a(E) = integral_E f dmu for all E in M; f is in L^1(mu) exactly when nu_a is a finite measure. The statement extends to nu a signed or complex measure of finite total variation with mu sigma-finite. WHERE IT FAILS: (a) sigma-finiteness of nu is essential for existence of the decomposition. Take X = [0,1] with the Borel sets, mu = Lebesgue measure and nu = counting measure. If nu = nu_a + nu_s with nu_a << mu and nu_s perp mu, pick E with mu(E) = 0 and nu_s(X minus E) = 0. For any x outside E we get nu({x}) = nu_a({x}), and mu({x}) = 0 forces nu_a({x}) = 0, contradicting nu({x}) = 1. So X minus E is empty, i.e. E = X, contradicting mu(X) = 1 > 0. (b) sigma-finiteness of mu is essential for the DENSITY. With mu = counting measure on [0,1] and nu = Lebesgue measure one has nu << mu, yet no f satisfies nu(E) = integral_E f dmu (evaluating on singletons forces f = 0). The decomposition itself survives here (nu_s = 0), but the Radon-Nikodym half does not. (c) Uniqueness is uniqueness of the pair of measures; the density f is only mu-almost everywhere unique.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["translation invariance","ergodicity under the translations","finite energy","an amenable transitive graph such as Z^d; the theorem FAILS on nonamenable graphs"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543290+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_19571635c9811ef2c4fa9bf7413abff7ada34807a8dc3b1fc48636004a01b663","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let mu be a probability measure on {0,1}^{E(Z^d)} that is (i) invariant under the lattice translations, (ii) ERGODIC with respect to them, and (iii) has the FINITE ENERGY property: for every edge e, the conditional probability that e is open given the states of all other edges lies almost surely strictly between 0 and 1. Then the number of infinite open clusters is almost surely a constant taking the value 0 or 1. Each of the three hypotheses does work. Ergodicity is what makes the number a constant rather than a random variable; without it a mixture of two percolation measures is a counterexample. Finite energy is what rules out infinitely many infinite clusters, by allowing local modifications; a measure that deterministically forbids certain local patterns can have infinitely many. And the argument uses AMENABILITY of Z^d - on a regular tree or another nonamenable transitive graph there is genuinely a regime with infinitely many infinite clusters, so the theorem is false there. Bernoulli percolation satisfies all three hypotheses for every p, so its infinite cluster is unique whenever it exists. [Burton and Keane (1989), Comm. Math. Phys. 121; see Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Theorem 8.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a Markov chain, here a Galton-Watson branching process, with an identified P-harmonic function h appropriate to the conditioning event","for Kesten's tree specifically: finite-mean offspring distribution with criticality or subcriticality correctly identified, and a precisely specified conditioning event","existence of the relevant weak-convergence limit of the conditioned law to the h-transformed law, which must be checked rather than assumed","correct identification of the size-biased offspring law along the spine, which differs from the original offspring law"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.994756+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_195cce09417950c349c4fdda5edd9f33edbe4cce03fe18f997181d11d952556c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Given a Markov chain with kernel P and a nonnegative P-harmonic function h, the Doob h-transform defines a new Markov chain with kernel P^h(x,y) = P(x,y) h(y)/h(x), representing the law of the original chain conditioned, in an appropriate limiting sense such as conditioning to survive forever or on an asymptotic event, to respect the weighting given by h. Applied to a critical or subcritical Galton-Watson branching process conditioned to survive forever, or, for critical trees, conditioned to have total size n with n -> infinity, the Kesten tree construction realizes the limiting law as an explicit infinite random tree: a single infinite spine, with each spine vertex additionally carrying an independent number of extra children distributed according to the size-biased-minus-one offspring law, each extra child then supporting an ordinary, unconditioned Galton-Watson subtree. This gives the exact local weak limit of large conditioned critical or subcritical branching trees and underlies scaling-limit results, such as convergence to the continuum random tree, that first pass through this explicit infinite-tree description. It does not directly give scaling limits of the whole tree's metric structure, which requires an additional contour or height-function argument, and the exact form of the spine's offspring law is specific to the conditioning event used, since conditioning on survival forever and conditioning on total size n give related but generally distinct limiting infinite trees. Typical failure: Confusing the different conditioning regimes for the conditioned Galton-Watson tree, such as conditioning on survival to infinity versus conditioning on total progeny exactly n as n -> infinity versus conditioning on height n, as if they all give the identical Kesten tree limit; they give related but generally distinct limiting infinite trees, differing in the spine's offspring bias and finer distributional details, and using one variant's known properties for a computation set up under a different conditioning is a frequent, easy-to-miss error. Canonical reference: Doob, 1957, Annales de l'Institut Fourier; Kesten, 1986, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare, Probabilites et Statistiques; Lyons, Pemantle and Peres, 1995, Annals of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

Unconstrained minimum variance depends on $\\hat\\Sigma^{-1}$, so its error is governed by the SPECTRUM of $\\hat\\Sigma$: the ratio $q = M/n$, the bulk edge, the near-null directions - the territory of random-matrix cleaning, where the Ledoit-Peche oracle, its analytical estimate and NERCOME differ from the sample covariance by design. The long-only plug-in's excess risk is bounded by twice the ENTRYWISE error $\\varepsilon = \\max_{ij}|\\hat\\Sigma_{ij} - \\Sigma_{ij}|$, which is $O(\\sqrt{\\log M/n})$ for the sample covariance and of the same order for every consistent estimator (a consistent nonlinear shrinkage moves the eigenvalues by $O(n^{-1/2})$ relative, hence the entries by the same order) - so all of them obey the same bound and, on the well-conditioned active submatrix, produce the same weights. A fixed floor $f\\sigma^2$ on the small eigenvalues, or a linear shrinkage $\\rho(\\mu I - \\hat\\Sigma)$, is a BIAS of size $f\\sigma^2$ (or $\\rho|\\mu - \\Sigma_{ii}|$) in the entries spanned by those directions that does not vanish with $n$; it cannot tighten the bound and it displaces the plug-in wherever an active member has weight in a floored direction. {"assumptions":["uniform product measure on the discrete cube {-1,1}^n","f real-valued and square integrable on the cube","C is a universal constant, in particular independent of n and of f"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628427+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_19af561bcf040b56cc9b3aa80d52d5dd62e1e00c1b7ecb97b574cbacb19b5603","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : {-1,1}^n -> R with the uniform product measure and let Delta_i f (x) = ( f(x) - f(x^{(i)}) ) / 2, where x^{(i)} flips coordinate i. Then there is a UNIVERSAL constant C with Var(f) <= C sum_{i=1}^n || Delta_i f ||_2^2 / ( 1 + log( || Delta_i f ||_2 / || Delta_i f ||_1 ) ), with the convention that a term is 0 when Delta_i f = 0. The unimproved bound Var(f) <= sum_i ||Delta_i f||_2^2 is the Efron-Stein inequality on the cube; Talagrand's refinement gains a LOGARITHMIC factor for every coordinate whose influence is spread out, that is whose L2 and L1 norms are far apart, and gains nothing for a coordinate whose discrete derivative is essentially an indicator. This is precisely the inequality Benjamini, Kalai and Schramm apply to first-passage percolation with two-valued weights to obtain Var <= C n / log n, and the reason their theorem carries a two-point weight hypothesis is that the L1-L2 comparison must be run on that specific cube structure. The p-biased and Gaussian analogues exist with modified constants; the Gaussian version replaces the log ratio by an entropy term (Falik-Samorodnitsky). {"assumptions":["the uniform product measure on {-1,1}^n","1 <= p <= q < infinity and 0 <= rho <= sqrt((p-1)/(q-1))","the constant is independent of n"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628214+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_19e3e9af2b5ddcfa431ba08524a9369ff10ac214b8a1b8391f61eaf614565d0c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : {-1,1}^n -> R with the uniform measure, with Fourier-Walsh expansion f = sum_{S subset [n]} fhat(S) chi_S where chi_S(x) = prod_{i in S} x_i. For 0 <= rho <= 1 define the noise operator T_rho f = sum_S rho^{|S|} fhat(S) chi_S. Then for all 1 <= p <= q < infinity, || T_rho f ||_q <= || f ||_p whenever rho <= sqrt( (p-1)/(q-1) ). Two standard specialisations: taking p = 2 gives || T_rho f ||_q <= || f ||_2 for rho = 1/sqrt(q-1); and for f of DEGREE at most d, meaning fhat(S) = 0 whenever |S| > d, one gets || f ||_q <= (q-1)^{d/2} || f ||_2 for every q >= 2, and by duality || f ||_2 <= (q-1)^{d/2} ||f||_{q'} for the conjugate exponent. The degree-d moment comparison is the workhorse: it says low-degree functions on the cube have all L^q norms comparable to their L^2 norm with a constant depending only on the degree and q, not on n, which is exactly the dimension-free input that KKL and Talagrand's variance inequality consume. The measure must be the UNIFORM (or a fixed p-biased, with a different constant) product measure - the theorem is about product measures on the cube. {"assumptions":["Omega is a bounded open subset of R^n, n >= 2","A is measurable, bounded and uniformly elliptic (no continuity assumed)","f is in L^1(Omega); the data may also be a bounded Radon measure with the same conclusions","the approximating data f_m are bounded, converge to f in L^1, and have L^1 norms bounded by ||f||_{L^1}","q is strictly less than n/(n-1)","conclusions are for the approximating sequence and its limit, not for an arbitrary distributional solution"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.396034+00:00","domain":"elliptic PDE, equations with measure or L^1 data","id":"claim_1a2ed3a0477ecc6b19ac15853dd25ba30feec9956659f5a93173e31f2bcfe10f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega be a bounded open subset of R^n with n >= 2, and let A be measurable, bounded and uniformly elliptic on Omega (alpha|xi|^2 <= A(x)xi.xi, |A(x)| <= Lambda, alpha > 0). Let f be in L^1(Omega) and let f_m be any sequence in L^infinity(Omega) with ||f_m||_{L^1} <= ||f||_{L^1} and f_m -> f in L^1 (for instance f_m = T_m(f), the truncation of f at level m). Let u_m in H^1_0(Omega) solve -div(A grad u_m) = f_m weakly. Then: (i) for every q with 1 <= q < n/(n-1) the sequence (u_m) is bounded in W^{1,q}_0(Omega) by a constant depending only on n, q, alpha, |Omega| and ||f||_{L^1}; (ii) up to a subsequence u_m converges strongly in W^{1,q}_0(Omega) and almost everywhere, together with its gradients, to a function u in W^{1,q}_0(Omega) which is a distributional solution: integral_Omega A grad u . grad phi = integral_Omega f phi for every phi in C_c^infinity(Omega); (iii) the limit satisfies the Marcinkiewicz (weak-Lebesgue) bounds u in M^(n/(n-2)) for n >= 3 and |grad u| in M^(n/(n-1)), with norms controlled by ||f||_{L^1}. WHERE IT FAILS: (a) the endpoint q = n/(n-1) is genuinely excluded - the fundamental solution of the Laplacian (the limit case f = Dirac mass) has |grad u| comparable to |x|^(1-n), which lies in weak-L^(n/(n-1)) but not in L^(n/(n-1)); (b) for n >= 3 one has n/(n-1) < 2, so the limit u need not belong to H^1_0 and the energy formulation is unavailable - u is only a distributional solution; (c) distributional solutions with L^1 data are NOT unique: Serrin's example gives a bounded measurable uniformly elliptic A and a nonzero u in W^{1,q}_0(Omega), q < 2, that solves the homogeneous equation distributionally. Uniqueness is restored only in the entropy-solution or renormalized-solution formulation of Benilan-Boccardo-Gallouet-Gariepy-Pierre-Vazquez. (d) The estimate is a bound on approximations plus a compactness statement; it does not by itself say that every distributional solution obeys it.","status":"unverified"}

L(u,v)=|A(u)v|^2/2:

    d_k=u_{k+1}-u_k
       =-eta v_k^T H'(u_k)v_k/2 -eta sigma z_k^T A'(u_k)v_k,
    v_{k+1}=(I-eta H(u_k))v_k-eta sigma A(u_k)^T z_k.

On v=0 its noise covariance is sigma^2 Hess L. The limiting ODE is

    U'=b(U),  b(u)=-sigma^2 tr H'(u)/4,  U(0)=u_0.

This is the known limiting flow of Li-Wang-Arora, Corollary 5.2, arXiv
2110.06914v4, printed pp.8-9 and 33. Their Theorem 4.6 supplies convergence,
not the explicit error estimate below. The hardest quantitative step here
is averaging with a coefficient that depends on u and shares the same noise
as the normal update. Section 4 computes that correlation rather than
discarding it as a martingale.

## 1. Constants and conclusion

Let F:R^{1+q}->R be bounded C^3, with bounded derivatives. Write
f(u)=F(u,0), F_j=sup |f^(j)|, j=1,2,3, and
F_vv=sup ||D_v^2 F||. The displayed bound uses only these seminorms.
Define

    c2=sigma^2 q M/m,
    c4=[sigma^2 M(2q+4)c2 + sigma^4 M^2 mu_4]/m,
    c6=[sigma^2 M(3q+12)c4 + 15 sigma^4 M^2 mu_4 c2
        + sigma^6 M^3 mu_6]/m,
    J2=B_1^2 c4/4+sigma^2 D^2 c2,
    Jcv=B_1^2 c6/4+B_1^2 sigma^2 M q c4/4
         +sigma^2 D^2 q c4+sigma^4 D^2 M mu_4 c2.

For j=0,1,2,3 put beta_j=sigma^2 q B_{j+1}/4. For T>=0 set

    G1=F_1 exp(beta_1 T),
    G2=exp(2 beta_1 T)(F_2+beta_2 T F_1),
    G3=exp(3 beta_1 T)[F_3+3 beta_2 T F_2
                     +(beta_3 T+3 beta_2^2 T^2/2)F_1],
    Gtu=beta_1 G1+beta_0 G2,
    Gtt=beta_0 beta_1 G1+beta_0^2 G2.

Define

    S0=B_1/(2m),
    S1=(B_2+2B_1 S0)/(2m),
    S2=(B_3+2B_2 S0+4B_1 S1)/(2m),
    C0=G1 S0/2,
    C1=(G2 S0+G1 S1)/2,
    C2=(G3 S0+2G2 S1+G1 S2)/2,
    Ct=Gtu S0/2.

Finally let

    Qg=G2 J2/2 + Gtu sqrt(J2) + Gtt/2,
    Qc=C0 M^2 c2
       +C1 B_1(c4+sigma^2 q M c2)/2
       +2 sigma^2 C1 sqrt(M) D c2
       +2 C2 Jcv + Ct c2,
    C(T)=(C0+F_vv/2)c2 + T(Qg+Qc).

Then, simultaneously for all integers 0<=k<=T/eta^2,

    |E F(u_k,v_k)-F(U(k eta^2),0)| <= C(T) eta.       (1)

The exponent is a=1. The finite constant is explicit in the hypotheses and

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:56:21.583919+00:00","domain":"algebraic number theory","id":"claim_1b7e3327494a2d86da57e3486e002e863fe896be76235e1a62d38263b27a90fd","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let K be a number field of degree n over the rationals, with r1 real embeddings and r2 pairs of complex conjugate embeddings, so n = r1 + 2 r2, and let O_K be its ring of integers. {"assumptions":["1 ≤ p < ∞","(A): u ∈ W^{1,p}_0(Ω), Ω contained in a slab of finite width d (no boundary regularity needed)","(B): Ω bounded, connected, Lipschitz boundary (or convex), u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω)"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492434+00:00","domain":"Sobolev inequalities, elliptic PDE, coercivity","id":"claim_1b864127f2bba872e9317da0f8bb92499ed6de1b5bd8779daf961da7ad1cb410","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Ω ⊂ R^n be open and 1 ≤ p < ∞.

(A) Poincaré–Friedrichs inequality (zero boundary values). Suppose Ω is bounded in one direction: Ω ⊂ {x : a < x_1 < a + d} for some a and some finite d (in particular any bounded Ω, with d = diam Ω). Then for every u ∈ W^{1,p}_0(Ω)
   ||u||_{L^p(Ω)} ≤ d ||∂_1 u||_{L^p(Ω)} ≤ d ||∇u||_{L^p(Ω)}.
For p = 2 the sharp constant for a slab of width d is d/π: ||u||_{L^2} ≤ (d/π)||∇u||_{L^2} for u ∈ H^1_0(Ω). NO regularity of ∂Ω is required and Ω need not be connected. Consequently ||∇u||_{L^p} is a norm on W^{1,p}_0(Ω) equivalent to the full W^{1,p} norm, the Dirichlet form ∫|∇u|^2 is coercive on H^1_0(Ω), and for bounded Ω the best constant C_P in ||u||_2 ≤ C_P||∇u||_2 satisfies 1/C_P^2 = λ_1(Ω), the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of −Δ.

(B) Poincaré–Wirtinger inequality (mean-zero functions). Suppose Ω is bounded, connected, and has Lipschitz boundary (or is bounded, connected and convex; more generally a bounded connected W^{1,p}-extension domain). Then there is C = C(Ω, p) with
   ||u − u_Ω||_{L^p(Ω)} ≤ C ||∇u||_{L^p(Ω)}  for all u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω),  u_Ω = (1/|Ω|) ∫_Ω u dx.
For convex Ω and p = 2 the sharp constant is diam(Ω)/π (Payne–Weinberger). Consequently u ↦ ||∇u||_{L^p} + |∫_Ω u| is a norm on W^{1,p}(Ω) equivalent to the W^{1,p} norm, and the Neumann problem is coercive on the mean-zero subspace.

Where it fails. (A) fails without zero boundary values: constants lie in W^{1,p}(Ω) with zero gradient. (A) fails on any domain containing balls of arbitrarily large radius (R^n, half-spaces, exterior domains): dilating one test function shows no constant works. (B) fails for disconnected Ω (a function equal to different constants on two components). (B) fails on some bounded connected domains with bad boundary (rooms-and-passages domains, sufficiently sharp outward cusps), where functions that are ≈0 in one part and ≈1 in another can have arbitrarily small gradient energy; Lipschitz boundary rules this out. In (B) the constant depends on Ω and blows up as the domain degenerates (e.g. a thin neck).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Bernoulli percolation with the ghost-field magnetisation M(p,h)","Russo's formula and the pivotal decomposition (Simon-Lieb type inequality)","Conclusions are one-sided mean-field bounds and sharpness, never continuity at p_c"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.988803+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1c135835662116d8bd927dc5acd650b6de0faa870e088f5dd7fd1ab1414511d1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Aizenman-Barsky (1987), for Bernoulli percolation on Z^d (and general transitive graphs), work with the magnetisation M(p,h) = P(0 is connected to a ghost vertex attached to every site with probability 1 - e^{-h}) and prove two differential inequalities: M <= h dM/dh + M^2 + p M dM/dp and dM/dp <= |J| M dM/dh (|J| the coordination constant), the first of Simon-Lieb type via the pivotal decomposition, the second from Russo's formula. Integrating them gives: (i) sharpness of the phase transition, i.e. the susceptibility chi(p) is finite for every p < p_c, hence exponential decay of connectivities below p_c; (ii) the mean-field bounds M(p_c,h) >= c h^{1/2} (delta >= 2) and theta(p) >= c (p - p_c) for p > p_c (beta <= 1). What they do NOT prove: continuity of theta at p_c (theta(p_c) = 0 is open for 3 <= d <= 10), or the matching upper bounds beta >= 1, delta <= 2 (those need the triangle condition, i.e. the lace expansion in high dimensions). The same inequalities transfer to the Ising model via the random-current representation (Aizenman-Barsky-Fernandez). Typical failure: Conflating the auxiliary percolation ghost field h with an actual physical parameter of the underlying model, or applying the conclusion theta(p_c)=0 to a percolation variant where FKG fails for the ghost-augmented measure, such as certain dependent percolation models; the entire argument rests on FKG holding for the specific augmented construction, and this needs to be re-verified for each new model rather than assumed to transfer automatically from ordinary Bernoulli percolation. Canonical reference: Aizenman and Barsky, 1987, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Aizenman, Kesten and Newman, 1987, Communications in Mathematical Physics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["complex (or real) terms; the ratio test needs a_n != 0 eventually","limsup and liminf are taken in [0, infinity]; when the limits exist the tests read with the plain limit"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479169+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_1c217f746d95c3909891090744a766ac7bb7f0c720afa221f92c52b6b464afc1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let sum a_n be a series of complex numbers. ROOT TEST (Cauchy): put L = limsup |a_n|^{1/n}. If L < 1 the series converges absolutely; if L > 1 it diverges (the terms do not tend to 0); if L = 1 the test is inconclusive. RATIO TEST (d'Alembert): suppose a_n != 0 for large n. If limsup |a_{n+1}/a_n| < 1 the series converges absolutely; if liminf |a_{n+1}/a_n| > 1 (in particular if |a_{n+1}/a_n| >= 1 for all large n) it diverges; otherwise the test is inconclusive. Comparison: for every sequence, liminf |a_{n+1}/a_n| <= liminf |a_n|^{1/n} <= limsup |a_n|^{1/n} <= limsup |a_{n+1}/a_n|, so whenever the ratio test decides, the root test decides the same way, and the root test is strictly stronger: for a_n = (1/2)^n for n even and (1/3)^n for n odd, the ratios oscillate between (2/3)^n -> 0 and (3/2)^{n} -> infinity so the ratio test says nothing, while |a_n|^{1/n} takes the values 1/2 and 1/3, limsup 1/2 < 1, and the series converges. Both tests are inconclusive for sum 1/n (divergent) and sum 1/n^2 (convergent), which have L = 1; the radius of convergence of a power series sum c_n z^n is 1 / limsup |c_n|^{1/n} (Cauchy-Hadamard), the root test in its most used form.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Ω ⊂ R^n open","F continuous on Ω × R × R^n","u continuous on Ω"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.415708+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: Hamilton-Jacobi equations","id":"claim_1e25d63418d6f4a5169a94db2c01063496e715960b47674a81764905279ec8b8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Ω ⊂ R^n be open and F: Ω × R × R^n → R continuous. A function u ∈ C(Ω) is a viscosity subsolution of F(x,u,Du) = 0 in Ω if for every φ ∈ C^1(Ω) and every x0 ∈ Ω at which u - φ has a local maximum, F(x0, u(x0), Dφ(x0)) ≤ 0. It is a viscosity supersolution if for every φ ∈ C^1(Ω) and every x0 ∈ Ω at which u - φ has a local minimum, F(x0, u(x0), Dφ(x0)) ≥ 0. It is a viscosity solution if it is both. For the evolution equation u_t + H(x,Du) = 0 in R^n × (0,T) apply the definition in the variables (x,t), with test functions φ(x,t) of class C^1 and F((x,t), r, (p,s)) = s + H(x,p); so at a local maximum of u - φ one requires φ_t + H(x0, Dφ) ≤ 0, and at a local minimum φ_t + H(x0, Dφ) ≥ 0. Equivalent variants giving the same class: C^1 test functions may be replaced by C^2 or C^∞ ones, local extrema by strict local extrema, and one may normalize φ(x0) = u(x0). The definition is NOT invariant under F ↦ -F: in general the viscosity solutions of F = 0 and of -F = 0 differ. The correct symmetry is: u is a viscosity subsolution of F(x,u,Du) = 0 iff -u is a viscosity supersolution of G(x,r,p) = 0, where G(x,r,p) := -F(x,-r,-p).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Discrete Gaussian free field on a two-dimensional lattice domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions","Gibbs-Markov (domain Markov) property and lattice Green function asymptotics","Random-walk-below-a-barrier (ballot) estimates for the scale walk"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1e595d1ddd4d31f5d20f20448b8cd74340f097f418011ebff2ea7ceb8a77b1af","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The concentric decomposition (Biskup-Louidor) describes the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field h in a box of side N as seen from a point x where the field is near its maximum. Around x one takes nested dyadic annuli; conditioning on the values of h on the boundaries of the concentric boxes, the Gibbs-Markov property splits h into (i) a random walk S_k along the scales, whose increments are the Gaussian binding fields' values at x, with variance of order g log 2 per scale, with the maximum constraint acting as a barrier the walk must stay below (entropic repulsion), (ii) independent zero-boundary fields in the annuli, and (iii) explicit bounded error terms from the non-exact scale invariance of the lattice Green function. The maximum-at-x event becomes a ballot-type event for the walk S_k, handled by random-walk-below-a-barrier estimates, which yield tightness of the centred maximum, the local limit law of the maximum, and the description of the cluster of near-maximal points around x (the cluster law nu). It is the tool behind the full extremal process of the DGFF (Biskup-Louidor 2016, 2018) and the intermediate level sets. It does not by itself give universality for other log-correlated fields: the binding-field structure uses the DGFF's exact Gibbs-Markov property. Typical failure: Treating the scale walk S_k as an exact random walk with identically distributed increments, as if the field were an exact branching random walk, and carrying a multiscale second-moment computation through without tracking the error terms; because the GFF is only log-correlated rather than an exact branching random walk, the comparison of S_k with a random walk (scale-dependent variances, the bounded error terms (iii)) must be explicitly controlled, while the Gibbs-Markov pieces themselves are exactly independent; skipping this control is a common source of unjustified exponent claims for GFF level-set percolation. Canonical reference: Biskup and Louidor, 2016, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Biskup and Louidor, 2018, Advances in Mathematics; Biskup, Extrema of the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field, PIMS-CRM lecture notes, 2020, Springer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["each K_eps is Lebesgue integrable"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.262329+00:00","domain":"real and harmonic analysis","id":"claim_1e5d0188dd28e245626b909ca5c58042ec03419fa53232852fb9172b6eb55d7d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A family $(K_\\varepsilon)_{\\varepsilon>0}$ in $L^1(\\mathbb R^d)$ (or a sequence $K_N$ with $N\\to\\infty$; the same definition works on $\\mathbb T$) is an approximate identity if (i) $\\int K_\\varepsilon=1$ for every $\\varepsilon$; (ii) $\\sup_\\varepsilon\\|K_\\varepsilon\\|_1<\\infty$; (iii) for every $\\delta>0$, $\\int_{|x|\\ge\\delta}|K_\\varepsilon(x)|\\,dx\\to0$ as $\\varepsilon\\to0$. If $K\\in L^1(\\mathbb R^d)$ with $\\int K=1$, the dilates $K_\\varepsilon(x)=\\varepsilon^{-d}K(x/\\varepsilon)$ form an approximate identity. Standard examples: the Gauss-Weierstrass (heat) kernel $\\varepsilon^{-d}e^{-\\pi|x|^2/\\varepsilon^2}$, the Poisson kernel of the half-space, the Fejer kernel $F_N$ and the Poisson kernel $P_r(x)=\\sum_n r^{|n|}e^{2\\pi i n x}$ ($r\\uparrow1$) on $\\mathbb T$. Non-example: the Dirichlet kernel $D_N$ satisfies (i) but not (ii), since $\\|D_N\\|_1\\to\\infty$; this is the root of the divergence phenomena for Fourier series. Some texts add the stronger condition $\\sup_{|x|\\ge\\delta}|K_\\varepsilon(x)|\\to0$, which is the convenient hypothesis for convergence at a point of continuity of a merely integrable $f$ (the tail is then controlled by $\\|f\\|_1$). Almost-everywhere convergence at Lebesgue points needs more than either condition: the usual hypothesis is the dilation structure $K_\\varepsilon(x)=\\varepsilon^{-d}K(x/\\varepsilon)$ together with an integrable radially nonincreasing majorant of $|K|$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the entries a_i are real and nonnegative","in the weighted form the weights are nonnegative and sum to exactly 1","the geometric mean is the nonnegative real root of the product","the convention 0^0 = 1 is used for zero weights"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090495+00:00","domain":"real analysis, classical inequalities","id":"claim_1f1e654f8c410c52b8d725a17d45f62a04496de0ecc32675cb38e67a595827dd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For NONNEGATIVE real numbers a_1, ..., a_n, (a_1 + ... + a_n)/n >= (a_1 a_2 ... a_n)^(1/n), with equality if and only if a_1 = ... = a_n. WEIGHTED FORM: if w_1, ..., w_n >= 0 with w_1 + ... + w_n = 1 and a_1, ..., a_n >= 0, then w_1 a_1 + ... + w_n a_n >= a_1^(w_1) ... a_n^(w_n), with the convention 0^0 = 1, and with equality if and only if all a_i with w_i > 0 are equal. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) nonnegativity is essential. With n = 2 and a_1 = a_2 = -1 the arithmetic mean is -1 while the product is 1 and its positive square root is +1, so the inequality as usually read reverses; the theorem is about nonnegative entries, never about arbitrary reals. (ii) With at least one zero entry and n >= 2 the geometric mean is 0 and the inequality is strict unless every entry is 0. (iii) The weights must be nonnegative AND sum to 1; dropping the normalisation makes the statement false, and the correct inhomogeneous relative is Young's inequality ab <= a^p/p + b^q/q with 1/p + 1/q = 1. (iv) The inequality is homogeneous of degree one, so it can be rescaled but never used to compare means of different orders; that is the power mean inequality, of which AM-GM is the limiting case as the exponent tends to 0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["E contains the empty set and admits countable covers of X, so every subset has at least one admissible cover","rho : E -> [0, +infinity] with rho(empty set) = 0; nonnegativity is essential for the rearrangement of the double sum","the family (A_n) is countable; the sets need not be measurable, disjoint or nested","the conclusion is an inequality only; additivity requires the Caratheodory criterion"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402499+00:00","domain":"measure theory, outer measures","id":"claim_1f8c36eb2db254c54ff701dd08d6243e0a9c40ab1d83ef4c3b9be279b1744140","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let E be a family of subsets of a set X with the empty set in E and with X covered by countably many members of E, let rho : E -> [0, +infinity] satisfy rho(empty set) = 0, and define mu*(A) = inf { sum over k of rho(E_k) : E_k in E, A contained in the union of the E_k } for every subset A of X. Then mu* is an outer measure: mu*(empty set) = 0; A contained in B implies mu*(A) <= mu*(B); and for EVERY countable family (A_n) of subsets of X, measurable or not, mu*(union of the A_n) <= sum of mu*(A_n). In particular Lebesgue outer measure on R^n is countably subadditive on all subsets of R^n, and finite subadditivity follows by padding the family with empty sets. WHERE THE INEQUALITY CANNOT BE IMPROVED: (a) equality fails in general even for pairwise DISJOINT sets. Let V be a Vitali set in [0,1] (one representative of each coset of the rationals) and let V_q = V + q for q in a countable enumeration of the rationals in [-1,1]. The V_q are pairwise disjoint, their union contains [0,1] and is contained in [-1,2], and by translation invariance all of them have the same Lebesgue outer measure; countable additivity would force that common value to be simultaneously 0 (giving outer measure 0 for [0,1]) and positive (to fill [0,1]), so the outer measure of the disjoint union is strictly less than the sum. Additivity is recovered exactly on the Caratheodory measurable sets. (b) Countable is sharp: the inequality does not extend to uncountable families - [0,1] is the union of its singletons, each of Lebesgue outer measure 0, while the union has outer measure 1. (c) No structure on rho is needed - rho need not be monotone, additive or a premeasure; that is why the construction is so robust, and also why mu* generally does not extend rho (mu*(E) <= rho(E) always, and equality for E in E requires rho to be a premeasure and E to be well behaved).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T_n is an ordered rooted tree, and its one-vertex fringe subtrees are leaves."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.363466+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1fb16adade5b99b6afb4fbfd858b71d368ab5f3b8075f27b19a7efee1501cb95","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; depends on the companion memo on Problem 20.2] This is the negative part of the answer recorded for Svante Janson's Problem 20.4 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510. Problem 20.4 asks for a Gaussian extension of Theorem 7.12, the law of large numbers for fringe-subtree counts. Let T_n be the simply generated tree, equivalently the conditioned Galton-Watson tree, with n vertices. Let N_T be the number of vertices whose fringe subtree equals a fixed finite ordered rooted tree T, and let N_d be the number of vertices with d children. For the one-vertex tree bullet, N_bullet = N_0 exactly, since its occurrences are precisely the leaves. {"assumptions":["psi(lambda) = log E e^{lambda X} finite for some lambda > 0 (otherwise the bound is vacuous)","for the i.i.d. rate statement: independent and identically distributed summands"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627588+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1fe4f3b747b727689cb17f579418ee4b2fd98070d9ff3fa9527f2e43df172cf8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a random variable with cumulant generating function psi(lambda) = log E[exp(lambda X)], finite on an interval containing 0 in its interior on the right. Then for every t, P(X >= t) <= exp(-psi^*(t)) where psi^*(t) = sup_{lambda >= 0} (lambda t - psi(lambda)) is the (one-sided) Legendre transform of psi. If X = sum_{i=1}^n X_i with the X_i independent and identically distributed with cumulant generating function psi_1, then psi = n psi_1 and P(X >= n t) <= exp(-n psi_1^*(t)): the exponent is LINEAR in n with rate psi_1^*(t), the Cramer rate function. Cramer's theorem says this exponential rate is exactly right, that is (1/n) log P(X >= n t) -> -psi_1^*(t) for t > E[X_1] under a finiteness condition on psi_1 near 0, so the Chernoff bound loses nothing at the level of the exponential rate although it can lose polynomial factors. The method requires SOME finite exponential moment: without it psi^* is identically 0 for t above the mean and the bound is vacuous, which is the correct behaviour for heavy-tailed laws. [standard; e.g. Dembo and Zeitouni, Large Deviations Techniques and Applications, 2nd ed., Chapter 2]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a topological space and T: X → X a map","for the orbit-closure characterization, T is continuous"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.111010+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics","id":"claim_20ab9dec4c9cbfd28df1fff4fca5251efcaf20965cb1e82ec6c01020cfd918be","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a topological space and T: X → X a map. A set A ⊂ X is (forward) invariant if T(A) ⊆ A. A minimal set is a nonempty closed invariant set M that contains no proper nonempty closed invariant subset. Some authors require T(M) = M (strict invariance); for a continuous T on a compact Hausdorff space a minimal set in the above sense automatically satisfies T(M) = M, since T(M) is then itself nonempty, closed (compact image) and invariant, hence equal to M. Characterization (T continuous): a nonempty closed invariant M is minimal if and only if for every x ∈ M the forward orbit {Tⁿx : n ≥ 0} is dense in M. Proof of the equivalence: for x ∈ M the orbit closure cl{Tⁿx : n ≥ 0} is nonempty, closed, contained in M, and invariant because continuity gives T(cl O) ⊆ cl T(O) ⊆ cl O; so minimality forces it to equal M; conversely, if every orbit in M is dense and N ⊂ M is nonempty closed invariant, any x ∈ N has its orbit inside N, so M = cl(orbit) ⊆ N. The system (X,T) itself is called minimal if X is a minimal set, i.e. every forward orbit is dense. Examples: a periodic orbit is a minimal set; an irrational rotation of the circle is minimal; the closure of a non-periodic orbit is in general NOT minimal (e.g. the orbit closure of a point of the doubling map whose orbit is dense contains the fixed point 0 as a smaller minimal set). Continuity is used in the orbit-closure characterization; the definition of a minimal set itself does not need it. For flows and group/semigroup actions the same definitions apply with 'orbit' read as the (semi)group orbit.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["INFINITE exchangeability; the theorem is false for finite exchangeable sequences","values in a Polish space, so that regular conditional distributions and a countable determining class exist"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.781914+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_20e7e94fd93a2e51ba5becdbc47068b21245cc7d9d4def4e9e32ec611d9265ad","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, X_2, ... be an INFINITE exchangeable sequence of random variables taking values in a Polish space S, meaning that for every n the law of (X_1, ..., X_n) is invariant under permutations of the n coordinates. Then there is a random probability measure Theta on S, measurable with respect to the exchangeable sigma-algebra, such that CONDITIONALLY on Theta the X_i are i.i.d. with common law Theta. Equivalently the law of the sequence is a MIXTURE of i.i.d. laws, and Theta is the almost sure limit of the empirical measures (1/n) sum_{i <= n} delta_{X_i}. The theorem is FALSE for finite exchangeable sequences. Counterexample with n = 2: let (X_1, X_2) be uniform on {(0,1), (1,0)}. This is exchangeable, but any mixture of i.i.d. Bernoulli sequences has Cov(X_1, X_2) = E[p^2] - (E p)^2 = Var(p) >= 0, whereas here E[X_1] = E[X_2] = 1/2 and E[X_1 X_2] = 0 give Cov = -1/4 < 0. Sampling without replacement is exactly the mechanism, and it produces the negative correlation that no mixture of i.i.d. can. What DOES survive in finite length is a quantitative approximation, due to Diaconis and Freedman: an exchangeable sequence of length n, restricted to k of its coordinates, is close in total variation to a mixture of i.i.d. sequences, with an error of order k/n. {"assumptions":["the chain is reversible with respect to pi (real eigenvalues); the bounds are stated for the absolute spectral gap","aperiodicity (e.g. laziness) so that gamma* > 0","the upper bound carries the factor log(1/pi_min); the lower bound holds for epsilon < 1/2"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.049135+00:00","domain":"Markov chains and mixing (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_2114caacee9ef704ca7243abee0f8be7a280413638cb34b387097351ec0f2be3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let P be the transition matrix of an irreducible, reversible Markov chain on a finite state space with stationary distribution pi, and let gamma* = 1 - max{|lambda| : lambda an eigenvalue of P other than 1} be the absolute spectral gap, with relaxation time t_rel = 1/gamma*. Then for every epsilon in (0, 1/2) the total-variation mixing time satisfies (t_rel - 1) log(1/(2 epsilon)) <= t_mix(epsilon) <= t_rel log(1/(epsilon pi_min)), where pi_min is the smallest stationary probability (Levin, Peres, Wilmer, Theorems 12.4 and 12.5). Mixing time is therefore the relaxation time up to a factor between log(1/(2 epsilon)) and log(1/(epsilon pi_min)); on a state space of size N the gap between the two sides can be as large as log N, and neither side can be dropped in general. For a lazy chain (holding probability at least 1/2) all eigenvalues are nonnegative, so the absolute gap equals the ordinary gap 1 - lambda_2; a periodic chain (a simple random walk on a bipartite graph) has an eigenvalue -1, gamma* = 0, and never mixes.","status":"unverified"}

Set U_t={u: integral (u-y)^(-2) mu(dy)>1/t}, with the integral allowed to be infinite, and v_t(u)=inf{v>=0: integral ((u-y)^2+v^2)^(-1) mu(dy)<=1/t}. In particular p_t is real analytic wherever positive, and 0<=p_t<=1/(pi*sqrt(t)). No moment, initial density, or compact-support assumption on mu is required. {"assumptions":["characteristic zero (or the general polynomial over any field of characteristic zero)","n >= 5","coefficients are independent indeterminates: particular degree-5 polynomials over Q may still be solvable by radicals"],"created_at":"2026-08-29T02:26:24.137447+00:00","domain":"algebra / Galois theory","id":"claim_2256ca4481d9e0acf08c9c091382001ee523cf5d05e7ef315770d80b729f7390","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let n >= 5 and let K = Q(a_0, ..., a_{n-1}) be the field of rational functions in independent indeterminates. The general polynomial x^n + a_{n-1} x^{n-1} + ... + a_1 x + a_0 over K is not solvable by radicals: no root of it lies in any radical extension of K (a tower K = K_0 < K_1 < ... < K_m in which each K_{i+1} = K_i(r) with r^{k} in K_i for some k >= 1). The reason is Galois' criterion: a polynomial is solvable by radicals exactly when its Galois group is a solvable group, and the general polynomial has Galois group the full symmetric group S_n over K, which is not solvable for n >= 5. For n <= 4 such formulas exist.","status":"unverified"}

On the torus T_{n,d} with volume V, a critical cluster of size V^{2/3} has intrinsic geometry of a critical tree embedded four-dimensionally, so its Euclidean diameter is of order (V^{2/3})^{1/4} = V^{1/6}, while the torus side is V^{1/d}. Since V^{1/6} > V^{1/d} iff d > 6, above six dimensions the window clusters wrap around the torus many times and see the torus uniformly; this is why the exploration process should have the same global (mass-proportional) depletion as in G(n,p), which is what the multiplicative-coalescent scaling limit (Heydenreich-van der Hofstad Open Problems 13.3 and 13.5) needs. The torus plateau theorem (Hutchcroft-Michta-Slade) is the two-point version of this uniformity; the open step is the exploration-level (higher-point) version. Same reason makes eps >> V^{-1/3} lie above the correlation-length crossover eps >> V^{-2/d} for d > 6 (Open Problem 13.2).","status":"unverified"}

If P projects onto range C and Q=I-P, put D=delta+||U_0Q||_F^2 and A=||JP||_F^2. Then the flow is global and converges to zero loss with v_infinity=sqrt((D+sqrt(D^2+4A))/2) and effective map G_infinity=JP+v_infinity U_0Q. The case C=0 is constant flow with the same formula. The invariants are v^2-||U||_F^2=delta and UQ=U_0Q. When delta=0, the strict loss gap Delta gives v^2>=Delta/||JC||_F>0; a PL estimate on the positive spectrum of C then proves exponential loss decay. In the square proxy J=I_d, z(w)=w, or augmented proxy J=[I_d,0], z(w)=(w,||w||^2/d+rho), C=(1/M)sum z(w_i)z(w_i)^T, use balanced isotropic initialization v_0=epsilon, U_0=epsilon J/sqrt(d), 0<epsilon<1. The initial effective map is epsilon^2 J/sqrt(d), giving the strict loss gap almost surely for iid Gaussian tasks. {"assumptions":["Galton-Watson with P(D=2) = 3/5, P(D=3) = 2/5","consistent equivariant flow rule choosing uniformly among same-coloured children"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:11:19.450036+00:00","domain":"probability, trees, ergodic theory","id":"claim_22df461caf6d08479ba0f1da9d8fdedbb4603bca52d4395ae62573d0bad9bec1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Lyons and Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks (version 19 August 2026), Question 17.18 (p. 575) asks whether a consistent equivariant flow rule admitting a stationary measure EQUIVALENT to Galton-Watson measure must induce an ergodic Markov chain; their Proposition 17.17 proves it when all child weights are strictly positive, and Exercise 17.22 gives a non-ergodic example whose stationary measure is only absolutely continuous, so equivalence is the point of the question. Our result (id P0033, 2026-09-08): NO. Take Galton-Watson with P(D=2) = 3/5, P(D=3) = 2/5 (mean 12/5) and an isomorphism-invariant colour in {0,1} defined by AND at two-child vertices and OR at three-child vertices; both preserve unanimity, so every vertex has at least one child of its own colour, and the flow chooses uniformly among those. Galton-Watson measure is stationary, the root colour is invariant along the chain and takes each value with probability 1/2 - a non-constant invariant function, hence no ergodicity - and the stationary measure equals Galton-Watson measure, trivially equivalent to it. The colour exists because F(p) = (3/5) p^2 + (2/5)[1 - (1-p)^3] fixes 1/2, and r_n = E[q_n^2] satisfies r_{n+1} = 3/10 + (3/5) r^2 + (2/5) r^3 whose increment factors as (r - 1/2)[(2/5) r^2 + (4/5) r - 3/5], driving r_n from r_0 = 1/4 up to 1/2 and giving E[q(1-q)] = 0. Verification as the source words it: the step the proof leaves implicit, and which was checked, is that Galton-Watson really is stationary - it holds because, conditioned on the children's colours, the child subtrees are independent, each distributed as Galton-Watson conditioned on its own colour, so the chosen subtree is exactly GW given colour = c, the uniform choice adds no bias, and mixing over c returns GW. Prior art unchecked; the tree-automaton and factor-of-iid literature is where to look.","status":"unverified"}

Weak form: every proper ideal of R has a common zero in k^n; equivalently, every maximal ideal of R is (x_1 - a_1, ..., x_n - a_n) for some a in k^n. Strong form: for every ideal I of R, the ideal of polynomials vanishing on V(I) is the radical of I, I(V(I)) = sqrt(I). {"assumptions":["X compact metric, T continuous and topologically exact","T is a local homeomorphism with finite fibres, so that L maps C(X) into C(X)","the weight w is continuous and strictly positive everywhere","there exist lambda > 0 and h in C(X) with h > 0 everywhere and L h = lambda h","there exists a Borel probability measure nu with L* nu = lambda nu (used only for algebraic simplicity)","the conclusion is about the eigenvalues of L acting on C(X); no Banach space of Holder or bounded-variation functions and no quasi-compactness is assumed"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090835+00:00","domain":"thermodynamic formalism, transfer operators, Perron-Frobenius theory","id":"claim_237e639d0e9ed9df151e70d43e37add45d9d02ba588674ca6999612a5fb36cf3","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"SETTING: X a compact metric space; T : X -> X a continuous, topologically exact map which is a local homeomorphism with finite fibres (so that the operator below sends continuous functions to continuous functions); w : X -> (0, infinity) a continuous weight. Define the transfer (Ruelle) operator on complex continuous functions by (L f)(x) = the sum of w(y) f(y) over the finitely many y with T(y) = x; L is a bounded positive operator on C(X). Assume the Perron data exist: a number lambda > 0 and a strictly positive h in C(X) with L h = lambda h, together with a Borel probability measure nu with L* nu = lambda nu, i.e. the integral of L f with respect to nu equals lambda times the integral of f with respect to nu for all f in C(X). CONCLUSION: (1) if f in C(X) is complex-valued and L f = z f with |z| = lambda, then z = lambda and f is a constant multiple of h - so lambda is the only eigenvalue of modulus lambda in C(X) and its eigenspace is one dimensional; (2) lambda is ALGEBRAICALLY simple: there is no f in C(X) with L f - lambda f = h, hence no Jordan block at lambda. WHERE THE HYPOTHESES BITE: (i) exactness cannot be weakened to minimality, unique ergodicity or transitivity. Take X the circle, T an irrational rotation and w identically 1, so that L f = f composed with T^{-1}: every character exp(2 pi i n x) is an eigenfunction with an eigenvalue of modulus 1, so the peripheral spectrum is infinite - and the system is minimal and uniquely ergodic but not exact (it is invertible, hence never exact). (ii) Strict positivity of the weight is essential. If w may vanish, the irreducibility can become periodic: in the finite-state model, where L is a nonnegative matrix, the statement above is the PRIMITIVE case of the Perron-Frobenius theorem, and an irreducible matrix of period p > 1 has exactly p eigenvalues of modulus equal to its spectral radius, so simplicity of the peripheral eigenvalue genuinely fails. (iii) The conclusion concerns the peripheral eigenvalue only and gives NO spectral gap: to place the rest of the spectrum in a strictly smaller disc one needs quasi-compactness (a Lasota-Yorke or Ionescu-Tulcea-Marinescu inequality on a Holder or bounded-variation space), a separate hypothesis on the regularity of w and the expansion of T. (iv) The existence of h and nu is assumed here, not proved; producing them is the other half of the Ruelle-Perron-Frobenius theorem and needs its own hypotheses.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A finite with at least two elements (for N = 1 the maximum has mean 0)","the signs are independent and symmetric; the bound is on the expectation over the signs only, the vectors are fixed"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:40:13.706093+00:00","domain":"probability and learning theory","id":"claim_238153b7dd2c94196c2f503107fe4086af1bd720d344b15f76689b1605667c76","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be a finite subset of R^n with N = |A| >= 2 elements, and let r = max_{a in A} ||a||_2. Let sigma_1, ..., sigma_n be independent Rademacher signs (uniform on {-1, +1}). Then E_sigma [ max_{a in A} sum_{i=1}^{n} sigma_i a_i ] <= r sqrt(2 log N), and consequently E_sigma [ max_{a in A} (1/n) sum_i sigma_i a_i ] <= r sqrt(2 log N) / n. Two consequences used constantly in learning theory: (1) for a finite class F of functions bounded by B on a sample x_1, ..., x_n, the empirical Rademacher complexity satisfies R_hat_S(F) = E_sigma sup_{f in F} (1/n) sum_i sigma_i f(x_i) <= B sqrt(2 log |F| / n), since each vector (f(x_1), ..., f(x_n)) has Euclidean norm at most B sqrt(n); (2) for a class C of sets of VC dimension d, restricting to the sample leaves at most s(C, n) <= (e n / d)^d distinct indicator vectors (Sauer-Shelah), each of norm at most sqrt(n), so R_hat_S(C) <= sqrt(2 d log(e n / d) / n) for n >= d. The logarithm cannot be removed at this generality: for A = {-1, +1}^n (N = 2^n, r = sqrt(n)) the maximum is exactly n while the bound reads n sqrt(2 log 2), so the lemma is sharp up to the constant sqrt(2 log 2) = 1.18; for VC classes Dudley's chaining removes the logarithm, R_hat_S(C) <= C sqrt(d / n).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:56:21.583278+00:00","domain":"graph theory","id":"claim_2391dac5df9a90395b1af7a294eca603716608168823cf2e7908d46e42b93d6a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In any bipartite graph, the maximum size of a matching (a set of edges no two of which share an endpoint) equals the minimum size of a vertex cover (a set of vertices meeting every edge). Both can be computed efficiently, and a minimum vertex cover can be extracted from a maximum matching via alternating paths from unmatched vertices. The equality can fail in non-bipartite graphs, where the minimum vertex cover can strictly exceed the maximum matching, for instance in an odd cycle. Proved by Denes Konig in 1931; equivalent to Hall's marriage theorem and a special case of the max-flow min-cut theorem.","status":"unverified"}

Balanced four-point frozen-model spectral interpolation only; actual nonlinear transfer remains open.

# C017 v1: rescaled noise restores two roots in the iid-head frozen precursor
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: bound. Target:1. Novelty unestablished.
A supporting frozen-model result, not full Target1 and not yet a nonlinear-network result.

## 1. Model and precise limit
For 0<e<1/4 set D=1+e^2+e^4 and x_(s,t)=(1,es,e^2t)/sqrt(D), s,t=+/-1.
Use the uniform four-point population and teacher direction
u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2). The letter u_e denotes this direction, not
nu, the fixed readout magnitude in (0,1]. Set c_e=e^2/sqrt(D(1+e^2)),
alpha=c_e/2, g(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-c_e/2. Its Walsh coefficients in modes
0,s,t,st are (0,alpha,alpha,alpha).
Initialize independent neurons with W_j~N(0,I_3) and heads independently +/-nu.
First take width to infinity at every fixed e, obtaining initial Gaussian
Walsh coefficients Z_(e,h). This is the ordinary fixed-width CLT of C016.
Then train the FROZEN deterministic full kernel
 H(x,z)=E[ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z]
with discrete step1/2. Write b_h=-log(1-lambda_h/2) for the normalized
four-point eigenvalues lambda_h. Use the settled clock premises
 b_s~nu^2 e/(4pi), b_t~b_st~nu^2 e^2/(8pi), b_0 bounded away from0.
Thus eta=(b_t+b_st)/b_s~e and b_t/(b_t+b_st)->1/2.

For fixed kappa>0 choose effective Walsh noise variance alpha^2 rho_e,
 rho_e=kappa/sqrt(e).
Four independent errors +/-sigma_e with sigma_e=2alpha sqrt(rho_e)
realize exactly this variance. In particular sigma_e~sqrt(kappa)e^(7/4),
so label noise remains <=1 for small e, but is not fixed as e decreases.
The noise-averaged clean risk conditional on initialization, in real-time
spectral interpolation of discrete GD, is
 Q_e(t)=sum_h [exp(-2b_h t)(Z_(e,h)-theta_h)^2
             +alpha^2 rho_e(1-exp(-b_h t))^2].             (1)
At integer t this is exactly discrete kernel GD. Real t is used only to
locate extrema of its spectral interpolation; no GD-to-flow limit is taken.

## 2. Joint initial-output covariance, on the relevant scales
Let phi_h(W)=(1/4)sum_(s,t) h(s,t) ReLU(W.x_(s,t)), and
lambda_h^RF=E phi_h(W)^2. The initial covariance is diagonal in Walsh modes,
Var(Z_(e,h))=nu^2 lambda_h^RF, by Gaussian coordinate sign symmetry.
In the Gaussian limit these modes are therefore independent.
C016 establishes lambda_s^RF/e^2->1/2 and the bounds
|phi_t|,|phi_st|<=e^2|W_2|/sqrt(D).
For W_0!=0, all four preactivations eventually have its sign. Consequently
phi_t/e^2 -> W_2 1{W_0>0}, and phi_st/e^2 ->0 almost surely.
Dominated convergence with the preceding bounds gives
 lambda_t^RF/e^4->1/2, lambda_st^RF/e^4->0.                (2)
On one probability space take independent standard normals G_0,G_s,G_t,G_st
and set Z_(e,h)=nu sqrt(lambda_h^RF)G_h for every e. This coupling has exactly
the required Gaussian law at each e. Since alpha~e^2/2, writing
A_(e,h)=(Z_(e,h)/alpha-theta_h/alpha)^2, we get almost surely
 e^2 A_(e,s)->a=2nu^2 G_s^2,
 A_(e,t)->(sqrt(2)nu G_t-1)^2, A_(e,st)->1.                (3)
Define B=((sqrt(2)nu G_t-1)^2+1)/2 >=1/2.
Here a>0 almost surely and a is independent of B. Independence is used only
after the joint Gaussian limit, not for finite-width output coefficients.

## 3. The new central derivative limit
For real s in a fixed compact interval set
 t_e(s)=((3/2)log(1/e)+s)/b_s, z=exp(-s).
Then q_s=exp(-b_s t_e(s))=e^(3/2)z exactly.
Normalize the risk derivative by 2alpha^2(b_t+b_st). Its fast contribution is
 [rho_e q_s-(A_(e,s)+rho_e)q_s^2]/eta
 =kappa(e/eta)z-[(e^2 A_(e,s))(e/eta)+kappa e^(5/2)/eta]z^2
 -> kappa z-a z^2.                                      (4)
For each slow mode q_h=1-O(e log(1/e)) uniformly on the compact interval.
Thus rho_e q_h(1-q_h)=O(sqrt(e)log(1/e))->0, while A_(e,h)q_h^2
has the limits in (3). The rate weights tend to1/2, giving their combined
contribution -B. The constant-mode contribution vanishes: its exponent
decays faster than every power of e and Z_(e,0)=O(1) in this coupling.
The same calculation after differentiating in s is valid: slow terms gain
a factor b_h/b_s=O(e), and even rho_e times that factor tends to0;
constant-mode exponentials dominate the additional polynomial factors.
Hence, almost surely in this coupling, uniformly on each compact s interval,

 Q'_e(t_e(s))/(2alpha^2(b_t+b_st)) -> H_kappa(s)
                                      =kappa exp(-s)-a exp(-2s)-B,
 and the derivatives in s converge too.                  (5)

## 4. Two-root criterion and peak time
On the event Delta=kappa^2-4aB>0 define
 z_+=(kappa+sqrt(Delta))/(2a), z_-=(kappa-sqrt(Delta))/(2a).
Both are positive and z_+>z_-. The classification is the elementary quadratic
criterion already used in C012, now with random coefficients a and B.
As s increases, H is negative, positive, then negative across
 s_min=-log z_+ and s_max=-log z_-.
The roots are simple. Uniform C1 convergence in (5) gives, for every such
fixed Gaussian realization, one nearby minimum and one nearby maximum of
the frozen interpolation for all sufficiently small e, converging to these
locations. Derivative convergence also gives strict decrease immediately
after the maximum. Thus there are two descents separated by a rise.
More precisely the peak satisfies
 b_s t_peak-(3/2)log(1/e) -> -log z_-,
 t_peak~(6pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e).                         (6)
The statements are pathwise in the coupling, on Delta>0. Random compact
neighborhoods are allowed: convergence on every integer-sized compact set
holds on one probability-one event. No deterministic width rate is asserted.
On Delta<0, H is negative on every compact s interval; this only addresses
this particular time window, not global absence of DD. Delta=0 is not treated.

For value-based nonlinear transfer, a useful additional consequence is this:
 d/ds [Q_e(t_e(s))/(2alpha^2 eta)] converges to H_kappa(s).
Therefore differences of the normalized risks converge to differences of
 V(s)=-kappa exp(-s)+(a/2)exp(-2s)-Bs.
Values across the two simple extrema have strict gaps of order alpha^2 eta.
An o(alpha^2 eta) uniform risk error over a containing compact interval would
preserve appropriately chosen decrease/rise/decrease witnesses and interval
peak localization. Such a nonlinear error is NOT supplied in this claim.

## 5. A tunable probability lower bound
The Gaussian independence in Section2 gives E a=2nu^2 and E B=1+nu^2,
so E[4aB]=8nu^2(1+nu^2). Markov's inequality yields
 P(Delta>0) >= 1-8nu^2(1+nu^2)/kappa^2.                   (7)
Choose kappa^2>8nu^2(1+nu^2)/delta for any prescribed delta in (0,1).
Then the frozen limiting construction has two simple central extrema with
probability greater than1-delta. The noise amplitude still tends to zero.
This is an initialization probability bound, with risk already averaged over
labels; it is not concentration for one realized label vector.
For fixed kappa the exact event probability need not equal this lower bound.

## 6. Scope and next unpaid step
C016's failed rho~1 route is avoided by changing BOTH noise scale and time
center; fixed nu and the unit-norm single-index teacher are retained.
This lemma concerns the balanced four-point frozen precursor only. It does
not yet prove the result for actual nonlinear GD, continuous iid input laws,
fixed label-noise amplitude, macroscopic feature learning, or full Target1.
The next step is a uniform-in-time risk transfer at order o(alpha^2 eta),
with nonzero iid initial output retained. C009's finite-horizon strategy is
a candidate; C015's zero-output paired argument cannot simply be substituted.
Independent mathematical and novelty review is pending. No paper-level
priority claim is made. Sources: own C009 clocks, C012 quadratic-root tool,
C016 Gaussian covariance and exact risk formula; the added slow-mode limits
and derivative scaling are proved above.","status":"unverified"}

# T422 Target 1: explicit constants for the optimal constant step

## Model and statement

Use the exact Gaussian second-moment recurrence established in the row diagnostics.
The covariance eigenvalues are h_j=j^(-alpha), alpha>1. The initial mode energies
are h_j a_j(0)=j^(-gamma), gamma>1. Labels have independent, mean-zero noise with
variance sigma2>=0. Each step uses B independent fresh examples, B a positive
integer. The batch gradient is their average. Put

    v_t = sum_j h_j a_j(t) = twice expected excess risk,
    Z_r = zeta(r),  v_0=Z_gamma,
    p=(gamma-1)/alpha >0, q=(2alpha-1)/alpha in (1,2).

This follows the existing diagnostics' gamma convention. If the target exponent
beta specifies a_j(0)=j^(-beta), then gamma=alpha+beta. If beta specifies the
risk mode energy h_j a_j(0)=j^(-beta), then gamma=beta. The two conventions must
not be interchanged. In Wang et al.'s Assumption 3.3, alpha is their beta and
p is their source exponent s.

Let S*(B,epsilon) be the minimum first hitting index of v_t<=epsilon v_0 over
ALL constant steps eta>0. No stability restriction is imposed on that minimum.
Define E*=B S*. For delta=epsilon Z_gamma, set

    eta_eff = min( 2B/Z_alpha, 2/(1+1/B), 4 delta B/(sigma2 Z_alpha) ),

where the third entry is omitted if sigma2=0, and

    Phi_1=epsilon^(-1/p)/eta_eff,
    Phi_2=(B epsilon)^(-1/q) eta_eff^(-(1-1/q)),
    Phi=max(Phi_1,Phi_2).

Here are explicit constants, all depending only on alpha,gamma:

    d=2^(-gamma-1-p)/(gamma-1),
    k=2^(-2alpha-1-q)/(2alpha-1),
    N=ceil(max(1, [2/((alpha-1) Z_alpha)]^(1/(alpha-1)))),
    T=N^alpha/2,
    epsilon_0=min(1/(8 Z_gamma), d/(2 Z_gamma T^p)).

For r>1 write s_r=(r-1)/alpha and define

    C(r)=2^s_r max( Z_r,
                   Gamma(s_r)/alpha + 2 [r/(e alpha)]^(r/alpha) ).
    C_D=C(gamma), C_K=C(2alpha).

If p<=q, define

    H=1+1/(1-p)                 if 0<p<1,
    H=1+1/(e(q-1))              if p=1,
    H=1+1/(p-1)                 if 1<p<=q,
    kappa=ceil(max(32, 1+4*2^p, 8*2^q C_K H/Z_alpha)),
    U=kappa (8 C_D/Z_gamma)^(1/p).

If p>q, define

    kappa=ceil(max(32, 1+4*2^p)),
    A=2^(q+4) C_K Z_(gamma-alpha),
    U=max( kappa (8 C_D/Z_gamma)^(1/p),
           kappa^(1-1/q) (A/Z_gamma)^(1/q) ).

Finally set

    c_minus=min( (d/Z_gamma)^(1/p)/4,
                 (k/(4 Z_gamma))^(1/q) 4^(-(1-1/q)) ),
    c_plus=2+U.

For every B>=1, sigma2>=0, and 0<epsilon<=epsilon_0, the claimed bounds are

    c_minus Phi <= S*(B,epsilon) <= c_plus Phi,
    c_minus B Phi <= E*(B,epsilon) <= c_plus B Phi.              (THEOREM)

The upper bound is achieved to these constants by the explicit stable choice
eta=eta_eff/kappa. The lower bound covers even a step that reaches the target
before subsequently diverging. Constants are deliberately conservative.

Then T*T is a compact positive self-adjoint operator on H, and |T| = (T*T)^{1/2} is compact and positive. The singular values (s-numbers) s_1(T) >= s_2(T) >= ... >= 0 of T are the eigenvalues of |T| (equivalently, the nonnegative square roots of the eigenvalues of T*T), listed in nonincreasing order and repeated according to multiplicity; if |T| has only finitely many nonzero eigenvalues the list is completed by zeros. Each nonzero singular value has finite multiplicity and s_n(T) -> 0. Basic facts: s_1(T) = ||T||; s_n(T*) = s_n(T); s_n(A T B) <= ||A|| s_n(T) ||B|| for bounded A, B; and for every n >= 0, s_{n+1}(T) = min{ ||T - F|| : F bounded, rank F <= n } (approximation numbers; the minimum is attained by a truncated Schmidt decomposition). If H = K and T is normal, the singular values are the absolute values of the eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity; for non-normal T they generally differ from the moduli of the eigenvalues.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Independent coordinates (product measure)","BKS noise sensitivity criterion: sum of squared influences tends to zero","Talagrand's logarithmic improvement needs hypercontractivity of the product measure"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.984548+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2735f9af03768ef56fdd8f2c95e272103da82734094d10270e1805b32cc1b47e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Efron-Stein: for f(X_1,...,X_n) with independent coordinates, Var f <= (1/2) sum_i E[(f(X) - f(X^{(i)}))^2], where X^{(i)} resamples coordinate i; for a Boolean function under a product measure the right side is a constant times the total influence sum_i I_i(f). This bounds variance by total influence and needs no monotonicity. Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm (1999): if f_n : {0,1}^{m_n} -> {0,1} satisfy sum_i I_i(f_n)^2 -> 0 then (f_n) is noise sensitive, i.e. Cov(f_n(omega), f_n(omega^eps)) -> 0 for every fixed noise level eps > 0; for monotone functions the converse also holds. The quantitative engine is Talagrand's inequality Var f <= C sum_i I_i(f)/log(e/I_i(f)) (hypercontractivity), which for functions with all influences at most n^{-a} improves Efron-Stein by a factor log n; the same mechanism gives the BKS sublinear variance bound Var(first-passage time to distance n) <= C n/log n for first-passage percolation with suitable edge weights. What these do NOT give: a lower bound on any individual influence (that is Kahn-Kalai-Linial: max_i I_i >= c Var(f) log n / n), or a power improvement n^{1-eps} on the variance, which remains open outside integrable models. Typical failure: Using the plain Efron-Stein variance bound and mistaking it for the BKS lower bound on the maximal individual influence, which is a distinct and much sharper statement requiring monotonicity and a total-influence hypothesis; conflating the two leads to claiming individual-coordinate sensitivity conclusions, needed for noise-sensitivity theorems, from a tool that in its basic form only controls the aggregate variance. Canonical reference: Efron and Stein, 1981, The Annals of Statistics; Benjamini, Kalai and Schramm, 1999, Publications Mathematiques de l'IHES.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["alpha irrational, phi continuous, and the non-coboundary condition for EVERY nonzero integer m - failing it for a single m already produces a second invariant measure, since a measurable transfer function conjugates the skew product to a product-like system with many invariant measures."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:04:29.026406+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, equidistribution","id":"claim_27d59969e006501ff4a353c3f75206770253125bc9e24dc25c44454a72d83cbc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let alpha be irrational, let T(x,y) = (x + alpha, y + phi(x)) be the skew product on the two-torus with phi continuous, and consider the associated cohomological condition.
