# C022 v1: continuous iid inputs and ONE realized noisy trajectory
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: narrowed. Target:1. Novelty unestablished.
Dependencies C009/C014/C015/C016/C020/C021 are also unaudited.
General T267 remains OPEN. No model training is used in this argument.

## 1. Exact model and restricted statement
Fix 0<nu<=1, kappa>0. For 0<e<1/4 put D=1+e^2+e^4 and
z_(s,t)=(1,es,e^2t)/sqrt(D), s,t=+/-1. Let tau=e^20 and let P_e be
the equal mixture of the uniform three-dimensional balls B(z_(s,t),tau).
Draw FOUR iid training inputs X_i from P_e. The test law is the same P_e.
Set u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2), c_e=e^2/sqrt(D(1+e^2)), alpha=c_e/2,
g_e(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-c_e/2. The direction u_e has norm1 and g_e is 1-Lipschitz.
Labels are y_i=g_e(X_i)+sigma_e xi_i, sigma_e=2alpha sqrt(kappa/sqrt(e)),
with four independent Rademacher signs xi_i, independent of inputs and
initialization. Each realized dataset trains ONE network, without averaging.
Use f_m(x)=m^(-1/2)sum_j a_j ReLU(w_j.x), iid w_j~N(0,I_3) and independent
iid a_j uniform {-nu,nu}. Both layers train by simultaneous GD step1/2 on
(1/8)sum_i(f_m(X_i)-y_i)^2; the gate derivative at zero is zero.
The individual clean test risk is R(k)=E_(x~P_e)(f_m(x;k)-g_e(x))^2.

For every epsilon>0, define E_(e,m)(epsilon) by existence of integers
0<=k0<k1<k2<k3 with R(k0)>R(k1), R(k2)>R(k1), R(k2)>R(k3),
k1 within relative epsilon of (3pi/nu^2)e^-1 log(1/e), and k2 within
relative epsilon of (9pi/nu^2)e^-1 log(1/e). Also require k2 to be an
interior maximum on an integer interval [l,k3] with k1<l<k2<k3,
and both endpoint risks strictly lower. Interior maximizing ties are allowed.
Then the claimed lower bound is
 liminf_(e downarrow0) liminf_(m to infinity) P(E_(e,m)(epsilon)) >=3/512. (1)
Probability includes inputs, label noise and initialization. This is a
positive-probability restricted width-first theorem on shrinking full-dimensional
continuous input laws, not a typical-data or feature-learning-regime theorem.
The earlier time is a cancellation witness, not a unique minimum claim.


For the CENTER Gram matrix H(z_i,z_j)/4, write its Walsh eigenvalues as
lambda_h, b_h=-log(1-lambda_h/2), and eta_e=(b_t+b_st)/b_s. The full
kernel H is defined in Section2. C009 supplies b_s~nu^2 e/(4pi),
b_t~b_st~nu^2 e^2/(8pi), eta_e~e and b_0 bounded away from zero.

## 2. General finite-horizon population transfer with NONZERO initial output
The following extension of C015 is needed. Fix finite d,n,T, gamma>0,
0<nu<=1, nonzero training points of norms <=M and an initialization-independent
law P on nonzero inputs with norms <=M. Bound labels by |y_i|<=Y.
Use iid Gaussian hidden weights and independent heads +/-nu, with the
same simultaneous GD loss (1/(2n))sum residual^2. Write
 H(x,z)=E[ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z].
Define deterministic-H frozen predictions with their ACTUAL RANDOM initial
function, not a zero replacement:
 F^m_0(x)=f_m(x;0),
 F^m_(k+1)(x)=F^m_k(x)-(gamma/n)sum_i H(x,x_i)(F^m_k(x_i)-y_i).
Then max_(k<=T)||f_m(k)-F^m_k||_(L2(P)) tends to zero in probability
as m tends to infinity, uniformly for bounded labels. The corresponding
finite training-point error and clean-risk error for a bounded teacher
also tend to zero. This is a fixed horizon before any scale limit.

Here are the modifications to the complete C015 Sections2-6 proof.
Let L>0 and first work on ||f_m(X;0)||/sqrt(n)<=L and
S_m=mean_j(1+||w_j(0)||)^2<=S, with S above its finite expectation.
By independent centered heads,
 E||f_m(X;0)||^2/n <=nu^2 M^2/2,
 E||f_m(.;0)||_(L2(P))^2<=nu^2 M^2/2.                   (2)
The first event has failure at most nu^2 M^2/(2L^2), and S_m<=S has
probability tending to1. In C015 Section2 use R_0=Y+L, rather than Y.
The exact simultaneous-update recurrences then give the same deterministic
finite movement radii through T on these events. No zero-output assumption
is used in deriving the recurrences after this initial residual bound.

C015 Section3's fixed-q weighted Gaussian band proof applies to iid
individual neurons just as to independent pairs: its integrable summands
and countable SLLN argument are unchanged. Consequently its sample gate
bands and population L2 gate bands vanish. Its Sections4-5 cross-kernel
and exact nonsmooth one-step remainder bounds are unchanged. The initial
kernel now averages m independent W summands instead of N pairs; its L2
cross-row variance bound has denominator m. All a_j(0)^2 still equal nu^2.
These are unconditional iid laws, restricted afterwards to the radius
event; conditioning is NOT used to claim independence of trained gates.

In Section6 compare training residuals starting with the SAME nonzero
vector (f_m(X;0)-y)/sqrt(n). Their initial discrepancy is exactly zero.
The finite induction there needs neither a contraction nor a gap and
still makes the sample discrepancy vanish. In the population telescoping
identity both initial functions are f_m(.;0), so they cancel POINTWISE.
The same cross-kernel and remainder estimates give the claimed L2 error.
For risks, ||F^m_k-g||_2 is tight: its initial norm is tight by (2), and
its finitely many kernel increments are bounded on the radius events.
Use | ||u-g||^2-||v-g||^2 |<=||u-v||(2||v-g||+||u-v||).
Finally send m to infinity, then L to infinity. The bounds are uniform
on the label cube because only Y enters them. This proves the extension;
it does not assert an L2-valued Gaussian process limit or a width rate.

## 3. Same-initializer perturbation of the frozen trajectories
Couple each training input as X_i=Z_i+tau V_i, where Z_i is uniform on
the four centers and V_i is uniform on the unit ball, independent.
Use the same construction independently for a test input X=Z+tau V.
Let A be the event that the four Z_i are all distinct, of probability3/32.
On A reorder canonically. Couple noisy labels to center labels
 y_i^0=g_e(Z_i)+sigma_e xi_i; |y_i-y_i^0|<=tau.
Use EXACTLY the same Gaussian weights and signed heads for initial outputs
on the perturbed points and on the centers. Independence and centered heads give
 E_init |f_m(x;0)-f_m(z;0)|^2
 =nu^2 E_W[ReLU(W.x)-ReLU(W.z)]^2
 <=nu^2 ||x-z||^2.                                      (3)
This is uniform in m. The cross-neuron terms vanish by the head signs;
ReLU Lipschitzness and E(W.v)^2=||v||^2 prove the bound. It would be false
with a tau^2 right side for two INDEPENDENT initial functions even at x=z.

Let fbar^tau and fbar^0 be deterministic-H frozen iterates with these
respective actual initial functions and labels. Work on the coupled test
space (Z,V) when taking population norms. Let a_m be the L2 norm of their
initial function difference and delta_m the Euclidean norm of the difference
of initial residual vectors normalized by sqrt(n). Then (3) and teacher
Lipschitzness give, conditional on any allowed input perturbations,
 E a_m^2<=nu^2 tau^2, E delta_m^2<=2(nu^2+1)tau^2.       (4)
Let Y_m be the norm of the center initial normalized residual. Uniformly
in m and small e, E Y_m^2<=C, since sigma_e<=1 for sufficiently small e,
the teacher is bounded on the centers and (2) applies.

C014 Section2's full ReLU-kernel modulus supplies the deterministic bounds
 ||K_tau-K_0||<=16sqrt(tau), ||b_tau-b_0||_(L2(row))<=16sqrt(tau),
where K=H(X,X)/n and b(x)=H(x,X)/sqrt(n). Both cross rows have norm
at most B_*=25/16 and both Gram matrices have trace at most25/16,
because norms of perturbed points are at most5/4. Thus for gamma=1/2
both I-gamma K are contractions. These are the settled C014 premises,
not estimates inferred from the training Gram matrix alone.

For completeness the nonzero-start prediction bound, for k<=T, is
 D_m(T):=max_k||fbar^tau_k(Z+tau V)-fbar^0_k(Z)||_2
 <=a_m+gamma T epsilon_b Y_m+gamma B_* T delta_m
       +gamma^2 B_* epsilon_K Y_m T(T-1)/2,              (5)
with epsilon_K,epsilon_b<=16sqrt(tau). To derive it, use
||v_tau,k-v_0,k||<=delta_m+gamma k epsilon_K Y_m from
noncommuting Duhamel and contraction; then sum prediction increments,
retaining the initial function difference a_m. No independence of the
random errors in (5) is assumed. Equations (4)-(5) imply uniformly in m
 E D_m(T)^2 <= C(1+T^4)tau.                             (6)
The constant is independent of e,m and the ball perturbations for small e.

On A the center population law is also its empirical training law.
Consequently its clean frozen-risk square root, uniformly in k, is at most
Y_m+sigma_e, by contraction of its training residual. This is uniformly
tight. The clean teacher difference on the coupled population is <=tau.
Therefore the square-norm risk inequality from Section2 gives
 max_(k<=T)|Rbar_tau(k)-Rbar_0(k)|
 <=(D_m(T)+tau)(2(Y_m+sigma_e)+D_m(T)+tau).               (7)
Choose T=ceil(e^(-3/2)), tau=e^20. By (6), D_m(T)=O_P(e^7), uniformly
in m, conditional on A. Since alpha^2 eta_e is asymptotic to (1/4)e^5,
(7) is o_P(alpha^2 eta_e), uniformly in m. Explicitly, first restrict
Y_m+sigma_e to a fixed bound using its uniform second moment, then use
(6) and Markov at the e^5 threshold; the failure bound there is O(e^4).
Finally let the fixed bound increase. This justifies the product estimate
without any independence assertion. Here eta_e is the CENTER clock ratio
(b_t+b_st)/b_s from C020, with eta_e~e.

## 4. Transfer strict witnesses and their probability
For fixed e, sample, labels and T as above, Section2 transfers actual
nonlinear risks to fbar^tau risks uniformly through T in probability as
width tends to infinity. For random training points, integrate the conditional
convergence over the sample; all labels are bounded and the points are
nonzero, so bounded convergence applies to the conditional failure probabilities.
The width limit is always taken at fixed e and its finite T.

On the two noise branches xi_(s,t)=chi*s in canonical center order,
C020v2 constructs, on compact subsets of the favorable Gaussian event
chi L<0, two early witness gaps of order alpha^2 e^(-1/2) and a central
endpoint gap bounded below by c alpha^2 eta_e, with c>0 depending only
on that compact set. It gives a deterministic bounded central clock window,
and an early cancellation window, each in the required relative time bands.
Both are inside T=ceil(e^(-3/2)) for sufficiently small e. The fixed-e
center initial finite vector obeys the same CLT as C020. Its open finite-array
witness event therefore has probability liminf at least that compact Gaussian
probability after the width limit. Section3's risk perturbation is negligible
on the SMALLEST gap scale, uniformly in width, so its failure probability
tends to zero as e decreases. Section2's actual-versus-frozen error vanishes
in the inner width limit. A union bound combines these errors; no independence
between the favorable initial output and perturbation error is needed.

The event of an interior peak is handled by a grid point strictly above
both endpoints of the fixed central interval. Strict gaps survive the two
risk comparisons. Any interval maximizer then lies inside; replacing the
grid witness by that maximizer preserves the earlier witness inequalities.
The whole central interval is in the desired relative peak-time band.
Send width to infinity, then e to zero, then exhaust compact favorable
Gaussian events exactly as C020 Section5. Conditional on A and either fixed
character branch, the resulting lower probability is1/2. Each character branch
has noise probability1/16. The latent occupancy event has probability3/32,
independent of noise and initialization. Thus the joint lower bound is
 (3/32)[(1/16)(1/2)+(1/16)(1/2)]=3/512,
which proves (1). No limiting operation is interchanged, and no conditional
variance is factored using an unproved independence assumption.

## 5. Scope and adversarial check
Unlike C015, this statement uses iid nonpaired readouts and ONE realized
label vector; unlike C020/C021, its sampling and test laws are absolutely
continuous in R^3. It retains shrinking clusters, shrinking label noise,
width-before-scale limits and a small positive event probability. It proves
finite decrease/rise/decrease witnesses and an interval peak, not full segment
monotonicity, unique stationary points, macroscopic feature learning, a full
noise window or general T267. Independent correctness and novelty review
remain pending; no claim of literature priority is made.
The strongest specific failure mode is replacing shared initialization in
(3) by independent initializers: the initial-output error would be order1,
destroying the e^5 risk-gap comparison. The exact finite covariance check
includes this negative arm and detects its nonzero variance at identical
inputs. Those finite checks do NOT certify the analytic transfer or novelty.
Sources: C014 full-kernel perturbation and clocks; C015 Sections2-6 weighted
population gate-band argument; C020v2 single-label witnesses; C021 occupancy.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["delta > 0, started at x > 0","the diffusion is considered on (0, infinity) up to the hitting time of 0","the integer case delta = d transfers to Brownian motion in R^d through the radial part"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543969+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_28ae49b4849a217435a2f33e1bff7911ba62b44c71425000ee08e45fdab6ac40","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a Bessel process of dimension delta > 0 started at x > 0, solving dX_t = dW_t + ((delta - 1)/(2 X_t)) dt on (0, infinity). Its SCALE FUNCTION is s(x) = x^{2 - delta}/(2 - delta) for delta != 2 and s(x) = log x for delta = 2. Consequently: for delta > 2 the process is TRANSIENT, never hits 0 from x > 0, and X_t -> infinity almost surely; for delta = 2 it never hits 0 and is NEIGHBOURHOOD RECURRENT, visiting every interval (a,b) with 0 < a < b at arbitrarily large times almost surely, while X_t -> infinity fails and liminf X_t = 0 with limsup X_t = infinity; for 0 < delta < 2 the process reaches 0 almost surely in finite time. Specialising to integer delta = d and using that |B| is BES^d recovers the classical dichotomy for Brownian motion in R^d: recurrent for d = 1 (point recurrent) and d = 2 (neighbourhood recurrent, never hitting a fixed point), transient for d >= 3. The critical dimension is exactly 2 and the transition is driven by whether the integral of s' diverges at 0 and at infinity. [standard; e.g. Revuz and Yor, Continuous Martingales and Brownian Motion, 3rd ed., Chapter XI, Proposition 1.5]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space","T is densely defined and symmetric","T is bounded below: ⟨Tx, x⟩ ≥ c‖x‖² on D(T)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.770573+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, elliptic operators, quantum mechanics","id":"claim_294eda050d48da488c1e81b1fd25b05ba335ce0de91817430155d293a96ecf69","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let T be a densely defined symmetric operator on a complex Hilbert space H which is bounded below: ⟨Tx, x⟩ ≥ c‖x‖² for all x ∈ D(T), with c ∈ ℝ. Let q(x, y) = ⟨Tx, y⟩ on D(T) and let Q be the completion of D(T) in the norm ‖x‖_q² = ⟨Tx, x⟩ + (1 − c)‖x‖², which embeds injectively into H as a dense subspace. Then there is a self-adjoint extension T_F of T (the Friedrichs extension) with the same lower bound, ⟨T_F x, x⟩ ≥ c‖x‖² for all x ∈ D(T_F), given by the closed form obtained as the continuous extension of q to Q; its domain is D(T_F) = D(T*) ∩ Q and T_F = T* restricted to that domain. T_F is the unique self-adjoint extension of T whose operator domain is contained in Q, and it is the unique self-adjoint extension whose form domain is Q. In particular every densely defined semibounded symmetric operator has at least one self-adjoint extension, so its deficiency indices are equal; T_F is the largest semibounded self-adjoint extension in the sense of quadratic forms, and it is the only one when T is essentially self-adjoint (in which case T_F = T̄).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["entries independent and uniform on {-1, +1}","the statement is asymptotic, with an o(1) inside the base","it is NOT a statement about symmetric random sign matrices"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.544307+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_29dc17afa1384af10ab2de54ecf88bb013b8c4634cd8ecae367cf91b3e346b1c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For each n let M_n be an n by n random matrix with INDEPENDENT entries each uniform on {-1, +1}. Then P( M_n is singular ) = ( 1/2 + o_n(1) )^n. The matching lower bound is elementary: the probability that two rows are equal, or two rows are opposite, or two columns are equal, or two columns are opposite, is already of order n^2 2^{-n} = (1/2 + o(1))^n, and each such coincidence forces singularity. The content of the theorem is the UPPER bound, which settled a long-standing conjecture: Komlos (1967) proved the probability is o(1), Kahn, Komlos and Szemeredi (1995) obtained 0.999^n, and Tao-Vu and Bourgain-Vu-Wood improved the base to (1/sqrt(2) + o(1))^n before Tikhomirov reached the conjectured (1/2 + o(1))^n. Note precisely what is claimed: the ENTRIES are independent uniform signs, and the statement is asymptotic in n with an o(1) in the base, so it gives no numerical bound at any fixed n. The analogous question for a random symmetric sign matrix is a separate problem, resolved later and by different methods, and the result stated here must not be quoted for it. [Tikhomirov (2020), 'Singularity of random Bernoulli matrices', Ann. of Math. 191; arXiv:1812.09016]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f integrable on the circle (or on R^d)","claims about rates require stated regularity of f"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264433+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, common errors","id":"claim_2be4b7e12c3e3f49eba47dda81e2c6f8756b4f804878db25d11f6a85781b81a8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"What the lemma says: $f\\in L^1$ implies $\\hat f(n)\\to0$ (on $\\mathbb T$) or $\\hat f(\\xi)\\to0$ as $|\\xi|\\to\\infty$ (on $\\mathbb R^d$), with $\\hat f$ continuous and bounded by $\\|f\\|_1$. What it does not say. (i) No rate is implied: for every even sequence $(a_n)$ of nonnegative reals with $a_n\\to0$ that is convex for $n\\ge1$ ($a_{n-1}+a_{n+1}-2a_n\\ge0$), there is a nonnegative $f\\in L^1(\\mathbb T)$ with $\\hat f(n)=a_n$ for all $n$; taking $a_n=1/\\log(|n|+e)$ shows the decay can be as slow as one likes. So an estimate like $|\\hat f(n)|\\le Cn^{-\\alpha}$ must come from extra regularity: e.g. $\\alpha$-Holder continuity gives $|\\hat f(n)|\\le\\frac{C}{2}(2|n|)^{-\\alpha}$ via $\\hat f(n)=\\frac12\\int(f(x)-f(x+\\tfrac1{2n}))e^{-2\\pi inx}dx$, and bounded variation gives $|\\hat f(n)|\\le V(f)/(2\\pi|n|)$. (ii) The converse fails: not every null sequence is the sequence of Fourier coefficients of an $L^1$ function. For odd $f\\in L^1(\\mathbb T)$ with sine coefficients $b_n$, the series $\\sum_nb_n/n$ must converge; since $\\sum_{n\\ge2}\\frac1{n\\log n}=\\infty$, the everywhere-convergent series $\\sum_{n\\ge2}\\frac{\\sin(2\\pi nx)}{\\log n}$ is not the Fourier series of any integrable function. (iii) Consequently 'the coefficients tend to 0' is never evidence that a given trigonometric series is a Fourier series, and never by itself a convergence statement.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. real observations","no assumption whatsoever on F","the uniformity is over half-lines; for a general class of sets a complexity condition is required"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.782115+00:00","domain":"statistics","id":"claim_2c322d793604c5ad716d92397e36484a3a1c70d121206cb63e12642f98799942","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, X_2, ... be i.i.d. real random variables with distribution function F, and let F_n(x) = (1/n) sum_{i <= n} 1{X_i <= x} be the empirical distribution function. Then sup_{x in R} | F_n(x) - F(x) | -> 0 almost surely. NO regularity of F is assumed: F may have atoms, may be singular, may be anything. The strong law alone gives only F_n(x) -> F(x) almost surely for each FIXED x, with a null set depending on x, and the union over uncountably many x of those null sets need not be null; the content of the theorem is that monotonicity upgrades pointwise convergence to UNIFORM convergence with a single null set. The quantitative companion is the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz inequality, P( sup_x |F_n(x) - F(x)| > t ) <= 2 exp(-2 n t^2) with Massart's sharp constant 2, valid for every n and t. The abstract generalisation replaces the class of half-lines by a general class of sets or functions, and then a combinatorial condition such as finite Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension is required - uniform convergence over an ARBITRARY class of sets is false. [Glivenko and Cantelli (1933); Massart (1990) for the sharp DKW constant; see van der Vaart, Asymptotic Statistics, Theorem 19.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:50:37.944175+00:00","domain":"hierarchical estimation","id":"claim_2c4ac5aa20827fd32b69fb4dd3efa5783003321360a715b05cdb388b2eb6b0e2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Consider $D$ related regressions whose coefficient vectors $w_d \\in \\mathbb{R}^p$ are modelled hierarchically, $w_d = w_0 + \\delta_d$ with $\\delta_d \\sim N(0, T)$ independent across $d$, observed through $\\hat w_d = w_d + z_d$ with known noise $z_d \\sim N(0, \\Sigma_d)$ (the sampling covariance of row $d$'s least-squares estimate). The posterior mean of $w_d$ given $\\hat w_d$ is the matrix shrinkage $$\\tilde w_d = w_0 + T\\,(T + \\Sigma_d)^{-1}(\\hat w_d - w_0),$$ which shrinks fully in the directions where the prior spread $T$ is small relative to the noise and not at all where it is large. Empirical Bayes estimates the unknowns from the rows themselves: $w_0$ by the row mean (or by a pooled fit such as the global convex weights of a stacking problem), and $T$ from the row covariance of the residuals $\\hat w_d - w_0$, whose expectation is $T + \\bar\\Sigma$: with a common noise covariance one whitens by $\\bar\\Sigma^{-1/2}$, forms the $p \\times p$ residual covariance $\\hat R = \\frac{1}{D}\\sum_d r_d r_d^T$ of the whitened rows, and takes $\\hat T = (\\hat R - I)_+$ (eigenvalues below one set to zero - the same 'subtract the noise level, keep the positive part' as the spiked-covariance debiasing, now at the aspect ratio $p/D$ of the row covariance, which is a random-matrix problem in its own right). The scalar positive-part James-Stein rule toward $w_0$ is the special case $T \\propto \\Sigma$. Two facts decide whether the construction helps in practice: the noise model $\\Sigma_d$ must be right (under heteroscedastic residuals the homoscedastic $\\sigma_d^2 (X_d^T X_d)^{-1}$ can understate the noise by a large factor in the ill-conditioned directions, making the estimated amount of shrinkage collapse to zero where cross-validation would shrink substantially - the sandwich covariance is the repair), and the gain is a variance reduction only, so it is largest when the rows are noisy relative to their spread, i.e. at small calibration sizes.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(G_n) decreasing with intersection G_infinity","Y integrable, or (X_n) a backward martingale with X_0 integrable"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627382+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2cc2222ab16695a55dfeff86ffc172230befd9f45d112c7f7776ea4b190fd13c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (G_n)_{n >= 0} be a DECREASING family of sub-sigma-algebras, G_0 containing G_1 containing G_2 and so on, and let G_infinity be their intersection. For Y in L^1, E[Y | G_n] converges almost surely and in L^1 to E[Y | G_infinity]. More generally a BACKWARD MARTINGALE, a family (X_n) with X_n G_n-measurable and E[X_n | G_{n+1}] = X_{n+1}, converges almost surely and in L^1 - and unlike the forward case NO extra hypothesis is required, because a backward martingale is automatically uniformly integrable: X_n = E[X_0 | G_n] is a family of conditional expectations of one integrable variable. This asymmetry with the forward theorem is the point: forward martingales need an L^1 bound for almost sure convergence and uniform integrability for L^1 convergence, backward martingales need neither. The classical application is the strong law of large numbers: with S_n the partial sums of an i.i.d. integrable sequence and G_n the exchangeable sigma-algebra generated by S_n, S_{n+1}, ..., one has E[X_1 | G_n] = S_n/n, so S_n/n converges almost surely and in L^1, and the Hewitt-Savage 0-1 law identifies the limit as E[X_1]. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 4.6.1]","status":"unverified"}

Define $$\\hat\\theta_{\\mathrm{JS}} = \\mu_0 + \\Big(1 - \\frac{(k - 2)\\sigma^2}{\\|X - \\mu_0\\|^2}\\Big)(X - \\mu_0), \\qquad \\hat\\theta_{\\mathrm{JS}+} = \\mu_0 + \\Big(1 - \\frac{(k-2)\\sigma^2}{\\|X - \\mu_0\\|^2}\\Big)_+ (X - \\mu_0).$$ Then for every $\\theta$: (i) $E\\|\\hat\\theta_{\\mathrm{JS}} - \\theta\\|^2 = k\\sigma^2 - (k-2)^2\\sigma^4\\, E\\big[\\|X - \\mu_0\\|^{-2}\\big] < k\\sigma^2 = E\\|X - \\theta\\|^2$, so the shrunk estimator strictly dominates the observation itself in total squared error, with the largest gain when $\\theta$ is near $\\mu_0$ (risk $\\to 2\\sigma^2$ at $\\theta = \\mu_0$); (ii) the positive-part version dominates the plain one, $E\\|\\hat\\theta_{\\mathrm{JS}+} - \\theta\\|^2 \\le E\\|\\hat\\theta_{\\mathrm{JS}} - \\theta\\|^2$ with strict inequality. {"assumptions":["The growth bound must be uniform in t on the time strip","Continuity at t = 0 and smoothness for t > 0 do not substitute for it","Nonnegativity (Widder) is an alternative hypothesis"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.106842+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_2db58f26b351f116cd637cc5b251283a346f12914a601ac338aa36ad4b299c46","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The load-bearing hypothesis in uniqueness for the Cauchy problem $u_t=\\Delta u$ on $\\mathbb R^n\\times(0,T)$, $u(\\cdot,0)=g$, is the growth bound $|u(x,t)|\\le Ae^{a|x|^2}$ with $A,a$ independent of $t$ (the Tychonoff class); smoothness of $u$ and continuity down to $t=0$ are not enough. Tychonoff's counterexample ($n=1$): let $g(t)=e^{-t^{-2}}$ for $t>0$, $g(0)=0$, and $u(x,t)=\\sum_{k\\ge0}\\frac{g^{(k)}(t)}{(2k)!}x^{2k}$. The Cauchy estimates for $g$ ($|g^{(k)}(t)|\\le k!\\,(\\theta t)^{-k}e^{-\\frac12t^{-2}}$ for some $\\theta>0$) make the series converge locally uniformly together with all its derivatives, and termwise differentiation gives $u_{xx}=u_t$; $u$ is continuous on $\\mathbb R\\times[0,\\infty)$ with $u(x,0)\\equiv0$, yet $u\\not\\equiv0$. So the zero initial datum admits the two distinct solutions $0$ and $u$, and by the uniqueness theorem $u$ cannot satisfy any uniform bound $|u|\\le Ae^{a|x|^2}$ on a strip. Two corollaries an auditor should apply: (1) a solution of the heat equation is not determined by its initial data unless a class is specified -- 'the' solution of a Cauchy problem is meaningless without one; (2) the Tychonoff solution necessarily changes sign, because nonnegative solutions with zero initial data are unique by Widder's theorem, so one-sided bounds are an alternative (and weaker) substitute for the growth class. The class is essentially sharp: the counterexample family with $g(t)=e^{-t^{-\\alpha}}$, $\\alpha>1$, shows uniqueness fails as soon as growth $e^{a|x|^{2+\\varepsilon}}$ is allowed, while $|u|\\le Ae^{a|x|^2}$ suffices.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["both measure spaces are sigma-finite","f is nonnegative (values in [0, infinity]) and measurable for the product sigma-algebra A (x) B","the product measure is the one determined by mu(A) nu(B) on rectangles (unique under sigma-finiteness)"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:23.251243+00:00","domain":"measure theory, integration, product measures","id":"claim_2db60f088285630433ee3f96f70f2774756e63f25313788bb43c846a2b2b7abe","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \\mathcal{A}, \\mu)$ and $(Y, \\mathcal{B}, \\nu)$ be $\\sigma$-FINITE measure spaces and let $f: X\\times Y \\to [0, \\infty]$ be measurable with respect to the product $\\sigma$-algebra $\\mathcal{A}\\otimes\\mathcal{B}$ (the $\\sigma$-algebra generated by the measurable rectangles $A\\times B$). Then: (i) for every $x \\in X$ the section $y \\mapsto f(x,y)$ is $\\mathcal{B}$-measurable and for every $y$ the section $x \\mapsto f(x,y)$ is $\\mathcal{A}$-measurable; (ii) the functions $x \\mapsto \\int_Y f(x,y)\\,d\\nu(y)$ and $y \\mapsto \\int_X f(x,y)\\,d\\mu(x)$ (with values in $[0,\\infty]$) are $\\mathcal{A}$- resp. $\\mathcal{B}$-measurable; (iii) $\\int_{X\\times Y} f\\,d(\\mu\\times\\nu) = \\int_X\\Big(\\int_Y f(x,y)\\,d\\nu(y)\\Big)d\\mu(x) = \\int_Y\\Big(\\int_X f(x,y)\\,d\\mu(x)\\Big)d\\nu(y)$, all three possibly $= +\\infty$, where $\\mu\\times\\nu$ is the (unique, by $\\sigma$-finiteness) product measure with $(\\mu\\times\\nu)(A\\times B) = \\mu(A)\\nu(B)$. Fubini's theorem is the companion for signed/complex $f$: if $f \\in L^1(\\mu\\times\\nu)$ - which by Tonelli applied to $|f|$ can be checked by ONE iterated integral of $|f|$ - then the sections are integrable for a.e. $x$ (resp. $y$), the partial integrals are integrable, and the three integrals agree as finite numbers. Sharp edges: (1) $\\sigma$-finiteness cannot be dropped: $X = Y = [0,1]$, $\\mu$ = Lebesgue, $\\nu$ = counting measure, $f = \\mathbf{1}_{\\{x = y\\}}$ (measurable for the product $\\sigma$-algebra since the diagonal is closed hence Borel); then $\\int_X\\int_Y f\\,d\\nu\\,d\\mu = 1$ while $\\int_Y\\int_X f\\,d\\mu\\,d\\nu = 0$; (2) nonnegativity (or integrability) cannot be dropped: $f(x,y) = (x^2 - y^2)/(x^2+y^2)^2$ on $(0,1)^2$ has iterated integrals $\\pi/4$ and $-\\pi/4$, and $f(x,y) = \\mathbf{1}_{\\{x = y\\}} - \\mathbf{1}_{\\{x = y+1\\}}$ on $\\mathbb{N}\\times\\mathbb{N}$ with counting measures has iterated sums $1$ and $0$ - in both $\\int|f| = \\infty$; (3) joint measurability cannot be dropped: assuming the continuum hypothesis there is a set $S \\subset [0,1]^2$ (Sierpinski) with every vertical section countable and every horizontal section co-countable, so the iterated integrals of $\\mathbf{1}_S$ are $0$ and $1$ - $S$ is not Lebesgue measurable in the plane; (4) for the COMPLETED product (Lebesgue measure on $\\mathbb{R}^{m+n}$ is the completion of $\\mathcal{L}^m\\otimes\\mathcal{L}^n$) the sections are measurable only for a.e. $x$ and the partial integral is defined a.e.; the equalities in (iii) still hold with this proviso; (5) the theorem gives equality of the iterated integrals with the DOUBLE integral - the existence and equality of the two iterated integrals of a signed function does not by itself imply integrability (example (2) reversed: symmetrise to make both iterated integrals 0).","status":"unverified"}

Then E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n ( f(X_i) - E f(X_i) ) | <= 2 E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n eps_i f(X_i) |, and in the other direction E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n eps_i ( f(X_i) - E f(X_i) ) | <= 2 E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n ( f(X_i) - E f(X_i) ) |. # C020 v2: a shifted peak for ONE realized label vector
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: narrowed. Target: 1. Novelty unestablished.
General T267 remains open. This is a restricted four-atom width-first theorem.

## 1. Model and precise probability statement
For 0<e<1/4 put D=1+e^2+e^4, x_(s,t)=(1,es,e^2t)/sqrt(D),
s,t in {-1,1}. The population is uniform on these four atoms and the
training set contains one observation at each atom (stratified, not iid).
Set u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2), c_e=e^2/sqrt(D(1+e^2)), alpha_e=c_e/2,
and g_e(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-c_e/2. Thus ||u_e||=1 and its four Walsh
coefficients (0,s,t,st) are (0,alpha_e,alpha_e,alpha_e).
Fix 0<nu<=1 and kappa>0. Independently draw four noise signs xi_(s,t),
each uniform {-1,1}, and label y_i=g_e(x_i)+sigma_e xi_i, where
 sigma_e=2alpha_e sqrt(kappa/sqrt(e))~sqrt(kappa)e^(7/4).
Initialize f_m(x)=m^(-1/2)sum_j a_j ReLU(w_j.x), with iid w_j~N(0,I_3)
and independent iid a_j uniform {-nu,nu}. Both layers undergo simultaneous
GD with step gamma=1/2 on loss (1/8)sum_i(f_m(x_i)-y_i)^2, using gate
derivative zero at zero. The individual clean risk is
 R_(e,m,xi)(k)=(1/4)sum_i(f_(m,xi)(x_i;k)-g_e(x_i))^2.
There is NO noise average anywhere in the claim.

Let H(x,z)=E[ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z], and let
lambda_h be the Walsh eigenvalues of H(X,X)/4, b_h=-log(1-lambda_h/2),
eta_e=(b_t+b_st)/b_s. C009's clock premises are
 b_s~nu^2 e/(4pi), b_t~b_st~nu^2 e^2/(8pi), eta_e~e,
with b_0 bounded away from zero.
For epsilon>0 let E_(e,m,xi)(epsilon) mean that there exist integer
k0<k1<k2<k3 with k0>=0, satisfying
 R(k0)>R(k1), R(k2)>R(k1), R(k2)>R(k3),                   (1)
 |k1/((3pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e))-1|<epsilon,
 |k2/((9pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e))-1|<epsilon,
and k2 is an interior maximum on a nontrivial integer interval [l,k3]
with k1<l<k2<k3 and both endpoint risks strictly below R(k2).
Ties between interior maximizing indices are allowed. The claim is
 liminf_(e downarrow0) liminf_(m to infinity)
 P_(xi,initialization)(E_(e,m,xi)(epsilon)) >= 1/16.       (2)
For each fixed chi in {-1,1}, conditional on xi_(s,t)=chi*s, the lower
bound over initialization alone is 1/2. The time k1 is a low-risk
cancellation WITNESS, not a claimed uniquely located stationary minimum.
The time k2 is an interval peak, not a unique stationary point theorem.
Equation (1) is the finite-witness meaning of two descents separated by a rise;
no monotonicity of every intervening nonlinear GD step is asserted.

## 2. Gaussian-width precursor and its exact unaveraged risk
C016/C017 supply, after the fixed-e width limit, independent Gaussian
Walsh initial outputs Z_(e,h) with covariance nu^2 lambda_h^RF. Couple them
for all e using independent standard G_0,G_s,G_t,G_st. Set
 U_(e,h)=Z_(e,h)/alpha_e-theta_h/alpha_e.
Then almost surely
 e U_(e,s)->L=sqrt(2)nu G_s,
 U_(e,t)->L_t=sqrt(2)nu G_t-1, U_(e,st)->-1.
These convergences are uniform when the four Gaussian coordinates range
over a fixed bounded set; the scalar variance coefficients are deterministic.
The constant initial output Z_(e,0)=O(1) in this coupling.

Fix the single label branch xi_(s,t)=chi*s. Its only nonzero normalized
noise Walsh coefficient is N_s=d e^(-1/4), d=2sqrt(kappa)chi;
N_0=N_t=N_st=0. Write N=N_s. The exact frozen clean risk is
 Q_(e,chi)(t)=alpha_e^2 sum_h [q_h U_(e,h)+(1-q_h)N_h]^2,
 q_h=exp(-b_h t).                                       (3)
At integer times this is discrete kernel GD, not gradient flow. In real
time it is only the spectral interpolation used to select integer witnesses.
Use the favorable initialization event chi*L<0, of probability1/2.
Every assertion below first refers to a fixed Gaussian realization in
this event, then is made probabilistic through compact exhaustion.

## 3. Early cancellation and two large value gaps
For small e, N and U_(e,s) have opposite signs. Thus
 q_*=-N/(U_(e,s)-N) belongs to (0,1),
 q_*~(-d/L)e^(3/4).
The fast residual N+q_*(U_(e,s)-N) is EXACTLY zero. Define
 t_1=-log(q_*)/b_s, t_0=-log(2q_*)/b_s.
Both are nonnegative for small e, t_0<t_1, and
 b_s t_1=(3/4)log(1/e)-log(-d/L)+o(1).                 (4)
Round these to nearest integers k0,k1. Their separation is (log2)/b_s,
which tends to infinity, so rounding preserves their order. A time change
of at most1/2 multiplies q_s by exp(O(b_s))=1+O(e). The residual error at
k1 is therefore O(|N|e)=O(e^(3/4)); at k0 it is -N+O(|N|e).
Slow-mode q_h tend to1 at both times and their U_h stay bounded. The
constant-mode residual is negligible faster than every power of e because
its initial normalized coefficient is O(e^(-2)) and b_0 is positive.
It follows that
 Q(k1)/alpha_e^2 -> L_t^2+1=2B,
 Q(k0)/(alpha_e^2 e^(-1/2)) -> d^2=4kappa,
where B=(L_t^2+1)/2>=1/2. In particular Q(k0)>Q(k1).
This proves the first descent witness and its leading clock; no derivative
argument or minimum uniqueness is needed.

## 4. The later single-label peak
Set t_e(v)=((9/4)log(1/e)+v)/b_s and z=exp(-v). Then q_s=e^(9/4)z.
Differentiate (3), using the exact derivative identity of C019:
 Q'(t_e(v))/(2alpha_e^2(b_t+b_st))
 =sum_h [b_h/(b_t+b_st)]
   [q_h N_h(N_h-U_h)-q_h^2(U_h-N_h)^2].                 (5)
The fast term -q_s N U_s/eta_e converges to -dL z=A z,
with A=-dL>0. Its other four expansion terms vanish uniformly on bounded
v intervals. Their orders are respectively e^(3/4), e^(3/2), e^(9/4), e^3,
for q_s N^2/eta_e, q_s^2 U_s^2/eta_e, q_s^2 U_s N/eta_e,
and q_s^2 N^2/eta_e. The slow terms, with N_t=N_st=0, tend to -B,
since their weights tend to1/2 and q_t,q_st=1-O(e log(1/e)).
The constant term is again exponentially negligible. Hence locally uniformly
 Q'(t_e(v))/(2alpha_e^2(b_t+b_st)) -> A exp(-v)-B.         (6)
Integration on bounded intervals gives convergence of centered risk differences:
 [Q(t_e(v))-Q(t_e(0))]/(2alpha_e^2 eta_e)
 -> V(v)-V(0), V(v)=-A exp(-v)-Bv.                     (7)
The function V is strictly concave, with its unique maximum at
 v_*=log(A/B), and has strict value gaps to either endpoint of any compact
interval containing v_* in its interior. Also, uniformly on compact v sets,
 Q(t_e(v))/(alpha_e^2 e^(-1/2)) -> d^2=4kappa.            (8)
Indeed q_s U_s=O(e^(5/4)) is negligible relative to N=O(e^(-1/4));
slow risk is O(alpha_e^2) and the constant-mode risk is negligible.
Equations (8) and Section3 give the second strict gap Q(peak)>Q(k1).
Equation (7) gives the third strict gap to a later time, now of order
alpha_e^2 eta_e. It is much smaller than the two early value gaps.

Round all central t_e(v) to the integer grid. The mesh in v is b_s->0,
so (7) remains uniform on the grid. On a fixed compact interval containing
v_* inside, an integer maximizing index is interior and its v coordinate
tends to v_*. This uses the positive gap between V(v_*) and the compact
complement of any neighborhood of v_*, not derivatives of nonlinear GD.
The central maximizing time consequently has leading term
 (9pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e).                              (9)
The early cancellation witness (4) precedes the entire central interval,
since their b_s-scaled time separation is (3/2)log(1/e)+O(1).
This completes the Gaussian frozen-array witness construction.

## 5. Probability and transfer to the actual BOTH-layer nonlinear updates
For an integer M>=1 restrict to the compact Gaussian event
 K_M={chi L<=-1/M, |G_0|,|G_s|,|G_t|,|G_st|<=M}.
These increasing events exhaust {chi L<0}. On K_M, A is bounded above
and away from zero and B is bounded above and below. Thus v_*, the offset
in (4), and all coefficients used above lie in deterministic bounded sets.
All estimates in Sections3-4 are uniform on K_M: the U limits have deterministic
coefficients linear in bounded G, the denominator L is bounded away from0,
and the exponentially small constant-mode bounds are uniform as well.
Choose a deterministic central v interval [-J,J] whose interior contains
all possible v_* on K_M, with a margin of at least1. Strict concavity and
compactness give uniform positive endpoint gaps for V. The two large early
gaps are also uniform. For small e, the entire central grid interval lies
inside the relative time tolerance epsilon in (2), and the cancellation
indices lie inside the stated earlier relative tolerance.

For each fixed e choose a finite integer horizon T_e(M) containing the
central grid interval and the possible earlier witnesses. C009 Section3,
as applied in C018 Section3, gives joint weak convergence of all actual
individual risks through that finite horizon to (3) when m tends to infinity.
The proof retains the actual nonzero initial output and controls both-layer
motion and gate-crossing remainders. The finite sixteen-label family is
covered, although here only the fixed single branch is used. Risk squaring
is continuous on the finite array, and the prediction arrays are tight.
No finite-width Gaussian-mode independence or e-uniform width bound is used.

For clarity about maxima and weak convergence, take the deterministic
central interval just specified. The event that there exist k0<k1 before
it and a grid index j in its interior, with the two early witness gaps
strictly positive and R(j) strictly above BOTH central endpoint values,
is open in the finite risk array: it is a finite union of finite intersections
of strict inequalities. Restrict k1 to its required relative time band.
The frozen arrays on K_M satisfy this open event for sufficiently small e.
Any maximum k2 over that central interval then lies in its interior;
replacing j by k2 only increases the witness gaps. The right endpoint is
k3, and k1 precedes the central interval. The entire central interval is
already in the required peak-time band, so all maximizers qualify.
The open-set Portmanteau inequality transfers the LOWER probability bound
to actual nonlinear risk arrays for each fixed e. Thus the two ordered
liminf limits have conditional probability at least P(K_M). Let M increase
to infinity to obtain the conditional lower bound1/2. This argument sends
width to infinity separately at every e and finite horizon, before e tends
to zero. No infinite-horizon NTK statement or interchange of limits occurs.

Finally the two noise events xi=+s and xi=-s are disjoint and each has
probability1/16 under the original four independent sign errors. Noise is
independent of initialization. Summing their conditional lower bounds gives
(1/16)(1/2)+(1/16)(1/2)=1/16, proving (2). Other sign patterns might add
probability, but they are not analyzed or counted in this claim.

## 6. Limits and unresolved piece
This is a single REALIZED label vector result, unlike C017/C018. It is
consistent with C019: its peak is at the later (9/4)log(1/e) clock, while
C019 addresses bounded offsets around (3/2)log(1/e).
The four input atoms cluster as e decreases; training inputs are stratified,
noise amplitude shrinks, width is taken first, and only a positive-probability
noise/initialization event is proved. No full typical-data theorem, macroscopic
feature learning, fixed-noise theorem, unique stationary points or complete
noise window is claimed. The hardest unpaid step is a general single-dataset
result beyond this shrinking four-atom, positive-probability construction.
Dependencies C009,C016,C017,C018,C019 and this claim all remain unaudited.
Independent correctness and novelty review are pending; no priority claim
is made. Sources: the named own proof files; the full ReLU kernel and clock
premises come from C009, with Heckel-Yilmaz 2007.10099v2 Section3 as its
primary kernel source. No new external literature result is claimed here.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the sequence is independent AND identically distributed","A invariant under permutations of finitely many coordinates"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.781848+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2f498bfa2a2e45261395e21060f28261d050042661f5980c3c3857ba42765667","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, X_2, ... be INDEPENDENT AND IDENTICALLY DISTRIBUTED. Call an event A EXCHANGEABLE if it is invariant under every permutation of finitely many indices, that is A is unchanged when the values of any finite set of coordinates are permuted. Then P(A) is 0 or 1 for every exchangeable A. This is strictly stronger than Kolmogorov's 0-1 law, which applies to TAIL events: every tail event is exchangeable, but not conversely. The standard separating example is A = { S_n = 0 for infinitely many n } for a simple random walk, which is exchangeable but NOT a tail event, since changing X_1 changes every partial sum. Identical distribution is essential and cannot be relaxed to mere independence. Minimal counterexample: let X_1 be Bernoulli(1/2) and let X_n = 0 deterministically for every n >= 2. These are independent but not identically distributed, and the event A = { x : x_n = 1 for some n } is invariant under every finite permutation of the coordinates, hence exchangeable, yet P(A) = P(X_1 = 1) = 1/2. The proof below breaks exactly where one needs it to: the permutation swapping the first n coordinates with the next n is not measure preserving unless the coordinates share a law. A standard use: for an i.i.d. sequence the events {limsup S_n = + infinity} and {liminf S_n = - infinity} are exchangeable, because permuting finitely many summands changes S_n for only finitely many n, so each has probability 0 or 1; for a non-degenerate mean-zero law a short further argument then shows both probabilities are 1, but that conclusion is NOT delivered by the 0-1 law alone. [Hewitt and Savage (1955); see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 4.1.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751901+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_302068305216ae5c066735895bb24468a7e83b19c56defd1453da6e28734f134","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TYPEWRITER (L^p convergence does not imply almost-everywhere convergence). On [0,1] write n = 2^k + j with 0 <= j < 2^k and let f_n be the indicator of [j 2^{-k}, (j+1) 2^{-k}). Then ||f_n||_p^p = 2^{-k} -> 0, so f_n -> 0 in L^p for every p < infinity and in measure. But for every x in [0,1) and every k there is exactly one j with f_{2^k + j}(x) = 1, so f_n(x) equals 1 for infinitely many n and 0 for infinitely many n: the sequence converges at NO point. This is why one extracts an a.e. convergent subsequence rather than hoping for the full sequence. SLIDING BUMP (pointwise convergence does not imply L^1 convergence). On [0,1] let g_n = n 1_{(0, 1/n)}. Then g_n(x) -> 0 for every x in (0,1], indeed the convergence is pointwise everywhere on (0,1], yet integral g_n = 1 for every n. The mass does not disappear, it concentrates. The dominated convergence theorem excludes exactly this: no integrable g dominates all g_n, since any such g would satisfy g >= n on (0,1/n) for every n, forcing integral_{(0,1/n)} g >= 1 for all n and contradicting absolute continuity of the integral. ESCAPING MASS is the third, distinct failure and lives on infinite measure spaces: h_n = 1_{[n, n+1]} on R is uniformly bounded, converges to 0 everywhere, and has ||h_n||_1 = 1. Three different mechanisms, three different repairs: a subsequence, a dominating function, and a tightness condition. [standard; the typewriter sequence is sometimes attributed to Kolmogorov]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a normed space (Banach for the uniform boundedness step in the failure remark and for the dual statement)","X* is the topological dual with the weak-star topology sigma(X*, X)","B is the closed unit ball of X*, or any bounded weak-star closed subset - the equivalence concerns bounded sets only","for the dual statement (weak metrizability of the ball of X iff X* separable), X is Banach"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.401830+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, duality and weak topologies","id":"claim_3068dbe8a1de19437f2a1e5ddde4699f874618668f487ef7075cce85ce2b6a54","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a normed space with dual X* carrying the weak-star topology sigma(X*, X). Then the closed unit ball B of X* is metrizable in the relative weak-star topology if and only if X is separable; in that case every bounded subset of X* is weak-star metrizable, and a compatible metric is d(f,g) = sum over n of 2^(-n) min(1, |f(x_n) - g(x_n)|) for any dense sequence (x_n) of the unit sphere of X. Combined with Banach-Alaoglu (B is weak-star compact), separability of X gives that B is weak-star compact and metrizable, hence weak-star SEQUENTIALLY compact: every bounded sequence in X* has a weak-star convergent subsequence. The dual statement also holds: for a Banach space X, the closed unit ball of X is metrizable in the weak topology sigma(X, X*) if and only if X* is separable. WHERE IT FAILS: (a) 'bounded' is essential - the weak-star topology on ALL of X* is metrizable only when X is finite dimensional; indeed if it were metrizable with countable base (U_m) at 0 and X is infinite dimensional, each U_m contains a nonzero subspace (it is cut out by finitely many functionals), so one can pick f_m in U_m with ||f_m|| >= m, and then f_m converges weak-star to 0 while being unbounded, contradicting the uniform boundedness principle; (b) the two directions are not interchangeable - separability of X does not imply separability of X*: X = l^1 is separable, so B of (l^1)* = l^infinity is weak-star metrizable, but (l^1)* = l^infinity is not separable, so the unit ball of l^1 is NOT weakly metrizable; (c) the metric above is not translation-invariantly compatible on the whole of X* and the equivalence is genuinely a statement about the relative topology on bounded sets; (d) for X = l^infinity, which is not separable, the unit ball of (l^infinity)* is weak-star compact but not weak-star metrizable, and weak-star compactness there is not sequential compactness.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:09:41.186720+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_31199ef303ea3dc048a12dfd4ffe05c9131d850a43b8c0ee851330f431bc4f9f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, Schur's lemma is an elementary but useful statement in representation theory of groups and algebras. In the group case it says that if M and N are two finite-dimensional irreducible representations of a group G and φ is a linear map from M to N that commutes with the action of the group, then either φ is invertible, or φ = 0. An important special case occurs when M = N, i.e. φ is a self-map; in particular, for representations over an algebraically closed field, any element of the center of a group must act as a scalar operator on M. The lemma is named after Issai Schur who used it to prove the Schur orthogonality relations and develop the basics of the representation theory of finite groups. Schur's lemma admits generalisations to Lie groups and Lie algebras, the most common of which are due to Jacques Dixmier and Daniel Quillen.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:00:09.358403+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning","id":"claim_3164e6f087edcf03d0ed5dc5b5362a181abb5563823cfe1cedcf020aa6b01bc9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Fitting a per-output affine stack directly in the per-sample relative metric - weighted least squares with case weights $1/\\|y_i\\|^2$, or a per-output simplex fit with the same weights - overfits badly: the weights concentrate the effective sample on the handful of smallest-norm cases and $M + 1$ coefficients fitted to them are unusable out of sample (measured on the EMIT pool, seed 101: 0.1236 against 0.0465 for ordinary least squares on Y1, 0.1591 against 0.1292 on Y2; cross-validation on the weighted fit chooses to discard it entirely). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:47:41.428399+00:00","domain":"Riemannian geometry","id":"claim_31b886d6ae5e89d7ba86732be244fd5ceb8c845f680edca8ffdf80a466f188ad","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (M,g) be a Riemannian manifold with Levi-Civita connection nabla. A smooth curve gamma: I -> M on an interval I subset R is a geodesic if its velocity field is parallel along itself: nabla_{gamma'(t)} gamma'(t) = 0 for every t in I. Equivalently, in local coordinates x^1,...,x^n a curve gamma(t) = (x^1(t),...,x^n(t)) is a geodesic iff it satisfies the second-order ODE system d^2x^k/dt^2 + sum_{i,j} Gamma^k_{ij}(gamma(t)) (dx^i/dt)(dx^j/dt) = 0 for k=1,...,n, where Gamma^k_{ij} are the Christoffel symbols of g. Geodesics are the critical points of the energy functional among curves with fixed endpoints, and, when locally minimizing, are the locally shortest paths between nearby points.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T07:57:26.142189+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_31bf23c8569447ad87fe2691c4a7ab91","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, Schur's lemma is an elementary but useful statement in representation theory of groups and algebras. In the group case it says that if M and N are two finite-dimensional irreducible representations of a group G and φ is a linear map from M to N that commutes with the action of the group, then either φ is invertible, or φ = 0. An important special case occurs when M = N, i.e. φ is a self-map; in particular, for representations over an algebraically closed field (e.g. $\\mathbb {C}$), any element of the center of a group must act as a scalar operator (a scalar multiple of the identity) on M. The lemma is named after Issai Schur who used it to prove the Schur orthogonality relations and develop the basics of the representation theory of finite groups. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T07:57:26.300439+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_32db5e05c2234ca8a4c051e226a841c9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, the free group $F_{S}$ over a given set $S$ consists of all words that can be built from members of $S$, considering two words to be different unless their equality follows from the group axioms (e.g. $st=suu^{-1}t$ but $s\\neq t^{-1}$ for $s,t,u\\in S$). This is a finite optimization of G+1 explicit rational values, not a

## Lower bound for every robustly calibrated generator

Fix g and its exact score partition Pi. Robust zero calibration makes
every p(B)=g(B) invariant across all compatible worlds. Since s<r<K,
swapping two residual L candidates in an A support forces all K-s
uncertified L atoms into a single score bin B*. Let k be the number
of known L truths OUTSIDE B*, so 0<=k<=s. In B* let u be the number
of known R truths, v the number of the F candidates outside C_R,
and w the number of fixed S atoms. Flipping orientation yields

 F*(u+k)=r*v.

Consequently v=F*j/G and u=r*j/G-k for an integer 0<=j<=G, with
k<=r*j/G. The size of B* is

For completeness the divisibility step uses Bezout: r/G and F/G are

gives (F/G)|v, then the displayed parametrization. The brain returned

and its common calibrated score, computed in the L-A world, is

 q*=lambda*(1-k*F/(r*L)).                               (3)

In any other bin let a be its known-L-truth count, u its known-R-
truth count and v its outside-C_R count. Orientation invariance gives
F*(u-a)=r*v. Its calibrated score is

Therefore in the actual compatible world R=A (whose support is C_R),
the false mass is at least

 H_R>=v*q*+(F-v)*lambda
    >=F*lambda*[1-(j/G)*(F/r)*k/(K+K*j/G-2k)].            (4)

The second inequality uses w>=0, which can only raise q* in (3).
For fixed j the function k/(K+K*j/G-2k) increases with k on the
feasible positive-denominator range: cross multiplication cancels the
quadratic terms and leaves K*(1+j/G)*(k_2-k_1)>=0. Thus its maximum
is at k=k_j. Formula (4) proves max_world H(g)>=the value (2).
It does not assume arbitrary bins are homogeneous in truth status.

## Attainer for each j

Fix any j and k=k_j. Choose k known L truths for a safe group T;
put all other L atoms in B*. In R put r*j/G-k known truths and
F*j/G outside-C_R atoms into B*. Put k of the remaining known R
truths in T alongside its k known L truths. Put all remaining R atoms
in Z. These choices are possible: k<=s and k<=r*j/G; also j<=G
ensures enough R known truths remain for T.

The groups have these source-invariant counts and scores:

* B*: K+K*j/G-2k atoms, score (3) with w=0;
* T: 2k known true atoms, score (1/r+1/K)/(2N), omitted if k=0;
* Z: r*(G-j)/G known R truths and F*(G-j)/G outside atoms,
  total K*(G-j)/G atoms, score lambda, omitted if j=G;
* fixed S atoms: score lambda.

T has source mass k/(Nr)+k/(NK). Z has source mass (G-j)/(GN)
in either orientation. B* has the remaining pair mass, or its
invariance follows directly from F*(u+k)=r*v. Thus every group has
an invariant p mass and g is its uniform coarsening; equal lambda
scores merge harmlessly. The total is one and g is robustly calibrated

If L=A its F false atoms all lie in B*, giving H_L=F*q*. If R=A,
H_R=(F*j/G)*q*+F*(1-j/G)*lambda. Since q*<=lambda, H_R>=H_L.
The worst risk is exactly F*lambda*(1-a_j). Maximizing a_j attains
the lower bound, proving (2).

The attaining rule uses only the observed known-truth unions and the

{"assumptions":["all examples are for Lebesgue measure on [0,1] or R, and counting measure on N"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.553628+00:00","domain":"real analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_33568bddd455c11696bbce09e0ff678cc9dd457d94aed6dcd3a4a493975ad160","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"There is NO inclusion between L^p and L^q on a general measure space, and the two familiar inclusions run in OPPOSITE directions. (b) Counting measure, p < q: l^p is contained in l^q, with ||a||_q <= ||a||_p - the reverse containment; strictness: a_n = 1/n is in l^2 but not l^1. (c) Lebesgue measure on R^n: NEITHER containment holds. On R, |x|^{-1/2} 1_{{|x|<1}} is in L^1 but not L^2, while (1 + |x|)^{-1} is in L^2 but not L^1 - the first fails by a local singularity, the second by slow decay at infinity. {"assumptions":["i.i.d. nonnegative weights on Z^d","existence holds in case (a) d=2 with no hypothesis, case (b) F(0) < p_c, case (c) F(0) > p_c with E tau_e < infinity; case (d) F(0) = p_c with d > 2 is OPEN","F continuous is a SUFFICIENT condition for uniqueness","the statement is about FINITE geodesics only"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542657+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3439799dcf869b96ef8603273809d352afd98579ca6a151dff8f1d66fd0af028","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Consider i.i.d. first-passage percolation on Z^d with weight law F. EXISTENCE of a finite geodesic between every pair of vertices, almost surely and simultaneously over all pairs, is known in each of the following cases, and the case division matters. (a) d = 2 and F ARBITRARY: Wierman and Reh proved that for any passage time distribution, with probability one there is a geodesic between any two points of Z^2. (b) Any d, with F(0) < p_c(d): existence follows from standard subcritical estimates. (c) Any d, with F(0) > p_c(d) and E[tau_e] < infinity: existence was proved by Zhang. (d) The remaining case F(0) = p_c(d) with d > 2 is STILL UNRESOLVED in general, though existence is known for distributions with F(0) = F(delta) = p_c for some delta > 0 in sufficiently high dimensions. So it is WRONG to say that geodesics need F(0) < p_c; that condition is sufficient and convenient, not necessary, and supercritical zero-weight percolation does not by itself destroy existence. UNIQUENESS is a separate matter: a continuous F is a SUFFICIENT condition for the model to be uniquely geodesic, since two distinct finite paths then have equal passage time with probability zero and there are countably many pairs of paths. With atoms - a two-valued weight law, say - ties are genuine and multiple geodesics occur with positive probability. All of the above is about FINITE geodesics; the existence, direction, uniqueness and coalescence of semi-infinite geodesics is a separate and largely open subject whose known results require differentiability or curvature assumptions on the limit shape. [Wierman and Reh (1978); Kesten, Aspects of First Passage Percolation, (9.23); Zhang; verified against Auffinger, Damron and Hanson, 50 Years of First-Passage Percolation, Section 4.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Primary-source scope record, not a new polynomial-gap theorem","Matrix sensing application assumes 1/20-RIP on all rank-at-most-2k matrices","The actual row has iid Gaussian rank-one measurements and m at least C d log^3 d"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T20:04:21.099115+00:00","domain":"sampling and nonconvex learning","id":"claim_35f9c193fc020fba4b06d0f0b693bea38742862f79e20a892b24d653fe16ba68","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"# Moitra-Risteski: relevant decomposition, uncovered phase-retrieval hypotheses

T321 Target 2. Literature applicability finding, not a new proof of Target 2.
Source: Fast Convergence for Langevin Diffusion with Manifold Structure,
arXiv:2002.05576, primary PDF saved under papers/.

Section 2, PDF page 3, requires the matrix-sensing operator to satisfy
(19/20)||M||_F^2 <= ||A(M)||_2^2 <= (21/20)||M||_F^2
for every matrix M of rank at most 2k. This is an operator-wide assumption,
not concentration for a fixed deterministic M.

For phase retrieval take k=1 and A_ph(M)_j=(a_j^T M a_j)/sqrt(m), so the
squared residual is precisely the normalized empirical quartic loss.
For every nonzero measurement a_i, set u=a_i/||a_i|| and M=uu^T. Then
rank(M)=1, ||M||_F=1 and

 ||A_ph(M)||_2^2=(1/m)sum_j(a_j.u)^4 >= ||a_i||^4/m.

Thus the upper RIP inequality would force
m >= (20/21)max_i||a_i||^4. The witness is allowed to depend on the sample,
because RIP quantifies over EVERY rank-one matrix. This is the exact
deterministic fourth-moment obstruction already relevant to this row,
applied to the paper's stated hypothesis; it is not presented as new.
For Gaussian measurements, ||a_1||^2/d tends to 1 in probability. Therefore
for m=C d log^3 d with fixed C, this necessary inequality fails with
probability tending to 1 as d grows. Multiplication by any fixed scalar
normalization of A_ph does not remove the growing d/log^3 d obstruction.
No claim is made here about operators obtained by data-dependent weighting,
truncation or a changed loss; those require their own arguments.

Section 4.1, Theorem 4, PDF page 7, is nevertheless a relevant generic
decomposition framework: along-level and across-level Poincare control,
control of changing conditional density/Jacobian, and finite-time retention
near the minimizer manifold combine into convergence to a restricted law.
These are hypotheses to establish, not consequences of benign landscape
alone. Our C007 is a different polar decomposition with the same unresolved
need for one conditional spectral-gap estimate.

Section 4.2, Theorem 5, PDF pages 7-8, assumes the matrix measurement
conditions above, a sufficiently large beta, and an absolutely continuous
initial law supported near one minimizer component. The target p_i is
defined just before the theorem as the Gibbs law restricted to points
closer to component E_i than the other component. The theorem's displayed
TV error includes an additive epsilon, as well as a decaying chi-square
term. It is not a statement of the full unrestricted even Poincare constant
for the empirical rank-one measurement model at beta~d/epsilon_loss.
The TV accuracy epsilon in the paper must not be identified silently with
the row's optimization/loss tolerance epsilon_loss.

The discussion on PDF page 9 explicitly leaves reaching the prescribed
initialization by unmodified Langevin for future work, while explaining
that optimization can supply such an initialization in the stated models.
Even if a warm-start sampling guarantee were imported, an additive-error
TV guarantee alone is not a variational Poincare inequality for the full law.

NEXT: adapt the near-well decomposition and retention estimates using the
actual rank-one measurement geometry, without imposing false global RIP;
then control the rest of the quotient to obtain the full polynomial gap.
No claim of a solved parameter range or a scored frontier move is made.
The rank-one diagnostic is analytic and unaudited, not a numerical bound
or a Lean-certified assertion.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["entries of Z i.i.d., mean zero, variance one (finite second moment suffices for the almost-sure convergence in the Bai-Silverstein form)","the spectral distribution of Sigma converges weakly to H; p/n -> c in (0, infinity)","Sigma and Z independent (Sigma may be random)"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_3625ab2a19639ec1e18b098bfb508774dc8680a3563d30345ceda3df84ad0c18","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $X = Z\\Sigma^{1/2}$ be $n \\times p$ with $Z$ having i.i.d. entries of mean $0$ and variance $1$, $\\Sigma$ positive semidefinite, and let $S = \\frac{1}{n}X^T X$. Then almost surely the empirical spectral distribution of $S$ converges weakly to a nonrandom probability measure $F = F^{c, H}$, characterised as follows: with $\\underline F = (1 - c)\\delta_0 + cF$ (the limiting spectral distribution of the $n \\times n$ companion $\\frac{1}{n}XX^T$) and $\\underline m(z) = \\int \\frac{d\\underline F(t)}{t - z} = -\\frac{1 - c}{z} + c\\,m_F(z)$, for every $z \\in \\mathbb{C}^+$ the value $\\underline m(z)$ is the unique solution in $\\mathbb{C}^+$ of $$z = -\\frac{1}{\\underline m} + c\\int \\frac{\\tau\\, dH(\\tau)}{1 + \\tau\\,\\underline m}.$$ Equivalently, $m_F$ solves $m_F(z) = \\int \\frac{dH(\\tau)}{\\tau\\,(1 - c - c z\\, m_F(z)) - z}$. For $H = \\delta_1$ (identity population covariance) the equation reduces to the quadratic $z\\,\\underline m^2 + (z + 1 - c)\\,\\underline m + 1 = 0$ for the companion transform (equivalently $c z\\, m_F^2 + (z - 1 + c)\\, m_F + 1 = 0$ for $m_F$ itself), whose solution is the Stieltjes transform of the Marchenko-Pastur law with ratio $c$; the support of $F$ and its density are read off by Stieltjes inversion, and the density is analytic inside the support and vanishes like a square root at each edge of the support other than $0$: for $c = 1$ the left edge is the hard edge $0$, where the density blows up like $x^{-1/2}$, and for $c > 1$ the measure $F$ also carries an atom of mass $1 - 1/c$ at $0$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. nonnegative edge weights on the nearest-neighbour edges of Z^d, d >= 2","E[min of 2d independent copies of tau_e] < infinity (implied by E[tau_e] < infinity); without it the limit exists only in probability","positivity of mu is NOT part of this theorem and holds exactly when F(0) < p_c"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542493+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_377aff255f0c4f83a8772b658e8326b0c3e89f3f2873cda60908dbe935ed4d02","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Consider i.i.d. first-passage percolation on Z^d with edge-weight law F supported on [0, infinity). Let Y be the minimum of 2d independent copies of tau_e - the smallest weight among the edges at a vertex. If E[Y] < infinity then the limit mu(e_1) = lim_{n -> infinity} T(0, n e_1)/n exists almost surely and in L^1 and is a deterministic constant in [0, infinity), and the same holds along every lattice direction, defining mu on Z^d and by homogeneity and convexity on all of R^d, invariant under the symmetries of the lattice; mu is either identically 0 or a genuine norm. Three companion facts, each with its own status. (i) WITHOUT the moment condition the limit still exists IN PROBABILITY, by Kesten, Cox-Durrett and Wierman, and when the moment condition does hold the two limits agree. (ii) 0 <= mu(e_1) <= E[tau_e], the upper bound by taking the direct path and applying the law of large numbers - so the finiteness of E[tau_e] gives the bound but is NOT needed for existence. (iii) POSITIVITY is a separate theorem and is not part of this one: mu(e_1) > 0 IF AND ONLY IF F(0) < p_c(d), the bond percolation threshold, and mu(e_1) > 0 if and only if mu(x) > 0 for every nonzero x. Let d>=3, m>=1, eta>0, A have iid real N(0,1) entries, x_* a deterministic unit signal, and independently x0~N(0,I_d/d). For f(x)=(1/(4m)) sum_i ((a_i^T x)^2-(a_i^T x_*)^2)^2 run unmodified GD. Excluding null events rho0*||v0||*||B^T v0||=0, define u=v0/||v0||, P=I-u*u^T, w=B^T*u, W=||w||^2, Q=I-w*w^T/W, b=B*w, r=P*b, a=P*v1, L=||a||^2, nu=Q*B^T*v1, gamma=eta*||v0||/m, kappa=-gamma-(eta/m)*(u^T*v1+r^T*v1/W). Observe in order w, then b (equivalently z1), then nu. Let F2=sigma(x0,g,h,w,b), F3=sigma(F2,nu). Conditional on F2, nu has Gaussian law with covariance L*Q. If L>0, B|F3 has mean M3=u*w^T+r*w^T/W+a*nu^T/L and residual law (P-a*a^T/L)*Z*Q for a fresh standard Gaussian matrix Z. Let mu be a probability measure on a finite distributive lattice satisfying the FKG lattice condition mu(x v y) mu(x ^ y) >= mu(x) mu(y) for all x, y, a condition automatically satisfied by any product measure on {0,1}^E, in which case the conclusion is called the Harris inequality. Then for any two increasing (or two decreasing) functions f, g in L^2(mu), E[fg] >= E[f]E[g]; equivalently, for increasing events A, B, mu(A ^ B) >= mu(A) mu(B), so increasing events are positively correlated. This is the basic monotone-coupling tool throughout percolation and interacting particle systems, lower-bounding joint probabilities of increasing events, such as several disjoint crossings occurring together, by the product of their individual probabilities, and it justifies a wide range of comparison and sprinkling arguments. It does not give any upper bound on the correlation, which requires separate and generally harder tools such as the van den Berg-Kesten inequality for disjoint occurrence; it does not apply to a mix of an increasing and a decreasing event without flipping a sign; and the strength of the positive correlation is not quantified beyond nonnegativity. Typical failure: Applying FKG to a pair of events where one is increasing and the other decreasing without flipping the sign, which reverses the direction of the inequality; or invoking FKG for a non-product Gibbs measure, such as a random-cluster model outside the ferromagnetic regime with cluster weight q<1, without checking the lattice condition, which is known to fail there. Canonical reference: Fortuin, Kasteleyn and Ginibre, 1971, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Harris, 1960, Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society.","status":"unverified"}

W^{k,p}(Ω) is the set of u ∈ L^p(Ω) all of whose distributional derivatives D^α u with |α| ≤ k lie in L^p(Ω): for each α there is g_α ∈ L^p(Ω) with ∫_Ω u D^α φ dx = (−1)^{|α|} ∫_Ω g_α φ dx for every φ ∈ C_c^∞(Ω); one writes D^α u = g_α (the weak derivative, unique a.e.). The norm is ||u||_{W^{k,p}} = ( Σ_{|α| ≤ k} ||D^α u||_{L^p}^p )^{1/p} (maximum over α for p = ∞). W^{k,p}(Ω) is a Banach space, separable for p < ∞ and reflexive for 1 < p < ∞. H^k(Ω) := W^{k,2}(Ω) is a Hilbert space with ⟨u, v⟩ = Σ_{|α| ≤ k} ∫_Ω D^α u D^α v dx. W^{k,p}_0(Ω) is the closure of C_c^∞(Ω) in W^{k,p}(Ω) (functions 'vanishing on the boundary' together with derivatives of order < k); H^1_0(Ω) := W^{1,2}_0(Ω). The Sobolev conjugate of p < n is p* = np/(n − p), i.e. 1/p* = 1/p − 1/n.\n\nFacts: C^∞(Ω) ∩ W^{k,p}(Ω) is dense in W^{k,p}(Ω) for p < ∞ and any open Ω (Meyers–Serrin); restrictions of C^∞(R^n) functions are dense when Ω is bounded with Lipschitz boundary; W^{k,p}_0(R^n) = W^{k,p}(R^n); for bounded Ω, W^{1,p}_0(Ω) is a proper closed subspace of W^{1,p}(Ω) (nonzero constants are excluded by the Poincaré inequality). On an interval, W^{1,p} functions have absolutely continuous representatives; in dimension n ≥ 2 a W^{1,p} function with p ≤ n can be unbounded and discontinuous. For a bounded Lipschitz domain, W^{1,∞}(Ω) is the space of Lipschitz functions on Ω̄.","status":"unverified"}

Somewhat more precisely, a problem is NP-complete when:It is a decision problem, meaning that for any input to the problem, the output is either \"yes\" or \"no\". Each input to the problem is associated with a collection of short solutions, which might or might not validly solve the input. The output is \"yes\" when at least one of these solutions is valid, and \"no\" when none of them are. The validity of each solution can be verified quickly, and a brute-force search algorithm can find a valid solution by trying all possible solutions. The problem can be used to simulate every other problem for which we can verify quickly that a solution is valid. Hence, if we could find valid solutions of some NP-complete problem quickly, we could quickly find valid solutions for every other problem in which a given solution can be easily verified.","status":"unverified"}

the Rellich formula expressing a Dirichlet eigenvalue by a boundary integral; equivalently 2λ||u||^2_{L^2(Ω)} = ∫_∂Ω (x·ν)(∂_ν u)^2 dS. For a domain star-shaped with respect to the origin (x·ν ≥ 0 on ∂Ω) the right side is nonnegative term by term. The same computation with −Δu = f(u), u = 0 on ∂Ω, is the Pohozaev identity.

Where it fails / hypotheses that matter. The integrated form needs enough regularity to give ∇u a boundary trace: u ∈ H^2(Ω) (or C^2 up to the boundary). A Dirichlet eigenfunction on a Lipschitz domain that is not convex (a re-entrant corner) need not belong to H^2(Ω), and the identity is then not available in this form without a separate justification. Without u = 0 on ∂Ω the tangential gradient contributes and the simplified boundary term (1/2)∫(x·ν)(∂_ν u)^2 is wrong: the full bracket must be kept. The sign of x·ν is not fixed for a general domain, so conclusions that use x·ν ≥ 0 (star-shapedness, Pohozaev-type nonexistence) fail otherwise. In dimension n = 2 the interior term ((n−2)/2)∫|∇u|^2 vanishes. The identity is for the Laplacian; for a variable-coefficient operator div(A∇u) extra terms involving x·∇A appear.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Sign convention: L u = -a^{ij} u_{x_i x_j} + b^i u_{x_i} + c u, subsolution means u_t + Lu <= 0","c identically zero for the full maximum principle","c >= 0 for the version with the positive part","bounded c of any sign for the comparison (sign) principle only"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.107002+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_3a4cafe9e19336aa105a2005fb7c65fd586ea28dc22562c2af3b9b1faed19d02","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For $u_t+Lu\\le0$ with $Lu=-a^{ij}u_{x_ix_j}+b^iu_{x_i}+cu$, the identity $\\max_{\\overline{U_T}}u=\\max_{\\Gamma_T}u$ requires $c\\equiv0$; with $c\\ge0$ only the weaker $\\max_{\\overline{U_T}}u\\le\\max_{\\Gamma_T}u^+$ survives; with $c$ of arbitrary sign even that fails. (a) $c<0$ destroys everything: on $U=(0,\\pi)$, $u(x,t)=e^t\\sin x$ satisfies $u_t-u_{xx}-2u=0$ (so $c=-2$), has $u=0$ on the lateral sides and $u=\\sin x\\le1$ at $t=0$, hence $\\max_{\\Gamma_T}u=1$, yet $u(\\pi/2,T)=e^T$ is arbitrarily large. A bounded operator T: H -> K is Hilbert-Schmidt if sum_{i in I} ||T e_i||^2 < infinity for some orthonormal basis (e_i)_{i in I} of H. The sum is then the same for every orthonormal basis of H, and ||T||_2 = (sum_i ||T e_i||^2)^{1/2} is the Hilbert-Schmidt norm. Equivalently, T is compact and sum_n s_n(T)^2 < infinity, with ||T||_2^2 = sum_n s_n(T)^2. Properties: ||T|| <= ||T||_2; ||T*||_2 = ||T||_2; every Hilbert-Schmidt operator is compact (it is the ||.||_2-limit, hence operator-norm limit, of finite-rank operators); the Hilbert-Schmidt operators S_2(H,K) form a Hilbert space under <A,B>_2 = sum_i <A e_i, B e_i> = tr(B*A), independent of the basis; and they form an ideal: ||A T B||_2 <= ||A|| ||T||_2 ||B|| for bounded A, B. Basis independence follows from sum_i ||T e_i||^2 = sum_i sum_j |<T e_i, f_j>|^2 = sum_j ||T* f_j||^2 for any orthonormal basis (f_j) of K.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.544171+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3b43ec8f5d0fa6d27d0e5752777028d785fae794a67b64a293ba500ca12736e7","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"The GAUSSIAN ORTHOGONAL ENSEMBLE GOE_n is the law of a real symmetric n by n matrix H whose entries are independent up to symmetry with H_{ii} distributed as N(0, 2/n) and H_{ij} distributed as N(0, 1/n) for i < j. Its density with respect to Lebesgue measure on the space of real symmetric matrices is proportional to exp( - (n/4) trace(H^2) ), and the law is invariant under H -> O H O^T for every orthogonal O. The GAUSSIAN UNITARY ENSEMBLE GUE_n is the law of a Hermitian H with H_{ii} distributed as N(0, 1/n) real and, for i < j, H_{ij} = x + i y with x and y independent N(0, 1/(2n)), so that E|H_{ij}|^2 = 1/n; its density is proportional to exp( - (n/2) trace(H^2) ) and it is invariant under H -> U H U^* for every unitary U. With THESE normalisations the empirical spectral distribution of either ensemble converges to the semicircle law on [-2, 2], the largest eigenvalue converges to 2, and the edge fluctuations are of order n^{-2/3} with Tracy-Widom limits (beta = 1 for GOE, beta = 2 for GUE). The DIAGONAL VARIANCE DIFFERS BETWEEN THE TWO ENSEMBLES - 2/n for GOE, 1/n for GUE - and that is what makes both densities come out as the invariant exponential of the trace; getting it wrong changes the density but not the limiting spectral law. Normalisation conventions vary widely across the literature: some authors use unnormalised entries of variance 1 and divide by sqrt(n) afterwards, some put the semicircle on [-1,1] or [-2 sqrt(2), 2 sqrt(2)], and some use exp(-trace(H^2)/2) with n absorbed elsewhere. Any imported constant must be checked against the convention it was derived under. [standard; e.g. Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni, An Introduction to Random Matrices, Sections 2.5 and 2.6]","status":"unverified"}

Condition on the rows indexed by $A$, let $E_A = \\operatorname{span}(A)^{\\perp}$, which has dimension $D$ almost surely, and let $Q_A : \\mathbb{R}^D \\to E_A \\subset \\mathbb{R}^m$ be any isometry (an $m \\times D$ matrix with orthonormal columns). Then the unit null normals $u_S, u_T$ of the two $(m-1) \\times m$ row submatrices satisfy $u_S = Q_A v$ and $u_T = Q_A w$, where $v, w \\in S^{D-1}$ are the null directions of the residual matrices $U = B Q_A$ and $V = C Q_A$. Conditionally on $A$ the matrices $U$ and $V$ are independent, each with iid rows of law $Q_A^{\\top} X$, and the pair correlation is preserved exactly: $\\rho_{ST}^2 = \\langle u_S, u_T \\rangle^2 = \\langle v, w \\rangle^2$. Writing $M_A = \\mathbb{E}[v v^{\\top} \\mid A]$ for the conditional second-moment matrix of the residual null line, $\\mathbb{E}[\\langle v,w\\rangle^2 \\mid A] = \\operatorname{tr}(M_A^2)$. {"assumptions":["f integrable on R","the pointwise identity is claimed at a specific point (typically x = 0)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264346+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, common errors","id":"claim_3b718e0037a91db9c64b0a4706cc1000aa0a6e3fe12673010be7f29fee1bf2dc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypotheses: the periodization $Pf(x)=\\sum_nf(x+n)$ must be continuous at the point where the identity is evaluated, and its Fourier series must converge there (absolute summability of $(\\hat f(k))_k$ is the usual sufficient condition). For a general $f\\in L^1(\\mathbb R)$ all that is true is $\\widehat{Pf}(k)=\\hat f(k)$, i.e. Poisson summation as an identity of Fourier series of an $L^1(\\mathbb T)$ function - which says nothing pointwise. Concrete failure: $f=\\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}$ (with $f(0)=f(1)=1$). Then $\\sum_nf(n)=f(0)+f(1)=2$, while $\\hat f(0)=1$ and $\\hat f(k)=\\int_0^1e^{-2\\pi ikx}dx=0$ for $k\\ne0$, so $\\sum_k\\hat f(k)=1\\ne2$. The periodization equals $1$ off $\\mathbb Z$ and $2$ on $\\mathbb Z$: it is discontinuous exactly where the identity is being evaluated, and the Fourier series converges to the midpoint $1$. Redefining $f(0)=f(1)=1/2$ restores the identity. Second trap: pure decay of $f$ is not enough - one needs decay (or summability) on the transform side as well, since the right-hand series must converge; $f$ continuous and integrable with $\\hat f$ merely tending to zero gives no pointwise statement. When quoting a rate, the clean hypothesis is $|f(x)|\\le C(1+|x|)^{-1-\\delta}$ and $|\\hat f(\\xi)|\\le C(1+|\\xi|)^{-1-\\delta}$ with $f$ continuous, or simply $f\\in\\mathcal S$.","status":"unverified"}
