{"assumptions":["(X,B,mu) is a probability space and T preserves mu","the partitions P_k are countable, measurable, and increasing: P_{k+1} refines P_k","H_mu(P_k) < infinity for each k","the union of the P_k generates B modulo mu-null sets","h_mu(T) is defined as the supremum of h_mu(T,Q) over countable partitions Q of finite entropy"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090319+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, entropy, generators","id":"claim_3c3e128038c699e9bd64175dd57d1489d79b6bc2f84bbdbc616d67a216487a92","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, B, mu) be a probability space and T : X -> X measure-preserving (invertibility is not assumed). Let P_1 <= P_2 <= ... be an increasing sequence of countable measurable partitions (each P_{k+1} refines P_k) with H_mu(P_k) < infinity for every k, and assume the sequence GENERATES: the sigma-algebra generated by the union of the P_k equals B up to mu-null sets. Then h_mu(T) = lim_k h_mu(T, P_k) = sup_k h_mu(T, P_k), where h_mu(T) is the supremum of h_mu(T,Q) over all finite-entropy partitions Q. The classical generator form is the special case: for an invertible T and a partition P with H_mu(P) < infinity whose two-sided join over all integer translates generates B, take P_k = the join of T^{-n}P over |n| <= k and conclude h_mu(T) = h_mu(T,P); for non-invertible T take the one-sided join over 0 <= n <= k. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) generation is the entire content. If the union of the P_k generates only a proper sub-sigma-algebra, the limit computes the entropy of the corresponding sub-process and can be strictly smaller than h_mu(T); with every P_k trivial the limit is 0 for a system of arbitrarily large entropy. In particular a partition that separates points topologically but only generates a smaller sigma-algebra modulo mu is not enough. (ii) Monotonicity of the sequence (or at least H_mu(Q | P_k) -> 0 for every finite-entropy Q) is used; an arbitrary sequence of partitions that 'converges' in some other sense need not have monotone entropies and the comparison step breaks. (iii) H_mu(P_k) < infinity is needed for the comparison inequality. (iv) Generation is modulo mu-null sets only, and the conclusion says nothing pointwise. (v) For non-invertible T the one-sided generator computes h_mu(T); using the two-sided join for a non-invertible map is meaningless.","status":"unverified"}

(a) Free homotopy: γ₀ and γ₁ are homotopic through closed curves in ℂ \\ {z₀} (a continuous H: [0,1]×[0,1] → ℂ \\ {z₀} with H(0,·) = γ₀, H(1,·) = γ₁ and H(s,0) = H(s,1) for every s) if and only if n(γ₀, z₀) = n(γ₁, z₀). (b) Based version: if γ₀(0) = γ₁(0) = p, they are homotopic through loops based at p in ℂ \\ {z₀} if and only if their winding numbers about z₀ agree. (c) Consequently the map π₁(ℂ \\ {z₀}, p) → ℤ, [γ] ↦ n(γ, z₀), is a well-defined group isomorphism; every integer k is realized by the circle t ↦ z₀ + r e^{2πikt} (moved to the base point along a path), and a loop in ℂ \\ {z₀} is null-homotopic exactly when its winding number about z₀ is zero. (1) Two or more punctures: in ℂ \\ {a, b} (a ≠ b) the fundamental group is free on two generators, hence non-abelian, and the pair of winding numbers does NOT classify loops: the commutator loop α β α⁻¹ β⁻¹ of small circles α about a and β about b has winding number 0 about both a and b (and about every point outside the domain) yet is not null-homotopic. {"assumptions":["n ≥ 2"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.723666+00:00","domain":"dispersive partial differential equations","id":"claim_3c61dddc2341b2fe03846c34c5f8fd2adaac49c5e5184bddc378dc2b3677df6a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let n ≥ 2. A pair (q,r) is wave-admissible (in the sense of Keel–Tao) if 2 ≤ q ≤ ∞, 2 ≤ r ≤ ∞, 1/q + (n−1)/(2r) ≤ (n−1)/4, and (q,r,n) ≠ (2,∞,3). It is sharp wave-admissible when equality holds, 1/q + (n−1)/(2r) = (n−1)/4. The exponent (n−1)/2 is the dispersive decay rate of frequency-localized waves; the associated regularity s is fixed separately by the scaling relation 1/q + n/r = n/2 − s. Examples in n = 3: (4,4) with s = 1/2, (5,10) and (4,12) with s = 1, and (∞,2) with s = 0, which is the bound ‖u‖_{L^∞_t L²_x} ≲ ‖u0‖_{L²} + ‖u1‖_{Ḣ^{−1}}. Note that the energy bound ‖u‖_{L^∞_t Ḣ¹} + ‖∂_t u‖_{L^∞_t L²} ≲ ‖u0‖_{Ḣ¹} + ‖u1‖_{L²} is not a different admissible pair: it is the pair (∞,2) applied at regularity s = 1, i.e. to |∇|u. The scaling relation always ties s to (q,r), so s = 0 is the only value that goes with (q,r) = (∞,2) in the Lebesgue-norm form of the estimate. Also note that r = ∞ is allowed in this definition but not in the Lebesgue-space wave Strichartz theorem, which requires r < ∞.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.626929+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3d2eccef094bb69e406fac092e701dccd48b74c6119162e597a97768bad97898","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (Omega, F, P) be a probability space with a filtration (F_n)_{n >= 0}, an increasing family of sub-sigma-algebras of F. A sequence (X_n)_{n >= 0} of random variables is a MARTINGALE with respect to (F_n) if (i) X_n is F_n-measurable for every n (adapted), (ii) E|X_n| < infinity for every n (integrable), and (iii) E[X_{n+1} | F_n] = X_n almost surely for every n. It is a SUBMARTINGALE if (iii) is weakened to E[X_{n+1} | F_n] >= X_n almost surely, and a SUPERMARTINGALE if E[X_{n+1} | F_n] <= X_n almost surely. Mnemonic: a supermartingale decreases in expectation, so it is what a gambler faces in an unfair game. All three notions are relative to a specified filtration; a process can be a martingale for its own natural filtration and fail to be one for a larger filtration. Integrability in (ii) is part of the definition, not a consequence: without it the conditional expectation in (iii) need not exist. If (X_n) is a martingale and phi is convex with phi(X_n) integrable for every n, then (phi(X_n)) is a submartingale by conditional Jensen; in particular |X_n| and X_n^2 are submartingales when integrable. [standard; e.g. Williams, Probability with Martingales, Chapter 10]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A and B are linear operators in the same Banach space","D(A) ⊂ D(B)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.769951+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, perturbation theory of operators","id":"claim_3e4fa40fff097dc9c86af5298ab723946a61639931a25125440e3ee34a2b916e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A and B be linear operators in a Banach space X. B is relatively bounded with respect to A (A-bounded) if D(A) ⊂ D(B) and there are constants a, b ≥ 0 with ‖Bx‖ ≤ a‖Ax‖ + b‖x‖ for all x ∈ D(A). The infimum of all admissible a is the A-bound (relative bound) of B; the corresponding b usually grows as a approaches the infimum, and the infimum itself need not be attained. In a Hilbert space the condition ‖Bx‖² ≤ a'²‖Ax‖² + b'²‖x‖² defines the same relative bound. Relative bound 0 means: for every ε > 0 there is b_ε with ‖Bx‖ ≤ ε‖Ax‖ + b_ε‖x‖. If A is closed, B is closable, and D(A) ⊂ D(B), then B is automatically A-bounded (closed graph theorem applied to B on the Banach space (D(A), graph norm of A)). The form analogue: for A ≥ 0 self-adjoint with form q_A(x) = ‖A^{1/2}x‖² on Q(A) = D(A^{1/2}), a symmetric form β is A-form-bounded with bound a if Q(A) ⊂ D(β) and |β(x, x)| ≤ a q_A(x) + b‖x‖² for x ∈ Q(A). Operator-boundedness with bound a implies form-boundedness with bound at most a, not conversely.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Finite d,q; constant SPD H with spectrum in [m,M]","Adapted states, deterministic u0, v0=0; jointly sampled oracle noise centered conditional on the past","Normal conditional covariance <=sigma^2 H; tangential conditional second moment <=sigma^2 D^2 |v|^2","0<rho<2; 0<eta<=rho/M; sigma,D>=0; F in C_b^2","Unbiased gradient oracle; individual random sample-loss gradient representation not asserted","For the proportional-covariance target subclass require normal covariance equality on v=0; proportionality is on the manifold only"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T19:49:38.596602+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_3eb7dc9fd7523a133f226b8bdae7ac45699057680f6ac8b7e79453b8cfe1178d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Status: proof (unaudited). Let d,q>=1 be finite, H a constant symmetric positive definite q by q
matrix, and 0<m<=lambda(H)<=M. Fix sigma,D>=0, 0<rho<2 and
0<eta<=rho/M. Let (F_k) be a filtration and (u_k,v_k) adapted, with
deterministic u_0 and v_0=0. At each step let the jointly sampled oracle
noise (xi_k^u,xi_k^v) in R^d x R^q be F_{k+1}-measurable, with

    E[xi_k^u|F_k]=0, E[xi_k^v|F_k]=0,
    E[xi_k^v (xi_k^v)^T|F_k] <= sigma^2 H,
    E[|xi_k^u|^2|F_k] <= sigma^2 D^2 |v_k|^2.           (1)

The matrix inequality is in Loewner order and holds almost surely.

    u_{k+1}=u_k-eta xi_k^u,
    v_{k+1}=B v_k-eta xi_k^v, B=I-eta H.               (2)

Here "oracle" means an unbiased estimator of grad L; this theorem does
not assert that every allowed noise field is the gradient of an individual
random sample loss. The label-gradient models of C005 are included.

For F in C_b^2(R^{d+q}), let f(u)=F(u,0), a(u)=D_v F(u,0), and define

    F_2=sup ||D^2 f||_op,
    F_vv=sup ||D_v^2 F||_op,
    F_uv=sup ||D_u a||_op,
    c=sigma^2 q/(2-rho), gamma=min{m,M(2-rho)/rho}.

Then, for every T>=0,

    sup_{integer 0<=K<=T/eta^2}
      |E F(u_K,v_K)-F(u_0,0)| <= eta C(T),
    C(T)=c[F_vv/2+T sigma^2 D^2 F_2/2+F_uv sigma D/gamma]. (3)

Thus a=1. If, in addition, the normal conditional covariance equals
sigma^2 H on the event v_k=0, then (1) forces xi_k^u=0 there almost
surely. Consequently the full noise covariance on the minimizing
manifold is sigma^2 diag(0,H), proportional to the population Hessian.

uses only domination. No global covariance proportionality is asserted.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X, Y Banach spaces"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492197+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator theory","id":"claim_3ecf47d2e1941e3ed3b704c1615dceb455e30d7da6c0085069f13dc22e065c98","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X, Y be Banach spaces. A linear operator K : X → Y is compact if it maps the closed unit ball of X onto a relatively compact subset of Y; equivalently, for every bounded sequence (x_n) in X the sequence (Kx_n) has a norm-convergent subsequence. Compact operators are bounded. They form a norm-closed two-sided ideal in the bounded operators: norm limits of compact operators are compact, and BK and KB are compact whenever K is compact and B is bounded. Every bounded finite-rank operator is compact; in a Hilbert space (and in every Banach space with the approximation property) every compact operator is a norm limit of finite-rank operators. K is compact iff its adjoint K* is compact (Schauder). The identity of an infinite-dimensional space is not compact (Riesz), so on an infinite-dimensional space a compact operator never has a bounded inverse. A compact operator maps weakly convergent sequences to norm-convergent sequences; the converse (complete continuity implies compactness) holds when X is reflexive, e.g. a Hilbert space, but fails in ℓ^1 (Schur property).\n\nExamples: diag(λ_n) on ℓ^2 is compact iff λ_n → 0; integral operators with L^2 kernels (Hilbert–Schmidt operators) are compact; the embedding H^1_0(Ω) → L^2(Ω) for bounded open Ω is compact (Rellich), so the inverse of the Dirichlet Laplacian is a compact self-adjoint operator on L^2(Ω). Non-examples: the shift operators on ℓ^2; multiplication by a function f on L^2[0,1] is compact only when f = 0 a.e.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space and T is continuous","the metric enters only through the compact topology"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438163+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, entropy","id":"claim_3fe95da80d1756dae2bb8c43b479ad29fb9efff8bf12406c39a668547d7335d9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $T: X \\to X$ be a continuous map of a compact metric space $(X, d)$. For $n \\ge 1$ define the dynamical metric $d_n(x, y) = \\max_{0 \\le k < n} d(T^k x, T^k y)$. A set $E \\subset X$ is $(n, \\varepsilon)$-separated if $d_n(x, y) > \\varepsilon$ for all distinct $x, y \\in E$; let $s(n, \\varepsilon)$ be the maximal cardinality of such a set (finite by compactness). A set $F$ is $(n, \\varepsilon)$-spanning if every $x \\in X$ has $d_n(x, y) \\le \\varepsilon$ for some $y \\in F$; let $r(n, \\varepsilon)$ be the minimal cardinality. The topological entropy is\n$$h_{top}(T) = \\lim_{\\varepsilon \\to 0} \\limsup_{n \\to \\infty} \\frac{1}{n} \\log s(n, \\varepsilon) = \\lim_{\\varepsilon \\to 0} \\limsup_{n \\to \\infty} \\frac{1}{n} \\log r(n, \\varepsilon) \\in [0, \\infty],$$\nusing $r(n,\\varepsilon) \\le s(n,\\varepsilon) \\le r(n, \\varepsilon/2)$; the limit in $\\varepsilon$ exists by monotonicity, and replacing the $\\limsup$ in $n$ by a $\\liminf$ gives the same value. The value is independent of the compatible metric (this uses compactness) and coincides with the open-cover definition $h_{top}(T) = \\sup_{\\mathcal{U}} \\lim_n \\frac1n \\log N(\\mathcal{U}^n_0)$ where $N$ counts the minimal subcover of the join $\\mathcal{U}^n_0 = \\bigvee_{k<n} T^{-k}\\mathcal{U}$. Basic properties: $h_{top}(T^m) = m\\, h_{top}(T)$ for $m \\ge 1$; $h_{top}(T^{-1}) = h_{top}(T)$ for homeomorphisms; $h_{top}$ is an invariant of topological conjugacy; a Lipschitz map of a compact metric space of finite box dimension has finite entropy, but a continuous map of a compact metric space can have $h_{top} = \\infty$. On a NON-compact space the separated-set quantity depends on the metric, not merely on the topology, and the equalities above can fail.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726542+00:00","domain":"dispersive partial differential equations","id":"claim_4035e0f47d8f89385856e3a0fa89ee495b32f2ab6d982252999b8813bc8feedd","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: finite speed of propagation and the domain-of-dependence cone are properties of the wave equation (and of symmetric hyperbolic systems), proved by a local energy identity on the cone. The Schrödinger equation has no such identity and propagates instantaneously. Concrete counterexample: let f ∈ L¹(R^n) be nonzero and compactly supported and let t ≠ 0. By the kernel formula, e^{itΔ}f(x) = (4πit)^{−n/2} e^{i|x|²/(4t)} · G(x/(2t)) where G is the Fourier transform of the compactly supported integrable function y ↦ e^{i|y|²/(4t)}f(y). By the Paley–Wiener theorem G extends to an entire function on C^n, and it is not identically zero, so its zero set contains no nonempty open set. Hence e^{itΔ}f is nonzero almost everywhere on every open subset of R^n at every t ≠ 0: compactly supported data instantly become globally supported. The same phenomenon rules out any cone-shaped domain of dependence, and the heat equation behaves the same way. What survives for Schrödinger are local smoothing, dispersive decay and (pseudo)locality statements about wave packets moving at velocity ≈ 2ξ, not a finite propagation speed; the wave equation's finite-speed argument must never be transplanted to a dispersive or parabolic equation.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-12T07:22:43.761193+00:00","domain":"graph theory","id":"claim_41f1607fe0ca61747b32e0ca370c278bba715b149e9ab306a7f07d7712059878","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A graph G = (V, E) is a finite set V of vertices together with a set E of edges, each an unordered pair of vertices; G is simple if it has no loops or repeated edges. A subgraph uses a subset of the vertices and edges. The degree of a vertex is the number of incident edges, and the handshake lemma gives sum of degrees = 2|E|. A walk is a vertex-edge alternation; a path has distinct vertices, a cycle is a closed path, and G is connected if every two vertices are joined by a path. Standard families: the complete graph K_n (all pairs adjacent), a tree (connected and acyclic, with |V|-1 edges), and a bipartite graph (vertices two-colorable so every edge crosses, equivalently no odd cycle). The vertex connectivity kappa(G) and edge connectivity lambda(G) are the least numbers of vertices, respectively edges, whose deletion disconnects G (or reduces it to a single vertex), and kappa(G) <= lambda(G) <= min-degree.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X and Y are Banach spaces","T is linear on a linear subspace D(T) of X"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.769166+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, unbounded operators","id":"claim_41fdcf41b301c72abeac970dc8d13d7e8412473ffc482e2582494edf964e1f49","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X, Y be Banach spaces and T: D(T) ⊂ X → Y a linear operator defined on a linear subspace D(T). Its graph is G(T) = {(x, Tx) : x ∈ D(T)} ⊂ X × Y. T is closed if G(T) is closed in X × Y; equivalently, whenever x_n ∈ D(T), x_n → x in X and Tx_n → y in Y, then x ∈ D(T) and Tx = y. Equivalently, D(T) is complete under the graph norm ‖x‖_T = ‖x‖ + ‖Tx‖. S is an extension of T (written T ⊂ S) if D(T) ⊂ D(S) and Sx = Tx for x ∈ D(T). T is closable if it has a closed extension; equivalently, x_n ∈ D(T), x_n → 0 and Tx_n → y imply y = 0; equivalently, the closure of G(T) is the graph of an operator, called the closure T̄ (the smallest closed extension). If T is closed, a subspace D_0 ⊂ D(T) is a core for T if D_0 is dense in D(T) for the graph norm, i.e. the closure of T restricted to D_0 equals T. A closed operator need not be bounded, and being closed says nothing about D(T) being dense; by the closed graph theorem a closed operator with D(T) = X is bounded.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X a normed space; no completeness of X is needed","for metrizability and sequential compactness of the ball: X separable","Tychonoff (hence a form of the axiom of choice) in the general case"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T15:38:23.784925+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_424daabf6bab4c23b100ce5671977a4d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a normed vector space over R or C. The closed unit ball B of the dual space X^* is COMPACT in the weak-* topology, that is the topology of pointwise convergence on X. Two refinements matter. (a) If X is SEPARABLE then the weak-* topology restricted to B is metrizable and B is weak-* SEQUENTIALLY compact, so bounded sequences of functionals have weak-* convergent subsequences; without separability compactness need not give sequential compactness. (b) The general theorem uses Tychonoff's theorem for a product of compact scalar discs and therefore, in ZF, is not provable without some choice; the separable case needs only a diagonal argument. The theorem does NOT say the ball is norm-compact: by Riesz's lemma the closed unit ball of a normed space is norm-compact if and only if the space is finite-dimensional. Nor does it say the ball of X itself is weakly compact - that characterises reflexivity (Kakutani). [standard; e.g. Rudin, Functional Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 3.15]\n\nFor every neighborhood U of 0 in X, its polar U^circ = {phi in X^*: |phi(u)| <= 1 for every u in U} is weak-* compact. Here X^* is the continuous dual and the weak-* topology is pointwise convergence on X; neither completeness nor separability of X is needed.","status":"unverified"}

Then (X_n,Y_n) converges jointly in distribution to (X,c). Consequently X_n+Y_n converges in distribution to X+c, X_n Y_n converges in distribution to cX, and, if c!=0, X_n/Y_n converges in distribution to X/c. For the quotient, define its value arbitrarily on {Y_n=0} when necessary; that event has probability tending to zero. Convergence Y_n=>c in distribution is equivalent to convergence Y_n->c in probability, so either hypothesis gives the same conclusion for a constant target. With a nonconstant target, separate marginal convergence alone does not identify the joint limit: if X is a nondegenerate symmetric random variable, X_n=X and Y_n=-X, then both marginal laws converge to the law of X, but X_n+Y_n=0 does not converge to the law of 2X. A random second limit is allowed when joint convergence (X_n,Y_n)=>(X,Y) is supplied; the continuous mapping theorem then gives the corresponding sum and product limits, and the quotient limit if P(Y=0)=0. [Re-derived local source, M9; textbook cross-reference: van der Vaart, Asymptotic Statistics, Theorem 2.8.]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. rows C^{1/2} z with z having i.i.d. mean-zero unit-variance entries and finite twelfth moment","p/n -> q_0 in (0, infinity)","the population spectral distribution converges to a limit with bounded support","the formula is used inside the bulk; isolated spikes are handled by the BBP correction"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T15:09:50+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_4371e12019521ab578f7c0a985513fd3b35fa6f43b024c62adc7360470e48a4a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $E = \\frac{1}{n} X^T X$ be the sample covariance of $n$ i.i.d. rows in $\\mathbb{R}^p$ with population covariance $C$ (rows $C^{1/2} z_i$ with $z_i$ having i.i.d. entries of mean zero, variance one and finite twelfth moment), in the regime $p, n \\to \\infty$ with $q = p/n \\to q_0 \\in (0, \\infty)$, and assume the spectral distribution of $C$ converges to a limit with bounded support. Let $\\lambda_k, u_k$ be the sample eigenvalues and eigenvectors and let $g_E(z) = \\frac{1}{p}\\operatorname{tr}(z I - E)^{-1}$ be the Stieltjes transform of the sample spectrum, and $g(z) = \\int (z - x)^{-1} F(dx)$ that of its almost-sure limit $F$, the limiting sample spectral distribution, with $g(\\lambda - i0) := \\lim_{\\eta \\downarrow 0} g(\\lambda - i\\eta)$ inside the bulk (the finite-sample $g_E(\\lambda - i\\eta)$ has no useful limit as $\\eta \\downarrow 0$: it diverges at each sample eigenvalue and is real between them). THEOREM (Ledoit and Peche, 2011, Theorem 4; in the form of Bun, Bouchaud and Potters 2017). The oracle eigenvalues $\\xi_k^{\\mathrm{or}} = u_k^T C u_k$, as the weighted measure $\\frac{1}{p}\\sum_k \\xi_k^{\\mathrm{or}} \\delta_{\\lambda_k}$, converge almost surely to $\\xi(\\lambda) F(d\\lambda)$ on $(0, \\infty)$, where $$\\xi(\\lambda) = \\frac{\\lambda}{\\big|\\, 1 - q_0 + q_0\\, \\lambda\\, g(\\lambda - i0) \\,\\big|^2};$$ informally $\\xi_k^{\\mathrm{or}} \\approx \\xi(\\lambda_k)$ for sample eigenvalues inside the bulk (the theorem is about the weighted measure, not a limit for each $k$). This limit depends on the population covariance $C$ only through the observable sample spectrum, so it is a consistent, computable estimator (the rotationally invariant estimator, RIE, or nonlinear shrinkage): replace each sample eigenvalue by $\\xi(\\lambda_k)$, keep the sample eigenvectors. In practice $g_E$ is evaluated at $\\lambda_k - i\\eta$ with a small $\\eta$ of order $n^{-1/2}$ times the eigenvalue scale, and the result is floored at a small positive fraction of the bulk level. When $C = \\sigma^2 I$ the formula returns $\\sigma^2$ for every eigenvalue (the Marchenko-Pastur spread is entirely removed); for a spike above the bulk it returns approximately the debiased population spike. Applying the formula to a matrix whose largest eigenvalue is a signal one is trying to keep, and flooring relative to that top eigenvalue, destroys the small eigenvalues that the inverse depends on.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:37:33.911755+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning","id":"claim_44346e151009d85ee2b6ef52041da819cd6f25e04627d15b65a60bf4ba58a87a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"When one ensemble of $M$ members predicts $D$ output coordinates (spectral bands, pixels, reduced coefficients) and a separate affine stack is fitted per output, the $D$ least-squares weight vectors form a matrix $\\hat W \\in \\mathbb{R}^{D \\times (M+1)}$ with $\\hat W = W + Z$: row $d$ of the noise $Z$ has covariance $\\sigma_d^2 (X_d^T X_d)^{-1}$, $X_d$ the calibration design of output $d$ and $\\sigma_d^2$ its residual variance, while the true $W$ has low effective rank whenever the optimal weighting varies smoothly across outputs (neighbouring bands weight the same members similarly). The relevant random-matrix ratio is then $\\beta = (M+1)/D$ - not $M/n_{\\mathrm{cal}}$ - and the problem is low-rank matrix denoising: after scaling row $d$ by $1/\\sigma_d$ (and, when the designs $X_d$ are nearly common across outputs, right-whitening by $\\bar G^{1/2}\\sqrt{n}$ with $\\bar G$ the average of $X_d^T X_d / n$), the Gavish-Donoho optimal singular-value shrinkage selects the rank as the number of singular values above the Marchenko-Pastur edge $1 + \\sqrt\\beta$ and debiases each retained singular value, with no cross-validation. Shrinking every row toward one global weight vector by a cross-validated scalar - the best heuristic found on the EMIT/OCO-2 pools, beating per-output least squares on 69 of 70 cells by 3.1 percent - is the rank-one special case of this estimator with the direction fixed and the amount tuned by hand. For EMIT ($M = 23$, $D = 285$) $\\beta = 0.084$; for OCO-2 ($M = 18$, $D = 40$) $\\beta = 0.475$, a wide bulk in which only strong structure clears the edge.","status":"unverified"}

The perturbed semigroup solves the variation-of-constants equation S(t)x = T(t)x + ∫_0^t T(t − s) B S(s)x ds for all x ∈ X, and is given by the Dyson-Phillips series S(t) = Σ_{n ≥ 0} S_n(t) with S_0(t) = T(t) and S_{n+1}(t)x = ∫_0^t T(t − s)B S_n(s)x ds, converging in operator norm uniformly on compact time intervals. {"assumptions":["the perturbation K is compact","lambda is a nonzero scalar","the ambient space is a Banach space (Hilbert space for the adjoint form with conjugated lambda)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.573224+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Fredholm theory","id":"claim_44c2b247a9f29b24f5479cb03b211daeeab0cd1b96adb5f6a3837b72135ca330","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The alternative 'injective implies surjective' for operators of the form lambda I - K is carried entirely by two hypotheses: K is compact, and lambda is nonzero. (1) Compactness is load-bearing. On l^2 the unilateral shift S(x_1, x_2, ...) = (0, x_1, x_2, ...) is bounded and injective but not surjective, and S = I - K with K = I - S bounded but not compact; its index is -1, not 0. So for a general bounded perturbation of the identity the two alternatives can both fail to be the right dichotomy: the equation x - K x = y can be uniquely solvable for some y and unsolvable for others, with no finite-dimensional solvability condition of equal dimensions on the two sides. What actually powers the alternative is that the index is 0, which compactness guarantees; a Fredholm operator of nonzero index (like S) is a counterexample to the dichotomy but not to Fredholm theory. (2) lambda nonzero is load-bearing. Take K = diag(1, 1/2, 1/3, ...) on l^2, which is compact and injective, with dense but proper range (the sequence (1/n) is not in ran K, since it would need preimage (1, 1, 1, ...)). So for lambda = 0, 'injective' does not give 'surjective', the range is not closed, and 0 is in the spectrum of every compact operator on an infinite-dimensional space. (3) In the Hilbert-space version the solvability condition uses the conjugate: lambda x - K x = y is solvable exactly when y is orthogonal to ker(conjugate of lambda times I - K*), not to ker(lambda I - K*); forgetting the conjugation is a common slip for complex lambda. (4) The dimension identity dim ker(lambda - K) = dim ker(lambda - K') is an identity of the two kernels, not a claim that the kernels correspond naturally, and it fails for non-compact perturbations (for S, ker S = 0 while ker S' is one-dimensional).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["C a class of measurable sets (or of {0,1}-valued functions); the suprema are assumed measurable (a countable class, or the standard measurability conditions)","i.i.d. sampling from an arbitrary P on X","the constants 4, 8 and 8, 32 are the classical ones; several textbooks state slightly different constants from the same proof"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:40:13.706632+00:00","domain":"statistical learning theory","id":"claim_44ca0346ee27a0d7980b7facd63807b8439c3deb8db5ffcd25f0f1d03c270b4a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"DEFINITIONS. For a class C of subsets of X and points x_1, ..., x_n, the number of distinct traces |{ A intersect {x_1, ..., x_n} : A in C }| is at most 2^n; the growth (shatter) function is s(C, n) = max over all n-point sets of this number; the VC dimension d = VC(C) is the largest n with s(C, n) = 2^n (infinite if s(C, n) = 2^n for all n). Sauer-Shelah: if d < infinity then s(C, n) <= sum_{i <= d} binom(n, i) <= (e n / d)^d for n >= d. THEOREM (Vapnik and Chervonenkis, 1971). Let X_1, ..., X_n be i.i.d. from P and P_n the empirical measure. For every eps > 0 and n >= 2 / eps^2, P( sup_{A in C} |P_n(A) - P(A)| > eps ) <= 4 s(C, 2n) exp( -n eps^2 / 8 ); a form valid for all n is P( sup_{A in C} |P_n(A) - P(A)| > eps ) <= 8 s(C, n) exp( -n eps^2 / 32 ). COROLLARIES. If VC(C) = d < infinity, then sup_A |P_n(A) - P(A)| -> 0 almost surely for EVERY P (C is a uniform Glivenko-Cantelli class), with E sup_A |P_n(A) - P(A)| <= C_0 sqrt(d / n) for an absolute constant C_0 (Talagrand's sharpening of the log-free bound); the sample size n = O( (d log(1/eps) + log(1/delta)) / eps^2 ) makes the sup at most eps with probability 1 - delta; and the condition is also necessary: if VC(C) = infinity there is a distribution P for which the sup does not converge to 0 in probability (Vapnik-Chervonenkis; Assouad; Dudley). In learning: for a class of classifiers of VC dimension d, every classifier's true error is within eps of its training error simultaneously once n is of order d / eps^2 (up to logarithms), so empirical risk minimisation is consistent exactly for finite VC dimension (the fundamental theorem of statistical learning, PAC learnability iff finite VC dimension).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["offspring distribution with finite mean m","Z_0 = 1 (otherwise q is raised to the power of the initial population)","the critical conclusion excludes the degenerate case p_1 = 1"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543433+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_45fc062a637215cf5de5e927c5e37e9088fb287a9abe4d2162d6b99b9588a972","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (Z_n) be a Galton-Watson branching process with Z_0 = 1 and offspring distribution (p_k)_{k >= 0} having generating function f(s) = sum_k p_k s^k and mean m = sum_k k p_k, assumed finite. Let q = P( Z_n = 0 for some n ) be the extinction probability. Then q is the SMALLEST root in [0,1] of the equation f(s) = s, and: if m < 1 (subcritical) then q = 1; if m = 1 (critical) then q = 1 UNLESS p_1 = 1, in which case the process is deterministic and never dies; if m > 1 (supercritical) then q < 1. The critical case is the one that gets misquoted: a critical branching process dies out almost surely even though E[Z_n] = 1 for every n, so the population is not uniformly integrable and the mean survives while the process does not. Excluding the degenerate p_1 = 1 is necessary. A second standard trap: q < 1 does not mean the process survives with probability 1 - it survives with probability exactly 1 - q, and conditioned on survival Z_n grows geometrically at rate m. [standard; e.g. Athreya and Ney, Branching Processes, Chapter I, or Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Section 4.3.3]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H a real or complex Hilbert space; X a normed space for the general remarks"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492120+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, weak topologies","id":"claim_46001c947b4cab76c499d85088d68c6f5587b6afdebff362beafde43fb023003","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"In a Hilbert space H a sequence (x_n) converges weakly to x, written x_n ⇀ x, if ⟨x_n, y⟩ → ⟨x, y⟩ for every y ∈ H; by the Riesz representation theorem this is convergence against every bounded linear functional. The weak topology on H is the coarsest topology making every functional x ↦ ⟨x, y⟩ continuous. Norm convergence implies weak convergence; the converse fails in infinite dimensions (an orthonormal sequence e_n converges weakly to 0 while ||e_n|| = 1). Weak limits are unique; weakly convergent sequences are norm-bounded (Banach–Steinhaus); the norm is weakly lower semicontinuous (||x|| ≤ liminf ||x_n|| when x_n ⇀ x); norm-closed convex sets are weakly closed (Mazur), and in infinite dimensions the weak closure of the unit sphere is the closed unit ball. If x_n ⇀ x and ||x_n|| → ||x|| then x_n → x in norm (Radon–Riesz property of Hilbert spaces). Bounded operators preserve weak convergence; compact operators turn weak convergence into norm convergence.\n\nIn a general normed space X the weak topology is the coarsest topology making every f ∈ X* continuous, and the weak-* topology on X* is the coarsest making every evaluation f ↦ f(x), x ∈ X, continuous. The weak-* topology on X* is in general coarser than the weak topology of X* (which is induced by X**); the two coincide when X is reflexive. In a Hilbert space, after identifying H* with H, weak and weak-* convergence are the same notion.","status":"unverified"}

Method: Identify what makes q = 1 and q = 2 expandable and whether a q-analogue of the random-current switching lemma exists. Result: q = 1 is Bernoulli percolation (independence gives the pivotal decomposition); q = 2 is expandable through the random-current representation and the switching lemma (Sakai's lace expansion for the Ising model). For integer q >= 3 the Potts model has a random-current-like representation (the 'random-current representation for Potts' via the Edwards-Sokal coupling with q colours) but the switching lemma fails because currents are Z_q-valued and the pairing structure that gives the switching identity is specific to Z_2. A lace expansion needs a 'pivotal' notion for which the model factorises across the pivotal: in FK with general q the cluster weight q^{k(omega)} couples the two sides of a pivotal edge only through the count of clusters, which changes by one when the pivotal is closed; this suggests an expansion in which each pivotal carries a factor q or 1 depending on whether closing it splits a cluster, i.e. a lace expansion for the two-point function with the cluster count as an extra variable, which is exactly the generating function in the number of clusters, i.e. the Tutte polynomial. So the expansion would be an expansion of the Tutte polynomial's two-point version, which is #P-hard to evaluate in general, suggesting no simple diagrammatic expansion exists for generic q; for the infrared bound one might instead use reflection positivity (available for integer q and for the FK model on Z^d with q >= 1 via the Potts representation), which gives the infrared bound for the Potts spin-spin covariance directly for integer q >= 1 (Frohlich-Simon-Spencer), without a lace expansion. Recorded: for integer q the infrared bound is available by reflection positivity (this is classical), so the source's 'and use it to derive an infrared bound' is partly moot for integer q; the genuinely open content is the expansion itself and the non-integer q infrared bound. Key identity: Reflection positivity gives the infrared bound for integer-q Potts covariances without any expansion; the open part is non-integer q and the expansion. Obstruction: No switching lemma for Z_q currents; the natural expansion variable is a Tutte-polynomial quantity.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(M,g) complete, without boundary, Ric >= 0 (M = R^n is the model case)","u > 0 everywhere on M x (0,infinity) and smooth","u solves the heat equation u_t = Delta u","in the integrated form: 0 < t_1 < t_2 and d the Riemannian distance"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.106567+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations / geometric analysis","id":"claim_47db85f6916ac54d9a66f428afda4251cde272229adb51598e29f6604b83e38b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(M,g)$ be a complete Riemannian manifold of dimension $n$ with nonnegative Ricci curvature and without boundary (for instance $M=\\mathbb R^n$), and let $u>0$ be a smooth solution of $u_t=\\Delta u$ on $M\\times(0,\\infty)$. Then the differential Harnack (Li-Yau) inequality holds pointwise: $\\frac{|\\nabla u|^2}{u^2}-\\frac{u_t}{u}\\le\\frac{n}{2t}$, equivalently $-\\Delta\\log u\\le\\frac n{2t}$. Integrating along geodesics gives the classical Harnack form: for $x_1,x_2\\in M$ and $0<t_1<t_2$, $u(x_1,t_1)\\le u(x_2,t_2)\\Big(\\frac{t_2}{t_1}\\Big)^{n/2}\\exp\\Big(\\frac{d(x_1,x_2)^2}{4(t_2-t_1)}\\Big).$ Both are sharp: equality in the differential form holds for the Gaussian $u=\\Phi(x,t)$ on $\\mathbb R^n$. Positivity of $u$ on the whole of $M\\times(0,\\infty)$ and $\\mathrm{Ric}\\ge0$ are both needed; if $\\mathrm{Ric}\\ge-K$ with $K>0$ the estimate degrades to $\\alpha\\frac{|\\nabla u|^2}{u^2}-\\frac{u_t}{u}\\le\\frac{n\\alpha^2}{2t}+\\frac{n\\alpha^2K}{2(\\alpha-1)}$ for any $\\alpha>1$.","status":"unverified"}

Not independently checked.
# T422 Target 2: an explicit lower tail bound for instantaneous noise scales

Status: proof (unaudited), C05 v1. This strengthens the positive-probability
scope obstruction C04. It is not an upper tail estimate or a typical-scale
calibration, and it makes no literature-priority claim.

## Statement and all constants

Use the noiseless fresh Gaussian online model of C04. Let alpha>1,
gamma>alpha+1, h_j=j^(-alpha), and deterministic e_0,j satisfy
e_0,j^2=j^(-(gamma-alpha)). Each update averages B independent samples,
B>=1 integer, with a fixed step eta>0. Fix finite integer t>=1, ell in {1,2},
and integer n>=1. Let u_n denote the nth coordinate unit vector, and put

    m=gamma-alpha>1, M=||e_0||=sqrt(zeta(m)), c=M/2,
    y=c u_n, A=<e_0-y,e_0>=M^2-c e_0,n,
    u=(e_0-y)/sqrt(eta A), R=||u||+1,
    r=c h_n^((ell+1)/2)/4,
    T=(1+eta R^2)^t-1,
    rho=min(1, r R/(4 M T)).

Here A>=M^2/2>0, T>0, M,R,r,rho>0. Every division is well defined.
The norm in R is explicit:

    ||u||^2=(M^2-2c e_0,n+c^2)/(eta A).

Choose the following explicit finite truncation:

    N=ceil(max(n,1,
         [16/(eta A (m-1)rho^2)]^(1/(m-1)),
         [32/((alpha-1)rho^2)]^(1/(alpha-1)))).

For a prescribed center w equal to either 0 or u, define

    a=rho/(2 sqrt(N)),
    P_N(w)= (1/2) [rho/sqrt(2 pi N)]^N
             (product_(j=1)^N h_j^(-1/2))
             exp[-(1/2) sum_(j=1)^N (|w_j|+a)^2/h_j].

These are finite explicit strictly positive real numbers, not floating-point
certificates. Put

    pi_event=P_N(0)^(B(t-1)) P_N(u)^B >0,
    L_n=1+(9/25)zeta(ell alpha)n^(ell alpha).

For the conditional single-example instantaneous scale R_ell of C04,

    P(e_t!=0 and R_ell(e_t)>=L_n) >= pi_event.             (Q1)

In particular, for any finite L choose n with L_n>L; the same explicit
pi_event lower-bounds P(e_t!=0 and R_ell(e_t)>L).
The theorem also applies when t is any finite first EXPECTED-risk hitting
index, since that index is deterministic. It does not apply to a realized-risk
stopping time chosen from the samples without an additional stopping argument.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["translation invariance, or more generally a transitive amenable group action, of the percolation measure","ergodicity of the measure under the translation group, needed to conclude N is almost surely constant","amenability of the underlying graph, i.e. subexponential boundary-to-volume ratio along a Folner sequence","finite energy or insertion and deletion tolerance for each edge's conditional state"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.981600+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4a75ca0603a5987c8ea2229b5f254b315be024ca14b43e8bb06290ff87223753","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a translation-invariant, ergodic percolation measure on Z^d, or more generally on an amenable transitive graph, satisfying finite energy (insertion and deletion tolerance for each edge conditionally on the rest of the configuration), the number N of infinite open clusters is almost surely a constant in {0, 1, infinity}, and Burton and Keane's argument rules out 2 <= N < infinity as well as N = infinity: if there were at least two infinite clusters with positive density, a positive density of trifurcation points (local configurations forcing at least three disjoint infinite paths) would be forced, but a discrete isoperimetric counting argument on a large box shows the number of trifurcation points cannot exceed a quantity of the order of the box's boundary, contradicting positive density in the bulk unless N <= 1. It follows that N is almost surely 0 or 1. The argument does not apply to non-amenable graphs, where coexistence of infinitely many infinite clusters is a genuine, well-studied phenomenon rather than a proof artifact, and constancy of N itself (ruling out a mixture over the value of N) is a separate ergodic-theory step, not part of the trifurcation-counting argument. Typical failure: Applying Burton-Keane uniqueness to a non-amenable graph, such as a regular tree or a graph with exponential volume growth, and expecting a unique infinite cluster; the trifurcation-point isoperimetric argument fundamentally requires amenability, and on non-amenable graphs the coexistence of infinitely many infinite clusters, studied by Haggstrom, Peres and others, is a real phenomenon that this theorem simply does not rule out. Canonical reference: Burton and Keane, 1989, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Gandolfi, Keane and Newman, 1992, Probability Theory and Related Fields.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the underlying space is a Lebesgue probability space (the unit interval with Lebesgue measure, after normalisation)","the construction uses three cuts and exactly one spacer above the middle subcolumn at every stage, with h_0 = 1 and h_{n+1} = 3h_n + 1","T is the induced a.e.-defined invertible measure-preserving map"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.814795+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, mixing and rank-one constructions","id":"claim_4b4d539c3f629ff9022575793ca66b8a2b15d3199dbed5c40bec97bddfa73324","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Chacon's transformation is the invertible, rank-one, measure-preserving transformation T of a Lebesgue probability space produced by the following cutting-and-stacking construction. Start with the column C_0 consisting of the single interval [0,1), of height h_0 = 1. Given the column C_n, a stack of h_n disjoint intervals ('levels') of equal width w_n, cut it vertically into three subcolumns of equal width w_n/3, place one new 'spacer' interval of width w_n/3, taken from the not-yet-used part of the line, on top of the MIDDLE subcolumn, and stack the three pieces in order: subcolumn 1 at the bottom, then subcolumn 2 with its spacer on top of it, then subcolumn 3. The result is the column C_{n+1} of height h_{n+1} = 3 h_n + 1. The map T sends each point of a level to the point directly above it in the current column; the columns exhaust the space in the limit, T is defined almost everywhere, is invertible, and preserves Lebesgue measure normalised to a probability measure. The same system appears symbolically as the subshift generated by the blocks B_0 = 0, B_{n+1} = B_n B_n 1 B_n, whose lengths satisfy the same recursion. STANDARD FACTS about this system: it is ergodic; it has rank one, hence simple spectrum and ZERO entropy; it is WEAKLY MIXING but NOT strongly mixing; del Junco, Rahe and Swanson proved that it has minimal self-joinings, from which it follows that it is prime (its only factors are the trivial ones) and that its centraliser consists of the powers of T alone. WHY MIXING FAILS, in one line one can check: let I be a level of C_n and let I_1, I_2, I_3 be the three pieces into which the cut splits I inside C_{n+1}, each of measure mu(I)/3. By construction T^{h_n} carries I_1 onto I_2, and I_2 is a subset of I; hence I_1 is contained in I ∩ T^{-h_n} I, so mu(I ∩ T^{-h_n} I) >= (1/3) mu(I). The same argument applied at every later stage m >= n gives mu(A ∩ T^{-h_m} A) >= (1/3) mu(A) for every A which is a union of levels of C_n and every m >= n. Mixing would force these correlations to converge to mu(A)^2, which is smaller than (1/3) mu(A) as soon as mu(A) < 1/3. SHARP EDGES. (a) This is THE standard witness that weak mixing does not imply strong mixing; do not use it as an example of a mixing system, and do not expect quantitative decay of correlations from it - along the tower heights h_n the correlations do not decay at all. (b) Its zero entropy and simple spectrum show that weak mixing carries no entropy or spectral-multiplicity information whatsoever. (c) Rank one and minimal self-joinings are properties of this specific construction, not of cutting-and-stacking systems in general; changing the number of cuts or the spacer pattern changes the mixing behaviour (some cutting-and-stacking constructions are mixing).","status":"unverified"}

For every locally Lipschitz f with f and grad f in L^2(gamma), Ent_gamma(f^2) <= 2 E_gamma[ |grad f|^2 ], where Ent(g) = E[g log g] - E[g] log E[g] for g >= 0. The constant 2 is sharp, with near-equality for exponentials f = e^{a . x / 2}. As with the Poincare inequality the constant is DIMENSION-FREE, obtained from the one-dimensional case by tensorization of entropy. Gross's theorem states that this inequality is EQUIVALENT to Nelson's hypercontractivity for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup, and it implies the Gaussian Poincare inequality by linearisation. Combined with the Herbst argument it yields Gaussian concentration for Lipschitz functions with the sharp sub-Gaussian variance proxy equal to the square of the Lipschitz constant. Care with normalisation: the inequality is often written as Ent(f) <= 2 E[ |grad sqrt(f)|^2 ] for f >= 0, which is the same statement after substituting f -> f^2, and some sources carry a factor 1/2 from using a different generator normalisation; the version stated here is the one matching the standard Gaussian and the generator L = Laplacian minus x . gradient. {"assumptions":["f is holomorphic on a neighborhood of the closed disk |z| ≤ R","f(0) ≠ 0 (otherwise divide by z^m)","zeros in the open disk are listed with multiplicity","no zeros on |z| = R in the stated form (the formula extends to that case)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.483367+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_4c20bd0201a9aff751ded5583603d49c0ce62d6d31f19a6b630a6fd68f837cd3","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let R > 0, let f be holomorphic on an open set containing the closed disk |z| ≤ R, with f(0) ≠ 0 and f having no zeros on the circle |z| = R. Equivalently, (1/2π)∫_0^{2π} log|f(Re^{iθ})| dθ - log|f(0)| = Σ_k log(R/|a_k|) = ∫_0^R n(t) dt/t, where n(t) is the number of zeros of f in |z| ≤ t counted with multiplicity. {"assumptions":["G finite, p prime with p dividing |G|"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.478772+00:00","domain":"group theory","id":"claim_4d35593daa64c444cac9ce0985344a1fd51aea56f0ba9d34f01bd81800978194","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let G be a finite group and p a prime dividing the order |G|. Then G contains an element of order exactly p, hence a subgroup of order p. More precisely (McKay), the number of solutions to x^p = e in G is a multiple of p, and since x = e is one of them, there are at least p - 1 elements of order p; in fact the number of elements of order p is congruent to -1 modulo p. Cauchy's theorem is the p^1 case of Sylow's first theorem (a subgroup of order p^a exists whenever p^a divides |G|) and is the converse of Lagrange's theorem for prime orders; the converse of Lagrange fails in general (A_4 has order 12 and no subgroup of order 6).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["phi_i 1-Lipschitz with phi_i(0) = 0","eps_i independent Rademacher signs","T bounded so the suprema are finite; constant 1 WITHOUT absolute values, 2 WITH them"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628629+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4d71e82701baa0652e97a3150c16f319f1bfdeca9e4a8d8cfae7f2157af90f94","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let T be a bounded subset of R^n, let eps_1, ..., eps_n be independent Rademacher signs, and let phi_i : R -> R be 1-Lipschitz with phi_i(0) = 0 for every i. Then E sup_{t in T} sum_{i=1}^n eps_i phi_i(t_i) <= E sup_{t in T} sum_{i=1}^n eps_i t_i. With ABSOLUTE VALUES inside the supremum the same statement holds with a factor 2: E sup_{t in T} | sum_i eps_i phi_i(t_i) | <= 2 E sup_{t in T} | sum_i eps_i t_i |. The distinction between the constants 1 and 2 is a standard source of misquotation; the constant 1 belongs to the version WITHOUT absolute values. The hypothesis phi_i(0) = 0 is needed for the version without absolute values and can be arranged by subtracting a constant, which is harmless for a symmetric process. In statistical learning the principle is what lets one strip a Lipschitz loss off a function class without changing the Rademacher complexity by more than a constant. [Ledoux and Talagrand, Probability in Banach Spaces, Theorem 4.12]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["F entire on C (or C^d)","claims of band limitation require the growth bound off the real axis","L^2 version needs square integrability on R; distributions need the polynomial-growth version"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264631+00:00","domain":"complex and harmonic analysis, common errors","id":"claim_4d88e0d15b6e8881d2eb18cd54107f75b8c1834afa521c13029e34cc2e348e2d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypotheses: (1) the growth bound $|F(z)|\\le Ce^{A|z|}$ must hold for all complex $z$, not merely on $\\mathbb R$; (2) $F$ must be square integrable on $\\mathbb R$ (for the $L^2$ version) or have controlled polynomial growth (for the distributional version). Failure of (1): $F(z)=e^{-z^2}$ is entire and its restriction to $\\mathbb R$ is in $L^2$, yet $|F(iy)|=e^{y^2}$, so $F$ is of order 2, not of exponential type; its Fourier transform is a Gaussian, supported everywhere - no band limitation. Failure of (2): $F(z)=\\cos(Az)$ is entire of exponential type exactly $A$ and bounded on $\\mathbb R$, but not in $L^2(\\mathbb R)$; it is not $\\int_{-A}^A\\varphi(t)e^{itz}dt$ for any $\\varphi\\in L^2$, only for the measure $\\frac12(\\delta_A+\\delta_{-A})$ - the correct statement in that regime is the Paley-Wiener-Schwartz theorem for compactly supported distributions, with a polynomial factor $(1+|\\zeta|)^N$ allowed. Similarly $F(z)=e^{Az}$ has type $A$ but grows on the real axis. Two further traps: the exponential factor in Paley-Wiener-Schwartz measures the support of the transform only through the supporting function of its convex hull, so the theorem detects $\\operatorname{ch}(\\operatorname{supp}u)$, not the support itself; and no such function can have both itself and its transform compactly supported, since a nonzero entire function cannot vanish on an open set (see Benedicks' theorem for the measure-theoretic strengthening).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_1, ..., X_n independent","Z = f(X) nonnegative with E[Z log Z] finite"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627951+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4dc336ffe1859932768872cd898d8a70b2b6935d4bd7b90c575ded181869d08f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent random variables and let Z = f(X_1, ..., X_n) be a nonnegative random variable with E[Z log Z] finite. Write Ent(Z) = E[Z log Z] - E[Z] log E[Z] and let Ent^{(i)}(Z) denote the same functional computed with respect to X_i alone, with the other coordinates held fixed. Then Ent(Z) <= sum_{i=1}^n E[ Ent^{(i)}(Z) ]. The same statement with variance in place of entropy is the Efron-Stein inequality, and the two are the p = 2 and p = 1 members of a family of phi-entropies that all tensorize. Tensorization is what converts a ONE-DIMENSIONAL functional inequality into an n-dimensional one with no loss of constant: if each coordinate's law satisfies a logarithmic Sobolev inequality with constant C, then the product law satisfies it with the SAME constant C, independent of n. That dimension-free feature is the whole reason the entropy method produces concentration bounds that do not degrade as n grows. Independence of the coordinates is essential. [standard; e.g. Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 4.10 and Section 4.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["both sequences (or functions) monotone in the same direction; opposite directions reverse the inequality","no independence or product structure needed beyond the single variable; the n-variable generalization is Harris-FKG"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.049386+00:00","domain":"correlation inequalities (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_4e33e7a855f3b1ed38c5b184f81787d0bc6049fa0a51bfd8ff8f2972faba1f89","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"If a_1 >= a_2 >= ... >= a_n and b_1 >= b_2 >= ... >= b_n (both sequences sorted the same way), then (1/n) sum a_i b_i >= ((1/n) sum a_i) ((1/n) sum b_i); if one sequence is increasing and the other decreasing, the inequality reverses. The integral form: for f and g both monotone in the same direction on [0,1], the integral of f g is at least the product of the integrals. Proof: the dimension of the measure is at most the entropy-over-Lyapunov ratio H(p)/log(3/2), and a measure on the line of dimension below one is not absolutely continuous; Hochman's theorem is needed only for the matching lower bound dim = min(1, H(p)/log(3/2)), which this does not use. Two further thresholds govern the Fourier criterion at this ratio. The biased factor |(1-p) + p e^{i phi}|^2 = 1 - 2p(1-p)(1 - cos phi) has arithmetic mean 1 - 2p(1-p) over the phase, which gives the annealed (main-term) exponent alpha(p) = 1 + log(1 - 2p(1-p))/log(3/2), zero at p(1-p) = 1/6, i.e. p = (1 - 3^{-1/2})/2 = 0.211325; and log-mean 2 log(1-p), which gives the quenched (typical) threshold (3/2)(1-p)^2 = 1 at p = 0.183503. As a calibration control for statistics on the unbiased Bernoulli convolution at 2/3 (the same ratio, frequencies and arithmetic, only the weights changed): below p* the measure is singular and a detection is expected; above 0.2113 the main term decays and a pass is expected; between 0.1403 and 0.2113 the measure has dimension one while the main term already diverges, so a reading there means nothing - controls belong at p <= 0.12 and p >= 0.35. Unlike the Pisot control lambda = 1/phi, where one localised cell forces the reading a priori, the absence of such a cell at ratio 3/2 is Mahler's open problem on ||(3/2)^m xi||, so the control's genuineness rests on an empirical extensiveness test: a flat per-step rate means one cell forces the reading, a wobbling rate means a real measurement (flat to 0.0005 at 1/phi from K = 8; wobbling by 0.028 at the unbiased 2/3).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T is measure-preserving","f is integrable","the sets are defined through the partial sums S_n f, n >= 1"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438013+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, maximal inequalities","id":"claim_4e5da40826ced68e04e188001f421a2ff04ef2165ef899ef0c91ed9c71f6fc4c","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \\mathcal{B}, \\mu)$ be a probability space (a finite or even $\\sigma$-finite measure suffices here), $T: X \\to X$ measure-preserving, $f \\in L^1(\\mu)$ real-valued. The maximal inequality follows: for $\\alpha > 0$, $\\mu\\big(\\{ \\sup_{n} \\tfrac{1}{n} S_n f > \\alpha \\}\\big) \\le \\tfrac{1}{\\alpha} \\int_{\\{\\sup_n S_n f / n > \\alpha\\}} f\\,d\\mu \\le \\tfrac{1}{\\alpha}\\|f\\|_1$ (apply the first statement to $f - \\alpha$; for the last step in infinite measure one needs $f \\ge 0$ or $\\mu$ finite, since $\\int (f - \\alpha)$ over the set is where $\\mu$ finite is used). Then there exists a function f meromorphic on U, holomorphic on U minus A, whose set of poles is exactly A and whose principal part at each a in A is P_a, i.e. f - P_a extends holomorphically across a. Any two such functions differ by a function holomorphic on all of U, so the general solution is f + h with h holomorphic on U. A standard instance is the pole structure of the Gamma function: U = C, A = {0, -1, -2, ...}, with prescribed principal part (-1)^n / (n! (z + n)) at the point z = -n for n = 0, 1, 2, ....","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["entries independent up to symmetry with mean 0 and variance 1 before scaling by 1/sqrt n","moments bounded uniformly in n (finite fourth moment suffices for the semicircle limit of the empirical spectral distribution; the diagonal entries may have a different variance)","the moment method identifies the limit because the semicircle law is determined by its moments (compact support)"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.049288+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_4f1567c38734286426940b4f4f52f264db38c2264b6a25725643dc91aea4918c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For the semicircle density (1/(2 pi)) sqrt(4 - x^2) on [-2, 2] (mean 0, variance 1), all odd moments vanish and the 2k-th moment equals the Catalan number C_k = (1/(k+1)) binom(2k, k): 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132, ... . A semicircle of radius R has 2k-th moment C_k (R/2)^{2k}. In the moment method for a Wigner matrix W = X / sqrt n, where X is real symmetric with independent entries above the diagonal, mean 0 and variance 1, the normalized traces satisfy E tr(W^{2k}) / n -> C_k: expanding the trace as a sum over closed walks of length 2k on the index set, only walks whose edges are each traversed exactly twice and whose underlying graph is a tree survive as n grows, and such walks are counted by C_k; the Catalan numbers determine the semicircle law uniquely because it has compact support. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.499458+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_4f46b2de22e7549670bcc1dce7b0f972c96bfd2b3336d5d4426cf06f59a598fa","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The Weierstrass convergence theorem (a locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic and derivatives converge locally uniformly) has no real-variable analogue and does not upgrade to uniform convergence on the whole domain. (1) Real failure: f_n(x) = sin(n^2 x)/n converges to 0 uniformly on R, but the derivatives f_n'(x) = n cos(n^2 x) do not converge to the derivative of the limit — at x = 0, f_n'(0) = n → ∞ — so uniform convergence of real functions carries no information about derivatives. More dramatically, by the Weierstrass approximation theorem every continuous nowhere differentiable function on [0,1] is a uniform limit of polynomials, so uniform limits of real-analytic functions need not be differentiable anywhere. The complex proof uses the Cauchy estimates, which need holomorphy on a two-dimensional neighborhood: a bound on |g| on a disk controls all derivatives at the center. (2) Only locally uniform: f_n(z) = z^n/n converges to 0 uniformly on all of D, yet f_n'(z) = z^{n-1} has supremum 1 on D for every n and does not converge uniformly on D. So the derivative statement must be quoted with 'uniformly on compact subsets'; deducing a uniform derivative bound up to the boundary from a uniform bound on the functions is a genuine error, and controlling it requires extra input (a larger domain of holomorphy, or boundary regularity). (3) The hypothesis is convergence on compact subsets of the open set, not convergence on the closed set: a sequence converging uniformly on the closed unit disk still gives derivative convergence only on |z| ≤ r < 1 unless the functions are holomorphic on a larger disk.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f ∈ C^1","u is a weak solution which is piecewise C^1 with C^1 shock curves and one-sided traces (the equivalence as stated is for this piecewise-smooth class; Kruzhkov's definition is what governs general L^∞ solutions)","the chord condition must hold at EVERY point of EVERY discontinuity curve","Rankine-Hugoniot alone is not sufficient: it fixes σ but permits inadmissible jumps"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.417666+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: hyperbolic conservation laws","id":"claim_502c4a8cf7e11bf1fd64197cea9e23277293f004895262e4972b802ea4718867","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f ∈ C^1(R) and let u ∈ L^∞(R × (0,∞)) be a weak solution of u_t + f(u)_x = 0 that is piecewise C^1: away from finitely many disjoint C^1 curves x = s_i(t) it is C^1, and it has C^1 one-sided traces u_-(t) (from x < s_i(t)) and u_+(t) (from x > s_i(t)) on each curve. Each curve then satisfies Rankine-Hugoniot, σ := s_i'(t) = ( f(u_-) - f(u_+) ) / ( u_- - u_+ ) when u_- ≠ u_+. Such a u is a Kruzhkov entropy solution if and only if at every point of every discontinuity curve the chord condition holds: for every k strictly between u_- and u_+, ( f(k) - f(u_-) ) / ( k - u_- ) ≥ σ ≥ ( f(k) - f(u_+) ) / ( k - u_+ ). Equivalently: if u_+ < u_-, the graph of f on [u_+,u_-] lies on or below the chord joining (u_+,f(u_+)) to (u_-,f(u_-)); if u_- < u_+, the graph of f on [u_-,u_+] lies on or above that chord. If f is strictly convex, this is equivalent to the Lax shock inequalities f'(u_-) ≥ σ ≥ f'(u_+), i.e. to u_- > u_+: a strictly convex flux admits only downward jumps.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["bond percolation on the square lattice Z^2","the Harris half as sketched uses Burton-Keane uniqueness, self-duality, the square-root trick and a planar topological argument","the Kesten half is stated but not proved in this node"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543220+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5050896df8f7fb9dbfa990fc0b0cefbd0928a39e58de37c123d446e63228d84e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For bond percolation on the square lattice Z^2, p_c = 1/2, and moreover theta(1/2) = 0: there is no infinite open cluster AT the critical point. The two halves have separate histories and separate proofs. HARRIS (1960) proved theta(1/2) = 0, which gives p_c >= 1/2. KESTEN (1980) proved that theta(p) > 0 for every p > 1/2, giving p_c <= 1/2. The self-duality of Z^2 bond percolation at p = 1/2 - the dual of the open configuration at parameter p is a configuration at parameter 1 - p on an isomorphic lattice - makes 1/2 the ONLY candidate but does not by itself decide the critical behaviour, which is why the theorem is hard. The corresponding value for SITE percolation on Z^2 is not known; for site percolation on the triangular lattice the answer is 1/2 by the same duality mechanism, and that is the case where conformal invariance at criticality is proved. {"assumptions":["odd m >= 5","simple random walk on the lexicographic product C_m[Kbar_2] (n = 2m vertices, 4-regular, arc-transitive, not a cycle)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:11:19.446810+00:00","domain":"probability, Markov chains, random walks on graphs","id":"claim_5397640b4878930b246260b0755cfb95ee891bc406442da83f632b64770faf2e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Aldous and Fill, Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, Open Problem 7.27 (Chapter 7, p. 259) asks whether, over arc-transitive graphs excluding the n-cycles, tau* = O(n log n), tau2 = O(n) and tau*/(2 tau0) = 1 + o(1). Our result (id P0208, 2026-09-08): all three claims are FALSE. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.376271+00:00","domain":"general topology","id":"claim_53b62a4d4b0ea879e3c5457fa6f8ecdb78aba2e92827a95ead2ce3351cd5f4ff","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A sequence (x_n) in a metric space (X, d) is Cauchy if for every epsilon > 0 there is an index N such that d(x_m, x_n) < epsilon for all m, n >= N. The metric space (X, d) is complete if every Cauchy sequence in X converges to a point of X. Every convergent sequence is Cauchy, but not conversely in general: the rationals with the usual distance are not complete, while the real line R and Euclidean space R^n are complete. A closed subset of a complete metric space is complete, and a complete subspace of any metric space is closed in it.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["F is continuous","u is continuous on Ω","the equation is written in the form F = 0 with a fixed sign convention"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.110816+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations, Hamilton–Jacobi equations","id":"claim_53dfc94ed0a9e05577bb2bf64ec2af288dc9f26b2353c233536514d102e5795c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Ω ⊂ ℝⁿ be open and F: Ω × ℝ × ℝⁿ → ℝ continuous; consider the equation F(x, u(x), Du(x)) = 0 in Ω. A function u ∈ C(Ω) is a viscosity SUBsolution if for every φ ∈ C¹(Ω) and every point x₀ ∈ Ω at which u − φ has a local maximum, F(x₀, u(x₀), Dφ(x₀)) ≤ 0. It is a viscosity SUPERsolution if for every φ ∈ C¹(Ω) and every local minimum point x₀ of u − φ, F(x₀, u(x₀), Dφ(x₀)) ≥ 0. It is a viscosity solution if it is both. (Equivalent reformulations: replace 'local' by 'strict local' or 'global' max/min, or use C^∞ test functions, or use super-/subdifferentials D⁺u(x₀) and D⁻u(x₀): the conditions read F(x₀, u, p) ≤ 0 for all p ∈ D⁺u(x₀) and ≥ 0 for all p ∈ D⁻u(x₀).) Every classical C¹ solution is a viscosity solution, and a viscosity solution that is differentiable at x₀ satisfies the equation pointwise there. For time-dependent equations u_t + H(x, Du) = 0 on Ω × (0,T) apply the same definition with the gradient variable (u_t, Du) and test functions of (x,t). SHARP EDGE — the sign of F matters: writing the same equation as −F = 0 interchanges the roles of sub- and supersolutions, so the two forms have DIFFERENT viscosity solutions. Example: on (−1,1) with boundary values u(±1) = 0, the function 1 − |x| is a viscosity solution of |u'| − 1 = 0 but NOT of 1 − |u'| = 0, while |x| − 1 is a viscosity solution of 1 − |u'| = 0 but not of |u'| − 1 = 0 (at the kink x = 0, a concave kink admits only test functions touching from above, and a convex kink only test functions touching from below). Viscosity solutions are in general only continuous, are stable under uniform limits, and for convex H coincide with Lipschitz solutions that are semiconcave; the notion is designed so that comparison/uniqueness theorems hold where classical and a.e. solutions are non-unique.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Real g in L^2 of the standard Gaussian measure; orthonormal probabilists Hermite convention.","For the finite-energy first-order expansion, also g in H^1(gamma)."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:46:50.165893+00:00","domain":"Gaussian analysis and neural-network capacity","id":"claim_546ec58f320bb143f8e7e8d299063a32dddcbcf5a1b864e0c2639fe6302e7d43","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let gamma be the standard normal probability measure on R and g be a real function in L^2(gamma). Use the orthonormal probabilists Hermite basis H_k=He_k/sqrt(k!) and coefficients a_k=E[g(Z)*H_k(Z)], Z~gamma. For jointly standard normal X,Y with correlation q in (-1,1), define C_g(q)=Cov(g(X),g(Y)) and V=Var_gamma(g). Then C_g(q)=sum_(k>=1) a_k^2*q^k and V=sum_(k>=1) a_k^2. {"assumptions":["the operator is densely defined but not assumed symmetric or closed","a closure or a core argument is being invoked"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.772684+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, unbounded operators","id":"claim_54940f80014d70dd9eb95c49c095eba47a53c4de71e730a15c0f74ec018b6e59","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: 'take the closure of T' presupposes that T is closable, i.e. that x_n ∈ D(T), x_n → 0 and Tx_n → y force y = 0; equivalently (in a Hilbert space) that D(T*) is dense. What fails: without closability the closure of the graph is not a graph, and 'the smallest closed extension' does not exist. Counterexample: H = ℓ², D(T) = finitely supported sequences, T x = (Σ_n x_n) e_1. T is densely defined and linear. Take x^{(k)} = (1/k, ..., 1/k, 0, 0, ...) with k entries: ‖x^{(k)}‖ = 1/√k → 0 while T x^{(k)} = e_1 for every k, so the graph closure contains both (0,0) and (0, e_1) and T is not closable. Consistently, ⟨Tx, y⟩ = (Σ x_n) conj(y_1) is ℓ²-bounded in x only if y_1 = 0, so D(T*) = {y : y_1 = 0} is not dense - exactly the criterion. The same phenomenon occurs for pointwise evaluation f ↦ f(0)g on L²(ℝ) restricted to continuous L² functions. Related traps: (i) an operator can be closable while its closure has strictly larger domain on which a defining formula no longer holds pointwise, so identities proved on D(T) must be re-derived by continuity in the graph norm; (ii) symmetry rescues closability (a symmetric operator is always closable, since T ⊂ T* and T* is closed), which is why this pitfall bites mainly for non-symmetric operators such as first order operators with unbalanced boundary conditions or multiplication-composition operators; (iii) a core argument ('it suffices to verify on a dense subspace') is valid only if the subspace is dense in the graph norm of the closed operator, not merely dense in the ambient space.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751292+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_54d64fad1e4608f5ad2108eaf3e69d53ceffd8a53470cf0276a225deb916e63a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Tonelli's theorem needs BOTH measures sigma-finite and the integrand nonnegative and product-measurable; it then asserts that the double integral and both iterated integrals agree in [0, infinity], with no integrability assumption. Fubini's theorem needs both measures sigma-finite and f in L^1(mu tensor nu); it then asserts the same equality with all three quantities finite. Two failure modes are standard and are NOT the same failure. (1) Integrability dropped, sigma-finiteness kept: on (0,1)^2 with Lebesgue measure take f(x,y) = (x^2 - y^2)/(x^2 + y^2)^2. Since d/dy [ y/(x^2+y^2) ] = (x^2 - y^2)/(x^2+y^2)^2, the inner integral over y in (0,1) is 1/(1+x^2), so integrating in x afterwards gives pi/4; f is antisymmetric under swapping x and y, so the other order gives -pi/4. Both iterated integrals exist and are finite and they differ, so f cannot be in L^1 of the product. (2) sigma-finiteness dropped, nonnegativity kept: let mu be Lebesgue measure on [0,1], nu counting measure on [0,1], and f the indicator of the diagonal. Then integral over x of (integral over y of f dnu) dmu = integral 1 dmu = 1, while integral over y of (integral over x of f dmu) dnu = integral 0 dnu = 0. Tonelli's conclusion fails although f >= 0, because nu is not sigma-finite. A third, quieter caveat: for COMPLETE measure spaces the correct statement is that ALMOST every section is measurable, not every section, since a null set in the product can have non-measurable sections; the theorem for the completed product measure is stated that way. In practice the usable recipe is: apply Tonelli to |f| first to decide integrability, then apply Fubini to f. [standard; e.g. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorems 2.37 and 2.39]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(L1) subadditivity","(L2) stationarity of the sequence of blocks of each fixed length","(L3) the row law does not depend on the starting index","(L4) E[X_{0,1}^+] finite and a linear lower bound on E[X_{0,n}]","ergodicity of the block sequences is needed only for a constant limit"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542341+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory","id":"claim_5512c8e378a10d1dd7b71a2d5741379e9a70c5f5d022ab969d1836e21965a057","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let {X_{m,n} : 0 <= m < n} satisfy: (L1) X_{0,n} <= X_{0,m} + X_{m,n} for every 0 < m < n; (L2) for each m >= 1 the sequence {X_{nm, (n+1)m} : n >= 1} is STATIONARY; (L3) the distribution of the row {X_{m, m+k} : k >= 1} does not depend on m; (L4) E[X_{0,1}^+] < infinity and E[X_{0,n}] >= -c_0 n for every n, for some finite c_0. Then: (a) gamma = lim_n E[X_{0,n}]/n = inf_n E[X_{0,n}]/n exists in [-c_0, infinity); (b) X = lim_n X_{0,n}/n exists almost surely and in L^1, with E[X] = gamma; (c) if in addition all the stationary sequences in (L2) are ERGODIC then X = gamma almost surely. The difference from Kingman is that (L2) and (L3) together are strictly WEAKER than joint stationarity of the whole array: they demand stationarity only along each fixed block length and equality of the row laws, not invariance of the full joint distribution. That weakening is what lets the theorem apply to models where the array is not generated by a single measure-preserving transformation. Note also that (L4) asks only for the POSITIVE part of X_{0,1} to be integrable, weaker than Kingman's E|X_{0,1}| < infinity. Quoting Kingman's hypotheses when using Liggett's conclusion, or the reverse, is the standard misquotation here. [Liggett (1985), 'An improved subadditive ergodic theorem', Ann. Probab. 13, 1279-1285; textbook form in Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 6.6.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["targets at every design point are mean plus noise with the noise independent of the calibration sample (so Cov(e, f(x)) = 0)","the weights on each point set sum to one; the family f_t is any family of fitted predictors (linearity in t is not needed for the identity, only for the cheap computation of the blend's cross-validated and bootstrap predictions)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T12:56:40.878952+00:00","domain":"regression / model assessment / transductive selection","id":"claim_553662417244b971618b1a8e4cc64e9cead1479c7050963b070adb0204ea329f","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f be a predictor fitted on a calibration sample, evaluated at design points x with targets y = mu(x) + e, where e has mean zero and variance sigma^2(x) and is independent of the sample. For a weighted average over a set of evaluation points E and the same average over the calibration points C (weights w_x summing to one on each set), write R_E = sum_E w_x E(y - f(x))^2 for the expected weighted risk on E, R_C the same on C, V_S = sum_S w_x Var f(x) for the average estimation variance on a set S, B_S = sum_S w_x (mu(x) - E f(x))^2 for the average squared bias, and N_S = sum_S w_x sigma^2(x) for the average noise. Then R_E = R_C + (V_E - V_C) + (B_E - B_C) + (N_E - N_C). Consequently, for a family of predictors f_t indexed by t (for instance a blend that is linear in t between two fitted bases), the minimiser over t of R_E(t) is the minimiser of R_C(t) + [V_E(t) - V_C(t)] + [B_E(t) - B_C(t)], the noise difference being free of t. A label-free criterion that replaces R_C(t) by the cross-validated risk on the calibration rows and V_E(t), V_C(t) by pairs-bootstrap estimates - the transductive covariance penalty used to choose the amount of simplex constraint at the scored rows - is this identity with the bias-shift term dropped; its single assumption is that the squared bias of the family shifts between the two point sets by an amount that does not depend on t, or does so less than the variance shift. What it cannot see is exactly the bias shift, which needs the targets at the new points; that is why such a criterion recovers only part of the hindsight-best t and errs toward the endpoint the calibration rows favour.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_i independent with E[X_i] = 0","one-sided bound X_i <= b almost surely (no lower bound needed for the upper tail)","v = sum_i E[X_i^2] finite"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627726+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5539ab1dd12776494ca55d16665e0670d5e85f01452dc2694daade30bd0d0cca","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent random variables with E[X_i] = 0 and X_i <= b almost surely for every i - a ONE-SIDED bound suffices for the upper tail - and let v = sum_{i=1}^n E[X_i^2]. Then for every t > 0, P( sum_i X_i >= t ) <= exp( - (v/b^2) h(bt/v) ) where h(u) = (1+u) log(1+u) - u. Bennett's inequality implies Bernstein's inequality through h(u) >= u^2/(2(1 + u/3)), which gives the familiar P(sum X_i >= t) <= exp(-t^2/(2(v + bt/3))), and it is strictly sharper in the large-deviation regime bt/v large, where Bennett decays like exp(-(t/b) log(bt/v)) - a Poisson tail - while Bernstein decays only like exp(-3t/(2b)). This is the right inequality when the summands are bounded but their variance is much smaller than the square of the bound, the regime where Hoeffding's inequality is badly lossy. [Bennett (1962); see Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 2.9]","status":"unverified"}
