{"assumptions":["(X, B, mu, T) is an invertible measure-preserving system on a standard (Lebesgue) probability space","T is ergodic with respect to mu","G is a compact metrizable group with normalized Haar measure m","phi : X -> G is measurable and the extension is T_phi(x,g) = (Tx, phi(x) g) on mu x m","solutions F of the transfer equation are required only to be measurable (matrix-valued), not continuous"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.732127+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, skew products, cocycles and group extensions","id":"claim_55b03d25b04f083e6d2634636c495b808dc293ac41f7f84754595cf15210a9be","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, B, mu, T) be an invertible measure-preserving system on a standard probability space with T ERGODIC. Let G be a compact metrizable group with normalized Haar measure m, let phi : X -> G be measurable, and let T_phi(x, g) = (T x, phi(x) g) be the associated group extension of (X x G, mu x m). Then:

  T_phi is ergodic  <=>  for EVERY nontrivial irreducible unitary representation pi : G -> U(d_pi), the functional (transfer) equation
        F(T x) = pi(phi(x)) F(x)      for mu-a.e. x
  has no nonzero MEASURABLE solution F : X -> M_{d_pi}(C).

Equivalently, ergodicity fails exactly when some nontrivial pi admits such a nonzero F. A nonzero solution can always be normalized so that its Hilbert-Schmidt norm is constant, because ||F(x)||_HS is then a T-invariant function and T is ergodic.

Abelian case (the form most often used). If G is abelian, the irreducible representations are the characters chi in the dual group, and the criterion reads: T_phi is ergodic if and only if for every nontrivial character chi there is NO measurable h : X -> S^1 with h(T x) = chi(phi(x)) h(x); i.e. no nontrivial character of phi is a measurable multiplicative coboundary. For G = S^1 and phi written additively this is: for every nonzero integer n, the equation u(T x) - u(x) = n * phi(x) (mod 1) has no measurable solution u.

SHARP EDGES. (1) Ergodicity of the BASE T is a hypothesis, not a conclusion: if T is not ergodic then T_phi is not ergodic either (invariant sets of the base lift), and the displayed equivalence is false as stated without it. (2) Compactness of G is essential -- the proof uses the Haar PROBABILITY measure and the Peter-Weyl decomposition of L^2(G); for noncompact G (e.g. G = R, cylinder flows) the natural invariant measure is infinite and ergodicity is a genuinely different problem. (3) 'Measurable' cannot be weakened to 'continuous': a cocycle can be a measurable coboundary without being a continuous one, so verifying that the equation has no CONTINUOUS solution does not certify ergodicity. (4) Every nontrivial irreducible pi must be tested, not one convenient one. Example: G = S^1 and phi taking values in {+1, -1} with the induced two-point extension ergodic. Then for the character chi_1(z) = z the equation has no solution (that is exactly ergodicity of the two-point extension), yet chi_2(z) = z^2 satisfies chi_2(phi(x)) = 1, so h identically 1 solves the equation for chi_2 -- and indeed T_phi is not ergodic, since phi lives in the proper closed subgroup {+1,-1}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["1 <= p < infinity","all three conditions (boundedness, uniform translation-continuity, uniform tightness); on a bounded domain tightness is automatic"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752488+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_55f7009e84a2c8aa0d6a0ebd9fd1b1397cfed669b44ad4e89536ea54eab897b5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let 1 <= p < infinity. A subset F of L^p(R^d) is relatively compact in the norm topology if and only if all three of the following hold: (i) F is BOUNDED, sup_{f in F} ||f||_p < infinity; (ii) F is uniformly continuous under translation, sup_{f in F} ||f(. + h) - f||_p -> 0 as h -> 0; (iii) F is uniformly TIGHT, sup_{f in F} integral_{|x| > R} |f|^p dx -> 0 as R -> infinity. Conditions (ii) and (iii) are each independent of the rest and cannot be dropped: the family {n^{d/p} 1_{B(0,1/n)}} is bounded in L^p and tight but not uniformly translation-continuous, since for |h| >= 2/n the translate is disjoint from the original; and the family {1_{[n, n+1]}} is bounded and uniformly translation-continuous but not tight, and has no L^p-convergent subsequence. Boundedness is listed as a separate condition here for safety - some treatments observe that it can be derived from the other two - and stating it explicitly costs nothing. On a bounded domain condition (iii) is automatic and the criterion reduces to (i) and (ii). The criterion is FALSE for p = infinity, where the analogue is Arzela-Ascoli on compacts plus a suitable equicontinuity. This is the L^p analogue of Arzela-Ascoli, with translation-continuity playing the role of equicontinuity. [Kolmogorov (1931), M. Riesz (1933), Frechet (1937); see Hanche-Olsen and Holden, 'The Kolmogorov-Riesz compactness theorem', Expo. Math. 28 (2010)]","status":"unverified"}

Fix D>=1 training examples and let d_k be the number whose task is k, so sum_{k=1}^{n_s} d_k=D. The source samples them iid from its task/bit distribution; the identity below holds conditional on any realized sample. Run continuous-time gradient flow with eta>0 on empirical half squared loss L_D=(1/(2D))*(sum_{k<=N} d_k*(S-a_k*b_k)^2+sum_{k>N} d_k*S^2). {"assumptions":["(X, Sigma, mu) is a measure space","f is Sigma-measurable","0 < p < infinity for the quasi-norm formula"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.551797+00:00","domain":"real analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_56428cce7b939634b8046806c62ca819a8a8f81caa9b6e1f7436a073f0e11f58","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a measurable f on a measure space (X, Sigma, mu), the distribution function is d_f(t) = mu({x : |f(x)| > t}) for t > 0; it is nonincreasing and right-continuous. It is a quasi-norm: ||f+g||_{L^{p,infinity}} <= max(2, 2^{1/p}) (||f||_{L^{p,infinity}} + ||g||_{L^{p,infinity}}), from d_{f+g}(t) <= d_f(t/2) + d_g(t/2). Chebyshev's inequality gives L^p contained in L^{p,infinity} with ||f||_{L^{p,infinity}} <= ||f||_p, and the inclusion is strict in general: on R^n, |x|^{-n/p} lies in L^{p,infinity} but not in L^p. {"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space","for the homeomorphism notion f is invertible; for positive expansiveness f is only assumed continuous"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.437766+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics","id":"claim_5676c1f151b4a57362148ab72f2407ae791df1e012af3b7099cc8435b4d96949","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, d)$ be a compact metric space. A homeomorphism $f: X \\to X$ is expansive with expansivity constant $\\varepsilon > 0$ if whenever $x \\ne y$ there is some $n \\in \\mathbb{Z}$ (positive OR negative) with $d(f^n x, f^n y) > \\varepsilon$; equivalently, $d(f^n x, f^n y) \\le \\varepsilon$ for all $n \\in \\mathbb{Z}$ forces $x = y$. A continuous map $f: X \\to X$ (not necessarily invertible) is positively expansive (forward expansive) with constant $\\varepsilon$ if $d(f^n x, f^n y) \\le \\varepsilon$ for all $n \\ge 0$ forces $x = y$. Positive expansiveness is much stronger than expansiveness: a positively expansive HOMEOMORPHISM of a compact metric space exists only when $X$ is finite (Schwartzman; Keynes-Robertson), so for an infinite compact space the notion is meaningful only for genuinely non-invertible maps such as expanding maps and one-sided shifts. On a compact space the property (with some constant) does not depend on the choice of compatible metric, though the constant does. Expansiveness is preserved by passing to $f^{-1}$ and to $f^k$, $k \\ne 0$; positive expansiveness is preserved by passing to $f^k$, $k \\ge 1$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["E finite (or the event depends on finitely many coordinates of an infinite product space)","the measure is a product of Bernoulli(p_e) coordinates; the single-parameter form takes p_e = p for all e","the pivotal (influence) form of the right-hand side needs A increasing; the general form P_p(A^e) - P_p(A_e) holds for every event","the sharp-threshold consequences are cited, not proved"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T15:38:02.592676+00:00","domain":"percolation and Boolean functions","id":"claim_569ccbdb68319948c30d7d0358dc8c699ed1907ce85a36c356879bd884bd847d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega = {0,1}^E for a finite set E (the coordinates e in E are 'edges' or 'bits'), and let P_p denote the product measure under which the coordinates omega_e are independent Bernoulli(p_e) variables, p = (p_e) in [0,1]^E; write P_p also for the case p_e = p for all e. For an event A (a subset of Omega) and a coordinate e write A^e = { omega : omega^e in A } and A_e = { omega : omega_e in A }, where omega^e and omega_e are omega with the coordinate e set to 1 and to 0 respectively; A^e and A_e do not depend on the coordinate e. The coordinate e is PIVOTAL for A at omega if exactly one of omega^e, omega_e lies in A; Piv_A(omega) is the set of pivotal coordinates and its size |Piv_A| is the number of pivotal coordinates. THEOREM (Margulis 1974, Russo 1981). For every event A, p |-> P_p(A) is a polynomial in the p_e and, for every coordinate e, d/dp_e P_p(A) = P_p(A^e) - P_p(A_e). With a single parameter p, d/dp P_p(A) = sum over e in E of ( P_p(A^e) - P_p(A_e) ). If A is INCREASING (closed under raising coordinates) then A_e is contained in A^e, A^e minus A_e is exactly the event that e is pivotal for A, and the formula reads d/dp P_p(A) = sum over e of P_p( e is pivotal for A ) = E_p |Piv_A| = sum over e of I_e^p(A), where I_e^p(A) = P_p(e pivotal for A) is the influence of e on A under P_p. In particular an increasing event's probability is nondecreasing in p (and in every p_e), and its derivative is the expected number of pivotal coordinates. The formula holds verbatim for an event on an infinite product space that depends on finitely many coordinates; for a general increasing event depending on infinitely many coordinates the right-hand side is only known to bound the derivative from below in the appropriate one-sided sense, and the finite-dimensional form is the one used in practice (finite boxes, then limits).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["m is Lebesgue measure on R^n and L is its completion of the Borel sigma-algebra B","f is Lebesgue measurable with values in the extended reals","for part (i): Lebesgue measure is sigma-finite and outer regular, which is what supplies the Borel hull and kernel","for part (iii): (X, M-bar, mu-bar) is the completion of a measure space (X, M, mu)","the conclusion is equality off a null set, not everywhere"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402310+00:00","domain":"measure theory, Borel versus Lebesgue measurability","id":"claim_56d067a642318476c9ea2c21c69cf1a4651cbf39b9d439c61824ee18654d3860","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let m denote Lebesgue measure on R^n, let B be the Borel sigma-algebra and let L be the Lebesgue sigma-algebra; recall that (R^n, L, m) is the completion of (R^n, B, m). (i) SETS: if E is in L then there are Borel sets B_1 contained in E contained in B_2 with m(B_2 minus B_1) = 0; consequently E = B_1 union N with N contained in a Borel set of measure zero, and every Lebesgue measurable set differs from a Borel set by a null set. (ii) FUNCTIONS: if f : R^n -> [-infinity, +infinity] is Lebesgue measurable, then there is a BOREL measurable g : R^n -> [-infinity, +infinity] and a Borel set N with m(N) = 0 such that g(x) = f(x) for every x outside N. One may take g with the same pointwise bounds as f (if a <= f <= b a.e. then a <= g <= b everywhere, and if f >= 0 then g >= 0). (iii) The same holds verbatim for the completion of any measure space: an M-bar-measurable function on the completion (X, M-bar, mu-bar) of (X, M, mu) agrees mu-almost everywhere with an M-measurable function. WHERE IT FAILS: (a) 'almost everywhere' cannot be strengthened to 'everywhere': let N be a non-Borel subset of the Cantor set (such subsets exist since the Cantor set has cardinality the continuum and carries continuum-many subsets, while there are only continuum-many Borel sets and all subsets of the Cantor set are Lebesgue null hence Lebesgue measurable); then the indicator of N is Lebesgue measurable but not Borel. (b) 'Borel' cannot be upgraded to 'continuous': Lusin's theorem only gives continuity of the restriction after deleting a set of arbitrarily small measure, not a continuous function agreeing almost everywhere (the indicator of [0,1] is a counterexample). (c) The distinction is not cosmetic in compositions: if h is continuous and f is Lebesgue measurable, f composed with h need not be Lebesgue measurable, whereas g composed with h is Borel measurable whenever g is Borel; this is the standard reason to replace f by its Borel representative before composing or before invoking a change of variables. (d) Statement (i) uses that Lebesgue measure is sigma-finite and Borel-regular; for a general non-regular measure there is no such inner and outer Borel approximation.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["independence within each row (nothing assumed across rows)","mean zero and finite variances, with sum_i E[X_{n,i}^2] -> sigma^2 > 0","Lindeberg's condition for sufficiency; additionally uniform asymptotic negligibility for the converse"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.781577+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_56f2f3ba378c4a6f96900d8c87012af674a778ae0963a2aedce836ff95c4516e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For each n let X_{n,1}, ..., X_{n,k_n} be INDEPENDENT random variables within each row, with E[X_{n,i}] = 0 and sum_{i=1}^{k_n} E[X_{n,i}^2] -> sigma^2 in (0, infinity). Suppose the LINDEBERG CONDITION holds: for every eps > 0, sum_{i=1}^{k_n} E[ X_{n,i}^2 1{ |X_{n,i}| > eps } ] -> 0 as n -> infinity. Then S_n = sum_i X_{n,i} converges in distribution to N(0, sigma^2). FELLER'S CONVERSE: if in addition the row is UNIFORMLY ASYMPTOTICALLY NEGLIGIBLE, max_{i <= k_n} E[X_{n,i}^2] -> 0, and S_n converges in distribution to N(0, sigma^2), then the Lindeberg condition holds - so under negligibility the condition is necessary as well as sufficient. LYAPUNOV'S CONDITION, sum_i E|X_{n,i}|^{2 + delta} -> 0 for some delta > 0, IMPLIES Lindeberg and is usually easier to check. Two things the theorem does not require: identical distribution within a row, and any relation between rows. Two things it does require: independence WITHIN each row, and the variance sum converging to a strictly positive limit. Without negligibility the converse fails - a single summand can already be Gaussian and carry the whole limit while the others are wild. [Lindeberg (1922), Feller (1935); see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorems 3.4.10 and 3.4.11]","status":"unverified"}

The lace expansion writes the two-point function of self-avoiding walk, Bernoulli percolation, oriented percolation or lattice trees as a renormalised random-walk Green function plus a correction series: for SAW, c_n(x) = sum_y D(y) c_{n-1}(x - y) + sum_{m=2}^{n} sum_y pi_m(y) c_{n-m}(x - y), with pi_m the alternating-sign lace coefficients obtained by inclusion-exclusion over self-intersections (for percolation the analogous expansion is in terms of pivotal bonds and sausages). The expansion is an exact identity; its use requires a bootstrap showing the coefficients are small in a norm controlled by a random-walk diagram: the bubble diagram for SAW (finite for d > 4), the triangle diagram for percolation (finite for d > 6) and the square diagram for lattice trees (d > 8). Proved regimes: nearest-neighbour SAW for d >= 5 (Hara-Slade), spread-out SAW for d > 4, nearest-neighbour percolation for d >= 11 (Fitzner-van der Hofstad) and spread-out percolation for d > 6 (Hara-Slade). Conclusions there: mean-field exponents (gamma = 1, eta = 0, beta = 1 and delta = 2 in bounded-ratio senses), Gaussian or super-Brownian scaling limits, and asymptotic expansions of critical points. It gives nothing at or below the upper critical dimension, and for nearest-neighbour percolation in 7 <= d <= 10 there is no small parameter, so the expansion holds only as an identity, not as a bound. Typical failure: Applying the expansion's mean-field conclusions (eta=0, Gaussian or super-Brownian scaling limit) to a model at or below its upper critical dimension without re-verifying the triangle or bubble condition; the coefficients pi_m are not shown small there, the bootstrap can fail to close, and the diagrammatic control silently assumed at the outset is exactly the open problem, which is why mean-field behaviour of nearest-neighbour percolation in dimensions 7 <= d <= 10 remains unproved although the spread-out (d > 6) and nearest-neighbour d >= 11 cases are resolved (below d = 6 mean-field behaviour is not expected, and at d = 6 logarithmic corrections are expected). {"assumptions":["Eikonal equation |u'| = 1 on (-1,1) with zero boundary data","The correct symmetry is: u solves F = 0 in the viscosity sense iff -u solves -F(x,-r,-p) = 0; simply flipping the sign of F does not preserve the solution set","The sign convention pairs with vanishing viscosity: the viscosity solution of F = 0 is the limit of solutions of F(x,u_ε,Du_ε) - εΔu_ε = 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418207+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: viscosity solution theory","id":"claim_573bfbe8e5c9cedb4b4e443a344bb159372ae5341600e867e80decd2533c1068","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing convention: the definition of viscosity solution is tied to the SIGN with which the equation is written (with the convention that F is nonincreasing in the second-order term, i.e. that the vanishing-viscosity approximation is F(x,u,Du) - εΔu = 0). Multiplying the equation by -1 changes the solution. Concrete counterexample: on Ω = (-1,1) with boundary data u(-1) = u(1) = 0, consider |u'| = 1. Written as F(x,r,p) = |p| - 1 = 0, the viscosity solution is u(x) = 1 - |x| (the distance to ∂Ω): at x = 0 the function has a concave kink, no C^1 function touches it from below there, and the subsolution test at the kink only requires |p| - 1 ≤ 0 for p ∈ [-1,1]. Written as G(x,r,p) = 1 - |p| = 0 (the same equation pointwise!), the viscosity solution is u(x) = |x| - 1: at its convex kink at x = 0 the supersolution test requires 1 - |p| ≥ 0 for the touching slopes p ∈ [-1,1], which holds. Moreover 1 - |x| is NOT a viscosity solution of G = 0 (the subsolution test at the concave kink would demand 1 - |p| ≤ 0 for p = 0) and |x| - 1 is not a viscosity solution of F = 0. Both functions are Lipschitz with |u'| = 1 a.e. and the same boundary data. Auditor's check: before citing a comparison or uniqueness theorem, verify that the equation is written in the same sign convention as the theorem (this bites when a Hamiltonian is moved across the equality, when time is reversed in u_t + H = 0, or when a maximization problem is rewritten as a minimization).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. observations with finite variance (Andrews states the result under moment conditions for the CLT)","the constraint is active at the true parameter (theta = 0); for theta > 0 the bootstrap is consistent"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T09:15:04.118127+00:00","domain":"resampling / constrained estimation","id":"claim_5803afc2cb107c5851acbdda8fe0e490d3b03266f3d6e659e596fdbcafb115fe","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $X_1, \\dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. with mean $\\theta \\ge 0$ and variance $\\sigma^2$, and let the estimator respect the constraint: $\\hat\\theta_n = \\max(0, \\bar X_n)$. When the true parameter is interior ($\\theta > 0$) the nonparametric bootstrap is consistent: the conditional law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n^* - \\hat\\theta_n)$ converges to $N(0, \\sigma^2)$, the law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n - \\theta)$. When the true parameter is on the boundary ($\\theta = 0$) it is not: $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n - \\theta) \\Rightarrow \\max(0, Z)$ with $Z \\sim N(0, \\sigma^2)$, a law with an atom of mass $1/2$ at zero, whereas the bootstrap law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n^* - \\hat\\theta_n)$ converges, conditionally on the data, to the law of $\\max(0, Z + \\zeta) - \\max(0, \\zeta)$ with $\\zeta \\sim N(0, \\sigma^2)$ a random shift that does not vanish - so the bootstrap distribution is random in the limit and does not equal the sampling distribution (Andrews 2000, Theorem 1). The same failure holds for maximum-likelihood and least-squares estimators under inequality constraints whenever the true parameter has an active constraint, in particular for nonnegatively constrained regression and portfolio weights with coordinates at zero: the bootstrap replicates flip the constrained coordinates between zero and positive values, and the spread of the replicates is not the spread of the estimator. Consistent alternatives: the $m$-out-of-$n$ bootstrap with $m \\to \\infty$, $m/n \\to 0$, and subsampling, both of which recover the limit law at the boundary.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:15:27.869621+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_581c9552f43e1f4cf92726d32a39b9a4720c921de8094cf33857ac37ef5fce39","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"FIRES WHEN a detection or coverage problem in a moving Boolean model has been reduced, correctly, to the volume of a union of swept regions, and you are about to call the problem solved. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.544044+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_59b71972a03cccd34a3b9f19358b0f2ad82bb2b26ccd049a537b06518a32a52b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a positive finite Borel measure mu on R, its STIELTJES TRANSFORM (also Cauchy transform) is m_mu(z) = integral (x - z)^{-1} mu(dx) for z in the open upper half plane C^+. It is analytic on C^+, maps C^+ into C^+ when mu is positive, and satisfies the a priori bound |m_mu(z)| <= mu(R)/Im(z). INVERSION: for a < b continuity points of mu, mu( (a,b) ) = (1/pi) lim_{eta decreasing to 0} integral_a^b Im m_mu(x + i eta) dx, so the transform determines the measure. CONTINUITY: a sequence of probability measures mu_n converges weakly to a probability measure mu if and only if m_{mu_n}(z) -> m_mu(z) for every z in C^+; convergence on any set with an accumulation point in C^+ suffices, by analyticity plus a tightness argument. In random matrix theory the transform of the empirical spectral distribution of a Hermitian matrix H is m_n(z) = (1/n) tr ( H - z I )^{-1}, the normalised trace of the RESOLVENT, which is why resolvent methods and Stieltjes-transform methods are the same method. Sign conventions differ across the literature: some authors define the transform with (z - x)^{-1}, which flips the sign of the whole calculus; the convention must be checked before importing a formula. [standard; e.g. Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni, An Introduction to Random Matrices, Section 2.4]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["conjugate exponents with 1 <= p <= 2","convention e^{-2 pi i x . xi}, for which the constant 1 is available on R^d","on T the transform is the coefficient sequence, with the counting measure on Z"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264720+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, common errors","id":"claim_5aeb07b2cba38ad9cc3665ecb9550bf24a5d74fc445f8cf0332b5120f3c59861","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The inequality $\\|\\hat f\\|_{p'}\\le\\|f\\|_p$, $\\frac1p+\\frac1{p'}=1$, holds for $1\\le p\\le2$ (Riesz-Thorin interpolation between $\\|\\hat f\\|_\\infty\\le\\|f\\|_1$ and Plancherel) - and only there. The restriction $p\\le2$ is load-bearing: (i) On $\\mathbb T$, $L^p\\subset L^2$ for $p>2$, so the coefficients are automatically in $\\ell^2$, but no better exponent is available: Carleman's example provides a continuous (hence in every $L^p$) function $f$ on $\\mathbb T$ with $\\sum_n|\\hat f(n)|^q=\\infty$ for every $q<2$. So no bound $\\|\\hat f\\|_{\\ell^{p'}}\\le C\\|f\\|_{L^p}$ with $p'<2$ can hold for any $p>2$. (ii) On $\\mathbb R^d$ and $p>2$, the Fourier transform of an $L^p$ function exists only as a tempered distribution and need not be representable by a locally integrable function, so the left-hand side of the inequality is not even defined in general. (iii) The direction matters too: the dual statement '$\\hat f\\in L^{p'}$ implies $f\\in L^p$' is false in general; what is true is the companion inequality $\\|f\\|_{p'}\\le\\|\\hat f\\|_p$ for $1\\le p\\le2$. (iv) On $\\mathbb R^d$ the constant $1$ is not sharp: Babenko-Beckner give $\\|\\hat f\\|_{p'}\\le\\big(p^{1/p}/(p')^{1/p'}\\big)^{d/2}\\|f\\|_p$ for $1<p<2$, attained by Gaussians, whereas on $\\mathbb T$ and $\\mathbb Z$ the constant $1$ is sharp.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f in L^2(R)","the Fourier transform vanishes a.e. outside [-W,W] (bandlimited)","the identity is for the continuous representative of f, at the sample rate 2W"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264078+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, signal analysis","id":"claim_5b13f31813707effd67637d18a57d7f164f03bdd14f035e44aa83cc3dc91a5ef","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Convention $\\hat f(\\xi)=\\int f(x)e^{-2\\pi i x\\xi}dx$. Let $W>0$ and let $f\\in L^2(\\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\\hat f=0$ a.e. outside $[-W,W]$. Then $\\hat f\\in L^1$, so $f$ has a (unique) continuous representative $f(x)=\\int_{-W}^{W}\\hat f(\\xi)e^{2\\pi i x\\xi}d\\xi$, and for that representative $$f(x)=\\sum_{n\\in\\mathbb Z}f\\!\\left(\\frac{n}{2W}\\right)\\operatorname{sinc}(2Wx-n),\\qquad \\operatorname{sinc}(t)=\\frac{\\sin(\\pi t)}{\\pi t},$$ the series converging in $L^2(\\mathbb R)$ and uniformly on $\\mathbb R$. Moreover $\\sum_n|f(n/2W)|^2=2W\\|f\\|_2^2$, so the samples determine $f$ isometrically. The sampling rate $2W$ (the Nyquist rate) is critical: functions bandlimited to $[-W,W]$ are in general not determined by samples at a slower rate, and the theorem's conclusion uses $f\\in L^2$ - the distributionally bandlimited function $\\sin(2\\pi Wx)$ has all samples $f(n/2W)=0$ without being zero, and it is excluded only because it is not in $L^2$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the ambient space is R^d with Lebesgue outer measure defined by countable covers by boxes","L is the sigma-algebra of Caratheodory-measurable sets and lambda = lambda* restricted to L","R^d is sigma-compact, locally compact and second countable, and lambda is finite on bounded sets - this is what drives regularity","the axiom of choice is used only for the remark that non-measurable sets exist"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.815011+00:00","domain":"measure theory, real analysis","id":"claim_5be137db7963f504ae7ade7e44a43ba8c850915205425ffc83a5dcc77d7cfe50","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let lambda* denote Lebesgue outer measure on R^d, defined by lambda*(E) = inf of sum of volumes of countably many open boxes covering E, let L be the sigma-algebra of Caratheodory-measurable (Lebesgue measurable) sets, and let lambda = lambda* restricted to L. Then: (1) OUTER REGULARITY, valid for EVERY set E contained in R^d, measurable or not: lambda*(E) = inf { lambda(U) : U open, U contains E }. (2) MEASURABILITY CRITERION: E is in L if and only if for every eps > 0 there is an open U containing E with lambda*(U \\ E) < eps, if and only if there is a G_delta set G containing E with lambda(G \\ E) = 0, if and only if there is an F_sigma set F contained in E with lambda(E \\ F) = 0. (3) INNER REGULARITY by compact sets, valid for every E in L: lambda(E) = sup { lambda(K) : K compact, K contained in E } (both sides may be +infinity). Equivalently, for E in L with lambda(E) < infinity and eps > 0 there is a compact K contained in E with lambda(E \\ K) < eps. Thus lambda is a Radon measure: it is finite on compacta, outer regular and inner regular. (4) COMPLETENESS: if lambda*(N) = 0 then N is in L and lambda(N) = 0, and hence every subset of a null set is measurable with measure zero. Equivalently, (R^d, L, lambda) is the completion of (R^d, Borel, lambda|Borel): L = { B union Z : B Borel, Z a subset of a Borel null set }. SHARP EDGES. (a) The Borel sigma-algebra itself is NOT complete: the Cantor set is Borel and null, it has 2^continuum subsets, all of them Lebesgue null and hence Lebesgue measurable, while there are only continuum many Borel sets; so L is strictly larger than the Borel sigma-algebra, and 'measurable' must never be silently upgraded to 'Borel'. (b) Regularity statements about the MEASURE are for measurable sets. Outer regularity in the form (1) does hold for arbitrary sets because it is the definition of the outer measure, but inner regularity fails badly for non-measurable sets: a Vitali set has inner measure 0 and positive outer measure, so the two approximations do not meet. It is exactly the meeting of the two that measurability expresses. (c) Completeness is what makes 'a.e. defined' harmless: if f = g almost everywhere and f is measurable then g is measurable. That inference is FALSE in the Borel sigma-algebra, and is a frequent silent error. (d) Regularity is not automatic for general Borel measures: on a non-sigma-compact or non-locally-compact space a finite Borel measure need not be inner regular by compact sets. Lebesgue measure is regular because R^d is sigma-compact, locally compact and second countable, and because lambda is finite on boxes. (e) Not every set is measurable: the existence of a non-measurable set uses the axiom of choice, and translation invariance plus countable additivity forbid extending lambda to all subsets of R^d.","status":"unverified"}

The Simon-Lieb inequality bounds G(x,y) across any finite set Lambda separating x from y (x in Lambda, y outside Lambda) by G(x,y) <= sum_{u in Lambda, v not in Lambda, u~v} G(x,u) J_{uv} G(v,y), a one-step recursive bound relating the two-point function across a separating surface to the two-point function up to the boundary of Lambda times the coupling crossing it. Iterating the inequality over a sequence of nested separating sets, such as concentric boxes, yields exponential decay of G(x,y) once the associated generating function drops below its self-consistency threshold, giving a classical route, predating and complementary to the Duminil-Copin-Tassion approach, to sharpness of the phase transition and analyticity of the free energy in the high-temperature regime. It does not determine the exact critical temperature directly, only characterizing it implicitly through the inequality's self-consistency condition, and it applies specifically to ferromagnetic spin systems with a workable notion of finite separating surfaces; it does not transfer automatically to percolation, which uses combinatorially different, though philosophically related, inequalities. Typical failure: Iterating the Simon-Lieb inequality across many nested separating surfaces while implicitly assuming a geometric decay rate that has not actually been verified to be summable; turning the one-step recursive bound into exponential decay requires checking that the relevant generating function, summing G times J over the boundary, lies strictly below its self-consistency threshold, and this check is exactly where the difficulty of locating beta_c resides, so skipping it silently assumes the conclusion. Canonical reference: Simon, 1980, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Lieb, 1980, Communications in Mathematical Physics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X, B, mu) is a probability space and T is measure-preserving","the partition is finite or countable and consists of measurable sets","for the two-sided join T must be invertible"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:23.250796+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, entropy","id":"claim_5c8ad06c4539071020c4a52ccb50fab1a5b23a0b5f4b9e11e00d40a599f8d3a6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \\mathcal{B}, \\mu, T)$ be a measure-preserving system on a probability space with $T$ invertible (a measure-preserving automorphism). A finite or countable measurable partition $\\xi = \\{A_1, A_2, \\dots\\}$ of $X$ is a (two-sided) generator if the smallest $\\sigma$-algebra containing all the sets $T^{-n} A_i$, $n \\in \\mathbb{Z}$, coincides with $\\mathcal{B}$ up to $\\mu$-null sets; in join notation, $\\bigvee_{n=-\\infty}^{\\infty} T^{-n}\\xi = \\mathcal{B}$ (mod $\\mu$). For a non-invertible $T$ one uses the one-sided join $\\bigvee_{n=0}^{\\infty} T^{-n}\\xi$ and speaks of a one-sided (strong) generator. Why it matters: by the Kolmogorov-Sinai theorem, if $\\xi$ is a generator with finite entropy $H_\\mu(\\xi) < \\infty$ then the measure-theoretic entropy of the system equals the entropy relative to $\\xi$, $h_\\mu(T) = h_\\mu(T, \\xi)$; no supremum over partitions is needed. Existence (Krieger): an ergodic automorphism of a Lebesgue probability space with $h_\\mu(T) < \\log k$ has a generator with $k$ atoms; a system with infinite entropy has no finite generator. # C018 v1: finite-width nonlinear transfer of the iid-head construction
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: narrowed. Target: 1. Novelty unestablished.
This is a four-point, label-noise-averaged witness theorem. It does not
claim double descent for one realized label vector or settle general T267.

## 1. Exact model and statement
Use C017's definitions: 0<e<1/4, D=1+e^2+e^4, uniform population on
x_(s,t)=(1,es,e^2 t)/sqrt(D), one training observation at each of these
four inputs, and u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2). The teacher is
 g_e(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-c_e/2, c_e=e^2/sqrt(D(1+e^2)), alpha_e=c_e/2.
Fix 0<nu<=1 and kappa>0. For each of the sixteen sign vectors
xi in {-1,1}^4, train a separate network with labels
 y_i=g_e(x_i)+sigma_e xi_i, sigma_e=2 alpha_e sqrt(kappa/sqrt(e)).
All sixteen networks share their initial parameters. At width m these are
 f_m(x)=m^(-1/2) sum_(j=1)^m a_j ReLU(w_j.x),
 w_j(0) iid N(0,I_3), a_j(0) iid uniform {-nu,nu}, independent of w_j(0).
Train BOTH layers by simultaneous discrete GD with step gamma=1/2 on
(1/8) sum_i (f_m(x_i)-y_i)^2. Set the derivative at a zero gate to zero.
No pairing, tying or resetting of the readout is imposed.
Define the clean population risk averaged over the sixteen trained networks:
 R_(e,m)(k)= (1/16) sum_xi (1/4) sum_i (f_(m,xi)(x_i;k)-g_e(x_i))^2.
Probability below is over initialization only. In particular R is NOT the
risk trajectory of any one of the sixteen networks.

Let lambda_h be the Walsh eigenvalues of C=H/4, where
 H(x,z)=E[ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z],
and let b_h=-log(1-lambda_h/2), eta_e=(b_t+b_st)/b_s.
The clock premises proved in C009 are b_s~nu^2 e/(4pi), eta_e~e.
Let independent standard normals G_s,G_t define
 a=2nu^2 G_s^2, B=((sqrt(2)nu G_t-1)^2+1)/2,
 p=P(kappa^2>4aB).

For every epsilon>0 define E_(e,m)(epsilon) as existence of integers
0<=k0<k1<k2<k3 such that
 R(k0)>R(k1), R(k2)>R(k1), R(k2)>R(k3),
and k2 maximizes R on the integer interval [k1,k3], with
 | k2 / ((6pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e)) - 1 | < epsilon.
Then
 liminf_(e downarrow 0) liminf_(m to infinity) P(E_(e,m)(epsilon)) >= p
 >= max(0,1-8nu^2(1+nu^2)/kappa^2).                       (1)
More precisely, for every zeta>0 there are constants c>0,L<infinity
such that the inner/outer liminf probability of witnesses with each of
the three displayed strict risk gaps >=c alpha_e^2 eta_e and
 |b_s k2-(3/2)log(1/e)|<=L
is at least p-zeta. Negative lower bounds are understood as vacuous.
This proves two descents separated by a rise in the finite-witness sense,
with an interior interval peak. It does not prove unique stationary points
or monotonicity of the intervening integer-time segments.

## 2. What the preceding proofs provide
C017 proves, in its joint Gaussian initialization coupling, locally uniform
convergence of centered risk differences
 [Q_e(t_e(s))-Q_e(t_e(0))]/(2alpha_e^2 eta_e)
       -> V(s)-V(0),
where t_e(s)=((3/2)log(1/e)+s)/b_s and
 V(s)=-kappa exp(-s)+(a/2)exp(-2s)-Bs.
The derivative converges too, although this proof only transfers values.
On Delta=kappa^2-4aB>0, V has a simple minimum r and a simple maximum v,
with r<v, decreasing before r, increasing on (r,v), decreasing after v.
Their formulas are r=-log((kappa+sqrt(Delta))/(2a)) and
v=-log((kappa-sqrt(Delta))/(2a)). The probability a=0 is zero.
C009 Section 3 proves the following finite-horizon fact for the SAME
nonzero iid initialization: for fixed e, bounded labels, and finite integer T,
actual nonlinear predictions at all four inputs, uniformly over k<=T and
all sixteen label patterns, approach frozen deterministic-C predictions
started from the actual initial vector, in probability as m tends to infinity.
That proof controls gates through initial weighted Gaussian bands and keeps
the exact simultaneous-update remainder. Its deterministic residual bounds
can use any finite initial residual bound; replacing its old teacher/labels
by the present bounded labels changes only this bound. Thus its argument
applies verbatim for each fixed e here. The small-e limit is taken AFTER the
width limit; no uniform width estimate in e or T is inferred.
These preceding claims are unaudited dependencies, not independent audits.

## 3. From nonlinear prediction transfer to the correct joint risk limit
For fixed e and T, the initial four-vector converges by the multivariate iid
CLT to C017's Gaussian Z_e (expressed in Walsh coordinates). The empirical
initial tangent kernel converges in probability to the deterministic C.
These facts hold jointly: no independence between the finite-width initial
output and its empirical kernel is needed, since the latter limit is constant.
C009's comparison is already to deterministic C with the same initial output.

Frozen predictions at times 0,...,T are affine continuous functions of the
initial four-vector, with labels fixed. For the finite sixteen-label family,
the corresponding frozen risk array is therefore a continuous function of
this vector. Actual and frozen risk arrays differ by o_P(1). Indeed for
vectors u,v measured in population L2, the exact bound
 | ||u-g||^2-||v-g||^2 | <= ||u-v||(2||v-g||+||u-v||)
applies; the finite frozen array is tight at fixed e,T by its continuous
Gaussian limit, and C009 supplies uniform o_P(1) prediction error. Averaging
a finite sixteen terms preserves this estimate. Slutsky then gives joint
weak convergence of the whole actual risk array to (Q_e(k))_(k=0)^T.
At fixed e, alpha_e^2 eta_e is strictly positive, so the same assertion holds
for risks centered at any fixed time and divided by this scale. There is
no claim that an unscaled o_P(1) error is uniform in e.

## 4. Finite witnesses, rounding, and the open-event argument
Fix a Gaussian realization in {Delta>0,a>0}. Choose small radii h0,h1>0
with r-h0<r<v<v+h1. Because V is strictly decreasing immediately before
r, increasing on (r,v), and decreasing after v, the values at
 r-h0, r, v, v+h1
have the required decrease/rise/decrease gaps. All are strict. On the
closed interval [r,v+h1], V has its unique global maximum at v. For any
sufficiently small d>0, the maximum over the complement of (v-d,v+d)
in that interval is strictly smaller than V(v), by continuity and compactness.

Convergence of centered risk differences locally uniformly in s therefore
preserves the three gaps, as well as the separated interval maximum, for
all sufficiently small e depending on this realization. Round all four
t_e anchor times to nearest integers. Their s coordinates change by at
most b_s/2, which tends to zero. They remain ordered because their fixed
s spacings are positive. The interpolation values at the rounded anchors
converge to the same V values. The same local uniform convergence controls
ALL integer times between the rounded second and fourth anchors. It gives
an interior maximizing grid index, with s coordinate in (v-d,v+d).
It follows pathwise that its s coordinate tends to v: apply this argument
for every rational d>0. Its peak-time leading coefficient is consequently
6pi/nu^2. This rounding step makes no claim about continuous interpolation
of actual nonlinear GD, which is only evaluated at integer times.

For precision in passing probabilities, fix zeta>0. The preceding pathwise
argument and a countable exhaustion allow deterministic c>0,L<infinity
such that, on an event of probability at least p-zeta, the three gaps of
the Gaussian-limit integer curves exceed 2c alpha_e^2 eta_e, all their
anchors lie in |s|<L-1, and an interior interval maximizer lies in |s|<L-1,
for all sufficiently small e in the following probabilistic sense: the
liminf of these event probabilities is at least p-zeta. One explicit
exhaustion bounds all four Gaussian coordinates, bounds a away from zero,
bounds Delta away from zero, bounds r and v, and then restricts each
positive limiting value gap and peak-separation margin away from zero.
These compact events exhaust {Delta>0,a>0}; local uniform convergence and
Fatou give the asserted liminf. Uniform convergence over compact Gaussian
parameters can also be used, but is not required.

For each fixed sufficiently small e, there are only finitely many indices
with |b_s k-(3/2)log(1/e)|<=L. Consider the following event in this FINITE
risk array: there exist k0<k1<j<k3 in this window such that all three
witness gaps at j exceed c alpha_e^2 eta_e, and every index in [k1,k3]
with a peak time outside the desired localization band has risk strictly
less than R(j). This is a finite union of finite intersections of strict
inequalities, hence open. If the excluded set is empty its inequalities
are vacuous. An interval maximizer then lies inside the desired band,
and substituting that maximizer for j preserves the three strict gaps.
The Gaussian arrays just constructed belong to such an open event (with
extra positive margins), taking either the band |s|<L or the relative
peak-time band of (1); for small e the whole fixed s window is inside the
relative band. Enlarge the finite horizon to include the whole window.
The joint weak convergence in Section 3 and the open-set Portmanteau
inequality transfer its probability LOWER bound to the nonlinear arrays.
Take liminf in e, then let zeta decrease to zero, proving (1).
For the refined gap statement retain zeta and c,L from the exhaustion.
Only fixed-e finite arrays are used in each width limit. There is no
exchange of the two limits, no infinite-horizon NTK claim, and no assertion
that finite-width Gaussian mode coefficients are independent.

## 5. Probability bound and scope
C017 gives E(4aB)=8nu^2(1+nu^2) using independence of G_s and G_t.
Markov's inequality bounds P(4aB>=kappa^2) and yields (1). Arbitrarily
large fixed kappa makes the bound approach one; sigma_e still tends to
zero and is <=1 for sufficiently small e. The teacher direction has norm
one. The input distribution is uniform on four shrinking, clustered atoms,
with a stratified training set of size four, not an iid Gaussian sample.
Width tends to infinity first, so this is an iterated-limit lazy-regime
result about actual nonlinear parameter updates, not macroscopic feature
learning. The risk average spans sixteen different GD trajectories.
The unresolved hardest piece for a one-dataset theorem is control of the
realized-noise cross terms on the alpha_e^2 eta_e central gap scale.
General Target 1, fixed-noise regimes, continuous iid-input extensions of

novelty review all remain open. Source dependencies: C009 Section 3,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.499003+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_5dc3c47c9309dce7fd49bcf52a42480f0accb33ab54ce677db12baa123bb1e4e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Hurwitz's theorem is often quoted as 'a locally uniform limit of zero-free holomorphic functions is zero-free'. Three hypotheses carry that conclusion. (1) Connectedness of the domain. On U = D(0,1) union D(3,1) put f_n = 1/n on the first disk and f_n = 1 on the second; each f_n is holomorphic and zero-free on U and f_n converges locally uniformly, but the limit is 0 on one component and 1 on the other: neither zero-free nor identically zero. The correct statement is the dichotomy component by component. (2) The degenerate alternative cannot be dropped even on a connected domain: f_n(z) = exp(z)/n is zero-free on C and converges locally uniformly to the identically zero function. Likewise the injectivity version must allow constants: f_n(z) = z/n is injective on D and converges to the constant 0. (3) Holomorphy, not just real analyticity: on the real line f_n(x) = x^2 + 1/n has no real zeros and converges uniformly on compacts to x^2, which has a zero; the complex statement survives because the complex zeros ±i/sqrt(n) move to 0. (4) The counting form requires that the boundary circle avoid the zeros of the limit: f_n(z) = z - 1 + 1/n has one zero in the unit disk for every n, while f_n(z) = z - 1 - 1/n has none, and both converge to z - 1, whose only zero sits on the circle |z| = 1. Never conclude equal zero counts from a circle through a zero of the limit.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-09T10:58:31+00:00","domain":"harvested statement (arXiv 2607.06055, 2026): mathematics","id":"claim_5dd3ddfaa1479d6173ecc873b861b91f8314530830d3ef6aca28ade20a1b4bd3","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Definition 4 (Edge type). Let G = (V, E, R, tau, w) be a base graph (Definition 1), where each node v in V carries a representational payload P_v as in Definition 2. The relation-type set R partitions into six pairwise-disjoint classes, R = R_causal U R_contain U R_temp U R_assoc U R_epist U R_spatial, each defined by an independent structural test below. For each edge e = (u, v) in E, the assigned type tau(e) in R belongs to exactly one class. A particular graph may employ only a subset; belief-graph and working-memory instantiations specify which classes appear in R_B and R_{W_t}. The six classes are: 1. Causal (R_causal). An edge (u, v) with tau(u, v) in R_causal asserts that node u produces, enables, probabilistically raises, or inhibits the occurrence of node v, independent of the payload types of u and v: R_causal = {r_causes, r_enables, r_inhibits, r_counterfactual}. Causal edges are antisymmetric: (u, v) in E_{R_causal} implies (v, u) not in E_{R_causal}. Acyclicity over R_causal is a structural forbidden pattern in S. When u is a distinguished agent node, an optional attribution tag a(u, v) in V records whose causal model the edge belongs to, e.g. 'agent a believes u causes v'. 2. Containment (R_contain). An edge (u, v) with tau(u, v) in R_contain asserts that v's existence or identity is nested inside u's scope, characterized by an existential-dependency test: (u, v) in E_{R_contain} iff removing u from G requires removing v as well. R_contain = {r_is-a, r_part-of, r_instance-of, r_role-of}. When v carries a graph payload G_v (Definition 2, item 5) or a structured perceptual payload (item 4), its internal subgraph is linked to v via r_part-of edges. Containment is transitive and irreflexive; a directed cycle over R_contain is a forbidden pattern in S. 3. Temporal (R_temp). An edge (u, v) with tau(u, v) in R_temp encodes ordering of nodes across time via a node timestamp function theta_V : V -> R (distinct from the working-memory time index t) such that (u, v) in E_{R_temp} implies theta_V(u) <= theta_V(v): R_temp = {r_before, r_after, r_during, r_next}. Here r_before and r_after are mutually exclusive on the same ordered pair (a predicate incompatibility in F); r_next is the sequential successor used in action-sequence and planning subgraphs. 4. Associative (R_assoc). An edge (u, v) with tau(u, v) in R_assoc encodes statistical co-occurrence or spreading-activation linkage with no stronger typed commitment: R_assoc = {r_related-to, r_co-occurs-with, r_similar-to}. Associative edges are undirected, represented as symmetric pairs (u, v), (v, u) in E with equal weights w(u, v) = w(v, u). This is the default class: any relation not warranting a stronger typed commitment from classes 1-3 or 5-6 defaults here. 5. Evidential (R_epist). An edge (u, v) with tau(u, v) in R_epist encodes inferential, evidential, or evaluative support between propositional or evaluative nodes: R_epist = {r_supports, r_contradicts, r_derived-from, r_supersedes}. Valence and deontic force are carried as signed edge weights on r_supports and r_contradicts edges (extending w to R on R_epist when needed); an obligation is an r_supports edge with |w(u, v)| = 1 directed at a norm node, and a prohibition is the corresponding r_contradicts edge. Here r_contradicts induces a conflict pair in (F, S); r_supersedes is generated by belief-update operators when a node is revised rather than deleted. 6. Spatial (R_spatial). An edge (u, v) with tau(u, v) in R_spatial encodes geometric relations, restricted to node pairs where at least one endpoint carries a perceptual or structured perceptual payload (Definition 2, items 3-4): R_spatial = {r_above, r_below, r_left-of, r_right-of, r_near, r_affords}. The sub-type r_affords links a body-schema node u to a perceptual node v, encoding a sensorimotor affordance relation. For any edge class R_k, write E_{R_k} = {(u, v) in E | tau(u, v) in R_k} for the induced edge set. {"assumptions":["two independent centered Gaussian fields on a common finite or suitably truncated index set","existence and enough regularity of the covariance functions to differentiate the interpolated expectation under the integral","a consistent-sign comparison, or specific structural relation, between the two covariance kernels","the test functional F smooth with the correct sign of mixed partial derivatives for the interpolation identity to yield a useful inequality rather than an uncontrolled remainder"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T15:09:50+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5fa8b83fd50055a08d35585e9f6488fdcbf8c30e41cd0f005a4089a7587fbe6d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For two independent centered Gaussian fields X, Y indexed by a common finite (or suitably truncated) set T with covariance functions C_X, C_Y, Kahane's interpolation forms Z(t,u) = sqrt(u) X(t) + sqrt(1-u) Y(t) for u in [0,1] and computes d/du E[F(Z(.,u))] for a smooth test function F, obtaining, since Z(.,u) has covariance u C_X + (1-u) C_Y, d/du E[F(Z(.,u))] = (1/2) sum_{s,t in T} (C_X(s,t) - C_Y(s,t)) E[d_s d_t F(Z(.,u))]. When C_X <= C_Y pointwise (or the relevant difference has a consistent sign) and F is chosen with matching sign of mixed partials, this yields a comparison inequality between functionals of X and Y, an approach that both generalizes Slepian-type comparisons and, in the Gaussian multiplicative chaos literature, is used to show that different regularizations of a log-correlated field, such as the two-dimensional Gaussian free field, converge to the same limiting chaos measure regardless of the approximation scheme, a key technical step in constructing Liouville quantum gravity measures. It does not apply to non-Gaussian fields, the interpolation is built from independent copies of the two fields (always available, since only their laws are compared; a dependent coupling adds cross-covariance terms to the derivative), and the sign or convexity conditions on F needed to obtain a clean inequality must be verified case by case rather than assumed. Typical failure: Running the interpolation on a dependent coupling of the two fields while dropping the cross-covariance terms, or to a family of regularizations whose covariance difference does not have a consistent sign across the whole index set, which is common when comparing regularizations of a log-correlated field near its singular set; either error breaks the monotonicity the interpolation is meant to exploit, and the resulting comparison can go in the wrong direction with no explicit error term to control it. {"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space and A is self-adjoint on it","psi lies in the absolutely continuous subspace of A and its spectral density is bounded by M almost everywhere","K is Hilbert-Schmidt (in particular compact); boundedness alone is not enough","the Fourier convention is exp(-i t lambda), which fixes the constant 2 pi","the estimate is uniform in psi given the density bound and in K given its Hilbert-Schmidt norm"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.091166+00:00","domain":"spectral theory, scattering theory, trace class perturbations","id":"claim_5fbe9483d9083c1e18b3ec600c653d4f2d8f70dfbfef14f47a1428b1b63ecc4f","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"CAUTION ON THE NAME: 'Rosenblum's argument' is used for at least two different results of M. Rosenblum; this entry is the scattering-theory one, the Plancherel estimate that drives the Kato-Rosenblum theorem on trace class perturbations and the standard existence proofs for wave operators. STATEMENT: let A be a self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space H with spectral measure E, let psi in H be a vector whose spectral measure mu_psi(S) = <psi, E(S) psi> is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure with density bounded by a constant M (that is, d mu_psi / d lambda <= M almost everywhere), and let K be a Hilbert-Schmidt operator on H. Then the map t -> K exp(-i t A) psi is square integrable on R as an H-valued function and the integral over R of the squared norm of K exp(-i t A) psi dt is at most 2 pi M times the square of the Hilbert-Schmidt norm of K. Consequently the quantity tends to 0 along a sequence of times, and combined with Cook's criterion this is what produces existence of wave operators for perturbations that factor through Hilbert-Schmidt operators; note that the bound is UNIFORM over all vectors psi with the same density bound M, which is how the estimate is bootstrapped from a dense set of vectors to the whole absolutely continuous subspace. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) the bounded density is essential. If psi has any point mass, for instance if psi is an eigenvector of A, then the norm of K exp(-i t A) psi equals the norm of K psi for all t and the time integral is infinite unless K psi = 0. The lemma is a statement about the absolutely continuous subspace with a locally bounded density, not about arbitrary vectors. (ii) 'Hilbert-Schmidt' cannot be relaxed to 'bounded': taking K the identity makes the left-hand side the integral of a positive constant over R, which diverges. (iii) The constant 2 pi is tied to the Fourier convention; with the kernel exp(-2 pi i t lambda) the constant is 1. (iv) Nothing is claimed about the pointwise decay of the norm of K exp(-i t A) psi in t; only its square integrability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["central sections (linear subspaces)","Q_n = [-1/2,1/2]^n","the density statement is for the uniform distribution on the cube only"],"created_at":"2026-09-23T01:01:03.840385+00:00","domain":"convex geometry","id":"claim_60a0a21170034ccb810c9ec9bf50076c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Q_n = [-1/2,1/2]^n and 1 <= k <= n. For every k-dimensional linear subspace H of R^n: vol_k(Q_n \\cap H) <= min{ (n/k)^{k/2}, 2^{(n-k)/2} }. The first bound is attained when k divides n (H spanned by the sums of the coordinate vectors over k disjoint blocks of size n/k); the second is the smaller one and is attained when k >= n/2. Equivalently, a central section of codimension m has volume <= min{ (n/(n-m))^{(n-m)/2}, 2^{m/2} }, with 2^{m/2} attained when m <= n/2. Probabilistic form: if U is uniform on Q_n and P is the orthogonal projection onto an m-dimensional subspace E, the density of PU is largest at 0, where it equals vol_{n-m}(Q_n \\cap E^perp); hence it is at most min{ (n/(n-m))^{(n-m)/2}, 2^{m/2} } <= 2^{m/2}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["h is a Gaussian free field with Dirichlet (or otherwise precisely specified) boundary conditions on domain D","U is a deterministic, or at least suitably measurable stopping-domain, subdomain of D","the Green's function and harmonic measure for D and U are well defined, requiring sufficient domain regularity","correct identification of phi_U as harmonic in U with boundary values equal to h on the boundary of U"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.988093+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_611d06babfa0bac3e6ad00051e94ec2a9160b2c2c47e76bdc0ac9037b7eb263d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Let h be a (discrete or continuum) Gaussian free field on a domain D with Dirichlet boundary conditions, and let U be a deterministic subdomain of D. The Gibbs-Markov (domain Markov) property states that h decomposes as h = h_U + phi_U, where h_U is a zero-boundary Gaussian free field on U, phi_U is the harmonic extension into U of the values of h on the boundary of U, h_U and phi_U are independent of each other, and phi_U is measurable with respect to the sigma-field generated by h restricted to the complement of U. This is the discrete and continuum analogue of the strong Markov property for Brownian motion and harmonic functions, and it is the fundamental tool enabling induction-on-scale arguments, the theory of local sets, and the construction of conformally invariant objects such as Liouville quantum gravity from the field. It does not hold for general non-Gibbsian or non-Gaussian log-correlated fields without separate verification, and it requires exact specification of the domain and boundary conditions, since the decomposition depends on the harmonic extension operator for the particular pair (D,U) being used. Typical failure: Applying the plain Gibbs-Markov decomposition with U chosen depending on the field h itself, such as a random subdomain determined by a level set or an exploration process, without checking that U is a valid stopping domain for the field's filtration; naively random domains destroy the independence between h_U and phi_U, and the correct fix requires the more delicate theory of local sets developed by Schramm and Sheffield, not the plain domain Markov property. Canonical reference: Sheffield, 2007, Probability Theory and Related Fields; Schramm and Sheffield, 2013, Probability Theory and Related Fields.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["All explicit definitions in proofs/BOUNDED_RELU_PAIRED.md","Even width; independent Gaussian hidden-weight pairs with equal hidden weights and opposite heads +/-nu, nu fixed in (0,1]; neurons are not iid","Unit-norm centered ReLU teacher with a nonzero interaction Walsh coefficient on the support","Noise standard deviation c_e=e^2/sqrt((1+e^2+e^4)(1+e^2)) tends to zero; n=4 stratified training and uniform test support","Risk averaged over sixteen independent label-noise sign patterns; GD step 1/2; width limit precedes feature-scale limit"],"created_at":"2026-10-22T00:34:14.190364+00:00","domain":"learning theory","id":"claim_6150b2543bd28a2853e880d5bd25f8624c1e1b6cb15383b4cea07167bb4daeae","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"# Unit-norm nonlinear ReLU teacher with paired initialization

T267 / Target 1 / C010 / proof draft (unaudited); novelty unestablished.

This removes the diverging teacher norm in C009, at the price of paired
initialization and noise that shrinks with the signal. It is a restricted
four-point, stratified-design, noise-averaged theorem. It does not establish
the generic iid Gaussian-input target or a fixed-positive-noise result.
The hardest remaining target step is sign-level population-risk control
for a genuinely sampled nonlinear model beyond this finite-support
infinite-width construction.

## Statement

Fix nu in (0,1]. For 0<e<1/4 let D=1+e^2+e^4 and use the same four inputs
x_(s,t)=(1,e s,e^2 t)/sqrt(D), s,t in {-1,1}. Training contains each once;
the test law is uniform on these four points. Let

u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2),
c_e=e^2/[sqrt(D)*sqrt(1+e^2)], alpha_e=c_e/2,
g_e(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-E_X ReLU(u_e.X).

The vector u_e has norm one. On this support u_e.x=c_e(s+t), so

g_e(x_(s,t))=alpha_e(s+t+st).

Thus the teacher is genuinely nonlinear even when restricted to the
support: no affine function of x has a nonzero st Walsh coefficient.
The centering constant is the population mean c_e/2. Labels are g_e(x_i)
plus independent equiprobable noise +/-c_e, so the noise standard deviation
is c_e, not a fixed positive constant as e decreases.

Take even width m=2N and initialize each independent pair by
w_(2j-1)=w_(2j)=W_j iid N(0,I_3),
a_(2j-1)=nu, a_(2j)=-nu.
Pairs are independent; the individual neurons are NOT iid. Initially f=0
exactly. Train both layers of every neuron by simultaneous GD at step 1/2,
loss ||f(X)-y||^2/(2n), n=4, with f=m^(-1/2) sum a ReLU(w.x) and gate
convention 1_{z>0}. No symmetry is imposed after initialization.

Let Q_(m,e)(k) be clean population squared risk, averaged over the sixteen
training-label-noise patterns, conditional on initialization. Let b_h be
C009's rates for the full initial tangent kernel h_nu=k+nu^2 g1, with mode
indices 0,1,2,12. Set

k0=ceil(e^(-1/2)), k1=floor(log(2)/b1),
k2=ceil(e^(-3/2)), k3=floor(log(2)/b2),
B=log[b1/(b2+b12)].

In the iterated limit m=2N->infinity first, then e->0, the probability of
failure of the strict witnesses

Q(k0)>Q(k1)<Q(k2)>Q(k3)

tends to zero. More precisely the four risks divided by alpha_e^2 converge
in probability, in that iterated sense, to 4,7/2,4,3.
For every fixed delta>0, every maximizer k_peak on the integer interval
I_e=[floor((B-1)/b1),ceil((B+1)/b1)] is interior and satisfies
|b1 k_peak-B|<delta with probability tending to one in the same iterated
sense. Consequently

k_peak ~ (4*pi/nu^2) e^(-1) log(1/e).

This localizes a central local peak, not a global maximum or all extrema.

## 1. Teacher identity and exact initialization

ReLU(s+t) takes values 2,0,0,0, whose mean is 1/2. Its centered version is
(s+t+st)/2. The unit norm and displayed teacher identity follow directly.
The nonzero interaction coefficient rules out an affine teacher on the
four inputs, even though two projections lie exactly at the teacher's
ReLU kink. No differentiability of the teacher is used in training.

Each pair has exactly cancelling outputs. Its two readout-Jacobian Gram
summands are identical. Its two hidden-Jacobian Gram summands are also
identical because their readout factors are squared. Dividing by m=2N
therefore gives the same expected full kernel as in C009:

C_(nu,e)(i,l)=[k(x_i.x_l)+nu^2 g1(x_i.x_l)]/4.

Strong laws apply to the N independent pairs. No independent-neuron
concentration or centered independent readout-sign argument is needed.

## 2. Transfer from the actual nonlinear GD

Here we specify why C009 Section 3 applies despite correlated pairs.
For e<1/4, c_e<e^2<1/16. The largest absolute teacher value is 3c_e/2;
the largest label magnitude is at most 5c_e/2<5/32. Thus ||y||<5/16<2.
The actual initial output is identically zero; use M=0 and R_0=2 in the
deterministic finite-horizon recurrences of C009 Section 3. Those bounds
are neuronwise and use no independence. They hold separately for both
members of every pair, even after their hidden weights separate.

The empirical mean of initial squared hidden norms converges almost surely
to 3 by the pairwise strong law. The weighted initial gate-band mass is
now exactly the mean over N independent W_j of
(1+||W_j||)^2 1{min_i|W_j.x_i| <= D_* (1+||W_j||)/sqrt(2N)}.
It tends to zero by the same rational-band strong-law and dominated-
convergence argument as C009. The initial kernel converges entrywise to
C by the pairwise strong law. These are the only probabilistic inputs to
the instantaneous-kernel and exact discrete-step remainder bounds in C009.
Their finite-horizon telescoping proof therefore gives

max_(k<=T) ||f_actual(k)-f_frozen(k)|| -> 0 in probability

for every fixed e,nu,T, uniformly over all sixteen noise patterns. The
frozen iteration starts at zero exactly. Here and below T may depend on e;
width tends to infinity separately for each fixed e. This does not claim a
uniform feature-scale rate or a feasible numerical width.

## 3. Risk margins

All three nonconstant teacher Walsh coefficients are alpha=alpha_e.
Independent +/-c_e label noise has Walsh variances c_e^2/4=alpha^2.
Parseval and the zero initial prediction give the exact frozen risk

Q_e^0(k)/alpha^2 = (1-q0^k)^2
                 + sum_(h=1,2,12) [q_h^(2k)+(1-q_h^k)^2],
q_h=exp(-b_h).

C009 Section 2 supplies b1~nu^2 e/(4pi), b2~nu^2 e^2/(8pi),
b12/b2->1, and b0 bounded away from zero. At k0 all nonconstant modes
remain unlearned, giving 1+1+1+1=4. At k1 the fast component has q1->1/2
and the two slow components remain at one, giving 1+1/2+1+1=7/2.
At k2 the fast component has q1->0 while slow components remain at one,
giving 4. At k3 both slow components have q->1/2, giving 1+1+1/2+1/2=3.
The three strict limiting margins are 1/2,1/2,1. For fixed e, alpha>0 and
the finite-horizon transfer changes risk by o_P(1), hence by o_P(alpha^2)
as width grows; division by a fixed positive alpha^2 is legitimate.
Then let e decrease. This proves the four strict actual-risk witnesses.

## 4. Central peak

Interpolate the frozen curve continuously and put z=(B+s)/b1 with
B=log[b1/(b2+b12)]. Uniformly for s in compact intervals,

(Q_e^0)'(z)/[2 alpha^2 (b2+b12)] -> exp(-s)-1,
(Q_e^0)''(z)/[2 alpha^2 b1 (b2+b12)] -> -exp(-s).

Indeed each nonconstant mode contributes 2 alpha^2 b_h q_h(1-2q_h).
The fast term contributes exp(-s); its quadratic correction is
O((b2+b12)/b1). The two slow terms contribute -b2/(b2+b12) and
-b12/(b2+b12), up to errors O(((b2+b12)/b1) B). The constant-mode
term and its derivatives vanish faster than any polynomial of e.
The same estimates after one further differentiation give the stated
second derivative. Thus the frozen central peak has scaled coordinate
s_e->0 and a strict value gap away from any fixed delta neighborhood,
of order alpha^2 (b2+b12)/b1, by integrating the derivative on [-1,1].
The grid spacing b1 tends to zero, so discrete maximizers obey the same
localization. When delta>=1, the conclusion follows from any smaller
positive delta, and interval endpoints are excluded as well.

For each fixed e the interval is finite and its positive peak gap is a
fixed positive number. Section 2 therefore transfers the maximizer
localization to the actual risk with probability tending to one as width
grows. No random initial-output perturbation occurs. Finally
b1/(b2+b12)~1/e and b1~nu^2 e/(4pi) give the peak asymptotic.

## Scope and dependencies

This proof depends on the unaudited deterministic bounds and Gaussian
kernel asymptotics in C009, not on an independent audit or a floating-point
fit. Pair cancellation is only an initial condition, not frozen weights.
The centering offset is part of the single-index link ReLU(z)-c_e/2.
The teacher has uniformly unit norm and is nonlinear on the support;
its variation and the label-noise standard deviation both vanish as e^2.
The design remains stratified, finite support, with every test input in
training, and risk averages over labels. No fixed-noise, iid-design,
macroscopic feature-learning, full-target or novelty claim is made.
Primary kernel source: Heckel--Yilmaz arXiv:2007.10099v2 Section 3 K1/K2.
The existence of two noise thresholds in Stephenson--Lee 2108.12006 is not
used to infer that this model has the same noise window.","status":"unverified"}

Use H(sigma)=-J sum_edges sigma_u sigma_v-B sum_v sigma_v with J>0,B>=0,Jh>B, and Gibbs law pi proportional to exp(-beta H). Consider any reversible single-spin continuous-time chain with each individual spin-flip rate at most1. Put A={number of plus spins< n/2}. Global spin reversal maps A bijectively onto its complement and does not decrease Gibbs weight, so pi(A)<=1/2. An A-to-complement jump must start with(n-1)/2 plus spins, whose energy exceeds the all-minus energy by at least(Jh-B)(n-1). There are at most2^n such states and total exit rate at most n per state. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726454+00:00","domain":"hyperbolic systems of partial differential equations","id":"claim_61f88f542a4ccb5b73d71ec83ca39d41269940f02589236c6fbe2be28d174a87","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: in ∂_t u + Σ_j A_j ∂_j u = 0 the estimate ‖u(t)‖_{L²} ≤ e^{Kt}‖u(0)‖_{L²} comes from the Hermitian symmetry of the A_j (which makes u* A_j ∂_j u an exact divergence up to lower order). Real eigenvalues alone (weak hyperbolicity) are not enough. Concrete counterexample in n = 1, m = 2: take A = [[0,1],[0,0]], a Jordan block whose only eigenvalue is 0 (real, so the system is weakly hyperbolic) but which is not symmetrizable. The system ∂_t u1 + ∂_x u2 = 0, ∂_t u2 = 0 with data (f,g) has the solution u2(t,x) = g(x), u1(t,x) = f(x) − t g'(x). So ‖u(t)‖_{L²} ≥ t‖g'‖_{L²} − ‖f‖_{L²}, which is not bounded by any function of t times ‖(f,g)‖_{L²}: one derivative is lost per unit time, and the Cauchy problem is ill-posed in L² (and in every H^s). Consequences for auditing: (i) hyperbolicity claims must say symmetric, symmetrizable or strictly hyperbolic, never merely 'real eigenvalues'; (ii) the constant K in the energy estimate depends on sup|Σ_j ∂_j A_j| and sup|B|, so the argument needs the coefficients to be differentiable in x with bounded derivative — Lipschitz in x is enough (the derivative then exists a.e. and is bounded), but mere continuity is not, and for merely continuous, non-Lipschitz coefficients well-posedness can genuinely fail with a loss of derivatives; (iii) after an approximate symmetrization, the estimate holds with the symmetrizer's constants, not with 1.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["N is a compact interval or the circle S^1 and f: N -> N is C^2 (not merely C^1)","Lambda is compact and forward invariant, f(Lambda) contained in Lambda","Lambda contains no critical point of f","every periodic point of f that lies in Lambda is hyperbolic repelling (no attracting or neutral periodic point in Lambda)","if N is the circle, f has at least one periodic point (excludes homeomorphisms of irrational rotation number, where the conclusion fails)"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:01:13.770157+00:00","domain":"one-dimensional real dynamics, hyperbolicity, interval and circle maps","id":"claim_626a47d09abfde2732f5b51624f4b49b88dc93b649aef5efde91c164e135a82b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Setting: $N$ is a compact interval or the circle $S^1$, and $f: N \to N$ is a $C^2$ map. Write $\mathrm{Crit}(f) = \{x : Df(x) = 0\}$ for the critical set. A periodic point $p$ of period $k$ is hyperbolic repelling if $|Df^k(p)| > 1$.

Theorem (Mañé, 1985). Let $\Lambda \subset N$ be a compact set which is forward invariant ($f(\Lambda) \subset \Lambda$) and such that
  (i) $\Lambda$ contains no critical point of $f$, and
  (ii) every periodic point of $f$ lying in $\Lambda$ is hyperbolic repelling (so $\Lambda$ contains no attracting and no neutral / indifferent periodic point);
  (iii) if $N = S^1$, assume in addition that $f$ has at least one periodic point in $N$. (This excludes in particular every circle homeomorphism of irrational rotation number, for which the conclusion is false; the literature states the caveat as 'f is not a homeomorphism without periodic points', and the hypothesis given here is the safe, slightly stronger form. Interval maps always have a fixed point, so (iii) is automatic on an interval.)
Then $\Lambda$ is uniformly expanding (a hyperbolic repelling set): there exist constants $C > 0$ and $\lambda > 1$, depending only on $f$ and $\Lambda$, such that
  $|Df^n(x)| \ge C \lambda^n$ for every $x \in \Lambda$ and every $n \ge 0$.

Standard corollary (the form usually quoted as the uniform expansion criterion). Suppose every periodic orbit of $f$ is hyperbolic repelling (and, on the circle, $f$ has a periodic point). Let $U$ be any open neighbourhood of $\mathrm{Crit}(f)$ and let $\Lambda(U) = \{x \in N : f^n(x) \notin U \text{ for all } n \ge 0\}$ be the set of points whose forward orbit never enters $U$. Then $\Lambda(U)$ is compact, forward invariant, disjoint from the critical set, and hence uniformly expanding: $|Df^n(x)| \ge C_U \lambda_U^n$ on $\Lambda(U)$. In words: 'all periodic orbits repelling' forces uniform expansion on any piece of the phase space that stays a fixed distance away from the critical points. Consequently every point either accumulates on the critical set or is uniformly expanded.

Where it FAILS if a hypothesis is dropped. (a) Without (i) the conclusion is false trivially: $Df = 0$ at a critical point. (b) Without (ii): an attracting or neutral periodic point in $\Lambda$ has $|Df^{nk}(p)| \le 1$. Attracting periodic orbits may exist elsewhere in $N$; the theorem only asks that none lies in $\Lambda$. (c) Without (iii): an irrational rotation, or any $C^2$ circle diffeomorphism with irrational rotation number, has $\Lambda = S^1$, no critical points and no periodic points at all (so (ii) holds vacuously), yet the derivatives $|Df^n|$ do not grow exponentially (each $f^n$ is a diffeomorphism of a circle of length 1, so $\min_x |Df^n(x)| \le 1$ for all $n$). (d) Smoothness: the proof uses $C^2$ (bounded distortion of iterates away from critical points); do not quote it for maps that are merely $C^1$. (e) Only one-dimensional: this is a theorem about interval and circle maps; there is no analogue for higher-dimensional maps or for holomorphic maps without further hypotheses. Note also that the theorem does NOT assume non-flat critical points and does NOT need to assume the absence of wandering intervals: both are handled inside the proof, and in particular no wandering interval can lie in a set $\Lambda$ satisfying (i)-(iii).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["F and its time derivative are continuous (F is C^1) on a neighbourhood of the closures of the moving domains","the domain is transported by a C^1 velocity field (one variable: the endpoints are C^1 functions of t)","the domain is bounded with Lipschitz boundary so that the divergence theorem applies","only the outward normal component of the boundary velocity enters the boundary term"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.437853+00:00","domain":"multivariable calculus, differentiation under the integral sign, continuum mechanics","id":"claim_62b43e5fca8e969efa6f05850018f3c363b1cc5d7374171927d6d89b2ccbc124","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"ONE VARIABLE. Let $a, b: (t_0, t_1) \to \mathbb{R}$ be $C^1$ and let $F(x, t)$ and $\partial_t F(x, t)$ be continuous on an open set of $\mathbb{R}^2$ containing $\{(x,t) : t \in (t_0,t_1),\ x \text{ between } a(t) \text{ and } b(t)\}$. Then for $t \in (t_0, t_1)$
$$\frac{d}{dt} \int_{a(t)}^{b(t)} F(x,t)\,dx = \int_{a(t)}^{b(t)} \partial_t F(x,t)\,dx + F(b(t),t)\, b'(t) - F(a(t),t)\, a'(t).$$

SEVERAL VARIABLES. Let $v(x,t)$ be a $C^1$ velocity field on an open set $U \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, $t \in (t_0, t_1)$, with flow $\varphi_t$ (so $\partial_t \varphi_t(y) = v(\varphi_t(y), t)$, $\varphi_{0} = \mathrm{id}$), and let $\Omega(t) = \varphi_t(\Omega_0)$ where $\Omega_0$ is a bounded open set with Lipschitz (e.g. piecewise $C^1$) boundary whose closure stays in $U$. Let $F(x,t)$ be $C^1$ on $U \times (t_0, t_1)$. Then
$$\frac{d}{dt} \int_{\Omega(t)} F\,dx = \int_{\Omega(t)} \partial_t F\,dx + \int_{\partial \Omega(t)} F\,(v \cdot \nu)\,dS = \int_{\Omega(t)} \big(\partial_t F + \nabla\cdot(F v)\big)\,dx,$$
where $\nu$ is the outward unit normal and $v \cdot \nu$ is the outward normal velocity of the boundary. Only the NORMAL component of the boundary velocity enters: two motions of the domain whose boundaries sweep the same sets (differing by a tangential reparametrisation) give the same derivative, so the formula can be stated with any $C^1$ boundary velocity having the correct normal component. The one-variable formula is the case $n = 1$, $\nu = \pm 1$ at $b$ and $a$.

WHERE IT FAILS OR NEEDS CARE. (1) $F$ must be continuous up to the moving boundary from inside; if $F$ jumps across $\partial\Omega(t)$ the boundary integrand is the one-sided limit from inside $\Omega(t)$. (2) $\partial_t F$ must be integrable over $\Omega(t)$ (continuity on a compact closure suffices); without domination, differentiation under the integral sign can fail. (3) The bounded-domain / Lipschitz-boundary hypothesis is what licenses the divergence theorem in the second equality; the first equality (Lagrangian form) needs only the change of variables. (4) If the domain is not transported by a $C^1$ flow but its boundary merely moves with a prescribed normal speed $w$, the same formula holds with $v \cdot \nu$ replaced by $w$, but the proof must build a flow with that normal speed.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542799+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_637545cab4581aec18b900458dddacc53f40eafaa957969735334b08e256a82f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be an event depending on the states of a finite set of edges, and let omega be a configuration. The edge e is PIVOTAL for A at omega if the occurrence of A is decided by the state of e alone, that is if omega with e forced open lies in A and omega with e forced closed does not, or the reverse. Pivotality is a function of the states of the OTHER edges only, so the event {e is pivotal for A} is independent of the state of e - a fact used constantly and easy to forget. The INFLUENCE of e on A under P_p is I_e(A) = P_p( e is pivotal for A ). Under the uniform measure on the discrete cube this coincides with the usual influence P( f(X) != f(X with coordinate e flipped) ) for the indicator f of A. The total influence sum_e I_e(A) is, by Russo's formula, exactly the derivative of p -> P_p(A) for increasing A, which is why influences govern the sharpness of the phase transition; and by the Kahn-Kalai-Linial theorem the maximum influence of a balanced Boolean function on n coordinates is at least of order log n / n, which is the quantitative input behind sharp-threshold results.
