{"assumptions":["mu is a T-invariant probability measure","partitions are finite or have finite static entropy"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T12:13:53+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, entropy","id":"claim_637c65a50c50c4a412cd1517de9fbd833d8ddce462113a909e4ca6ed27e8e5e4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \\mathcal{B}, \\mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system. For a finite (or countable, with finite entropy) measurable partition $\\xi = \\{A_1, \\dots, A_k\\}$ put $H_\\mu(\\xi) = -\\sum_i \\mu(A_i) \\log \\mu(A_i)$ (with $0 \\log 0 = 0$), and $\\xi^n_0 = \\bigvee_{j=0}^{n-1} T^{-j}\\xi$, the partition into sets $A_{i_0} \\cap T^{-1}A_{i_1} \\cap \\dots \\cap T^{-(n-1)}A_{i_{n-1}}$ (the $n$-step itineraries). The entropy of $T$ relative to $\\xi$ is $h_\\mu(T, \\xi) = \\lim_{n\\to\\infty} \\frac1n H_\\mu(\\xi^n_0)$ (the limit exists because $n \\mapsto H_\\mu(\\xi^n_0)$ is subadditive; it also equals $\\inf_n \\frac1n H_\\mu(\\xi^n_0)$ and $\\lim_n H_\\mu(\\xi \\mid \\xi^n_1)$). The Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy is $h_\\mu(T) = \\sup_\\xi h_\\mu(T, \\xi)$ over finite partitions, in $[0, \\infty]$. Facts used constantly: $h_\\mu(T, \\xi) \\le H_\\mu(\\xi) \\le \\log k$; $h_\\mu(T, \\xi) \\le h_\\mu(T, \\eta) + H_\\mu(\\xi \\mid \\eta)$ for partitions $\\xi, \\eta$; $h_\\mu(T^m) = m\\, h_\\mu(T)$ for $m \\ge 1$; the Kolmogorov-Sinai generator theorem: if $\\xi$ is a generator ($\\bigvee_{j \\ge 0} T^{-j}\\xi$ generates $\\mathcal{B}$ mod $\\mu$, or $\\bigvee_{j\\in\\mathbb{Z}}$ for invertible $T$) then $h_\\mu(T) = h_\\mu(T, \\xi)$; and if $\\xi_m$ is an increasing sequence of partitions generating $\\mathcal{B}$ then $h_\\mu(T, \\xi_m) \\uparrow h_\\mu(T)$. On a compact metric space, finite Borel partitions $\\xi_m$ with $\\mathrm{diam}(\\xi_m) \\to 0$ also give $h_\\mu(T, \\xi_m) \\to h_\\mu(T)$ (for every finite partition $\\eta$, $H_\\mu(\\eta \\mid \\xi_m) \\to 0$), but not monotonically in general, since such partitions need not refine one another. The map $\\mu \\mapsto h_\\mu(T)$ on invariant measures is affine, but it is NOT in general continuous or even upper semicontinuous in the weak* topology; upper semicontinuity holds when $T$ is expansive (and for $C^\\infty$ maps of compact manifolds by Newhouse), which is what guarantees measures of maximal entropy exist in those cases.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["All explicit definitions and width/scale limit order in proofs/IID_FIXED_NOISE.md","Uniform four-atom input law, unit-norm centered-ReLU single-index teacher; n(e)~4sigma^2 e^-4","Label noise independent symmetric +/-sigma, sigma fixed in (0,1]; clean risk averages over labels conditional on input sample and initialization","Paired Gaussian hidden initialization and opposite nonzero heads +/-nu, nu fixed in (0,1]; step 1/2, both layers trained","Finite-horizon comparison through T_e=ceil(e^-5/2); population support remains finite and initialization is not iid across individual neurons"],"created_at":"2026-10-22T00:34:54.664213+00:00","domain":"learning theory","id":"claim_63eeb2ba518fa80ea62431166cebf7979ced645d133468563296bbc7eb2cb3ce","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"# Iid finite-support samples with fixed label noise and unit-norm ReLU teacher

T267 / Target 1 / C013 / proof draft (unaudited); novelty unestablished.
This removes stratification and vanishing label-noise amplitude from C010.
The remaining finite population support, paired initialization, tangent-
kernel limit and averaging over label noise are substantive restrictions.

## 1. Statement

Use C010's four unit inputs x_(s,t), uniform population distribution and
centered unit-norm ReLU teacher g_e=alpha_e(s+t+st). Fix nu in (0,1] and
label-noise amplitude sigma in (0,1], independently of feature scale e.
Take n(e)=ceil(sigma^2/alpha_e^2) independent population input samples,
and label each by g_e(x)+epsilon, with independent epsilon uniform +/-sigma.
Initialize an even-width two-layer ReLU net by independent Gaussian pairs
with equal hidden weights and opposite readouts +/-nu, as in C010.
Training inputs, label noises and initialization are mutually independent.
Train all parameters by simultaneous GD at step gamma=1/2 on empirical
squared loss divided by 2n(e). No post-initialization parameter tying.

Let Q_(m,e)(k) be clean population squared risk averaged over all training
label noises, conditional on input samples and network initialization.
Use C010's rates b_h and witness times k0,k1,k2,k3, and its central integer
interval I_e with B=log[b1/(b2+b12)]. Then in the iterated even-width-first,
feature-scale-second limit, with probability tending to one over iid
training inputs and initialization:

Q(k0)>Q(k1)<Q(k2)>Q(k3),
(Q(k0),Q(k1),Q(k2),Q(k3))/alpha_e^2 -> (4,7/2,4,3),

and every maximizer k_peak on I_e is interior and satisfies
b1 k_peak-B ->0. In particular

k_peak ~ (4pi/nu^2) e^(-1) log(1/e).

All convergence in probability uses the order lim_(e->0) limsup_(m->infinity)
of each failure probability. Sample size n(e) grows as 4sigma^2 e^(-4);
it is fixed during each width limit. The theorem does not assert high
probability over realized labels; risk itself averages over label noise.
No Gaussian-input or full Target1 solution is claimed.

## 2. Collapse repeated inputs exactly

Let N_i be the count of population point i, p_i=N_i/n, and
D=diag(4p_i). On the event all N_i>0 let bar y_i be the mean label in cell i.
The empirical loss equals

(1/2) sum_i p_i (f(x_i)-bar y_i)^2 + a parameter-independent constant.

Consequently every parameter update is exactly the update on these four
cell means with weights p_i. Conditional on counts, the cell-mean noise
has mean zero and diagonal covariance

V=diag(sigma^2/N_i)=(4sigma^2/n)D^(-1).

No Gaussian approximation or independence of Walsh coefficients is used.
The test law remains uniform on the population support, including when
the realized training counts are unequal.

## 3. Count concentration

Put delta=||D-I||. Each diagonal deviation has mean zero and variance 3/n,
because N_i is binomial(n,1/4). Chebyshev plus a union bound gives

P(delta>r)<=12/(n r^2).

Take r=e^(3/2). Since n is asymptotic to 4sigma^2 e^(-4), the failure
probability is O(e), for fixed sigma. For all small e, on the resulting
good event delta<=e^(3/2)<1/2, every cell is nonempty and
D lies between (1-delta)I and (1+delta)I. This is the only sample-count
event used. There is no fixed-count conditioning in the final theorem.

## 4. Weighted frozen-kernel stability without a slow-gap denominator

Let C be C009's deterministic full initial tangent matrix, with ||C||<=1,
and A=I-gamma C, gamma=1/2. Compare zero-start prediction iterations
using C and C D, both with the SAME cell-mean label vector bar y.
Write their residuals r_I(k),r_D(k) and prediction difference d(k).

The matrix I-gamma C D is similar, by D^(1/2), to the symmetric matrix
I-gamma D^(1/2) C D^(1/2). The latter has eigenvalues in [0,1] when
delta<=1/2, since gamma||D|| ||C||<=3/4. Thus

||r_D(k)|| <= kappa_delta ||bar y||,
kappa_delta=sqrt((1+delta)/(1-delta))<=sqrt(3)<2.

Subtracting the two iterations and using d(0)=0 gives

d(k)=-gamma sum_(j=0)^(k-1) A^(k-1-j) C(D-I)r_D(j).

For l>=0, spectral calculus yields
||gamma C A^l||<=1/(l+1): each eigenvalue is a(1-a)^l with a in [0,1/2],
whose maximum is bounded by 1/(l+1). Therefore

||d(k)||<=kappa_delta delta H_k ||bar y||,
H_k=sum_(j=1)^k 1/j <=1+log k, k>=1.

The crucial feature is logarithmic time growth rather than division by
the smallest eigenvalue of C. This argument does not assume that C and D
commute. For k=0 the difference is zero and H_0=0.

## 5. Uniform noise-averaged risk comparison

Let Q_D(k) denote the clean frozen risk using C D and the actual cell-
mean noise. Let Q_I,V(k) use C and the same noise covariance V. Since
||g||^2=12alpha^2 and tr V<=32alpha^2 on delta<=1/2 (n>=sigma^2/alpha^2),
E||bar y||^2<=44alpha^2<49alpha^2 and ||g||<4alpha.
The unweighted predictor has norm at most ||bar y||, and the weighted
predictor has norm at most (1+kappa_delta)||bar y||. Combining the risk
identity | ||a||^2-||b||^2 |<=||a-b||(||a||+||b||) with Section4 and
Cauchy--Schwarz, and dividing by four for the uniform population, gives

max_(k<=T)|Q_D(k)-Q_I,V(k)|/alpha^2 <=126 delta H_T.

For clarity this constant follows from kappa_delta<2,
(2+kappa_delta)E||bar y||^2+2||g||E||bar y|| <=252alpha^2;
the outside factor is kappa_delta delta H_T/4<delta H_T/2.

Now compare V with the balanced covariance V0=(4sigma^2/n)I.
The unweighted prediction noise map B_k=I-A^k has norm at most one.
Its risk covariance perturbation is at most

(1/4)||V-V0||_* <=4(sigma^2/n)delta/(1-delta)<=8alpha^2 delta.

Balanced covariance has Walsh variance sigma^2/n, while C010 uses alpha^2.
Let rho_round=sigma^2/(nalpha^2). Rounding n upward gives
0<=1-rho_round<=alpha^2/sigma^2. Each of four mode noise filters is at
most one, so the corresponding risk error is at most 4alpha^4/sigma^2.
Consequently, for C010's baseline zero-output curve Q_e^0,

max_(k<=T)|Q_D(k)-Q_e^0(k)|/alpha^2
 <=126 delta H_T+8delta+4alpha^2/sigma^2.

Choose T=ceil(e^(-5/2)). On the count-good event the right side is
O(e^(3/2)log(1/e))+O(e^4)=o(e). This is smaller than both C010's constant
normalized witness margins and its normalized central peak gap of order e.
All covariance arguments use exact second moments, not a central limit
approximation or a numerical experiment.

## 6. Actual nonlinear GD comparison under cell weights

We spell out the weighted extension of C010's finite-horizon argument.
On the count-good event ||D||<=3/2. For small e, each cell-mean label has
absolute value at most sigma+3alpha<2, hence ||bar y||<=4. The network
starts at zero. Use the deterministic neuronwise bounds of C009 with
R_0=4, S=14, L=2, n0=4, and replace its c_k by

gamma L (3/2)R_k/n0.

In its residual recurrence multiply the readout-kernel gradient term by
3/2 as well; the feature-motion term is already expressed through c_k.
This follows directly from replacing r by D r in both exact parameter
updates and bounding ||D r||<=3R/2. All resulting constants through a
fixed T are finite and uniform over D in [I/2,3I/2] and labels in [-2,2]^4.

Gaussian norm bounds, independent-pair strong laws, initial kernel
convergence and weighted initial gate-band mass are unchanged, since the
four possible input vectors are unchanged. Kernel drift and the exact
discrete-step gate remainder tend uniformly to zero. The frozen iteration
uses C D; its powers are bounded by sqrt(3) by Section4, so telescoping
still transfers predictions uniformly through T. Crucially the argument
is uniform over all bounded cell-mean label vectors; it does not take a
union over 2^n noise realizations or assume independent adaptive gates.
Uniform prediction control and the finite-horizon deterministic bounds
transfer noise-averaged risks as width tends to infinity for each fixed e.
Division by the fixed positive alpha^2 e is legitimate at this stage.

Thus max_(k<=T)|Q_actual(k)-Q_D(k)|/(alpha^2 e)->0 in probability over
initialization as width grows, on the count-good event, uniformly in its
counts. This claim does not give a uniform-in-e practical width threshold.

## 7. Witness and peak transfer, and remaining scope

The sample event fails with probability O(e). On it, Section5 gives
uniform surrogate-risk error o(alpha^2 e), and Section6 adds a vanishing
fixed-e width error. C010's positive risk witnesses and central peak
value gaps therefore transfer, first taking width to infinity and then
e to zero. Its entire integer peak interval and k3 lie below T for all
small e. The teacher identity and full tangent-kernel clocks are unchanged.
This proves the stated restricted theorem.

Fixed label noise, unit teacher norm and iid sampling are now explicit,
but n grows as e^(-4), the test population has only four atoms, readouts
are paired, risk averages over label noise and the proof is in a tangent-
kernel limit. It is not a generic Gaussian-design, macroscopic feature-
learning, realized-label high-probability, fixed-n, all-time, full-target
or novelty claim. C009/C010 and the uniform weighted nonlinear extension
await independent review. That extension is the least-trusted proof step.
No network training, dataset generation or large computation is needed.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Ising model, or a model with an analogous current/high-temperature expansion, with ferromagnetic couplings J_xy>=0","finite volume, or a well-defined infinite-volume limit, so the current sums converge","correct bookkeeping of source sets and the associated parity constraints defining valid currents","the switching lemma's precise combinatorial hypotheses on which pairs of currents are being exchanged"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.988477+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_646353a0e9728355c63142b0d86b9eb47ec1664b2c790cc1273707fc13579553","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For the Ising model with ferromagnetic couplings J_xy >= 0, the random-current representation writes correlation functions as sums over integer-valued edge configurations n = (n_xy) weighted by prod_{xy} (beta J_xy)^{n_xy} / n_xy!, subject to a source condition specifying a subset A of vertices where the total current degree is odd (and even elsewhere); the two-point function <sigma_x sigma_y> is proportional to the sum of weights over currents with sources {x,y}, with higher correlations expressed via larger source sets. The switching lemma is the key combinatorial identity underlying this representation: summing over pairs of independent currents with sources A and B and comparing to pairs with sources determined by the symmetric difference of A and B allows swapping which edges are assigned to which current while preserving all parity constraints, reducing correlation inequalities such as the Griffiths and Lebowitz inequalities, and Aizenman's tree-graph inequality used in proving triviality of the phi^4 field theory scaling limit in dimension d>=4 (or d=4 with logarithmic corrections), to purely combinatorial statements about current configurations. The representation does not extend beyond the Ising model or closely related models admitting an analogous high-temperature expansion, and it requires ferromagnetic couplings for the current weights to be nonnegative and hence probabilistically interpretable. Typical failure: Attempting to apply the random-current representation and switching lemma to models with mixed-sign (non-ferromagnetic) couplings, where the current weights are no longer nonnegative and the entire probabilistic interpretation, along with any downstream FKG-type consequences, breaks down; a further common error is misidentifying the source-set parity condition when composing several currents, which silently produces an identity for a different correlation function than intended. Canonical reference: Griffiths, Hurst and Sherman, 1970, Journal of Mathematical Physics; Aizenman, 1982, Communications in Mathematical Physics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n for all m, n >= 1","nothing else; the limit may be -infinity"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542097+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_64ec21a222975d147ed73e8e88f795ade040338e0b25c8717e8284dec60c0d3e","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (a_n)_{n >= 1} be a sequence of reals with a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n for all m, n >= 1. Then lim_{n -> infinity} a_n / n exists in [-infinity, +infinity) and equals inf_{n >= 1} a_n / n. In particular the limit is finite if and only if a_n / n is bounded below. The SUPERadditive version, a_{m+n} >= a_m + a_n, gives lim a_n/n = sup_n a_n/n in (-infinity, +infinity]. The lemma requires nothing beyond subadditivity - no monotonicity, no positivity, no continuity - and the limit can be minus infinity, as with a_n = -n^2. Fekete's lemma is the deterministic skeleton of Kingman's subadditive ergodic theorem: applying it to a_n = E[X_{0,n}] gives the existence of the constant that the ergodic theorem then identifies as the almost sure limit. [Fekete (1923); standard, e.g. Steele, Probability Theory and Combinatorial Optimization, Chapter 1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a centered Gaussian process, almost surely bounded on the index set, for Borell-TIS","for Slepian/Sudakov-Fernique: two Gaussian processes on the same index set with pointwise increment-variance domination E[(X_s-X_t)^2]<=E[(Y_s-Y_t)^2]","for the classical Slepian tail comparison specifically: equal marginal variances or a nonnegative-correlation condition, beyond the plain increment domination Sudakov-Fernique needs","measurability and separability of the process so the supremum is well defined"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.986173+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_65504cb28ab92ac996647f611e0658cd9e04f5e99731dc3bc37859c9883f39af","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a centered, almost surely bounded Gaussian process (X_t)_{t in T}, let M = sup_t X_t and sigma^2 = sup_t Var(X_t). The Borell-TIS inequality states P(|M - E[M]| >= u) <= 2 exp(-u^2/(2 sigma^2)) for all u >= 0, giving Gaussian concentration of the supremum around its mean at the scale of the process's maximal pointwise variance, regardless of the cardinality or geometry of the index set. Separately, Slepian's inequality compares two centered Gaussian processes on the same index set with equal marginal variances: if E[(X_s-X_t)^2] <= E[(Y_s-Y_t)^2] for all s,t, then E[sup X] <= E[sup Y], and in its classical strong form also gives a tail comparison, typically under an additional nonnegative-correlation condition. The Sudakov-Fernique inequality removes the equal-variance requirement, needing only the pointwise increment domination, but concludes only the expectation comparison E[sup X] <= E[sup Y], not the stronger distributional comparison. Together these tools reduce bounding E[sup] of a complicated Gaussian field to bounding it for a simpler, dominating comparison field. Borell-TIS does not give the value of E[M] itself, which requires a separate chaining or Dudley-integral bound, and Sudakov-Fernique is strictly weaker in conclusion than the classical Slepian inequality even when both sets of hypotheses happen to hold. Typical failure: Invoking the classical Slepian inequality's tail or distributional comparison after only verifying the weaker Sudakov-Fernique hypotheses, namely increment domination without equal variances or a correlation-sign condition; Sudakov-Fernique licenses comparing E[sup X] to E[sup Y] only, and treating the two comparison theorems as interchangeable overstates what has actually been proven. Canonical reference: Borell, 1975, Inventiones Mathematicae; Tsirelson, Ibragimov and Sudakov, 1976, in Proceedings of the School-Seminar on Random Processes; Slepian, 1962, Bell System Technical Journal; Fernique, 1975, Ecole d'Ete de Probabilites de Saint-Flour, Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics.","status":"unverified"}

A mixed strategy for player i is a probability distribution sigma_i over S_i, and the expected payoff to player i under a profile of mixed strategies sigma = (sigma_1,...,sigma_n), with players randomizing independently, is the expectation of u_i(s_1,...,s_n) over s_i drawn from sigma_i for each i.","status":"unverified"}

In full R^3 almost every initialization escapes with kq,v of matching infinite sign, factors O(sqrt(log |v|)), head-normalized limit +/-e_v and margin Gamma_+ or Gamma_-. # Target 1: almost-everywhere full-space factored gradient-flow classification

Version 1, proof unaudited. Owner own work; novelty unestablished.
This concerns continuous gradient flow, not arbitrary-step GD.

## Statement

For n>=2, b_i,kappa_i>0, 0<a_i<b_i, set
h_i(s)=a_i+b_i tanh(kappa_i s) and
L(v,k,q)=mean_i log(1+exp(-v h_i(kq))).
Let p_bar be the unique zero of mean_i h_i. For every initial point with
C=k^2-q^2!=0, the Euclidean gradient flow exists globally forward and has
exactly one of these outcomes:

1. convergence to a finite point on the stationary curve v=0,kq=p_bar;
2. v,kq->+infinity, loss->0, normalized direction (v,k,q)/norm ->(1,0,0);
3. v,kq->-infinity, loss->0, normalized direction ->(-1,0,0).

The set in outcome 1, together with the excluded balanced surfaces C=0,
has three-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Hence almost every finite
initialization belongs to one of the two escaping basins. Both basins
are open in the FULL parameter space, are nonempty, and have respective
normalized minimum margins Gamma_+=min_i(a_i+b_i) and Gamma_-=min_i(b_i-a_i).
The second is strictly inferior, as in claim 010. The known imbalance
invariant is used for reduction, not claimed as a new result.

We do not classify trajectories on C=0 in this theorem. They really allow
another fate: on k=q=0, v solves v_dot=mean_i a_i/(1+exp(v a_i))>0,
so v->infinity and L->0 while attention stays uniform. In fact a relatively
open subset of the balanced plane has this fate: if k=-q!=0, v>0 and
R<kq<0, where R=max_i rho_i<0, then v increases, s increases toward zero,
and k,q tend to zero. To check this, all h_i(s)>=c>0, forcing v->infinity.
If s tended to a strictly negative limit, alpha=2|s| and all h_i' would
be bounded below there; ds/dv>=c_1 v would contradict bounded s. Thus
s->0 and both factors vanish. Its normalized margin is min_i a_i.
These null sets demonstrate why the almost-everywhere qualification
must not be omitted.

## Reduction and global existence

Put s=kq, F=mean_i g_i h_i(s), G=mean_i g_i h_i'(s)>0,
g_i=(1+exp(v h_i(s)))^-1. Flow equations are

 v_dot=F, k_dot=vqG, q_dot=vkG.

Differentiating gives d(k^2-q^2)/dt=0. Also
(k^2+q^2)^2=C^2+4s^2. Thus on a fixed nonzero-C leaf,

 v_dot=F(v,s), s_dot=alpha_C(s) vG(v,s),
 alpha_C(s)=sqrt(C^2+4s^2)>0.

If H=max_i(a_i+b_i), M=max_i b_i kappa_i, then |v_dot|<=H.
On any finite time interval v is bounded, and
|k_dot|+|q_dot|<=M|v|(|k|+|q|). Gronwall gives finite factors on that
interval. The smooth full flow therefore has no finite-time blow-up,
in either time direction. Nonzero-C leaf coordinates are global charts on
each sheet: for C>0 fix sign k, solve
k=sign(k)sqrt((alpha_C(s)+C)/2), q=s/k;
for C<0 instead fix sign q and use the symmetric formula.

## Leaf saddle and trapping

Let A=H^2/4 and F_0(s)=F(0,s)=mean_i h_i(s)/2. Then
-A<=F_v<=0, F_0 strictly increases with unique zero p_bar, and G>0.
The sole reduced equilibrium is (0,p_bar), corresponding to one point
on each sheet. With u=s-p_bar, the two good quadrants v,u>0 and v,u<0
are forward invariant: s_dot has sign v; on the boundary v=0 the vector
field F_0(s) points into the respective quadrant. More explicitly, in
the positive quadrant v_dot>=-A v, so a strictly positive v cannot hit zero
in finite time, and u increases. Reflection treats the negative quadrant.

In a bad quadrant v>0,u<0, F(v,s)<=F_0(s)<0 and s_dot>0.
Both coordinates move monotonically toward their axes until one axis is
crossed or the orbit stays forever. Crossing an axis enters a good quadrant;
uniqueness excludes hitting the equilibrium in finite time. If the orbit
stays in the bad quadrant, it has a finite limit. Continuity and monotonicity
force F=alpha_C vG=0 at that limit, hence it is the saddle.
The other bad quadrant is handled by the reflected links -h_i(-s).
Nonstationary points on an axis enter a good quadrant immediately.

## Escape from good quadrants

Consider the positive quadrant. Then s increases from s_0>p_bar.
Suppose s tends to finite P. If v is bounded, compactness and
alpha_C G>0 imply integral_0^infinity v(t)dt<infinity.
Since |v_dot|<=H, the nonnegative function v is uniformly continuous;
the elementary disjoint-triangle argument gives v->0. But then
v_dot->F_0(P)>0, contradiction.

If v is unbounded, put R=max_i rho_i, h_i(rho_i)=0. If P<=R,
an example j with root R has h_j(s(t))<=0, hence g_j>=1/2;
on the compact s interval its derivative is >=d>0. Consequently
s_dot>=|C| d v/(2n). A finite P again implies integral v<infinity
and, by the same bounded-derivative argument, v->0: contradiction.
If P>R, eventually all h_i>=c>0. Then v increases without bound and

 ds/dv=alpha_C(s) v (mean g_i h_i')/(mean g_i h_i)
       >=|C| d v/H,

contradicting finite P. Thus s->infinity. Eventually all h_i>=c>0;
v increases and cannot remain bounded, since bounded v keeps every g_i
bounded below. Therefore v->infinity. Reflection proves negative escape.

For the direction, let kappa_0=min_i kappa_i. On the positive tail,
alpha_C(s)<=|C|+2s and

 ds/dv<=(4M/c)(|C|+2s)v exp(-2kappa_0 s).

Thus d[exp(kappa_0 s)]/dv <=C_1 v, because
(|C|+2s)exp(-kappa_0 s) is bounded on the positive tail.
Integration gives s=O(log v). Since k^2+q^2=alpha_C(s), both
factors are O(sqrt(log v)) and are negligible relative to v.
The negative branch is identical after reflection. Endpoint margin and
zero-loss limits follow. By fixed C and |s|->infinity, both |k| and |q|
also tend to infinity (their squared difference is constant).

## Leaf-null implies full-space-null

At the reduced equilibrium the linearization is

 [[-A_s,B_s],[alpha_C(p_bar) B_s,0]],
 A_s=mean h_i(p_bar)^2/4, B_s=mean h_i'(p_bar)/2>0.

Its determinant is negative; it is a hyperbolic saddle. The local stable
manifold is one-dimensional. The global stable set on a leaf is contained
in its countably many backward integer-time flow images, so is planar null;
the flow is a smooth local diffeomorphism (indeed globally defined here).

The full stationary curve E={v=0,kq=p_bar} is closed. The set
S={initial points whose distance to E tends to zero} is Borel: express
the limiting condition using countable thresholds and integer times.
For C!=0 our classification shows S is exactly the convergent set;
the leaf coordinate formulas also show convergence of k,q when s->p_bar.
Use coordinates (v,s,C) on the four open regions C>0,sign k fixed and
C<0,sign q fixed. Each coordinate map is a smooth diffeomorphism.
Every fixed-C slice of S is planar null by the preceding argument.
Fubini gives a null set in these coordinates; local diffeomorphisms
preserve null sets under a countable cover. Finally C=0 is the union of
the two planes k=q and k=-q, also null. This proves the asserted full-space
almost-everywhere dichotomy, without assuming independence across examples.

The escaping basins are open even at balanced initial points: any escaping
orbit eventually enters a strict region v>0,s>max(R,0) or v<0,s<min rho_i.
Those regions are invariant and escape, also when C=0, by the same proof
with alpha=2|s| bounded below there. (Requiring s>0 on the positive branch
is essential; a balanced negative product can instead collapse to zero.)
The union of their finite-time preimages
is open. For arbitrary escaping points the converse follows from divergence
of s. They are nonempty by claim 010's sign regions. No assertion that every
balanced trajectory escapes is needed.

## Literature scope and remaining obstruction

The comparisons in proof 008 apply: 2308.16898 and 2403.08699 treat
fixed-head factored attention, while this is the stated scalar joint-head
logistic family. The balance reduction is standard and is not a novelty claim.
For simultaneous GD, C_+=(1-eta^2 v^2 G^2)C, so these invariant leaves
are unavailable. Extending this full-space result to GD remains open here;
claim 010 proves only its arbitrary-step open sign basins.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["all moments m_k of the measure are finite","the specific growth rate of the even moments m_{2k}, needed to check whether sum m_{2k}^{-1/(2k)} diverges","if a simpler sufficient condition is invoked instead, such as compact support or subgaussian tails, that condition must itself be independently verified","the moment-convergence method is being used to establish convergence in distribution to a specific candidate limit that is separately known to be moment-determinate"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.994936+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_66433380dc750c0be230a31fb21285dac83b7ea69a958dffd48040d2335c57a8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). A probability measure mu on R is moment-determinate if it is the unique probability measure sharing its full sequence of moments (m_k)_{k>=0}. The Carleman condition gives a simple sufficient criterion: if sum_{k=1}^infinity m_{2k}^{-1/(2k)} = infinity, then mu is moment-determinate. In practice this is most often invoked via a stronger, easier-to-check sub-condition, such as subgaussian or lighter tails, for instance P(|X|>t) <= C exp(-ct^2), which implies the even moments grow at most at Gaussian rate and hence satisfy Carleman's sum divergence; a common proof strategy in random matrix theory and random measure convergence is to show convergence of all moments to those of a known moment-determinate limit, such as the compactly supported semicircle law, and then invoke Carleman's condition, or compact support directly, to upgrade moment convergence to convergence in distribution. It does not hold automatically for every measure with finite moments of all orders: the classical log-normal distribution is the standard counterexample, having finite moments of every order yet failing to be moment-determinate, so other measures share its entire moment sequence, meaning that verifying Carleman's sum diverges, or invoking compact support, is a genuinely necessary step, not a formality. Typical failure: Assuming that finiteness of all moments, or even termwise convergence of a sequence's moments to a limit's moments, is sufficient to conclude convergence in distribution, without checking that the limit measure is itself moment-determinate; the log-normal-type failure of moment determinacy is the standard cautionary example, and in random matrix or random measure contexts, using the method of moments toward a limit whose determinacy has not been separately established, as happens for some heavy-tailed spectral limits, can produce a plausible-looking but invalid convergence claim. Canonical reference: Carleman, 1926, Les Fonctions Quasi Analytiques, Gauthier-Villars; Akhiezer, The Classical Moment Problem, 1965, Hafner Publishing; Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni, An Introduction to Random Matrices, 2010, Cambridge University Press.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Counterexample flux f(u) = u^4 - 5u^2 with states u_- = 2, u_+ = -2, shock speed σ = 0","Lax inequalities compare σ only with f'(u_-) and f'(u_+)","Oleinik's condition requires the graph of f between the two states to lie on the correct side of the chord at EVERY intermediate value","For nonconvex flux the Riemann solution is generally a composite of shocks and rarefactions given by the convex (or concave) hull construction"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418807+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: hyperbolic conservation laws","id":"claim_665fbc7218ee86a7f2a8fde5b2aa270eb45fa9903d84e1f03383d32859a141ad","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: the equivalence 'admissible shock ⇔ Lax inequalities f'(u_-) ≥ σ ≥ f'(u_+)' requires the flux to be convex (genuinely nonlinear) on the range of the data. For a nonconvex flux one must use Oleinik's full chord condition, which involves f at every intermediate state, not only the two endpoint derivatives. Counterexample: f(u) = u^4 - 5u^2 (so f'(u) = 4u^3 - 10u), left state u_- = 2, right state u_+ = -2. Since f(2) = f(-2) = -4, Rankine-Hugoniot gives the stationary shock σ = 0, and the Lax inequalities hold strictly: f'(2) = 12 > 0 > f'(-2) = -12. Yet the shock is NOT admissible: the chord joining (-2,-4) and (2,-4) is the constant -4, while f(0) = 0 lies ABOVE it, so Oleinik's condition fails; equivalently the Kruzhkov inequality with k = 0 requires σ(k - u_-) ≥ f(k) - f(u_-), i.e. 0 ≥ 4, which is false. The correct entropy solution of this Riemann problem is read off the least concave majorant of f on [-2,2] (the hull construction for a decreasing jump u_l > u_r): a shock from u_- = 2 down to u* = (√7 - 2)/3 ≈ 0.2153, the point at which the line through (2, f(2)) is tangent to the graph of f, then an attached rarefaction from u* down to -u*, then, by symmetry, a shock from -u* to u_+ = -2. The two shock speeds are -(16 + 14u*)/9 ≈ -2.113 and +(16 + 14u*)/9 ≈ +2.113, and the rarefaction sweeps the speeds between them. Recurrence of M(1,1) would follow if the walk returns to the origin infinitely often; since the second coordinate performs a simple random walk on the column above the current first coordinate whenever the vertex was visited before, the walk behaves in each column like a 1D random walk (recurrent) until it hits an unvisited vertex, at which time the first coordinate steps. The number of new visits up to time n is the range R_n; the first coordinate after n steps is a simple random walk at time R_n, so |X^1_n| is of order sqrt(R_n), and the range of a planar walk-like process is at most n, giving |X^1_n| <= sqrt n; a return to the origin requires both coordinates to vanish. A rigorous partial fact: M(1,1) is recurrent if and only if the first coordinate returns to 0 infinitely often at times when the second coordinate is 0; since within a column the second coordinate is a recurrent 1D walk that keeps returning to 0 until it finds a new vertex, and new vertices in a column are found at the ends of the visited interval, the question is whether the first-coordinate walk (which is a simple random walk in the clock of new visits) visits 0 infinitely often, which it does a.s. (1D recurrence), and whether at those visits the second coordinate is 0 - not automatic. So recurrence of M(1,1) reduces to: at the (infinitely many) times the first coordinate is 0, the second coordinate, which then performs a 1D walk in the column of 0 with the visited interval of that column, returns to height 0 before finding a new vertex - which has probability bounded below by a constant each time if the visited interval around height 0 in column 0 has length bounded... the visited interval in column 0 grows, and the probability of returning to 0 from the boundary of an interval of length L before exiting is of order 1/L... summing over the visits to column 0 gives a divergent series only if the interval lengths grow slowly enough. This is the crux and I did not settle it; the reduction is recorded. Key identity: M(1,1) recurrent iff, at the infinitely many returns of the first coordinate to 0, the second coordinate returns to 0 in column 0 before finding a new vertex; the return probability is of order 1/(visited interval length). {"assumptions":["Both semigroups strongly continuous with the SAME generator including the same domain - two operators that agree on a common core but have different domains can generate different semigroups, which is precisely the non-uniqueness phenomenon for symmetric operators with several self-adjoint extensions."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:06:45.871339+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, semigroup theory","id":"claim_684380ee4334e17df539211dc9360d736e96ca633045262ed3ef27d741f7e789","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be the infinitesimal generator of a strongly continuous (C_0) semigroup on a Banach space. Then the semigroup is UNIQUELY determined by A: if (S(t)) and (T(t)) are C_0-semigroups with the same generator then S(t) = T(t) for every t >= 0. Equivalently, the Laplace transform of the semigroup is the resolvent of A, and the resolvent determines the semigroup. {"assumptions":["Counterexample: sawtooth functions u_k = dist(·, (1/k)Z) for the eikonal equation |u'| = 1 on R","Viscosity stability requires locally uniform convergence of the solutions (convergence of the equations must also be locally uniform)","Half-relaxed limit techniques replace uniform convergence only when combined with semicontinuous envelopes, not with a.e. solutions"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418309+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: viscosity solution theory","id":"claim_686c4951f47d3257d9394437cec0033cb5f7dec3b6ad9bdad4ce29fab5a2d321","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis in the stability theorem: the approximating functions must be VISCOSITY sub/supersolutions and the convergence must be LOCALLY UNIFORM. Neither can be dropped. (1) Almost-everywhere solutions are not closed under uniform convergence: let u_k(x) := dist(x, (1/k)Z) on R. Then |u_k'| = 1 at every point of differentiability, 0 ≤ u_k ≤ 1/(2k), so u_k → 0 uniformly, yet the limit u ≡ 0 satisfies |u'| = 0 and solves the eikonal equation nowhere. The u_k are not viscosity solutions of |u'| - 1 = 0 (at each of their convex kinks, on (1/k)Z, the supersolution test with the touching slope p = 0 fails), which is exactly why the stability theorem does not apply. (2) The convergence hypothesis cannot be weakened to pointwise or weak-* convergence. What goes wrong in the a.e. setting is already visible in (1): Du_k = ±1 a.e. while Du_k ⇀ 0 weakly-*, and the nonlinear expression H(Du_k) does not pass to weak limits. For genuine viscosity sub/supersolutions the proof of the stability theorem uses LOCALLY UNIFORM convergence to move maximum points of u_k - φ to a maximum point of u - φ; for a family that is merely locally uniformly bounded the correct substitutes are the half-relaxed limits limsup* u_k and liminf* u_k (Barles-Perthame), which are respectively a subsolution and a supersolution but in general differ from a pointwise limit. (If the u_k are locally equi-Lipschitz, pointwise convergence already forces locally uniform convergence, so the gap between the two modes of convergence bites only in the absence of equicontinuity.) Auditor's check: any passage to the limit in a nonlinear first-order PDE that is justified only by 'u_k → u and each u_k solves the equation a.e.' is invalid.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.477138+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_68724c8134dfcc0ae4992f700876980e044d69d7ce8ec6254ca4f97fecc65d60","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (S, A) be a measurable space and mu a sigma-finite measure on it, the intensity measure. A Poisson point process with intensity mu is a random counting measure N on S (N(A) is a random element of {0, 1, 2, ...} union {infinity} for each A in A, and N is a measure for each outcome) such that (i) for every A with mu(A) < infinity, N(A) has the Poisson distribution with mean mu(A), and (ii) for pairwise disjoint A_1, ..., A_k the counts N(A_1), ..., N(A_k) are independent. Such a process exists for every sigma-finite mu (construct it on each piece of finite measure by throwing a Poisson(mu(A)) number of independent points with law mu restricted to A and normalised, then superpose the pieces). When mu has no atoms the points are almost surely distinct; when mu is a multiple of Lebesgue measure on R^d the process is homogeneous with rate equal to that multiple. Basic calculus: the mapping theorem (the image of a Poisson process under a measurable map is Poisson with the image intensity), superposition (independent Poisson processes add to a Poisson process with the summed intensity), thinning (keeping each point independently with probability p(x) gives a Poisson process with intensity p mu), and Campbell's formula E sum_{x in N} f(x) = integral f d mu.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A is self-adjoint","the perturbation is claimed to be small relative to A"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.772201+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, perturbation theory, Schrodinger operators","id":"claim_6a489f3aa69fc8c053255532a89d8dafa488b42e2454afe14d89e8625076239b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypotheses: (i) B is symmetric; (ii) D(A) ⊂ D(B); (iii) ‖Bx‖ ≤ a‖Ax‖ + b‖x‖ on D(A) with a strictly less than 1. What fails. Dropping symmetry: take A self-adjoint unbounded and B = icA with 0 < c < 1. Then D(A) = D(B) and ‖Bx‖ = c‖Ax‖, so the relative bound is c < 1, yet A + B = (1 + ic)A has spectrum (1 + ic)σ(A), which is not contained in ℝ, so A + B is not self-adjoint; it is not even symmetric. Losing the strict inequality: take B = −A (symmetric, relative bound exactly a = 1, b = 0). Then A + B = 0 on D(A), which is symmetric and essentially self-adjoint but not self-adjoint on D(A), since D(A) ≠ H when A is unbounded; the conclusion 'self-adjoint on D(A)' is false at a = 1, and only Wüst's weaker conclusion (essential self-adjointness) survives. Dropping relative boundedness entirely: A = −d²/dx² on H²(ℝ) and B = multiplication by −x⁴ (maximal domain) are both self-adjoint and C_c^∞(ℝ) is a common dense invariant-looking core, but −d²/dx² − x⁴ is not essentially self-adjoint on C_c^∞(ℝ) (it is in the limit circle case at both ±∞, with deficiency indices (2,2)); the sum of two self-adjoint operators is in general neither self-adjoint nor essentially self-adjoint on the intersection of their domains, and that intersection can even be {0}. Also note that the relative bound of the perturbation must be measured against A itself, not against A + B, and that the infimum defining the relative bound need not be attained, so 'a ≤ 1' in a cited inequality is not the same as 'relative bound a < 1'. Audit rule: check symmetry of B, the domain inclusion, and the strict inequality with the constants actually produced by the estimate.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T is trace class (or positive) for the diagonal sum to be basis-independent","cyclicity tr(AB) = tr(BA) needs one factor trace class and the other bounded, or both Hilbert-Schmidt","Hilbert-Schmidt does not imply trace class"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.573399+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator ideals","id":"claim_6b062606a8899853447fad7c25599be3992c8f16f17ceb5224a67851c9805cf3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The expression sum_i <T e_i, e_i> is basis-independent and deserves the name 'trace' only when T is trace class (or T >= 0, where the sum is basis-independent in [0, infinity]). Two concrete failures. (1) Conditional convergence, basis-dependent value: on l^2 let T = diag((-1)^{n+1}/n) with respect to the standard basis. T is self-adjoint, compact and Hilbert-Schmidt, but not trace class since sum_n 1/n = infinity. In the standard basis sum_n <T e_n, e_n> converges conditionally to log 2, and permuting the orthonormal basis rearranges the series, so by the Riemann rearrangement theorem the 'trace' can be made any real number or made to diverge. (2) An absolutely convergent, even identically zero, diagonal without trace class: let T be the block-diagonal operator on l^2 whose n-th two-by-two block is [[0, 1/n], [1/n, 0]]. Every diagonal entry in the standard basis is 0, so the diagonal sum is 0, yet the singular values are 1/n twice each, so sum s_n = infinity and T is not trace class; the eigenvalues are plus and minus 1/n and no trace can be assigned consistently. Related traps: tr(AB) = tr(BA) requires a hypothesis such as A trace class and B bounded, or A and B both Hilbert-Schmidt. For merely bounded A, B the commutator identity fails: on l^2 with the unilateral shift S, the commutator [S*, S] = I - S S* is the rank-one projection onto the first coordinate, so it is trace class with trace 1, not 0, even though it is a commutator. Finally, 'T is Hilbert-Schmidt' does not imply 'T is trace class': sum s_n^2 < infinity is strictly weaker than sum s_n < infinity, as diag(1, 1/2, 1/3, ...) on l^2 shows.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(S, d) is a metric space with its Borel sigma-algebra","the members of the family are Borel probability measures"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:01:13.770398+00:00","domain":"probability, weak convergence of measures, tightness","id":"claim_6b379f9f39b8f899e353d04b96592d438754cd075fffcd3c5f233e7113013891","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(S, d)$ be a metric space. A family $\\Gamma$ of Borel probability measures on $S$ is tight (uniformly tight) if for every $\\varepsilon > 0$ there is a compact set $K_\\varepsilon \\subset S$ such that $\\mu(S \\setminus K_\\varepsilon) \\le \\varepsilon$ for EVERY $\\mu \\in \\Gamma$ - the same compact set works for all members of the family. A single measure $\\mu$ is tight if $\\{\\mu\\}$ is.\n\nFacts to keep straight. (1) On a Polish space (separable and complete metric space) every single Borel probability measure is tight (Ulam), and a finite family is then tight as well. (2) On a separable metric space that is not complete a single Borel probability measure can fail to be tight: for a set $S \\subset [0,1]$ with Lebesgue outer measure 1 and inner measure 0 (a Bernstein-type set) the trace of Lebesgue measure is a Borel probability measure on $S$ whose compact subsets are all null. (3) In a compact metric space every family is tight (take $K = S$). (4) On $\\mathbb{R}^k$ tightness of $\\Gamma$ means $\\sup_{\\mu \\in \\Gamma} \\mu(\\{|x| > R\\}) \\to 0$ as $R \\to \\infty$, i.e. no mass escapes to infinity uniformly in the family; in $C[0,1]$ tightness is characterised by the Arzelà-Ascoli type conditions (bounded initial values plus a uniform modulus-of-continuity control). (5) Tightness is the hypothesis of Prokhorov's theorem, which turns it into relative compactness in the weak topology.","status":"unverified"}

The explicit choice C=0.4748 is valid for every n>=1 (Shevtsova, 2011, Theorem 2 and Corollary 1, https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.6554); it is a proven historical upper bound, not an assertion of the exact or currently best constant. The conjecture asks whether repeating two simple arithmetic operations will eventually transform every positive integer into 1. It concerns sequences of integers in which each term is obtained from the previous term as follows: if a term is even, the next term is one half of it. If a term is odd, the next term is 3 times the previous term plus 1. The conjecture is that these sequences always reach 1, no matter which positive integer is chosen to start the sequence. {"assumptions":["Finite one-hot task identifiers with positive power-law task weights; independent uniform skill bits.","Fixed task parity functions; first N supplied as basis functions; noiseless target amplitude S>0."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:24:35.629108+00:00","domain":"Multitask sparse parity and skill emergence","id":"claim_6b8bb2f11abe9145368bad240c2dab04e24a2526e3b98efbfeac8938553e0ab6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Nam-Fonseca-Lee-Mingard-Louis fixed-basis multitask parity model. Fix integers n_s,n_b,m with 1<=m<=n_b, alpha>0 and S>0. The task I in {1,...,n_s} has probabilities p_k=A*k^(-alpha-1), A=(sum_{j=1}^{n_s} j^(-alpha-1))^(-1), and is represented by a one-hot n_s-bit control vector. Independently, X is uniform on {0,1}^{n_b}. For each task choose an m-element subset A_k of skill-bit coordinates and set g_k(i,x)=1_{i=k}*(-1)^(sum_{j in A_k} x_j). Distinct tasks have disjoint task support, so E[g_j(I,X)*g_k(I,X)]=p_k*1_{j=k}; these basis functions are not unit-normalized in the population measure. The noiseless target is f_star(i,x)=S*sum_{k=1}^{n_s} g_k(i,x). For 1<=N<=n_s the source multilinear model fixes the N most frequent skill functions in advance and trains only the 2N real scalars in f(i,x)=sum_{k=1}^N a_k*b_k*g_k(i,x). Its represented skill strengths are R_k=a_k*b_k. Define R_k=E_X[g_k(k,X)*f(k,X)] and conditional MSE L_k=(1/2)*E_X[(S*g_k(k,X)-f(k,X))^2]. For this model L_k=(1/2)*(S-R_k)^2 when k<=N, and L_k=S^2/2 when k>N. In contrast, for an arbitrary predictor f the definition gives L_k=(1/2)*(S^2+E_X[f(k,X)^2]-2*S*R_k), so skill strength alone need not determine skill loss. Population MSE is sum_k p_k*L_k. The skill functions in this exactly solvable model are supplied, rather than learned from examples.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a moment bound with a STRICTLY positive exponent to spare (beta > 0)","a complete metric target space","the conclusion is about a modification, not the original process"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.782051+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6bc3c6154eb242793c2a5c251a34ca7565adf2b8c40b69ee5551e9af7d6209b4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X_t)_{t in [0,T]} be a stochastic process with values in a complete metric space, and suppose there are constants alpha > 0, beta > 0 and C < infinity with E[ d(X_t, X_s)^alpha ] <= C |t - s|^{1 + beta} for all s, t in [0,T]. Then X admits a MODIFICATION Xtilde - a process with P(X_t = Xtilde_t) = 1 for every fixed t - whose sample paths are almost surely continuous, and indeed almost surely HOLDER continuous of every exponent gamma in (0, beta/alpha). The exponent beta/alpha is the boundary and is generally not attained. Applications: for Brownian motion E|B_t - B_s|^{2m} = c_m |t-s|^m, so taking alpha = 2m and beta = m - 1 gives Holder exponents up to (m-1)/(2m), which approaches 1/2 as m grows - matching the known fact that Brownian paths are Holder of every exponent below 1/2 and of no exponent at or above 1/2. The theorem produces a MODIFICATION, not the original process: the original may have wildly discontinuous paths, and the two agree at each fixed time but not, in general, simultaneously at all times. The strictly positive beta is essential: E|X_t - X_s|^alpha <= C|t-s| with no exponent to spare does not suffice, as the Poisson process shows, where E|N_t - N_s| = |t - s| exactly and the paths are genuinely discontinuous. The d-dimensional time-parameter version holds with 1 + beta replaced by d + beta. [Kolmogorov, published by Slutsky and by Chentsov; see Revuz and Yor, Continuous Martingales and Brownian Motion, 3rd ed., Theorem I.2.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628833+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6c8676d825f4a55fd3a14f69b1c08c5a1e3f9cf9297d3f4f48fbb82aef6f2234","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X >= 0 with 0 < E[X^2] < infinity. The second moment method is the chain of consequences of Paley-Zygmund and Chebyshev. FIRST FORM: P(X > 0) >= (E X)^2 / E[X^2]. This gives only a LOWER BOUND ON THE PROBABILITY, bounded away from 0 when the second moment is comparable to the square of the first; it does NOT give an event of probability tending to 1. SECOND FORM: if Var(X) / (E X)^2 -> 0 along a sequence of models, then X / E[X] -> 1 in probability by Chebyshev, so X > 0 with probability tending to 1 and moreover X is concentrated. Confusing the two is the standard error: E[X^2] <= C (E X)^2 with C > 1 fixed gives positive probability at least 1/C, and no amount of that alone upgrades to high probability. The repair when only the first form is available is usually a 0-1 law or a sprinkling or self-improvement argument that turns positive probability into probability one, not a better moment estimate. The typical use is a counting random variable X = number of structures of a given type: the first moment method (Markov: P(X >= 1) <= E X) gives the upper threshold, and the second moment method gives the lower one, and the two match only when the second moment is not inflated by correlated pairs. {"assumptions":["P is a product measure (independent coordinates)","A and B are increasing events (van den Berg-Kesten); Reimer's inequality removes this hypothesis","A box B is the disjoint-occurrence event, witnessed by disjoint coordinate sets, not the intersection"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.048828+00:00","domain":"percolation and correlation inequalities (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_6e1b259086d35f04b2f1c00edbbb017feb2ef912f0a7984e0cd00e9e6739eb28","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let P be a product measure on {0,1}^n and let A and B be increasing events. Write A box B for the disjoint occurrence of A and B: the set of configurations omega for which there are disjoint index sets I and J such that every configuration agreeing with omega on I lies in A and every configuration agreeing with omega on J lies in B. Then P(A box B) <= P(A) P(B) (van den Berg and Kesten 1985). This runs in the opposite direction to the Harris-FKG inequality for the plain intersection, P(A and B) >= P(A) P(B); the two are not in conflict because A box B is a subset of A and B. In percolation the standard use is P(two disjoint open paths) <= P(open path)^2.","status":"unverified"}

Method: Design the algorithm and check whether the exploration frontier remains Markov. Result: For bond percolation the peeling frontier is a two-colour boundary (free/blocked edges) and the algorithm peels the edge at the colour change, keeping the unexplored region a Boltzmann map with a boundary of the same type. For site percolation the colour lives on vertices and after peeling a face the newly exposed boundary vertices are uncoloured; the natural algorithm peels the edge whose left endpoint is black and right endpoint is uncoloured, colouring the new vertices as they appear. The unexplored region is then a Boltzmann map with a boundary condition that is a word in {black, white, uncoloured}, and the difficulty is that the length of the black segment is no longer a Markov chain by itself: the future depends on the positions of uncoloured vertices along the boundary. The frontier becomes Markov if one records the boundary word, which is an infinite-dimensional state. On triangulations the problem was solved (Angel-Curien) because degree-3 faces expose at most one new vertex per step, keeping the state finite; for general Boltzmann maps with large faces a peeled face exposes many uncoloured vertices at once. So a Markov site-percolation peeling exists exactly when faces expose boundedly many vertices, i.e. for bounded face degrees, and the general Boltzmann case requires a state space of boundary words; whether the threshold can still be computed from a word-valued Markov chain is the open part. Obstruction: Unbounded face degrees expose many uncoloured boundary vertices at once; the frontier state is a word, not an integer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a well-defined Dirichlet form and reversible Markov chain with a reference measure mu","a valid Nash-type functional inequality with a specified effective dimension d","for two-sided estimates: matching volume-growth and effective-resistance-growth bounds on balls","typically also an elliptic Harnack inequality, or comparable regularity, to establish the matching lower heat-kernel bound"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.993577+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f33033cc6c015e74e17ecf03f84254fb9e59f13180becd49ac22b25d7db440b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). A Nash inequality on a graph with Dirichlet form E and reference measure mu has the form ||f||_2^{2+4/d} <= C E(f,f) ||f||_1^{4/d} for all f in the domain of the form, where d is an effective dimension parameter. Such an inequality is classically equivalent, by results of Nash and later Carlen-Kusuoka-Stroock, to an on-diagonal heat-kernel upper bound p_t(x,x) <= C' t^{-d/2} for the associated Markov semigroup, and combining it with matching volume-growth and effective-resistance-growth estimates, within the general framework relating resistance growth to heat-kernel decay used for fractal-like and random graphs, yields two-sided sub-Gaussian or Gaussian heat-kernel bounds. On graphs where effective resistance to the complement of a ball of radius n grows like n^zeta and volume grows like n^alpha, this gives sub-Gaussian heat-kernel estimates with off-diagonal decay governed by the exponent alpha+zeta, a technique central to analysis on fractals and on random graphs such as critical percolation clusters or random walk among random conductances. The technique does not give the resistance or volume exponents themselves, which are separate geometric inputs, and a full two-sided heat-kernel estimate typically requires both the Nash-type inequality, giving the upper bound, and a separate lower-bound argument, often via a chaining construction or an elliptic Harnack inequality. Typical failure: Assuming ordinary Euclidean Gaussian heat-kernel scaling, of the t^{-d/2} exp(-|x-y|^2/4t) form, transfers automatically to a random or fractal-like graph without re-deriving the resistance exponent zeta; on structures such as the incipient infinite cluster of critical percolation, or random conductance models with heavy-tailed conductances, the correct scaling is sub-Gaussian with zeta != 1, and using the Euclidean exponent silently mis-states both the walk dimension and the tail behavior of the heat kernel. Canonical reference: Nash, 1958, American Journal of Mathematics; Carlen, Kusuoka and Stroock, 1987, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare; Barlow, 2004, Annals of Probability; Kumagai, Random Walks on Disordered Media and their Scaling Limits, 2014, Springer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:09:41.190331+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_6f5cfee93cb76cd8d74924060da891f5b4881b2215fe5aa410d44ee0474d26de","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, the term homology, originally introduced in algebraic topology, has three primary, closely related usages. First, there is the homology of a chain complex, a sequence of abelian groups, called homology groups, which are regarded as fundamental invariants of the chain complex. Secondly, when one can associate a chain complex to a different mathematical object, one can also associate its homology to that object. Distinct procedures of associating chain complexes to a given object are grouped into homology theories. Finally, homology is important in the study of topological spaces. Under nice conditions in which distinct homology theories for a single topological space produce the same homology groups, one can define a single homology of a topological space. This last notion of homology is closely related to topological ideas frequently discussed in popular mathematics such as the holes of a surface or the cycles of a graph. There is also a related notion of the cohomology of a cochain complex, giving rise to various cohomology theories, in addition to the notion of the cohomology of a topological space.","status":"unverified"}

    The upper bound | e^{2 pi i q alpha} - 1 | <= 2 pi ||q alpha|| always holds, so the two sides are comparable to ||q alpha||.

(ii) (solving the cohomological equation) Let R_alpha(x) = x + alpha on the circle T = R/Z and let f be a C^infinity function on T with mean zero. Then the equation u(x + alpha) - u(x) = f(x) has a C^infinity solution u, unique up to an additive constant, given on Fourier coefficients by u-hat(q) = f-hat(q) / (e^{2 pi i q alpha} - 1) for q nonzero. Quantitatively |u-hat(q)| <= |q|^{tau} |f-hat(q)| / (4C), so one loses tau derivatives: in Sobolev scale ||u||_{H^{s - tau}} <= (4C)^{-1} ||f||_{H^s}, and the analogous statement holds in Holder scale with an epsilon loss.

(iii) (how common the hypothesis is) For every tau > 1, Lebesgue-almost every alpha is Diophantine of type (C, tau) for some C = C(alpha) > 0; for tau = 1 the alpha satisfying the condition are exactly the badly approximable ones (bounded partial quotients), a set of Lebesgue measure zero and full Hausdorff dimension; for tau < 1 no alpha satisfies it at all, by Dirichlet's theorem.

WHERE IT FAILS. If alpha is LIOUVILLE (no such C, tau exist), the conclusion of (ii) fails badly: choose q_1 < q_2 < ... with ||q_k alpha|| < q_k^{-k} and define f by f-hat(q_k) = f-hat(-q_k)-bar = ||q_k alpha||^{1/2} and all other coefficients zero. These coefficients decay faster than any power of q_k, so f is C^infinity with mean zero, yet |u-hat(q_k)| >= ||q_k alpha||^{1/2} / (2 pi ||q_k alpha||) = 1 / (2 pi ||q_k alpha||^{1/2}), which blows up faster than any polynomial in q_k. Hence no solution u exists in L^2, and not even a distributional solution exists. So the Diophantine condition is not a technical convenience: it is what separates solvability from non-solvability. Note also that (ii) gives no information at all about the SPEED of ergodic averages by itself, and that the estimates degrade as C -> 0, so any application that needs uniformity must track C and tau explicitly.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f measurable and a.e. finite","|E| < infinity (or E sigma-finite, applied piecewise)","the measure is Borel regular, so that inner regularity by closed sets is available"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751562+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_70f1790178f49b91f5ee0ff4790936831774e34f8e840b54c67bc80f664a49ab","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : R^d -> C be Lebesgue measurable and finite almost everywhere, let E be a measurable set of FINITE measure, and let eps > 0. Then there is a CLOSED set F contained in E with |E \\ F| < eps such that the RESTRICTION of f to F is continuous. Moreover one may take g in C_c(R^d) with g = f on F and sup |g| <= sup |f|. The theorem does not assert that f is continuous AT the points of F as a function on R^d: the indicator of the rationals is nowhere continuous on R, yet it agrees with the zero function off a set of measure zero, and Lusin's F can be taken to be any closed set of irrationals of nearly full measure. Finiteness of |E| may be relaxed to sigma-finiteness by exhausting E, at the price of stating the conclusion with |E \\ F| < eps for each piece. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 2.24]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:00:45.293334+00:00","domain":"QA-corrected (round 3, audit-driven)","id":"claim_715f4fa3e031a45505b144f07e822269b3a28da69fba6d6d2d8695650633769d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Finitely generated abelian group: An abelian group (G, +) is called finitely generated if there exist finitely many elements x_1, x_2, ..., x_s in G such that every x in G can be written as x = n_1 x_1 + n_2 x_2 + ... + n_s x_s for some integers n_1, n_2, ..., n_s. Minimizing mu(P) is the convex semidefinite program: minimize real s subject to -sI <=_PSD P-(1/n)11^T <=_PSD sI, P_ij>=0 entrywise, P1=1, P=P^T, and P_ij=0 for (i,j) outside E. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:00:09.358321+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning","id":"claim_725b1291163158659b5a95f154eb99cbd5bf0e3c3895a5a6a7c646f4cd804d39","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In a multi-output stacking problem scored by the mean per-sample relative error $\\frac{1}{n}\\sum_i \\|\\hat y_i - y_i\\|/\\|y_i\\|$, the per-output least-squares stack minimises the unweighted squared error, which is dominated by the cases with the largest $\\|y_i\\|$, while the score is dominated by the cases with the smallest. Interpolating the per-output weights toward one pooled simplex weight vector fitted on the relative error therefore improves the score even IN-SAMPLE on the very calibration rows on which least squares is optimal in squared error - the signature that distinguishes an objective mismatch from a generalisation (variance) effect, which can only appear out of sample. Measured on the EMIT lookup-table pool (seed 101, component Y2, 23 members, 932 calibration rows, 285 outputs): in-sample relative error 0.1105 for least squares against 0.1026 at interpolation weight 0.4 (-7.2 percent), the in-sample optimum at the same weight as the out-of-sample optimum (0.1292 to 0.1186), while the in-sample squared error is minimal at least squares (8.8e-5 against 1.2e-4); the out-of-sample gain is +15.9 percent in the smallest-norm quartile of targets and -9.6 percent in the largest, and 45 percent of the least-squares score comes from its worst decile of cases. Consequently no model of the sampling noise of the weight rows reproduces the cross-validated interpolation weight: the known-noise James-Stein amount is 0.00 and the heteroscedasticity-robust amount 0.03-0.05 where cross-validation chooses 0.10-0.40. Shrinking toward the pooled UNCONSTRAINED least-squares weights (entries up to 90 in magnitude) or toward the mean of the rows is much worse; the simplex constraint together with the relative objective carries the effect. The practical rule: when a stack is scored in a metric that weights cases differently from the fitting loss, the first question is the objective, not the estimator's variance.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["𝔄 is a unital Banach algebra (e.g. bounded operators on a Banach space, or square matrices)","A and B are elements of 𝔄 (bounded operators)","AB = BA"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.111181+00:00","domain":"operator theory, matrix analysis, one-parameter groups","id":"claim_72638ddfde3be7c71bd07c8d293de0f5da0036958c9131cd1b17e4853a1f9986","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let 𝔄 be a unital Banach algebra (for instance the algebra B(E) of bounded linear operators on a Banach space E, or the n×n complex matrices), and for A ∈ 𝔄 define exp(A) = e^A := Σ_{k=0}^∞ A^k / k!, a series that converges absolutely in norm for every A (‖A^k/k!‖ ≤ ‖A‖^k/k!), so that ‖e^A‖ ≤ e^{‖A‖}. If A, B ∈ 𝔄 COMMUTE, AB = BA, then e^{A+B} = e^A e^B = e^B e^A. Consequences: for every A and all scalars s, t, e^{(s+t)A} = e^{sA} e^{tA} (the one-parameter group law), e^A is invertible with (e^A)⁻¹ = e^{−A}, e^0 = 1, and t ↦ e^{tA} is norm-differentiable with derivative A e^{tA} = e^{tA} A. If P is invertible, e^{PAP⁻¹} = P e^A P⁻¹. Sharp edges. (1) Commutativity cannot be dropped: for the 2×2 matrices A = [[0,1],[0,0]] and B = [[0,0],[1,0]] one has e^A = I + A, e^B = I + B, so e^A e^B = [[2,1],[1,1]], whereas A + B = [[0,1],[1,0]] gives e^{A+B} = [[cosh 1, sinh 1],[sinh 1, cosh 1]] ≠ e^A e^B (and e^B e^A = [[1,1],[1,2]] ≠ e^A e^B, so the two products differ as well). For non-commuting A, B the product e^A e^B is instead described by the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff series e^{A+B+[A,B]/2+…} when it converges, and by the Lie–Trotter formula e^{A+B} = lim_{n→∞} (e^{A/n} e^{B/n})ⁿ. (2) The converse is false in general: e^A e^B = e^{A+B} does not imply AB = BA (there are non-commuting complex matrices with e^A = e^B = e^{A+B} = I); it does hold for Hermitian (self-adjoint) matrices A, B, because then e^{A+B} Hermitian forces e^A e^B = (e^A e^B)* = e^B e^A, so the positive definite matrices e^A and e^B commute, and hence so do their unique Hermitian logarithms A and B. (3) For UNBOUNDED operators (generators of semigroups) the series definition is unavailable and 'commuting' must be formulated with care (e.g. commuting resolvents / commuting semigroups); this statement is only about bounded operators and Banach algebras.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["α irrational (for the rational case the expansion terminates)","regular (simple) continued fraction with integer partial quotients a_k ≥ 1 for k ≥ 1","||t|| denotes the distance from t to the nearest integer"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492004+00:00","domain":"Diophantine approximation, circle rotations, continued fractions","id":"claim_7271e0510379bbe55262f0b504298ebded2c36c4dd6bb321ac077750203941b8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let α be irrational with regular continued fraction [a_0; a_1, a_2, ...], convergents p_n/q_n (p_{-1} = 1, q_{-1} = 0, p_0 = a_0, q_0 = 1, p_{n+1} = a_{n+1}p_n + p_{n-1}, q_{n+1} = a_{n+1}q_n + q_{n-1}) and complete quotients α_{n+1} = [a_{n+1}; a_{n+2}, ...], so a_{n+1} < α_{n+1} < a_{n+1} + 1. Write ||t|| = dist(t, Z) and δ_n = |q_n α − p_n| (so δ_{-1} = 1).

(1) Exact size and alternating sign. For all n ≥ 0, q_n α − p_n = (−1)^n / (q_n α_{n+1} + q_{n-1}). Hence 1/(q_n + q_{n+1}) < δ_n < 1/q_{n+1}, the errors alternate in sign, δ_n is strictly decreasing, and δ_n = ||q_n α|| for every n ≥ 1 (because q_{n+1} ≥ 2 gives δ_n < 1/2); for n = 0 this holds when a_1 ≥ 2.

(2) The distances obey the same recursion as the denominators: δ_{n-1} = a_{n+1} δ_n + δ_{n+1} for all n ≥ 0. Equivalently δ_n = 1/(α_1 α_2 ··· α_{n+1}).

(3) Closest returns (Lagrange's theorem on best approximations of the second kind). For every n ≥ 0 and every integer q with 1 ≤ q < q_{n+1}: ||q α|| ≥ δ_n, with equality if and only if q = q_n. In dynamical words: for the rotation t ↦ t + α (mod 1), among all times 1 ≤ q < q_{n+1} the orbit of any point comes closest to its starting point exactly at time q_n; the record-breaking (closest-return) times of the orbit are precisely the denominators q_0 (when a_1 ≥ 2), q_1, q_2, ..., and successive closest returns land on alternate sides of the starting point, at distances δ_n.

(4) Growth. q_{n+1} ≥ q_n + q_{n-1}, hence q_n ≥ F_{n+1} (Fibonacci) and q_n ≥ 2^{(n−1)/2} for n ≥ 1; the golden ratio (all a_k = 1) is the slowest case.

Where it fails. For rational α the expansion terminates, the last δ is 0 and the recursion (2) stops. Statement (3) is about ||qα|| = min_p |qα − p| (best approximations of the SECOND kind). For the FIRST-kind problem of minimising |α − p/q| over q ≤ Q, intermediate fractions (p_{n-1} + k p_n)/(q_{n-1} + k q_n) with k > a_{n+1}/2 can also be best approximations, so the two notions must not be conflated. When a_1 = 1 one has q_0 = q_1 = 1, the n = 0 case of (3) is vacuous, and ||α|| equals δ_1, not δ_0.","status":"unverified"}
