Every continuous real symmetric PSD kernel of rank <=p and diagonal <=R^2 on a nonempty compact X subset R^d admits an explicit raw-input normalized-ReLU-attention transformer for uniform noisy predictive forward KL <=eps, with positive noise s, labels bounded by B, and contexts <=n. The complete width/depth/MLP/head bound is given in C005 Section 1 in terms of the canonical kernel modulus Omega(r), a finite h-net cardinality J, and the solver constants. A fixed finite Gram factorization supplies all encoder feature values; no feature computation is hidden outside the count. Status: proof (unaudited), T336-w727-C005 v2. Complete theorem, constants and scope:
# Target 1 for continuous finite-rank kernels on compact raw domains

Claim T336-w727-C005 v2. Status: proof (unaudited), dependent on C002 v1 and the deterministic perturbation/encoder constructions in C004 v1. The entire result is not Lean-checked. No independent review or novelty certification is claimed.

The hardest step is removing the supplied-feature oracle without adding a hidden feature-computation cost. A finite Gram factorization fixes the encoder weights; a kernel modulus controls its error. The size explicitly includes the resulting encoder.

## 1. Statement and all parameters

Let X be a nonempty compact subset of R^d, d>=1. Let k:X times X -> R be a continuous real symmetric positive-semidefinite kernel of rank at most p, p>=1, with k(x,x)<=R^2 for R>=0. The prior is the zero-mean GP with kernel k. Observation noise is independent N(0,s), s>0. Labels are bounded by B>=0, contexts have length <=n with n>=0 an integer, and eps>0. The prediction concerns a new noisy observation.

Define the canonical kernel modulus in the ambient L1 metric by

    Omega(r)=sup_{x,y in X, ||x-y||_1<=r}
                sqrt(k(x,x)+k(y,y)-2k(x,y)).

The expression is nonnegative by positive semidefiniteness. Omega(r) tends to zero as r decreases to zero, as proved below.

Retain the following explicit constants from C004's deterministic perturbation bound:

    S=R+1, C_A=n(2R+1),
    C_m=nB[(R+S)/s+S C_A R/s^2],
    C_v=R+S+S^2 C_A/s>0,
    eta=min(1,sqrt(s eps)/(2(1+C_m)),s sqrt(eps)/(2C_v),s/(4C_v)),
    eps0=min(eps/4,1/16), e=eta/sqrt(p)>0.

Choose any **fixed admissible** r>0 with Omega(r)<=e/2. An explicit upper modulus for k can be used to choose r; continuity guarantees existence, not an algorithm for computing a modulus of an arbitrary black-box kernel. Put

    A_cone=(2R+e)/r>0, h=e/(2A_cone)>0.

Choose a finite h-net G contained in X, of cardinality J>=1. The size bound is explicit in J (or in a known upper bound for the covering number). For X=[0,1]^d one may take the regular grid with

    m=max(1,ceil(d A_cone/e)), J=(m+1)^d.

For the attention solver define

    kappa=1+max(1,n)S^2/s, M=nS^2B/s,
    delta0=min(1/2,s/(2S^2),sqrt(s eps0)/(1+M),s sqrt(eps0)/S^2),
    T=ceil(sqrt(kappa) log(2/delta0)/2).

There is a transformer, using normalized residual ReLU attention and tokenwise residual ReLU MLPs, with

    D=7p+6+d+Jd+pJ,
    H=2Jd+pJ+4p+1,
    L_total=T+5+ceil(log_2 J),
    at most five attention heads per layer,
    at most L_total(15D^2+2DH)+2D dense scalar parameters,

whose positive-variance Gaussian output has forward KL<=eps from the exact noisy GP predictive, uniformly over all admissible raw-input contexts and queries. Its input contains only raw coordinates, labels, fixed context/query flags, and constants. The encoder is counted. These are arbitrary-real-weight size bounds; no finite-bit, kernel-evaluation, offline factorization-time, SGD, or ERM-generalization bound is asserted.

## 2. Canonical finite-dimensional features and the kernel modulus

Form the vector space of finite formal combinations of symbols delta_x with bilinear form

    <sum_i a_i delta_{x_i},sum_j b_j delta_{y_j}>
       =sum_{i,j}a_i b_j k(x_i,y_j).

Positive semidefiniteness makes this a nonnegative quadratic form. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality follows by applying nonnegativity to u+t v for all real t; in particular a zero-norm vector is orthogonal to every vector. Quotient by the zero-norm subspace. For any finite list of symbols, the dimension of their quotient span is the rank of their Gram matrix. Every finite list of quotient vectors is contained in the span of finitely many symbols. Thus the dimension of the resulting inner-product space is the supremum of these Gram ranks, which is the kernel rank and is at most p. It is finite dimensional, so no completion issue remains.

Choose an orthonormal basis and pad with zeros in R^p. The coordinates z(x) of delta_x then satisfy

    k(x,y)=z(x)^T z(y), ||z(x)||<=R,
    ||z(x)-z(y)||^2=k(x,x)+k(y,y)-2k(x,y).

Thus z is continuous and ||z(x)-z(y)||<=Omega(r) whenever ||x-y||_1<=r. To justify Omega(r)->0 directly, suppose the contrary. There are sequences r_j->0 and x_j,y_j in X at distance <=r_j with feature distance bounded away from zero. Compactness supplies a subsequence x_j->x; then y_j->x as well. Continuity of k makes the squared feature distance tend to k(x,x)+k(x,x)-2k(x,x)=0, a contradiction. The supremum is finite because the kernel is continuous on the compact product. In particular every fixed positive e admits the required r.

The factorization at the finite net does not require evaluating any feature map on runtime inputs. Form the fixed J-by-J Gram matrix K_G=(k(a,b))_{a,b in G}. It is PSD of rank <=p, so a finite spectral factorization gives vectors v_a in R^p with v_a^T v_b=k(a,b). There is an isometry between the spans of z(a) and v_a: the map sum c_a z(a) -> sum c_a v_a is well defined and norm preserving because both squared norms equal c^T K_G c. Extend orthonormal bases of the two spans to R^p. The isometry extends to an orthogonal map on R^p. Applying it to all z(x) gives a representation, still called z, with z(a)=v_a for every a in G and with the same norm and modulus bounds.

Consequently **all feature values used as weights below can be obtained from the finite prior Gram matrix on G**. Computing this fixed factorization is preprocessing of the fixed prior, not an input-dependent inverse hidden in the predictive head. Its real entries are included in the encoder's parameter count.

## 3. Cone envelope for a general continuous feature map

Define, using the finite Gram feature values,

    ztilde_j(x)=min_{a in G}[v_{a,j}+A_cone ||x-a||_1].

This formula is valid even though z_j need not be Lipschitz. We claim |ztilde_j(x)-z_j(x)|<=e for every j,x.

For a with ||x-a||_1<=r, the modulus gives v_{a,j}>=z_j(x)-Omega(r)>=z_j(x)-e/2. Adding a nonnegative cone term preserves this lower bound. For a with ||x-a||_1>r, the coordinate bound |z_j|<=R gives

    v_{a,j}+A_cone ||x-a||_1
      >z_j(x)-2R+A_cone r=z_j(x)+e.

So every candidate is >=z_j(x)-e/2, and the finite minimum is too.

For the upper bound choose a net point with ||x-a||_1<=h. Since h=e r/(2(2R+e))<=r/2, the modulus bound applies. Therefore

    ztilde_j(x)<=z_j(x)+Omega(r)+A_cone h
                  <=z_j(x)+e/2+e/2=z_j(x)+e.

It follows that sup_x ||ztilde(x)-z(x)||<=sqrt(p)e=eta and ||ztilde(x)||<=R+eta<=S. All denominators above are positive, including R=0. For a cube grid, coordinate rounding gives L1 distance <=d/(2m)<=e/(2A_cone)=h, which verifies the displayed grid size.

## 4. Exact network realization and original-posterior KL

Use C004 Section 4's explicit register construction, with the J centers now the net points a and with the slope K in the cone layer replaced by A_cone. Layer 1 computes all Jd absolute differences with 2Jd ReLUs. Layer 2 forms the pJ affine cone values using these nonnegative absolute registers and the constant register. A balanced residual-min tournament takes ceil(log_2 J) layers, including zero layers when J=1. The last gating layer, using the binary context/query flags and |ztilde_j|<=S, writes the context/query feature registers exactly. For padding choose a fixed anchor point in X as its raw coordinates, rather than assuming the ambient origin belongs to X. Its flags are zero, so the computed features are gated to zero.

This uses E=3+ceil(log_2 J) encoder layers and precisely the width and hidden-width bounds in Section 1. This invokes the exact algebraic encoder construction, **not the Lipschitz-error assertion** of C004 Section 3. Section 3 above supplies the replacement uniform approximation guarantee.

C004 Section 2's perturbation proof uses only ||ztilde-z||<=eta<=1, not feature Lipschitzness. It therefore gives original-versus-encoded predictive errors

    |mu-mutilde|<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    |v-vtilde|<=min(s/4,s sqrt(eps)/2).

Apply C002 v1 to the encoded features with bound S and accuracy eps0. The one-head query broadcast, T five-head Chebyshev layers, and four-head readout produce muhat,vhat with vhat>=s and errors

    |mutilde-muhat|<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    |vtilde-vhat|<=min(s/4,s sqrt(eps)/2).

The original predictive variance is also >=s. Adding scalar errors gives |mu-muhat|<=sqrt(s eps) and |v-vhat|<=min(s/2,s sqrt(eps)). The Gaussian calculation in C002 Section 5 then yields forward KL<=eps from the **original kernel** predictive distribution to the transformer output. No triangle inequality for KL is used.

Combining the E encoder layers with the T+2 solver layers gives the depth. Count three D-by-D matrices for each of at most five heads, two MLP matrices of dimensions H-by-D and D-by-H per layer (even counting zeros), and a two-coordinate linear readout. This proves the displayed parameter bound.

## 5. Exact scope

C005 covers every continuous bounded finite-rank kernel on a nonempty compact Euclidean domain, with an explicit bound in terms of a kernel modulus and a finite covering number. It includes continuous kernels whose features are not Lipschitz. C004 gives the simpler closed grid formula when a coordinatewise Lipschitz feature bound is available. C002 is smaller when features are supplied directly.

C003 proves that the bounded-kernel statement without continuity can fail for continuous raw-input Gaussian-output architectures. Thus these results distinguish the feature-input interpretation from the regularity needed for a raw-input theorem. They do not claim that a raw-input size bound can ignore the fixed kernel's modulus or its feature-computation complexity. All three constructive claims remain independently unaudited.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X,B,mu) is a probability space and T preserves mu (invertibility is not needed)","P and Q are countable measurable partitions","H_mu(P) < infinity and H_mu(Q) < infinity","entropies are taken with a fixed logarithm base throughout"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090248+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, entropy","id":"claim_73e397e27849e65c29b0ad85dd4fc2d78bd89a46e9ea1748bcc9855a192424af","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let T be a measure-preserving transformation of a probability space (X, B, mu) and let P and Q be countable measurable partitions with H_mu(P) < infinity and H_mu(Q) < infinity. Write P_n for the join of T^{-i}P over 0 <= i <= n-1 and h_mu(T,P) = lim_n (1/n) H_mu(P_n) (the limit exists by subadditivity and equals the infimum over n). Then h_mu(T, Q) <= h_mu(T, P) + H_mu(Q | P). Two standard consequences: if P refines Q then H_mu(Q | P) = 0 and hence h_mu(T, Q) <= h_mu(T, P), so the partition entropy is monotone under refinement; and |h_mu(T,P) - h_mu(T,Q)| <= H_mu(P | Q) + H_mu(Q | P), i.e. the map P -> h_mu(T,P) is 1-Lipschitz for the Rokhlin metric. WHERE IT FAILS: finiteness of H_mu(P) and H_mu(Q) is used - with infinite-entropy partitions both sides can be infinite and the inequality carries no information. The inequality is one-sided: nothing bounds h_mu(T,P) from below in terms of h_mu(T,Q) unless the conditional entropy in the other direction is also controlled. It is an inequality between the entropies of PROCESSES, not of the partitions: H_mu(Q) <= H_mu(P) + H_mu(Q|P) is the (easier) static statement and must not be quoted in its place.","status":"unverified"}

F is normal (in the finite sense) if every sequence in F has a subsequence converging uniformly on every compact subset of U; the limit is then automatically holomorphic, and it need not belong to F. F is normal in the extended sense if every sequence in F has a subsequence which, on each connected component of U, either converges uniformly on compact subsets to a holomorphic function or tends to ∞ uniformly on compact subsets (equivalently, the reciprocals tend to 0 uniformly on compact subsets). For families of meromorphic functions, normality means that every sequence has a subsequence converging uniformly on compact subsets with respect to the chordal metric of the Riemann sphere; restricted to holomorphic families this coincides with the extended sense, because a spherical limit of zero-free reciprocals is, by Hurwitz's theorem, either holomorphic or identically ∞ on each component. Normality is a local property: F is normal on U if and only if every point of U has a neighborhood on which F is normal. Normality asserts the existence of convergent subsequences only; it does not assert convergence of the family itself, and the limit function may leave the family (for instance the limit of injective functions may be constant).","status":"unverified"}

Exact constants are T=3/2, fourth moment9/5, t=6/5,
e=8/35, z=2/35, a=3/5, b=h=0.
Gaussian priors also satisfy (1) with tau=1,eta=x,zeta=0.
The result applies to every fixed law satisfying the stated kernel
conditions, not just these examples. Discrete Rademacher priors do
not satisfy (1) for arbitrary smooth tests and are not covered.
Specifically choose a compact smooth cutoff of (3*x-x^3)/2 which
equals that polynomial near {-1,1}. At a Rademacher input, h(u)=u
and h'(u)=0, so E[u*h(u)]=1 while E[tau(u)*h'(u)]=0 for every
finite function tau on its support. This is an obstruction to
applying the present derivative-transfer route to that law, not a
counterexample to quartic universality for discrete priors.

More concretely, each of U and V may have any standardized beta
law, with its own arbitrary fixed positive shape parameters p,q.
Let k=p+q, C=1/k, B=(q-p)*sqrt(k+1)/(k*sqrt(p*q)), and
x=(t-p/k)/sqrt(p*q/[k^2*(k+1)]) for t~Beta(p,q). Then

 tau(x)=1+C+B*x-C*x^2,
 eta(x)=tau(x)*(x+B)/(1+C),
 zeta(x)=B*tau(x)-C*eta(x).

The beta density times tau vanishes at both endpoints, including
when the density itself is unbounded there, because p,q>0.
Direct integration of its derivative proves E[x h]=E[tau h'].
Writing Q=x^2-1, the identity tau-1=B*x-C*Q and applying this
first identity to x*h(x) give
(1+C)E[Q*h]=E[tau*(x+B)*h']; this proves the eta identity.
The zeta identity follows by the same linear relation tau-1.
All kernels are bounded on the compact standardized support, so
every hypothesis of (1) is paid. This covers two asymmetric beta
priors as well as the symmetric subfamily. For an asymmetric exact
check, Beta(2,3) standardized as x=5*t-2 has

For a sequence of finite, possibly random, rooted graphs G_n, local weak (Benjamini-Schramm) convergence means that for every finite radius r, the distribution of the isomorphism class of the r-ball around the (uniformly, or otherwise canonically) chosen root converges weakly to that of a limiting, typically infinite, random rooted graph (G*, o). The objective method, due to Aldous and Steele, is the broader program of analyzing this limiting infinite object directly, such as a Poisson weighted infinite tree or a unimodular Galton-Watson tree, to compute limiting constants for combinatorial optimization functionals on the finite graphs, such as the minimum spanning tree constant or the limiting value in the random assignment problem, by solving a recursive distributional (fixed-point) equation on the infinite limit rather than working with finite-n computations directly. It does not by itself establish that a given sequence converges locally weakly, which typically must be separately verified via a subsequential compactness argument together with uniqueness of subsequential limits, and it does not directly give convergence of global, extensive functionals without an additional concentration or summation argument beyond the purely local statement. Typical failure: Assuming that local weak convergence of the underlying random graph automatically implies convergence of a global extensive functional, such as the total weight of a minimum spanning tree, at the same per-vertex limiting rate; local convergence controls only typical local neighborhoods, and passing to a global average requires an additional uniform-integrability or concentration argument, often the genuinely hard part of an objective-method proof, which is easy to overlook once the local limit has been identified. Canonical reference: Benjamini and Schramm, 2001, Electronic Journal of Probability; Aldous and Steele, 2004, in Probability on Discrete Structures, Springer; Aldous and Lyons, 2007, Electronic Journal of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X, M) is a measurable space","mu and nu are positive measures on M (for signed or complex measures the definition is applied to their total variations)","the separating set E is required to belong to M"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402012+00:00","domain":"measure theory, decomposition of measures","id":"claim_7949ee76619d07edbf68d03f6116561c0881f49a0a0bfc5d35c33818a908ff98","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let mu and nu be positive measures on M. One says that mu and nu are MUTUALLY SINGULAR, written mu perp nu, if there exists a set E in M with mu(E) = 0 and nu(X minus E) = 0; equivalently, X splits into two measurable pieces, one carrying all of nu and mu-null, the other carrying all of mu and nu-null. The relation is symmetric. For signed or complex measures the definition is applied to the total variations: mu perp nu means |mu| perp |nu|. Basic consequences: mu perp mu holds if and only if mu = 0; if nu is absolutely continuous with respect to mu (nu << mu) and nu perp mu, then nu = 0; if nu_1 perp mu and nu_2 perp mu then (nu_1 + nu_2) perp mu. CAUTIONS. (1) Mutual singularity is much stronger than 'nu is not absolutely continuous with respect to mu': a measure can fail to be absolutely continuous without being singular, and in general a measure splits into an absolutely continuous and a singular part (Lebesgue decomposition). (2) Singularity is a measure-theoretic, not a topological, smallness statement: the measure sum over n of 2^(-n) times the Dirac mass at the n-th rational is mutually singular with Lebesgue measure on R yet has full support, and the Cantor-Lebesgue measure is mutually singular with Lebesgue measure while being atomless. (3) The witness set E must be measurable; without that requirement the notion is vacuous or ill-posed. (4) Mutual singularity is not preserved by arbitrary uncountable sums of measures.","status":"unverified"}

A rank-one bounded PSD kernel on [-1,1], k(x,xprime)=1{x>=0}1{xprime>=0}, with observation noise variance 1, prevents every continuous raw-input Gaussian predictor from achieving uniform forward KL below log(9/8)/4 > 1/36. An empty context, or one observation (-1,0), yields predictive variances 1 left of zero and 2 at zero. Status: proof (unaudited), T336-w727-C003 v1. Complete theorem, constants and scope:
# Raw-input obstruction for Target 1

Claim T336-w727-C003 v1. Status: proof (unaudited). This is a scope obstruction to the literal bounded-kernel raw-input statement; it does not contradict C002's supplied-feature theorem. No novelty or Lean certification is claimed.

## Statement

There is a rank-one bounded positive-semidefinite kernel on the compact raw-input domain [-1,1], observation-noise variance s=1, and bounded context labels, such that every predictor with continuous Gaussian output parameters (mu(x),v(x)), v(x)>0, has worst-case noisy predictive forward KL at least

    c0=(1/4) log(9/8)>1/36.

The conclusion applies in particular to every finite transformer whose raw-input encoding and subsequent operations are continuous and whose output is a Gaussian with positive continuous variance. It applies to normalized ReLU attention and softmax attention under these conditions. Therefore boundedness, compactness, finite rank, and positive observation noise alone cannot imply the raw-input version of Target 1 for arbitrarily small eps.

## Kernel and posterior

Define phi(x)=0 for x<0 and phi(x)=1 for x>=0. Set k(x,x')=phi(x)phi(x'). For any finite coefficients a_i,

    sum_{i,j} a_i a_j k(x_i,x_j)=(sum_i a_i phi(x_i))^2>=0.

Thus k is positive semidefinite, bounded by 1, and of rank exactly one (because k(0,0)=1). The GP can be represented as f(x)=Z phi(x), with Z~N(0,1). Observations add independent N(0,1) noise.

Use the empty context if allowed. Alternatively, for any n>=1 use one observation at x=-1 with label y=0, which satisfies every B>=0. This observation is pure noise independent of Z, so the posterior law of Z remains N(0,1). For either context, the new noisy predictive distribution is

    P_x=N(0,1) for x<0; P_x=N(0,2) for x>=0.

Hence the example does not rely on whether a context of length zero is included.

## Continuity forces two incompatible approximation requirements

Fix this context and any continuous output mu(x),v(x)>0. Let E=sup_x KL(P_x || N(mu(x),v(x))). If E is infinite the bound is immediate. Otherwise put mu0=mu(0),v0=v(0)>0. At x=0,

    D_2:=KL(N(0,2)||N(mu0,v0))<=E.

Take x_j=-1/j tending to zero from below. Since mu,v are continuous and v0>0, the explicit Gaussian KL formula is continuous along this sequence; all denominators remain positive near the limit. Therefore

    D_1:=KL(N(0,1)||N(mu0,v0))<=E.

No dominated convergence, probabilistic conditioning argument, or exchange of a supremum with a limit is used: every term in this deterministic convergent sequence is <=E.

For a>0 define

    D_a=(1/2)(log(v0/a)+(a+mu0^2)/v0-1).

Writing w=3/(2v0)>0 and combining logarithms gives the exact identity

    (D_1+D_2)/2
      = (1/4)log(9/8)+(1/2)(w-1-log w)+mu0^2/(2v0).

The inequality log w<=w-1 follows by integrating 1/t from 1 to w, separately for w>=1 and 0<w<=1, or by differentiating w-1-log w. Both additional terms are nonnegative. Consequently

    E >= (D_1+D_2)/2 >= (1/4)log(9/8).

Finally log(9/8)=integral_1^{9/8} dt/t > (1/8)(8/9)=1/9, since 1/t>8/9 except at the right endpoint. Thus c0>1/36. Every denominator and logarithm argument above is strictly positive.

## Interpretation for the dossier

C002 supplies phi as an input, so its input encoding itself is discontinuous as a function of raw x in this example; the continuity hypothesis here then fails. There is no contradiction. To close Target 1, the architecture must explicitly permit the fixed feature map in the input representation, or the theorem must add assumptions that make raw-input feature computation possible and account for its cost. Merely calling the kernel finite rank does not settle this issue.

The example is an obstruction to a named target interpretation, not a claimed solution of the entire T336 problem. The remaining feature-input theorem C002 and this obstruction both await independent review.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space","T : X -> X is continuous and surjective","the definition quantifies over all nonempty OPEN subsets U"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090776+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, mixing properties of non-invertible maps","id":"claim_79ea44cf7b3dcd7452df709c8e293198d63314337814289a89d9a84e9a0edffe","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a compact metric space and T : X -> X a continuous surjection. T is TOPOLOGICALLY EXACT, also called locally eventually onto, if for every nonempty open set U there is an integer n >= 1 with T^n(U) = X. Two consequences are what proofs actually use. (a) UNIFORMITY IN n: if T^n(U) = X then T^m(U) = X for every m >= n, because T is onto; hence for each nonempty open U there is N with T^n(U) = X for ALL n >= N. (b) DENSE BACKWARD ORBITS WITH ALL LARGE PERIODS: for every x in X and every nonempty open U there is N with U intersect T^{-n}(x) nonempty for every n >= N; in particular the full backward orbit of any point is dense. Property (b) is a genuine aperiodicity statement that topological transitivity does not give and that even topological mixing of an invertible system cannot give. Relations: topological exactness implies topological mixing, which implies topological transitivity; the converses are false. An invertible map is never topologically exact unless X is a single point, since T^n(U) = X forces U = X for a homeomorphism, so exactness is a hypothesis reserved for genuinely non-invertible maps: expanding maps of the circle or of a compact manifold, one-sided mixing subshifts of finite type, and Chebyshev-like interval maps are the standard examples.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["K ⊂ ℝⁿ is nonempty and closed","the Euclidean norm is used (for the eikonal equation |Du| = 1 the ball of the same norm is the unit speed set)","the eikonal equation is taken in the form |Du| − 1 = 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.110904+00:00","domain":"Hamilton–Jacobi equations, optimal control, distance functions","id":"claim_7a06bdbc5ba6d57f83322f14777c062b65834326f61029190ba7a9d22b579f18","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let K ⊂ ℝⁿ be nonempty and closed and let d(x) := dist(x, K) = min_{y ∈ K} |x − y| (the minimum is attained because K is closed). Then: (a) d is 1-Lipschitz, d ≥ 0, and d(x) = 0 exactly when x ∈ K. (b) [minimal-time / control representation] d(x) = inf { T ≥ 0 : there is an absolutely continuous ξ: [0,T] → ℝⁿ with |ξ'(s)| ≤ 1 for a.e. s, ξ(0) = x, ξ(T) ∈ K } = inf { ∫_0^T |ξ'(s)| ds : ξ absolutely continuous, ξ(0) = x, ξ(T) ∈ K, T ≥ 0 } — the distance is the value function of the minimal-time problem for the control system ξ' = α, |α| ≤ 1, with target K, and the straight segment from x to a nearest point of K is an optimal trajectory. (c) [variational characterization] d is the largest 1-Lipschitz function that is ≤ 0 on K: if u: ℝⁿ → ℝ is 1-Lipschitz and u ≤ 0 on K then u ≤ d everywhere, and d itself is admissible; equivalently d(x) = max { u(x) : u 1-Lipschitz, u ≤ 0 on K }. Exact normal linear-stability classification of every finite fixed point of joint-head factored-attention GD at every eta>0: the stationary curve v=0,kq=p_bar has tangent multiplier 1 and normal multipliers 1-eta lambda_+/- with lambda_+/-=(A +/- sqrt(A^2+4B^2(k^2+q^2)))/2. One normal direction is always repelling; the other attracts exactly when k^2+q^2<(4/eta^2-2A/eta)/B^2, is neutral at equality, and repels beyond. Every positive fixed step loses the attracting normal direction at sufficiently unbalanced factorizations.

# Target 1: exact normal stability of the factored GD stationary curve

Version 1, proof unaudited. This is a linearized stability classification;
it does not claim a nonlinear flip bifurcation or a full-space GD basin theorem.

Assume precisely the n-example factored model of claim 010:
0<a_i<b_i, b_i,kappa_i>0, logistic average loss of
v h_i(kq), h_i(s)=a_i+b_i tanh(kappa_i s), and simultaneous Euclidean GD
with any fixed eta>0. Let p_bar<0 be the unique mean root and define

 A=mean_i h_i(p_bar)^2/4>=0,
 B=mean_i h_i'(p_bar)/2>0.

All finite stationary points, equivalently all GD fixed points, form the
curve E={v=0,kq=p_bar}. At such a point write S=k^2+q^2>=2|p_bar|.
The GD Jacobian has tangent multiplier 1 and normal multipliers

 mu_-=1-eta lambda_-, mu_+=1-eta lambda_+,
 lambda_+/-=(A +/- sqrt(A^2+4B^2 S))/2.

Here lambda_-<0<lambda_+, hence mu_->1 everywhere: no point of E is
linearly attracting in all normal directions. The other normal direction is

* strictly attracting in the linearization when eta lambda_+<2;
* neutral with multiplier -1 when eta lambda_+=2;
* strictly repelling with multiplier less than -1 when eta lambda_+>2.

Let
 J_eta=(4/eta^2-2A/eta)/B^2.

The first case is EXACTLY S<J_eta, the middle case exactly S=J_eta,
and the last exactly S>J_eta. Equivalently, with C=k^2-q^2,
S=sqrt(C^2+4p_bar^2): there is an attracting normal direction only if
J_eta>2|p_bar|, and then precisely at

 |C|<sqrt(J_eta^2-4p_bar^2).

Equality gives neutral normal points when J_eta>=2|p_bar|. If J_eta
is smaller than 2|p_bar|, every point is repelling in both normal directions.
In particular, for EVERY eta>0, sufficiently unbalanced factorizations on
E are normally repelling in both directions. There is no positive constant
step that preserves the flow's one attracting normal direction uniformly
along the entire stationary curve. This does NOT imply an open basin of
cycles or disprove a full-space almost-everywhere GD endpoint theorem.

## Proof

The fixed-point condition is gradient L=0, classified in proof 008.
Its loss Hessian at E is
 [[A,-Bq,-Bk],[-Bq,0,0],[-Bk,0,0]].
The tangent vector (0,k,-q) is in its kernel. In the orthonormal basis
e_v=(1,0,0), e_s=(0,q,k)/sqrt(S) of the normal plane, the Hessian is
 [[A,-B sqrt(S)],[-B sqrt(S),0]].
The quadratic characteristic polynomial is lambda^2-A lambda-B^2 S,
which yields lambda_+/- and their signs. The GD Jacobian is I-eta Hessian,
proving the multipliers and their linear classifications.

For equivalence with J_eta, consider the polynomial
f(z)=z^2-Az-B^2 S, whose positive zero is lambda_+ and negative zero
lambda_-. Since 2/eta>0, lambda_+<2/eta is equivalent to
f(2/eta)>0, or S<J_eta; equality and the reverse inequality follow likewise.
This avoids squaring a potentially negative expression 4/eta-A.
Finally S^2=C^2+4p_bar^2 by algebra, and S is unbounded along E by
taking k->infinity, q=p_bar/k. All asserted threshold statements follow.

## Scope of the obstruction

The obstruction is to a PARTICULAR transfer from flow to GD: retaining
one attracting normal direction uniformly on every imbalance leaf at fixed
step. It is not an obstruction to every possible discrete-time proof.
The imbalance leaves themselves are not invariant under GD:
C_+=(1-eta^2 v^2 G^2)C. Both facts must be accounted for in further work.
Normal multipliers on the unit circle require separate nonlinear analysis;
no attracting two-cycle is claimed. Scalar genuine self-attention embeddings
of this family are supplied in claim 008.","status":"unverified"}

# Balanced opposite-head two-cycles: complete implicit parametrization

T328-W698-017 v1, Target 1, proof (unaudited).

Consider L(v,k,q)=log(1+exp(-v h(kq))), h(s)=a+b*tanh(kappa*s),
0<a<b, kappa>0 and simultaneous Euclidean GD with fixed eta>0.
For this scalar signed link, every balanced period-two orbit whose heads have
opposite signs is covered by the following construction, up to interchanging
the two phases and simultaneously negating both factors. The construction
parametrizes cycles across the data/step parameters; for prescribed a,b,kappa,
eta these parameter equalities are necessary and sufficient, not a claim that
every prescribed model has such a cycle.

## Construction from four positive parameters

Choose 0<r<1 and T,y0,kappa>0. Define

    A=tanh T, B=tanh(r^2*T),
    D=cosh(T)^2/cosh(r^2*T)^2,
    sig(y)=1/(1+exp(-y)), f(y)=y*sig(y)^2.

There is a unique y1>0 solving

    f(y1)=f(y0)/(r*D).

Indeed f'(y)=sig(y)^2*[1+2y*(1-sig(y))]>0 on y>0,
and f increases continuously from 0 to infinity. Put

    g0=sig(y0), g1=sig(y1), c=g0/g1,
    t=y1/(y0*c),
    v0=sqrt((1-r)*(A-B)/((1+t)*(1+c)*kappa*sech(T)^2)),
    H0=y0/v0, H1=c*H0,
    b=H0*(1+c)/(A-B), a=b*A-H0,
    eta=v0*(1+t)/(g0*H0), w=sqrt(T/kappa).

All denominators are strictly positive. Also a/b=(c*A+B)/(1+c) lies
strictly between B and A, hence 0<a<b. These parameters give the exact
period-two orbit

    (v0,w,-w) <-> (-t*v0,r*w,-r*w).

The two signed margins are -y0 and -y1. In particular the logistic factors
are exactly g0 and g1, not factors obtained from a limiting approximation.

## Verification

h(-w^2)=-H0 and h(-r^2*w^2)=H1. Thus g0*H0=g1*H1 and
the two head increments are respectively -v0*(1+t) and v0*(1+t).
Let d0=b*kappa*sech(T)^2, d1=b*kappa*sech(r^2*T)^2=D*d0.
The first factor coefficient is

    delta0=eta*v0*g0*d0
          =v0^2*(1+t)*(1+c)*kappa*sech(T)^2/(A-B)=1-r.

For the second coefficient, the scalar equation gives

    t*(g1/g0)*D = y1*g1^2*D/(y0*g0^2)=1/r.

Consequently delta1=eta*(-t*v0)*g1*d1=-(1-r)/r=1-1/r.
On k=-q the factor multipliers 1-delta0=r and 1-delta1=1/r
return the factors exactly. The head changes sign, so the orbit is nonfixed.

## Completeness within the stated class

Balance means k^2=q^2. If k=q, the product is nonnegative, h(kq)>0,
and the head strictly increases at every finite point, so there is no finite
cycle. If k=q=0 the same argument applies. Thus a balanced cycle must lie
on k=-q with nonzero k. Interchange phases so v0>0>v1 and simultaneously
negate both factors so k0=w>0. Since delta_j=eta*v_j*g_j*h'_j,
delta0>0>delta1. The returning-factor equation is

    (1-delta0)*(1-delta1)=1.

The second factor is >1; therefore 0<1-delta0<1. Write this number r.
It follows that k1=r*w and delta1=1-1/r. In particular no factor sign flip
is possible for an opposite-head balanced two-cycle in this class.
The head update v1-v0<0 forces h0<0, and the reverse update forces h1>0.
Set H0=-h0, H1=h1, t=-v1/v0, T=kappa*w^2,
y0=v0*H0, y1=t*v0*H1. These are positive. The equal and opposite
head increments imply H1/H0=g0/g1=c, whence t=y1/(y0*c).
Dividing the two factor coefficients gives r*D*f(y1)=f(y0).
The identities h1-h0=b*(A-B), delta0=1-r and the head increment then
recover precisely the formulas for b,a,v0,eta above. This proves completeness.

## Full Jacobian test and its present limit

The normal two-step multiplier is exactly

    mu_U=(1+delta0)*(1+delta1)=(2-r)*(2-1/r)=5-2r-2/r.

It satisfies |mu_U|<1 precisely for (3-sqrt(5))/2<r<1,
equals -1 at the left endpoint, and is <-1 below it. It is zero at r=1/2.
The other two multipliers are exactly the eigenvalues of J1*J0, using
the general balanced Jacobian given in proofs/014_opposite_head_cycles.md.
This is an exact formula for the full spectrum, but no uniform inequality
for that balanced block has been proved for unequal head magnitudes.

The reproducible script scripts/asymmetric_cycles.py sampled 576 choices:
r in {.1,.2,.35,.4,.5,.65,.8,.9,.98}, T in {.1,.3,.6,.9,1.3,2,3,5},
y0 in {.01,.1,.4,1,2,4,8,16}, with kappa=1. It solved the monotone
equation by floating-point bisection and differentiated the full 3D loss.
It found zero attracting candidates; the smallest observed full spectral
radius was approximately 8.9666956. The largest relative cycle residual was
approximately 2.56e-13. These are numerical evidence, not rigorous bounds,
and cannot establish instability throughout the parametrization.

Claim 016 proves full instability and the complete second-multiplier phase
diagram on the equal-head-magnitude subfamily r=1/2,
cosh(T)^2=2cosh(T/4)^2. The SINGLE remaining hard step for upgrading
the wider numerical finding to a theorem is a rigorous spectral-radius
inequality for J1*J0 throughout (r,T,y0)>0 with 0<r<1. This proof
does not claim that step or almost-everywhere factored-GD convergence.","status":"unverified"}

Method: Analyse M(1,1) on Z^2 through the range of the first-coordinate walk. Result: In M(1,1) the first coordinate moves only at first visits and the second at later visits; the set of visited vertices is the range, and the first-coordinate process is a simple random walk on Z run at the rate of new visits. Recurrence of M(1,1) would follow if the walk returns to the origin infinitely often; since the second coordinate performs a simple random walk on the column above the current first coordinate whenever the vertex was visited before, the walk behaves in each column like a 1D random walk (recurrent) until it hits an unvisited vertex, at which time the first coordinate steps. The number of new visits up to time n is the range R_n; the first coordinate after n steps is a simple random walk at time R_n, so |X^1_n| is of order sqrt(R_n), and R_n <= n, so |X^1_n| is typically at most of order sqrt n - not deterministically: n first-visit moves to the right, which have probability 2^-n, give X^1_n = n; a return to the origin requires both coordinates to vanish. A heuristic: if R_n ≍ n/log n as for planar simple random walk then the first coordinate is diffusive at the slower clock, and the walk is 'more recurrent' than planar simple random walk, supporting the conjecture; but the range of M(1,1) is not that of simple random walk because the exploration is column-wise. A rigorous partial fact: M(1,1) is recurrent if and only if the first coordinate returns to 0 infinitely often at times when the second coordinate is 0; since within a column the second coordinate is a recurrent 1D walk that keeps returning to 0 until it finds a new vertex, and new vertices in a column are found at the ends of the visited interval, the question is whether the first-coordinate walk (which is a simple random walk in the clock of new visits) visits 0 infinitely often, which it does a.s. (1D recurrence), and whether at those visits the second coordinate is 0 - not automatic. So recurrence of M(1,1) reduces to: at the (infinitely many) times the first coordinate is 0, the second coordinate, which then performs a 1D walk in the column of 0 with the visited interval of that column, returns to height 0 before finding a new vertex - which has probability bounded below by a constant each time if the visited interval around height 0 in column 0 has length bounded... the visited interval in column 0 grows, and the probability of returning to 0 from the boundary of an interval of length L before exiting is of order 1/L... summing over the visits to column 0 gives a divergent series only if the interval lengths grow slowly enough. This is the crux and I did not settle it; the reduction is recorded. Key identity: M(1,1) recurrent iff, at the infinitely many returns of the first coordinate to 0, the second coordinate returns to 0 in column 0 before finding a new vertex; the return probability is of order 1/(visited interval length). Obstruction: Growth rate of the visited interval in column 0 not controlled.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a Hilbert space","T is a bounded linear operator on H"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.571526+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator ideals","id":"claim_7d3da9c3c18db6a4a1b175a83b3a4853fd1bc3c0008d3153ce0be80e2db8b984","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H be a Hilbert space. A bounded operator T on H is trace class (nuclear) if it is compact and ||T||_1 := sum_n s_n(T) < infinity. Equivalently: sum_i <|T| e_i, e_i> < infinity for some (hence every) orthonormal basis (e_i), where |T| = (T*T)^{1/2}, and this sum then equals ||T||_1; equivalently, T = AB with A and B Hilbert-Schmidt operators. The trace of a trace-class T is tr T = sum_i <T e_i, e_i>; this series converges absolutely for every orthonormal basis and its sum does not depend on the basis. The trace-class operators S_1(H) form a two-sided ideal of B(H) and a Banach space under ||.||_1, with ||T|| <= ||T||_2 <= ||T||_1; finite-rank operators are ||.||_1-dense in S_1(H); under the pairing (T, B) -> tr(TB), S_1(H) is isometrically the dual of the compact operators K(H) and the predual of B(H). For a positive operator T >= 0 the sum sum_i <T e_i, e_i> in [0, infinity] is basis-independent and is finite exactly when T is trace class; for operators that are not positive, convergence (even absolute convergence) of sum_i <T e_i, e_i> in one basis does not imply trace class.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Counterexample: F(p,z,x) = p_1 (equation u_x = 0), Γ = {y=0}","Noncharacteristic condition: D_pF(p0,z0,x0)·ν(x0) ≠ 0","Compatibility (admissibility): F(p0,z0,x0) = 0 and p0 agrees with the tangential gradient of g on Γ","Even when the conditions hold, the conclusion is only local in a neighbourhood of the point"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418512+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: first-order equations, method of characteristics","id":"claim_7d8c544f22ddfa6bc426587ded0c72b9450163a966ed4890aa02b90253645958","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: local solvability of F(Du,u,x) = 0 with u = g on Γ requires D_pF(p0,z0,x0)·ν(x0) ≠ 0, i.e. the characteristic direction must be transversal to the data surface; and the initial triple must be admissible (the tangential derivatives of g must match p0). If the surface is characteristic, existence can fail outright and uniqueness can fail catastrophically. Counterexample: the equation u_x = 0 in R^2 (F(p,z,x) = p_1, so D_pF = (1,0)) with data on Γ = { y = 0 }, whose normal is ν = (0,1): D_pF·ν = 0, so Γ is characteristic — indeed the characteristics are the horizontal lines y = const, which lie IN Γ. Every C^1 solution satisfies u(x,y) = u(0,y), so u(·,0) must be constant: if g is not constant there is NO solution in any neighbourhood of a point of Γ; if g ≡ c there are infinitely many solutions u(x,y) = h(y) with h ∈ C^1 arbitrary and h(0) = c. The same pathology occurs for u_t + u_x = 0 with data prescribed on the characteristic line { x = t }. Auditor's check: before invoking local existence by characteristics, compute D_pF·ν at the point in question; for quasilinear equations a(x,u)·Du = b this is a(x0,g(x0))·ν(x0) ≠ 0, and for the Cauchy problem u_t + H(x,Du) = 0 on { t = 0 } it is automatic (the coefficient of u_t is 1).","status":"unverified"}

For the Erdos-Renyi random graph G(n,p) near the critical window p = 1/n + lambda n^{-4/3}, Aldous's exploration process encodes a depth-first search of the graph as a random-walk-like process Z_n(t) whose excursions above past running minima correspond exactly to the connected components, with excursion lengths equal to component sizes. After rescaling space by n^{-2/3} and time correspondingly, this process converges to a limiting process W(t) = B(t) + lambda t - t^2/2, a Brownian motion with parabolic drift, whose excursions above its running minimum encode the limiting rescaled sizes of the largest components in the critical window; the associated merging dynamics of component sizes as edges are added form the \"standard multiplicative coalescent\", a Markov process on sequences of masses matching the excursion structure. This gives the precise scaling limit, order n^{2/3} for the largest components with an explicit limiting joint law, for the Erdos-Renyi critical phase transition. It does not extend directly to other random graph models without re-deriving an analogous exploration or walk encoding, which may not exist in closed form, and the specific n^{2/3} spatial and n^{-1/3} time-window scaling is particular to models in the Erdos-Renyi (mean-field) universality class. {"assumptions":["The two cylinders must be separated in time, past on the left of the inequality","Nonnegativity is required on the entire cylinder","Time-slice and reversed-time versions are false","Cylinders must respect the parabolic scaling t ~ r^2"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.107085+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations / Harnack inequalities","id":"claim_7f4575933b50f01a827886bdb34f32f9b2fc796f45ba59f43b34b0e99f0abc08","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Moser's inequality reads $\\sup_{Q^-}u\\le C\\inf_{Q^+}u$ with $Q^-$ strictly earlier than $Q^+$. Three hypotheses are load-bearing, and all three fail for the naive elliptic-style statement. (1) No inequality at a single time: on $\\mathbb R^n$ the positive solution $u_k(x,t)=e^{kx_1+k^2t}$ has, on $B_1\\times\\{t\\}$, $\\sup u_k/\\inf u_k=e^{2k}\\to\\infty$, so $\\sup_{B_1\\times\\{t\\}}u\\le C\\inf_{B_1\\times\\{t\\}}u$ cannot hold with $C$ independent of the solution; the same family (or the shifted heat kernel $\\Phi(x-y,t+\\varepsilon)$ as $\\varepsilon\\downarrow0$) shows that even the elliptic Harnack constant for the Laplacian does not transfer. (2) The time direction cannot be reversed: $\\sup_{Q^+}u\\le C\\inf_{Q^-}u$ is false, since $u_k$ grows like $e^{k^2t}$; information propagates forward in time only. Intuitively, a heat distribution can be large now and tiny in the past. (3) Nonnegativity on the whole cylinder is needed, not just on $Q^-\\cup Q^+$: the inequality is applied to $u$ and to $\\sup u-u$ in the derivation of Holder continuity, and both must be nonnegative on the full cylinder $B_{2r}\\times(t_0-4r^2,t_0)$. Also parabolic, not Euclidean, scaling governs the geometry: the cylinder for radius $r$ must have time length comparable to $r^2$, so an auditor should check that a cited Harnack inequality is applied on cylinders of the correct aspect ratio, with the two sub-cylinders separated in time by a fixed multiple of $r^2$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:15:27.869314+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_800182846141774e70b9296f79e5eab92b4ed12261fc2c10ba2ec3e50d8353b6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"FIRES WHEN a source, or your own reading of one, states a stochastic dominance between two random variables that you can check have equal means. MINIMAL COUNTEREXAMPLE, or rather the minimal IMPOSSIBILITY: if X >= Y in the usual stochastic order and E X = E Y < infinity, then E(X - Y) = integral (P(X > t) - P(Y > t)) dt = 0 with a nonnegative integrand, so the survival functions agree everywhere and X and Y are equal in law. There is no example to find; the hypothesis is already the conclusion. CONDITION UNDER WHICH THE ROUTE FAILS: equal means. WHAT TO DO INSTEAD: the intended relation is the CONVEX or dilation order, under which the variance inequality c^2 >= 1 is immediate. In the E0078 case this is a reading issue in the source's own statement, not a mathematical obstacle - and reading it as the usual stochastic order would have made Conjecture 4.2 imply Conjecture 4.1 for a trivial and wrong reason. The lesson generalises past this problem: when a claimed ordering would be vacuous under a moment identity the problem also asserts, the ordering has been mis-transcribed.","status":"unverified"}

# C006: prior-averaged Gaussian log-loss generalization

Claim T336-w727-C006 v1. Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: bound.
Target: none (reviewer-authorized generalization half of the T336 statement).
This is an explicit adaptation of standard covering and exponential-moment
arguments, not a claim of a new learning-theory principle or a new solver.
The hardest step is uniform concentration for the unbounded query loss.

## 1. Statistical statement

Let (W_i,Y_i), i=1,...,m, be independent identically distributed tasks, m>=1.
W contains the context and query features, including all information on which
the predictive is conditioned. Assume the conditional law is exactly

    Y | W ~ N(a(W), b(W)), |a(W)|<=M, 0<b(W)<=V,

where M>=0 and V>0 are fixed. The law of W is otherwise arbitrary. In
particular no independence between the query and context features is required.
For the GP application this conditional-law premise must be checked; it is
not inferred just from a marginal GP label law or an arbitrary feature-selection
mechanism. A fixed GP, exogenous input design, and rejection of tasks based only
on their context labels satisfy it. Conditioning on query labels would not.

Assume the token encoding of W is measurable. Let H be the family of clipped
transformer predictions described in Section 2,
with outputs mu_theta(W) in [-U,U] and v_theta(W) in [v0,v1], where
U>=0 and 0<v0<=v1 are fixed. Define the normalized negative log loss

    ell_theta(W,Y) = (1/2)log(v_theta/v0)
                    +(Y-mu_theta)^2/(2v_theta).

The usual Gaussian negative log density differs by the same constant
(1/2)log(2 pi v0) for every theta, so its ERM and excess risk are identical.
Let R(theta)=E ell_theta and Rhat(theta)=m^(-1) sum_i ell_theta(W_i,Y_i).
An approximate ERM satisfies Rhat(thetahat)<=inf_theta Rhat(theta)+xi,
with xi>=0. No efficient algorithm for finding it is asserted.

For gamma>0 and alpha in (0,1), use the explicit architecture quantities
P,Lambda from Section 2 and set

    q = max(1,ceil(2 Wmax Lambda/gamma)), J=(q+1)^P,
    D0=M+U,
    C=(1/2)log(v1/v0)+D0^2/v0, A=V/v0, K=4(C+A),
    u=log(4J/alpha), t=log(4m/alpha),
    T=M+sqrt(2V t),
    Q=1/(2v0)+(D0+sqrt(V))/v0+(D0^2+V)/v0^2,
    L_T=1/(2v0)+(T+U)/v0+(T+U)^2/(2v0^2),
    beta=4sqrt(2) K sqrt(u/m)+2K u/m,
    E_m=beta+gamma(Q+L_T).

Then, with probability at least 1-alpha, simultaneously for all theta,

    |R(theta)-Rhat(theta)| <= E_m,
    R(thetahat) <= inf_theta R(theta)+2E_m+xi.             (1)

Let P_W=N(a(W),b(W)) and h_theta=N(mu_theta(W),v_theta(W)). Subtracting
the integrable conditional Gaussian entropy gives equivalently

    E_W KL(P_W || h_thetahat(W))
       <= inf_theta E_W KL(P_W || h_theta(W))+2E_m+xi.   (2)

For (2), assume also b(W)>=b0>0, as in the noisy-GP application. This
makes the conditional entropy finite and justifies subtracting it. Without
that lower bound (1) still holds, but (2) is not asserted via subtraction
of potentially infinite entropies.

## 2. Explicit parameter entropy for normalized ReLU attention

Fix N tokens, token dimension D>=1, L>=0 residual attention layers, at
most H>=1 heads per layer, and a linear two-output readout. No trainable
tokenwise MLP, softmax, or layer normalization is included in this architecture.
Pad unused heads by zero matrices. There are

    P=3HLD^2+2D

trainable scalar entries, all in [-Wmax,Wmax], with Wmax>=1. The encoding
of W into tokens is fixed and has every scalar coordinate bounded in
absolute value by K0>=1. One layer is exactly

    h_i^+ = h_i + N^(-1) sum_heads sum_j
                    ReLU(<Q h_i,K h_j>) V h_j.

Optionally apply a fixed coordinatewise clip onto [-Kcap,Kcap] after each
attention layer, with Kcap>=K0. This is fixed tokenwise ReLU postprocessing,
not a trainable MLP or layer normalization. For this variant use K_l=Kcap
for every l in the recurrences below instead of the growing K recurrence.
Clipping is nonexpansive, so the same E recurrence remains valid.

The readout acts on one fixed token. Apply coordinatewise interval clipping
to its two outputs. This postprocessing uses fixed, nontrainable constants;
each scalar clip is representable by two ReLUs. Count P as the trainable
parameters, not as every fixed scalar in this postprocessing.

Define deterministic nonnegative recurrences

    K_{l+1}=K_l+H D^4 Wmax^3 K_l^3,       K_0=K0,
    E_0=0,
    E_{l+1}=(1+3H D^4 Wmax^3 K_l^2) E_l
                       +3H D^4 Wmax^2 K_l^3,
    Lambda=D Wmax E_L+D K_L > 0.

For any two parameter vectors theta,theta' in the cube at sup distance
rho, the outputs obey

    sup_W max(|mu_theta-mu_theta'|,|v_theta-v_theta'|)
        <= Lambda rho.                                  (3)

To verify this, use the sup norm across all tokens and coordinates. Each
transformed coordinate Qh has magnitude <=D Wmax K_l; each score has
magnitude <=D^3 Wmax^2 K_l^2; each Vh coordinate has magnitude
<=D Wmax K_l. The normalized sum cancels N and proves the K recurrence.

At fixed weights, changing inputs by d changes one head by at most
3D^4 Wmax^3 K_l^2 d: two terms differentiate the score and one term
the value; ReLU is 1-Lipschitz. At fixed inputs of size K_l, changing
matrix entries by rho changes a head by at most
3D^4 Wmax^2 K_l^3 rho, by the same three-term product split. Splitting
the joint change into these two changes and adding the residual proves
the E recurrence by induction. The readout change is bounded by
D Wmax E_L rho+D K_L rho. Clipping is 1-Lipschitz, proving (3).
These estimates compare actual heads directly, and require no independence
among tokens or between successive layers.

Divide [-Wmax,Wmax] into q equal intervals. There are q+1 grid values;
each parameter has a grid value within 2Wmax/q<=gamma/Lambda.
Thus the full grid has J elements and gives a gamma cover in the output
metric of (3). It is fixed before seeing the training tasks. In particular
log J <= P log(2+2Wmax Lambda/gamma) except when the max with 1 is active;
in that case q=1 and the same bound still holds since 2+2Wmax Lambda/gamma>=2.

## 3. A uniform exponential moment and finite-cover concentration

Write Z=(Y-a(W))/sqrt(b(W)). Its conditional law given W is standard
normal, hence Z is independent of W. For every theta,

    0 <= ell_theta <= C+A Z^2.

Indeed |Y-mu_theta|<=D0+sqrt(V)|Z| and (r+s)^2<=2r^2+2s^2.
Since C/K<=1/4 and A/K<=1/4, Gaussian integration yields

    E exp(ell_theta/K)
       <= exp(C/K)(1-2A/K)^(-1/2)
       <= exp(1/4)sqrt(2) < 2.                           (4)

The last inequality follows from log(2)>1/2 (integrate 1/x on [1,2]).
It follows from the nonnegative exponential series that
E ell_theta^k <= 2 k! K^k for every integer k>=1. For
X=ell_theta-E ell_theta, convexity gives

    E|X|^k <= 2^k E ell_theta^k <= 2^(k+1) k! K^k.

For |z|<1/(2K), the centered exponential series therefore gives

    log E exp(z X) <= 8K^2 z^2/(1-2K|z|).              (5)

Interchange of expectation and the series is justified by the absolute
moment series, which converges at these z. Independence across the m
tasks gives for their centered sum the same bound with 8mK^2 in
the numerator. Chernoff's inequality and (5) give each one-sided tail

    Pr(|Rhat(theta)-R(theta)| >
                  sqrt(32)K sqrt(u/m)+2K u/m) <= 2exp(-u).

For completeness, the generic bound log E exp(z S)<=v z^2/[2(1-cz)]
implies Pr(S>=sqrt(2vu)+cu)<=exp(-u): substitute
z=r/(1+cr), r=sqrt(2u/v), into the exponential Markov bound.
Here v=16mK^2, c=2K; apply it also to -S and divide by m.
No bounded-label assumption has been used.

A union bound on the J fixed grid predictors, with u=log(4J/alpha),
shows all their risk deviations are <=beta except on probability alpha/2.

## 4. From the grid to every parameter

For two clipped predictors within gamma in both output coordinates,
the elementary log derivative and a difference-of-squares split give

    |ell_theta(W,Y)-ell_theta'(W,Y)| <= gamma L(Y),
    L(Y)=1/(2v0)+(|Y|+U)/v0+(|Y|+U)^2/(2v0^2).       (6)

In detail, the log term costs gamma/(2v0). Hold v fixed and vary the
mean to get gamma(|Y|+U)/v0. Hold the new mean fixed and vary 1/v to
get gamma(|Y|+U)^2/(2v0^2). Both denominators use the common positive
floor v0. Thus E L(Y)<=Q: E|Y|<=M+sqrt(V) and
E(|Y|+U)^2<=2D0^2+2V.

The standard-normal exponential integral E exp(zZ)=exp(z^2/2), followed
by exponential Markov at z=x, gives Pr(|Z|>x)<=2exp(-x^2/2).
For t=log(4m/alpha), a union bound gives |Y_i|<=T for all i except
on probability alpha/2. On that event the empirical average of L(Y_i)
is at most L_T. Combine this event with the grid concentration event.
For each theta choose a grid point theta' satisfying (3). Insert
R(theta') and Rhat(theta') and use (6) to obtain the first line of (1).
The approximate-ERM inequality then gives the second line of (1).
The same event works for all approximate ERMs, without a union over
their potentially data-dependent choice. This proves (1) and (2).

## 5. GP comparator and scope

For the finite-rank noisy GP in C002, with supplied features bounded by R,
context length <=n and context labels bounded by B, one can use

    M=nR^2 B/s, V=s+R^2.

Take a desired comparator accuracy eps_c>0, U=M+sqrt(s eps_c),
v0=s, v1=V+s min(1/2,sqrt(eps_c)). C002's scalar error estimates
ensure its outputs lie in these intervals and its expected forward KL
is <=eps_c. Its padded encoding has K0=max(1,R,B,s), width D=7p+4,
at most H=5 heads and L=T_c+2 layers. The construction gives fixed
explicit matrices and readout. Choose Wmax at least 1 and their largest
absolute scalar entry; this is an explicitly computable maximum of the
finite matrices specified by C002 Section 4, independent of task data.
The class of Section 2 then contains that comparator, and (2) implies

    E_W KL(P_W || h_thetahat(W)) <= eps_c+2E_m+xi.        (7)

One may use the internally clipped variant with the explicit common cap

    Kcap=max(1,R,B,s,2nRB/s,2R/s,U,v1).

It preserves the C002 comparator exactly: its feature and query registers
are bounded by R; for every Chebyshev iteration j, |r_j(lambda)|<=1,
so the mean-solve iterates have norm <=2nRB/s and the variance-solve
iterates have norm <=2R/s. The previous-iterate registers have the same
bounds. Initialization, broadcast, constants, and final output registers
are covered by the other displayed terms. Thus clipping changes none
of its states. For this class the parameter Lipschitz recurrence uses a
constant Kcap, and log Lambda grows at most linearly with depth, avoiding
the very loose cubic growth of the unclipped K recurrence. The statistical
bound (7) is consequently explicit for a class containing the comparator
with either choice of internal clipping. All added clipping parameters
are fixed, so P still counts exactly the trainable entries.

For R=0 use a constant exact comparator instead of C002's formulas that
divide by R. The class can contain it by initializing a constant coordinate
and choosing a readout that outputs (0,s).

If training uses rejection to enforce bounded context labels, (7) concerns
the resulting conditioned task distribution. It is not silently a theorem
for the original unconditioned GP context law. With unconditioned contexts,
the C002 comparator guarantee and this bounded-input parameter cover do
not apply as stated. This is the precise remaining distributional scope
issue, separate from the unbounded Gaussian query labels handled above.

All constants here are explicit but loose. The parameter cube and finite
cover give a statistical ERM guarantee, not SGD convergence, efficient
enumeration of the cover, a finite-bit realization theorem for the original
solver, or a claim that Chebyshev depth beats Newton-type solvers.

{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space","T is a homeomorphism of X (bijective, continuous, continuous inverse)","the expansive constant delta is strictly positive and depends on the metric"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:23.250591+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, expansive maps","id":"claim_81a7ef561e0af1f85a9f7f77df488257576c032550ed3b546d86f1abbe6a19db","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space and $T: X \\to X$ a homeomorphism. $T$ is called expansive if there is a constant $\\delta > 0$ (an expansive constant) such that for every pair of distinct points $x \\neq y$ in $X$ there exists an integer $n \\in \\mathbb{Z}$ (positive, zero or negative) with $d(T^n x, T^n y) > \\delta$. Equivalently: two orbits that stay within distance $\\delta$ of each other for all times $n \\in \\mathbb{Z}$ are the same orbit, i.e. the same point. Any $\\delta' < \\delta$ is again an expansive constant; on a compact metric space the property (though not the constant) does not depend on the choice of a compatible metric. A map $T$ (not necessarily invertible) is positively expansive if the same holds with $n$ restricted to $n \\geq 0$. Examples: the full shift on $k$ symbols and every subshift (with $\\delta$ below the distance between two sequences differing in the zeroth coordinate); hyperbolic toral automorphisms; Axiom A restricted to a basic set. Non-examples: the identity, any isometry (e.g. a circle rotation), any map with a nontrivial equicontinuous factor of the same type. Warning: the definition uses two-sided time for homeomorphisms; a homeomorphism of an infinite compact metric space is never positively expansive.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f is 1-periodic and Lebesgue integrable over one period"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.262136+00:00","domain":"Fourier series on the circle","id":"claim_82389d4e8f4fb9ac13809cff86a8079ad0ec59befe3fccefb0bd229569f870b4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $\\mathbb{T}=\\mathbb{R}/\\mathbb{Z}$, identified with $[0,1)$ with Lebesgue measure, and $f\\in L^1(\\mathbb{T})$. The Fourier coefficients are $\\hat f(n)=\\int_0^1 f(x)e^{-2\\pi i n x}\\,dx$, $n\\in\\mathbb{Z}$, with $|\\hat f(n)|\\le\\|f\\|_1$; the Fourier series is $\\sum_n\\hat f(n)e^{2\\pi i n x}$. Convolution on $\\mathbb T$ is $(f*g)(x)=\\int_0^1 f(x-y)g(y)\\,dy$ and $\\widehat{f*g}(n)=\\hat f(n)\\hat g(n)$. The symmetric partial sums are $S_Nf(x)=\\sum_{|n|\\le N}\\hat f(n)e^{2\\pi i n x}=(f*D_N)(x)$ with the Dirichlet kernel $D_N(x)=\\sum_{|n|\\le N}e^{2\\pi i n x}=\\sin((2N+1)\\pi x)/\\sin(\\pi x)$; $D_N$ is even, $\\int_0^1 D_N=1$, but it changes sign and its Lebesgue constants $\\|D_N\\|_{L^1(\\mathbb T)}=\\frac{4}{\\pi^2}\\log N+O(1)$ tend to infinity. The Fejer (Cesaro) means are $\\sigma_Nf=\\frac{1}{N+1}\\sum_{k=0}^N S_kf=f*F_N$ with the Fejer kernel $F_N(x)=\\frac{1}{N+1}\\left(\\frac{\\sin((N+1)\\pi x)}{\\sin(\\pi x)}\\right)^2=\\sum_{|n|\\le N}\\left(1-\\frac{|n|}{N+1}\\right)e^{2\\pi i n x}$; $F_N\\ge0$, $\\int_0^1F_N=1$, and $F_N(x)\\le\\min\\{N+1,\\;1/((N+1)\\sin^2(\\pi x))\\}$. Periods other than 1 are handled by rescaling (for period $2\\pi$: $\\hat f(n)=\\frac1{2\\pi}\\int_{-\\pi}^{\\pi}f(t)e^{-int}dt$).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-07T14:01:11.606209+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_82b243bfd1bdebcf927fafa46de1d7d9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 2.5 of arXiv:2512.19517v1, 'Spiking and Resetting' (Cédric Bernardin and Vsevolod Vladimirovich Tarsamaev); numbered Proposition 6 in the earlier card; corrected to the increment form]

## Proposition 2.5 (increment form)

Assume the standing hypotheses of Section 1: (f,h\in C^2([0,1])), (f(1)<0<f(0)), (h(1)=0), (h'(1)\ne0), and (h(x)>0) on ([0,1)). Let

\[
e_1^\varepsilon=\inf\{t\ge0:X_t^\varepsilon>y_*^\varepsilon\},\qquad
e_2^\varepsilon=\inf\{t\ge e_1^\varepsilon:X_t^\varepsilon=0\},
\]

and define the post-(e_1^\varepsilon) holding time

\[
d_2^\varepsilon:=e_2^\varepsilon-e_1^\varepsilon.
\]

Then, for every (t\ge0),

\[
\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathbb P(d_2^\varepsilon>t)=e^{f(1)t},
\]

so (d_2^\varepsilon\Rightarrow \operatorname{Exp}(-f(1))).

The proof in the paper restarts the deterministic flow at (e_1^\varepsilon) with local time (s=0); its displayed survival integral is therefore for (d_2^\varepsilon), not the absolute epoch (e_2^\varepsilon). The source says that after the stopping time “the process evolves deterministically until the next reset” (v1 HTML lines 252-257), which is precisely an increment statement.

## Later alternating holding-time sentence

For the recursively defined epochs (e_k^\varepsilon), the strong Markov property applies to the increments

\[
e_{2k+1}^\varepsilon-e_{2k}^\varepsilon,
\qquad
e_{2k+2}^\varepsilon-e_{2k+1}^\varepsilon,
\]

not to the increasing absolute epochs themselves. The alternating increments are the quantities that can be independent and have the two respective holding-time laws. Any downstream card should preserve this distinction.

## Why the absolute-time statement cannot hold as written

For every (\varepsilon), (e_2^\varepsilon\ge e_1^\varepsilon), hence

\[
\mathbb P(e_2^\varepsilon>t)\ge\mathbb P(e_1^\varepsilon>t).
\]

This stochastic order must persist at continuity points of any weak limits. Yet the paper permits (f(x)=1-3x) and (h(x)=1-x), for which (f(0)=1) and (f(1)=-2). Its two displayed absolute-time limits would require (e^{-2t}\ge e^{-t}) for (t>0), an immediate contradiction. No additional relation between (f(0)) and (f(1)) is present in the standing hypotheses.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f in L^1(R^d) for the weak (1,1) bound; f in L^p for the strong bound","Lebesgue measure on R^d (the doubling property of the measure is what the proof uses)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751428+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis","id":"claim_83dc1a42b76b6de69325a6175207b7e1669093bf0f53df5985f5dc3e5cdce959","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For f in L^1_loc(R^d) define the centred maximal function Mf(x) = sup_{r > 0} (1/|B(x,r)|) integral_{B(x,r)} |f(y)| dy. {"assumptions":["X takes values in a finite set of size m","X_hat is a function of Y alone, so X -> Y -> X_hat is a Markov chain","P_e = Pr(X_hat != X)"],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:43:37.236127+00:00","domain":"information theory","id":"claim_83dc491008b3e031d0e3a0ac5475fb48986b2f077baf5876dcd333a684d89f6b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a discrete random variable taking values in a finite set of size m, let Y be any random variable jointly distributed with X, and let X_hat = g(Y) be any estimator of X computed from Y alone, so that X -> Y -> X_hat forms a Markov chain. Let P_e = Pr(X_hat != X) be the error probability. Then H(X|Y) <= H_b(P_e) + P_e * log(m-1), where H_b(p) = -p*log p - (1-p)*log(1-p) is the binary entropy function. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:43:37.236543+00:00","domain":"numerical analysis","id":"claim_8448b322d9af94267599948f7ac8e35e7642de9c07050163cb44f14c3c789388","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"An explicit s-stage Runge-Kutta method for the initial value problem y' = f(t,y), y(t_0) = y_0, advances y_n to y_{n+1} = y_n + h * sum_{i=1}^{s} b_i * k_i, where k_i = f( t_n + c_i*h, y_n + h*sum_{j<i} a_{ij}*k_j ), and the coefficients a_{ij}, b_i, c_i (the Butcher tableau) typically satisfy c_i = sum_{j<i} a_{ij}. The method has order p if, for sufficiently smooth f, its Taylor expansion in h agrees with the Taylor expansion of the exact solution through the h^p term (equivalently, the local truncation error is O(h^{p+1})). Matching these Taylor expansions imposes polynomial equations on (a_{ij}, b_i, c_i) called order conditions: for example, order 1 requires sum_i b_i = 1, and order 2 additionally requires sum_i b_i*c_i = 1/2. In Butcher's rooted-tree theory there is one order condition per rooted tree up to order p, and the number of independent conditions grows faster than the number of stages s, which is why, for instance, no explicit Runge-Kutta method can reach an order equal to its stage count once the order exceeds 4.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the group is the two-element Cayley group; the claim is a counterexample, not a general theorem","relaxation time is 1/(1 - lambda_2), the standard spectral-gap convention","the target is the geometric-time law of the base walk at tilt p"],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:15:27.869264+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_8494f2b7e60391b8ead2ab87b96e7454cadc38307316484de8264628972059fc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign status: author_checked_limited_argument - a first-pass structural calculation; no independent review, prior art unverified, and the other questions in the source are untouched] For Metropolis chains targeting a geometric-time law on a Cayley group, the source asks whether the relaxation time decreases monotonically in the tilt p. CLAIM: NO, and the counterexample is the smallest possible one - the two-element group - with relaxation defined the standard way as 1/(1 - lambda_2). (i) NONLAZY BASE. The base walk flips the two states; the target is mu_p = (1/(2-p), (1-p)/(2-p)); the Metropolis matrix is [[p, 1-p],[1, 0]], whose second eigenvalue is p - 1, so tau(p) = 1/(2 - p), STRICTLY INCREASING in p. (ii) LAZY BASE, which removes the convention ambiguity because its spectrum is nonnegative. The base matrix has all entries 1/2, mu_p = ((1+p)/2, (1-p)/2), the Metropolis off-diagonal rates are (1-p)/(2(1+p)) and 1/2, and tau(p) = 1 + p, again increasing. (iii) If laziness is imposed AFTER forming the nonlazy Metropolis kernel, tau(p) = 2/(2 - p), still increasing. WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO: it refutes the literal monotonicity direction only. It does not answer the source's other universal-bound questions and does not resolve its undefined tau(infinity). CONVENTION CAVEAT recorded with the result: if 'relaxation' meant the inverse absolute spectral gap of a nonlazy chain, that convention differs - the lazy example exists precisely to remove the ambiguity.","status":"unverified"}

Among all estimators of the form $\\rho_1 I + \\rho_2 S$ with nonrandom $\\rho_1, \\rho_2$, the expected loss $E\\|\\hat\\Sigma - \\Sigma\\|^2$ is minimized by $$\\Sigma^* = \\frac{\\beta^2}{\\delta^2}\\, \\mu I + \\frac{\\alpha^2}{\\delta^2}\\, S,$$ a convex combination of the sample covariance and the scaled identity, with expected loss $\\alpha^2 \\beta^2 / \\delta^2$. The constants have consistent plug-in estimates under general asymptotics $p/n \\to \\gamma \\in (0, \\infty)$: $\\hat\\mu = \\operatorname{tr}(S)/p$, $\\hat\\delta^2 = \\|S - \\hat\\mu I\\|^2$, $\\hat{\\bar b}^2 = \\frac{1}{n^2}\\sum_i \\|x_i x_i^T - S\\|^2$, $\\hat\\beta^2 = \\min(\\hat{\\bar b}^2, \\hat\\delta^2)$, $\\hat\\alpha^2 = \\hat\\delta^2 - \\hat\\beta^2$, and the resulting estimator $\\hat\\Sigma^* = \\frac{\\hat\\beta^2}{\\hat\\delta^2}\\hat\\mu I + \\frac{\\hat\\alpha^2}{\\hat\\delta^2} S$ has the same asymptotic loss as $\\Sigma^*$, is always well conditioned and invertible, and is uniformly no worse than $S$. The shrinkage target is the scaled identity, so the estimator pulls all eigenvalues of $S$ toward their mean $\\hat\\mu$; when one eigenvalue of $\\Sigma$ dominates the trace (a strong spike), $\\hat\\mu$ is dominated by that spike and the target is far from the small eigenvalues.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f measurable and a.e. finite","|E| < infinity (or E sigma-finite, applied piecewise)","the measure is Borel regular, so that inner regularity by closed sets is available"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T17:07:35.550181+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_85c2d201a83f46e0b6df467d153d01f4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : R^d -> C be Lebesgue measurable and finite almost everywhere, let E be a measurable set of FINITE measure, and let eps > 0. Then there is a compact (hence closed) set F contained in E with |E \\ F| < eps such that the RESTRICTION of f to F is continuous. Moreover one may take g in C_c(R^d) with g = f on F and sup |g| <= sup |f|. The theorem does not assert that f is continuous AT the points of F as a function on R^d: the indicator of the rationals is nowhere continuous on R, yet it agrees with the zero function off a set of measure zero, and Lusin's F can be taken to be any closed set of irrationals of nearly full measure. Finiteness of |E| may be relaxed to sigma-finiteness by exhausting E, at the price of stating the conclusion with |E \\ F| < eps for each piece. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 2.24]\n\nConverse (Lusin's criterion): let E be a Lebesgue measurable subset of R^d of finite measure and let f:E->C be a function. If for every eps>0 there is a closed F contained in E with |E\\F|<eps such that f restricted to F is continuous, then f is Lebesgue measurable on E. Thus measurability of an a.e.-finite function on such E is equivalent to continuity of its restriction on closed subsets missing arbitrarily small measure. Applied on every bounded measurable piece, this gives the local criterion on R^d.","status":"unverified"}

Equivalently, T_rho f = sum_S rho^{|S|} hat{f}(S) chi_S, and the inequality forces the Fourier weight of f on high-degree levels to decay geometrically once rho<1, giving sum_S rho^{2|S|} hat{f}(S)^2 <= (E[|f|^p])^{2/p} for suitable p. This is the central tool converting L^2 Fourier information into higher-moment (typically L^4) control, and it underlies the Kahn-Kalai-Linial theorem on the existence of an influential coordinate, the Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm noise-sensitivity theorems, and Friedgut's junta theorem for low-influence functions. It does not directly give influence bounds without further combination with such machinery, and the sharp constant and range of rho given here hold for the uniform measure on {-1,1}^n; biased-p product measures or non-product (dependent) measures require different, generally weaker, p-biased or dependency-adjusted hypercontractive inequalities. Typical failure: Applying the sharp uniform-measure {-1,1}^n hypercontractive constant to a biased-p product measure or to a dependent measure such as the random-cluster or Ising Gibbs measure without switching to the correct p-biased or dependency-adjusted hypercontractivity inequality, whose constants generally degrade as p approaches 0 or 1; this silently invalidates quantitative noise-sensitivity conclusions claimed for critical percolation at p != 1/2 or for genuinely non-product models. Let X_1', ..., X_n' be an independent copy of the X_i and Z_i' = f(X_1, ..., X_i', ..., X_n) the value with the i-th coordinate resampled. Then Var(Z) <= (1/2) sum_{i=1}^n E[(Z - Z_i')^2] = sum_{i=1}^n E[(Z - E_i Z)^2], where E_i denotes expectation over X_i alone (Efron and Stein 1981; Steele 1986 for the constant 1/2). Equivalently Var(Z) <= sum_i E[Var_i(Z)]. The inequality is tight for linear f. It needs independence of the coordinates (it is the sum over coordinates of one-coordinate variances, a tensorization statement) but no boundedness; the bounded-differences (McDiarmid) inequality is the exponential-tail counterpart under the extra assumption that changing one coordinate changes f by at most c_i, in which case Var(Z) <= (1/4) sum c_i^2.","status":"unverified"}

The converse needs the domain to be reflexive, because the proof runs 'bounded sequence -> weakly convergent subsequence -> norm convergent image', and the first arrow is exactly reflexivity (with the Eberlein-Smulian theorem). The counterexample is the identity of l^1: by Schur's property, every weakly convergent sequence in l^1 converges in norm, so the identity is completely continuous, yet it is not compact because l^1 is infinite-dimensional. A related trap in the other direction is the use of weak sequential compactness of the unit ball: in a nonreflexive space such as c_0 or L^1([0,1]) a bounded sequence need not have any weakly convergent subsequence, so arguments of the form 'the sequence is bounded, so pass to a weakly convergent subsequence, and then apply compactness of T' are invalid there. Also note that the older literature uses 'completely continuous' as a synonym for 'compact'; when reading a classical source, check which meaning is in force before transporting a statement.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["mu_1 and mu_2 strictly positive on a common finite distributive lattice closed under meet and join","the pointwise Holley ratio condition mu_1(x v y) mu_2(x ^ y) >= mu_1(x) mu_2(y) holding for all pairs x, y","events being compared are increasing with respect to the same partial order used to define the lattice"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.972949+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8778e7a65e49c4be1f23175bfeb78103a14f5cdd5ed03f4f8cc84200ea1e4687","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Let mu_1, mu_2 be strictly positive probability measures on a common finite distributive lattice (e.g. {0,1}^E ordered coordinatewise). If the Holley condition holds, mu_1(x v y) mu_2(x ^ y) >= mu_1(x) mu_2(y) for all configurations x, y, then mu_1 stochastically dominates mu_2, meaning mu_1(A) >= mu_2(A) for every increasing (monotone) event A. This is a purely combinatorial, pointwise sufficient condition for stochastic domination between two measures that need not be product measures, and it strictly generalizes the FKG inequality, which is recovered as the special case mu_1 = mu_2. It is the standard tool for comparing Gibbs measures with different boundary conditions or parameters in the Ising model, the random-cluster model, and other lattice systems, and for monotone-coupling arguments more generally. The theorem does not establish the Holley condition itself, which can be as hard to verify as the comparison one is trying to prove; it gives only qualitative stochastic domination, with no quantitative bound on the total-variation distance between mu_1 and mu_2; and it requires strict positivity of both measures on the entire lattice. Typical failure: Assuming the Holley condition holds because mu_1 looks larger than mu_2 in some averaged or marginal sense; the condition is a pointwise, multiplicative statement that must hold for every pair of configurations including their join and meet, and it can fail even when mu_1 does stochastically dominate mu_2 for unrelated reasons, or when only checked on a generating set of configurations rather than genuinely all pairs. Canonical reference: Holley, 1974, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Georgii, Haggstrom and Maes, 2001, in Phase Transitions and Critical Phenomena, vol. 18, Academic Press.","status":"unverified"}
