{"assumptions":["(X,d) is a compact metric space","T: X -> X is continuous","for the non-compact extension, T is uniformly continuous and the entropy is taken as a supremum over compact subsets, and then depends on the uniform equivalence class of d"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.814666+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, entropy","id":"claim_885e1c5ce5a142a5b0817a051568e1c6290d72f8e2a8225eed7dad76bf607388","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X,d) be a compact metric space and T: X -> X continuous. For n >= 1 define the Bowen metric d_n(x,y) = max_{0 <= i <= n-1} d(T^i x, T^i y). A set E contained in X is (n, eps)-SEPARATED if d_n(x,y) > eps for all distinct x, y in E; let s_n(eps) be the largest cardinality of an (n, eps)-separated set. A set F is (n, eps)-SPANNING if for every x in X there is y in F with d_n(x,y) <= eps; let r_n(eps) be the smallest cardinality of an (n, eps)-spanning set. Both are finite by compactness. THEOREM (Bowen, Dinaburg): h_top(T) = lim_{eps -> 0+} limsup_{n -> infinity} (1/n) log s_n(eps) = lim_{eps -> 0+} limsup_{n -> infinity} (1/n) log r_n(eps), and this common value coincides with the Adler-Konheim-McAndrew topological entropy defined through open covers. The limits in eps exist in [0, +infinity] because s_n(eps) and r_n(eps) are nonincreasing in eps, so the inner quantities are nonincreasing in eps. The two counts are comparable at shifted scales: r_n(eps) <= s_n(eps) <= r_n(eps/2). SHARP EDGES. (a) The order of the limits is not negotiable: for a FIXED eps the quantity limsup_n (1/n) log s_n(eps) is in general strictly smaller than h_top(T) (it is the 'entropy at scale eps'), and it is only after eps -> 0 that one gets the entropy. The single exception worth remembering is an expansive homeomorphism, where any eps below the expansive constant already gives the answer. (b) Compactness is used to make the counts finite and to make the value a topological invariant. Bowen's extension to a uniformly continuous map of a possibly non-compact metric space, taking the supremum of the above over compact subsets, defines a quantity h_d(T) that depends on the METRIC and not only on the topology: uniformly equivalent metrics give the same value, but merely topologically equivalent ones need not, so on non-compact spaces 'the topological entropy' is not well defined without naming the metric. (c) Separated and spanning counts measure ORBIT distinguishability over a finite time window; they say nothing by themselves about invariant measures. The link to measures is the variational principle, h_top(T) = sup over T-invariant Borel probabilities mu of h_mu(T), which is a separate theorem and is not proved by the counting argument below. (d) The definition uses only forward iterates 0, ..., n-1, and for a homeomorphism this already gives the entropy of T; the two-sided window max over |i| <= n gives the same number, not twice it.","status":"unverified"}

Reduction recorded. Key identity: t_cov ~ |E| (E max GFF)^2 when t_cov/t_hit -> infinity (Ding; Zhai), so (1+eps)-approximation reduces to approximating a Gaussian expected maximum. {"assumptions":["f ∈ C^2 with f'' > 0 everywhere (genuine nonlinearity); for nonconvex f the Riemann solution is a composite of shocks and rarefactions given by the convex/concave hull construction","initial datum exactly the two-state Riemann datum","entropy (Kruzhkov / Oleinik) admissibility is what excludes the nonphysical expansion shock when u_l < u_r"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418000+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: hyperbolic conservation laws","id":"claim_8ac03e996b3b87a605fc6323901992a6fdd8ce364550e7a1265b2c2093413b70","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f ∈ C^2(R) with f''(s) > 0 for all s, and let u_l, u_r ∈ R with initial datum u0(x) = u_l for x < 0 and u0(x) = u_r for x > 0. The unique Kruzhkov entropy solution of u_t + f(u)_x = 0 is: (a) if u_l > u_r (shock): u(x,t) = u_l for x < σ t and u(x,t) = u_r for x > σ t, with σ = ( f(u_l) - f(u_r) ) / ( u_l - u_r ); this jump satisfies the Lax inequalities f'(u_l) > σ > f'(u_r); (b) if u_l < u_r (rarefaction wave): u(x,t) = u_l for x ≤ f'(u_l) t, u(x,t) = (f')^{-1}( x/t ) for f'(u_l) t ≤ x ≤ f'(u_r) t, u(x,t) = u_r for x ≥ f'(u_r) t; this function is continuous on t > 0 and Lipschitz away from t = 0. {"assumptions":["f continuous (or merely integrable) on the circle","symmetric partial sums S_N of the Fourier series"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264258+00:00","domain":"Fourier series, common errors","id":"claim_8ac39be5488e62ef2062744a8805090f4ff3f7a198a608caf56cfdc735eca673","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: a local regularity condition (Dini, Holder, bounded variation), not mere continuity. The evaluation functionals $f\\mapsto S_Nf(0)$ on $C(\\mathbb T)$ have norms equal to the Lebesgue constants $\\|D_N\\|_{L^1}=\\frac4{\\pi^2}\\log N+O(1)\\to\\infty$, so by Banach-Steinhaus the set of continuous $f$ with $\\sup_N|S_Nf(0)|=\\infty$ is a dense $G_\\delta$ in $C(\\mathbb T)$; du Bois-Reymond (1873) gave the first explicit example. Kahane-Katznelson: for every set $E\\subset\\mathbb T$ of measure zero there is a continuous $f$ whose Fourier series diverges at every point of $E$. Kolmogorov (1926): there is $f\\in L^1(\\mathbb T)$ whose Fourier series diverges at every point. What is true: Carleson (1966) - $f\\in L^2(\\mathbb T)$ implies $S_Nf\\to f$ a.e.; Hunt - the same for $L^p$, $p>1$; Riesz - $S_Nf\\to f$ in $L^p$ for $1<p<\\infty$, but this fails in $L^1$ and in the uniform norm; Fejer - $\\sigma_Nf\\to f$ uniformly for continuous $f$. Also note convergence in norm does not repair the pointwise picture near a jump: for a function with a jump $J$, the partial sums overshoot by $\\big(\\frac1\\pi\\int_0^\\pi\\frac{\\sin t}{t}dt-\\frac12\\big)J\\approx0.0895\\,J$ on each side (Gibbs phenomenon), so $\\|S_Nf-f\\|_\\infty$ does not tend to 0 even though $\\|S_Nf-f\\|_2\\to0$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a product probability measure on independent, not necessarily identically distributed coordinates","the function or event of interest admits a certifiable Lipschitz-type structure with bounded, possibly nonuniform, weights","measurability of the relevant sets","typically only median concentration is obtained directly; mean concentration needs a separate argument"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.985402+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8bc6218023d8f024ef67f80f2057021b0e367a5c321ceeb28f5937f91f9987b7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). On a product probability space (Omega_1 x ... x Omega_n, mu), define the convex distance d_T(x,A) = sup_{alpha>=0, |alpha|=1} inf_{y in A} sum_i alpha_i 1_{x_i != y_i}, a weighted Hamming-type distance from x to a set A, maximized over convex combinations of nonnegative unit-norm weight vectors. Talagrand's inequality states integral exp(d_T(x,A)^2/4) dmu(x) <= 1/mu(A), which implies mu(A) mu({x : d_T(x,A) >= t}) <= exp(-t^2/4), a strong concentration of any set A around itself in convex distance. Applied to a function f that is certifiable, meaning any difference f(x) - f(y) can be witnessed by a bounded number of coordinates with bounded weight, this yields subgaussian concentration of f around its median without requiring f to be linear or even close to it, making the method far more flexible than Azuma-Hoeffding for combinatorial optimization functionals such as the longest increasing subsequence, bin-packing cost, or chromatic number. It does not directly give concentration around the mean, only the median, so a separate median-to-mean gap argument is needed, and it requires exhibiting an explicit certificate structure for f, which can be technically demanding to construct. Typical failure: Applying Talagrand concentration by treating f as ordinary Hamming-Lipschitz (uniform weight 1 per coordinate change) when the natural certificate for f actually requires nonuniform or superlinear weighting, since changing one coordinate can move f by an amount depending on many other coordinates; using the wrong or absent certificate yields either the wrong concentration scale or, more commonly, no valid proof at all, since the convex-distance formulation is easy to state and easy to misapply. Canonical reference: Talagrand, 1995, Publications Mathematiques de l'IHES; Steele, Probability Theory and Combinatorial Optimization, 1997, SIAM.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["each F_n nondecreasing, right-continuous, with values in [0,1]","no tightness is assumed, and without it the limit can be defective"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T12:13:53+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8c5cd17030a65ecdbe60f4f7255a5f34afa5ee5bff2e761be63adba0ecc0f134","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (F_n) be a sequence of distribution functions on R, that is nondecreasing right-continuous functions with values in [0,1]. Then there exist a subsequence (F_{n_k}) and a nondecreasing right-continuous F : R -> [0,1] such that F_{n_k}(x) -> F(x) at every continuity point x of F. The limit F need NOT be a distribution function: mass can escape to plus or minus infinity, and with F_n the distribution function of the point mass at n one gets F identically 0. This is exactly the gap that tightness closes: when every F_n is a proper distribution function (F_n(x) -> 0 as x -> -infinity and F_n(x) -> 1 as x -> +infinity), the family is tight, meaning sup_n (1 - F_n(M) + F_n(-M)) -> 0 as M -> infinity, if and only if every such subsequential limit is a proper distribution function, which is Prokhorov's theorem on R (without properness the 'if' fails: a single improper F_1 makes the family non-tight while every subsequential limit can be proper). For the selection itself nothing is assumed about the F_n beyond monotonicity, right-continuity and the range [0,1] - no continuity, no tightness, no common support. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 3.2.6]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the series is real-valued and conditionally convergent","for the affine-subspace conclusion: finite-dimensional target R^d and a convergent (not necessarily conditionally convergent) series"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752356+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_8cac9c7bdc207f01ab297921ae09bfe7234b1fd5d6dee6f7121badbca7085a69","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let sum_n a_n be a series of REAL numbers that converges but not absolutely (a conditionally convergent series). Then for every alpha in the extended reals [-infinity, +infinity] there is a permutation sigma of the indices with sum_n a_{sigma(n)} = alpha, and there are permutations for which the partial sums have any prescribed pair liminf <= limsup in the extended reals. Consequently a real series is unconditionally convergent (every rearrangement converges to the same sum) if and only if it is absolutely convergent. In R^d with d >= 2 the analogous statement is FALSE and is replaced by the Levy-Steinitz theorem: the set of sums achievable by rearranging a convergent series in R^d is an AFFINE SUBSPACE of R^d, that is a translate of a linear subspace, so it can be a single point, a line, a plane, or all of R^d, but never for instance a disc or two isolated points. In infinite-dimensional Banach spaces unconditional and absolute convergence differ (Dvoretzky-Rogers), so the equivalence in the first sentence is a strictly finite-dimensional phenomenon. [Riemann (1854); Levy (1905) and Steinitz (1913); Dvoretzky and Rogers (1950)]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["U ⊂ C is open","every member of F is holomorphic on U","F is uniformly bounded on each compact subset of U"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.482349+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_8d2196586281fbe29fe2e8e264eed8aa8081e271ecbfcd1b06c6fdf3c582a836","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let U ⊂ C be open and let F be a family of holomorphic functions on U that is locally uniformly bounded: for every compact K ⊂ U there is M_K < ∞ with |f(z)| ≤ M_K for all f in F and all z in K (equivalently, every point of U has a neighborhood on which F is uniformly bounded). Then F is a normal family: every sequence in F has a subsequence converging uniformly on every compact subset of U, and the limit is holomorphic on U (it need not belong to F). Conversely, a family of holomorphic functions in which every sequence has a locally uniformly convergent subsequence with finite limit is locally uniformly bounded. Pointwise boundedness alone is not sufficient.","status":"unverified"}

Conditional on Y, the planted latent variable and all replicas are iid with the same posterior law. Therefore E f(Y,Theta_star,Theta_1,...,Theta_k)=E f(Y,Theta_{k+1},Theta_1,...,Theta_k) for every measurable f for which the expectations are absolutely finite. If Theta is a pair of coupled latent matrices, each replica is sampled as a whole pair; the identity supplies no independence between the two components within that pair. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149689+00:00","domain":"elliptic regularity, boundary regularity","id":"claim_8db5bb04ea0ba49df7ad1e7b2be77bd57ef67c284c1ead04a14cdb02d09b5503","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: for the global statement 'u in H^1_0(Omega), Laplacian u in L^2(Omega) implies u in H^2(Omega) with ||u||_{H^2} <= C ||Laplacian u||_{L^2}', the boundary must be C^{1,1} (C^2 in the usual textbook proof) or Omega must be convex. Lipschitz is not enough. Counterexample (reentrant corner): in the plane let Omega be the sector {0 < theta < beta, 0 < r < 1} with pi < beta < 2 pi (a nonconvex Lipschitz domain) and put v(r,theta) = r^{pi/beta} sin(pi theta/beta), which is harmonic and vanishes on the two straight edges. Let eta be a smooth cutoff equal to 1 near the vertex and supported in {r < 1/2}, and set u = eta v. Then u is in H^1_0(Omega) (grad v is comparable to r^{pi/beta - 1}, which is square integrable in the plane for every beta, since pi/beta > 0) and f = -Laplacian u = -(2 grad v . grad eta + v Laplacian eta) is smooth and bounded (it is supported in an annulus away from the vertex). But near the vertex |D^2 u| is comparable to r^{pi/beta - 2}, and integral of r^{2(pi/beta - 2)} r dr diverges precisely when pi/beta <= 1, i.e. when beta >= pi. So u is not in H^2(Omega) although the data are smooth: the singularity is created by the geometry, not by the coefficients or the right-hand side. Remarks an auditor should keep in mind: interior H^2 regularity is untouched (it needs only Lipschitz coefficients and no boundary hypothesis); on a convex domain, even a convex polygon, the H^2 estimate does hold (Kadlec/Grisvard), which is why finite-element arguments often assume convexity; on a general polygon the solution splits into an H^2 part plus explicit corner singularities r^{k pi/beta} sin(k pi theta/beta); and the analogous failure occurs for the W^{2,p} estimate, so a C^{1,1} (or convexity) hypothesis cannot be quietly weakened to Lipschitz.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["uniform measure on {-1, 1}^n, n >= 1","phi, psi >= 0 with mean 1","A nonempty"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T09:29:33.705360+00:00","domain":"analysis of Boolean functions","id":"claim_8dd7b9661fcb5526be1aca1d53a252de4e5711d0c2eca02d0d139066cc2d9225","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"On {-1, 1}^n (n >= 1) with the uniform probability measure mu, chi_S(x) = prod over i in S of x_i for S inside [n], and f^(S) = E[f chi_S] is the Walsh-Fourier coefficient of a real function f, so f = sum over S of f^(S) chi_S. A probability density is phi >= 0 with E phi = 1; it gives the law P(Y = y) = 2^(-n) phi(y), and then E[g(Y)] = E[phi g] for every real g. For nonempty A, phi_A = 1_A / mu(A) = (2^n/|A|) 1_A is a density whose law is uniform on A. The normalized convolution is (f * g)(x) = E_y[f(y) g(x y)] with y uniform and x y the coordinatewise product (addition on F_2^n written multiplicatively), and (f * g)^(S) = f^(S) g^(S) for every S. If phi is a density then (phi * g)(x) = E[g(x Y)] for Y with density phi, and if Y and Z are independent with densities phi and psi, then phi * psi is a density and it is the density of the coordinatewise product Y Z.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479922+00:00","domain":"commutative algebra","id":"claim_8de0f9044164fe2b452d0173a984390480cda436dec0025cb6e5cbbb40cebac3","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A commutative ring R is Noetherian if every ideal is finitely generated; equivalently every ascending chain of ideals I_1 <= I_2 <= ... stabilises, equivalently every nonempty set of ideals has a maximal element. Facts: fields, Z, and principal ideal domains are Noetherian; quotients and localisations of Noetherian rings are Noetherian; the Hilbert basis theorem says R[x] is Noetherian when R is, hence every finitely generated algebra over a field or over Z is Noetherian; a Noetherian ring has finitely many minimal primes and every ideal has a primary decomposition (Lasker-Noether); the power series ring R[[x]] over a Noetherian ring is Noetherian; a subring of a Noetherian ring need not be (the ring of all algebraic integers is not Noetherian). The KRULL DIMENSION dim R is the supremum of the lengths n of chains of prime ideals P_0 < P_1 < ... < P_n. Facts: a field has dimension 0, and a Noetherian ring has dimension 0 exactly when it is Artinian (Akizuki); Z and every principal ideal domain that is not a field have dimension 1, as does every Dedekind domain; dim k[x_1, ..., x_n] = n for a field k (Krull's principal ideal theorem and Noether normalisation), and more generally dim R[x] = dim R + 1 for Noetherian R; the dimension of a finitely generated k-algebra that is a domain equals the transcendence degree of its field of fractions over k; Krull's height theorem: in a Noetherian ring a minimal prime over an ideal generated by n elements has height at most n; a Noetherian LOCAL ring (R, m) has finite dimension, equal to the least number of generators of an m-primary ideal, and dim R <= dim_k (m / m^2) with equality exactly for regular local rings. Non-Noetherian rings can have infinite dimension, and there are Noetherian rings of infinite dimension (Nagata's example), though every Noetherian local ring has finite dimension.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:57:59.663755+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory","id":"claim_8de81c29a1406da7f47b7819df7f69538247ac004b47bf6b106fafdadffdc25b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, F, mu) be a measure space with mu(X) < infinity and let T: X -> X be measurable and measure-preserving, meaning mu(T^{-1}A) = mu(A) for every measurable A. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.376759+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_8e61bd090f62d43a44ea41fdfc55f56cf5875d06c224e218013ae47a821947fe","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A family {e_i : i in I} in a Hilbert space H is orthonormal if <e_i, e_j> = 0 for i distinct from j and ||e_i|| = 1 for every i. An orthonormal basis (complete orthonormal system) of H is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is all of H. Equivalent characterizations: the family is a maximal orthonormal set; the only vector orthogonal to every e_i is 0; every x in H has the expansion x = sum over i of <x, e_i> e_i, where at most countably many coefficients <x, e_i> are nonzero and the series converges in norm regardless of ordering. Every Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis (by Zorn's lemma), any two orthonormal bases of H have the same cardinality, and H is separable exactly when it has a countable orthonormal basis. An orthonormal basis of an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is not a vector-space (Hamel) basis.","status":"unverified"}

D(P||Q) is in general not symmetric (D(P||Q) need not equal D(Q||P)) and does not satisfy the triangle inequality, so it is not a metric, but it is the standard measure of how much one probability distribution P differs from a reference distribution Q.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T_n is an ordered rooted tree, and its one-vertex fringe subtrees are leaves."],"created_at":"2026-10-12T15:09:50+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8eeb93530b800f12c01ed104639a108b8119a9456beb5c141963fc3c2a9de5b8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; depends on the companion memo on Problem 20.2] This is the negative part of the answer recorded for Svante Janson's Problem 20.4 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510. Problem 20.4 asks for a Gaussian extension of Theorem 7.12, the law of large numbers for fringe-subtree counts. Let T_n be the simply generated tree, equivalently the conditioned Galton-Watson tree, with n vertices. Let N_T be the number of vertices whose fringe subtree equals a fixed finite ordered rooted tree T, and let N_d be the number of vertices with d children. For the one-vertex tree bullet, N_bullet = N_0 exactly, since its occurrences are precisely the leaves. In both constructions of the companion memo on Problem 20.2, the subcritical law of its Theorem A (nu < 1) and the critical infinite-variance law of its Theorem B (nu = 1, sigma^2 = infinity), most vertices have degree 0 or 1, but N_0 = n - N_1 - sum_{d>=2} N_d and sum_{d>=2} N_d is of order n whenever pi_d > 0 for some d >= 2, so N_0 = n - N_1 + O(1) does not follow. Since N_0 - n pi_0 = -(N_1 - n pi_1) - sum_{d>=2} (N_d - n pi_d), N_bullet inherits, with the sign reversed, the non-Gaussian limit of (N_1 - n pi_1)/sqrt(n) (a two-point law in the first construction, a mixture of two Gaussians in the second) if sum_{d>=2} (N_d - n pi_d) = o(sqrt n) in probability, which is not shown; otherwise its limit depends on the joint fluctuations of all the degree counts. So the negative answer, that fringe-subtree counts are not asymptotically normal in general when nu < 1, nor when nu = 1 with sigma^2 = infinity, is not established by this reduction. The finite-variance critical case is resolved in the literature by Janson (Random Structures Algorithms 48, 2016, Theorem 1.5) and is not included here as own work. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-09T06:55:03+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_901c0a8cd124bb8d518e1184c9227edfe32dcfdd9106fe5b7c65b23e17e91da4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 2.5 of arXiv:2512.19517v1, 'Spiking and Resetting' (Cédric Bernardin and Vsevolod Vladimirovich Tarsamaev); numbered Proposition 6 in the earlier card; corrected to the increment form]

## Proposition 2.5 (increment form)

Assume the standing hypotheses of Section 1: (f,h\in C^2([0,1])), (f(1)<0<f(0)), (h(1)=0), (h'(1)\ne0), and (h(x)>0) on ([0,1)). Let

\[
e_1^\varepsilon=\inf\{t\ge0:X_t^\varepsilon>y_*^\varepsilon\},\qquad
e_2^\varepsilon=\inf\{t\ge e_1^\varepsilon:X_t^\varepsilon=0\},
\]

and define the post-(e_1^\varepsilon) holding time

\[
d_2^\varepsilon:=e_2^\varepsilon-e_1^\varepsilon.
\]

Then, for every (t\ge0),

\[
\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathbb P(d_2^\varepsilon>t)=e^{f(1)t},
\]

so (d_2^\varepsilon\Rightarrow \operatorname{Exp}(-f(1))).

The proof in the paper restarts the deterministic flow at (e_1^\varepsilon) with local time (s=0); its displayed survival integral is therefore for (d_2^\varepsilon), not the absolute epoch (e_2^\varepsilon). The source says that after the stopping time “the process evolves deterministically until the next reset” (v1 HTML lines 252-257), which is precisely an increment statement.

## Later alternating holding-time sentence

For the recursively defined epochs (e_k^\varepsilon), the strong Markov property applies to the increments

\[
e_{2k+1}^\varepsilon-e_{2k}^\varepsilon,
\qquad
e_{2k+2}^\varepsilon-e_{2k+1}^\varepsilon,
\]

not to the increasing absolute epochs themselves. The alternating increments are the quantities that can be independent and have the two respective holding-time laws. Any downstream card should preserve this distinction.

## Why the absolute-time statement cannot hold as written

For every (\varepsilon), (e_2^\varepsilon\ge e_1^\varepsilon), hence

\[
\mathbb P(e_2^\varepsilon>t)\ge\mathbb P(e_1^\varepsilon>t).
\]

This stochastic order must persist at continuity points of any weak limits. Yet the paper permits (f(x)=1-3x) and (h(x)=1-x), for which (f(0)=1) and (f(1)=-2). Its two displayed absolute-time limits would require (e^{-2t}\ge e^{-t}) for (t>0), an immediate contradiction. No additional relation between (f(0)) and (f(1)) is present in the standing hypotheses.","status":"unverified"}

# C016 v1: why fixed iid heads do not inherit the paired construction
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: route-failure. Target: 1.
This is an obstruction to the existing witness route, not absence of epochwise
double descent in iid-initialized networks. Novelty is unestablished.

## 1. Precisely the precursor model considered
Let 0<e<1/4, D0=1+e^2+e^4, x_(s,t)=(1,es,e^2t)/sqrt(D0), s,t in {+1,-1}.
The population is uniform on these four points. Set
u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2), c_e=e^2/sqrt(D0(1+e^2)), alpha=c_e/2.
The teacher g(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-c_e/2 has Walsh coefficients
(theta_0,theta_s,theta_t,theta_st)=(0,alpha,alpha,alpha).
Here the name u_e denotes the teacher direction; nu below is a different,
fixed readout magnitude in (0,1]. Initialize m independent neurons with
W_j~N(0,I_3), a_j independently uniform on {+nu,-nu}, independently of W_j.
Let z_h^(m) be the Walsh coefficients of the random initial output.
Consider the deterministic FULL initial kernel H_nu from C009/C014,
including both trained layers, and real-time-interpolated kernel GD
with step gamma=1/2. If lambda_h are its normalized four-point eigenvalues,
put b_h=-log(1-lambda_h/2), q_h(t)=exp(-b_h t).
The phrase interpolation only means allowing real t in this exact spectral
formula; at integer t it is precisely discrete GD, not gradient flow.
Use centered independent effective label errors of Walsh variance alpha^2.
For instance, four independent errors +/-2alpha have exactly this property.
Balanced replication with fixed sigma and n chosen so sigma^2/n~alpha^2
also gives the same conclusions with rho_e= sigma^2/(n alpha^2)->1.

The noise-averaged clean risk, conditional on initialization, is exactly
 Q_e(t;z)=sum_h [q_h(t)^2(z_h-theta_h)^2
                         +alpha^2(1-q_h(t))^2].           (1)
No independence between noise Walsh modes is needed: Parseval removes
cross-mode terms. The derivative below refers to this interpolated FROZEN
risk, not derivatives of finite-width ReLU iterates.
We use the already recorded full-kernel clocks
 b_s~nu^2 e/(4pi), b_t~b_st~nu^2 e^2/(8pi),
 b_0 -> a positive constant, eta=(b_t+b_st)/b_s~e.
This is the four-point balanced precursor of C015, NOT its continuous,
iid-input-count, actual-network model. No automatic transfer of the negative
result to that stronger model is asserted.

## 2. Initial covariance on the correct signal scale
Let phi_h(W)=one-quarter sum_(s,t) h(s,t) ReLU(W.x_(s,t)).
For each fixed e, ordinary finite-dimensional iid CLT gives
 z^(m) => Z_e as m->infinity, a centered Gaussian four-vector with
 Var(Z_(e,h))=nu^2 lambda_h^RF, lambda_h^RF=E phi_h(W)^2.
The covariance is diagonal by invariance of W under coordinate sign flips.
One can get the vector CLT by applying the scalar finite-variance CLT to
every linear combination. Width is deterministic, not a stopped random list.
All moments used are finite since |phi_h|<=||W|| on the unit inputs.

For almost every W with W_0 !=0,
 phi_s(W)/e -> W_1 1{W_0>0}.
Group the two s values for each t and use ReLU's Lipschitz property to get
 |phi_s(W)|<=e |W_1|/sqrt(D0).
Dominated convergence therefore proves
 lambda_s^RF/e^2 -> E[W_1^2 1{W_0>0}]=1/2.              (2)
Grouping instead by the t coordinate similarly gives
 |phi_t(W)|, |phi_st(W)|<=e^2 |W_2|/sqrt(D0),
so their variances are O(e^4). The constant-mode variance is O(1).
Since alpha~e^2/2, the fast standardized initial output satisfies
 Var(Z_(e,s)/alpha)~2nu^2/e^2.                            (3)
Thus the initial fast prediction error is not negligible on the teacher's
scale. Let A_e=(Z_(e,s)/alpha-1)^2. For any fixed C>0, the Gaussian maximum
density bound gives
 P(eta A_e<=C) <= 2 sqrt(C/eta)/sqrt(2pi Var(Z_(e,s)/alpha))
                    =O(sqrt(Ce)/nu) ->0.                 (4)
Hence eta A_e diverges to infinity in probability. This uses no independence
between A_e and the other modes.

## 3. The old fast-minimum witness diverges on its normalized scale
Let k_1=floor(log(2)/b_s), the C010/C015 precursor's fast witness.
Then q_s(k_1)->1/2. From the single nonnegative term in (1), for any fixed C,
 P(Q_e(k_1;Z_e)/alpha^2<=C)
 <= P(|Z_(e,s)/alpha-1|<=sqrt(C)/q_s(k_1))=O(sqrt(C)e/nu)->0. (5)
Thus Q_e(k_1;Z_e)/alpha^2 ->infinity in probability, rather than 7/2.
This is an iterated width-then-e statement for the iid initialization;
finite-width convergence in distribution follows from the preceding CLT.
For an upper bound at a distributional event boundary one may enlarge C
arbitrarily and use Portmanteau; no uniform-in-e CLT rate is claimed.
The paired-initialization witness statement itself is unaffected.

## 4. The old central peak window is decreasing in the frozen model
Put B_e=log(1/eta), t_e(s)=(B_e+s)/b_s. For any fixed L<infinity,
q_s(t_e(s))=eta exp(-s). Differentiate (1), divide by
2 alpha^2(b_t+b_st), and separate the fast mode. Its contribution is exactly
 exp(-s)-eta(A_e+1)exp(-2s).                              (6)
For the two slow modes, (Z_h/alpha-1)^2 is tight by the O(e^4) covariance
bound. Their rate ratios b_h/(b_t+b_st) are bounded and q_h<=1, hence their
combined contribution is uniformly O_P(1) over |s|<=L.
The constant-mode contribution is o_P(1): b_0 is bounded away from zero,
Z_0=O_P(1), alpha^2~e^4/4, and q_0(t_e(s)) decays faster than every power
of e uniformly on this fixed s interval. Consequently

 sup_|s|<=L Q'_e(t_e(s);Z_e)/(2alpha^2(b_t+b_st))
 <= exp(L)-eta A_e exp(-2L)+O_P(1) -> -infinity
                                                        (7)
by (4). With probability tending to one this entire old peak window is
strictly decreasing in the frozen-risk interpolation. In particular, its
interval maximum lies at the left endpoint, not at the paired model's
interior peak. Tightness plus (4), rather than independence, is sufficient.
The same proof works when the effective noise factor rho_e tends to1:
replace exp(-s) in (6) by rho_e exp(-s) and1 by rho_e.

## 5. What this settles and what remains open
Merely replacing paired heads by fixed-variance iid heads while retaining
the unit-teacher scaling, noise scaling and peak witnesses does NOT preserve
C010/C015's precursor argument: the witness risk diverges and the old
central peak interval has the wrong derivative sign in the limiting frozen
model. This is the exact failure point, not a theorem of global monotonicity.
Other times, other teachers/noise scales, non-lazy learning, the continuous
iid-input model and the actual finite-width derivative pattern remain open.
In particular, C015's positive paired-initialization result is not retracted.
Next route: choose teacher/noise scales jointly with initial GP covariance
before proposing iid-head witnesses. Shrinking readout variance changes the
full-kernel clocks, so one cannot keep fixed-nu clock asymptotics silently.

{"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space","the operator in question is densely defined and symmetric but its adjoint has a strictly larger domain"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.771968+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, spectral theory, quantum mechanics","id":"claim_90607036aaf6052e0e3969770549f68d2f6a3b0e0d151f0440b57246950ca254","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: self-adjointness requires the equality of domains D(T) = D(T*), not merely ⟨Tx, y⟩ = ⟨x, Ty⟩ on D(T). Everything that makes an operator usable - the spectral theorem, the Borel functional calculus, real spectrum, the unitary group e^{itT}, the resolvent bound 1/|Im z| - fails for a merely symmetric operator. What fails: a closed symmetric operator T that is not self-adjoint never has spectrum inside ℝ; its spectrum is all of ℂ when both n_+ ≥ 1 and n_- ≥ 1 (in particular whenever n_+ = n_- ≥ 1), and a closed half plane when exactly one of n_+, n_- is 0, so 'eigenvalue' and 'spectral decomposition' statements are void. Counterexample: on H = L²(0,1) let T = −i d/dx with D(T) = {f ∈ H¹(0,1) : f(0) = f(1) = 0}. T is densely defined, closed and symmetric, and T* = −i d/dx on all of H¹(0,1). Deficiency: ker(T* − i) = span{e^{−x}} and ker(T* + i) = span{e^{x}}, so n_+ = n_- = 1 and T is not self-adjoint. For every λ ∈ ℂ, Ran(T − λ)^⊥ = ker(T* − λ̄) = span{e^{iλ̄x}} ≠ {0}, so σ(T) = ℂ. Its self-adjoint extensions are the operators T_θ = −i d/dx on {f ∈ H¹(0,1) : f(1) = e^{iθ}f(0)}, θ ∈ [0, 2π), with spectrum {θ + 2πk : k ∈ ℤ} - a different physical momentum operator for each θ. Second counterexample, where no self-adjoint extension exists at all: S = −i d/dx on D(S) = {f ∈ H¹(0, ∞) : f(0) = 0} in L²(0, ∞) is closed and symmetric with ker(S* − i) = span{e^{−x}} and ker(S* + i) = {0}, so n_+ = 1, n_- = 0; S is maximal symmetric and has no self-adjoint extension in L²(0, ∞), so there is no unitary group it generates. Audit rule: whenever a proof invokes the spectral theorem, functional calculus, Stone's theorem, Kato-Rellich or 'the eigenvalues of T', check that self-adjointness (or essential self-adjointness plus passing to the closure) has actually been established, typically via Ran(T ± i) dense or a semibounded range condition.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the target space has the approximation property (automatic in Hilbert spaces and in spaces with a Schauder basis)","in a general Banach space compactness alone does not give norm approximation by finite-rank operators"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.573577+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Banach space theory","id":"claim_9063aacd7b762796789db5a4019c2eadcd50f3f3cee806ae5cdd905624995622","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In Hilbert space every compact operator is an operator-norm limit of finite-rank operators, and many arguments quietly reuse this in a Banach setting, where it can be false. A Banach space Y has the approximation property (AP) if the identity of Y is a limit of finite-rank operators uniformly on compact subsets of Y; Grothendieck proved that Y has AP if and only if, for every Banach space X, the finite-rank operators are norm dense in K(X,Y). Enflo (1973) produced a separable reflexive Banach space without AP, and Davie and Szankowski showed that l^p for p not equal to 2, and c_0, have closed subspaces without AP; consequently there are Banach spaces X, Y and a compact operator X -> Y that is not a norm limit of finite-rank operators. Szankowski further showed that B(l^2) itself fails AP. What breaks without AP: (a) proofs of Fredholm-type results that first replace a compact K by a finite-rank F with ||K - F|| small; (b) attempts to define a trace on nuclear operators (the trace is well defined on the nuclear operators of X exactly when X has AP; without it the same nuclear operator has representations with different 'traces'); (c) approximation-number arguments imported from Hilbert space. Safe hypotheses to state instead: the space is a Hilbert space, or has a Schauder basis, or has the (bounded) approximation property; classical spaces such as C(K), L^p(mu) for 1 <= p <= infinity, and c_0 all have AP, so the pitfall bites only in exotic settings - but the hypothesis must be present, not assumed silently.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["coordinates of X independent, mean zero, sub-Gaussian with psi_2 norms at most K","A an arbitrary real n by n matrix; no symmetry is required","c is an absolute constant"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628497+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_908badbf12a5ec45572dec14ab5daa9643b8baf082a5a148183ab488fa20801c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) be a random vector with INDEPENDENT, mean-zero, sub-Gaussian coordinates with sub-Gaussian norms bounded by K, and let A be an n by n real matrix. Then there is an absolute constant c > 0 such that for every t >= 0, P( | X^T A X - E[X^T A X] | > t ) <= 2 exp( - c min( t^2 / (K^4 ||A||_F^2) , t / (K^2 ||A||_op) ) ), where ||A||_F is the Frobenius norm and ||A||_op the spectral norm. The two regimes are the sub-Gaussian one governed by the Frobenius norm and the sub-exponential one governed by the operator norm; this is the quadratic-form analogue of Bernstein's inequality and reduces to it for diagonal A. The coordinates must be INDEPENDENT and sub-Gaussian: independence cannot be weakened to uncorrelatedness, and heavier tails change the shape of the bound. E[X^T A X] equals the trace of A when the coordinates have unit variance, but in general it is sum_i A_{ii} E[X_i^2]. A standard corollary is a concentration bound for the Euclidean norm of a random vector, ||BX||_2 concentrated around ||B||_F within K^2 ||B||_op scales. [Hanson and Wright (1971); modern proof in Rudelson and Vershynin, 'Hanson-Wright inequality and sub-gaussian concentration', arXiv:1306.2872]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the operator is given by a differential expression on a domain with boundary or on a punctured space","essential self-adjointness on the chosen core is not verified"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.772085+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Schrodinger operators, boundary value problems","id":"claim_9144d6537a78e5261760c787afb10663c3eb5665068915709c8ea0cb0eddfa3a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: 'the operator −Δ' or 'the Schrodinger operator H = −Δ + V' is not defined by its formula; the domain is part of the data, and essential self-adjointness on a chosen core is a theorem, not a convention. What fails without it: two different self-adjoint operators can agree on a common dense domain, with different spectra, different semigroups and different dynamics; semiboundedness does not select a unique extension either. Counterexamples. (1) −d²/dx² on C_c^∞(ℝ) is essentially self-adjoint with closure the operator on H²(ℝ); but −d²/dx² on C_c^∞(0, ∞) in L²(0, ∞) has deficiency indices (1, 1), and its self-adjoint extensions are the Dirichlet realization {f ∈ H²(0,∞) : f(0) = 0} and the Robin family {f ∈ H²(0,∞) : f'(0) = α f(0)}, α ∈ ℝ. All extend a nonnegative symmetric operator, yet for α < 0 the Robin extension has the eigenvalue −α² with eigenfunction e^{αx}: the lower bound 0 valid on C_c^∞(0,∞) is not inherited by every self-adjoint extension. The Friedrichs extension (here the Dirichlet realization) is the one that always inherits the lower bound; the Robin extensions with α ≥ 0 happen to stay nonnegative as well, so the lower bound alone singles out nothing. (2) −d²/dx² on C_c^∞(0, 1) has deficiency indices (2, 2); the Dirichlet, Neumann and periodic realizations are distinct self-adjoint extensions with eigenvalues {(kπ)² : k ≥ 1}, {(kπ)² : k ≥ 0} and {(2πk)² : k ∈ ℤ} respectively. (3) −Δ on C_c^∞(ℝⁿ ∖ {0}) is essentially self-adjoint if and only if n ≥ 4; for n ≤ 3 removing a single point changes the operator, and the extensions in n = 3 are the point-interaction ('delta potential') Hamiltonians. Audit rule: a claim 'H is self-adjoint' must name the domain or the core, and a claim that a computation on smooth compactly supported functions determines the operator must cite an essential self-adjointness theorem (Kato-Rellich, Faris-Lavine, Nelson's analytic vectors, or a limit-point analysis).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T is measure-preserving on a probability space","A is measurable","integrability of log^+ ||A|| is the standing hypothesis for the multiplicative ergodic theorem"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438394+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, Lyapunov exponents","id":"claim_920354a52c00e42c3e25c80f9069506badd8e398097645124d1386fa4d04f5aa","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \\mathcal{B}, \\mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system and $A: X \\to M_d(\\mathbb{R})$ a measurable matrix-valued function. The linear cocycle generated by $A$ over $T$ is $A^n(x) = A(T^{n-1}x) \\cdots A(Tx)\\,A(x)$ for $n \\ge 1$, $A^0 = I$; it satisfies the cocycle identity $A^{n+m}(x) = A^m(T^n x) A^n(x)$. (If $T$ is invertible and $A(x) \\in GL_d$, one also sets $A^{-n}(x) = A^n(T^{-n}x)^{-1}$.) The cocycle is (forward) integrable if $\\log^+ \\|A\\| \\in L^1(\\mu)$, where $\\log^+ t = \\max(\\log t, 0)$ and $\\|\\cdot\\|$ is any matrix norm; it is two-sidedly integrable if also $A(x)$ is invertible a.e. and $\\log^+\\|A^{-1}\\| \\in L^1$. For $v \\in \\mathbb{R}^d \\setminus \\{0\\}$ the (forward) Lyapunov exponent of $v$ at $x$ is $\\lambda(x, v) = \\lim_{n\\to\\infty} \\frac1n \\log \\|A^n(x) v\\|$ when the limit exists (in $[-\\infty, \\infty)$); more generally $\\bar\\lambda(x, v) = \\limsup$. The function $v \\mapsto \\bar\\lambda(x, v)$ takes finitely many values and satisfies $\\bar\\lambda(x, u + v) \\le \\max(\\bar\\lambda(x,u), \\bar\\lambda(x,v))$, so for each $x$ the sets $\\{v : \\bar\\lambda(x, v) \\le c\\} \\cup \\{0\\}$ are linear subspaces and form a filtration of $\\mathbb{R}^d$. The prototype is the derivative cocycle $A(x) = Df_x$ of a smooth map $f$ on a manifold (trivialised bundle), whose exponents measure exponential rates of divergence of nearby orbits. Warning: $\\|A^n(x)\\|^{1/n}$ and $|\\text{eigenvalues of } A^n(x)|^{1/n}$ are different things; Lyapunov exponents are the growth rates of SINGULAR values of $A^n(x)$, not eigenvalues, and for non-commuting products the two can differ.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the axiom of choice (used in step 3 to select orbit representatives; the result is not a theorem of ZF alone)","n >= 3 for the paradox; rigid motions of R^n (isometries); 'pieces' are arbitrary sets, necessarily non-measurable"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.480173+00:00","domain":"measure theory and geometry","id":"claim_926a5872eb18b627a0e7fd10743a1293421bfa6309bdf99c41e9eb5a25b9a1d1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Assuming the axiom of choice, the closed unit ball B in R^3 can be partitioned into finitely many pieces which can be reassembled by rigid motions (rotations and translations) into two disjoint copies of B; five pieces suffice (Robinson), and four do not. More generally (the strong form) any two bounded subsets of R^n, n >= 3, with nonempty interior are equidecomposable: one can be cut into finitely many pieces and moved by isometries onto the other. The pieces are necessarily non-measurable, so no contradiction with Lebesgue measure arises - the theorem shows that no finitely additive, isometry-invariant measure defined on ALL subsets of R^3 and normalising the ball can exist. In dimensions 1 and 2 the paradox fails: Banach showed that Lebesgue measure on R and R^2 extends to a finitely additive isometry-invariant measure on all subsets, because the isometry groups of R and R^2 are amenable (solvable), while SO(3) contains a free group on two generators, which is the source of the paradox (Hausdorff, 1914). Tarski's theorem (1929) makes this exact: a group action admits a paradoxical decomposition if and only if it carries no finitely additive invariant probability measure, i.e. it is non-amenable. With choice the result is a theorem; in ZF plus the axiom of determinacy, or in Solovay's model, every set of reals is measurable and the decomposition does not exist.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Definition of the specific source model; beta>1,s>0,uniform power-law comparison constants.","Fresh independent Gaussian features and independent Gaussian constant-order label noise; averaged minibatch gradients.","Zero initial iterate and zero initial momentum for the scaling-law protocol."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:47:26.804438+00:00","domain":"Kernel regression and stochastic optimization","id":"claim_92bc45c903189bf192adf6404c4679485e5e9b8150fad2524367d7a2833ca314","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"The model used by Wang-Huang-Li-Wu in arXiv:2609.02728 is Gaussian-feature, online least-squares regression. In the covariance eigenbasis, a feature vector phi has centered Gaussian law N(0,H) with H=diag(lambda_1,lambda_2,...) positive trace class, lambda_1>=lambda_2>=...>0. A label is y=<phi,theta_star>+epsilon with epsilon~N(0,sigma^2) independent of phi. The target has finite prediction energy sum_j lambda_j*|theta_star_j|^2<infinity; the pairing can equivalently be read as its mean-square-convergent Gaussian series. The population risk is R(theta)=E(<phi,theta>-y)^2/2, and the excess risk is Ecal(theta)=sum_j lambda_j*|theta_j-theta_star_j|^2/2=R(theta)-sigma^2/2. Their source/capacity assumptions are beta>1,s>0, lambda_j asymp j^(-beta) and lambda_j*|theta_star_j|^2 asymp j^(-(1+s*beta)), where asymp means upper and lower bounds by fixed positive constants, uniform in j. The label-noise standard deviation sigma is bounded above and away from zero by fixed constants (the constant-order noisy setting). At iteration k a fresh IID batch of B examples, independent of all past batches, gives the AVERAGED gradient g(theta;batch)=B^(-1)*sum_i phi_(k,i)*(<phi_(k,i),theta>-y_(k,i)). For a constant eta>0 and constant rho in[0,1), SGD uses theta_(k+1)=theta_k-eta*g(theta_k;batch); Polyak uses theta_(k+1)=theta_k-eta*g(theta_k;batch)+rho*(theta_k-theta_(k-1)); Nesterov first sets theta_k_la=theta_k+rho*(theta_k-theta_(k-1)) and uses theta_(k+1)=theta_k_la-eta*g(theta_k_la;batch). The source scaling-law analysis takes theta_0=theta_-1=0. For a one-pass data budget D, take T=D/B updates (or integer rounding at the exponent level), and B=D^(b+o(1)) with fixed b in[0,1). Hyperparameters can depend on D but are constant within each run. This protocol concerns final expected excess risk; it is not a finite-data repeated-epoch protocol, nor a theorem giving explicit constants in the critical-batch trade-off.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the graph is planar (embeddable in the plane without crossings) and loopless; multiple edges do not matter for colouring","proper colouring: adjacent vertices differ","the proof is computer-assisted; the sketch names the method and the published verifications"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.476890+00:00","domain":"graph theory","id":"claim_92e5db9a713cd3ef2d22a18a59a18840aa7e87870d30226a7a633987fb4d11b1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Every loopless planar graph is properly 4-colourable: its vertices can be coloured with four colours so that adjacent vertices receive different colours. Equivalently, the regions of any map drawn in the plane (each region connected) can be coloured with four colours so that regions sharing a boundary segment differ. Four is best possible (the complete graph K_4 is planar and needs four colours). The five-colour theorem (Heawood 1890) has a short proof; the four-colour theorem was proved by Appel and Haken in 1976 with a computer check of 1,936 reducible configurations, reproved by Robertson, Sanders, Seymour and Thomas in 1997 with 633 configurations and 32 discharging rules, and formally verified in the Coq proof assistant by Gonthier in 2005. No proof is known that a human can check unaided; every published proof rests on a machine-checked case analysis.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["mu a finite positive Borel measure on the real line","for the density statement: mu absolutely continuous with a density continuous at x; for the real-part statement: the density Hölder continuous near x"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T07:52:29.172721+00:00","domain":"complex analysis / spectral theory / random matrix theory","id":"claim_930971f2e2958ad4b39127882e7fb8c2f41978d305608de432e06a9933e30a3d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $\\mu$ be a finite positive measure on $\\mathbb{R}$ with Stieltjes transform $m(z) = \\int \\frac{d\\mu(t)}{t - z}$, defined and analytic for $\\operatorname{Im} z > 0$, with $\\operatorname{Im} m(z) > 0$ there. Then for every $a < b$ that are continuity points of $\\mu$, $\\mu((a, b]) = \\lim_{\\eta \\downarrow 0} \\frac{1}{\\pi}\\int_a^b \\operatorname{Im} m(x + i\\eta)\\,dx$, and if $\\mu$ has a continuous density $f$ at $x$ then $f(x) = \\frac{1}{\\pi}\\lim_{\\eta \\downarrow 0} \\operatorname{Im} m(x + i\\eta)$. The real part has the companion limit $\\operatorname{Re} m(x + i\\eta) \\to \\pi H_f(x) := \\mathrm{PV}\\int \\frac{f(t)}{t - x}\\,dt$ wherever $f$ is Hölder continuous, so the boundary value $\\breve m(x) = \\lim_{\\eta\\downarrow0} m(x + i\\eta) = \\pi H_f(x) + i\\pi f(x)$ (Sokhotski-Plemelj). In particular two measures with the same Stieltjes transform on $\\mathbb{C}^+$ coincide, and a sequence of probability measures converges weakly if and only if the Stieltjes transforms converge pointwise on $\\mathbb{C}^+$ (to the transform of a probability measure).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f : {-1,1}^n -> {0,1} Boolean, uniform product measure","c is a universal constant","the conclusion bounds only the MAXIMUM influence, not any specific coordinate"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T15:09:50+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_94198fd805d1f2269bd7bd89b92062349f91be394349788a2f4df1ea2bf88af8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : {-1,1}^n -> {0,1} be a Boolean function on the uniform product measure, and define the influence of coordinate i as Inf_i(f) = P( f(X) != f(X^{(i)}) ) where X^{(i)} flips the i-th coordinate. Then there is a universal constant c > 0 with max_{i <= n} Inf_i(f) >= c Var(f) log n / n, where Var(f) = p(1-p) with p = E[f]. This does not bound the TOTAL influence by c Var(f) log n: a dictator f(x) = (1 + x_1)/2 has total influence 1 and Var(f) = 1/4 for every n. The total-influence form of the theorem is sum_i Inf_i(f) >= c' Var(f) log(1/max_i Inf_i(f)) for nonconstant f, with c' > 0 universal, and the maximum bound follows from it. The bound is SHARP up to the constant: the tribes function, a read-once DNF on blocks of size about log_2 n - log_2 log_2 n, is balanced and has all influences of order log n / n. The theorem is about the uniform measure on the cube; the analogous statement for p-biased measures carries an extra factor and is the Friedgut-Kalai sharp-threshold machinery. Note what it does NOT say: it does not bound the influence of any PARTICULAR coordinate, only the maximum, and it says nothing when Var(f) is 0, that is when f is constant. [Kahn, Kalai and Linial (1988); see O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, Chapter 9]","status":"unverified"}

# C024 v2: fixed-radius thickening fails the vanishing initial-function comparison
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: route-failure. Target:1.
General T267 OPEN. This is a precise obstruction to one proof route, not a
counterexample to nonlinear epochwise double descent. Novelty unestablished.

1. Statement
Let Z have ANY initialization-independent probability law on unit vectors in R^3,
and let V be uniform on the unit three-dimensional ball, independent of Z.
Fix 0<nu<=1, 0<tau<=1/4 and any integer m>=1. Independently initialize
 f_m(x;0)=m^(-1/2)sum_(j=1)^m a_j ReLU(W_j.x),
where W_j are iid N(0,I_3), a_j are iid uniform {-nu,nu}, and all are independent.
The SAME network is evaluated at Z+tau V and Z. Conditional on its initialization
put Y_m=E_(Z,V)|f_m(Z+tau V;0)-f_m(Z;0)|^2.
Define the strictly positive Gaussian-box probability
 p=P(1<=G_0<=2, |G_1|<=1, |G_2|<=1)
  =(Phi(2)-Phi(1))*(2Phi(1)-1)^2, for independent standard normals G_i.
Then, uniformly in m and the law of Z,
 E_init Y_m >=nu^2 tau^2 p/5,
 E_init Y_m^2 <=3nu^4 tau^4,
 P_init(Y_m>=nu^2 tau^2 p/10)>=p^2/300.                 (1)
In particular, at a FIXED positive tau the coupled initial-function discrepancy
cannot vanish in probability as width increases, even though initializations
are shared exactly. No training, Gram approximation or kernel-width limit is
needed for this conclusion.

2. Gaussian active-region lower bound
Fix a unit z and choose orthonormal coordinates with first axis z. Rotational
invariance of N(0,I_3) gives the same probability p to
 A_z={1<=W.z<=2, absolute values of the two orthogonal coordinates <=1}.
On this event ||W||<=sqrt(6). For EVERY ||v||<=1 and tau<=1/4,
 W.z>=1 and W.(z+tau v)>=1-tau sqrt(6)>0,
since 6/16<1. Thus both ReLUs are active and their difference is EXACTLY
 tau W.v. Uniform-ball covariance is E VV^T=I_3/5: its radial density is
3r^2 on [0,1], so E||V||^2=3/5, and symmetry divides this equally among axes.
Consequently
 E_(W,V)[ReLU(W.(z+tau V))-ReLU(W.z)]^2
 >=tau^2 E_W[1_(A_z)||W||^2/5]>=tau^2 p/5.            (2)
The integrand is nonnegative, so restriction to A_z is legitimate. This
bound is uniform in z; the orthonormal coordinates need not be chosen jointly
measurably because the pointwise bound is already independent of z.

3. Independent centered heads and the second moment
For fixed z,v put delta_j=ReLU(W_j.(z+tau v))-ReLU(W_j.z), T_j=a_j delta_j.
The T_j are independent centered variables; centering follows from the
independent head sign, without requiring delta_j itself to be centered.
Therefore
 E_init |m^(-1/2)sum_j T_j|^2=nu^2 E_W delta_1^2.
Integrate over (Z,V) and apply (2), using Tonelli, to obtain the first
inequality in (1). There is no 1/m decay in this initial output fluctuation:
the summation has scale 1/sqrt(m), whereas a kernel sample mean has scale 1/m.
The conclusion does not apply to paired antithetic initialization with
identical hidden weights and opposite heads; that violates the iid hypothesis
and can make the initial function identically zero.

4. Fourth moment and a probability lower bound
ReLU is 1-Lipschitz, hence |delta_j|<=tau |W_j.v|. For fixed z,v, write
mu_2=E T_1^2 and mu_4=E T_1^4. Gaussian second and fourth moments give
 mu_2<=nu^2 tau^2 ||v||^2,
 mu_4<=3nu^4 tau^4 ||v||^4.
These Gaussian moments follow by rotating v to a coordinate axis and using
E G^2=1, E G^4=3 (integration by parts for the standard normal density).
In the expansion of E(sum_j T_j)^4, a term survives only if every index
occurs an even number of times. There are m all-equal terms and
6*binom(m,2) two-pair terms. Thus exactly
 E_init |m^(-1/2)sum_j T_j|^4
 =mu_4/m+3(1-1/m)mu_2^2
 <=3nu^4 tau^4 ||v||^4<=3nu^4 tau^4.                 (3)
Jensen on the (Z,V) probability space gives Y_m^2<=E_(Z,V)|D_m(Z,V)|^4,
where D_m is the same initial prediction difference. Integrating (3) proves
the second inequality in (1). All moments are finite by the displayed bounds.

For completeness, the one-sided moment step does not assume concentration.
Set a=nu^2 tau^2 p/5, b=3nu^4 tau^4 and E={Y_m>=a/2}. Then
 E Y_m<=a/2+E[Y_m 1_E]<=a/2+sqrt(b P(E))
by splitting at a/2 and applying Cauchy-Schwarz. Since E Y_m>=a,
P(E)>=a^2/(4b)=p^2/300. This is precisely the last inequality in (1).
It is a probability lower bound, not a conclusion from mean error alone.

5. Consequence for the C022/C023 transfer route
In those constructions Z is uniform on four unit centers. At initialization,
the coupled center-to-ball population L2 error is sqrt(Y_m). It is part of
D_m(T)=max_(0<=k<=T)||F_ball,k(Z+tau V)-F_center,k(Z)||_2,
so D_m(T)>=sqrt(Y_m) for every horizon T, regardless of subsequent updates.
The bound (1) therefore holds for an initial discrepancy inside exactly the
same coupling used there, for every e, every width, and every fixed tau>0.
Directly replacing tau=e^20 by a positive constant cannot retain the
vanishing prediction comparison D_m(T)=o_P(1), let alone o_P(e^5).
More generally, with fixed nu>0 and tau=tau_e<=1/4, any argument that requires
D_m(T)=o_P(e^5) in width-before-scale limits must have tau_e=o(e^5): if not,
a subsequence has tau_e/e^5 bounded below, and (1) gives a fixed positive
probability of D_m(T)/e^5 being bounded away from zero. This is only a
necessary condition for THAT prediction-error route; C022's e^20 radius
satisfies it. It says nothing about optimal radius exponents.

This does NOT prove that actual population-risk differences cannot cancel,
that no alternative nonshrinking-geometry proof exists, or that double descent
fails for fixed-radius input laws. A proof for such laws must analyze their
nonconstant initial function and population dynamics directly, or use an
alternative comparison. The obstruction identifies why the present center
comparison cannot simply be thickened.

6. Finite checks and audit scope
The accompanying exact Fraction script enumerates independent head signs
for several deterministic increment vectors and widths1 through8. It checks
second and fourth moment expansions and detects a deliberately omitted
mixed fourth-moment term. Its paired-head negative control yields zero
initial difference where the independent-head computation is positive.
These checks concern the finite combinatorial step only; they are not an
independent audit of the Gaussian, population or limiting arguments. No Lean
certificate or literature-priority claim is made. Reviewer PASS is pending.

Brain use: q022 returned the standard second-moment technique; its warning
against drawing a probability conclusion from a mean alone is addressed in
Section4. The population Jensen step assumes no independence across inputs.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Omega is an open subset of R^N","u belongs to W^{1,p}(Omega) for the chain rule to apply","k > 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:23.250886+00:00","domain":"elliptic PDE, Sobolev spaces, truncation method","id":"claim_94ec221464adf6dc620b348214224d1a08fe5b06010d5e14cd92e3e805a01a53","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For $k > 0$ the truncation at level $k$ is $T_k(s) = \\max(-k, \\min(k, s))$, $s \\in \\mathbb{R}$: it equals $s$ for $|s| \\leq k$ and $\\pm k$ outside. $T_k$ is Lipschitz with constant 1, odd, and $T_k(0) = 0$. Chain rule (Stampacchia): if $\\Omega \\subset \\mathbb{R}^N$ is open and $u \\in W^{1,p}(\\Omega)$, $1 \\leq p \\leq \\infty$, then $T_k(u) \\in W^{1,p}(\\Omega)$ with $\\nabla T_k(u) = \\nabla u \\cdot \\mathbf{1}_{\\{|u| < k\\}}$ almost everywhere; if $u \\in W_0^{1,p}(\\Omega)$ then $T_k(u) \\in W_0^{1,p}(\\Omega)$, and $|T_k(u)| \\leq \\min(|u|, k)$. In particular $\\nabla u = 0$ a.e. on every level set $\\{u = c\\}$. Companion functions: the positive part $u^+ = \\max(u,0)$ and $G_k(u) = u - T_k(u)$ (the part of $u$ beyond level $k$); all such compositions satisfy the same chain rule $\\nabla(\\phi \\circ u) = \\phi'(u)\\nabla u$ a.e. for piecewise $C^1$ Lipschitz $\\phi$ with finitely many corners (with $\\phi(0) = 0$ to stay in $W_0^{1,p}$). The truncation method uses $T_k(u)$ (or $G_k(u)$) as a test function in a weak formulation; because it is bounded by $k$ it is admissible against $L^1$ right-hand sides, and $\\int_\\Omega |\\nabla T_k(u)|^p$ measures the energy of $u$ on the set where $|u| < k$. Sharp edges: the chain rule needs $\\phi$ Lipschitz (a merely continuous or unbounded-derivative $\\phi$ can leave $W^{1,p}$); for a function that is only in $L^1_{loc}$ with no Sobolev regularity, $T_k(u) \\in W_0^{1,p}$ for all $k$ is a genuine extra hypothesis, and this is exactly the class in which entropy solutions of $L^1$-data problems live.","status":"unverified"}

The lace expansion writes the two-point function of self-avoiding walk, Bernoulli percolation, oriented percolation or lattice trees as a renormalised random-walk Green function plus a correction series: for SAW, c_n(x) = sum_y D(y) c_{n-1}(x - y) + sum_{m=2}^{n} sum_y pi_m(y) c_{n-m}(x - y), with pi_m the alternating-sign lace coefficients obtained by inclusion-exclusion over self-intersections (for percolation the analogous expansion is in terms of pivotal bonds and sausages). The expansion is an exact identity; its use requires a bootstrap showing the coefficients are small in a norm controlled by a random-walk diagram: the bubble diagram for SAW (finite for d > 4), the triangle diagram for percolation (finite for d > 6) and the square diagram for lattice trees (d > 8). Proved regimes: nearest-neighbour SAW for d >= 5 (Hara-Slade), spread-out SAW for d > 4, nearest-neighbour percolation for d >= 11 (Fitzner-van der Hofstad) and spread-out percolation for d > 6 (Hara-Slade). Typical failure: Applying the expansion's mean-field conclusions (eta=0, Gaussian or super-Brownian scaling limit) to a model at or below its upper critical dimension without re-verifying the triangle or bubble condition; the coefficients pi_m are not shown small there, the bootstrap can fail to close, and the diagrammatic control silently assumed at the outset is exactly the open problem, which is why four-dimensional nearest-neighbor percolation mean-field behavior remains open despite the spread-out and high-dimension cases being resolved. {"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space","T is continuous","the supremum is over T-invariant Borel probability measures; it need not be attained"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438290+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, topological dynamics, entropy","id":"claim_95cd3f5a581ee5b3b33c5ba6ef9422e6da7205ab57a2fb35db6f9be50cdf92b0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $T: X \to X$ be a continuous map of a COMPACT metric space and let $M(X, T)$ be the (nonempty, by Krylov-Bogolyubov) set of $T$-invariant Borel probability measures. Then
$$h_{top}(T) = \sup\{ h_\mu(T) : \mu \in M(X, T) \},$$
and the supremum may be restricted to ERGODIC invariant measures. The inequality $h_\mu(T) \le h_{top}(T)$ for every invariant $\mu$ is Goodwyn's half; the existence, for every $c < h_{top}(T)$, of an invariant $\mu$ with $h_\mu(T) > c$ is the Dinaburg-Goodman half (Misiurewicz's proof below). Both sides may be $+\infty$. A measure attaining the supremum is a measure of maximal entropy; it need NOT exist for a general continuous $T$ (there are continuous maps, and even homeomorphisms, with $h_{top} < \infty$ and no measure of maximal entropy), but it exists whenever $\mu \mapsto h_\mu(T)$ is upper semicontinuous, e.g. for expansive maps and for $C^\infty$ maps of compact manifolds. The variational principle is the case $\varphi = 0$ of the variational principle for topological pressure, $P(T, \varphi) = \sup_\mu \{ h_\mu(T) + \int \varphi\,d\mu \}$.

WHERE IT FAILS OR NEEDS CARE. (1) Non-compact $X$: the statement depends on which notion of topological entropy is used; for the Bowen metric entropy on a non-compact space the supremum over invariant measures can be strictly smaller, and $M(X,T)$ may be empty (translation on $\mathbb{R}$). (2) The supremum need not be a maximum (see above). (3) Restricting to a non-invariant measure is meaningless: $h_\mu(T)$ is defined only for invariant $\mu$. (4) The principle relates ENTROPY to entropy; it does not say that a generic point has orbit-growth rate $h_{top}$, nor that the measure of maximal entropy is unique (uniqueness = intrinsic ergodicity, a much stronger property that holds e.g. for topologically mixing shifts of finite type but fails for many systems).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["k algebraically closed; the curves are projective and have no common component","intersection multiplicity is the local-ring dimension (equivalently Fulton's axiomatic multiplicity)","over non-closed fields or in affine coordinates only the upper bound mn on the number of points holds"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.626765+00:00","domain":"algebraic geometry","id":"claim_9689091d3f27a70eb1bd6d2e53f2f98d9030885135749952fef3396e0d0e9bcd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let C and D be projective plane curves over an algebraically closed field k, defined by homogeneous polynomials F, G in k[X, Y, Z] of degrees m and n with no common factor (the curves share no component). Then C and D meet in exactly mn points of the projective plane P^2(k) when each intersection point P is counted with its intersection multiplicity I_P(C, D) = dim_k O_P / (F, G) (the local ring at P modulo the ideal of the two curves); in particular they meet in at least one and at most mn distinct points. The multiplicity is at least m_P(C) m_P(D), the product of the multiplicities of the two curves at P, with equality exactly when the curves have no common tangent at P. Over a non-closed field, or in the affine plane, the count mn is only an upper bound on the number of points (missing points are at infinity, in a field extension, or hidden in multiplicities). {"assumptions":["K is a compact metric space","F is a uniformly bounded family in C(K)","F is equicontinuous on K"],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.377034+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_969621bacd8c4d8d1d18dc91064c5582eb98fa2cd21ef76831aadd2757e586da","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let K be a compact metric space and let F be a family of real- or complex-valued continuous functions on K. Suppose F is (i) uniformly bounded: there is M with |f(x)| <= M for all f in F and all x in K, and (ii) equicontinuous: for every epsilon > 0 there is delta > 0 such that d(x, y) < delta implies |f(x) - f(y)| < epsilon for every f in F simultaneously. Then every sequence in F has a subsequence converging uniformly on K (to a continuous limit); equivalently, F is relatively compact in C(K) with the supremum norm. Conversely, a relatively compact subset of C(K) is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. (Pointwise boundedness plus equicontinuity already implies uniform boundedness on compact K; the classical statement on K = [a,b] is the special case.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["F a class of measurable functions with values in a bounded interval [a, b] (for the two-sided form with the stated constant the class should be closed under negation or one accepts an extra factor; see the references)","the sample is i.i.d. from P; delta in (0, 1)","measurability of the suprema (a countable class, or the usual separability assumptions) is assumed throughout"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:40:13.706434+00:00","domain":"statistical learning theory","id":"claim_97839b3fb5a128a097b064c2e4b18409edd68bbc82e49a4901fe22e9f110c5d0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"DEFINITIONS. Let F be a class of measurable functions f: X -> [a, b], let S = (X_1, ..., X_n) be an i.i.d. sample from a distribution P on X, and let sigma_1, ..., sigma_n be independent Rademacher signs, independent of S. The empirical Rademacher complexity of F on S is R_hat_S(F) = E_sigma [ sup_{f in F} (1/n) sum_{i=1}^{n} sigma_i f(X_i) ], and the Rademacher complexity is R_n(F) = E_S [ R_hat_S(F) ]. Write P f = E f(X) and P_n f = (1/n) sum_i f(X_i). THEOREM. For every delta in (0, 1), with probability at least 1 - delta over the sample, simultaneously for all f in F: P f - P_n f <= 2 R_n(F) + (b - a) sqrt( log(1/delta) / (2n) ), and also P f - P_n f <= 2 R_hat_S(F) + 3 (b - a) sqrt( log(2/delta) / (2n) ) (a bound computable from the data). If F is closed under negation (f in F implies -f in F), the two-sided version sup_{f in F} |P f - P_n f| <= 2 R_n(F) + (b - a) sqrt(log(2/delta) / (2n)) holds with probability at least 1 - delta (for a general F apply the one-sided bound to F and to -F, each with delta/2, which replaces R_n(F) by R_n(F union -F)). Since E sup_f (P f - P_n f) <= 2 R_n(F), a class is uniformly Glivenko-Cantelli whenever R_n(F) -> 0. Standard values of R_n: a finite class bounded by B has R_n <= B sqrt(2 log |F| / n) (Massart); a class of indicators of VC dimension d has R_n <= sqrt(2 d log(e n / d) / n) and in fact O(sqrt(d / n)) (Dudley); linear predictors x -> <w, x> with ||w||_2 <= Lambda on inputs with ||x||_2 <= r have R_n <= Lambda r / sqrt(n); and for L-Lipschitz phi, R_n(phi o F) <= L R_n(F) (Ledoux-Talagrand contraction), which is how the bound passes from a class of predictors to a class of losses. In learning, with f the loss of a hypothesis, the theorem says the true risk of EVERY hypothesis in the class exceeds its empirical risk by at most 2 R_n plus a term of order sqrt(log(1/delta)/n), the modern replacement for VC bounds when the class is not a class of sets.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a set and mu* is defined on the entire power set of X","for the construction: E contains the empty set and some countable subfamily of E covers X, so that every subset has at least one admissible cover","rho maps E into [0, +infinity] with rho(empty set) = 0; no additivity or monotonicity of rho is assumed","countable, not arbitrary, families are used in the subadditivity axiom"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402410+00:00","domain":"measure theory, Caratheodory construction","id":"claim_9861570c368e84c1c207e946455b7453e592c4255152ddc4ad3423bc0df71072","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a set. A function mu* from the FULL power set of X to [0, +infinity] is an OUTER MEASURE if (1) mu*(empty set) = 0, (2) it is monotone: A contained in B implies mu*(A) <= mu*(B), and (3) it is countably subadditive: mu*(union over n >= 1 of A_n) <= sum over n >= 1 of mu*(A_n) for every countable family of subsets A_n of X, MEASURABLE OR NOT. Note that subadditivity is part of the definition in the abstract setting; the mathematical content lies in the fact that the standard constructions produce it. CONSTRUCTION FROM A COVERING FAMILY (a gauge): let E be a family of subsets of X containing the empty set and covering X by countably many of its members, and let rho : E -> [0, +infinity] with rho(empty set) = 0. Define mu*(A) = inf { sum over k >= 1 of rho(E_k) : E_k in E for all k and A contained in the union of the E_k }, with the convention that the infimum of the empty set is +infinity. Lebesgue outer measure on R^n is the case where E is the family of boxes (or open boxes, or cubes) and rho is the elementary volume. A set A is CARATHEODORY MEASURABLE for mu* if mu*(T) = mu*(T intersect A) + mu*(T minus A) for every test set T; these sets form a sigma-algebra on which mu* restricts to a complete countably additive measure (Caratheodory's theorem). CAUTIONS: an outer measure is defined on all subsets but is in general NOT additive on disjoint sets; it is not a measure on the power set; and the Caratheodory criterion, not the mere inequality in (3), is what recovers additivity.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.375169+00:00","domain":"general topology","id":"claim_987a713ab2d41c965d796f3285a70f19fefacd5934de0e8382701f1d12d8b510","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A collection B of subsets of a set X is a basis (base) for a topology on X if (i) every point of X lies in at least one member of B, and (ii) whenever a point x lies in the intersection of two members B1, B2 of B, there is a member B3 of B with x in B3 and B3 contained in the intersection of B1 and B2. {"assumptions":["all F_k lie in the SAME fixed chaos of order n >= 2","E[F_k^2] -> sigma^2 > 0","the equivalence is FALSE for sequences not confined to one chaos"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543836+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_987c81863f8063bc739cd937cd38fc426cd1f16bcd26e3a30b1ba5274965a462","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Fix an integer n >= 2 and let F_k = I_n(f_k) be a sequence living in the SAME n-th Wiener chaos, with E[F_k^2] = n! ||f_k||^2 converging to sigma^2 > 0. Then the following are EQUIVALENT: (i) F_k converges in distribution to N(0, sigma^2); (ii) E[F_k^4] -> 3 sigma^4; (iii) the contractions satisfy || f_k contracted with f_k at r indices || -> 0 for every r = 1, ..., n-1. The theorem replaces the infinitely many moment conditions of the method of moments by a SINGLE fourth-moment condition. The hypothesis that the chaos order n is FIXED and the same for every k is essential and is the standard misquotation: for a general sequence of random variables, or for a sequence whose chaos order drifts, matching the fourth moment says nothing about normality - the fourth moment of a suitable two-point law is also 3 times the square of its variance. Also essential is sigma^2 > 0; degenerating variance is excluded. The quantitative form is due to Nourdin and Peccati via Malliavin-Stein: for F in the n-th chaos with E[F^2] = sigma^2, the total variation distance to N(0, sigma^2) is bounded by a constant depending only on n times the square root of ( E[F^4] - 3 sigma^4 ), so the fourth cumulant controls the rate as well as the limit. [Nualart and Peccati (2005), Ann. Probab. 33; Nourdin and Peccati (2009); see Nourdin and Peccati, Normal Approximations with Malliavin Calculus, Theorem 5.2.7]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.499252+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_98c8bf02b194191751d59e544407d2b5ddcfe2816446a87e8a3d6e57a9ae7c3e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"(1) U ≠ C is essential: there is no biholomorphism from C onto D, since any holomorphic map C → D is bounded, hence constant by Liouville's theorem. C and D are the two conformal types of simply connected Riemann surfaces with the sphere. (2) Simple connectivity is essential and is not repaired by 'the domain has no holes that matter'. The punctured disk D minus {0} is not conformally equivalent to D: a biholomorphism F : D minus {0} → D would be bounded, hence extend holomorphically to 0 with |F(0)| ≤ 1; the extension maps the disk into D by the open mapping theorem, so F(0) = F(z1) for some z1 ≠ 0, and openness near both points contradicts injectivity on D minus {0}. Likewise two annuli {1 < |z| < R} and {1 < |z| < R'} are conformally equivalent only when R = R': conformal type has a modulus, so 'both are doubly connected' is not enough. (3) The conclusion is interior. The Riemann map need not extend continuously to the boundary, and when it does it need not be injective there. For the slit disk U = D minus [0,1) (which is simply connected), the inverse of the Riemann map extends continuously to the closed disk, but each point of the open slit is the image of two boundary points, so no homeomorphism of the closures exists. The correct boundary statement is Carathéodory's theorem: if U is bounded by a Jordan curve, then the Riemann map extends to a homeomorphism of the closed domains. {"assumptions":["(F_n) increasing, F_infinity generated by their union","Y integrable"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627314+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_990c757f8a69205734bf9eaa5f8523ff03979cc297993560b1152fd27fd6f9f2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (F_n) be an increasing filtration with F_infinity the sigma-algebra it generates, and let Y be in L^1. Then E[Y | F_n] converges almost surely and in L^1 to E[Y | F_infinity]. Taking Y = 1_A for A in F_infinity gives LEVY'S 0-1 LAW: P(A | F_n) -> 1_A almost surely, so the conditional probability of any event in the limit sigma-algebra converges to 0 or 1. Applied to a tail event of an independent sequence, where F_n is generated by the first n variables and P(A | F_n) = P(A) by independence, this yields Kolmogorov's 0-1 law as a corollary. The theorem is about an INCREASING family; the corresponding statement for a decreasing family is Levy's downward theorem and needs its own proof. The limit is conditional on F_infinity and not on F - the two differ, and writing E[Y | F] would be wrong unless F_infinity = F up to null sets. [standard; e.g. Williams, Probability with Martingales, Theorem 14.2]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149419+00:00","domain":"elliptic regularity theory","id":"claim_994ea180f3136425e554f422a5cd28077f4672f5e5871e28d1685f524f0bcfca","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Three hypotheses of the De Giorgi-Nash-Moser theorem are load-bearing, and each fails concretely. (1) Scalar. The theorem is false for systems: De Giorgi (1968) exhibited, for n >= 3, a linear elliptic system with bounded measurable coefficients satisfying the Legendre-Hadamard and even the strong ellipticity condition whose weak solution is u(x) = x |x|^{-gamma} for an explicit gamma with 1 < gamma < n/2 - a solution in H^1 that is unbounded, hence not even locally bounded, let alone Hoelder. So a referee must check that an application of De Giorgi-Nash-Moser or of Moser's Harnack inequality is to a single equation, not to a system, and that the maximum-principle-based truncations used in the proof are available. (2) The energy class u in H^1_loc. A distributional solution whose gradient is only in L^p for some p < 2 need not be bounded. In the plane take A(x) = I + (mu - 1) x x^T/|x|^2 with mu > 1 (uniformly elliptic, bounded, measurable, discontinuous only at the origin). In polar coordinates div(A grad u) = (1/r) d/dr ( r mu u_r ) + (1/r^2) u_{theta theta}, so u = r^s cos(theta) solves the equation away from 0 exactly when mu s^2 = 1. The choice s = -1/sqrt(mu) in (-1,0) gives u = r^{-1/sqrt(mu)} cos(theta), which is unbounded at 0, lies in W^{1,p}_loc precisely for p < 2/(1 + 1/sqrt(mu)) < 2, and is a distributional solution across the origin (the flux through small circles tends to 0 because s > -1). (3) The Hoelder exponent depends on the ellipticity ratio and cannot be improved to Lipschitz. The same coefficients with s = +alpha, i.e. mu = 1/alpha^2, give the H^1 solution u = r^alpha cos(theta) of a uniformly elliptic equation with ellipticity ratio alpha^{-2}: it is exactly C^{0,alpha} at the origin and no better. Hence the exponent alpha(n, Lambda/lambda) in the theorem must degenerate to 0 as Lambda/lambda tends to infinity, and 'bounded measurable coefficients give Lipschitz solutions' is false. Gradient bounds require continuity (or Dini/Hoelder continuity) of the coefficients.","status":"unverified"}
