{"assumptions":["the walk is on the incipient infinite cluster or a similarly statistically self-similar critical random graph","a known or boundable volume-growth exponent d_f for balls in the cluster","a known or boundable effective-resistance-growth exponent reflecting the bottleneck/dangling-end structure","typically also requires the cluster's law to have appropriate scale-invariance, or at least comparable behavior across scales"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T15:09:50+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_995bb1851ff2b7c32ba0e7dcdd60e02e63ccc5cf1891c73d2c0eefad0e85bbb6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For simple random walk on the incipient infinite cluster of critical percolation, or more generally on critical random media with anomalous volume growth, Kesten's argument establishes subdiffusive behavior, that the walk's typical displacement after n steps is of order n^{1/d_w} with walk dimension d_w > 2 rather than the diffusive n^{1/2}, by combining a volume-growth estimate showing balls of radius r typically contain of order r^{d_f} points, with d_f the fractal (volume) dimension of the cluster, and an effective-resistance estimate R_eff(0, B(0,r)^c) of order r^{zeta}, reflecting the long dangling ends and low-conductance bottlenecks characteristic of the critical cluster. The expected exit time from a ball of radius r is then of order r^{d_f+zeta} (volume times resistance: the Einstein relation d_w = d_f + zeta), so the displacement is of order n^{1/(d_f+zeta)}, subdiffusive when d_f + zeta > 2; the Nash/heat-kernel machinery or a direct expected-exit-time computation turns the two estimates into bounds. In balls of the intrinsic (graph) metric with unit conductances R_eff(0, B(0,r)^c) <= r, so zeta <= 1 there: for the high-dimensional incipient infinite cluster the intrinsic volume grows as r^2 and the resistance as r, giving d_w = 3. The argument does not give the exact value of the subdiffusivity exponent in most dimensions, only bounds, with the precise exponent known rigorously only in specific settings such as sufficiently high dimension or tree-like/hierarchical models, and it is specific to critical (not subcritical or supercritical) percolation geometry, where the fractal, tree-like structure with many bottlenecks is essential to the argument. Typical failure: Assuming the subdiffusivity exponent established for one setting, such as high-dimensional or tree-based incipient infinite clusters where exact computation is possible, transfers to two-dimensional critical percolation, where the exact random-walk dimension remains a major open problem; volume-growth and resistance-growth exponents are model- and dimension-specific quantities that must be independently estimated rather than imported across models with superficially similar critical geometry. Canonical reference: Kesten, 1986, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare, Probabilites et Statistiques; Barlow, Jarai, Kumagai and Slade, 2008, Communications in Mathematical Physics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542424+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9983acdd24bab7573598cbe43c588211e9e1d72227253d0cb43782e29ec19a49","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Fix d >= 2 and let E(Z^d) be the set of nearest-neighbour edges of the integer lattice. Assign to each edge e an independent random weight tau_e >= 0 with common distribution F; the collection (tau_e) is the environment. The PASSAGE TIME of a finite lattice path gamma is T(gamma) = sum over the edges of gamma of tau_e, and the passage time between vertices x and y is T(x,y) = inf over finite paths from x to y of T(gamma). T is a random pseudometric on Z^d: it is symmetric, satisfies the triangle inequality, and vanishes on the diagonal, but T(x,y) = 0 is possible for x != y when F has an atom at 0. A GEODESIC from x to y is a path attaining the infimum. Geodesics need not exist for a general F, and when F(0) is at least the critical probability p_c(d) the infimum can be 0 and attained by infinitely many paths; when F(0) < p_c a geodesic exists almost surely for every pair, and it is almost surely unique for every pair when F is continuous, since ties then have probability 0. The standing notation in the literature is T(0, x) for the point-to-point time, mu or g for the time constant, chi for the fluctuation exponent and xi for the wandering exponent; the store already records that those exponents are DEFINED differently by different theorems and are not interchangeable. [standard; e.g. Auffinger, Damron and Hanson, 50 Years of First-Passage Percolation, Chapters 1 and 4]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Burgers' equation f(u) = u^2/2 in one dimension","Weak solutions are only required to satisfy the integral identity; jumps must satisfy Rankine-Hugoniot but may still be inadmissible","Uniqueness is restored by the Kruzhkov entropy inequalities (equivalently, for piecewise smooth solutions, by Oleinik's chord condition at each jump)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418611+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: hyperbolic conservation laws","id":"claim_99a13816dfad50d260100b726c1812dec833cb5ab9500c5108e4748d4cdc77db","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: uniqueness in Kruzhkov's theorem is for ENTROPY solutions; the integral (weak) formulation alone, even with Rankine-Hugoniot satisfied at every jump, does not determine the solution. Counterexample 1 (Burgers, f(u) = u^2/2, datum u0 ≡ 0): besides u ≡ 0 the function u(x,t) = 0 for x < -t/2, u = -1 for -t/2 < x < 0, u = 1 for 0 < x < t/2, u = 0 for x > t/2 is a weak solution — every jump satisfies Rankine-Hugoniot (speeds -1/2, 0, 1/2 respectively) — yet it is not an entropy solution (the jump from -1 up to 1 is an expansion shock violating Oleinik/Lax). Counterexample 2 (Burgers with u0 = 0 for x < 0, u0 = 1 for x > 0): the stationary-in-shape expansion shock u = 0 for x < t/2, u = 1 for x > t/2 satisfies Rankine-Hugoniot, but the entropy solution is the rarefaction u = 0 for x ≤ 0, u = x/t for 0 ≤ x ≤ t, u = 1 for x ≥ t. In both cases the wrong solutions create information (characteristics emanate from the shock) instead of destroying it, and they are not vanishing-viscosity limits. Hamming codes are perfect codes, that is, they achieve the highest possible rate for codes with their block length and minimum distance of three. Richard W. A has a factorisation A = L U with L unit lower triangular (ones on the diagonal) and U upper triangular if and only if every leading principal submatrix A_k = A[1..k, 1..k], k = 1, ..., n - 1, is invertible (for invertible A this is equivalent to all n leading principal minors being nonzero); when it exists the factorisation is unique for invertible A, and u_kk = det A_k / det A_{k-1}. In general, for every A there is a permutation matrix P with P A = L U (Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting: at each step the row with the largest remaining entry in the pivot column is swapped into the pivot position); for invertible A the factors are then unique given P. The elimination costs 2 n^3 / 3 flops; solving A x = b afterwards costs 2 n^2 by one forward and one back substitution; the determinant is the product of the u_kk times the sign of P. Partial pivoting is backward stable in practice (the growth factor is bounded by 2^{n-1} in the worst case, attained by Wilkinson's example, but is small on almost all matrices), whereas elimination without pivoting can be unstable on matrices with small pivots even when A is well conditioned. Symmetric positive definite matrices need no pivoting (Cholesky); diagonally dominant matrices need none either.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T is measurable","invariance is expressed through preimages T^{-1}A"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.437948+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, foundations","id":"claim_9ba1defc34ee3afb4584a993f111afbfc82e7640f9230052afb1810248d72dbf","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \\mathcal{B}, \\mu)$ be a measure space. A measurable map $T: X \\to X$ is measure-preserving if $\\mu(T^{-1} A) = \\mu(A)$ for every $A \\in \\mathcal{B}$ (preimages, not images: $T$ need not be injective, and for non-invertible $T$ the condition $\\mu(TA) = \\mu(A)$ is neither implied nor required). The system is a probability-preserving system when $\\mu(X) = 1$. A set $A$ is (strictly) invariant if $T^{-1}A = A$, and invariant mod $\\mu$ if $\\mu(T^{-1}A \\,\\triangle\\, A) = 0$; every set invariant mod $\\mu$ differs from a strictly invariant set by a null set. $T$ is ergodic if every invariant set has measure $0$ or full measure; equivalently (for a probability measure) every measurable $f$ with $f \\circ T = f$ a.e. is a.e. constant; equivalently every set $A$ with $T^{-1}A \\subset A$ mod $\\mu$ (or $T^{-1}A \\supset A$ mod $\\mu$) has measure 0 or 1. The invariant $\\sigma$-algebra $\\mathcal{I} = \\{A : T^{-1}A = A\\}$ is what the ergodic averages converge to conditional expectations onto. Ergodicity is not the same as mixing (mixing implies ergodic, not conversely: an irrational rotation of the circle is ergodic but not mixing), and it is not preserved by passing to powers ($T^2$ may fail to be ergodic when $T$ is, e.g. the rotation by $1/2$ on two points).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["examples use Lebesgue measure on [0,1] and a one-point space of infinite measure","statements about (L^infinity)* use the axiom of choice via Hahn-Banach","the degenerate exception in (1) is a measure that is a finite sum of atoms of finite measure"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.553548+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_9c99a22f279aba04c24062eeaa629c6222d83b8f4cd18106908536d318f9894e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The identification of the dual of L^p has two genuine exceptions. (1) p = infinity fails in general: apart from the degenerate case of finitely many atoms all of finite measure (where L^1 = L^infinity is finite-dimensional and the duality is trivially true), L^1 is a proper closed subspace of (L^infinity)*. On [0,1] with Lebesgue measure, C[0,1] embeds isometrically in L^infinity (for continuous functions the sup norm equals the essential sup norm); extend the evaluation functional h -> h(0) from C[0,1] to a norm-one functional Lambda on L^infinity by Hahn-Banach. If Lambda were integration against some g in L^1, then taking continuous h_n with h_n(0) = 1, 0 <= h_n <= 1, supported in [0, 1/n], dominated convergence would give int h_n g -> 0 while Lambda(h_n) = 1. (Concretely, (L^infinity)* is the space of finitely additive bounded measures absolutely continuous with respect to mu.) (2) p = 1 without sigma-finiteness (or localizability) fails: let X = {pt} with mu({pt}) = infinity. Then L^1(mu) = {0}, so (L^1)* = {0}, while L^infinity(mu) is one-dimensional; the canonical map L^infinity -> (L^1)* is not injective, let alone onto. {"assumptions":["two-dimensional planar lattice model satisfying the FKG inequality","translation invariance and, in the classical gluing constructions, reflection symmetry of the lattice","an a priori lower bound on square-crossing probabilities, which is a hypothesis to be separately established, not a free consequence of RSW","independence, or at least positive association, of the underlying edge or site variables"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9ca68baa0660aa59223fcaebbdec10b169d0c2892b9d78d08095d1f75675fc1d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). In two-dimensional critical or near-critical percolation, RSW theory states that if crossing probabilities of n x n squares are uniformly bounded away from 0 as n grows, then crossing probabilities of rho n x n rectangles, for any fixed aspect ratio rho, are also uniformly bounded away from 0 by a constant depending on rho but not on n. The matching bound away from 1 needs the same input for the dual model (at criticality on a self-dual lattice it follows by duality); a lower bound for the primal model alone does not give it, since in the supercritical phase both crossing probabilities tend to 1. The classical proof glues together several square-crossing events using the FKG inequality and translation and reflection symmetry of the lattice. RSW estimates are the essential multi-scale input for proving arm-exponent bounds, conformal-invariance-adjacent results, and, via the Duminil-Copin-Tassion approach, for establishing sharpness of the phase transition without relying on exact self-duality. RSW does not by itself prove existence of a scaling limit as n -> infinity, does not give the exact value of any crossing probability, only two-sided bounds; and the classical form required exact self-duality (p=1/2 on the square lattice), so extending the theory to general planar lattices or to p != 1/2 required a genuinely new, duality-free argument (Tassion, 2016). Typical failure: Assuming that RSW-type bounded-away-from-0/1 crossing estimates transfer automatically to a new planar model merely because it is monotone and planar; RSW requires either exact self-duality or the more robust but still nontrivial Tassion-style construction, and models without FKG, or with strong enough long-range dependence, can fail to admit the needed gluing arguments even though they look superficially similar to Bernoulli percolation. Canonical reference: Russo, 1978, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Seymour and Welsh, 1978, Annals of Discrete Mathematics; Tassion, 2016, Probability Theory and Related Fields.","status":"unverified"}

(1) If A is dissipative and Ran(λ_0 − A) = X for some λ_0 > 0, then A is closed, Ran(λ − A) = X for every λ > 0, and A generates a contraction C_0-semigroup. (2) If A is dissipative and Ran(λ_0 − A) is merely dense for some λ_0 > 0, then A is closable, its closure Ā is dissipative with Ran(λ − Ā) = X for all λ > 0, and Ā generates a contraction C_0-semigroup. (3) Conversely, if A generates a contraction C_0-semigroup, then A is densely defined, closed, Ran(λ − A) = X for all λ > 0, and A is dissipative in the strong sense that Re⟨Ax, x*⟩ ≤ 0 for every x ∈ D(A) and every x* ∈ J(x). (4) If X is reflexive, a dissipative A with Ran(λ_0 − A) = X for some λ_0 > 0 is automatically densely defined. (5) Hilbert space corollary: if A is densely defined and closed and both A and A* are dissipative, then A generates a contraction C_0-semigroup; and a densely defined symmetric operator S with S ≤ 0 that is self-adjoint generates the contraction semigroup e^{tS}. {"assumptions":["X a Banach space","K compact and linear","the statement is about I - K; for lambda I - K with lambda not zero divide by lambda"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.476530+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_9cd24333d102074cf31fdaac1e3b28d41b51bfe803503d2d5cfac25fbe524fc7","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a Banach space, K : X -> X a compact linear operator, and T = I - K. Then: (i) ker T is finite-dimensional and the range of T is closed; (ii) T is injective if and only if it is surjective, and in that case T has a bounded inverse; (iii) dim ker T = dim ker T* where T* = I - K* is the adjoint on the dual X*, and the equation T x = y is solvable exactly when y annihilates ker T* (the closed-range theorem). So either T x = y has a unique solution for every y, or the homogeneous equation T x = 0 has a nontrivial finite-dimensional solution space and T x = y is solvable exactly for y orthogonal (in the duality sense) to the finitely many solutions of the adjoint homogeneous equation. For a Hilbert space and a self-adjoint compact K this is the classical alternative for integral equations of the second kind; the same conclusions hold for lambda I - K with any nonzero lambda.","status":"unverified"}

For raw inputs in [0,1]^d, every bounded rank-at-most-p GP with coordinatewise K-Lipschitz feature map has an explicit residual ReLU-attention transformer attaining uniform noisy predictive forward KL <= eps over contexts of length <=n and labels bounded by B. Unlike C002, feature computation is counted. The constants, grid size, width, heads, hidden width, and depth are explicit in C004 Sections 1-5. Status: proof (unaudited), T336-w727-C004 v1. Complete theorem, constants and scope:
# Target 1 with raw inputs and an explicit Lipschitz feature encoder

Claim T336-w727-C004 v1. Rung: proof (unaudited), subject to recorded checks and dependent on unaudited C002 v1. No Lean certification or independent audit is claimed. This gives a quantitative raw-input subclass of Target 1, rather than assuming exact feature computation outside the size count.

The hardest steps are the explicit residual-MLP encoder and the perturbation budget linking its feature errors to the original GP predictive distribution. The proof does not use a triangle inequality for KL.

## 1. Assumptions and explicit size

Fix integers d,p>=1,n>=0, real s>0, B>=0,R>=0,K>=0,eps>0. The raw domain is X=[0,1]^d. The fixed zero-mean GP prior has kernel k(x,x')=z(x)^T z(x'), where z:X->R^p satisfies ||z(x)||_2<=R and, for each coordinate j,

    |z_j(x)-z_j(x')|<=K ||x-x'||_1.

The observation noise is independent N(0,s). Context labels satisfy |y_i|<=B, and contexts have length t<=n. The target is the predictive law of a new noisy observation. The input encoding supplies only raw coordinates, labels, two binary role flags (context and query), and fixed constants. Zero padding fixes N=n+1 tokens. A padding token has raw coordinates zero and both flags zero; the query has only its query flag set; actual context tokens have only their context flag set. No label is supplied for the query.

Define the following fixed constants:

    S=R+1,
    C_A=n(2R+1),
    C_m=nB[(R+S)/s + S C_A R/s^2],
    C_v=R+S+S^2 C_A/s > 0,
    eta=min(1, sqrt(s eps)/(2(1+C_m)), s sqrt(eps)/(2 C_v), s/(4 C_v)),
    eps0=min(eps/4,1/16),
    m=max(1,ceil(K d sqrt(p)/eta)), J=(m+1)^d, E=3+ceil(log_2 J).

For the solver set

    kappa=1+max(1,n)S^2/s, M=nS^2B/s,
    delta0=min(1/2,s/(2S^2),sqrt(s eps0)/(1+M),s sqrt(eps0)/S^2),
    T=ceil(sqrt(kappa) log(2/delta0)/2).

There is a residual normalized ReLU-attention transformer (Bai et al. Definition 1 and Definition 2) with

    token width D=7p+6+d+Jd+pJ,
    depth L_total=E+T+2=T+5+ceil(log_2 J),
    at most five attention heads per layer,
    tokenwise MLP hidden width at most H=2Jd+pJ+4p+1,

whose Gaussian output satisfies forward KL<=eps uniformly over all these raw-input contexts and queries. A dense parameter upper bound is

    L_total(15D^2+2DH)+2D.

Fixed affine input placement is not counted; all nonlinear feature computation is counted. Every weight is specified below or in C002 v1 and depends only on the fixed prior feature map (through finitely many grid samples) and the displayed bounds, never on observed contexts, query labels, or future data. This is a real-weight size theorem, not a finite-bit complexity theorem or training guarantee.

## 2. Posterior perturbation caused by an approximate feature map

First suppose a map ztilde satisfies sup_x ||ztilde(x)-z(x)||<=eta<=1. Then ||ztilde||<=R+eta<=S. For any fixed admissible context and query, put

    A=sI+sum_i z_i z_i^T, b=sum_i z_i y_i, q=z(x_*),
    Atilde=sI+sum_i ztilde_i ztilde_i^T, btilde=sum_i ztilde_i y_i, qtilde=ztilde(x_*).

Both matrices are symmetric positive definite with inverse operator norm <=1/s. For vectors u,v,

    ||uu^T-vv^T||_op
      =||(u-v)u^T+v(u-v)^T||_op
      <=||u-v|| (||u||+||v||).

Thus

    ||A-Atilde||<=n(2R+eta)eta<=C_A eta,
    ||b-btilde||<=nB eta, ||b||<=nRB,
    ||A^{-1}-Atilde^{-1}||
      =||A^{-1}(Atilde-A)Atilde^{-1}||<=C_A eta/s^2.

The true and perturbed noisy predictive parameters are

    mu=q^T A^{-1}b, v=s+s q^T A^{-1}q,
    mutilde=qtilde^T Atilde^{-1}btilde,
    vtilde=s+s qtilde^T Atilde^{-1}qtilde.

Both variances are >=s. Add and subtract qtilde^T A^{-1}b and qtilde^T Atilde^{-1}b. Cauchy-Schwarz and the preceding bounds give

    |mu-mutilde|
      <=eta nRB/s + S C_A eta nRB/s^2 + S nB eta/s
      =C_m eta.

For the variance, first replace both q factors while retaining A^{-1}, and then replace the inverse. This gives

    |v-vtilde|
      <=s[eta(R+S)/s+S^2 C_A eta/s^2]=C_v eta.

The definition of eta ensures

    |mu-mutilde|<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    |v-vtilde|<=min(s/4,s sqrt(eps)/2).

No probabilistic context distribution or independence between observed features is needed here.

## 3. A finite-grid cone encoder

Let G={0,1/m,...,1}^d, so |G|=J. For each feature coordinate define

    ztilde_j(x)=min_{a in G}[z_j(a)+K sum_{r=1}^d |x_r-a_r|].

The Lipschitz assumption shows every term in this minimum is >=z_j(x). Choose a nearest grid point coordinate by coordinate; its L1 distance is <=d/(2m). The same Lipschitz bound then gives

    0<=ztilde_j(x)-z_j(x)<=Kd/m.

Consequently ||ztilde(x)-z(x)||<=sqrt(p)Kd/m<=eta. This also holds for K=0, when the error is zero and m=1. In particular |ztilde_j(x)|<=||ztilde(x)||<=S on the whole input cube.

The encoder is exact as an implementation of this finite minimum, including all absolute values. It is not a numerical approximation to the finite minimum.

## 4. Exact tokenwise residual-MLP construction

Use the 7p+4 core registers of C002. Add d registers for raw x, Jd zero-initialized absolute-value registers, pJ zero-initialized cone registers, and two role flags. This is D=7p+6+d+Jd+pJ. Initially the feature registers z_c,z_q are zero. The core constant is one=1; the variance-output register starts at s, and the query/padding label register is zero. Encoder MLP layers preserve raw x, the flags, and all core constants.

Each MLP has the residual form h^+=h+W2 ReLU(W1 h), with a constant register implementing affine biases. All unspecified matrix entries are zero. The attention block in each encoder layer is the identity (all value matrices zero).

Layer 1 uses 2Jd hidden units for ReLU(x_r-a_r) and ReLU(a_r-x_r), for all a in G,r. Their sums are written into the initially zero absolute-value registers, yielding |x_r-a_r| exactly.

Layer 2 uses Jd identity-ReLU units on the nonnegative absolute registers and one unit on the constant one. Its output matrix writes

    F_{j,a}=z_j(a)+K sum_r |x_r-a_r|

into each initially zero cone register. Negative fixed grid values cause no difficulty: they occur in the output matrix applied to the constant unit.

Next compute the minimum independently for each coordinate j by a balanced binary tournament on the J cone registers. A pair of current registers u,v is replaced in the first slot by

    u-ReLU(u-v)=min(u,v),

leaving the other slot unused thereafter. This is one residual MLP unit: W1 reads u-v and W2 subtracts its ReLU from the u register. Distinct pairs at the same level use disjoint output slots. An unpaired register passes unchanged. After ceil(log_2 J) levels one designated cone slot contains ztilde_j(x). Each level uses at most p floor(J/2) units, bounded by pJ. This works for signed cone values and for every J, not only powers of two.

One final gating layer writes the feature registers. For any |f|<=S and binary flag r define

    g(f,r)=ReLU(f+S(r-1))-ReLU(-f+S(r-1)).

If r=1, this equals f; if r=0, both arguments are <=0 and it equals zero. Apply g to every computed feature with the context flag to populate z_c, and with the query flag to populate z_q. The registers start at zero, so the residual connection adds precisely the desired values. This uses 4p units. Query, padding, and context feature routing now matches C002 exactly. Both flags and the raw x registers are preserved throughout.

There are E=3+ceil(log_2 J) MLP encoder layers. The stated H bounds every hidden width. Biases are realized through the constant register, rather than being omitted from the construction. All grid feature values are fixed weights of the known prior; no context-dependent parameter is selected.

## 5. Solver composition and KL budget

Apply C002 v1 to ztilde with feature bound S and accuracy eps0. Its core 7p+4 registers embed in the larger width D; all additional registers are preserved by zero extension of its matrices. The solver uses its one-head broadcast layer, T five-head Chebyshev layers, and four-head readout layer. All solver MLPs are identities. The resulting parameters muhat,vhat obey

    vhat>=s,
    |mutilde-muhat|<=sqrt(s eps0)<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    |vtilde-vhat|<=s sqrt(eps0)<=min(s/4,s sqrt(eps)/2).

Combine these with Section 2 using ordinary triangle inequalities for scalar errors, not for KL:

    |mu-muhat|<=sqrt(s eps),
    |v-vhat|<=min(s/2,s sqrt(eps)).

Since v,vhat>=s, put h=(v-vhat)/vhat in [-1/2,1/2]. As proved directly in C002 Section 5,

    KL(N(mu,v)||N(muhat,vhat))
      <=(mu-muhat)^2/(2s)+(v-vhat)^2/(2s^2)<=eps.

The depth is E+T+2. There are at most five heads, each with three D-by-D matrices. Counting two D-by-H/H-by-D MLP matrices at every layer, even when they are zero, and a two-coordinate linear readout, gives the stated dense parameter bound.

## 6. What this does and does not settle

This is a quantitative raw-input theorem for every bounded finite-rank GP feature map satisfying the displayed Lipschitz assumption, in every fixed input dimension. It counts the encoder rather than treating it as a free feature oracle. The bound is deliberately explicit and can be very large because J=(m+1)^d.

C003 shows that dropping all raw-feature regularity makes the literal bounded-kernel statement false for continuous Gaussian-output transformers. C004 therefore supplies a precise constructive assumption, while C002 remains the smaller theorem when features are supplied directly.

The finite-grid envelope and ReLU min/max identities are classical elementary constructions, not claims of new approximation theory. The claimed target contribution is their fully costed composition with the accelerated posterior solver and a uniform original-posterior forward-KL budget. C004 remains a proof candidate dependent on C002 until independent review passes both exact versions.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-12T06:09:38.198131+00:00","domain":"general topology","id":"claim_9e45874fad796149c5ac8f2b58760157b9ee22954ae7f56d86aa7e03bdd65509","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a subset A of a topological space X: the interior int(A) is the union of all open sets contained in A (the largest open set inside A); the closure cl(A) is the intersection of all closed sets containing A - which is closed, being an arbitrary intersection of closed sets, contains A, and lies inside every closed superset of A, hence is the smallest closed set containing A; the boundary is cl(A) minus int(A), equivalently cl(A) intersect cl(X\\A). Then A is open iff A = int(A) and closed iff A = cl(A). Point characterization: x is in cl(A) iff every open neighborhood of x meets A (if not, X\\cl(A) is an open neighborhood of x missing A; conversely a neighborhood U of x missing A makes X\\U a closed superset of A avoiding x). The closure operator satisfies the Kuratowski axioms - cl(empty)=empty, A subset of cl(A), cl(cl(A))=cl(A), cl(A union B)=cl(A) union cl(B) - and these four axioms on a set determine a unique topology whose closed sets are exactly the closure-fixed subsets.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["All paired four-point model definitions and restrictions of C010","Noise-to-signal Walsh variance ratio rho>0 fixed as e decreases; actual noise standard deviation tends to zero","Width tends to infinity before feature scale decreases; nonlinear comparison is only through finite T_e for each fixed e","Clean risk averages over all sixteen training-label-noise sign patterns"],"created_at":"2026-10-22T00:34:45.041953+00:00","domain":"learning theory","id":"claim_9ffa636677134a5540e6a704a86f6f5fe37015b52ad2241f167a16f3bc581359","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"# Co-scaled noise phases: double descent versus preference for late stopping

T267 / Target 2 / C011 / proof draft (unaudited); novelty unestablished.
This is an asymptotic phase comparison in C010's restricted model, not
an exact finite-scale two-critical-noise-level theorem.

## 1. Model and statement

Keep the four-point design, unit-norm centered-ReLU teacher, paired
nonzero initialization and both-layer GD of BOUNDED_RELU_PAIRED.md.
Write alpha=alpha_e and replace label noise +/-2alpha by
+/-2alpha sqrt(rho), for any fixed rho>0. Thus the noise standard deviation
is c_e sqrt(rho), which tends to zero. Each Walsh noise variance is
rho alpha^2. Average clean risk over the sixteen noise patterns as before.
All width limits are over even widths m=2N, before e decreases to zero.

Let b_h be the full-kernel rates of C009, q_h=exp(-b_h), and define

K_e=ceil(e^(-3/2)), T_e=ceil(e^(-5/2)),
E(rho)=rho+2+rho/(1+rho),
L(rho)=2rho+2rho/(1+rho).

For small e, K_e<T_e. The following minima of the ACTUAL nonlinear risk
converge in probability in the iterated width-then-scale sense:

min_(0<=k<=K_e) Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2 -> min{3,E(rho)},
min_(K_e<=k<=T_e) Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2 -> L(rho),
min_(0<=k<=T_e) Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2 -> min{3,L(rho)}.

Here convergence means for every epsilon>0, lim_(e->0) limsup_(N->infinity)
P(absolute discrepancy>epsilon)=0. These statements do not control actual
nonlinear risk after T_e or exchange the two limits.

Moreover there are strict descent-rise-descent witnesses at every fixed
rho>0. With k0=ceil(e^(-1/2)),
k1=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b1), k2=K_e,
k3=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b2), their risks divided by alpha^2 converge to

rho+3, E(rho), 2rho+2, L(rho).

Their three limiting strict margins are
1/(1+rho), rho^2/(1+rho), 2/(1+rho).
For all fixed rho<1, the best risk in the late phase is strictly lower
than the best in the early phase with probability tending to one.
For all fixed rho>1, the early phase is strictly better. At rho=1 the
leading phase minima tie at 3; no finite-e ordering is asserted.

Thus rho=1 is the limiting late-versus-early preference boundary in this
model, whereas strict double descent survives on both sides. No lower
critical-noise rate or exact finite-e second threshold is established.

## 2. Exact frozen risk and nonlinear transfer

The frozen zero-output curve is

F_e(k)=Q_e^0(k)/alpha^2
      =rho(1-q0^k)^2
       +sum_(h=1,2,12)[q_h^(2k)+rho(1-q_h^k)^2].

This follows from Walsh Parseval, identical teacher coefficients alpha
and Walsh noise variances rho alpha^2. The paired initialization gives
zero output exactly. Let p_r(q)=q^2+rho(1-q)^2. Completing the square,

p_r(q)=(1+rho)(q-rho/(1+rho))^2+rho/(1+rho).

For each fixed e and rho the labels are bounded; indeed max|y_i| is at
most (3+2sqrt(rho))alpha, which tends to zero. For all sufficiently small
e the residual bound R_0=2 used in C010 is therefore valid. Its pairwise
finite-horizon transfer applies uniformly through T_e (a finite integer
for this fixed e), and over all noise patterns. It follows that

max_(k<=T_e)|Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2-F_e(k)| ->0 in probability as N->infinity.

For this step alpha^2 is a FIXED positive number; no uniform-in-e width
bound is inferred. Consequently it suffices to prove the deterministic
frozen limits for the two ranges and the four witnesses.

## 3. Early-phase minimum

At k=0, F_e=3 exactly. At
k1=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b1), the constant mode has learned, q1^k1 tends to
rho/(1+rho), and q2^k1,q12^k1 tend to one. Hence F_e(k1)->E(rho).
These give the upper bound min{3,E(rho)} for the limiting early minimum.

For the lower bound, take any sequence e->0 and early-phase integers
k_e<=K_e. Choose a subsequence such that k_e is bounded or tends to
infinity, and such that b1 k_e converges in [0,infinity].
If k_e is bounded, all nonconstant q_h^k_e tend to one, so liminf F_e>=3.
If k_e tends to infinity, q0^k_e tends to zero. Uniformly for k<=K_e,
b2 k and b12 k tend to zero, since b2 K_e=O(e^(1/2)). Thus the slow-mode
contribution tends to two, while the fast-mode contribution is at least
rho/(1+rho) by the exact completed square. The limit inferior is at least
E(rho), whether the fast scaled time is finite or infinite. This proves
the matching early lower bound. The subsequence argument applies to
minimizers, which exist because the integer range is finite.

## 4. Late-phase minimum

Uniformly for k>=K_e, q0^k and q1^k tend to zero, since b1 K_e tends to
infinity. Their combined risk tends to 2rho, uniformly in this range.
Each of the two slow contributions is bounded below by rho/(1+rho),
so the late minimum has limit inferior at least L(rho).
For k3=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b2), both slow q's tend to rho/(1+rho), because
b12/b2->1. Also K_e<k3<T_e for all small e, since b2 K_e->0 and
b2 T_e->infinity. Thus F_e(k3)->L(rho), proving the matching upper bound.
Combining Sections 3-4 gives the full finite-horizon minimum as
min{3,E(rho),L(rho)}. The simplification in Section 6 proves the stated
min{3,L(rho)} form.

## 5. Strict double-descent witnesses

At k0 all nonconstant modes remain at one and the constant noise mode
has saturated, so F_e(k0)->rho+3. At k1 the limit is E(rho).
At K_e fast q1 tends to zero and the slow q's to one, giving 2rho+2.
At k3 the limit is L(rho). Subtraction gives exactly the three positive
margins in Section 1. This applies to every fixed rho>0, including rho>1.
The strict finite-e margins transfer to nonlinear GD by Section 2.

For rho=0 the frozen curve is sum_(h=1,2,12)q_h^(2k), strictly decreasing.
This zero-noise frozen statement does not imply monotonic actual nonlinear
risk for all times, nor locate a finite-e onset as rho_e tends to zero.
Pointwise positive-rho results must not be promoted to such a uniform
noise-window theorem.

## 6. Which phase wins?

Exact subtraction yields

E(rho)-L(rho)=(2-rho^2)/(1+rho),
L(rho)-3=(rho-1)(2rho+3)/(1+rho).

If 0<rho<1, then L<3 and L<E, so late training beats the entire early
phase, not just its fast-mode stationary point. If rho>1, then L>3,
so the early phase containing k=0 beats the late phase. Also E>3 for
rho>1, since E-3=(rho^2+rho-1)/(1+rho)>0. Consequently the overall
minimum is min{3,L}. At rho=1 the leading early and late values both
are 3, so a finer expansion is needed to decide finite-scale ordering.

Comparing ONLY E and L would instead produce sqrt(2). That would be the
wrong early-stopping boundary because it omits the allowed initialization
time k=0. This is why the early-phase minimization includes every time
from zero rather than only the first fast-signal minimum. The tiny initial
transient may shift the finite-e preference threshold; it does not change
these strict comparisons for rho bounded away from one.

## Scope and source distinction

Stephenson--Lee, arXiv:2108.12006, Section4, EDD-NES/EDD-ES phases and
P3/P4, distinguish onset of double descent from the higher noise level
where early stopping is preferable. This source does not supply this
model's threshold. Our computation is self-contained and restricted to
the paired four-point model. The lower onset at finite scale, its rate,
a full two-threshold window, iid Gaussian inputs, fixed-positive-noise
unit-teacher dynamics, high probability over label noise, and actual
nonlinear convergence after T_e remain open. Mathematical and novelty
review are pending; no independent audit or full Target2 solution.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Allen-Cahn on the 1-d torus with 1-d quadratic noise, critical gamma^2 = 2","deterministic constant initial data u_0 = a > 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:11:19.448302+00:00","domain":"stochastic partial differential equations, critical spaces","id":"claim_a215289259f9cccbe1cb7c19d537e22e0c0239f3b17a21caf7771d147f98140b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Agresti and Veraar, Nonlinear parabolic stochastic evolution equations in critical spaces (journal version 2025, p. 130), Problem 4 asks whether in the variational setting of their Theorem 6.4 there is a constant C_T with E sup_{t <= T} ||u(t)||_H^2 <= C_T (1 + E ||u_0||_H^2) for all u_0 in L^2(Omega; H). With deterministic constant data u_0 = a > 0 the solution stays spatially constant, and the substitutions Y = 1/U, Y = e^{-t} V, time change s = (e^{2t} - 1)/2 and R = V / sqrt 2 turn the SDE into R being a four-dimensional Bessel process started at R_0 = 1/(sqrt 2 a), with U_t = e^t / (sqrt 2 R_s). X) is a martingale. If (X_n) is a SUPERMARTINGALE and in addition H_n >= 0 for every n, then (H . X) is a supermartingale; the same with submartingale. {"assumptions":["phi is continuous on the unit circle (for merely bounded measurable symbols the criterion is different)","T_phi acts on the Hardy space H^2 of the circle","the winding number is that of the curve phi about 0, defined because phi is nonvanishing"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.573131+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Toeplitz operators, index theory","id":"claim_a336e41f1363f4a04acdf30204d079af81761e9aab33543cfff3898ac6f7532f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H^2 be the Hardy space of the unit circle T, realised as the closed subspace of L^2(T) spanned by the exponentials z^n with n >= 0, and let P: L^2(T) -> H^2 be the orthogonal projection. For a continuous symbol phi in C(T) define the Toeplitz operator T_phi on H^2 by T_phi f = P(phi f); the bound ||T_phi|| <= ||phi||_infinity is immediate from ||P|| = 1, and in fact ||T_phi|| = ||phi||_infinity. Then T_phi is Fredholm if and only if phi has no zero on T, and in that case ind T_phi = - wind(phi), the negative of the winding number of the closed curve phi about the origin. In particular T_phi is invertible if and only if phi is nonvanishing with winding number 0, and a Fredholm Toeplitz operator with continuous symbol is never invertible when its winding number is nonzero, even though it may be injective or surjective.","status":"unverified"}

The minimum-variance weights subject to $\\mathbf{1}^T w = 1$ are $w^* = \\Sigma^{-1}\\mathbf{1} / (\\mathbf{1}^T \\Sigma^{-1}\\mathbf{1})$ with risk $R^* = w^{*T}\\Sigma w^* = 1/(\\mathbf{1}^T \\Sigma^{-1}\\mathbf{1})$. Let $S$ be the sample covariance of $n > M + 1$ i.i.d. Gaussian observations with covariance $\\Sigma$ and let $\\hat w = S^{-1}\\mathbf{1}/(\\mathbf{1}^T S^{-1}\\mathbf{1})$ be the plug-in weights. THEOREM (Pafka and Kondor, 2003; the finite-$n$ moments are those of the inverse Wishart law). In the limit $M, n \\to \\infty$ with $q = M/n \\in (0, 1)$: (i) the true (out-of-sample) risk of the plug-in portfolio satisfies $\\hat w^T \\Sigma \\hat w / R^* \\to \\frac{1}{1 - q}$; (ii) the in-sample risk $\\hat w^T S \\hat w / R^* \\to 1 - q$; so the realized risk exceeds the optimum by the factor $1/(1-q)$ while the naive in-sample estimate understates the optimum by the factor $1 - q$, the two differing by $1/(1-q)^2$. {"assumptions":["A Hermitian (symmetric in the real case)","positive definite for existence with a strictly positive diagonal and for uniqueness"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479375+00:00","domain":"numerical linear algebra","id":"claim_a456a3e325bc76743808041802880a3b7d0b3e39a7260821e678465f0bff4aaf","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"A Hermitian matrix A in C^{n x n} is positive definite if and only if it can be written as A = L L^* with L lower triangular having strictly positive real diagonal entries; when it exists this factorisation is unique. For real symmetric positive definite A the factor L is real, A = L L^T. Equivalently A = R^* R with R = L^* upper triangular. The factor is computed by the Cholesky algorithm in n^3 / 3 flops (half the cost of LU, no pivoting needed): for j = 1..n, l_jj = sqrt(a_jj - sum_{k<j} |l_jk|^2) and l_ij = (a_ij - sum_{k<j} l_ik conj(l_jk)) / l_jj for i > j; the algorithm is backward stable (Wilkinson), and it fails - a nonpositive quantity under the square root - exactly when A is not positive definite, which makes it the standard numerical test of positive definiteness. For positive semidefinite A a factorisation A = L L^* with nonnegative diagonal still exists but is no longer unique. Uses: solving A x = b by two triangular solves, sampling Gaussian vectors with covariance A (x = mu + L z), least squares via the normal equations, and the Kalman filter.","status":"unverified"}

The largest gap G_N satisfies theta G_N - (1/2) log N - log(2 theta) - c_b => Gumbel, with theta = zeta(3/2)/(2 sqrt(2 pi)) = 0.5210934894 and c_b = log 2 - 1/4 + (1/(4 pi)) sum_{n>=2} (1/n)(-pi + sum_{m=1}^{n-1} 1/sqrt(m(n-m))) = 0.0625786, the bulk gap constant conjectured by Forrester and proved by FitzGerald, Tribe and Zaboronski; so G_N ~ log N/(2 theta). Then for every t > 0, P(|X - mu| >= t) <= sigma^2 / t^2; when sigma > 0 this is equivalent to P(|X - mu| >= k sigma) <= 1/k^2 for every k > 0 (for sigma = 0 the standardized form fails: X = mu almost surely and the left side is 1). The inequality is sharp: for t >= sigma the variable taking the values mu - t and mu + t with probability sigma^2 / (2 t^2) each and the value mu otherwise has mean mu, variance sigma^2 and P(|X - mu| >= t) = sigma^2 / t^2 exactly. It gives no information for t <= sigma, and it is the classical route to the weak law of large numbers: for i.i.d. X_i with finite variance, P(|(X_1 + ... + X_n)/n - mu| >= eps) <= sigma^2 / (n eps^2) -> 0.","status":"unverified"}

Edgar Gilbert introduced the other model contemporaneously with and independently of Erdős and Rényi. {"assumptions":["independent (product) Bernoulli measure, possibly with coordinate-dependent parameters","A is a monotone (increasing) event depending on finitely many coordinates","differentiability in p, automatic for finite-dimensional product measures"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.974074+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a6e95b98b55e5073a7f62110341ac5fe86d89ae81b909d71bb1c753c13feb7de","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For the product measure mu_p on {0,1}^E with each coordinate independently open with probability p and an increasing event A depending on finitely many edges, Russo's formula states d/dp mu_p(A) = sum_{e in E} mu_p(e is pivotal for A), where e is pivotal for A at a configuration omega if flipping the state of e changes the indicator of A. When different edges carry different parameters p_e, the analogous statement is d/dp_e mu(A) = mu(e is pivotal for A). This identity converts questions about how quickly an event's probability crosses a threshold into questions about counting or bounding pivotal edges, which is the basic engine behind sharp-threshold theorems when combined with the Margulis-Russo framework and tools such as hypercontractivity, the Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm influence bound, or the OSSS inequality. Russo's formula does not by itself give sharp thresholds; it requires monotonicity of A, since non-monotone events need a more complex signed-pivotal generalization; and it is stated for independent-coordinate measures, so applying it to dependent measures such as the random-cluster model requires a separate Glauber-dynamics-based generalization rather than the naive product-measure formula. Typical failure: Using Russo's formula on a non-monotone event without its signed-pivotal generalization, or applying the plain product-measure version of the formula to a dependent measure such as a random-cluster or Ising Gibbs measure, where the correct analogue requires the generator of an associated Glauber dynamics rather than a simple coordinatewise derivative; both errors produce a derivative formula that looks structurally similar but is simply wrong. Canonical reference: Russo, 1981, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Margulis, 1974, Problemy Peredachi Informatsii; Grimmett, Percolation, second edition, 1999, Springer, Chapter 2.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space and T : X -> X is continuous","M(X,T) carries the weak-star topology and is nonempty (guaranteed by Krylov-Bogolyubov)","h*(T) = 0 (asymptotic h-expansiveness); h-expansiveness and expansiveness are sufficient special cases","h_mu(T) is the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy of the measure-preserving system (X, mu, T)","the existence corollary uses the variational principle, which itself needs only compactness and continuity"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090700+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, entropy, measures of maximal entropy","id":"claim_a77bafb383fb156acf97fdf0ec6338f3cdb7ec81469c4cf42ee27a80550d59df","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a compact metric space, T : X -> X continuous, and let M(X,T) be the set of T-invariant Borel probability measures with the weak-star topology, a nonempty compact convex metrisable set. Suppose T is ASYMPTOTICALLY h-EXPANSIVE, i.e. its tail entropy h*(T) = lim as eps -> 0 of sup over x of h(T, Gamma_eps(x)) vanishes; this holds in particular when T is h-expansive, and a fortiori when T is expansive. THEN the entropy map mu -> h_mu(T) is upper semicontinuous on M(X,T): whenever mu_k -> mu weak-star inside M(X,T), limsup_k h_{mu_k}(T) <= h_mu(T). CONSEQUENCES: an upper semicontinuous function on a nonempty compact set attains its supremum, so by the variational principle a measure of maximal entropy exists and h_top(T) = max over mu in M(X,T) of h_mu(T); the entropy function is then a bounded, affine, upper semicontinuous function on a Choquet simplex, which is what makes the theory of maximal measures and of symbolic extensions run. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) some hypothesis of this kind is necessary. For a general continuous map the entropy map need not be upper semicontinuous and a measure of maximal entropy need not exist; this is why smoothness matters - Newhouse proved that C^infinity diffeomorphisms of compact manifolds are asymptotically h-expansive and therefore always carry maximal measures, while for finite smoothness there are counterexamples. (ii) The conclusion is strictly one-sided and cannot be improved to continuity even for expansive systems: in a mixing shift of finite type the periodic-orbit measures, all of entropy 0, are weak-star dense, so they converge to the measure of maximal entropy and the entropy map is not lower semicontinuous. (iii) Compactness of X (hence of M(X,T)) is what converts upper semicontinuity into existence of a maximiser; on a noncompact space the existence conclusion fails even when the map is upper semicontinuous. (iv) The implication is stated in one direction only: upper semicontinuity of the entropy map is a strictly weaker property than asymptotic h-expansiveness, so do not run the criterion backwards.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["two independent centered Gaussian fields on a common finite or suitably truncated index set","existence and enough regularity of the covariance functions to differentiate the interpolated expectation under the integral","a consistent-sign comparison, or specific structural relation, between the two covariance kernels","the test functional F smooth with the correct sign of mixed partial derivatives for the interpolation identity to yield a useful inequality rather than an uncontrolled remainder"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.986351+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a7b6b7b2b6ff3d35232e25a83c85018f52e970e60f45507e62d94c80f06513bc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For two independent centered Gaussian fields X, Y indexed by a common finite (or suitably truncated) set T with covariance functions C_X, C_Y, Kahane's interpolation forms Z(t,u) = sqrt(u) X(t) + sqrt(1-u) Y(t) for u in [0,1] and computes d/du E[F(Z(.,u))] for a smooth test function F, obtaining an integral expression involving (C_Y(s,t) - C_X(s,t)) times a mixed second derivative of F, evaluated against the law of Z(.,u). When C_X <= C_Y pointwise (or the relevant difference has a consistent sign) and F is chosen with matching sign of mixed partials, this yields a comparison inequality between functionals of X and Y, an approach that both generalizes Slepian-type comparisons and, in the Gaussian multiplicative chaos literature, is used to show that different regularizations of a log-correlated field, such as the two-dimensional Gaussian free field, converge to the same limiting chaos measure regardless of the approximation scheme, a key technical step in constructing Liouville quantum gravity measures. It does not apply to non-Gaussian fields, it requires the two fields being compared to be independent for the interpolation construction itself, and the sign or convexity conditions on F needed to obtain a clean inequality must be verified case by case rather than assumed. Typical failure: Applying the interpolation to fields that are not independent, or to a family of regularizations whose covariance difference does not have a consistent sign across the whole index set, which is common when comparing regularizations of a log-correlated field near its singular set; either error breaks the monotonicity the interpolation is meant to exploit, and the resulting comparison can go in the wrong direction with no explicit error term to control it. Canonical reference: Kahane, 1986, Annales des Sciences Mathematiques du Quebec; Robert and Vargas, 2010, Comptes Rendus Mathematique; Berestycki, 2017, Electronic Communications in Probability.","status":"unverified"}

Equivalently, T_rho f = sum_S rho^{|S|} hat{f}(S) chi_S, and the inequality forces the Fourier weight of f on high-degree levels to decay geometrically once rho<1, giving sum_S rho^{2|S|} hat{f}(S)^2 <= (E[|f|^p])^{2/p} for suitable p. This is the central tool converting L^2 Fourier information into higher-moment (typically L^4) control, and it underlies the Kahn-Kalai-Linial theorem on the existence of an influential coordinate, the Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm noise-sensitivity theorems, and Friedgut's junta theorem for low-influence functions. It does not directly give influence bounds without further combination with such machinery, and the sharp constant and range of rho given here hold for the uniform measure on {-1,1}^n; biased-p product measures or non-product (dependent) measures require different, generally weaker, p-biased or dependency-adjusted hypercontractive inequalities. Typical failure: Applying the sharp uniform-measure {-1,1}^n hypercontractive constant to a biased-p product measure or to a dependent measure such as the random-cluster or Ising Gibbs measure without switching to the correct p-biased or dependency-adjusted hypercontractivity inequality, whose constants generally degrade as p approaches 0 or 1; this silently invalidates quantitative noise-sensitivity conclusions claimed for critical percolation at p != 1/2 or for genuinely non-product models. Canonical reference: Bonami, 1970, Annales de l'Institut Fourier; Beckner, 1975, Annals of Mathematics; O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, 2014, Cambridge University Press.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f : {-1,1}^n -> {0,1} Boolean, uniform product measure","c is a universal constant","the conclusion bounds only the MAXIMUM influence, not any specific coordinate"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628283+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a7d3fa81d9e828619a0897ad9b5e1de549e37211c93fe093b3a6f7e2f0ac728c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : {-1,1}^n -> {0,1} be a Boolean function on the uniform product measure, and define the influence of coordinate i as Inf_i(f) = P( f(X) != f(X^{(i)}) ) where X^{(i)} flips the i-th coordinate. Then there is a universal constant c > 0 with max_{i <= n} Inf_i(f) >= c Var(f) log n / n, where Var(f) = p(1-p) with p = E[f]. Equivalently the TOTAL influence satisfies sum_i Inf_i(f) >= c Var(f) log n. The bound is SHARP up to the constant: the tribes function, a read-once DNF on blocks of size about log_2 n - log_2 log_2 n, is balanced and has all influences of order log n / n. The theorem is about the uniform measure on the cube; the analogous statement for p-biased measures carries an extra factor and is the Friedgut-Kalai sharp-threshold machinery. Note what it does NOT say: it does not bound the influence of any PARTICULAR coordinate, only the maximum, and it says nothing when Var(f) is 0, that is when f is constant. [Kahn, Kalai and Linial (1988); see O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, Chapter 9]","status":"unverified"}

If every f_i is upper semicontinuous - in particular if every f_i is continuous - then the pointwise infimum inf_i f_i is upper semicontinuous. Dually, a pointwise supremum of lower semicontinuous functions is lower semicontinuous. The family may be uncountable, and no uniformity is needed. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149018+00:00","domain":"elliptic partial differential equations, maximum principles","id":"claim_a7ff9de16f2bbefc6c4fe4f5adbe349d50f8611965c390800f138c4833c83567","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: c <= 0 in the nondivergence convention Lu = sum a^{ij}D_{ij}u + b.Du + cu (equivalently c >= 0 in the divergence convention -div(A grad u) + b.grad u + cu). The same function shows uniqueness fails: u and 0 both solve the Dirichlet problem. In n dimensions the first Dirichlet eigenfunction of the Laplacian does the same on any bounded domain. Sharp form: for L = Laplacian + c with constant c on a bounded Omega, the weak maximum principle in the H^1 sense (if u in H^1(Omega), Lu >= 0 weakly and u^+ in H^1_0(Omega), then u <= 0) holds if and only if c < lambda_1(Omega), the first Dirichlet eigenvalue. Example: on (-1,1), u(x) = -cosh x satisfies u'' - u = 0 (so c = -1 <= 0), u(0) = -1 while u(-1) = u(1) = -cosh 1 which is about -1.543; the interior supremum strictly exceeds the boundary supremum, and only the truncation at 0 saves the statement. {"assumptions":["X integrable with X in an open interval I almost surely","phi convex on I","E[phi(X)^-] < infinity, so that E[phi(X) | G] is defined"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752623+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a82c08a702478464e662ccbbaeeea30b77120ba9b85679d10ca8d340f884bc36","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be an integrable random variable taking values almost surely in an open interval I of R, let phi : I -> R be convex, and let G be a sub-sigma-algebra. If phi(X) is integrable, or more generally if E[phi(X)^-] < infinity so that E[phi(X) | G] is well defined in (-infinity, +infinity], then phi(E[X | G]) <= E[phi(X) | G] almost surely. Taking G trivial recovers the unconditional Jensen inequality. Two hypotheses do real work: X must lie in the interval where phi is convex, and some one-sided integrability of phi(X) is needed for the right-hand side to be defined. Convexity cannot be weakened to midpoint convexity without measurability, and the inequality REVERSES for concave phi. A standard consequence is that for a convex phi and a martingale (M_n), the process phi(M_n) is a submartingale whenever it is integrable. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 4.1.10]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X and Y are Banach spaces over the same field","T is a bounded linear operator from X to Y"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.571248+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Fredholm theory","id":"claim_a8d654dd18a265403bd8a3b84aa51c1024872fabf26f962e91167e35b5920dca","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X and Y be Banach spaces and T in B(X,Y) a bounded linear operator. T is a Fredholm operator if (a) its kernel ker T is finite-dimensional and (b) its range ran T has finite codimension, i.e. the quotient vector space Y / ran T is finite-dimensional. The index of a Fredholm operator is the integer ind T = dim ker T - dim(Y / ran T). The range of a Fredholm operator is automatically closed (a bounded operator between Banach spaces whose range has finite algebraic codimension has closed range), so texts that add 'ran T is closed' to the definition define the same class. For Fredholm T one has dim(Y / ran T) = dim ker T', where T': Y' -> X' is the Banach-space adjoint, so ind T = dim ker T - dim ker T'. Examples on l^2: an invertible operator has index 0; the unilateral shift S(x_1, x_2, ...) = (0, x_1, x_2, ...) is injective with range of codimension 1, so ind S = -1, and its adjoint (the backward shift) has index +1; I + K with K compact has index 0. The set of Fredholm operators X -> Y is written Phi(X,Y).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["R associative with identity; 'semisimple' means semisimple as a left module over itself (equivalent to the right-module version)","the division rings need not be commutative (the real quaternions H occur, e.g. in R[Q_8])"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479831+00:00","domain":"ring theory and representation theory","id":"claim_a8dff8cc7fd1ebc995d2f1c2cd5a96f7c66d395874540b73e9f3e7c21eab6fcc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"A ring R (associative, with 1) is semisimple - every left R-module is a direct sum of simple modules, equivalently R is a finite direct sum of simple left modules, equivalently R is left Artinian with zero Jacobson radical - if and only if R is isomorphic to a finite product of matrix rings over division rings: R = M_{n_1}(D_1) x ... x M_{n_r}(D_r). The integers r and n_i and the division rings D_i (up to isomorphism) are determined by R: r is the number of isomorphism classes of simple left R-modules, and the simple module S_i = D_i^{n_i} has End_R(S_i) = D_i (opposite conventions aside). A simple left Artinian ring is a single matrix ring M_n(D). Consequences: for a finite group G and a field k of characteristic not dividing |G| (Maschke), the group algebra k[G] is semisimple, so k[G] = prod M_{n_i}(D_i); over an algebraically closed field the D_i are k itself, the n_i are the degrees of the irreducible representations, r is the number of conjugacy classes, and |G| = sum n_i^2. A commutative semisimple ring is a finite product of fields. Wedderburn's little theorem (finite division rings are fields) then gives: a finite semisimple ring is a product of matrix rings over finite fields.","status":"unverified"}

For arbitrary n>=2 scalar three-token first-token-query self-attention examples with distinct signed values, negative minimum, positive maximum, and positive signed first token, joint-head logistic GD has two open endpoint-selection basins. Invariant subregions escape for every eta>0; for eta<=min(2/H^2,1/(2D)), every finite initialization outside a null saddle-stable set escapes to one endpoint pattern. Interior and mixed endpoint hard patterns are impossible. Normalized margins are min maxima and min negated minima, so unequal margins give a positive-measure inferior basin.

# Target 1: scalar three-token self-attention under joint training

Version 1, unaudited. Owner own work; novelty not established globally.
This extends the scalar family, not arbitrary vector-valued token geometry.

## Data, model and conclusions

For each i=1,...,n, n>=2, take a label y_i in {-1,+1} and three distinct
signed token values c_ij. Their minimum m_i is negative, maximum M_i positive,
and the FIRST token c_i1 is positive. Let raw tokens x_ij=y_i c_ij and use
the actual first token x_i1 as the self-attention query. With jointly trained
scalar head v and scalar attention weight p, signed prediction is v h_i(p),

 h_i(p)=sum_j c_ij exp(zeta_i c_ij p)/sum_j exp(zeta_i c_ij p),
 zeta_i=c_i1>0.

The loss is average logistic loss. Let
 H=max_i max(|m_i|,|M_i|), D=max_i zeta_i(M_i-m_i)^2,
 eta_*=min(2/H^2,1/(2D)).

For every fixed eta in (0,eta_*], simultaneous GD in (v,p) has precisely
three possible limits: the unique finite saddle (0,p_bar), where
mean_i h_i(p_bar)=0; matching-positive escape v,p->+infinity; or
matching-negative escape v,p->-infinity. The saddle's global stable set is
planar null. Both escaping basins are open and nonempty. Their hard selections
are respectively the maximum signed token in EVERY example and the minimum
signed token in EVERY example. No interior token, or mixed pattern of extrema,
is a hard-selection limit in this scalar model. On escaping trajectories
p=O(log |v|), loss->0 and the normalized joint directions are (+1,0),(-1,0).
The corresponding minimum signed margins, normalized by sqrt(v^2+p^2),
are Gamma_+=min_i M_i and Gamma_-=min_i(-m_i).

In addition, for EVERY eta>0 the regions
 Q_+={v>0,p>max_i rho_i}, Q_-={v<0,p<min_i rho_i},
where h_i(rho_i)=0, are forward invariant and satisfy the same respective
escape/margin conclusions. Thus if Gamma_+>Gamma_-, the inferior basin is
open and positive measure even without a step-size restriction. A sufficient
strict inequality is M_i+m_i>0 for every example.

## Scalar softmax link estimates

Write alpha_ij(p) for the three softmax weights. Direct differentiation gives
h_i'=zeta_i[sum alpha_ij c_ij^2-h_i^2]
     =zeta_i sum_{j<l} alpha_ij alpha_il(c_ij-c_il)^2>0.
Also |h_i|<=H, h_i'<=zeta_i(M_i-m_i)^2<=D, and h_i tends to m_i,M_i
at the two infinities. Thus each root rho_i exists uniquely.

Let delta be the minimum over i of zeta_i times either adjacent gap of its
sorted three token values. It is strictly positive. For p>=0, the total
softmax mass on nonmaximum tokens is <=2 exp(-delta p).
Variance is no larger than the second moment about the maximum token,
so h_i'(p)<=2D exp(-delta p). Reflecting yields the same upper bound
2D exp(-delta |p|) for p<=0. Every h_i is real analytic, strictly increasing,
bounded, and has exponentially decaying derivative.

## Full-plane trapping and escape

For g_i=(1+exp(v h_i(p)))^-1 put F=mean g_i h_i and G=mean g_i h_i'>0.
GD is v_+=v+eta F, p_+=p+eta vG. The following estimates are identical
to those needed in proof 005, now established for genuine three-token links:

 -H^2/4<=F_v<=0,
 F(0,p)=mean h_i(p)/2=:F_0(p), 0<F_0'<=D/2, G<=D.

There is a unique mean root p_bar. Set u=p-p_bar, A=H^2/4.
In v,u>0, v_+>=(1-eta A)v+eta F_0(p)>0 and p increases; reflecting gives
invariance in v,u<0. In a bad quadrant v>0,u<0, v decreases and u increases
until it exits or converges to the saddle. Double crossing would require

 (1-eta A)v<=eta(D/2)|u|<=eta^2 D^2 v/2,

impossible since eta A<=1/2 and eta D<=1/2. The other bad quadrant is the
reflection. An axis point other than the saddle enters a good quadrant after
one step. A bad-quadrant orbit staying there is bounded and monotone; continuity
of increments gives vG=F=0 at its limit, hence the saddle.

Consider a positive good-quadrant orbit. If p had a finite limit P and v were
bounded, compactness would give G bounded below; Delta p->0 would force v->0,
but F_0(P)>0 contradicts convergence of v to zero. If v were unbounded and
P<=R:=max rho_i, an example with root R has h_j(p)<=0 and therefore g_j>=1/2.
On the compact p interval its derivative is bounded below, so
Delta p>=eta d v/(2n), contradicting finite P. If P>R, eventually all links
are >=c>0; v then increases without bound and
Delta p/Delta v>=d v/H again contradicts finite P. Thus p->infinity.
Eventually all h_i>=c, forcing v->infinity (bounded v would keep the g_i
uniformly positive). Negative escape follows by reflection using -h_i(-p).

This proof also applies directly within Q_+ or Q_- at any eta>0: both
coordinates are monotone from the start and all signed links are positive
after reflection. Only the full-plane trapping argument uses eta_*.

## Rates, margin, and the null exceptional set

On a positive escaping trajectory, h_i>=c>0 eventually, so
Delta p<=eta D v exp(-cv)->0. Moreover
Delta p/Delta v<=2D v exp(-delta p)/c.
Once Delta p<=1, the mean value theorem gives
Delta exp(delta p)<=C v Delta v. Telescoping against v^2 gives
exp(delta p)<=C'(1+v^2), so p=O(log v). Reflection proves the other branch.
Loss and normalized margin limits now follow. For any parameter pair,
the endpoint bounds and sqrt(v^2+p^2)>=|v| show the normalized minimum
margin cannot exceed max(Gamma_+,Gamma_-); the larger branch attains it.

At the saddle, the update Jacobian is
[[1-eta A_s,eta B_s],[eta B_s,1]],
where A_s=mean h_i(p_bar)^2/4<=A and B_s=mean h_i'(p_bar)/2 in (0,D/2].
Its determinant >=7/16 and det(DT-I)<0: one eigenvalue lies in (0,1),
the other exceeds 1. The analytic update map has a Jacobian determinant
not identically zero; the zero set is null. Away from that set its local
inverse maps preserve null sets. By a countable cover, preimages of null
sets are null. The local stable-manifold theorem and countably many iterated
preimages therefore give a null global stable set. Each escaping basin is
the union of preimages of its open good quadrant, hence open. This is the
same null-preimage argument detailed in proofs/003 and 005, not an assumption
that the GD map is globally invertible.

## Which locally optimal selections, and comparison with prior art

For p->+infinity only the largest signed c_ij can dominate; for p->-infinity
only the smallest can dominate. Because all zeta_i>0 these choices must be
consistent across examples. At finite p all weights are strictly positive,
so an interior token cannot become a hard selection. For a fixed v>0, the
maximum-token pattern is the only locally optimal feasible hard selection;
for fixed v<0 the minimum-token pattern is the only one. Both are stable
under joint training, by the open basins above. The minimum pattern can
nevertheless be inferior when comparing the two JOINT normalized margins.

Tarzanagh et al., 2306.13596, Definition 2 (PDF p.5) compares the chosen token
score only to its active SVM neighbors, with a FIXED head. Their Theorem 3
(PDF p.6) gives convergence from cones C_{mu,R} around such locally optimal
directions. It already includes a three-token illustration immediately after
the theorem. The present scalar result is not the discovery of that phenomenon:
it classifies the scalar joint-head basins and excludes mixed/interior hard
patterns in this stated geometry. General vector-valued three-token locally
optimal selections and their joint-head basins remain open here.

## Explicit distinct mixed-label witness

Take signed triples (3/2,1/4,-1/2) and (3/2,1/8,-1), with labels +1,-1.
Raw triples are (3/2,1/4,-1/2),(-3/2,-1/8,1); actual first-token queries
are 3/2,-3/2. Both zeta_i=3/2. H=3/2, D=75/8, eta_*=4/75.
Gamma_+=3/2 and Gamma_-=1/2. The conditions are strict and persist in an
open neighborhood of these data. This witness is illustrative; the theorem
covers the whole family above rather than just this isolated case.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the operator is compact on a Hilbert space","self-adjointness or normality is what the eigenbasis conclusion needs","for a general compact operator only the Riesz-Schauder conclusions and the singular value decomposition are available"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.573312+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, spectral theory of compact operators","id":"claim_ab876a6af8757c91d5eb78a56fd013d6691bfc416c7fa2ac4c3ae96614531a82","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators (an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, real eigenvalues tending to 0, ||T|| = max |eigenvalue|, min-max characterisation of eigenvalues) requires self-adjointness or at least normality. Compactness alone gives only the Riesz-Schauder picture: the nonzero spectrum consists of eigenvalues of finite algebraic multiplicity accumulating only at 0, and the set of such eigenvalues may be empty. The standard counterexample is the Volterra operator on L^2([0,1]), (V f)(x) = integral from 0 to x of f(t) dt, which is Hilbert-Schmidt (kernel k(x,t) = 1 for t < x, 0 otherwise) hence compact, but has no eigenvalues at all: V f = lambda f with lambda nonzero forces f to be absolutely continuous with f' = f/lambda and f(0) = 0, so f = 0; and V f = 0 forces f = 0 a.e. Thus sigma(V) = {0}, spectral radius 0, while ||V|| = 2/pi; the singular values of V are 1/((n + 1/2) pi), n >= 0, so V is Hilbert-Schmidt but not trace class, and the moduli of its eigenvalues (all zero) are nowhere near its singular values. Consequences for an auditor: (a) 'compact, so expand in eigenfunctions' is invalid without normality; the right substitute is the Schmidt decomposition in singular values, which always exists; (b) 'compact, so the spectral radius equals the norm' is false; (c) Rayleigh-quotient and min-max formulas for eigenvalues are statements about self-adjoint operators and become statements about singular values otherwise; (d) Mercer-type positivity conclusions require a self-adjoint positive kernel, not just an L^2 kernel.","status":"unverified"}

 p(B)=lambda*(m+2),
 p(T)=lambda*(4m-2),

Define g as the uniform coarsening of these groups:

 g(B atom)=lambda*(m+2)/(m+4)=q,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.627182+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_ac75738e8e3dabce1159fdd76643746f5142db1f8704a7114eee97125f9e99b8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A function f: [a, b] -> R has bounded variation if its total variation V(f; [a, b]) = sup over all partitions a = x_0 < x_1 < ... < x_n = b of sum_{i=1}^{n} |f(x_i) - f(x_{i-1})| is finite; the space of such functions is BV[a, b]. Facts (Jordan, Lebesgue): (1) f is of bounded variation if and only if f = g - h with g and h nondecreasing on [a, b] (Jordan decomposition; one may take g(x) = V(f; [a, x]), the variation function, and h = g - f, both nondecreasing); (2) a BV function is bounded, has one-sided limits at every point, has at most countably many discontinuities, all of them jumps, and is differentiable Lebesgue-almost everywhere with f' integrable and integral_a^b |f'(x)| dx <= V(f; [a, b]), with equality if and only if f is absolutely continuous; (3) monotone functions and Lipschitz functions are BV (a Lipschitz function with constant L has V <= L (b - a)), while a continuous function need not be: x sin(1/x) on (0, 1] (extended by 0) has infinite variation, and the Cantor function is continuous, nondecreasing, BV, yet has f' = 0 almost everywhere with total variation 1 (so it is not absolutely continuous); (4) BV[a, b] is a Banach space under ||f|| = |f(a)| + V(f; [a, b]); (5) f is BV exactly when the Riemann-Stieltjes integral integral_a^b g df exists for every continuous g, and then g -> integral g df is a bounded linear functional on C[a, b] of norm V(f; [a, b]) - the Riesz representation of the dual of C[a, b] (normalised BV functions correspond to finite signed Borel measures). In higher dimensions BV functions are those whose distributional gradient is a finite vector measure.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149510+00:00","domain":"elliptic regularity, L^p theory","id":"claim_ac7bfef65ba08df89da6d269b48b216132d2600e11e7ada5844f2602810376eb","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: in the Calderon-Zygmund theory for Lu = sum a^{ij}D_{ij}u + b.Du + cu the leading coefficients must be continuous (uniform continuity on the relevant compact set), or at least of vanishing mean oscillation; only then does the freezing-and-absorption step work for every 1 < p < infinity. Mere measurable uniform ellipticity is not enough, and the failure is not a technicality: both the estimate and uniqueness fail. Counterexample (Gilbarg-Serrin type): on the unit ball B_1 in R^n, n >= 2, fix lambda in (0,1) and set a^{ij}(x) = delta^{ij} + beta x_i x_j/|x|^2 with 1 + beta = (n-1)/(1 - lambda) > 0. These coefficients are bounded, symmetric, uniformly elliptic (eigenvalues 1 with multiplicity n-1 and (n-1)/(1-lambda)) and continuous except at the origin. For radial u, D_{ij}u = u''(r) x_i x_j/r^2 + (u'(r)/r)(delta_{ij} - x_i x_j/r^2), hence Lu = (1 + beta) u'' + (n-1) u'/r, and u(x) = |x|^lambda gives Lu = r^{lambda - 2} [ (1 + beta) lambda(lambda - 1) + (n-1) lambda ] = 0. Now w = |x|^lambda - 1 lies in W^{2,p}(B_1) for every p < n/(2 - lambda), lies in W^{1,p}_0(B_1) for those p, satisfies Lw = 0 almost everywhere, and is not identically zero (w(0) = -1). Consequences: the Dirichlet problem is not uniquely solvable in W^{2,p} intersect W^{1,p}_0 for p < n/(2 - lambda), so no global estimate ||w||_{W^{2,p}} <= C ||Lw||_{L^p} can hold there; the maximum principle also fails for such strong solutions (w attains its minimum -1 at an interior point while Lw = 0 and w = 0 on the boundary). Note n/(2 - lambda) < n and lambda may be taken as close to 1 as desired, so the failure reaches every exponent below n. What survives with only measurable coefficients: the Aleksandrov-Bakelman-Pucci estimate and Krylov-Safonov theory, both of which require the solution to be in W^{2,n}_loc - which is exactly the class this example escapes.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X a normed space; no completeness of X is needed","for metrizability and sequential compactness of the ball: X separable","Tychonoff (hence a form of the axiom of choice) in the general case"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752423+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_ad0f3a207b3c5379410429f086bcbbeb1babd7dfb64560bd3c03ab098d3b5d3e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a normed vector space over R or C. The closed unit ball B of the dual space X^* is COMPACT in the weak-* topology, that is the topology of pointwise convergence on X. Two refinements matter. (a) If X is SEPARABLE then the weak-* topology restricted to B is metrizable and B is weak-* SEQUENTIALLY compact, so bounded sequences of functionals have weak-* convergent subsequences; without separability compactness need not give sequential compactness. (b) The general theorem uses Tychonoff's theorem for a product of compact scalar discs and therefore, in ZF, is not provable without some choice; the separable case needs only a diagonal argument. The theorem does NOT say the ball is norm-compact: by Riesz's lemma the closed unit ball of a normed space is norm-compact if and only if the space is finite-dimensional. Nor does it say the ball of X itself is weakly compact - that characterises reflexivity (Kakutani). [standard; e.g. Rudin, Functional Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 3.15]","status":"unverified"}
