{"assumptions":["Omega is a compact metric space and T: Omega -> Omega is a homeomorphism","(Omega, T) is minimal","V: Omega -> R is continuous","H_omega is the discrete Schrodinger operator with potential n -> V(T^n omega) on l^2(Z) (equivalently, the continuum Schrodinger operator over a minimal flow)","E is a real energy","uniform hyperbolicity is understood with constants uniform over all of Omega"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.814897+00:00","domain":"spectral theory of ergodic Schrodinger operators, hyperbolic cocycles","id":"claim_ae02788a467b182215c0322bd89b1ed9531f9fb0c3a5dbf18d877ba74f12ef05","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (Omega, T) be a MINIMAL topological dynamical system, Omega a compact metric space and T a homeomorphism, and let V: Omega -> R be continuous. For each omega in Omega let H_omega be the discrete Schrodinger operator on l^2(Z) given by (H_omega u)(n) = u(n+1) + u(n-1) + V(T^n omega) u(n). By minimality the spectrum sigma(H_omega) is one and the same compact set Sigma contained in R for every omega. For an energy E in R define the Schrodinger cocycle (T, A^E) over (Omega,T), where A^E(omega) is the SL(2,R) matrix with rows (E - V(omega), -1) and (1, 0); its iterates are A^E_n(omega) = A^E(T^{n-1}omega) ... A^E(omega), and they transfer solutions of the difference equation u(n+1) + u(n-1) + V(T^n omega)u(n) = E u(n). The cocycle is UNIFORMLY HYPERBOLIC if there is a continuous T-invariant splitting R^2 = E^s(omega) + E^u(omega) and constants C > 0, lambda > 1 with ||A^E_n(omega)v|| <= C lambda^{-n}||v|| for v in E^s(omega) and ||A^E_{-n}(omega)v|| <= C lambda^{-n}||v|| for v in E^u(omega), for all n >= 0 and all omega; equivalently (for SL(2,R) cocycles over a compact base) ||A^E_n(omega)|| >= C lambda^n for all omega and all n >= 0. THEOREM (R. Johnson): E belongs to R \\ Sigma if and only if the cocycle (T, A^E) is uniformly hyperbolic. Equivalently, Sigma is exactly the set of real energies at which the Schrodinger cocycle fails to be uniformly hyperbolic. The same statement holds in the continuum setting for Schrodinger operators -u'' + V(T_t omega)u on the line with a minimal flow, which is Johnson's original formulation, and it is the standard dictionary between spectral theory and the dynamics of the transfer-matrix cocycle. SHARP EDGES. (a) UNIFORM hyperbolicity is far stronger than a positive Lyapunov exponent, and this is the single most often misused point. In the supercritical almost Mathieu operator, and more generally in the localisation regime, the Lyapunov exponent L(E) is positive at EVERY energy of the spectrum; those energies are in Sigma, so the cocycle there is non-uniformly hyperbolic. 'Positive exponent' therefore does NOT imply 'in the resolvent set'; only uniformity does. (b) Minimality of the base is used twice: to make sigma(H_omega) independent of omega, and to propagate the exponential dichotomy from one orbit to all of Omega. For a non-minimal base the spectrum can genuinely depend on omega and the statement must be reformulated (typically with the union of the spectra over the support of an ergodic measure, or over the whole base), so do not apply the equivalence verbatim outside minimality. (c) The theorem characterises the RESOLVENT set, which is open; correspondingly uniform hyperbolicity is an open condition in E and in the cocycle, whereas positivity of the Lyapunov exponent is not open. (d) The statement is for real E; for non-real E the operator is invertible anyway and the associated cocycle is not an SL(2,R) cocycle.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a topological space","f takes values in the extended reals (-infinity, +infinity]","for the liminf characterisation, X is first countable (e.g. metric)","for the attainment-of-the-infimum statement, X is compact","for the approximation by Lipschitz functions, X is metric and f is bounded below"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.814277+00:00","domain":"general topology, real analysis, calculus of variations","id":"claim_ae0d76cf084a3679aa5c60bc21a5f1aa5a7d55e81a31da780dbc20178aa9cae5","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a topological space and f: X -> (-infinity, +infinity] an extended-real function. f is lower semicontinuous (lsc) at a point x0 if for every real a < f(x0) there is a neighbourhood U of x0 with f(x) > a for all x in U. f is lsc on X iff any one of the following equivalent conditions holds: (i) the superlevel set {x : f(x) > a} is open for every real a; (ii) the sublevel set {x : f(x) <= a} is closed for every real a; (iii) the epigraph {(x,t) in X x R : t >= f(x)} is closed in X x R. If X is first countable (in particular metric), lower semicontinuity at x0 is equivalent to liminf_{x -> x0} f(x) >= f(x0). f is upper semicontinuous iff -f is lsc, and f is continuous iff it is both. Standard facts, each of which is the reason lsc is worth naming: (1) the pointwise SUPREMUM of an arbitrary family of lsc functions is lsc; (2) a sum of finitely many lsc functions is lsc provided no (+infinity) + (-infinity) occurs, and a nonnegative multiple of an lsc function is lsc; (3) a nondecreasing pointwise limit of continuous functions is lsc, and conversely on a METRIC space every lsc function bounded below is the pointwise nondecreasing limit of a sequence of Lipschitz functions (Baire); (4) the indicator 1_A is lsc iff A is open; (5) WEIERSTRASS FORM: if X is compact and f is lsc then f attains its infimum on X, because the sublevel sets {f <= a} are closed and have the finite intersection property. This is the form in which lsc is used in the direct method of the calculus of variations: coercivity plus lsc on a compact (or weakly compact) set yields a minimiser. SHARP EDGES, i.e. what is NOT true. (a) lsc buys you MINIMA only, never maxima: on the compact space [0,1] the function f(x) = x for x < 1, f(1) = 0 is lsc (every superlevel set {f > a} is (a,1) or [0,1] or empty), its supremum is 1 and it is not attained. (b) The supremum of lsc functions is lsc but the INFIMUM of infinitely many lsc functions need not be: on R the continuous functions f_n(x) = max(0, 1 - n|x|) have pointwise infimum the indicator of {0}, whose superlevel set {f > 1/2} = {0} is not open. (c) 'lsc at every point' is genuinely weaker than continuity; an lsc function may be discontinuous on a dense set. (d) Statement (3) uses metrizability of X; on a general topological space an lsc function need not be a pointwise limit of continuous functions (it is a supremum of continuous functions on compact Hausdorff or, more generally, normal spaces, by Urysohn/Katetov-Tong, but for arbitrary X no such representation is available). (e) In integration theory the useful instance is Fatou's lemma, which says exactly that f -> integral f is lsc along pointwise convergence of nonnegative measurable functions; no upper semicontinuity holds there without a domination hypothesis.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A is a square real matrix with nonnegative entries"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438555+00:00","domain":"linear algebra, nonnegative matrices","id":"claim_ae5c6a4cb8084ef24a18e45632bcc8943945094a5e71de887f9245aa6e393816","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A real $n \\times n$ matrix $A = (a_{ij})$ is nonnegative ($A \\ge 0$) if all entries are $\\ge 0$, and positive ($A > 0$) if all entries are $> 0$. Associate to $A \\ge 0$ the directed graph $G(A)$ on vertices $1, \\dots, n$ with an edge $i \\to j$ iff $a_{ij} > 0$; then $(A^m)_{ij} > 0$ iff there is a walk of length $m$ from $i$ to $j$. $A$ is irreducible if $G(A)$ is strongly connected (every vertex reaches every other), equivalently if there is no permutation matrix $P$ with $P A P^{\\mathsf T} = \\begin{pmatrix} B & C \\\\ 0 & D\\end{pmatrix}$ with $B, D$ square nonempty blocks, equivalently (for $n \\ge 2$) if $(I + A)^{n-1} > 0$; a $1 \\times 1$ matrix is irreducible by convention (some authors exclude the zero $1\\times1$ matrix). The period (index of imprimitivity) $h$ of an irreducible $A$ is the greatest common divisor of the lengths of all closed walks in $G(A)$; it does not depend on the vertex, and $h = 1$ iff $A$ is aperiodic. $A$ is primitive if $A \\ge 0$ and $A^m > 0$ for some $m \\ge 1$; for nonnegative matrices, primitive $\\iff$ irreducible and aperiodic, and then $A^m > 0$ for all $m \\ge (n-1)^2 + 1$ (Wielandt's bound). Every positive matrix is primitive. Warnings: irreducible does not imply primitive (the cyclic permutation matrix of an $n$-cycle is irreducible with period $n$); a matrix with a positive diagonal entry that is irreducible is automatically primitive; irreducibility is a property of the zero pattern only, not of the magnitudes; a matrix with some negative entries is outside this theory entirely.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space","every A_n and A is self-adjoint (so the resolvent set contains C minus R and the resolvent norm bound 1/|Im z| holds)","no relation between the domains of the A_n and of A is assumed","convergence is of the resolvents, applied to a fixed vector (strong) or in operator norm (norm)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090914+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, unbounded self-adjoint operators","id":"claim_aefd17250c9ea1190635da34d922379fe94928d2718e0131592cbabceafdf37c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A_n (n = 1, 2, ...) and A be self-adjoint operators on a Hilbert space H, each on its own dense domain; the domains are not assumed equal or even comparable. One says A_n -> A in the STRONG RESOLVENT SENSE if for every psi in H and every z in C with nonzero imaginary part, (A_n - z)^(-1) psi converges in norm to (A - z)^(-1) psi. Because each operator is self-adjoint, the resolvent (A_n - z)^(-1) is bounded with norm at most 1 / |Im z|, so the family is uniformly bounded and it is enough to verify the convergence for a SINGLE non-real z: one z in the upper half plane suffices, the conjugate point following by taking adjoints and the remaining z by the resolvent identity together with the uniform bound. The NORM RESOLVENT SENSE is the same statement with convergence in operator norm; it implies the strong resolvent sense and is strictly stronger. Practical criterion: if all the A_n and A are essentially self-adjoint on a common core D and A_n psi -> A psi for every psi in D, then A_n -> A in the strong resolvent sense. Without such a hypothesis convergence on a dense subspace says nothing, which is precisely why the resolvent formulation, and not naive pointwise convergence of unbounded operators, is the notion that interacts with the spectral theorem.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["real variable on [-1, 1] for the extremal statements; the polynomials themselves are defined on all of R and C"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479741+00:00","domain":"approximation theory","id":"claim_af2c306d13e82f8e10b1a499cd863744a70e37247652744c79e094c450f9b166","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"The Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind are defined on [-1, 1] by T_n(cos theta) = cos(n theta), n = 0, 1, 2, ...; equivalently T_0 = 1, T_1 = x and T_{n+1}(x) = 2 x T_n(x) - T_{n-1}(x). {"assumptions":["the Marchenko-Pastur-Silverstein setting (i.i.d. rows with finite twelfth moments in Ledoit-Wolf's statement), p/n -> c in (0, 1)","estimators restricted to the rotation-equivariant class (sample eigenvectors kept)","the identity making the two oracles' limits reciprocal is cited from the paper, not re-derived above"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T09:21:49.110177+00:00","domain":"covariance estimation / portfolio optimization","id":"claim_af6709ee5777434e2a0ecbeedc7d640c4e67e6b22be7b38c5f3187f98400f874","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $S = \\sum_i \\lambda_i u_i u_i^T$ be the sample covariance of $n$ observations in $\\mathbb{R}^p$ with population covariance $\\Sigma$, $p/n \\to c \\in (0, 1)$, in the setting of the Marchenko-Pastur-Silverstein theorem. Consider rotation-equivariant estimators $\\hat\\Sigma = \\sum_i d_i u_i u_i^T$ and the global minimum-variance portfolio $\\hat w = \\hat\\Sigma^{-1}\\mathbf{1}/(\\mathbf{1}^T\\hat\\Sigma^{-1}\\mathbf{1})$ built from them, scored by its true out-of-sample variance $\\hat w^T \\Sigma \\hat w$. Ledoit and Wolf (2017) show: (i) the finite-sample oracle for this loss is $d_i^{\\mathrm{mv}} = 1 / (u_i^T \\Sigma^{-1} u_i)$ (the 'inverse' oracle), whereas the Frobenius-loss oracle is $d_i^{\\mathrm{fro}} = u_i^T \\Sigma u_i$; (ii) in the large-dimensional limit both oracles converge to the SAME nonlinear shrinkage $\\tilde d_i = \\lambda_i / |1 - c - c\\lambda_i \\breve m_F(\\lambda_i)|^2$ (the Ledoit-Peche formula), because the Ledoit-Peche limits of the two quadratic forms $u_i^T\\Sigma u_i$ and $u_i^T\\Sigma^{-1}u_i$ are reciprocal to each other; so the nonlinear shrinkage estimator that is optimal for estimating the covariance in Frobenius loss is also asymptotically optimal for the minimum-variance portfolio - neither too much shrinkage (the linear shrinkage's) nor too little (the sample covariance's). {"assumptions":["i.i.d. nonnegative weights on Z^d, d >= 2","F(0) < p_c(d), so the time constant is a norm and the shape is bounded","E min{t_1^d, ..., t_{2d}^d} < infinity, equivalently E[Y^d] < infinity for Y the minimum of 2d independent copies of tau_e - and this condition is necessary, not just sufficient","no curvature, strict convexity or differentiability of B_nu is asserted; those are open"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542575+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_af7572591de074922b3c8bcd06ef7d3cfa5df7ed73222e70cd4667e68059f97c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Consider i.i.d. first-passage percolation on Z^d, d >= 2, with edge-weight law nu. Assume the two conditions (i) E min{ t_1^d, ..., t_{2d}^d } < infinity, where the t_i are 2d independent copies of tau_e - equivalently E[Y^d] < infinity where Y is the MINIMUM of 2d copies, the two being the same because x -> x^d is increasing on [0, infinity) - and (ii) F(0) < p_c(d). Let B(t) = {x : T(0, x) <= t}, the random ball. Then there is a DETERMINISTIC, convex, COMPACT set B_nu in R^d with NON-EMPTY INTERIOR, symmetric about the axes, such that for every eps > 0, P( (1-eps) B_nu is contained in B(t)/t which is contained in (1+eps) B_nu for all large t ) = 1. The set B_nu is the unit ball of the time constant. Condition (i) is NOT merely convenient: if it fails then for every C > 0 the sum over x of P(m(x) > C|x|) diverges, where m(x) is the minimum weight over the edges at x, and Borel-Cantelli forces T(0,x)/|x| > C for infinitely many x almost surely, so the shape statement itself fails. Condition (ii) is what keeps the shape bounded: if F(0) >= p_c then zero-weight edges percolate, the time constant vanishes and B_nu is all of R^d. What is NOT known, and is repeatedly imported elsewhere as an unproven hypothesis: whether the boundary of B_nu is STRICTLY CONVEX, whether it is DIFFERENTIABLE, and whether it has uniformly positive CURVATURE. Those are open for every non-degenerate weight distribution in every dimension, which is why the Newman-Piza exponent bounds and the directed-geodesic results carry non-constructive curvature or differentiability hypotheses. B_nu is not computed explicitly for any non-trivial F. [Cox and Durrett (1981), verified against Auffinger, Damron and Hanson, 50 Years of First-Passage Percolation, Section 2.2]","status":"unverified"}

Colour the edges of the complete graph on n vertices red or blue independently and uniformly at random. The expected number of monochromatic k-cliques is C(n,k) 2^{1 - C(k,2)}; when n = floor(2^{k/2}) this expectation is below 1 for k >= 3, so some colouring has no monochromatic k-clique, and R(k,k) > n. This is the first-moment method (a union bound over the C(n,k) cliques); only linearity of expectation is used, and no clique needs to be independent of another. With Stirling's formula the same count gives R(k,k) >= (1 + o(1)) (k / (e sqrt 2)) 2^{k/2}; the Lovasz local lemma (Spencer 1975) improves the constant to (1 + o(1)) (sqrt 2 / e) k 2^{k/2} and nothing better than the exponent k/2 is known. {"assumptions":["N>=5,d=2,K=3,r=2,ell=0,n=6; two A/S pairs and remaining known S contexts","Actual iid factual samples without tags; p uniform on contexts then true candidates; all A truth supports allowed","Each data-dependent generator robustly exact-level source-calibrated at zero in every compatible world","Conditional V(D) maximizes after data; global Gamma_N maximizes over a fixed world before data"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T21:04:18.141881+00:00","domain":"statistical learning; calibrated generation; global minimax and actual iid data","id":"claim_b06700a866ade064c72020029c1c0095e0197f769e2a689f4972776a20807bd5","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited), independent mathematical, priority and target-scope review pending. # A genuine zero-budget global averaging obstruction from repeated facts

T379-C020 v2, proof (unaudited), exact all-world checks PASS; audit pending.
Target 1, secondary target 2: auxiliary-route obstruction, not an exact
global frontier. This concerns actual iid training, not only an
artificial conditional posterior or a handpicked world.

## Experiment and objectives

Fix any N>=5. Set d=2,K=3,r=2,ell=0,n=6. There are two A/S pairs,
one A and one S each, and N-4 fixed S contexts. A has an arbitrary
uniform two-element truth support; S has all three truths. Source p
chooses contexts uniformly and then truths uniformly. Observe six
iid factual samples WITHOUT orientation labels or verifier information.
Require every data-dependent generator to have source Mis_infinity=0
in EVERY world compatible with its observed facts, at exact score bins.

For data D let V(D) be the conditional minimum over robustly calibrated
generators of their maximum compatible-world false mass. Let

 B_N=E_w[V(D)],
 Gamma_N=inf_policy max_fixed_world w E_w[H(policy(D))].

B_N is independent of the fixed actual world w: sibling permutations
and within-context candidate permutations map any world to any other,
preserve the model and compatibility, and carry source calibration,
false mass and V(D) with them. The data laws are carried along by the
same bijections. Thus V(D)'s distribution is identical in all worlds.

The candidate strict inequality is

 Gamma_N <= B_N-5/(1008*N^7) < B_N.                      (1)

No numerical value of B_N or Gamma_N is claimed. The point is that
expected conditional worst-world risk overstates global expected
minimax risk even at ZERO source calibration budget.

## Finite conditional selectors exist

There are finitely many actual worlds and finitely many score
partitions of the NK atoms. For a zero-calibrated g its score partition
Pi satisfies g=p_w,Pi for every compatible w, so a fixed Pi admits at
most one such g. Merging equal-score cells preserves this property.
The one-cell uniform generator is always feasible, so each V(D) is
attained among finitely many candidates. Choose any deterministic
conditional minimizer g*_D by a fixed tie rule. This selector is an
existence construction, not a claim of computational efficiency.
For every actual w it satisfies H_w(g*_D)<=V(D) pointwise.
Datasets incompatible with every source world may use the uniform
fallback; they have probability zero under every actual world.

## Observable rare event and its conditional value

Let E be the event that all six samples have this pattern:

* Four copies of ONE candidate in ONE context of one pair;
* one fact in each of the two contexts of the other pair;
* no other observations.

The pair roles, repeated context, candidate identities and sample
order are unrestricted. E is recognizable from the data alone.
Its known-truth counts are (1,0) in the repeated pair and (1,1) in
the other pair, all strictly below r=2. Thus C017's exact zero-budget
frontier, with pairwise minima 0 and 1, gives

 V(D)=1/(3N)+7/(24N)=5/(8N) on E.                        (2)

For clarity, the (1,0) pair's zero-calibrated bins must contain whole
contexts: support swaps make each uncertified set constant-score and
orientation invariance with the zero-known sibling leaves no known
truths available to peel from that context. Forgetting the repeated
fact therefore preserves all source-bin and false-count information.
The resulting balanced (0,0)/(1,1) game has artificial mean densities
1/(3N),7/(24N) on its residual groups, with false risks 1/6,1/4;
safe densities are higher. The per-bin low-density tail argument
gives the lower value (2), and the invariant-group mean attains it
worldwise. This is a conditional worst-world assertion, not an
actual-orientation posterior calculation.

## A causal calibrated generator on E

Let x be the observed four-repeat context. Let a,b be the two contexts
of the other pair and let their single observed candidates be c_a,c_b.
Form B from ALL THREE atoms of x plus the four atoms of a,b other
than c_a,c_b. Its source mass is 1/N+7/(6N)=13/(6N) in every
compatible world; its seven atoms get score q=13/(42N).
Give the two observed atoms in a,b score 5/(12N). Give every other
atom score lambda=1/(3N), including the untouched sibling of x and
all fixed S contexts. The group masses sum to one. All source group
masses are invariant across orientations and supports, so exact-score
mergers preserve source Mis_infinity=0. The rule uses observed context
counts and observed truths only; it never reads the hidden orientation.

If x is actually A, false mass is H_A=2q=13/(21N).
If x is actually S, false mass is H_S=q+lambda=9/(14N).
These identities hold for every compatible truth-support choice.

## Fixed-world event probabilities, not a posterior shortcut

In ANY fixed actual world, summing over the repeated candidate
identity gives repeated-four-fact weights proportional to

 r*(1/(Nr))^4=1/(N^4*r^3) for the A context,
 K*(1/(NK))^4=1/(N^4*K^3) for the S context.

Consequently, conditional on E, the repeated context is actually A
with probability K^3/(K^3+r^3)=27/35, uniformly in every fixed world.
The exponent is THREE, not four: the number of available true
candidate identities must be included. The other pair's one sample
per context contributes 1/N^2 after its identities are summed out.

There are two choices of repeated pair and 6!/(4!1!1!)=30 orders.
Thus in every fixed world

 P_w(E)=60/N^6*(1/8+1/27)=175/(18N^6),                  (3)
 E_w[H_pool|E]=(27/35)*13/(21N)+(8/35)*9/(14N)
             =153/(245N),
 V(E)-E_w[H_pool|E]=1/(1960N).                           (4)

These are ordinary disjoint-event sums under the fixed sampling law;
no independence of learned events or hidden labels is assumed.

## Global policy and strict separation

Use the explicit pooling generator on E and g*_D otherwise. Every
outcome is robustly zero-calibrated. For every fixed actual world,

 E_w H <= E_w[1_{not E}V(D)]+P_w(E)*153/(245N)
       =B_N-P_w(E)/(1960N)
       =B_N-5/(1008N^7).

Taking the maximum over w proves (1). At N=5 the exact strict gap
certified by this construction is 1/15750000. This is an upper bound
on Gamma_N relative to B_N, not an exact value for either objective.

The result complements C014's positive-budget example and C015's
single-outcome pointwise control. Here the improvement is realized
under actual iid data, uniformly for EVERY fixed world, at zero
budget. A global expected lower bound must therefore use a valid
fixed-prior/per-world argument rather than average conditional maxima.

{"assumptions":["H must be convex and superlinear for the Hopf-Lax (Lax-Oleinik) representation with L = H*","The Hopf formula requires convex initial datum g instead, with H merely continuous","Counterexample: H(p) = (p^2-1)^2, g(x) = x/2, where Hopf-Lax returns the solution for H** and misses the flux by H(1/2) - H**(1/2) = 9/16"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418414+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: Hamilton-Jacobi equations","id":"claim_b153eb3a5fb04c6f5b11975f8d220003ec053be109078039e18bb58d9896bdc1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: in u(x,t) = min_y ( t L((x-y)/t) + g(y) ) with L = H*, the Hamiltonian H must be CONVEX (and superlinear). For a nonconvex H the formula does not solve u_t + H(Du) = 0: since H* = (H**)*, the formula reproduces the equation with H replaced by its convex envelope H**. Counterexample (n = 1): H(p) = (p^2 - 1)^2 is continuous and superlinear but not convex, and H**(p) = 0 for |p| ≤ 1, H**(p) = H(p) for |p| ≥ 1. Take the Lipschitz datum g(x) = x/2. The true solution is the classical (hence viscosity) solution u(x,t) = x/2 - t H(1/2) = x/2 - (9/16) t. The Hopf-Lax expression gives min_y ( tL((x-y)/t) + y/2 ) = x/2 - t L*(1/2) = x/2 - t H**(1/2) = x/2, which satisfies u_t + H(u_x) = 0 + (1/4 - 1)^2 = 9/16 ≠ 0 at EVERY point — it is not even an almost-everywhere solution. The correct nonconvex counterpart is the Hopf formula u(x,t) = sup_p ( x·p - t H(p) - g*(p) ), valid for continuous H when the DATUM g is convex; for nonconvex H and general Lipschitz g there is no closed formula and one works with viscosity solutions directly. Auditor's check: whenever a proof writes a value function / Hopf-Lax representation, confirm convexity (of H for Hopf-Lax, of g for Hopf) before trusting it; the corresponding control interpretation (L as a running cost) also fails without convexity.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-14T12:08:18+00:00","domain":"probability / combinatorics (sharp Rademacher singularity campaign)","id":"claim_b1866ba9ebe77b0039db98d4a1b0706e55d081a0b85c4c05bb355f88250fc4db","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Lemma (campaign status: proved): Let $n\\ge3$, let $u_1,\\dots,u_n$ be the standard basis of $\\mathbb F_2^n$, and take indices cyclically ($u_{n+1}=u_1$). Put $\\mathcal S_n=\\{0\\}\\cup\\{u_i:1\\le i\\le n\\}\\cup\\{u_i+u_{i+1}:1\\le i\\le n\\}\\subseteq\\mathbb F_2^n$, a set of $2n+1$ vectors. For every subspace $W\\le\\mathbb F_2^n$ of dimension $w$, the number of cosets of $W$ that meet $\\mathcal S_n$ satisfies $\\boxed{|\\mathcal S_n/W|\\ge2n+1-3w}$ (tag 36). Neither hypothesis can be dropped: for $n=2$ the two cycle edges give the same vector $u_1+u_2$ and $|\\mathcal S_2|=4<5$, for $n=1$ one has $u_1+u_1=0$ and $|\\mathcal S_1|=2<3$ (both at $W=0$), and with path indices ($1\\le i\\le n-1$) $|\\mathcal S_n|=2n<2n+1$ at $W=0$ for every $n$. Transfer to real residuals (tag 37): let $e_0,\\dots,e_n$ be the standard basis of $\\mathbb R^{n+1}$ and $D_n=\\{A,B_i,C_i:i\\in\\mathbb Z/n\\mathbb Z\\}$ with $A=e_0$, $B_i=e_i$, $C_i=e_0+e_i+e_{i+1}$. For a real residual subspace $R\\le\\mathbb R^{n+1}$ of dimension $d$ (in the source, a signed-difference residual), let $k_{D_n}(R)$ be the number of signed projective classes that $R$ induces on $D_n$: two members $f,g$ lie in one class when $f\\equiv\\pm g\\pmod R$, and the members lying in $R$ form one zero class, counted once if it occurs. Replace $R$ by the rational span $R_0\\subseteq R$ of its actual class witnesses (the members of $D_n$ in the zero class and the differences $f-\\sigma g\\in R$, $\\sigma=\\pm1$, that witness a class equality), so that $d_0=\\dim R_0\\le d$ and $R_0$ induces the same classes, and reduce the saturated lattice $\\Lambda=R_0\\cap\\mathbb Z^{n+1}$ modulo two to $\\overline\\Lambda\\le\\mathbb F_2^{n+1}$, $\\dim\\overline\\Lambda=d_0$; signed equality becomes ordinary coset equality. Translating the binary reductions by $A$ sends $A\\mapsto0$, $B_i\\mapsto u_i'$, $C_i\\mapsto u_i'+u_{i+1}'$, where $u_i'=e_0+e_i$ ($1\\le i\\le n$) form a basis of the even-weight hyperplane $E\\le\\mathbb F_2^{n+1}$, and two translated members lie in one $\\overline\\Lambda$-coset exactly when their difference lies in $W=\\overline\\Lambda\\cap E$, $\\dim W\\le d_0$. Identifying $E$ with $\\mathbb F_2^n$ through the basis $u_i'$, (36) gives $k_{D_n}(R)\\ge|\\mathcal S_n/W|\\ge2n+1-3d_0\\ge2n+1-3d$ (tag 37). Notes: Proof of (36): the images $u_i+W$ span $\\mathbb F_2^n/W$, which has dimension $n-w$, so some $n-w$ of them, indexed by $Q$, form a quotient basis, and zero and these $n-w$ singleton images are distinct cosets. For $n\\ge3$ the cycle $C_n$ is a simple graph in which every vertex has degree two, so removing the other $w$ cycle vertices destroys at most $2w$ cycle edges and at least $n-2w$ edges keep both endpoints in $Q$; their images are sums of two distinct basis vectors, hence distinct from each other, from zero and from the singleton images. This gives $1+(n-w)+(n-2w)=2n+1-3w$ occupied cosets when $w\\le n/2$; when $w\\ge n/2$ the first two terms alone give $1+n-w\\ge2n+1-3w$. The coefficient 3 is exact: for $w\\le n/2$, $W=\\langle u_j:j\\in P\\rangle$ with $P$ a set of $w$ pairwise non-adjacent cycle vertices meets exactly $2n+1-3w$ cosets. The source states the lemma under its standing assumption $n\\ge4$; the proof needs only $n\\ge3$. {"assumptions":["X is a real random variable","E[X^2] < infinity","a > 0"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T04:51:55.036210+00:00","domain":"real random variables with finite variance","id":"claim_b1909fbdc8598cb9caebc1fdbbcb39a4039fb8630ed1ebe942721471c698c2dd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a real random variable with mean mu and finite variance sigma^2. For every a > 0, P(X - mu >= a) <= sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + a^2), and by symmetry P(X - mu <= -a) <= sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + a^2). For sigma^2 > 0 this is strictly smaller than the bound min(1, sigma^2 / a^2) that Chebyshev's inequality gives for the one-sided tail; at sigma^2 = 0 both are 0. The bound is attained for every sigma^2 > 0 and a > 0: the law that puts mass sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + a^2) at mu + a and mass a^2 / (sigma^2 + a^2) at mu - sigma^2 / a has mean mu, variance sigma^2 and P(X - mu >= a) = sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + a^2).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Omega is bounded and open in R^n","L is locally uniformly elliptic: a^{ij} symmetric with a^{ij} xi_i xi_j >= lambda(x)|xi|^2, lambda(x) > 0 in Omega","|b^i|/lambda is bounded on Omega","c <= 0 in Omega (identically 0 for the sharper form (i))","u is in C^2(Omega) and continuous up to the closure of Omega","the differential inequality L u >= 0 holds pointwise in Omega"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.396277+00:00","domain":"elliptic PDE, maximum principles","id":"claim_b1af22df20531351edcba66ebf511db40a02c503c0d643a4140f3798e72e41d2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega be a BOUNDED open subset of R^n and let L u = a^{ij}(x) D_{ij} u + b^i(x) D_i u + c(x) u with a^{ij} = a^{ji}, L locally uniformly elliptic in the sense that a^{ij}(x) xi_i xi_j >= lambda(x)|xi|^2 with lambda(x) > 0 for every x in Omega, and with |b^i(x)|/lambda(x) bounded on Omega. Let u be in C^2(Omega) intersect C^0(closure of Omega). (i) If c is identically 0 and L u >= 0 in Omega, then max over the closure of u = max over the boundary of u (and if L u <= 0, min over the closure = min over the boundary). (ii) If c <= 0 in Omega and L u >= 0 in Omega, then max over the closure of u <= max over the boundary of u^+, where u^+ = max(u, 0); if L u <= 0 then min over the closure of u >= -max over the boundary of u^-. (iii) If c <= 0 and L u = 0, then max over the closure of |u| = max over the boundary of |u|. Nothing is assumed about continuity of the coefficients, and no sign condition is placed on a^{ij} beyond positive definiteness. WHERE IT FAILS: (a) the sign condition c <= 0 cannot be dropped - on Omega = (0,pi) x (0,pi) the function u(x_1,x_2) = sin(x_1) sin(x_2) satisfies Laplacian(u) + 2u = 0 (so c = 2 > 0), vanishes on the whole boundary and is strictly positive inside; (b) with c <= 0 but not identically 0 the positive part in (ii) is necessary: on Omega = (0,1) with L = d^2/dx^2 - k^2 the function u(x) = -cosh(k(x - 1/2))/cosh(k/2) solves L u = 0, equals -1 at both endpoints and equals -1/cosh(k/2) > -1 at the midpoint, so max over Omega of u strictly exceeds max over the boundary of u, while remaining below max of u^+ = 0; (c) boundedness of Omega cannot be dropped - u(x) = x_n is harmonic on the half-space {x_n > 0}, vanishes on its boundary and is unbounded above; on unbounded domains one needs a Phragmen-Lindelof growth restriction; (d) |b|/lambda must be bounded and lambda > 0 - degenerate ellipticity or unbounded drift relative to lambda destroys the auxiliary-function step. {"assumptions":["members fitted on training rows only; calibration and evaluation rows are disjoint subsets of the test rows","paired comparisons cell by cell; small-calibration arms use the same subsample draws for every estimator"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T09:17:06.630206+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning","id":"claim_b1af80c830980c68889b9acac6f530d6836b4a70edf57875df3cb64a911900ce","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Measured 2026-09-05 on two stacking pools with the same protocol (test rows split 40/60 by a fixed permutation into calibration and evaluation, per-sample relative $L_2$ metric, paired gains): EMIT (10 seeds x 4 components = 40 cells; 23 members, 285 outputs, 932 calibration rows) and OCO-2 (10 seeds x 3 bands = 30 cells; 18 members, 40 outputs, 800 rows). {"assumptions":["L is a vector lattice of real-valued (finite everywhere) functions on a set X","Stone's condition: f in L implies min(f,1) in L","I : L -> R is linear","I is positive: f >= 0 implies I(f) >= 0","Daniell continuity: f_n in L with f_n decreasing pointwise to 0 implies I(f_n) -> 0","for the uniqueness clause only: there are f_n in L increasing pointwise to the constant 1","no topology on X is assumed, and no regularity of the resulting measure is claimed"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090141+00:00","domain":"measure theory, integration, representation of positive functionals","id":"claim_b330fea79f8371289214536b62fd4e02f8348d302f06b862ea12c798689edb94","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a nonempty set and let L be a vector lattice of real-valued functions on X: L is a real vector space of functions X -> R, and f, g in L implies max(f,g) and min(f,g) are in L. Assume STONE'S CONDITION: f in L implies min(f, 1) in L. Let I : L -> R satisfy (i) linearity; (ii) positivity: f >= 0 pointwise implies I(f) >= 0 (equivalently f <= g implies I(f) <= I(g)); (iii) the DANIELL CONTINUITY CONDITION: whenever f_n in L decrease pointwise to 0 at every point of X, I(f_n) -> 0. Granted (i) and (ii), condition (iii) is equivalent to: f_n in L increasing pointwise to f with f in L implies I(f_n) -> I(f). CONCLUSION (Daniell-Stone): there is a measure mu on sigma(L), the smallest sigma-algebra on X making every member of L measurable, such that every f in L is mu-integrable and I(f) equals the integral of f with respect to mu. If moreover there exist f_n in L increasing pointwise to the constant function 1 (an exhaustion, i.e. sigma-finiteness along L), then mu is unique on sigma(L). WHERE IT FAILS: (a) condition (iii) is the whole content and cannot be dropped. On X = (0,1] take L to be the set of restrictions to (0,1] of the continuous functions on the closed interval [0,1] - a vector lattice satisfying Stone's condition - and let I(f) be the limit of f(x) as x decreases to 0, which exists for every member of L. This I is linear and positive, but f_n(x) = max(0, 1 - n x) lies in L and decreases pointwise to 0 on (0,1] while I(f_n) = 1 for every n, and I is not integration against any Borel measure on (0,1]: the 'missing' representing measure is a unit mass at the point 0, which does not lie in the space. A positive linear functional on a lattice always yields a finitely additive set function; (iii) is exactly what upgrades finite additivity to countable additivity. (b) Stone's condition is what manufactures indicator functions: for f in L and c > 0 the functions min(n (f - c)^+, 1) lie in L and increase pointwise to the indicator of {f > c}, which is how the measure of a generating set is defined. Without it one still gets a representation, but on a lattice of sets rather than on a sigma-algebra. (c) Without the exhaustion hypothesis uniqueness can fail: sets that no member of L 'sees' are unconstrained. Example: X = {p} union (0,1] with L the continuous compactly supported functions on (0,1] extended by the value 0 at p; then {p} lies in sigma(L) but its measure may be chosen freely without changing any I(f). (d) The theorem produces a measure on sigma(L) only; regularity (inner or outer) of mu is NOT part of the conclusion and needs topological hypotheses, which is where Riesz-Markov-Kakutani differs from Daniell-Stone.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T is measurable with respect to Σ","invariance is defined through preimages T⁻¹(E), not images T(E)"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.110366+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, measure-preserving dynamics","id":"claim_b37bfdbafedccacf12edc1ee9bd940c9966158655c818a0c9f8f9b11bdc70a19","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, Σ) be a measurable space and T: X → X a measurable map (T⁻¹(E) ∈ Σ for every E ∈ Σ). A measure μ on Σ is T-invariant (equivalently: T preserves μ, or T is a measure-preserving transformation of (X, Σ, μ)) if μ(T⁻¹(E)) = μ(E) for every E ∈ Σ, i.e. the push-forward T_*μ := μ∘T⁻¹ equals μ. Equivalent formulation for a finite measure: ∫ f∘T dμ = ∫ f dμ for every bounded measurable f; when X is a compact metrizable space with its Borel σ-algebra and T is continuous, it suffices to test f ∈ C(X), because finite Borel measures on such a space are determined by their integrals against continuous functions. Note the direction: invariance is stated with the PREIMAGE T⁻¹(E), not the image T(E); for non-injective T the image condition μ(T(E)) = μ(E) is a different (and generally false) statement, e.g. the doubling map x ↦ 2x mod 1 preserves Lebesgue measure but doubles the length of short intervals. For a flow (φ_t)_{t∈ℝ} invariance means φ_t*μ = μ for every t.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["γ is a continuous closed curve in ℂ","z₀ does not lie on the image of γ"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.110598+00:00","domain":"algebraic topology, complex analysis","id":"claim_b3a02e8f0726857a802fa42855fcd7acf8b442a81228e97aa6f877a727c5c99f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let γ: [a,b] → ℂ be a continuous closed curve (γ(a) = γ(b)) and let z₀ ∈ ℂ be a point NOT on the curve, z₀ ∉ γ([a,b]). Because γ(t) − z₀ never vanishes, there is a continuous function θ: [a,b] → ℝ (a continuous choice of argument) with γ(t) − z₀ = |γ(t) − z₀| e^{iθ(t)}; θ is unique up to adding a constant integer multiple of 2π. The winding number of γ about z₀ is n(γ, z₀) := (θ(b) − θ(a)) / (2π). It is an integer (since γ(b) = γ(a) forces θ(b) − θ(a) ∈ 2πℤ) and does not depend on the choice of θ. For piecewise C¹ curves it equals the contour integral (1/2πi) ∮_γ dz/(z − z₀). Basic properties: z₀ ↦ n(γ, z₀) is constant on each connected component of ℂ \\ γ([a,b]) and equals 0 on the unbounded component; it is additive under concatenation of closed curves at a common point and changes sign when the orientation of γ is reversed; it is invariant under homotopies of closed curves that avoid z₀ (see the classification theorem). SUDAKOV-FERNIQUE: if E[(X_s - X_t)^2] <= E[(Y_s - Y_t)^2] for all s, t in T, then E[ sup_t X_t ] <= E[ sup_t Y_t ]. Note that only the increment variances are compared and the individual variances may differ; the conclusion is about EXPECTED suprema only. SLEPIAN: if in addition E[X_t^2] = E[Y_t^2] for every t - so that the increment comparison is equivalent to E[X_s X_t] >= E[Y_s Y_t] for all s, t - then the stronger distributional conclusion P( sup_t X_t >= u ) <= P( sup_t Y_t >= u ) holds for every u, and indeed the whole joint law is stochastically ordered coordinatewise. Slepian's extra hypothesis of equal variances is not decorative: without it the distributional conclusion is false, while the Sudakov-Fernique conclusion about expectations survives. Both require CENTRED and GAUSSIAN; there is no comparable general statement for non-Gaussian processes. The finite index set is a convenience; both extend to separable processes by approximation. [Slepian (1962), Sudakov (1971), Fernique (1975); see Adler and Taylor, Random Fields and Geometry, Chapter 2, or Boucheron-Lugosi-Massart Section 13.3]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["d >= 3, G connected and d-regular (bipartite graphs have lambda_n = -d, which is excluded from the Ramanujan condition together with +d)","the Alon-Boppana bound is asymptotic in n for fixed d","existence results are cited, not proved"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T15:17:03.041240+00:00","domain":"spectral graph theory","id":"claim_b4cff0d243e113602094a9e01462d26887e25896b93bb86c6b28ac1795f048d4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let G be a connected d-regular graph on n vertices with adjacency eigenvalues d = lambda_1 >= lambda_2 >= ... >= lambda_n >= -d. G is Ramanujan if every eigenvalue other than +-d satisfies |lambda| <= 2 sqrt(d - 1); the number 2 sqrt(d-1) is the spectral radius of the infinite d-regular tree. Alon-Boppana theorem: for every fixed d >= 3 and every epsilon > 0, every d-regular graph with sufficiently many vertices has lambda_2 >= 2 sqrt(d - 1) - epsilon; more precisely lambda_2 >= 2 sqrt(d-1) (1 - O(1/ log^2 n)) (Friedman; Nilli). So Ramanujan graphs are the best possible spectral expanders. Existence: Lubotzky, Phillips and Sarnak (1988) and independently Margulis constructed explicit infinite families of (p+1)-regular Ramanujan graphs for every prime p congruent to 1 mod 4 (Cayley graphs of PSL(2, Z/qZ) or PGL(2, Z/qZ) according to the Legendre symbol of p modulo q, the eigenvalue bound coming from the Ramanujan-Petersson conjecture for modular forms proved by Deligne), later extended to all prime powers (Morgenstern 1994); Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava proved by the method of interlacing families, non-constructively, that infinite families of bipartite Ramanujan graphs of every degree d >= 3 exist (Ann. Math. 2015, via 2-lifts) and then that bipartite Ramanujan graphs of every degree exist on every even number of vertices (interlacing families IV, 2018); Friedman (2008) proved Alon's conjecture that a random d-regular graph is nearly Ramanujan, lambda_2 <= 2 sqrt(d-1) + epsilon with high probability, and Bordenave (2020) gave a shorter proof. Ramanujan graphs give the optimal expander mixing lemma constant and near-optimal derandomisation gadgets.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H: R^n → R is finite everywhere and convex (hence continuous)","H is superlinear: H(p)/|p| → ∞ as |p| → ∞","for part (iv): H ∈ C^2 and D^2H ≥ θI with θ > 0 (which already implies superlinearity)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.415976+00:00","domain":"convex analysis for Hamilton-Jacobi equations","id":"claim_b547a366acd0d9caa05bd0fd6c74e4b7c9b6d81ddd9e55157d9fc2c6927f0355","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H: R^n → R be convex and superlinear, i.e. H(p)/|p| → +∞ as |p| → ∞. Then: (i) the supremum is attained for every q, and L is finite, convex and superlinear; (ii) L* = H, i.e. H(p) = sup_q ( p·q - L(q) ) (duality of H and L); (iii) Fenchel-Young: p·q ≤ H(p) + L(q) for all p,q, with equality iff q ∈ ∂H(p) iff p ∈ ∂L(q); (iv) if in addition H ∈ C^2 with D^2H(p) ≥ θ I for all p and some θ > 0, then DH: R^n → R^n is a bijection, L ∈ C^1, DL = (DH)^{-1}, DL is Lipschitz with constant 1/θ, and consequently L(q+w) + L(q-w) - 2L(q) ≤ |w|^2/θ for all q,w.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the walk is on the incipient infinite cluster or a similarly statistically self-similar critical random graph","a known or boundable volume-growth exponent d_f for balls in the cluster","a known or boundable effective-resistance-growth exponent reflecting the bottleneck/dangling-end structure","typically also requires the cluster's law to have appropriate scale-invariance, or at least comparable behavior across scales"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.993751+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b5e3fa35e1a6d931ebdc3e155642b0dc3bd61f17553d02dc415ed8ee523ff71e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For simple random walk on the incipient infinite cluster of critical percolation, or more generally on critical random media with anomalous volume growth, Kesten's argument establishes subdiffusive behavior, that the walk's typical displacement after n steps scales as n^{1/(2+theta)} for some theta>0 rather than the diffusive n^{1/2}, by combining a volume-growth estimate showing balls of radius r typically contain of order r^{d_f} points, with d_f the fractal (volume) dimension of the cluster, and an effective-resistance estimate showing R_eff(0, B(0,r)^c) grows faster than linearly, of order r^{1+theta}, reflecting the long dangling ends and low-conductance bottlenecks characteristic of the critical cluster. Combining volume growth and resistance growth via the Nash/heat-kernel machinery, or a direct expected-exit-time computation, gives the subdiffusive exponent. The argument does not give the exact value of the subdiffusivity exponent in most dimensions, only bounds, with the precise exponent known rigorously only in specific settings such as sufficiently high dimension or tree-like/hierarchical models, and it is specific to critical (not subcritical or supercritical) percolation geometry, where the fractal, tree-like structure with many bottlenecks is essential to the argument. Typical failure: Assuming the subdiffusivity exponent established for one setting, such as high-dimensional or tree-based incipient infinite clusters where exact computation is possible, transfers to two-dimensional critical percolation, where the exact random-walk dimension remains a major open problem; volume-growth and resistance-growth exponents are model- and dimension-specific quantities that must be independently estimated rather than imported across models with superficially similar critical geometry. Canonical reference: Kesten, 1986, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare, Probabilites et Statistiques; Barlow, Jarai, Kumagai and Slade, 2008, Communications in Mathematical Physics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["1 ≤ p < ∞","Ω = R^n, or Ω bounded open with Lipschitz boundary (an extension domain); for W^{1,p}_0 any open Ω","compactness statements require Ω bounded"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492521+00:00","domain":"Sobolev spaces, embedding theorems, compactness","id":"claim_b6b2ca78bf6d58de47692329336d31951c68502f00143a7631b268179675e75b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let n ≥ 1, 1 ≤ p < ∞, and let Ω ⊂ R^n be either all of R^n or a bounded open set with Lipschitz boundary (more generally a bounded W^{1,p}-extension domain). For p < n write p* = np/(n − p) (Sobolev conjugate, 1/p* = 1/p − 1/n).

(i) Subcritical case p < n (Gagliardo–Nirenberg–Sobolev). W^{1,p}(Ω) ↪ L^{p*}(Ω) continuously. On R^n one has the scale-invariant form ||u||_{L^{p*}(R^n)} ≤ C(n,p) ||∇u||_{L^p(R^n)} for every u ∈ W^{1,p}(R^n). For bounded Ω, W^{1,p}(Ω) ↪ L^q(Ω) for every 1 ≤ q ≤ p*, and the embedding is COMPACT for every q < p* (Rellich–Kondrachov), but not for q = p*.

(ii) Critical case p = n ≥ 2. W^{1,n}(Ω) ↪ L^q(Ω) for every q ∈ [1, ∞), compactly when Ω is bounded, but W^{1,n}(Ω) is NOT contained in L^∞(Ω): in the unit disc of R^2, u(x) = log log(1 + 1/|x|) belongs to W^{1,2} and is unbounded. (For n = 1, W^{1,1} on an interval consists of absolutely continuous functions and does embed into the continuous functions.)

(iii) Supercritical case p > n (Morrey). W^{1,p}(Ω) ↪ C^{0,γ}(Ω̄) with γ = 1 − n/p: every u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω) has a representative that is Hölder continuous with exponent γ, and ||u||_{C^{0,γ}(Ω̄)} ≤ C ||u||_{W^{1,p}(Ω)}. For bounded Ω the embedding into C^{0,β}(Ω̄) is compact for every β < γ, in particular into C(Ω̄).

(iv) Higher order, Ω bounded Lipschitz, k ≥ 1. If kp < n then W^{k,p}(Ω) ↪ L^q(Ω) with 1/q = 1/p − k/n, compactly into L^r for r < q. If kp > n then W^{k,p}(Ω) ↪ C^{k − ⌊n/p⌋ − 1, γ}(Ω̄), where γ = ⌊n/p⌋ + 1 − n/p when n/p is not an integer, and γ is any number in (0,1) when n/p is an integer.

(v) Zero boundary values. Every statement holds for W^{1,p}_0(Ω) (resp. W^{k,p}_0) on an ARBITRARY open set Ω, bounded for the compactness claims, with no regularity of ∂Ω, because such functions extend by zero to W^{1,p}(R^n).

Where it fails. Without an extension property (Lipschitz or comparable boundary) the embedding W^{1,p}(Ω) ↪ L^{p*}(Ω) can fail for bounded Ω: there are bounded domains with a sufficiently sharp outward cusp on which it is false. Compactness fails at the critical exponent q = p* (the rescaled bubbles u_λ(x) = λ^{(n−p)/p} u(λx) keep constant L^{p*} norm and W^{1,p} seminorm but converge weakly to 0) and fails on unbounded domains such as R^n (translates of one bump). The inequality ||u||_{L^q(R^n)} ≤ C||∇u||_{L^p(R^n)} is FALSE for every q ≠ p*: dilation invariance forces q = p*. W^{1,n} ↪ L^∞ fails for n ≥ 2 as shown. The Hölder exponent in (iii) cannot be improved beyond 1 − n/p in general.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["independent (product) probability measure on the input coordinates","f is a bounded, typically boolean, function of finitely many coordinates","existence of a randomized decision tree computing f exactly, with well-defined per-coordinate revealments","revealments computed under the same measure used for Var(f) and Inf_i(f)"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.972746+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b71abce6cf84475d6e6984b0c6a4d7ee2a29f331d669301354889ab502d006c7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Let f: {0,1}^n -> {0,1} be evaluated exactly by a randomized decision-tree algorithm T that, over its internal randomness, queries coordinate i with probability delta_i(T) (its revealment), and let Var(f) denote the variance of f under a product probability measure on the input. The OSSS inequality states Var(f) <= sum_{i=1}^n delta_i(T) Inf_i(f), where Inf_i(f) is the influence of coordinate i under the same measure. Consequently, exhibiting an algorithm with small maximal revealment forces the sum of influences to be large, giving lower bounds on total influence and noise sensitivity via algorithmic constructions; for critical planar percolation, an exploration-path algorithm gives revealments comparable to arm-event probabilities, and combined with quasi-multiplicativity this yields sharp bounds on noise sensitivity and, via the Duminil-Copin-Raoufi-Tassion route, on sharpness of the phase transition in all dimensions without reflection positivity or duality. The inequality does not directly compute Inf_i itself, does not apply to non-product (dependent-coordinate) measures without a separate generalization, and it is an inequality rather than an identity, so it can be loose or even vacuous if the algorithm chosen is not well matched to f's structure. Typical failure: Plugging in a naive, non-adaptive algorithm (e.g. querying coordinates in a fixed deterministic order) and expecting a sharp bound; the inequality is only informative when the algorithm is cleverly matched to the function's geometric structure, such as an exploration process for a crossing event, and a poorly chosen algorithm produces a valid but essentially vacuous bound that is easy to mistake for a genuine obstruction to sharper influence or sensitivity estimates. Canonical reference: O'Donnell, Saks, Schramm and Servedio, 2005, Proceedings of the 46th Annual IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science; Duminil-Copin, Raoufi and Tassion, 2019, Annals of Mathematics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_1, ..., X_n independent (arbitrary measurable state spaces, not necessarily identically distributed)","E[Z^2] < infinity","X_i' an independent copy of X_i"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T04:29:00.269210+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b7911cc88f0c4e9cbcd38f7c8f3a5c04","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_n be INDEPENDENT random variables taking values in arbitrary measurable spaces - they need NOT be identically distributed and need not be real-valued - and let Z = f(X_1, ..., X_n) with E[Z^2] < infinity. Let X_i' be an independent copy of X_i, independent of everything else, and put Z^{(i)} = f(X_1, ..., X_{i-1}, X_i', X_{i+1}, ..., X_n). Then Var(Z) <= (1/2) sum_{i=1}^n E[ (Z - Z^{(i)})^2 ] = sum_{i=1}^n E[ ((Z - Z^{(i)})_+)^2 ]. Equivalently, and often more convenient, Var(Z) <= sum_{i=1}^n E[ (Z - Z_i)^2 ] for ANY random variables Z_i that are measurable functions of the n-1 variables other than X_i; taking Z_i = inf over the i-th coordinate of f gives the version used for suprema and for first-passage times. Equality in the replace-one bound (in either form) holds if and only if f is a sum of functions of the individual coordinates; equality in the bound with arbitrary Z_i holds if and only if, in addition, Z_i = E[Z | X_j, j != i] almost surely for every i. Independence is the only structural hypothesis and it is essential; the inequality is FALSE for dependent coordinates. Applied with a bounded-difference function it recovers the variance half of McDiarmid's inequality; applied to first-passage percolation with the geodesic length as the influence bound it produces the linear variance upper bound. [Efron and Stein (1981), Steele (1986); see Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 3.1]","status":"unverified"}

Let Delta be any nonzero m-by-p matrix of rank at most r and X a fixed full-row-rank p-by-n design. For noiseless Y=Delta X, the global rank-r empirical least-squares estimate equals Delta, so its isotropic population parameter risk is zero. Simultaneous factor GD from B0=0 and nondegenerate Gaussian A0, with any step schedule fixed conditional on X independently of A0, almost surely has B_t A_t != Delta at every finite t. {"assumptions":["i.i.d. nonnegative edge weights on Z^2 with F(0) = 0","mu is the axial time constant; the comparison is with the expectation of the minimum of four independent weights","the refutation is Ahlberg's (2019/2020); this is a rederivation with an explicit instance"],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:15:27.869107+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_b80639d38026a14989da0a86aa6755d6ea3593aa2551d349ffb00e6d55126985","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign status: literature_counterexample_rederived - the primary two-page proof was read and the arithmetic author-checked; the result is Ahlberg's, not ours, and novelty is not claimed] For i.i.d. nonnegative edge weights on Z^2 with F(0) = 0, Auffinger, Damron and Hanson (50 years of first-passage percolation, Question 12) ask whether the axial time constant mu is at least the expected minimum of four independent edge weights. CLAIM: NO, and the question was already settled in the literature by Ahlberg (2019/2020), whose bound mu <= 2 t_{2/3} - twice the 2/3-quantile - refutes it. EXPLICIT INSTANCE: take tau = eta + epsilon U with P(eta = 0) = 3/4 and U uniform on [0,1]. For epsilon > 0 this law is atomless and bounded with F(0) = 0. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:43:37.236593+00:00","domain":"numerical analysis","id":"claim_b8a68d2eccee5860bfb70fd0f24e13b2b7626e3471541b131b79447a4472e0ff","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"In a floating-point number system, the machine epsilon eps is the smallest positive representable number such that 1 + eps, computed with that system's rounding rule, is strictly greater than 1; equivalently, eps is the gap between 1 and the next larger representable floating-point number. {"assumptions":["a well-defined electrical network with nonnegative conductances, on a finite graph or an infinite graph with appropriate limiting or boundary conditions","the comparison is between two networks differing only in conductance values on a common edge set, or related by a clean edge addition, deletion, or vertex identification","finite total energy for the relevant flows or potentials, so the variational characterization is well posed","for random-walk conclusions, the standard correspondence between the electrical network and a reversible Markov chain"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.993128+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b9387245512e1cdb33d492e04652cfd536ce550cebd97a2fc52f4dd9dc6c0a91","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For an electrical network on a graph with nonnegative edge conductances c_e, the effective resistance R_eff(a,b) between vertices a, b is defined variationally, via Thomson's principle, as the minimum of sum_e (1/c_e) i_e^2 over unit flows i from a to b obeying Kirchhoff's node law, or equivalently via Dirichlet's principle over voltage functions. Rayleigh's monotonicity law states that R_eff(a,b) is monotone nonincreasing as a function of each conductance: increasing any conductance, adding an edge, or short-circuiting (identifying) any pair of vertices can only decrease or preserve R_eff(a,b), while decreasing a conductance, or deleting an edge, can only increase or preserve it. This purely variational fact underlies comparisons between random walks on different graphs via the resistance-recurrence correspondence, that a network is recurrent for its associated random walk if and only if R_eff(a,infinity)=infinity, comparisons of hitting and commute times, and resistance-based bounds on percolation-type crossing quantities. It gives only monotone comparisons, no quantitative rates, and using it for random-walk conclusions requires the standard electrical network-reversible Markov chain correspondence, with conductances proportional to transition rates, to be correctly set up first. Typical failure: Applying Rayleigh monotonicity to compare effective resistances between two networks that differ in more than conductance values on a shared edge set, such as networks on genuinely different vertex sets or after a modification that is not literally a conductance increase/decrease, edge addition/deletion, or vertex identification; the monotonicity is a coupling statement about the same underlying network with modified weights, and applying it across structurally different networks without an explicit embedding produces an unjustified comparison. Canonical reference: Rayleigh, 1871, Philosophical Magazine; Doyle and Snell, Random Walks and Electric Networks, 1984, Mathematical Association of America; Lyons and Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks, 2016, Cambridge University Press.","status":"unverified"}

A strongly continuous semigroup (C_0-semigroup) on X is a family (T(t))_{t ≥ 0} of bounded linear operators on X with T(0) = I, T(t + s) = T(t)T(s) for all t, s ≥ 0, and t ↦ T(t)x continuous from [0, ∞) to X for every x ∈ X (for a semigroup this is equivalent to T(t)x → x as t ↓ 0 for every x, and also equivalent to weak continuity, i.e. continuity of t ↦ ⟨T(t)x, x*⟩ on [0, ∞) for every x ∈ X and every x* ∈ X*). Every C_0-semigroup is exponentially bounded: there are M ≥ 1 and ω ∈ ℝ with ‖T(t)‖ ≤ M e^{ωt} for all t ≥ 0; the growth bound is ω_0 = inf of such ω. It is a contraction semigroup if ‖T(t)‖ ≤ 1 for all t, and quasi-contractive if ‖T(t)‖ ≤ e^{ωt}. Its (infinitesimal) generator is the operator A with D(A) = {x ∈ X : lim_{t↓0} (T(t)x − x)/t exists} and Ax equal to that limit. One says A generates T and writes T(t) = e^{tA}. Norm continuity of t ↦ T(t) at 0 (a uniformly continuous semigroup) holds if and only if the generator is bounded, in which case T(t) = Σ t^n A^n / n!; the typical generators of PDE semigroups are unbounded and the semigroup is only strongly continuous.","status":"unverified"}

Condition on center +1 and every interval variable OTHER than the whole-word interval being vacant. This event has positive finite-volume probability. The whole interval then has conditional occupation probability h_l(theta)/(1+h_l(theta)), since the only remaining sets have weights 1 and h_l. {"assumptions":["mu is a probability measure","T is measure-preserving, not necessarily invertible","mu(A) > 0","the value 1/mu(A) for the mean return time requires ergodicity; the general identity does not"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T12:13:53+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, recurrence, induced maps","id":"claim_baade9096b6824c73152f5700a64977d653156c661b715154a8e597b0e136142","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu)$ be a probability space, $T: X \to X$ measure-preserving (not necessarily invertible), $A \in \mathcal{B}$ with $\mu(A) > 0$, and $n_A(x) = \min\{n \ge 1 : T^n x \in A\}$ the first return time (finite for a.e. $x \in A$ by Poincare recurrence; set $n_A = \infty$ where no return occurs). Then, in general,
$$\int_A n_A\,d\mu = \mu\Big(\bigcup_{j \ge 0} T^{-j} A\Big),$$
the measure of the set of points whose forward orbit ever meets $A$. In particular $\int_A n_A\,d\mu \le 1$ always, so $n_A$ is integrable over $A$ for EVERY positive-measure set in a probability-preserving system, ergodic or not. If $T$ is ERGODIC, the union has full measure and
$$\int_A n_A\,d\mu = 1, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \frac{1}{\mu(A)} \int_A n_A\,d\mu = \frac{1}{\mu(A)}:$$
the mean return time to $A$, with respect to the normalised measure $\mu_A = \mu(\cdot \cap A)/\mu(A)$, is exactly $1/\mu(A)$. The induced (first-return) map $T_A = T^{n_A}$ on $A$ preserves $\mu_A$. When $T$ is invertible and ergodic, $(X, \mu, T)$ is isomorphic mod 0 to the tower (Kakutani skyscraper) over $(A, \mu_A, T_A)$ with height $n_A$, of total mass $\int_A n_A\,d\mu / \mu(A)$ in units of $\mu_A$; for non-invertible $T$ the tower map $(x, j) \mapsto T^j x$ is in general only a factor map (for the doubling map with $A = [0, 1/2)$ it is many-to-one).

WHERE IT FAILS. (1) Without ergodicity the mean return time can be strictly less than $1/\mu(A)$: if $A$ is itself invariant then $n_A = 1$ on $A$ and $\int_A n_A = \mu(A) < 1$. (2) In an infinite measure space $\int_A n_A\,d\mu$ can be infinite even for a conservative ergodic $T$ (in fact for an ergodic conservative infinite-measure system it is always infinite for sets of finite positive measure), so 'mean return time $= 1/\mu(A)$' is a finite-measure statement. (3) The lemma controls only the MEAN of $n_A$: no bound on its variance or tail follows; $n_A$ need not be in $L^2$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["mu is a probability measure","T is measure-preserving, not necessarily invertible","mu(A) > 0","the value 1/mu(A) for the mean return time requires ergodicity; the general identity does not"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438087+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, recurrence, induced maps","id":"claim_bb6dcbe5ce02085d2e2e48afcaee2028d3f09a38e89e185dcbbbb02136dd47f5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu)$ be a probability space, $T: X \to X$ measure-preserving (not necessarily invertible), $A \in \mathcal{B}$ with $\mu(A) > 0$, and $n_A(x) = \min\{n \ge 1 : T^n x \in A\}$ the first return time (finite for a.e. $x \in A$ by Poincare recurrence; set $n_A = \infty$ where no return occurs). Then, in general,
$$\int_A n_A\,d\mu = \mu\Big(\bigcup_{j \ge 0} T^{-j} A\Big),$$
the measure of the set of points whose forward orbit ever meets $A$. In particular $\int_A n_A\,d\mu \le 1$ always, so $n_A$ is integrable over $A$ for EVERY positive-measure set in a probability-preserving system, ergodic or not. If $T$ is ERGODIC, the union has full measure and
$$\int_A n_A\,d\mu = 1, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \frac{1}{\mu(A)} \int_A n_A\,d\mu = \frac{1}{\mu(A)}:$$
the mean return time to $A$, with respect to the normalised measure $\mu_A = \mu(\cdot \cap A)/\mu(A)$, is exactly $1/\mu(A)$. Equivalently, the induced (first-return) map $T_A = T^{n_A}$ on $A$ preserves $\mu_A$ and $(X, \mu, T)$ is recovered from $(A, \mu_A, T_A, n_A)$ as a tower of total mass $\int_A n_A\,d\mu / \mu(A)$.

WHERE IT FAILS. (1) Without ergodicity the mean return time can be strictly less than $1/\mu(A)$: if $A$ is itself invariant then $n_A = 1$ on $A$ and $\int_A n_A = \mu(A) < 1$. (2) In an infinite measure space $\int_A n_A\,d\mu$ can be infinite even for a conservative ergodic $T$ (in fact for an ergodic conservative infinite-measure system it is always infinite for sets of finite positive measure), so 'mean return time $= 1/\mu(A)$' is a finite-measure statement. (3) The lemma controls only the MEAN of $n_A$: no bound on its variance or tail follows; $n_A$ need not be in $L^2$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:16:35.596991+00:00","domain":"statistical learning theory","id":"claim_bbd3a83729c8d9e501cff01bc27d1df869d97b124fee1913e254632b046cae12","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For kernel ridge regression with power-law spectrum $\\eta_k = k^{-\\alpha}$ ($\\alpha>1$, the capacity) and teacher coefficients $\\theta_k = k^{-(1+\\alpha(2r-1))/2}$ ($r \\ge 0$, the source), with label noise of variance $\\sigma^2$ and ridge $\\lambda = n^{-\\ell}$, the excess risk of the ridgeless estimator ($\\ell \\ge \\alpha$, including interpolation) is of order $\\max(\\sigma^2, n^{-2\\alpha\\min(r,1)})$, while the optimally regularised excess risk is of order $n^{-2\\alpha\\min(r,1)}$ for $n$ below a crossover $n_* \\asymp \\sigma^{-1/(\\alpha\\min(r,1))}$ and of order $n^{1/(1+2\\alpha\\min(r,1)) - 1}$ above it (Cui, Loureiro, Krzakala, Zdeborova, NeurIPS 2021). {"assumptions":["v_1, ..., v_n linearly independent in a real or complex inner product space","for a dependent family the process produces a zero u_k, which is skipped and yields an orthonormal basis of the span"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.476812+00:00","domain":"linear algebra","id":"claim_bc01791ccad0fb7bcf635158f0db13bcca11c5b76eca0ae6dceb03aec1fed455","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let v_1, ..., v_n be linearly independent vectors in an inner product space. Define recursively u_1 = v_1 and u_k = v_k - sum_{j < k} <v_k, e_j> e_j with e_j = u_j / |u_j|. Then every u_k is nonzero, the vectors e_1, ..., e_n are orthonormal, and span(e_1, ..., e_k) = span(v_1, ..., v_k) for every k; the e_k are unique up to the sign (or unit scalar) of each vector given this nested-span condition. Applied to a countable linearly independent sequence the process yields an orthonormal sequence with the same nested spans, which is why every separable Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis. In matrix language, applying it to the columns of an m x n matrix A of full column rank gives the QR factorisation A = Q R with Q having orthonormal columns and R upper triangular with positive diagonal. (Numerically the modified Gram-Schmidt variant, which subtracts each projection as soon as it is formed, loses orthogonality far more slowly in floating point.)","status":"unverified"}

Present the stored pattern xi^nu; the local field at neuron i is h_i = sum_j W_{ij} xi_j^nu = ((N-1)/N) xi_i^nu + C_i, where the crosstalk C_i = (1/N) sum over mu not equal to nu, sum over j not equal to i, of xi_i^mu xi_j^mu xi_j^nu has mean 0 and variance (P-1)(N-1)/N^2, which tends to alpha = P/N as N -> infinity with P/N -> alpha. The (P-1)(N-1) summands are pairwise uncorrelated products of independent signs, so by the central limit theorem C_i is approximately N(0, alpha) for large N and P, and the probability that the update flips neuron i away from the pattern - the event xi_i^nu h_i < 0, that is xi_i^nu C_i < -(N-1)/N - is approximately Phi(-1/sqrt(alpha)) = (1/2) erfc( 1/sqrt(2 alpha) ). {"assumptions":["i.i.d. summands with mean zero and finite variance","the constant sqrt(2) inside the normalisation is not adjustable; it is the correct almost sure envelope"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.781780+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_be6c233b3f80b2ad7b180f07b82c12b5a10e4b84732b718a58c52d3c3540a594","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, X_2, ... be i.i.d. with E[X_1] = 0 and E[X_1^2] = sigma^2 < infinity, and let S_n = X_1 + ... + X_n. Then almost surely limsup_{n -> infinity} S_n / sqrt( 2 n log log n ) = sigma and liminf_{n -> infinity} S_n / sqrt( 2 n log log n ) = - sigma. Consequently the set of limit points of S_n / sqrt(2 n log log n) is exactly the interval [-sigma, sigma], and the sequence oscillates: it comes arbitrarily close to both endpoints infinitely often and does not converge. STRASSEN'S CONVERSE: if limsup_n |S_n| / sqrt( 2 n log log n ) < infinity with positive probability, then E[X_1] = 0 and E[X_1^2] < infinity, so the two-moment hypothesis is exactly right and not merely convenient. The theorem sits strictly between the strong law, which says S_n/n -> 0, and the central limit theorem, which describes S_n/sqrt(n) in distribution but says nothing about the almost sure oscillation; in particular the CLT does NOT imply that S_n/sqrt(n) is almost surely bounded, and indeed it is not - the iterated logarithm is the correct almost sure envelope. [Hartman and Wintner (1941); Strassen (1966); see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 8.5.2]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["M is a compact Riemannian manifold and f a C^1 diffeomorphism of M","mu is an f-invariant Borel probability measure (compactness makes the Oseledets integrability condition automatic)","the exponents and multiplicities are measurable and f-invariant, constant a.e. when mu is ergodic; the subspaces are measurable and Df-equivariant","the Oseledets splitting is measurable, generally not continuous, and the Pesin blocks are not invariant"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"smooth ergodic theory, Lyapunov exponents","id":"claim_bf769101c6fe8505c33df1958690eca784e10a921c4b8007d731b67c59e25eca","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f be a C^1 diffeomorphism of a compact Riemannian manifold M and mu an f-invariant Borel probability measure. Since M is compact, log of the norm of Df and of Df^{-1} are bounded, hence integrable, so Oseledets' multiplicative ergodic theorem applies: for mu-a.e. x there are finitely many numbers lambda_1(x) > lambda_2(x) > ... > lambda_{k(x)}(x) (the LYAPUNOV EXPONENTS at x) and a Df-invariant splitting of the tangent space

  T_x M = E_1(x) + ... + E_{k(x)}(x),   Df_x E_i(x) = E_i(f x),

such that for every nonzero v in E_i(x) the limit of (1/n) log |Df^n_x v| as n -> +-infinity exists and equals lambda_i(x). The functions x -> lambda_i(x) and the multiplicities dim E_i(x) are measurable and f-invariant, and if mu is ergodic they are constant almost everywhere; the subspaces E_i(x) are measurable and Df-equivariant, Df_x E_i(x) = E_i(fx). The splitting is in general only MEASURABLE, not continuous, and the convergence is not uniform in x.

Two structural facts that every application uses. (1) TEMPEREDNESS: any measurable positive function that is subexponential along orbits -- such as the angle between the Oseledets subspaces, or the norm of the change to Lyapunov (adapted) coordinates -- can be chosen tempered, meaning (1/n) log of its value at f^n x tends to 0; this is what lets one build Lyapunov charts in which Df is uniformly contracting on the negative-exponent bundle at the cost of a chart size that shrinks subexponentially along the orbit. (2) PESIN BLOCKS: for each l one collects the points where the Oseledets estimates hold with uniform constants depending on l; the resulting sets Lambda_l are COMPACT (after discarding a null set and restricting the subbundles continuously), increase in l, exhaust a full-measure set, and carry uniform hyperbolic-like estimates. They are NOT f-invariant -- an orbit wanders between blocks -- which is exactly why non-uniformly hyperbolic statements are local-and-measurable rather than uniform.

A point x is called (non-uniformly) hyperbolic when no exponent at x is zero; the stable bundle E^s(x) is the sum of the E_i(x) with lambda_i(x) < 0 and the unstable bundle the sum of those with lambda_i(x) > 0. Zero exponents are the obstruction: nothing in this framework says anything about directions with zero exponent.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f in L^1_loc(R^d), Lebesgue measure","averaging sets shrink nicely to x (bounded eccentricity); unbounded eccentricity breaks the theorem"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751496+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_bf8b9a4334173b1b42ad155604b5dabb90ceb6c0b2b33e20cc69bf001127fc26","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f be in L^1_loc(R^d). Then for Lebesgue-almost every x, (1/|B(x,r)|) integral_{B(x,r)} |f(y) - f(x)| dy -> 0 as r -> 0; such an x is called a Lebesgue point of f. In particular the averages of f over shrinking balls converge to f(x) for a.e. x. The result persists if balls are replaced by any family of sets U_r shrinking NICELY to x, meaning U_r is contained in B(x,r) and |U_r| >= c |B(x,r)| for a fixed c > 0 (cubes centred at x, for instance). It FAILS for families of arbitrary eccentricity: in R^2 there is an integrable f whose averages over rectangles centred at x with sides parallel to the axes and both side lengths tending to 0 fail to converge at almost every x, because the strong maximal function is not of weak type (1,1). The a.e. exceptional set genuinely depends on f and cannot be taken empty. [standard; e.g. Stein and Shakarchi, Real Analysis, Chapter 3, Corollary 1.5 and Section 1.4]","status":"unverified"}
