{"assumptions":["Fixed finite d,n,T and step gamma>0; bounded nonzero training inputs and bounded nonzero-input population independent of initialization","m=2N independent Gaussian hidden pairs with opposite fixed heads +/-nu,0<nu<=1; all parameters subsequently trained without tying","Squared empirical loss normalized by n; bounded labels; zero ReLU derivative at zero","Width tends to infinity before any time, sample-size or input-law limit; mathematical and literature review pending"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T18:15:10.683358+00:00","domain":"two-layer ReLU learning; population neural tangent kernel limits","id":"claim_c05778d0768f5d9377765bf96953205bc672897c685dd1f7ce32845f258f62b0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited); independent mathematical review pending; novelty unestablished. This is a finite-horizon supporting method, not full Target1 closure.

## 1. Finite-horizon transfer statement
Fix finite d,n,T, gamma>0, 0<nu<=1, Y<infinity, nonzero training inputs
x_1,...,x_n with norms <=M, and a probability law P supported on nonzero
inputs of norm <=M. Inputs and P are independent of initialization.
The loss is (1/(2n)) sum_i (f(x_i)-y_i)^2, with |y_i|<=Y.
Use m=2N neurons, f(x)=m^(-1/2) sum_j a_j ReLU(w_j.x).
For each independent W_l~N(0,I_d), initialize one pair at (nu,W_l),
(-nu,W_l); update every parameter by ordinary simultaneous GD of step gamma,
with derivative 1{w.x>0}. The pairing is only at initialization, not enforced.
Let H be the deterministic full initial kernel from C014 Section2:
H(x,z)=E[ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z].
Let f^H_k be zero-start kernel GD with this H, the same sample and labels.
Then, as N tends to infinity,

 max_{k<=T} ||f_k-f^H_k||_{L2(P)} -> 0 in probability.       (1)

The event bounds proving this hold uniformly for every y in [-Y,Y]^n.
No positive training eigenvalue or nonzero gate margin is assumed. T is
fixed before this width limit; constants below can grow rapidly with T.

## 2. Width-independent finite-horizon bounds
Write u_j=1+||w_j(0)||. The empirical mean S_m=m^(-1)sum u_j^2 is a pair
average and tends almost surely to E(1+||W||)^2. Fix S above that expectation
and work on S_m<=S, an event eventually true almost surely.
Define H_0=D_0=0, R_0=Y. Given H_k,D_k,R_k, set
 A_k=1+H_k, B_k=1+D_k, c_k=gamma M R_k,
 H_{k+1}=H_k+c_k B_k, D_{k+1}=D_k+c_k A_k,
 R_{k+1}=R_k+M c_k S[B_k(B_k+c_k A_k)+A_k^2].
Induction gives, uniformly over the label cube,
 |a_j(k)-a_j(0)|<=H_k u_j/sqrt(m),
 ||w_j(k)-w_j(0)||<=D_k u_j/sqrt(m),
 |a_j(k)|<=A_k u_j, ||w_j(k)||<=B_k u_j,
 ||r_k||/sqrt(n)<=R_k, where r_i=f_k(x_i)-y_i.
Indeed Cauchy-Schwarz in the exact parameter updates gives
 |Delta a_j|<=c_k B_k u_j/sqrt(m),
 ||Delta w_j||<=c_k A_k u_j/sqrt(m).
ReLU is 1-Lipschitz and homogeneous, so at every ||x||<=M,
 |Delta f_k(x)|<=||x|| c_k S[B_k(B_k+c_k A_k)+A_k^2].
This proves the induction and a finite uniform output bound through T.
Let H,D,A,B,c denote maxima of these constants through the required steps.

## 3. Population gate bands shrink in L2, not just on the sample
Put L_m(x)=m^(-1)sum_j u_j^2 1{|w_j(0).x|<=D u_j||x||/sqrt(m)}.
For each training x_i, L_m(x_i)->0 almost surely. Also

 ||L_m||_{L2(P)} -> 0 almost surely.                         (2)

Proof: for fixed q>0, the pair-averaged integrable function
 Z_q(W)=(1+||W||)^2 P_x{|W.x|<=q(1+||W||)||x||}
has its empirical average tending to E Z_q by the ordinary scalar SLLN.
For m large with D/sqrt(m)<=q, integral L_m dP is bounded by that average.
For every fixed nonzero x, Gaussian W.x has no atom at zero; Fubini and
dominated convergence imply E Z_q->0 as q decreases to zero. Apply SLLN
simultaneously on countably many q=1,1/2,1/3,..., then let q decrease.
Thus integral L_m->0 almost surely. Since 0<=L_m<=S_m, its squared L2 norm
is at most S_m integral L_m. The finite training-point assertion follows
by the same fixed-q argument without integration over P.
This is uniform over trajectories obeying Section2; no independence between
trained gates and initialization is asserted or needed.

## 4. Both train and cross kernels remain close
Let H^m_k be the empirical full tangent kernel at step k. Product expansion
and the movement bounds give, for every training point x_i,

 |H^m_k(x,x_i)-H^m_0(x,x_i)|
 <= ||x||||x_i|| [C S/sqrt(m)+nu^2(L_m(x)+L_m(x_i))],       (3)

where C=D(B+1)+H(A+1) is finite. The RF-product part is bounded by
D(B+1)u_j^2/sqrt(m). The readout-square change is bounded by
H(A+1)u_j^2/sqrt(m). A changed gate at x forces the initial weight into
the band defining L_m(x); likewise at x_i. These inequalities remain valid
when a trained preactivation equals zero, using the stated derivative.
Equations (2),(3) imply uniform-in-k convergence of the training normalized
Gram matrices and of the population cross rows, relative to their INITIAL
empirical kernels. In particular define K^m_k=(H^m_k(x_i,x_l)/n),
b^m_k(x)=(H^m_k(x,x_i)/sqrt(n))_i. Their respective operator and L2(row)
differences from step0 tend to zero; the latter is bounded by
M^2[C S/sqrt(m)+nu^2(||L_m||_2+max_i L_m(x_i))].

At initialization, each independent pair contributes the same feature
kernel F_W(x,z)=ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z.
It satisfies |F_W(x,z)|<=M^2(||W||^2+1). Its squared envelope is integrable.
Thus the empirical initial training kernel tends to K=(H(x_i,x_l)/n).
For the population cross row b(x)=(H(x,x_i)/sqrt(n))_i, independence of pairs
and Fubini give E||b^m_0-b||_2^2<=M^4 E(||W||^2+1)^2/N.
Hence this difference tends to zero in probability too. This explicitly
controls the missing test-to-training kernel; it is not inferred from K.

## 5. Discrete-step gate remainder off the sample
The exact prediction update is
 f_{k+1}(x)=f_k(x)-gamma b^m_k(x).v_k+Z_k(x), v_k=r_k/sqrt(n),
where, writing h=ReLU(w.x), h'=ReLU((w+Delta w).x),
 Z_k(x)=m^(-1/2)sum_j[Delta a_j(h'-h)
             +a_j(h'-h-1{w.x>0}Delta w_j.x)].
If the second summand is nonzero, the segment from w to w+Delta w crosses
its gate at x. Because both endpoints are within the Section2 cumulative
radius of w(0), the initial preactivation lies in the D-band above.
The Lipschitz inequality therefore gives

 |Z_k(x)|<=||x||[c^2 A B S/sqrt(m)+c A^2 L_m(x)].           (4)

It follows that max_{k<T}||Z_k||_{L2(P)}->0 and max_{k<T,i}|Z_k(x_i)|->0.
No approximation replaces discrete GD by flow.

## 6. Close the training and population prediction recurrences
Let v^H_{k+1}=(I-gamma K)v^H_k, v^H_0=-y/sqrt(n).
The true normalized residual update is
 v_{k+1}=(I-gamma K^m_k)v_k+z_k,
where ||z_k||<=max_i |Z_k(x_i)|. Sections2,4,5 imply by finite induction
max_{k<=T}||v_k-v^H_k||->0 in probability, uniformly over bounded labels.
For example each error is bounded by ||I-gamma K|| times the previous
error plus gamma ||K^m_k-K|| R_k+||z_k||. The multiplier is finite; neither
a contraction nor a spectral gap is required at this finite horizon.
Both output initializations are exactly zero. Sum the prediction updates:
 f_k-f^H_k=-gamma sum_{j<k}[(b^m_j-b).v_j+b.(v_j-v^H_j)]
                         +sum_{j<k}Z_j.
The population L2 norm is bounded by the sum of cross-kernel errors times
R_j, deterministic ||b||_2 times training residual errors, and remainder
norms. Every term tends to zero by the preceding sections, proving (1).
The same controlling random bounds work for all bounded label vectors.
For any bounded teacher, clean risks averaged over the bounded independent
label noises consequently converge uniformly through T in probability,
by Cauchy-Schwarz and the finite uniform output bound from Section2.


Here zero-start kernel GD means f^H_{k+1}(x)=f^H_k(x)-(gamma/n)sum_i H(x,x_i)(f^H_k(x_i)-y_i), with f^H_0=0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["U is an open subset of C","S ⊂ U has no accumulation point in U","f is holomorphic (single-valued) on U minus S","γ is a cycle of closed piecewise C^1 curves in U minus S","γ is null-homologous in U: n(γ,w) = 0 for all w not in U"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.481612+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_c06a4addcacadd823305bc30a444fb82b5f0e61db090ada5bdf7da7ba0dd5c8c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let U be an open subset of C, let S be a subset of U with no accumulation point in U (so S is discrete and closed in U), and let f be holomorphic on U minus S. Let γ be a cycle (a finite formal sum with integer coefficients of closed piecewise C^1 curves) whose trace lies in U minus S, and assume γ is null-homologous in U, i.e. the winding number n(γ,w) = 0 for every w in C minus U. Then n(γ,a) is nonzero for only finitely many a in S, and ∫_γ f(z) dz = 2πi Σ_{a in S} n(γ,a) Res(f,a). Most-used special case: if γ is a positively oriented piecewise C^1 Jordan curve such that γ together with its interior region lies in U and no point of S lies on γ, then ∫_γ f(z) dz = 2πi times the sum of Res(f,a) over the (finitely many) points a of S inside γ. By the two-regimes corollary those are Aitken's variance-stabilising weights exactly when the error scale is proportional to the target norm (multiplicative error, elasticity of log ||e_i|| on log ||y_i|| equal to one); then the relative-metric fit is the efficient one and its optimism is 2m/n relative to its own noise level, regardless of how concentrated 1/||y_i||^2 is. If the error carries an additive floor, the rows with the smallest targets - exactly the rows the relative weights concentrate on - have the largest floor relative to their target, the concentration re-enters, and Kish's n_eff of the relative weights measures how far the fit is from balanced. The discriminating measurement is the elasticity of the out-of-fold residual norm to the target norm and the nonnegative fit ||e_i||^2 = a + b ||y_i||^2 (the floor share a / (a + b median ||y||^2)) on the calibration rows; on a pool whose targets vary by orders of magnitude (the EMIT radiance outputs) the question is live, on one whose targets are homogeneous (the OCO-2 retrievals, n_eff within a few percent of n) the two metrics coincide and it is moot.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["finite simple graphs (loops make P identically 0; parallel edges do not change P)","k a nonnegative integer in the counting definition; the polynomial identity then holds for all k"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479653+00:00","domain":"graph theory","id":"claim_c11359eb703fe597fd324079d34608d788354417c8b886cc4a0e84bab112bea7","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a finite graph G and a positive integer k let P(G, k) be the number of proper colourings of the vertices of G with k colours (adjacent vertices receive different colours). THEOREM (Birkhoff, Whitney): P(G, k) is a polynomial in k of degree |V|, the chromatic polynomial, determined by the deletion-contraction recurrence P(G, k) = P(G - e, k) - P(G / e, k) for any edge e (G - e deletes the edge, G / e contracts it, merging its endpoints and removing loops and parallel copies), with P(empty graph on n vertices, k) = k^n. Facts: P(K_n, k) = k (k - 1) ... (k - n + 1); P(tree on n vertices, k) = k (k - 1)^{n-1}; P(C_n, k) = (k - 1)^n + (-1)^n (k - 1); P is multiplicative over connected components; its coefficients alternate in sign, the leading coefficient is 1, the coefficient of k^{|V| - 1} is -|E|, and the constant term is 0 for a graph with a vertex; the chromatic number is the least positive integer that is not a root; k = 0, 1, ..., chi(G) - 1 are roots; the chromatic polynomial is a specialisation of the Tutte polynomial, P(G, k) = (-1)^{|V| - c(G)} k^{c(G)} T(G; 1 - k, 0). {"assumptions":["Little: f entire and nonconstant","Great: f holomorphic on a punctured disk about a with an isolated essential singularity at a"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.482747+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_c11eee83f3cff31aeab34ce71916569c41ce2b6c167fbad02599fabb55fea697","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Little Picard theorem: if f is entire and nonconstant, then the complement of its image, C minus f(C), contains at most one point; i.e. a nonconstant entire function omits at most one complex value. Great Picard theorem: if f is holomorphic on a punctured disk 0 < |z - a| < r and has an essential singularity at a, then for every ε in (0,r) the image of the punctured disk 0 < |z - a| < ε is all of C with at most one point removed, and every value so attained (again with at most one exception) is attained infinitely often. Both exceptional values are genuinely possible and the count is sharp: exp(z) is entire and omits exactly the value 0, and exp(1/z) has an essential singularity at 0 and omits exactly 0 near 0. Meromorphic versions: a nonconstant meromorphic function on C omits at most two values of the Riemann sphere, and near an essential singularity a meromorphic function takes every spherical value with at most two exceptions.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Omega is bounded and open in R^n with C^1 (or piecewise C^1) boundary, so the divergence theorem applies","u is in C^2 up to the closure of Omega","for the Pohozaev form: u = 0 on the boundary, f is continuous, F(t) = integral_0^t f and F(0) = 0","for the nonexistence corollary: n >= 3, Omega star-shaped about the origin, f(u) = |u|^(p-1)u with p >= (n+2)/(n-2), and strict star-shapedness plus Hopf or unique continuation in the critical case"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.396148+00:00","domain":"elliptic PDE, variational identities and nonexistence","id":"claim_c1db80201085a9bde5ef4703381e7acf672f7231bfba2a288812bae9f615e2b6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega be a bounded open subset of R^n with boundary of class C^1 and outward unit normal nu. RELLICH IDENTITY: for every u in C^2(closure of Omega) one has integral_Omega (x . grad u) Laplacian(u) dx = ((n-2)/2) integral_Omega |grad u|^2 dx - (1/2) integral_{boundary} (x . nu) |grad u|^2 dS + integral_{boundary} (x . grad u)(du/dnu) dS. POHOZAEV IDENTITY: if in addition u = 0 on the boundary of Omega and -Laplacian(u) = f(u) in Omega with f continuous and F(t) = integral_0^t f(s) ds, then, since on the boundary grad u = (du/dnu) nu, the two boundary terms collapse and one gets ((n-2)/2) integral_Omega |grad u|^2 dx + (1/2) integral_{boundary} (x . nu) |du/dnu|^2 dS = n integral_Omega F(u) dx. CONSEQUENCE (nonexistence): let n >= 3, let Omega be star-shaped with respect to the origin (x . nu >= 0 on the boundary) with C^1 boundary, and let f(u) = |u|^(p-1) u with p >= (n+2)/(n-2). Multiplying the equation by u gives integral |grad u|^2 = integral |u|^(p+1), while Pohozaev gives ((n-2)/2) integral |u|^(p+1) + (1/2) integral_{boundary}(x . nu)|du/dnu|^2 = (n/(p+1)) integral |u|^(p+1). Since p >= (n+2)/(n-2) is exactly n/(p+1) <= (n-2)/2, the boundary term is <= 0 while star-shapedness makes it >= 0; hence it vanishes and integral |u|^(p+1) = 0 for p > (n+2)/(n-2). In the critical case p = (n+2)/(n-2) the two bulk terms cancel identically and one concludes only that (x . nu)|du/dnu|^2 = 0 on the boundary; if Omega is strictly star-shaped (x . nu > 0) this forces du/dnu = 0 on the whole boundary and then u = 0 by the Hopf lemma or unique continuation. WHERE IT FAILS: star-shapedness is essential, not technical - on an annulus {a < |x| < b} in R^n there exist positive radial solutions of -Laplacian(u) = u^p vanishing on both boundary spheres for EVERY p > 1, including supercritical p (Kazdan-Warner). Regularity is also essential: the identity is proved for u in C^2 up to the boundary (it is valid for H^1_0 weak solutions only after elliptic regularity has upgraded them, which requires growth conditions on f), and the boundary must be regular enough for the divergence theorem. The origin matters: star-shapedness is with respect to the point used in the multiplier x . grad u.","status":"unverified"}

If 2/q + n/r ≠ n/2 the ratio of the two sides is λ^{n/2 − 2/q − n/r}, which is unbounded as λ → 0 or λ → ∞ for any fixed f ≠ 0. So an estimate off the scaling line fails for every nonzero f. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_c26dbe1967eabd9968a58da43f41afdfaebe56d66241b6d5ae45dbc5bb37aa7a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Localized regime of the bounded-density conjecture for quadratic forms (Proposition 4). Let X_1..X_n be independent with densities <=1 and Q(x)=x^T A x with A symmetric. (a) If some 2x2 PRINCIPAL submatrix B of A (two original coordinates i, j) is definite, then ||p_Q||_inf <= pi/sqrt(det B). Proof: condition on the other n-2 ORIGINAL coordinates (independent, so Fubini is genuine); given them Q is a quadratic-plus-linear form in (X_i, X_j); complete the square (B invertible), which shifts (X_i, X_j) and keeps their joint density <=1; for definite B each set {s <= y^T B y <= s+h} is an elliptic annulus of area at most pi h/sqrt(det B), so the conditional density is at most pi/sqrt(det B); average. (b) Hence if A has a 3x3 PRINCIPAL submatrix A_[S] all of whose eigenvalues have modulus >= c>0, and A_[S] is definite or diagonal, then ||p_Q||_inf <= pi/c: for definite A_[S], Cauchy interlacing puts both eigenvalues of every 2x2 principal block of A_[S] at modulus >= c with one sign, so det >= c^2; for diagonal A_[S], two of the three diagonal entries share a sign and form a definite diagonal block with det >= c^2. This contains the separable case. (c) For other well-conditioned blocks the bound K/c is not proved. A block may have no definite 2x2 principal block at all, e.g. [[0,1,1],[1,0,1],[1,1,0]] (eigenvalues 2, -1, -1), and the rank-3 coarea bound ||p_S||_inf <= K||rho||_inf^{2/3} is false for general bounded densities on R^3: a density rho <= B placed on a thin shell around {S = s} gives p_S of order B s^{1/2}/sqrt(l1 l2 l3) for a definite form, unbounded in s. So the localized regime is settled for forms with a definite 2x2 principal block of determinant >= c^2, in particular when a well-conditioned 3x3 principal block is definite or diagonal; the other localized forms stay open, together with the DELOCALIZED forms (every 3x3 principal block near-singular), which is the CLT regime.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["mu and nu are measures on a common measurable space (X, Sigma); nu may be signed or complex","the epsilon-delta characterisation requires nu finite"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:23.251367+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_c2889b5313a76c0af8fa3f49c365322c4a2e27291177d6ab0a182d09f34f8d7d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $\\mu$ and $\\nu$ be measures on the same measurable space $(X, \\Sigma)$, with $\\nu$ possibly signed or complex. $\\nu$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\\mu$, written $\\nu \\ll \\mu$, if $\\nu(A) = 0$ for every $A \\in \\Sigma$ with $\\mu(A) = 0$ (for signed $\\nu$, equivalently $|\\nu|(A) = 0$, where $|\\nu|$ is the total variation). If $\\nu$ is FINITE (or finite signed/complex), this is equivalent to the $\\varepsilon$-$\\delta$ condition: for every $\\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\\delta > 0$ with $|\\nu(A)| < \\varepsilon$ whenever $\\mu(A) < \\delta$; for infinite $\\nu$ the $\\varepsilon$-$\\delta$ condition is strictly stronger (e.g. $\\nu(A) = \\int_A |x|^{-1}dx$ on $(0,1)$ has $\\nu \\ll$ Lebesgue but fails $\\varepsilon$-$\\delta$). Any measure of the form $\\nu(A) = \\int_A f\\,d\\mu$ with $f \\geq 0$ measurable (or $f \\in L^1(\\mu)$ for signed $\\nu$) satisfies $\\nu \\ll \\mu$; the Radon-Nikodym theorem is the converse under $\\sigma$-finiteness. $\\mu$ and $\\nu$ are mutually singular, $\\mu \\perp \\nu$, if there is $A \\in \\Sigma$ with $\\mu(A) = 0$ and $\\nu(X\\setminus A) = 0$. Lebesgue decomposition: for $\\sigma$-finite $\\mu, \\nu$ there is a unique splitting $\\nu = \\nu_{ac} + \\nu_s$ with $\\nu_{ac} \\ll \\mu$ and $\\nu_s \\perp \\mu$. Related but different: a FUNCTION $F: [a,b]\\to\\mathbb{R}$ is absolutely continuous iff its Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure is absolutely continuous w.r.t. Lebesgue measure iff $F(x) = F(a) + \\int_a^x F'$ with $F' \\in L^1$; the Cantor function is continuous, increasing, but not absolutely continuous (its measure is singular). Sharp edge: $\\nu \\ll \\mu$ is not symmetric, and $\\nu \\ll \\mu$ with $\\mu \\ll \\nu$ (equivalence) does not make the density bounded or bounded below.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a Banach space","A is dissipative","the range condition Ran(λ_0 − A) = X (or dense) is the hypothesis at issue"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.772454+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator semigroups, boundary value problems","id":"claim_c354d651b0d3d4c7e46b9aa4b5480a1f39abee205e5d85399db455e11dffea4d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypotheses: A is densely defined, dissipative, AND Ran(λ_0 − A) = X (or at least dense) for some λ_0 > 0. What fails without the range condition: a dissipative operator can be closed and densely defined and still generate nothing. Counterexample: X = L²(0, 1), A f = f' with D(A) = {f ∈ H¹(0,1) : f(0) = f(1) = 0}. Then A is densely defined and closed, and Re⟨f', f⟩ = (|f(1)|² − |f(0)|²)/2 = 0, so A is dissipative (indeed both A and −A are). But solving λf − f' = g with f(0) = 0 gives f(x) = −∫_0^x e^{λ(x−s)}g(s) ds, and the second boundary condition f(1) = 0 forces the constraint ∫_0^1 e^{−λs} g(s) ds = 0: Ran(λ − A) is a closed subspace of codimension 1, not dense, for every λ > 0. Hence A is not a generator, although dropping one boundary condition (D = {f ∈ H¹ : f(1) = 0}) gives exactly the generator of the left shift semigroup. The range condition is what encodes 'the right number of boundary conditions'. What fails without density: X = C[0,1] with the sup norm, A f = f' on D(A) = {f ∈ C¹[0,1] : f(1) = 0}. Solving λ f − f' = g with f(1) = 0 gives f(x) = ∫_x^1 e^{λ(x−s)}g(s)ds, so ‖f‖ ≤ ‖g‖/λ: A is dissipative and Ran(λ − A) = X for every λ > 0. Yet the closure of D(A) is {f ∈ C[0,1] : f(1) = 0}, a proper closed subspace, so A generates no C_0-semigroup on C[0,1] (generators are densely defined); it generates one on the smaller space. Density is automatic only when X is reflexive, which C[0,1] is not. Related trap: for the norm inequality version, dissipativity means ‖(λ − A)x‖ ≥ λ‖x‖ for all λ > 0 - checking it for a single λ, or checking Re⟨Ax, x⟩ ≤ 0 only on a core without knowing the operator is closed or closable there, proves nothing about the closure being a generator unless the range condition is verified on that same core.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X, B, mu, T) is measure-preserving on a standard Borel (Lebesgue) probability space","mu is T-invariant; entropies are Kolmogorov-Sinai entropies with values in [0, +infinity]","the ergodic decomposition is taken over the sigma-algebra of T-invariant sets","convex combinations are of T-INVARIANT measures only","no finiteness of entropy and no continuity of the entropy map is assumed or asserted"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.732492+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, entropy","id":"claim_c423ff08a284a7ccfc7dc1d8f089019abb153806f7c00355fd50d003464125fc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, B, mu, T) be a measure-preserving system on a STANDARD Borel (Lebesgue) probability space, and let I be the sub-sigma-algebra of T-invariant sets.

ERGODIC DECOMPOSITION. There is a measurable family x -> mu_x of T-invariant Borel probability measures on X such that (i) mu_x is a version of the conditional measure of mu given I, so mu(A) = integral of mu_x(A) d mu(x) for every A in B and integral of f d mu = integral over x of (integral of f d mu_x) d mu(x) for f in L^1(mu); (ii) mu_x is ERGODIC for mu-a.e. x; (iii) the family is essentially unique. Writing P for the law of the random measure x -> mu_x, one gets mu = integral of nu dP(nu) supported on the ergodic T-invariant measures -- the Choquet representation of mu in the simplex of invariant measures.

AFFINITY OF ENTROPY. Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy is affine in the measure, with values in [0, +infinity]:
  for every finite measurable partition Q,   h_mu(T, Q) = integral of h_{mu_x}(T, Q) d mu(x);
  and                                        h_mu(T)    = integral of h_{mu_x}(T) d mu(x).
In particular, for T-invariant mu and nu and t in [0,1],  h_{t mu + (1-t) nu}(T) = t h_mu(T) + (1-t) h_nu(T).

SHARP EDGES. (1) AFFINE IS NOT CONTINUOUS: nu -> h_nu(T) is affine on the simplex of invariant measures but is in general NOT weak-* continuous; for expansive homeomorphisms it is upper semicontinuous, and in general it can fail even that. Do not use affinity to pass to weak-* limits. (2) The decomposition genuinely needs a standard/Lebesgue space; on a pathological measure space conditional measures need not exist and the statement can fail. (3) The convex combination must be of INVARIANT measures -- entropy is undefined for a non-invariant measure, so there is no affinity statement along an arbitrary path in the space of measures. (4) The identity holds in [0, +infinity]; if h_mu(T) = +infinity the integral is +infinity, and no finiteness is assumed anywhere. (5) The affinity is a property of measure-theoretic entropy, not of topological entropy: the variational principle gives h_top(T) = sup over invariant nu of h_nu(T), which is a supremum over the simplex, so it is attained (if at all) at ergodic measures precisely BECAUSE h is affine -- but h_top itself is not an average.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. real summands","Lambda finite in a neighbourhood of 0, which makes Lambda^* a good rate function","the rate is exponential in n; polynomial prefactors are NOT captured"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.782174+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4dfaffbd4e619148e1df048b6bc2f3b8bb7627b05d4a288d55a3707d2b749ea","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, X_2, ... be i.i.d. real random variables with cumulant generating function Lambda(lambda) = log E[ exp(lambda X_1) ] and Legendre transform Lambda^*(x) = sup_{lambda in R} ( lambda x - Lambda(lambda) ). Assume Lambda(lambda) < infinity for every lambda in a neighbourhood of 0. Then the empirical means S_n/n satisfy the LARGE DEVIATION PRINCIPLE with speed n and good convex rate function Lambda^*: for every closed set C, limsup_n (1/n) log P( S_n/n in C ) <= - inf_{x in C} Lambda^*(x), and for every open set G, liminf_n (1/n) log P( S_n/n in G ) >= - inf_{x in G} Lambda^*(x). In particular, for x > E[X_1], (1/n) log P( S_n/n >= x ) -> - Lambda^*(x), so the Chernoff upper bound is exact at the level of the exponential rate although it can be off by polynomial factors: the sharper Bahadur-Rao asymptotic supplies a factor of order n^{-1/2}. The exponential moment hypothesis is what makes Lambda^* a GOOD rate function, meaning its sublevel sets are compact; on the real line the large deviation principle itself continues to hold without it, but the rate function may fail to be good and the statement must then be handled with care. Heavy-tailed laws with no exponential moments have Lambda^* identically 0 above the mean, and their large deviations are governed by a single big jump rather than by a rate function of this shape. (or stationary ergodic with care) elliptic environment on Z^d","The statement concerns the UNION of the two directional events","Directional 0-1 law is open for d >= 3"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.990370+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4f0b35296bb24abc03e25c08c3620d73cbcb1dad336577101e148e2359e4818","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Kalikow's zero-one law (1981; Zerner-Merkl 2001 for the sharp form): for random walk in an i.i.d. elliptic random environment on Z^d and a direction l, let A_l = {X_n . l -> +infinity}. Then P_0(A_l union A_{-l}) is 0 or 1. It does NOT say that P_0(A_l) itself is 0 or 1: the directional zero-one law P_0(A_l) in {0,1} is a theorem in d = 1 (Solomon) and d = 2 (Zerner-Merkl, using planarity: two walks in the same environment must intersect), and is an OPEN PROBLEM for d >= 3 (Drewitz-Ramirez Open Question 3.2; Kalikow's law is often misquoted as the directional one). Kalikow's proof: the event A_l union A_{-l} is invariant under a coupling of walks started at different points that follow the same environment after they meet in a slab, and its probability is a function of the environment's tail sigma-field, hence 0 or 1 by Kolmogorov. Consequences: under transience in some direction the regeneration structure of Sznitman-Zerner applies to the union event; Zerner's law of large numbers then gives X_n/n -> v or -c v. Typical failure: Treating Kalikow's zero-one law as if it determines transience, mistaking the statement that the probability is 0 or 1 for a claim that it equals 1; the theorem only rules out intermediate probabilities and leaves open, often genuinely unresolved, which side of the dichotomy holds for a specific environment law, which is precisely the content of the still largely open general ballisticity conjecture for random walk in random environment in dimension d>=2. Canonical reference: Kalikow, 1981, Annals of Probability; Zeitouni, 2004, Ecole d'Ete de Probabilites de Saint-Flour, Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.499560+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_c53552d7811e343a9c322a0f0f633c47f09d36f9fce8bd51339ed0e1ea11dbf9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"(1) One omitted value is not enough. The family {exp(nz) : n ≥ 1} on the unit disk omits the value 0 everywhere, but it is not normal, not even in the extended sense: on the left half of the disk exp(nz) → 0 while on the right half |exp(nz)| → ∞, and a locally uniform limit on the connected set D would have to be holomorphic throughout or identically ∞. Montel's fundamental normality test needs two distinct omitted values, and that is sharp. (2) When two values are omitted, the conclusion is normality in the extended sense: the constant functions f_n = n omit 0 and 1 and converge to ∞, so a proof that assumes the limit is a finite holomorphic function must first exclude the ∞ branch (typically by a bound at one point or by the maximum principle). (3) Pointwise bounds are not local bounds. Montel's first theorem needs a bound uniform on each compact set; pointwise boundedness of the family is genuinely weaker (Runge's theorem produces sequences of polynomials converging pointwise on C to a discontinuous function, so such a sequence is pointwise bounded and not normal). (4) Normality is not convergence: it only yields subsequences, and the limit may leave the class one is working in — the injective maps z/n converge to a constant, and the limit of a normal family of functions in some prescribed family need not satisfy the same constraint unless Hurwitz-type arguments are added.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-12T12:13:53+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c574fba2347e734a070686822f78efb69bc3f308b61775e623e7cd7013108c3f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a real parameter delta >= 0 the SQUARED BESSEL PROCESS of dimension delta started at y >= 0, written BESQ^delta, is the unique strong solution of dY_t = 2 sqrt( |Y_t| ) dW_t + delta dt with Y_0 = y; the solution is nonnegative, and pathwise uniqueness holds despite the non-Lipschitz diffusion coefficient by the Yamada-Watanabe criterion, which requires only Holder continuity of exponent 1/2. The BESSEL PROCESS of dimension delta, BES^delta, is X_t = sqrt(Y_t); for X > 0 it solves dX_t = dW_t + ((delta - 1)/(2 X_t)) dt. When delta = d is a positive INTEGER, BES^d started at |x| has the law of the radial part |B_t| of a d-dimensional Brownian motion started at x - a fact that makes the family the natural interpolation of radial Brownian motion to non-integer dimension. ADDITIVITY: BESQ^delta started at y and an independent BESQ^{delta'} started at y' add to a BESQ^{delta + delta'} started at y + y'; this holds for the SQUARED process and is false for the Bessel process itself. The index nu = delta/2 - 1 is the other common parameterisation and is the one that appears in the modified Bessel functions of the transition density; delta and nu must not be confused. For 0 <= delta < 2 the point 0 is reached from y > 0, and the BESQ^delta equation itself fixes what happens there: 0 is absorbing for delta = 0 and instantaneously reflecting for 0 < delta < 2, so the squared process needs no extra boundary convention (the equation for X = sqrt(Y) holds only while X_t > 0). For delta >= 2 the point 0 is never reached from y > 0. [standard; e.g. Revuz and Yor, Continuous Martingales and Brownian Motion, 3rd ed., Chapter XI]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-06T17:07:35.313136+00:00","domain":"set theory","id":"claim_c619e145faa54d71a70d2a407f2b55f1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"The axiom of choice (AC) states: for every family (A_i)_{i in I} of nonempty sets, indexed by a set I, there exists a function c on I with c(i) in A_i for every i. Equivalently, every family of nonempty sets admits a choice function selecting one member of each set; every Cartesian product of nonempty sets is nonempty; every surjection has a right inverse; and every set of nonempty pairwise disjoint sets has a transversal selecting exactly one element from each. Over Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory ZF, AC is equivalent to Zorn's lemma, the well-ordering theorem, and Tychonoff's theorem for arbitrary compact spaces. AC asserts existence, not a specified construction; Zermelo formulated it in 1904 in order to prove the well-ordering theorem. AC is independent of ZF, assuming ZF is consistent: Godel (1938) established relative consistency of ZF+AC using the constructible universe, and Cohen (1963) established relative consistency of ZF+not-AC by forcing. Choice for every finite index set is a theorem of ZF. Choice for arbitrary countable families of nonempty sets is not provable in ZF in general.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The allocations are defined along sizes with positive conditioning probability.","0 < nu < lambda and the boundary-tilted law pi has generating-function radius one."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.362761+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c701f819aa156cb392336f5dc77d31cdfefe98e256ab50479dcc6ee2e7e58553","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author_checked; reduction plus asserted conditional, not a solution] Svante Janson's Problem 18.39 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510, asks whether Y_(1)/n -> 0 in probability is possible in the condensation regime 0 < nu < lambda. Janson conjectures that it is not possible for the full sequence and, more strongly, that there are always epsilon > 0 and a subsequence along which Y_(1) >= epsilon n w.h.p. {"assumptions":["(a): f integrable on R","(b): the periodization converges everywhere to a continuous function AND the Fourier transform is absolutely summable over the integers","(c): f continuous with (1+|x|)^{-1-delta} decay of both f and its transform","integrability alone does NOT give the pointwise identity"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.263262+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis on Euclidean space","id":"claim_c871045185872c50e3ad107b05bbe60ce99326ffffae1aec8481b784ad7e885a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Convention $\\hat f(\\xi)=\\int_{\\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-2\\pi i x\\xi}dx$. (a) (Always, as an $L^1$ identity) If $f\\in L^1(\\mathbb R)$, the periodization $Pf(x)=\\sum_{n\\in\\mathbb Z}f(x+n)$ converges absolutely for a.e. $x$, $Pf\\in L^1(\\mathbb T)$ with $\\|Pf\\|_{L^1(\\mathbb T)}\\le\\|f\\|_1$, and $\\widehat{Pf}(k)=\\hat f(k)$ for all $k\\in\\mathbb Z$. (b) (Pointwise identity) If in addition $\\sum_nf(x+n)$ converges for every $x$ to a continuous function and $\\sum_k|\\hat f(k)|<\\infty$, then $\\sum_{n\\in\\mathbb Z}f(x+n)=\\sum_{k\\in\\mathbb Z}\\hat f(k)e^{2\\pi i kx}$ for every $x$; taking $x=0$, $\\sum_nf(n)=\\sum_k\\hat f(k)$. (c) (Convenient sufficient condition) If $f$ is continuous and there are $C,\\delta>0$ with $|f(x)|\\le C(1+|x|)^{-1-\\delta}$ and $|\\hat f(\\xi)|\\le C(1+|\\xi|)^{-1-\\delta}$, then (b) applies and both series converge absolutely; this holds for every $f\\in\\mathcal S(\\mathbb R)$. (d) Scaled and multidimensional forms: for $T>0$, $\\sum_nf(nT)=T^{-1}\\sum_k\\hat f(k/T)$; for $f\\in\\mathcal S(\\mathbb R^d)$ and the lattice $\\mathbb Z^d$, $\\sum_{n\\in\\mathbb Z^d}f(x+n)=\\sum_{k\\in\\mathbb Z^d}\\hat f(k)e^{2\\pi i k\\cdot x}$; more generally for a full-rank lattice $\\Lambda$ with dual $\\Lambda^*$ and covolume $|\\Lambda|$, $\\sum_{\\lambda\\in\\Lambda}f(\\lambda)=|\\Lambda|^{-1}\\sum_{\\mu\\in\\Lambda^*}\\hat f(\\mu)$. Classic application (Jacobi theta transformation): $\\sum_ne^{-\\pi n^2t}=t^{-1/2}\\sum_ne^{-\\pi n^2/t}$ for $t>0$.","status":"unverified"}

ADDITIVITY: BESQ^delta started at y and an independent BESQ^{delta'} started at y' add to a BESQ^{delta + delta'} started at y + y'; this holds for the SQUARED process and is false for the Bessel process itself. The index nu = delta/2 - 1 is the other common parameterisation and is the one that appears in the modified Bessel functions of the transition density; delta and nu must not be confused. For delta < 2 the boundary point 0 is reached and a boundary convention (absorbing or instantaneously reflecting) must be specified; for delta >= 2 the point 0 is never reached from y > 0 and no convention is needed. The column player's LP, minimize w subject to sum_{j=1}^{n} A_{ij} * y_j <= w for all i=1,...,m, y_j >= 0, sum_j y_j = 1, is exactly the LP dual of the row player's program. Because both programs are feasible and bounded, strong LP duality guarantees their optimal values agree (v* = w*), recovering von Neumann's minimax theorem as a consequence of linear programming duality; standard LP algorithms, such as the simplex method or interior-point methods, applied to either program simultaneously compute the game's value and both players' optimal mixed strategies.","status":"unverified"}

Suppose the sequence is monotone in n at every point (f_n(x) <= f_{n+1}(x) for all n and all x, or the reverse for all n and all x), that f_n -> f pointwise, and that the limit f is continuous. Then f_n -> f UNIFORMLY on K. All four hypotheses carry weight: (a) compactness - on the non-compact [0,1) the sequence f_n(x) = x^n decreases continuously to the continuous limit 0 but not uniformly; (b) continuity of the limit - on the compact [0,1] the same f_n(x) = x^n is monotone and continuous with a discontinuous limit and the convergence is not uniform; (c) monotonicity - the moving bump f_n which is the piecewise-linear tent of height 1 on [1/(n+1), 1/n] and 0 elsewhere on [0,1] converges pointwise to 0 with all data continuous and compact, but sup |f_n| = 1; (d) continuity of each f_n - on [0,1] the indicators of the OPEN intervals, f_n = 1_{(0, 1/n)}, decrease pointwise to the identically zero function, which is continuous, on a compact space, so every hypothesis except the continuity of the f_n holds, yet sup |f_n| = 1 for every n. Monotonicity is required POINTWISE IN THE SAME DIRECTION for all x, not merely that each f_n is a monotone function of x. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 7.13]","status":"unverified"}

Then there are open intervals I containing a and J containing b and a unique continuously differentiable function g : I -> J such that g(a) = b and, within the rectangle I x J, the solution set of F(x, y) = 0 is exactly the graph {(x, g(x)) : x in I}; moreover g'(x) = -F_x(x, g(x)) / F_y(x, g(x)). Example: for F(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 - 1 (the unit circle) at (a, b) = (0, 1) one gets g(x) = sqrt(1 - x^2), the upper semicircle; no such g exists near (1, 0), where F_y = 0. General version: if F : R^{n+m} -> R^m is C^1 near (a, b), F(a, b) = 0, and the m x m Jacobian of F with respect to the y-variables at (a, b) is invertible, then near (a, b) the equation F(x, y) = 0 determines a unique C^1 map y = g(x) with g(a) = b and F(x, g(x)) = 0.","status":"unverified"}

Then the L^p(mu) norm of the y-average dominates in the direction: || integral_Y f(., y) dnu(y) ||_{L^p(dmu)} <= integral_Y || f(., y) ||_{L^p(dmu)} dnu(y). For signed or complex f the same holds provided the right-hand side is finite, and then the inner integral converges absolutely for mu-a.e. x. The inequality is the continuous form of the triangle inequality for the L^p norm and reduces to it when nu is counting measure on two points. The reverse inequality is false for p > 1 and TRUE for 0 < p <= 1 with the roles of the two sides exchanged. Special case worth naming: taking nu counting measure on the integers gives || sum_n f_n ||_p <= sum_n || f_n ||_p. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:37:33.911677+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning","id":"claim_cb9f0a5bfb69e6d801c7f9b4c969831d7a650fa1a7cd92d88cc350fba9aa3034","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $M$ predictors $f_1, \\dots, f_M$ of a target $y$ have errors $e_m = f_m - y$ with error covariance $\\Sigma_E$ (the $M \\times M$ covariance of the vector $(e_1, \\dots, e_M)$ over the population of inputs). An affine stack $\\sum_m w_m f_m + b$ with $\\sum_m w_m = 1$ has error $\\sum_m w_m e_m + b$, so after the intercept removes the mean error its risk is $w^T \\Sigma_E w$, and the optimal weights are the minimum-variance portfolio $w^* = \\Sigma_E^{-1}\\mathbf{1} / (\\mathbf{1}^T \\Sigma_E^{-1}\\mathbf{1})$; without the sum constraint the least-squares stack is the ordinary regression of $y$ on $(f_1, \\dots, f_M, 1)$. Consequently every random-matrix result about the noisy-covariance portfolio problem transfers to ensemble weighting with $q = M / n_{\\mathrm{cal}}$, $n_{\\mathrm{cal}}$ the number of calibration cases the weights are fitted on: the plug-in (least-squares) stack's out-of-sample risk is inflated by the factor $1/(1 - q)$ relative to the optimum, its in-sample risk understates the optimum by $1 - q$, and any cleaning of the covariance must be applied to $\\Sigma_E$. The covariance of the predictions themselves, $\\operatorname{Cov}(f_1, \\dots, f_M)$, is NOT the object to clean: writing $f_m = y + e_m$ it equals $\\operatorname{Var}(y)\\mathbf{1}\\mathbf{1}^T + (\\text{cross terms}) + \\Sigma_E$, a rank-one spike of the size of the signal variance over the error covariance. The stacking weight's departure from equal weights, $w - \\mathbf{1}/M$, is orthogonal to $\\mathbf{1}$, so it lives entirely in the small-eigenvalue subspace of the prediction covariance; a bulk-versus-spike cleaner applied to that matrix (Marchenko-Pastur truncation, shrinkage toward $\\operatorname{tr}/p \\cdot I$, a rotationally invariant estimator floored relative to the top eigenvalue) keeps the signal spike and destroys exactly the directions stacking needs. At $q = 0.025$ (23 members, 932 calibration rows) the whole prize from cleaning $\\Sigma_E$ is bounded by about $2.5$ percent; the prize grows like $q/(1-q)$ as the calibration set shrinks.","status":"unverified"}

Conversely, if an entire $U$ on $\\mathbb C^d$ satisfies $|U(\\zeta)|\\le C(1+|\\zeta|)^{N}e^{R|\\operatorname{Im}\\zeta|}$ for some constants $C,N$, then $U=\\hat u$ for a unique $u\\in\\mathcal E'(\\mathbb R^d)$ with $\\operatorname{supp}u\\subset B_R$. The support-and-growth correspondence is an exact equivalence; the order is not preserved in both directions - the forward implication gives the exponent $N$ from the order $N$, while the converse only returns a distribution of order at most $N+d+1$. Consequence: the exponential factor records the size of the (convex hull of the) support, the polynomial factor records smoothness versus singularity order. {"assumptions":["Counterexample: u_t + (u^2/2)_x = 0 versus (u^2/2)_t + (u^3/3)_x = 0 with left state 1 and right state 0","Rankine-Hugoniot: σ = [flux]/[density], so both entries matter","Chain-rule manipulations of the flux are valid only where the solution is C^1"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418709+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: hyperbolic conservation laws","id":"claim_cd2c0cd0a6c998918c8d20dec220a3380322e8bf670c19046ddde117aec30ea3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: the Rankine-Hugoniot condition, and hence the whole notion of weak solution, is attached to a specific pair (conserved density, flux) — not to the PDE as an equation for smooth functions. Counterexample: for smooth u, Burgers' equation u_t + (u^2/2)_x = 0 is equivalent to (u^2/2)_t + (u^3/3)_x = 0 (multiply the first by u; conversely divide where u ≠ 0). But a jump from u_l = 1 (left) to u_r = 0 (right) travels with speed [f]/[u] = (1/2 - 0)/(1 - 0) = 1/2 for the first form, and with speed (1/3 - 0)/(1/2 - 0) = 2/3 for the second: the two weak solutions are genuinely different. The same phenomenon makes the nonconservative form u_t + u u_x = 0 meaningless across a shock (the product u u_x is not a distribution for discontinuous u). Physically, the model must specify which quantity is conserved; numerically, only schemes written in the conservative form of the true conserved quantity (Lax-Wendroff theorem) converge to the correct shock speeds. Auditor's check: when a proof rewrites the flux (multiplying the equation by a function of u, changing variables u = φ(v), or using a chain rule), the manipulation is legitimate for smooth solutions only; across discontinuities it changes the answer.","status":"unverified"}

For example, the Möbius strip is not the product space of a line segment with a circle, but locally on any segment of the circle it resembles an ordinary rectangle without the global twist. {"assumptions":["T is consistent","T is effectively axiomatized (computably enumerable axiom set)","T interprets Robinson arithmetic Q"],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.378582+00:00","domain":"mathematical logic","id":"claim_cde8bcbf7d8ce7708f2314743185825fb5c4235f909300f46e471371d1a885c8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let T be a first-order theory satisfying all three hypotheses: (i) T is consistent; (ii) T is effectively axiomatized: its set of axioms is computably enumerable (equivalently, by Craig's trick, computably decidable after re-axiomatization), so theoremhood is computably enumerable; (iii) T interprets enough arithmetic - it suffices that T contains or interprets Robinson arithmetic Q. Then T is incomplete: there is a sentence G in the language of T (arithmetical under the interpretation) such that T proves neither G nor the negation of G. Consequently no consistent, effectively axiomatized theory interpreting Q is complete; in particular Peano arithmetic and ZFC, if consistent, are incomplete. Godel's original 1931 argument additionally assumed omega-consistency to rule out T proving the negation; Rosser's 1936 refinement, stated here, needs only consistency. All three hypotheses are necessary: complete consistent extensions of Q exist but are not effectively axiomatized (e.g. true arithmetic), effectively axiomatized complete consistent theories exist that do not interpret Q (e.g. the theory of dense linear orders, or Presburger arithmetic), and an inconsistent theory proves everything.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["M a local martingale with M_0 = 0","for 0 < p < 1: M continuous","for p >= 1: cadlag suffices","constants depend on p only"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627451+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cf80a57cbccec160cd5893a5f18cbdc60f4fa6097c1a6f73d35f5f00697e2593","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let M be a local martingale with M_0 = 0, let M^*_T = sup_{t <= T} |M_t| for a stopping time T, and let [M] be the quadratic variation. There are constants 0 < c_p <= C_p < infinity depending ONLY on p such that c_p E[ [M]_T^{p/2} ] <= E[ (M^*_T)^p ] <= C_p E[ [M]_T^{p/2} ]. The admissible range of p differs by regularity: for CONTINUOUS local martingales the two-sided bound holds for every 0 < p < infinity; for general cadlag local martingales it holds for every p >= 1, and the case 0 < p < 1 genuinely requires continuity (Davis' theorem covers p = 1 in the general case). In discrete time the same holds with [M]_n = sum_{k <= n} (M_k - M_{k-1})^2 the square function, for 1 <= p < infinity. The constants are UNIVERSAL in the sense of depending on p alone - not on the martingale, the filtration, the time horizon or the dimension - and they blow up as p decreases to 0 and as p increases to infinity; explicit admissible choices grow like p for the upper constant. For p = 2 the inequality is an identity with c_2 = C_2 replaced by the Ito isometry together with Doob's L^2 maximal inequality, which is the cheap case one should reach for first. [Burkholder (1973), Davis (1970), Burkholder-Davis-Gundy (1972); see Revuz and Yor, Continuous Martingales and Brownian Motion, 3rd ed., Theorem IV.4.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Little: f entire and nonconstant","Great: f holomorphic on a punctured disk about a with an isolated essential singularity at a"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T09:45:15.353295+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_cfb6b34b04c740458f4aa7f731e3fa6b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Little Picard theorem: if f is entire and nonconstant, then the complement of its image, C minus f(C), contains at most one point; i.e. a nonconstant entire function omits at most one complex value. Great Picard theorem: if f is holomorphic on a punctured disk 0 < |z - a| < r and has an essential singularity at a, then for every ε in (0,r) the image of the punctured disk 0 < |z - a| < ε is all of C with at most one point removed, and every value so attained (again with at most one exception) is attained infinitely often. Both exceptional values are genuinely possible and the count is sharp: exp(z) is entire and omits exactly the value 0, and exp(1/z) has an essential singularity at 0 and omits exactly 0 near 0. Meromorphic versions: a nonconstant meromorphic function on C omits at most two values of the Riemann sphere, and near an essential singularity a meromorphic function takes every spherical value with at most two exceptions. If f is entire and transcendental (not a polynomial), then f takes every complex value, with at most one exception, infinitely often.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["consistency of the finite-dimensional distributions under permutation and marginalisation","the state space Polish (or otherwise inner regular by compacts); the theorem fails for general measurable spaces","the conclusion is on the PRODUCT sigma-algebra only"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.781981+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cff4b22d3f4e9f129de820bfc924fd6ae8ae16e1c64314c11984e1f4a5a4588a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let T be an arbitrary index set and suppose that for every finite subset {t_1, ..., t_n} of T a probability measure mu_{t_1, ..., t_n} on R^n (or on S^n for a Polish space S with its Borel sigma-algebra) is given. Suppose the family is CONSISTENT: (i) permuting the indices permutes the measure correspondingly, and (ii) the marginal of mu_{t_1, ..., t_n, t_{n+1}} on the first n coordinates is mu_{t_1, ..., t_n}. Then there is a probability measure P on the product space S^T equipped with the PRODUCT sigma-algebra whose finite-dimensional marginals are exactly the given family, and P is unique. TWO LIMITATIONS, both routinely forgotten. FIRST, the topological hypothesis is essential: for general measurable spaces the theorem is FALSE, and there are consistent families with no extension (Andersen and Jessen); what is really needed is that the marginals be inner regular in a suitable sense, which Polish spaces provide. SECOND, the resulting measure lives on the PRODUCT sigma-algebra, every member of which is determined by countably many coordinates. When T is uncountable, sets such as {the path is continuous}, {sup_t X_t <= c}, or {the path is bounded} are therefore NOT measurable for that sigma-algebra, so the theorem does not by itself construct Brownian motion as a continuous process; it constructs a process with the right finite-dimensional laws, and a separate regularity theorem - Kolmogorov's continuity criterion - is needed to produce a modification with continuous paths. [Kolmogorov (1933); see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 2.1.21, and Billingsley, Probability and Measure, Section 36]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.477019+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d007b509b76b2574e8db1cb4d99bb511beec50788f3846f5da7d43e190951280","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For two probability measures mu and nu on a measurable space (S, A), the total variation distance is d_TV(mu, nu) = sup over A in A of |mu(A) - nu(A)|, a number in [0, 1]. If mu and nu have densities f and g with respect to a common reference measure lambda (which always exists, for instance lambda = mu + nu), then d_TV(mu, nu) = (1/2) integral |f - g| d lambda = 1 - integral min(f, g) d lambda, and the supremum is attained at A = { f > g }. Equivalent characterisations: d_TV is half the supremum of |integral h d mu - integral h d nu| over measurable h with |h| <= 1; and by the coupling characterisation, d_TV(mu, nu) = min P(X not equal to Y) over all couplings (X, Y) with X distributed as mu and Y as nu, the minimum being attained by the maximal coupling. Convergence in total variation is strictly stronger than weak convergence (point masses at 1/n converge weakly to the point mass at 0 but stay at total variation distance 1). The normalisation matters: some texts use the un-halved integral |f - g| d lambda, which lies in [0, 2].","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Boundedness of Omega is essential (the embedding is never compact on R^n, by translating a fixed bump), and for W^{1,p} rather than W_0^{1,p} some boundary regularity is needed so that an extension operator exists.","Compactness FAILS at the critical exponent q = p*, which is exactly the loss of compactness behind concentration phenomena in critical problems."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:06:45.870307+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations, Sobolev spaces","id":"claim_d00bdbb3a32698c4ecb614feccf503f1db25275537f989f81c44012bb8fa3418","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega be a bounded open subset of R^n with C^1 boundary (or any bounded extension domain, for instance a bounded Lipschitz domain), let 1 <= p < n and let p* = np/(n-p) be the Sobolev conjugate exponent. {"assumptions":["edges are present independently with the same probability p (the binomial model; the uniform model G(n,m) has the analogous statement with m = (n/2)(log n + c))","the statement is about the window p = (log n + c)/n with c fixed as n grows","the Poisson approximation is for the count of isolated vertices; other small components are negligible in this window"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.049186+00:00","domain":"random graphs (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_d041dda48ec32c5f52986ec651884b81edb7100fb10f41b597a06330618dfc66","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In the binomial random graph G(n,p) with p = (log n + c)/n for a fixed real c, the number of isolated vertices converges in distribution to a Poisson random variable with mean e^{-c} (the method of moments: the factorial moments of the count converge to those of the Poisson law), and the probability that G(n,p) is connected tends to exp(-e^{-c}) (Erdos and Renyi 1959, 1960). The obstruction to connectivity in this window is isolated vertices alone: P(G connected) - P(G has no isolated vertex) tends to 0. {"assumptions":["S symmetric positive semidefinite","the feasible set is nonempty (it always is: the simplex)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:16:12.170261+00:00","domain":"portfolio optimization / covariance estimation","id":"claim_d0a23007d09157190578bc34001ca8ab56a2324c0cee39b19878ff5e75ad0f46","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $S$ be a symmetric positive semidefinite $M \\times M$ matrix (a sample covariance) and consider the long-only minimum-variance problem $\\min_w w^T S w$ subject to $\\mathbf{1}^T w = 1$ and $w \\ge 0$. Let $w^+$ be a solution and $\\delta \\in \\mathbb{R}^M$, $\\delta \\ge 0$, the Lagrange multipliers of the nonnegativity constraints ($\\delta_m > 0$ only where $w^+_m = 0$). THEOREM (Jagannathan and Ma, 2003). $w^+$ is also the UNCONSTRAINED minimum-variance solution (subject only to $\\mathbf{1}^T w = 1$) for the modified covariance $$\\tilde S = S - \\delta \\mathbf{1}^T - \\mathbf{1}\\delta^T,$$ which is symmetric, positive semidefinite on the relevant set, and differs from $S$ by lowering the covariances of the constrained (excluded) assets with every other asset by $\\delta_m$ and their variances by $2\\delta_m$. Imposing the no-short constraint is therefore equivalent to shrinking the large entries of the sample covariance toward zero by data-determined amounts - which is why the constraint improves out-of-sample risk even when the true covariance would not call for it (\"why imposing the wrong constraints helps\"): it acts as a covariance-shrinkage estimator whose amount is chosen implicitly by the optimisation, without cross-validation.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["K symmetric positive definite","G symmetric positive semidefinite","rounding modelled as a symmetric perturbation E of G with spectral norm at most epsilon times the spectral norm of G"],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:16:35.596684+00:00","domain":"numerical linear algebra","id":"claim_d244969753d3b8416c6319f8f2c5f4c515fce7100d74b357e01c4e2202aa7d48","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $K$ be symmetric positive definite with eigenvalues $w_1 \\le \\dots \\le w_n$ and eigenvectors $U$, and let $G$ be symmetric positive semidefinite. The exact identity $V = \\mathrm{Tr}(K^{-1} G K^{-1}) = \\sum_k \\tilde G_{kk} / w_k^2$ with $\\tilde G = U^\\top G U$ holds, but if $G$ is replaced by $G + E$ with $\\|E\\|_2 \\le \\varepsilon \\|G\\|_2$ (rounding of relative size $\\varepsilon$ in the entries of $G$), the computed value changes by at most $\\varepsilon \\|G\\|_2 \\sum_k w_k^{-2} \\le \\varepsilon\\, n\\, \\|G\\|_2 / w_1^2$. When $\\|G\\|_2$ is comparable to $\\|K\\|_2^2 = w_n^2$ (as for $G = \\Phi D \\Phi^\\top$ built from the same features as $K = \\Phi\\Phi^\\top$), this is an absolute error of order $\\varepsilon\\, \\kappa(K)^2$ per eigendirection, so the trace form is not a usable number once $\\varepsilon \\kappa(K)^2 \\gtrsim 1$. If instead $G = \\Phi D \\Phi^\\top$ and $K = \\Phi \\Phi^\\top$ share a factor $\\Phi$ with $D$ diagonal nonnegative, then $V = \\sum_j D_{jj} \\|K^{-1} \\Phi_{\\cdot j}\\|^2$, and a perturbation $\\Delta$ of $\\Phi$ with $\\|\\Delta\\|_F \\le \\delta$ changes $V$ to first order by at most $2 \\sqrt{V}\\, \\sqrt{D_{\\max}}\\, \\delta / w_1$: one inverse, and the error enters through a single factor of $1/w_1$ rather than $1/w_1^2$. Measured instance: Gaussian kernel on the sphere, $d=12$, $n=4096$, $\\kappa(K) = 1.3\\times 10^{10}$, $\\varepsilon \\kappa^2 = 4\\times 10^4$: the trace form reads $3.09$, a factored form through an eigendecomposition of $G$ alone reads $25.7$ (the rounding directions of $G$ still divided by $w_k^2$), the shared-factor form reads $2.653$, and a Monte-Carlo evaluation of the same quantity reads $2.657 \\pm 0.003$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f lower semicontinuous AND bounded below (boundedness below can be relaxed to a linear minorant);","the approximation is from BELOW and increasing.","For an upper semicontinuous f bounded above the dual sup-convolution gives a decreasing sequence of Lipschitz functions."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:01:51.298930+00:00","domain":"real analysis, convex analysis","id":"claim_d260b03e2f3333274936e1cd451507f7f128ecfe5257b820323708fee2f6bbf4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X,d) be a metric space and let f : X -> (-infinity, +infinity] be lower semicontinuous and bounded below. For each n define f_n(x) = inf over y in X of ( f(y) + n d(x,y) ). Then each f_n is real-valued and n-Lipschitz, the sequence is nondecreasing, f_n <= f for every n, and f_n(x) increases to f(x) at every x. So a lower semicontinuous function bounded below is the pointwise increasing limit of Lipschitz functions. On a Hilbert space with the quadratic kernel (1/(2t))||x-y||^2 in place of n d(x,y) the same construction gives the Moreau envelope of a convex f, which is convex, differentiable with Lipschitz gradient, and increases to f as t decreases to 0.","status":"unverified"}

For the Ising model, or more generally ferromagnetic spin systems with finite-range interactions (with merely summable long-range couplings G(x,y) >= tanh(beta J_xy) by Griffiths' inequality, so exponential decay can fail), let G(x,y) = <sigma_x sigma_y> be the two-point function. The Simon-Lieb inequality bounds G(x,y) across any finite set Lambda separating x from y (x in Lambda, y outside Lambda) by G(x,y) <= sum_{u in Lambda, v not in Lambda} G_Lambda(x,u) beta J_{uv} G(v,y), with G_Lambda the two-point function of the model restricted to Lambda (free boundary condition) and beta the inverse temperature (forms with tanh(beta J_{uv}) in place of beta J_{uv} are also used), a one-step recursive bound relating the two-point function across a separating surface to the two-point function up to the boundary of Lambda times the coupling crossing it. Iterating the inequality over a sequence of nested separating sets, such as concentric boxes, yields exponential decay of G(x,y) once the associated generating function drops below its self-consistency threshold, giving a classical route, predating and complementary to the Duminil-Copin-Tassion approach, to sharpness of the phase transition and analyticity of the free energy in the high-temperature regime. It does not determine the exact critical temperature directly, only characterizing it implicitly through the inequality's self-consistency condition, and it applies specifically to ferromagnetic spin systems with a workable notion of finite separating surfaces; it does not transfer automatically to percolation, which uses combinatorially different, though philosophically related, inequalities. Typical failure: Iterating the Simon-Lieb inequality across many nested separating surfaces while implicitly assuming a geometric decay rate that has not actually been verified to be summable; turning the one-step recursive bound into exponential decay requires checking that the relevant generating function, summing G times J over the boundary, lies strictly below its self-consistency threshold, and this check is exactly where the difficulty of locating beta_c resides, so skipping it silently assumes the conclusion. {"assumptions":["a specified target distribution with a known, workable Stein characterizing operator or equation","an auxiliary coupling structure connecting to W, such as an exchangeable pair, a size-biased coupling, or a dependency graph","sufficient smoothness or explicit derivative bounds on the solution f of the Stein equation for the specific target distribution","control of the resulting expectation bound in terms of the coupling's own closeness or error parameters"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.996944+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d39aa2bb9e25135cdd42c23538dfcea568834d63bc2b2b834c74380b75fd1b82","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). To bound the distance, in Kolmogorov, Wasserstein, or total variation metric, between the law of a random variable W and a target distribution, classically the standard normal but also Poisson, exponential, and other targets, Stein's method characterizes the target law via a characterizing (Stein) equation: for the normal, E[f'(Z) - Zf(Z)] = 0 for all sufficiently smooth f if and only if Z is standard normal. Given a test function h, one solves the associated Stein equation f'(x) - xf(x) = h(x) - E[h(Z)] for f, and then bounds E[f'(W) - Wf(W)] directly using structural information about W, typically supplied by an auxiliary coupling such as an exchangeable pair, a size-biased coupling, or a dependency-graph/local-dependence construction, without going through characteristic functions or moment matching. This yields explicit, often near-optimal-rate, quantitative bounds on distributional distance for sums of dependent or weakly dependent random variables and for counts in combinatorial structures, settings where classical central limit theorem machinery is difficult to apply directly because of dependence. It does not automatically give a good bound for an arbitrary random variable, since constructing the right coupling matched to the problem's dependence structure is the substantive and typically hardest step, and the quality of the final bound is entirely determined by the quality of that coupling. Typical failure: Treating Stein's method as an automatic black box that produces a good rate on its own, when in fact the rate is entirely determined by the quality of the coupling constructed for the specific problem, such as an exchangeable pair with a large error term or a dependency graph with high maximum degree; a poorly constructed coupling yields a valid but far-from-optimal, or even useless, bound, and this construction step, rather than the abstract Stein equation itself, is where nearly all the technical difficulty and risk of error lies. Canonical reference: Stein, 1972, Proceedings of the Sixth Berkeley Symposium on Mathematical Statistics and Probability; Chen, Goldstein and Shao, Normal Approximation by Stein's Method, 2011, Springer.","status":"unverified"}

There are an open neighbourhood W of p in U and constants theta in (0,1) and c > 0 such that |f(x) - f(p)|^theta <= c |grad f(x)| for every x in W. Consequence (finite length and convergence of bounded gradient trajectories). Let x: [0, infinity) -> U solve x'(t) = -grad f(x(t)) and suppose the trajectory {x(t): t >= 0} has compact closure in U. Along the lacunary orbit 2^n, |hat_mu(2^n)| reduces to the exact arithmetic product prod_{k>=0} |cos(pi 2^{n+k}/3^{k+1})|, each factor depending only on 2^{n+k} mod 2 * 3^{k+1} (verified digit-for-digit against the direct Fourier product for n=0..16), with only k up to about 1.71n contributing; because 2 is a primitive root mod every 3^j, the exact period-average of log|cos(pi u/3^{k+1})| over units u equals -log 2 for every k, predicting an average decay of about 1.185 per level n, while the MEASURED slope of log|hat_mu(2^n)| over n=0..16 is about 1.0 per level - the decay itself is bursty (0.31 at n=0, 4.1e-8 at n=7, back up to 1.7e-5 at n=10, 4.3e-9 at n=15), the small factors being exactly the k where 2^{n+k+1} lands near an odd multiple of 3^{k+1}, though the trend matches the prediction; the exchange of sums behind the prediction is rigorous only for k up to about log_3 n, where the window covers the period 2 * 3^k. For the rational, non-Pisot ratio lambda=2/3, the currently PROVED decay rate of hat_mu is only logarithmic in the frequency (giving deficits of order n^{-c}, not summable - the family a related paper bound n^{-13/25} belongs to), while the measured/predicted decay is vastly faster; the gap between the proved logarithmic rate and the faster measured rate is exactly the missing ingredient - a lacunary Fourier estimate for the 2/3 Bernoulli convolution better than logarithmic - and closing it requires simultaneous equidistribution of 2^{n+k} mod 3^{k+1} across k up to about 1.71n, an unproved, Erdos-Kahane-barrier-type statement (a literature check found proved Fourier decay for rational lambda=p/q is logarithmic-power in general, and known absolute-continuity results for algebraic parameters reach down to about lambda=0.7995, above 2/3=0.667). {"assumptions":["independence of the matrix entries or summands, each with finite moments up to the order being matched, typically four","matching of the first four (or the relevant number of) moments between the actual entry distribution and the Gaussian reference, up to a specified small error","sufficient smoothness, typically several bounded derivatives, of the test function F used in the swapping argument","a separate mechanism, such as local relaxation flow or a priori rigidity estimates, to transfer from smooth-test-function statements to the actual eigenvalue statistics of interest"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.997682+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d62d01195d629cfaace32a339dd8b3931fc1ee479898a520c29aeefdbd2472a7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The Lindeberg exchange (swapping) principle proves distributional limit theorems by replacing the summands or matrix entries of a random object one at a time with Gaussian (or other reference) analogues, bounding the resulting change in E[F] for a sufficiently smooth test function F via a Taylor expansion at each swap, provided the relevant moments, typically up to third or fourth order depending on the smoothness assumed of F, agree between the original and replacement distributions. In random matrix theory, the Tao-Vu four-moment theorem states that for Wigner matrices, local eigenvalue statistics such as gap distributions at a fixed bulk location are universal, independent of the specific entry distribution, provided the first four moments of the off-diagonal entries match those of the Gaussian (GOE/GUE) case up to a small, quantified error, with a weaker three-moment matching sufficing for some global statistics; this is the primary technical engine behind Wigner-Dyson-Mehta universality results beyond the exactly solvable Gaussian ensembles. It does not apply directly to test functions or statistics that are insufficiently smooth, requiring a separate regularization step, typically via a local relaxation flow or Dyson Brownian motion argument, to pass from smooth test functions to eigenvalue counting functions or individual eigenvalue locations, and it requires the specific moment-matching order assumed, with fewer matched moments giving correspondingly weaker conclusions. Typical failure: Applying the four-moment theorem's universality conclusion directly to a non-smooth statistic, such as the exact location or gap of a specific eigenvalue or an indicator-type event, without the additional Green's function comparison or local relaxation machinery needed to pass from smooth test functions to such statistics; the raw Lindeberg swapping argument by itself only controls E[F(eigenvalues)] for smooth F, and asserting the full local universality conclusion from moment matching alone skips this substantial extra step. Canonical reference: Lindeberg, 1922, Mathematische Zeitschrift; Tao and Vu, 2011, Acta Mathematica; Erdos and Yau, A Dynamical Approach to Random Matrix Theory, 2017, American Mathematical Society (Courant Lecture Notes).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["mu is a T-invariant probability measure","partitions are finite or have finite static entropy"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438227+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, entropy","id":"claim_d643cf301f6f85cdf8c9e8de5370d025f0501ae66a766e597b735e7610396bee","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \\mathcal{B}, \\mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system. For a finite (or countable, with finite entropy) measurable partition $\\xi = \\{A_1, \\dots, A_k\\}$ put $H_\\mu(\\xi) = -\\sum_i \\mu(A_i) \\log \\mu(A_i)$ (with $0 \\log 0 = 0$), and $\\xi^n_0 = \\bigvee_{j=0}^{n-1} T^{-j}\\xi$, the partition into sets $A_{i_0} \\cap T^{-1}A_{i_1} \\cap \\dots \\cap T^{-(n-1)}A_{i_{n-1}}$ (the $n$-step itineraries). The entropy of $T$ relative to $\\xi$ is $h_\\mu(T, \\xi) = \\lim_{n\\to\\infty} \\frac1n H_\\mu(\\xi^n_0)$ (the limit exists because $n \\mapsto H_\\mu(\\xi^n_0)$ is subadditive; it also equals $\\inf_n \\frac1n H_\\mu(\\xi^n_0)$ and $\\lim_n H_\\mu(\\xi \\mid \\xi^n_1)$). The Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy is $h_\\mu(T) = \\sup_\\xi h_\\mu(T, \\xi)$ over finite partitions, in $[0, \\infty]$. Facts used constantly: $h_\\mu(T, \\xi) \\le H_\\mu(\\xi) \\le \\log k$; $h_\\mu(T, \\xi) \\le h_\\mu(T, \\eta) + H_\\mu(\\xi \\mid \\eta)$ for partitions $\\xi, \\eta$; $h_\\mu(T^m) = m\\, h_\\mu(T)$ for $m \\ge 1$; the Kolmogorov-Sinai generator theorem: if $\\xi$ is a generator ($\\bigvee_{j \\ge 0} T^{-j}\\xi$ generates $\\mathcal{B}$ mod $\\mu$, or $\\bigvee_{j\\in\\mathbb{Z}}$ for invertible $T$) then $h_\\mu(T) = h_\\mu(T, \\xi)$; and if $\\xi_m$ is an increasing sequence of partitions generating $\\mathcal{B}$ then $h_\\mu(T, \\xi_m) \\uparrow h_\\mu(T)$. On a compact metric space, partitions of diameter $< \\varepsilon$ with $\\varepsilon \\to 0$ are such a sequence. The map $\\mu \\mapsto h_\\mu(T)$ on invariant measures is affine, but it is NOT in general continuous or even upper semicontinuous in the weak* topology; upper semicontinuity holds when $T$ is expansive (and for $C^\\infty$ maps of compact manifolds by Newhouse), which is what guarantees measures of maximal entropy exist in those cases.","status":"unverified"}

Then for every x with |x - x0| = r < R, R^{n-2} (R - r)/(R + r)^{n-1} u(x0) <= u(x) <= R^{n-2} (R + r)/(R - r)^{n-1} u(x0). {"assumptions":["free entries independent standard Gaussian, H = W/sqrt(n)","f Lipschitz; no other regularity","the bound is around the mean, which is not identified here"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.544234+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d6862b4e3c8c63b6e20e398a7e0d94968e582011da1837ac900c1fbb41e8f5be","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let W be a real symmetric n by n matrix whose entries W_{ij} for i <= j are independent standard Gaussians, and let H = W / sqrt(n) with eigenvalues lambda_1, ..., lambda_n. Let f be Lipschitz with constant ||f||_L. Then for every t > 0, P( | (1/n) sum_{i=1}^n f(lambda_i) - E (1/n) sum_i f(lambda_i) | >= t ) <= 2 exp( - n^2 t^2 / (4 ||f||_L^2) ). The exponent scales like n^2 t^2, not n t^2: linear eigenvalue statistics are FAR more concentrated than an average of n independent samples would be, and their fluctuations are of order 1/n rather than 1/sqrt(n). This is a consequence of the eigenvalue repulsion built into the matrix model, and it is one of the few places where a naive independence heuristic gives the wrong exponent by a whole power of n. The result needs only Lipschitz f - no smoothness, no boundedness - and it is a statement about concentration around the MEAN, not about identifying the mean, which is the separate content of Wigner's theorem. The constant 4 in the denominator is tied to the stated normalisation (independent standard Gaussians for the free entries, then divided by sqrt(n)); a different convention rescales it. [standard; the argument is Hoffman-Wielandt plus Gaussian Lipschitz concentration, e.g. Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni, An Introduction to Random Matrices, Theorem 2.3.5]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a metric space","Y is a topological space (metric suffices, and is the usual case)","f: X x Y -> R is separately continuous: continuous in each variable with the other held fixed","for the residual-set-of-continuity-points consequence, X x Y is a Baire space (e.g. X, Y complete metric)","values are real (or in a metric space in which the partition-of-unity averaging makes sense, e.g. a locally convex space)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.815145+00:00","domain":"real analysis, Baire classes, separate continuity","id":"claim_d6a3e76764dc5394e33eca6c37c02af4c15a58c1386d4a14e4041123cff48df9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Recall that a real function g on a topological space Z is of BAIRE CLASS ONE if it is the pointwise limit of a sequence of continuous real functions on Z. THEOREM (Baire for R x R; Rudin in this generality): let X be a METRIC space, let Y be a topological space (in particular a metric space), and let f: X x Y -> R be SEPARATELY CONTINUOUS, i.e. for each fixed y the map x -> f(x,y) is continuous on X and for each fixed x the map y -> f(x,y) is continuous on Y. Then f is of Baire class one on X x Y: there is a sequence of continuous functions f_n: X x Y -> R with f_n(x,y) -> f(x,y) for every (x,y). CONSEQUENCE (Baire's theorem on functions of the first class): if in addition X x Y is a Baire space - for instance if X and Y are both complete metric, or both locally compact Hausdorff - then the set of points at which f is JOINTLY continuous is a dense G_delta subset of X x Y, and its complement is meagre. So a separately continuous function is jointly continuous at 'most' points, in the sense of category. CLASSICAL EXTENSION: a function of n variables that is separately continuous in each variable is of Baire class n - 1 (Lebesgue); the case n = 2 is the theorem above. SHARP EDGES. (a) Separate continuity does NOT give joint continuity: f(x,y) = xy/(x^2 + y^2) with f(0,0) = 0 is separately continuous on R^2, indeed continuous on each line through the origin, and is discontinuous at the origin (it equals 1/2 on the diagonal). The theorem therefore cannot be strengthened to continuity anywhere in particular, only to a residual set of continuity points. (b) The metric structure of the first factor is essential to the proof, which builds a locally finite partition of unity on X; for arbitrary topological factors the statement requires extra hypotheses and should not be quoted in that generality. (c) The consequence about continuity points needs X x Y to be a Baire space; on a non-Baire domain 'dense G_delta' carries no information, and the conclusion is vacuous. (d) Baire class one is a statement about POINTWISE limits; it gives no uniform convergence, and the limit functions f_n constructed in the proof are not monotone in n. (e) The converse is false and is not being claimed: plenty of Baire class one functions on a product are not separately continuous.","status":"unverified"}
