{"assumptions":["d is an integer >=2","Independent standard Gaussian input blocks a,b in R^d","Noiseless binary labels and disagreement loss","Independent training examples; randomized learners allowed","Orthogonal equivariance is required only for the single-target corollary","0<epsilon<c/2; fixed 0<delta<1 for the stated asymptotic; use epsilon<c/4 in the expected-risk formula"],"created_at":"2026-10-22T02:42:45.469501+00:00","domain":"statistical learning theory","id":"claim_d78c59562ff1370a5f041f4a2d1471299a379d138c7e30cc148d6d85948c6dce","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let d>=2 be an integer, let X=(a,b) have the standard Gaussian law on R^(2d), and let H_d={h_U(a,b)=sign(a^T U b): U in O(d)}. Define rho(h,g)=Pr[h(X)!=g(X)], and let D(H_d,rho,t) be its t-packing number. There is an absolute c>0 such that D(H_d,rho,t)>=(c/t)^(d(d-1)/2). Consequently any learner which, for each h in H_d, achieves disagreement error at most epsilon with probability at least 1-delta from n independent labeled examples must satisfy n >= (d(d-1)/2) log_2(c/(2epsilon)) + log_2(1-delta). This is useful for 0<epsilon<c/2 and fixed delta in (0,1). The class H_d is contained in the orthogonal orbit of f(x)=sign(sum_{i=1}^d x_i^2-sum_{i=d+1}^{2d} x_i^2). Thus an orthogonally equivariant learner of this single target under the standard Gaussian law has a fixed-confidence Omega(d^2 log(1/epsilon)) lower bound as epsilon decreases below an absolute constant. With expected disagreement risk epsilon, the corresponding explicit bound is (d(d-1)/2) log_2(c/(4epsilon))-1. This is an existing result of Li, Zhang and Arora, not new research; it concerns classification, not square-loss regression.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751964+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_d808bc15a0303b9690e36c075fb8407e6aa1c7ddf475cac89c2eb1a5636847d8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The monotone convergence theorem for an INCREASING sequence 0 <= f_1 <= f_2 <= ... needs no integrability hypothesis at all: integral f_n dmu increases to integral (lim f_n) dmu in [0, infinity]. The downward statement is FALSE without an extra hypothesis. On R with Lebesgue measure, f_n = 1_{[n, infinity)} decreases pointwise to 0, yet integral f_n = infinity for every n. The correct downward version requires f_1 in L^1 (equivalently, on a finite measure space with a bounded f_1): if f_n decreases pointwise to f and f_1 is integrable then integral f_n -> integral f, which follows from applying upward monotone convergence to f_1 - f_n. FATOU'S LEMMA, integral liminf f_n <= liminf integral f_n for f_n >= 0, is strict in general and its strictness is exactly the escaping-mass and concentrating-mass phenomena: with f_n = 1_{[n, n+1]} on R, liminf f_n = 0 pointwise so the left side is 0 while the right side is 1; with f_n = n 1_{(0, 1/n)} on [0,1] the left side is 0 and the right side is again 1. Reverse Fatou, limsup integral f_n <= integral limsup f_n, requires an integrable UPPER bound f_n <= g in L^1, and fails without one: for f_n = n 1_{(0, 1/n)} on [0,1] the pointwise limsup is 0 with integral 0, while limsup integral f_n = 1, so the inequality is violated - and no integrable g dominates all the f_n. [standard; e.g. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorems 2.14 and 2.15]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X and Y are topological spaces and X x Y carries the product topology","for the equality: both X and Y are second countable (a countable base of open sets); separable metric suffices","B(X) tensor B(Y) denotes the sigma-algebra generated by measurable rectangles, not its completion","the inclusion B(X) tensor B(Y) inside B(X x Y) needs no countability hypothesis"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402216+00:00","domain":"measure theory and topology, Borel structures on products","id":"claim_d85e091e5868ae9cbf056305f26be57cebf2da93d681eeb18aff1182d687f85d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X and Y be topological spaces and give X x Y the product topology. Write B(Z) for the Borel sigma-algebra of a space Z and B(X) tensor B(Y) for the product sigma-algebra, i.e. the sigma-algebra on X x Y generated by the measurable rectangles A x B with A in B(X) and B in B(Y). Then: (i) ALWAYS B(X) tensor B(Y) is contained in B(X x Y), because the two coordinate projections are continuous, hence Borel measurable. (ii) If X and Y are both SECOND COUNTABLE (each has a countable base of open sets), then equality holds: B(X x Y) = B(X) tensor B(Y). In particular this applies to separable metric spaces, so B(R^(m+n)) = B(R^m) tensor B(R^n), and to Polish spaces and to countable products of second countable spaces. Practical consequence: for second countable targets, a map into X x Y is Borel measurable exactly when both components are, and Borel functions of two variables are jointly measurable in the product sense - which is what lets Fubini-Tonelli be applied to Borel functions. WHERE IT FAILS: second countability is not a technicality. Let X be a set of cardinality strictly greater than the continuum equipped with the discrete topology, so that B(X) is the full power set and X x X is discrete. The diagonal {(x,x)} is closed, hence Borel in X x X, but by a classical theorem (B. V. Rao) the diagonal of X belongs to P(X) tensor P(X) if and only if the cardinality of X is at most the continuum. So B(X x X) strictly contains B(X) tensor B(X). The underlying reason is structural: every set in a product sigma-algebra is already measurable with respect to a countably generated pair of sub-sigma-algebras, so a product sigma-algebra can only see countably many 'coordinates' at a time, while the product topology of a non-second-countable space produces open sets that need uncountably many. A second warning of the same kind: for Lebesgue sigma-algebras the analogous equality is FALSE - the Lebesgue sigma-algebra of R^(m+n) is strictly larger than the product of the Lebesgue sigma-algebras of R^m and R^n; it is its completion.","status":"unverified"}

paired nonzero initialization with fixed nu in (0,1], both-layer GD with
step 1/2, and label-noise-averaged clean risk Q. Let alpha=alpha_e and
let b_h denote C009's full-kernel rates. Set

eta_e=(b2+b12)/b1 ~ e,
rho_e=kappa sqrt(eta_e), kappa>0 fixed,
sigma_e=2alpha sqrt(rho_e),
t0_e=log(1/sqrt(eta_e)).

Here sigma_e is the amplitude of independent symmetric label noise.
It is asymptotic to sqrt(kappa) e^(9/4). The network step size remains
1/2; eta_e in this proof is a spectral ratio, not that step size.

Let F_e(z) be the continuously interpolated frozen risk divided by
alpha^2. Define its central-time version
G_e(s)=F_e((t0_e+s)/b1). Then, uniformly on compact real s intervals,

G_e'(s)/(2 eta_e) -> H_kappa(s)
       =kappa exp(-s)-exp(-2s)-1,
G_e''(s)/(2 eta_e) -> H_kappa'(s)
       =-kappa exp(-s)+2exp(-2s).

Equivalently, the normalized value differences converge locally uniformly:

[G_e(s)-G_e(0)]/(2 eta_e) -> V_kappa(s)-V_kappa(0),
V_kappa(s)=-kappa exp(-s)+(1/2)exp(-2s)-s.

If kappa>2, define z_+=(kappa+sqrt(kappa^2-4))/2 and
z_-=(kappa-sqrt(kappa^2-4))/2. The frozen curve has a central strict local
minimum at scaled time tending to s_min=-log z_+, and a subsequent strict
local maximum at scaled time tending to s_max=-log z_-.
In small fixed neighborhoods of those two points there is exactly one
frozen stationary point of the indicated type for sufficiently small e.
The actual nonlinear discrete-GD risk has strict descent-rise-descent
witnesses near these points, with probability tending to one in the
iterated even-width-then-feature-scale limit. Its interval minimizers and
maximizers on these separate neighborhoods have the same scaled limits.
Its resulting central local peak obeys

b1 k_peak-t0_e -> s_max,
k_peak ~ (2pi/nu^2) e^(-1) log(1/e),

in that iterated probabilistic sense. The first assertion refers to every
maximizer in a chosen sufficiently small neighborhood of s_max; it does
not assert that all actual extrema are unique.

For 0<kappa<2, the FROZEN interpolated risk is strictly decreasing on any
fixed compact central s window for sufficiently small e. No monotonicity
of actual finite-width risk is asserted. At kappa=2 the leading derivative
has a degenerate zero; this proof does not resolve its finite-e unfolding.
Thus 2 is a threshold for this limiting central-window shape, not a proved
global critical noise level or a global absence theorem.

## 2. Uniform derivative limit

The exact frozen curve is
F_e(z)=rho_e(1-exp(-b0 z))^2
      +sum_(h=1,2,12)[exp(-2b_h z)+rho_e(1-exp(-b_h z))^2].
Its nonconstant h derivative with respect to z is
2 b_h q_h [rho_e-(1+rho_e)q_h], q_h=exp(-b_h z).
At z=(t0_e+s)/b1, q1=sqrt(eta_e)exp(-s). Therefore its contribution to
G_e'(s)/(2eta_e) is exactly
kappa exp(-s)-(1+kappa sqrt(eta_e))exp(-2s).

For h=2,12, b_h/b1=O(eta_e) and
q_h=1+O(eta_e log(1/eta_e)), uniformly on compact s sets. Their combined
contribution to G_e'(s)/(2eta_e) tends to -1, since their b_h/b1 weights
sum to eta_e. Differentiating with respect to s makes their contribution
tend to zero: the extra b_h/b1 factor is O(eta_e).
The constant-mode term and its s derivatives tend to zero after division
by eta_e. Indeed b0/b1 is of order 1/e, t0_e is of order log(1/e), and
exp[-(b0/b1)(t0_e+s)] decays faster than every power of e on compact s
sets. These exact formulas prove both uniform derivative limits.
Integration from zero proves the uniform value-difference limit.

## 3. Limiting stationary points and risk witnesses

Writing z=exp(-s)>0, H_kappa=kappa z-z^2-1.
For kappa>2 its roots are z_+>1 and z_-<1 with product one.
At s_min=-log z_+, H_kappa'=z_+ sqrt(kappa^2-4)>0;
at s_max=-log z_-, H_kappa'=-z_- sqrt(kappa^2-4)<0.
Thus V has a strict minimum then a strict maximum. Compact uniform
convergence of H and H' gives a unique frozen critical point near each,
of the same type; the derivative is bounded away from zero outside small
root neighborhoods inside a fixed central compact window.

Choose delta>0 sufficiently small. The four scaled times
s_min-delta, s_min, s_max, s_max+delta are increasing and have strict
limiting value inequalities descent-rise-descent. Rounded integer times
floor((t0_e+s)/b1) have scaled grid error at most b1, which tends to zero.
The associated frozen risk differences therefore have strictly positive
margins of order alpha^2 eta_e. The same value convergence provides a
strict gap away from the unique minimum or maximum in each separate
small neighborhood.

For 0<kappa<2, completion of the square gives
H_kappa=-(z-kappa/2)^2+kappa^2/4-1<0 for every z>0.
Its maximum is strictly negative, so compact uniform derivative
convergence implies the stated frozen decrease on each fixed compact
s window. This does not control scaled times escaping all compacts.

## 4. Actual nonlinear GD and order of limits

For each fixed e, rho_e, alpha_e and all interval endpoints are fixed
numbers, and all involved integer times lie below T_e=ceil(e^(-5/2))
for sufficiently small e. Labels remain bounded. C010's independent-pair
finite-horizon comparison therefore controls every involved actual risk
uniformly through T_e as width grows, including all sixteen noise
patterns. Multiplication of the error by the fixed positive factor
1/(alpha_e^2 eta_e) preserves convergence to zero for this FIXED e.
It follows, first taking width to infinity then e to zero, that the
actual risk value differences converge to the same V differences and
inherit the strict four witnesses. The positive local value gaps transfer
the interval minimizers and maximizers to s_min and s_max. No derivative
comparison for the actual nonlinear network is needed or claimed.

Finally eta_e~e, b1~nu^2 e/(4pi), so t0_e~(1/2)log(1/e) and the displayed
peak time follows. This theorem concerns a different joint-noise regime
from C011's fixed-rho phase comparison; neither proof exchanges limits.

## 5. Exact concrete witness certificate, kappa=5/2

Here z_+=2, z_-=1/2. Use z values 3,2,1/2,1/4 in decreasing order,
so the corresponding s=-log z and integer times increase. The primitive
values are respectively

-3+log 3, -3+log 2, -9/8-log 2, -19/32-2log 2.

Their required margins are
log(3/2), 15/8-2log 2, log 2-17/32, all strictly positive.
For fully checkable bounds, log(3/2)>1/3 and
7/12<log 2<3/4 follow from integrals of 1/t: the lower bound splits
[1,2] into [1,3/2] and [3/2,2] and uses right-endpoint rectangles.
For the upper bound write t=1+x and use
1/(1+x)<=1-x/2 on [0,1], strict in the interior, since the difference
has numerator x(1-x)/2. The margins exceed 1/3,3/8,5/96 respectively.
This certifies a specific joint-noise witness choice by exact rational
bounds, not a floating-point estimate of a bifurcation.

## Remaining scope

The exact finite-e global onset, the degenerate kappa=2 case, interaction
with the initial constant-mode transient, iid sampling, fixed-positive
noise and all-time nonlinear dynamics remain open. These restrictions
matter: a central-window derivative result cannot imply that no other
double-descent pattern occurs elsewhere in time. Pairing and finite
support remain as in C010. Dependencies C009/C010 and this argument
await independent mathematical review; specialist novelty is unestablished.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726283+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis / dispersive PDE","id":"claim_d948b0ea69eecd49bd6d6367620cfaf6003daf10d9fece613e380a2beca5623f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: the Christ–Kiselev lemma passes from an untruncated space-time bound L^p_t → L^q_t to its causal truncation ∫_{s<t} only when p < q strictly. At p = q the truncation can be unbounded even when the full operator is bounded. Concrete counterexample on L²(R): let K(t,s) = sin(t−s)/(t−s) (continuous, locally bounded). The full operator is convolution with the sinc kernel, whose Fourier multiplier is π·1_{[−1,1]}(ξ) (up to normalization), so it is bounded on L² with norm ≈ π. Its causal truncation is convolution with k(u) = 1_{u>0} sin(u)/u, whose multiplier is m(ξ) = ∫_0^∞ e^{−iuξ} sin(u)/u du; using ∫_0^∞ sin(u) sin(uξ)/u du = (1/2) log |(1+ξ)/(1−ξ)|, the imaginary part of m is −(1/2) log|(1+ξ)/(1−ξ)|, which is unbounded as ξ → ±1. A convolution operator on L²(R) is bounded if and only if its multiplier is in L^∞, so the truncated operator is unbounded on L²: p = q = 2 fails. Consequence for PDE: the retarded (Duhamel) Strichartz estimate at the double endpoint q = q̃ = 2 cannot be obtained from the untruncated estimate by Christ–Kiselev; it is exactly the case Keel–Tao had to prove directly. {"assumptions":["for the smoothing transform: existence of alpha solving E[sum_i T_i^alpha]=1 in the admissible range, plus regularity conditions such as E[sum_i T_i^alpha log^+ T_i]<infinity from Durrett-Liggett/Biggins theory","for Poisson-Dirichlet: a well-defined subordinator, or fragmentation/coalescent structure, whose ranked, normalized jump sizes are being studied","independence of (T_i) from the i.i.d. copies (W_i) in the smoothing transform equation","non-degeneracy conditions ruling out the trivial Dirac-mass-at-0 solution"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.998030+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d95edc3570f77641129fb8247438ed5ea704bbccb6be4cad5233917af61c0692","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The smoothing transform concerns fixed points of the distributional equation W =_d sum_i T_i W_i, where (T_i) is a given, typically random, sequence of nonnegative weights and (W_i) are i.i.d. copies of W independent of (T_i); such fixed points arise as limits of branching random walk martingales, including derivative martingale limits, or of Mandelbrot multiplicative cascades, and their tail behavior, characterized by a power-law index alpha solving E[sum_i T_i^alpha]=1 or a related equation, governs the limit's regular variation. Durrett and Liggett characterized the solution set of the smoothing transform equation, establishing existence, uniqueness up to a scaling constant, and the precise tail index under moment conditions on (T_i), a result foundational for analyzing branching random walk boundary and derivative martingale limits and related models such as the random energy model. Separately, Poisson-Dirichlet distributions PD(alpha,theta) arise as the limiting law of ranked, normalized jump sizes of a subordinator, of ranked cycle lengths in random permutations, or of ranked masses in fragmentation and coalescent processes, characterized via the stick-breaking (GEM) construction or via a Poisson process of jumps of a stable subordinator normalized by its total mass. Neither result gives an explicit closed-form density for the general fixed point or limit; the smoothing transform's fixed point is typically characterized only implicitly, through its tail index and functional equation, and both results require specific moment or regular-variation conditions on the input weights or subordinator to hold. Typical failure: Assuming the smoothing transform has a unique nontrivial fixed point up to scale without checking that the characteristic equation E[sum T_i^alpha]=1 actually has a solution in the admissible range, or without the Durrett-Liggett/Biggins regularity conditions, particularly in boundary cases such as the critical branching random walk where the derivative martingale, rather than the ordinary martingale, is the relevant object; applying the generic smoothing-transform tail behavior in a boundary or degenerate parameter regime without re-deriving it is a common source of incorrect tail-index claims. Canonical reference: Durrett and Liggett, 1983, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Biggins and Kyprianou, 2005, Electronic Journal of Probability; Pitman and Yor, 1997, Annals of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

The notion of absolute continuity allows one to obtain generalizations of the relationship between the two central operations of calculus—differentiation and integration. This relationship is commonly characterized in the framework of Riemann integration, but with absolute continuity it may be formulated in terms of Lebesgue integration. For real-valued functions on the real line, two interrelated notions appear: absolute continuity of functions and absolute continuity of measures. These two notions are generalized in different directions. The usual derivative of a function is related to the Radon–Nikodym derivative, or density, of a measure. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726371+00:00","domain":"hyperbolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_dbf122d5a238489aa083fdb44f89336d4d034fb877e0be5e3ba3b1dc4f1ae3c4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: 'the solution at (t,x) depends only on the data on the sphere ∂B(x,t)', i.e. sharp propagation on the light cone with no tail, holds only in odd space dimensions n ≥ 3. Finite speed of propagation (support in {|x| ≤ t + R}) holds in every dimension; the sharp inner edge does not. Counterexample n = 1: with u0 = 0 and u1 = 1_{[−1,1]}, d'Alembert's formula gives u(t,x) = (1/2)∫_{x−t}^{x+t} u1, so u(t,0) = 1 for every t ≥ 1 — the disturbance never leaves the origin. Counterexample n = 2: with u0 = 0 and u1 = 1_{B(0,1)}, Poisson's formula gives u(t,0) = (1/2π)∫_{|y|<1} (t² − |y|²)^{−1/2} dy > 0 for every t > 1 — a decaying tail behind the wavefront (this is why a splash on a pond is felt long after the front passes, while a sound pulse in three dimensions is heard once). Practical consequence: statements like 'the data inside B(x,t) do not matter' or 'the solution vanishes after the front passes' are valid only for odd n ≥ 3, and any argument that tacitly extends them to n = 1, 2 or to even dimensions (or to variable-coefficient / curved-background wave equations, where strong Huygens generally fails even in odd dimensions) is unsound.","status":"unverified"}

A cold arrival triggers deterministic setup tau>=0, which is never cancelled; arrivals during setup wait. Set p=exp(-lambda g), x=lambda tau and rho=lambda/mu. Busy, on-idle, off and setup occupy fractions rho, (1-rho)(1-p)/(1+xp), (1-rho)p/(1+xp), and (1-rho)xp/(1+xp). {"assumptions":["U open with lambda_1 > 0 on H^1_0(U) (e.g. U bounded, or bounded in one direction, or of finite measure)","g in L^2(U)","u the weak solution of the Dirichlet heat equation with u(0) = g","the equality case requires the infimum defining lambda_1 to be attained, e.g. U bounded"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.105957+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_dccca23e6eedae7c488796bf4490a59edff019e1d479e546a6dbd3a3e781c655","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $U\\subset\\mathbb R^n$ be open with $\\lambda_1=\\inf\\{\\|\\nabla v\\|_{L^2}^2/\\|v\\|_{L^2}^2:v\\in H^1_0(U),v\\ne0\\}>0$; this positivity holds in particular when $U$ is bounded, when $U$ is merely bounded in one direction, and when $U$ has finite measure. Among nonnegative randomized weights S satisfying E[S|X]=1 and E[P(S>0|X)]=gamma, the minimum of J(S)=E[S^2 Z(X)] is attained by S_star=I/pi_star(X), where I conditional on X is Bernoulli(pi_star(X)) and pi_star(X)=min(1,c*sqrt(Z(X))). {"assumptions":["(X, B, mu, T) is a measure-preserving system on a standard (Lebesgue) probability space","G is a compact metrizable group, m its normalized Haar measure","phi : X -> G is Borel measurable","the fibre action is by left translation, T_phi(x,g) = (Tx, phi(x) g)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.731878+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, skew products and cocycles","id":"claim_ddecdf9c38acba7f9d1a20280128c4273217092304e304e1c131cecbf3f30d61","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, B, mu, T) be a measure-preserving system on a standard probability space, let G be a compact metrizable group with normalized Haar measure m, and let phi : X -> G be measurable (the cocycle generator). The G-extension, or skew product, is the transformation

  T_phi(x, g) = (T x, phi(x) g)   on   (X x G, B x Borel(G), mu x m).

It preserves mu x m: for fixed x the fibre map g -> phi(x) g is a left translation, and Haar measure on a compact group is left invariant (compactness is what makes Haar a probability measure, so that mu x m is a probability measure). Iterating, T_phi^n(x, g) = (T^n x, phi_n(x) g) with the cocycle phi_n(x) = phi(T^{n-1} x) * ... * phi(T x) * phi(x), which satisfies the cocycle identity phi_{n+k}(x) = phi_k(T^n x) * phi_n(x).

Two standard obstructions to ergodicity are built into the definition. (i) If phi takes values in a proper closed subgroup H of G, then every set of the form X x (union of right cosets H g) is T_phi-invariant, so T_phi is not ergodic. (ii) More generally if there is a measurable u : X -> G with phi(x) = u(T x)^{-1} h(x) u(x) for h taking values in a proper closed subgroup, the same conclusion holds after the measurable change of coordinates (x, g) -> (x, u(x) g); cocycles differing in this way are called cohomologous, and ergodicity of T_phi depends only on the cohomology class. Note the sides: with the convention above the cocycle acts by LEFT translation and the invariant objects are RIGHT cosets; the opposite convention T_phi(x,g) = (Tx, g phi(x)) swaps them, and mixing the two conventions is the usual source of sign/side errors in the ergodicity criteria.","status":"unverified"}

Assume xi_0 has finite second moment and that, conditional on z_k, the next chain state is independent of xi_k (in particular deterministic initial xi_0 with the natural chain filtration suffices). Define p_k^i=P(z_k=i), q_k^i=E[xi_k 1_{z_k=i}], Q_k^i=E[xi_k xi_k^T 1_{z_k=i}]. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.627278+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_de27015aaa0fed8be3e6e4717dc3b361b73aac1ab1054852f520fd6389b23345","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A linear operator T: X -> Y between Banach spaces is compact if the image T(B_X) of the closed unit ball is relatively compact in Y; equivalently, every bounded sequence (x_k) in X has a subsequence along which (T x_k) converges in Y. A compact operator is bounded. Facts: (1) the compact operators K(X, Y) form a closed linear subspace of the bounded operators B(X, Y), and compositions of a compact operator with bounded operators on either side are compact, so K(X) = K(X, X) is a closed two-sided ideal of B(X); (2) every finite-rank bounded operator is compact, and a norm limit of finite-rank operators is compact; when Y is a Hilbert space (more generally when Y has the approximation property) every compact operator is such a limit - for Banach spaces in general this fails (Enflo, 1973); (3) the identity of an infinite-dimensional Banach space is not compact (Riesz's lemma: the unit ball is not compact), so a compact operator on an infinite-dimensional space is never invertible; (4) Riesz-Schauder theory: for compact T on an infinite-dimensional Banach space the spectrum sigma(T) is a countable (possibly finite) set whose only possible accumulation point is 0, 0 belongs to sigma(T), every nonzero spectral value is an eigenvalue with finite-dimensional generalised eigenspace, and for lambda != 0 the operator lambda - T is injective if and only if it is surjective (the Fredholm alternative: either (lambda - T) x = y has a unique solution for every y, or the homogeneous equation has a nontrivial solution, and then the inhomogeneous one is solvable exactly for y annihilated by the kernel of the adjoint); (5) a compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues tending to 0 (the spectral theorem); (6) integral operators (Kf)(x) = integral k(x, y) f(y) dy with a continuous kernel on a compact domain, or with an L^2 kernel (Hilbert-Schmidt operators), are compact, and so is every diagonal operator on l^2 whose entries tend to 0. Compact perturbations preserve the essential spectrum and the Fredholm index (Atkinson).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space","a one-parameter family of unitaries or an exponential e^{itT} is being used","the continuity and self-adjointness hypotheses are the ones at issue"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.772569+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, spectral theory, quantum dynamics","id":"claim_df9328ea820c9b58103e280388d82cc43f63148f9a76b0b2e1fdd63f459b8d1b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypotheses: (i) U(t) is unitary for every t ∈ ℝ and satisfies the group law on all of ℝ; (ii) t ↦ U(t)x is continuous (weak continuity or, on a separable space, weak measurability suffices, but some regularity is required); (iii) the generator is self-adjoint. What fails. Without any continuity: pick a discontinuous additive function φ: ℝ → ℝ (a Hamel basis construction) and set H = ℂ, U(t) = e^{iφ(t)}. This is a one-parameter group of unitaries with U(0) = 1, but φ is non-measurable and unbounded on every interval, so U(t) is not of the form e^{ita} for any real a; no generator exists. Hence 'one-parameter unitary group' without a continuity hypothesis carries no spectral information. Overshooting in the other direction: if one assumes t ↦ U(t) is continuous in operator norm, then the generator is necessarily bounded, so norm continuity is the wrong hypothesis for Schrodinger evolutions, where A is unbounded. With a symmetric but not self-adjoint generator: on L²(0, ∞) the right translation semigroup (T(t)f)(x) = f(x − t) for x > t, 0 for x ≤ t, is a C_0-semigroup of isometries that is not a group (T(t) is not surjective), and its generator is A = −d/dx on {f ∈ H¹(0, ∞) : f(0) = 0}, i.e. A = −iS with S = −i d/dx closed and symmetric with deficiency indices (1, 0). There is no unitary group whose generator extends S, so exponentiating a symmetric operator to 'e^{itS}' is not legitimate: only self-adjointness (or essential self-adjointness followed by taking the closure) licenses the unitary group. Audit rule: in quantum dynamics arguments, check that the Hamiltonian has been shown self-adjoint on a stated domain before using e^{itH}, unitarity, conservation of norm, or invariance of D(H).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["M is a compact Riemannian manifold and f a C^1 diffeomorphism of M","mu is an f-invariant Borel probability measure (compactness makes the Oseledets integrability condition automatic)","the exponents, multiplicities and subspaces are measurable and f-invariant; constant a.e. when mu is ergodic","the Oseledets splitting is measurable, generally not continuous, and the Pesin blocks are not invariant"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.732600+00:00","domain":"smooth ergodic theory, Lyapunov exponents","id":"claim_dfb0e656c58d4f14dd665a85b8ce62d25a662a2455b987541fa0436ab64565e1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f be a C^1 diffeomorphism of a compact Riemannian manifold M and mu an f-invariant Borel probability measure. Since M is compact, log of the norm of Df and of Df^{-1} are bounded, hence integrable, so Oseledets' multiplicative ergodic theorem applies: for mu-a.e. x there are finitely many numbers lambda_1(x) > lambda_2(x) > ... > lambda_{k(x)}(x) (the LYAPUNOV EXPONENTS at x) and a Df-invariant splitting of the tangent space

  T_x M = E_1(x) + ... + E_{k(x)}(x),   Df_x E_i(x) = E_i(f x),

such that for every nonzero v in E_i(x) the limit of (1/n) log |Df^n_x v| as n -> +-infinity exists and equals lambda_i(x). The functions x -> lambda_i(x), the multiplicities dim E_i(x), and the subspaces are measurable and f-invariant; if mu is ergodic they are constant almost everywhere. The splitting is in general only MEASURABLE, not continuous, and the convergence is not uniform in x.

Two structural facts that every application uses. (1) TEMPEREDNESS: any measurable positive function that is subexponential along orbits -- such as the angle between the Oseledets subspaces, or the norm of the change to Lyapunov (adapted) coordinates -- can be chosen tempered, meaning (1/n) log of its value at f^n x tends to 0; this is what lets one build Lyapunov charts in which Df is uniformly contracting on the negative-exponent bundle at the cost of a chart size that shrinks subexponentially along the orbit. (2) PESIN BLOCKS: for each l one collects the points where the Oseledets estimates hold with uniform constants depending on l; the resulting sets Lambda_l are COMPACT (after discarding a null set and restricting the subbundles continuously), increase in l, exhaust a full-measure set, and carry uniform hyperbolic-like estimates. They are NOT f-invariant -- an orbit wanders between blocks -- which is exactly why non-uniformly hyperbolic statements are local-and-measurable rather than uniform.

A point x is called (non-uniformly) hyperbolic when no exponent at x is zero; the stable bundle E^s(x) is the sum of the E_i(x) with lambda_i(x) < 0 and the unstable bundle the sum of those with lambda_i(x) > 0. Zero exponents are the obstruction: nothing in this framework says anything about directions with zero exponent.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X,d) is a compact metric space","T: X -> X is a homeomorphism","T is expansive with expansive constant c > 0 for the metric d","alpha is a finite Borel partition with diam(A) < c for every A in alpha","for the cover statement, U is a finite open cover with mesh(U) < c","for the entropy consequence, mu is a T-invariant Borel probability measure"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.814532+00:00","domain":"topological and ergodic dynamics, entropy","id":"claim_e0991e6f5703dfafed9b8ef66c327d54b46c44f7e1c7b2d0847a9c270a85228d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X,d) be a compact metric space and let T: X -> X be a homeomorphism which is EXPANSIVE with expansive constant c > 0, meaning: for every pair of distinct points x, y in X there exists an integer n with d(T^n x, T^n y) > c. Let alpha = {A_1, ..., A_k} be a finite Borel partition of X whose mesh is below the expansive constant, i.e. diam(A_i) < c for every i. CONCLUSION: alpha is a two-sided generator. Precisely, the smallest sigma-algebra containing T^{-n}(A_i) for all n in Z and all i is the full Borel sigma-algebra of X. Consequently, for EVERY T-invariant Borel probability measure mu, alpha is a generator mod mu, and the Kolmogorov-Sinai theorem gives h_mu(T) = h_mu(T, alpha) = lim_n (1/n) H_mu(alpha v T^{-1}alpha v ... v T^{-(n-1)}alpha): the measure-theoretic entropy is already computed by that one fixed finite partition, with no refinement over scales. TOPOLOGICAL COUNTERPART, same hypotheses: if U is a finite OPEN cover of X with mesh(U) < c, then h_top(T) = h_top(T, U); in particular an expansive homeomorphism of a compact metric space has finite topological entropy, and the entropy is reached at one fixed finite scale. SHARP EDGES. (a) Expansiveness is indispensable, not a convenience: for the identity map on [0,1] (which is not expansive) every finite partition alpha satisfies alpha v T^{-n}alpha = alpha for all n, so the generated sigma-algebra is the finite algebra generated by alpha and never the Borel sigma-algebra, however small the mesh. More generally, for a non-expansive system no bound on the mesh forces the generator property. (b) The constant c depends on the metric even though expansiveness itself does not: on a compact metric space expansiveness is independent of the choice of compatible metric, but 'mesh below c' must be read in the SAME metric for which c is an expansive constant. (c) The conclusion is about the TWO-SIDED sigma-algebra, using T^{-n} for all n in Z. For a one-sided generator (only n >= 0), which is what is needed for one-sided entropy statements and for non-invertible maps, one needs POSITIVE expansiveness (some n >= 0 with d(T^n x, T^n y) > c); a homeomorphism of an infinite compact metric space is never positively expansive, so that strengthening is not available here. (d) The theorem says the entropy is captured by alpha; it does NOT say h_mu(T) = H_mu(alpha) or that alpha is independent under T.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the optimism theorem for weighted least squares; weights normalised to sum to one","regime (2) beyond the Loewner bounds uses row exchangeability given the weights as a first-order approximation of the two moment matrices"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T11:47:28.060880+00:00","domain":"regression / model assessment","id":"claim_e133d7fdae691c4a0638ff9a8fb3a814a36acd27f937ccf5fa74ff1dd0aeeb11","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"In the setting of the optimism theorem for weighted least squares, normalise the weights to sum_i s_i = 1. (2) Concentrated weights with homoscedastic errors: the Loewner bounds s_min X'SX <= X'S^2 X <= s_max X'SX give 2 sigma^2 m s_min <= optimism <= 2 sigma^2 m s_max, and when the rows are exchangeable given the weights (E[x x'] = G for every row) the two moment matrices are (sum s_i) G and (sum s_i^2) G to first order, so the optimism is 2 sigma^2 m sum_i s_i^2 = 2 sigma^2 m / n_eff with Kish's n_eff = (sum s)^2 / sum s^2; relative to the noise level sigma^2 of the loss the gap is 2 m / n_eff, and a concentrated weighting behaves as a small sample. (3) Variance-stabilising weights s_i = c / sigma_i^2 (Aitken's weights) give S^2 Sigma = c S, the trace collapses to c m, the optimism is 2 c m whatever the concentration of the weights, and relative to the noise level c n of the loss it is 2 m / n again: under Aitken weights a small Kish n_eff is not a small sample but the balanced sample of the stabilised problem. {"assumptions":["f holomorphic on all of U (a single pole inside the curve breaks the conclusion)","gamma null-homotopic in U, or U simply connected"],"created_at":"2026-08-29T02:26:24.138942+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_e1ac45e32ccdf39cbe875f20ffbbf2cbbc88ded86e4deb4194390e29be3272f7","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let U be an open subset of C and f holomorphic on U. If gamma is a closed piecewise smooth curve in U that is null-homotopic in U - in particular, any closed curve when U is simply connected - then the integral of f over gamma is zero. Homology form: the integral of f over a cycle gamma in U vanishes for every holomorphic f on U if and only if the winding number n(gamma, a) is zero for every point a outside U. Consequently, on a simply connected domain every holomorphic function has a holomorphic primitive.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Lebesgue measure on [0,1] for the counterexample","0 < p < 1"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.553704+00:00","domain":"real analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_e1f1d09dab661f59168150611995537e63e0f249b26c9ceb645e324eb84a1360","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For 0 < p < 1 the functional ||f||_p = (int |f|^p)^{1/p} is NOT a norm and the triangle inequality is false. Counterexample: on [0,1] with Lebesgue measure take f = 1_{[0,1/2]} and g = 1_{(1/2,1]}. Then ||f+g||_p = ||1_{[0,1]}||_p = 1, while ||f||_p + ||g||_p = 2 * (1/2)^{1/p} = 2^{1 - 1/p} < 1 for every p < 1 (e.g. 2^{-1} = 0.5 at p = 1/2). What survives: (i) the reverse inequality ||f+g||_p >= ||f||_p + ||g||_p for nonnegative f, g when 0 < p < 1; (ii) the quasi-triangle inequality ||f+g||_p <= 2^{1/p - 1}(||f||_p + ||g||_p); (iii) the p-th power is subadditive, int |f+g|^p <= int |f|^p + int |g|^p, so d(f,g) = ||f - g||_p^p is a complete translation-invariant metric and L^p (0 < p < 1) is a complete metric topological vector space - but it is not locally convex on a nonatomic space, and its dual is {0}. Related trap: the generalized Hölder inequality with 1/r = sum 1/p_i remains valid for r < 1, but the TWO-exponent Hölder inequality with a negative conjugate exponent (0 < p < 1, q = p/(p-1) < 0) points the other way under the appropriate positivity and finiteness hypotheses, so the standard direction may not be quoted when p < 1.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a Hilbert space","a is bounded sesquilinear on H × H","the claimed coercivity constant α > 0 must hold on all of H"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.772311+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, elliptic PDE, finite element analysis","id":"claim_e2aa108ac361aa69126eca86591b9d8beaedd4bc7bdd886699f31c317c3ce026","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: Re a(u, u) ≥ α‖u‖² for all u in the Hilbert space H, with a fixed α > 0 and the norm of H itself (the trial and test space). What fails: strict positivity a(u, u) > 0 for u ≠ 0, or injectivity of the associated operator, is not enough - the solution operator need not be bounded and the problem need not be solvable. Counterexample 1: H = ℓ², a(u, v) = Σ_{n ≥ 1} n^{-1} u_n conj(v_n). Then a is bounded (C = 1), Hermitian, and a(u, u) > 0 for every u ≠ 0, but the associated operator is the injective compact diagonal operator with entries 1/n, whose range is not closed. For f = (1/n)_n ∈ ℓ², the equation a(u, v) = ⟨f, v⟩ for all v forces u_n = 1 for all n, which is not in ℓ²: no solution exists. Counterexample 2 (the practical one): on a bounded connected Lipschitz domain Ω, a(u, v) = ∫_Ω ∇u·∇v̄ on H = H¹(Ω) is bounded and positive semidefinite but not coercive, since a(1, 1) = 0; the Neumann problem −Δu = f, ∂_ν u = 0 is solvable only under the compatibility condition ∫_Ω f = 0, and is never uniquely solvable in H¹(Ω) (constants can be added). Coercivity is recovered only on the subspace {u ∈ H¹(Ω) : ∫_Ω u = 0} via the Poincaré-Wirtinger inequality; on H_0^1(Ω) it is recovered via the Poincaré inequality, which is why the Dirichlet problem is the easy case. Other silent hypotheses: H must be complete (a coercive bounded form on a dense non-closed subspace gives no existence), and the coercivity constant α must be uniform, not depending on u. Note a is not assumed symmetric - that part is genuinely unnecessary. For non-coercive but well-posed problems (e.g. mixed or saddle point formulations, convection dominated problems, different trial and test spaces), the correct replacement is the Banach-Necas-Babuska inf-sup theorem: an inf-sup condition on a plus injectivity of the adjoint form, of which coercivity is only a sufficient condition.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["conditioned Galton-Watson (simply generated) tree with n vertices","N_d = number of vertices of outdegree d"],"created_at":"2026-09-24T23:46:59.318625+00:00","domain":"probability/random trees","id":"claim_e3850e9afeb448f99ec9561d012acf69","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Janson's Problem 20.2 (Probability Surveys 2012, Section 20.2) asks whether the outdegree counts N_d of a conditioned Galton-Watson (simply generated) tree are asymptotically normal. (a) nu = 1 with finite variance: yes, jointly with the covariances (Janson, Random Structures Algorithms 48 (2016), Theorem 1.13 with Example 2.2 and Section 8). (b) nu = 1 with infinite variance and (c) nu < 1: yes when the offspring law is regularly varying (Thevenin, Electron. J. Probab. 25 (2020), Theorems 6.2 and 6.7, variance pi_d(1 - pi_d)), but not in general. A subcritical law whose bulk sits on {0, 1}, with two rare atoms at (1 - q - c) n_r +/- A sqrt(n_r), each of probability n_r^{-4}, makes the conditioned tree carry exactly one of the two with probability tending to 1/2 each, so N_1 = n pi_1 -/+ A sqrt(n) up to smaller terms, a near two-point law (Theorem A, full proof); the critical infinite-variance case is the same construction with the pair straddling the missing mass of an absent rarer atom (Theorem B, a sketch that still needs a lattice local moderate-deviation expansion). Thevenin's conjecture that normality holds for every such law is therefore false. The regularly varying case survives because the giant's law is locally flat at scale sqrt(n).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["product measure on a FINITE index set","BK: both events increasing","Reimer: no monotonicity hypothesis"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542992+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e3854fb8e108d83f54f7a2c762956ced396b14b16573131eabefa9f8eab4f84b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let P be a product measure on {0,1}^E with E FINITE. For events A and B define the DISJOINT OCCURRENCE A box B as the set of configurations omega for which there exist DISJOINT sets of coordinates K and L such that every configuration agreeing with omega on K lies in A and every configuration agreeing with omega on L lies in B - informally, A and B occur for disjoint reasons. VAN DEN BERG-KESTEN: if A and B are both INCREASING then P(A box B) <= P(A) P(B). REIMER: the same inequality holds for ARBITRARY events A and B, with no monotonicity hypothesis. The direction is opposite to Harris-FKG, which is the point: increasing events are positively correlated, but requiring them to occur on disjoint witnesses destroys that correlation and more. The finiteness of E is a genuine hypothesis of the standard statements; infinite index sets are handled by approximation, and the definition of disjoint occurrence itself needs care there. Typical use: bounding the probability of two disjoint open crossings, or of a self-avoiding open path of length n, by a product. [van den Berg and Kesten (1985); Reimer (2000), Combin. Probab. Comput. 9; see Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.12]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Conclusion is constancy on the closure of U x [0,t_0] only","U must be connected","The maximum must be attained at a point with x_0 in U and t_0 > 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.106923+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_e5db45cf444dc11d943ed80dd9009a1a1904ce853e38b9031ae8a4e06c9b3559","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"If a solution of the heat equation attains its maximum over $\\overline{U_T}$ at an interior point $(x_0,t_0)\\in U_T$, the conclusion is that $u$ is constant on $\\overline U\\times[0,t_0]$ -- the past of $t_0$ -- and nothing at all is claimed for $t>t_0$. Heat is not time-reversible, and the mean value property over heat balls only looks backwards. Counterexample: on $U=(0,\\pi)$, $T=2$, let $h(t)=1$ for $t\\le1$ and $h(t)=1-e^{-1/(t-1)}$ for $t>1$ (smooth, $h\\le1$, $h<1$ for $t>1$), and let $u$ be the solution of $u_t=u_{xx}$ with $u(\\cdot,0)\\equiv1$ and $u(0,t)=u(\\pi,t)=h(t)$. On $[0,1]$, $u\\equiv1$ by uniqueness; the weak maximum principle gives $\\max_{\\overline{U_T}}u=1$, attained at the interior point $(\\pi/2,1)\\in U_T$; but for $t>1$, $u$ is not constant (its boundary values are $<1$ while, by continuity, $u$ stays near $1$ in the middle). So constancy holds exactly up to $t_0=1$ and fails afterwards. A second load-bearing hypothesis is connectedness of $U$: for $U=(0,1)\\cup(2,3)$ the solution equal to $1$ on the first component and to $e^{-\\lambda_1t}\\phi_1$ on the second attains its maximum at an interior point of the first component and is not constant on $U$. Finally, the interior maximum must be attained in $U_T$, i.e. at a point with $x_0\\in U$: a maximum on the lateral boundary says nothing about constancy (that is the Hopf lemma's domain, which asserts instead that the outward normal derivative is strictly positive there).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The counterexample uses H(p) = p^2 (smooth, uniformly convex) and zero data, so no exotic Hamiltonian is needed","'Solution a.e.' means Lipschitz plus the equation at points of differentiability","Uniqueness is restored by the viscosity property or, equivalently for convex superlinear H, by the semiconcavity bound of the Hopf-Lax solution"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418105+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: Hamilton-Jacobi equations","id":"claim_e6002f2b1fb67f105d5effe237759fa92f79220ba532358144c459114f6ad305","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: in any uniqueness statement for u_t + H(Du) = 0 the solution must be a VISCOSITY solution (equivalently, for convex superlinear H, a Lipschitz a.e. solution satisfying the one-sided semiconcavity estimate). Satisfying the equation at almost every point plus the initial condition is far too weak. Counterexample (n = 1): H(p) = p^2, initial datum g ≡ 0. Both u ≡ 0 and v(x,t) := min(0, |x| - t) are Lipschitz on R × [0,∞), vanish at t = 0, and satisfy v_t + v_x^2 = 0 at every point of differentiability: for |x| < t one has v = |x| - t, v_t = -1, v_x = ±1; for |x| > t one has v ≡ 0. Only u ≡ 0 is the viscosity solution (it is also what the Hopf-Lax formula gives, since L(q) = q^2/4 and min_y ( |x-y|^2/(4t) ) = 0). Why v fails: at a point (0,t) with t > 0, v has a local minimum in x with a convex kink, so φ ≡ v(0,t) + c(t'-t) touches from below with φ_x = 0, φ_t = -1, and the supersolution inequality φ_t + φ_x^2 ≥ 0 reads -1 ≥ 0. Equivalently v violates semiconcavity: v(z,t) - 2v(0,t) + v(-z,t) = 2|z|, which is not O(|z|^2). Auditor's check: whenever a proof concludes 'u is the solution' from 'u is Lipschitz and solves the PDE a.e.', the argument is incomplete unless viscosity, semiconcavity, or a variational (Hopf-Lax) representation is verified.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149207+00:00","domain":"functional analysis for elliptic PDE","id":"claim_e668a967db6b2df1576259501b51767438bb0d124e237c2d8edd4b1aa48d5602","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: there is beta > 0 with B[u,u] >= beta ||u||^2 for every u in the Hilbert space H. Strict positivity (B[u,u] > 0 for u nonzero) is not enough, and neither is injectivity of the associated operator. Counterexample: H = l^2, B(u,v) = sum_k u_k v_k / k. This form is bounded (|B(u,v)| <= ||u|| ||v||), symmetric and strictly positive, but B(e_k, e_k) = 1/k tends to 0, so it is not coercive. The bounded functional F(v) = sum_k v_k / k is represented by the sequence (1/k) in l^2, yet B(u, .) = F forces u_k = 1 for all k, which is not in l^2: the equation has no solution. PDE instances of the same failure: (i) on H^1_0(Omega) the form B[u,v] = integral (grad u . grad v - lambda_1 u v) satisfies B[u,u] >= 0 with equality exactly on the first eigenfunction, and the Dirichlet problem for -Laplacian - lambda_1 is not solvable for general right-hand sides (the Fredholm orthogonality condition appears); (ii) on H^1(Omega) the Neumann form integral grad u . grad v annihilates constants, and integral f = 0 is necessary for solvability; (iii) on an unbounded Omega the Poincare inequality may fail, so integral (grad u . grad v) is not coercive for the full H^1 norm. Two further points a careful reader should keep straight: coercivity is sufficient but not necessary (for lambda strictly between two Dirichlet eigenvalues the form of -Laplacian - lambda is indefinite, yet the problem is uniquely solvable by the Fredholm alternative), and Lax-Milgram does not require B to be symmetric - symmetry only turns the solution into the minimizer of a quadratic energy (Riesz representation / Dirichlet principle).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T07:57:26.103264+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_e68f193186254c789712f4d9509a62ad","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, specifically in homology theory and algebraic topology, cohomology is a way of attaching algebraic invariants to a topological space or other mathematical object that encode its properties in a way that is often computable. Cohomology is often related to questions of whether some local property of the space is obstructed when passing to a global property. For example, the Möbius strip is not the product space of a line segment with a circle (i.e., a cylinder), but locally on any segment of the circle it resembles an ordinary rectangle (product of two line segments) without the global twist. The obstruction to making the product structure global is encoded in the first cohomology of the underlying circle, which classifies the two inequivalent ways a line can twist around a circle (an even number of twists or an odd number of twists). The fact that there are only two inequivalent ways of twisting a line around a circle is encoded in the relevant cohomology group $H^{1}(S^{1},\\{+1,-1\\})$ which can be computed as isomorphic to the group $\\{+1,-1\\}$ where $+1$ corresponds to an even number of twists, and $-1$ to an odd number.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f in L^2(R^d)","the Plancherel transform is the L^2 extension of the L^1 transform"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264524+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, common errors","id":"claim_e6a7de372efdb69b5dda51fbcd54ebeef72e1430e1bd848aa9b086939563f833","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing distinction: for $f\\in L^1$ the transform is an honest absolutely convergent integral, bounded, continuous, defined at every $\\xi$; for $f\\in L^2\\setminus L^1$ it is defined only as the $L^2$-limit $\\hat f=\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}\\widehat{f\\mathbf 1_{\\{|x|\\le R\\}}}$ (the unique continuous extension from the dense subspace $L^1\\cap L^2$), hence is an equivalence class defined only almost everywhere. Example: $f(x)=\\sin(\\pi x)/(\\pi x)\\in L^2\\setminus L^1$, whose Plancherel transform is $\\mathbf 1_{[-1/2,1/2]}$ a.e.; the truncated integrals converge to $1$ for $|\\xi|<1/2$, to $0$ for $|\\xi|>1/2$ and to $1/2$ at $\\xi=\\pm1/2$, but no value at $\\pm1/2$ is meaningful for the $L^2$ transform. Consequences an auditor should check: (i) claims like '$\\hat f(\\xi_0)=0$' or '$\\hat f$ is continuous' are meaningless for $L^2$ data without naming a representative (the usual legitimate versions are 'a.e.' statements or support statements up to null sets); (ii) $\\|\\hat f\\|_\\infty\\le\\|f\\|_1$ is unavailable; (iii) that $\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}\\int_{-R}^Rf(x)e^{-2\\pi ix\\xi}dx$ exists for a.e. $\\xi$ when $f\\in L^2(\\mathbb R)$ is a deep result (the Fourier-integral form of Carleson's theorem), not a corollary of Plancherel, which only gives $L^2$ convergence and hence a.e. convergence along some subsequence of radii. On $L^1\\cap L^2$ the two definitions agree a.e., which is what makes the extension consistent.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the joint law of the points is invariant under reflection of any subset through the origin","the points are almost surely in general position (every d or fewer are linearly independent)","independence of the points is not required"],"created_at":"2026-10-14T12:08:18+00:00","domain":"geometric probability","id":"claim_e6ae446cd6fd7036517cf71cccaaa1cb4fa2b1cf94cd433f14ec3cf8acbcb1e8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $x_1,\\dots,x_N$ be random points in $\\mathbb{R}^d$ whose joint law is invariant under reflection of any subset of them through the origin, and which are almost surely in general position. Then the probability that all of them lie in a single open halfspace whose boundary contains the origin, equivalently the probability that the origin is not in their convex hull, equals $2^{-N+1}\\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\\binom{N-1}{k}$. In particular this probability is $1$ whenever $N \\le d$. Note that symmetry alone does not suffice: general position is needed, since for instance two points i.i.d. uniform on $\\{\\pm e_1\\} \\subset \\mathbb{R}^2$ are symmetric (their joint law is invariant under reflection of any subset of them through the origin) but not in general position, and they lie in a common open halfspace whose boundary contains the origin with probability $1/2$ (exactly when the two points coincide; $e_1$ and $-e_1$ lie in no such halfspace, and the origin is in their convex hull), whereas the formula gives $2^{-1}\\left(\\binom{1}{0}+\\binom{1}{1}\\right)=1$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["rows are i.i.d. Gaussian with covariance sigma^2 (I + theta u u^T)","p/n -> gamma in (0, 1]","the spike rank r is fixed as p, n -> infinity"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_e75253c32e05d555c04fc1b98cd0a36914ac029db4849bdb4ba0e4dd287fb429","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $S$ be the sample covariance of $n$ i.i.d. Gaussian rows in $\\mathbb{R}^p$ with population covariance $\\Sigma = \\sigma^2 (I_p + \\theta u u^T)$, $\\|u\\| = 1$, $\\theta > 0$, in the regime $p/n \\to \\gamma \\in (0, 1]$. Let $\\hat\\lambda$ be the largest eigenvalue of $S$ and $\\hat u$ its unit eigenvector. THEOREM (Baik, Ben Arous, Peche 2005 for the eigenvalue in the complex case; Paul 2007 for real Gaussian data, eigenvalue and eigenvector; Baik-Silverstein 2006 in general). (i) If $\\theta \\le \\sqrt{\\gamma}$ then $\\hat\\lambda \\to \\sigma^2 (1 + \\sqrt{\\gamma})^2$ almost surely, the bulk edge of the Marchenko-Pastur law, and $|\\langle \\hat u, u \\rangle|^2 \\to 0$: the spike is invisible. (ii) If $\\theta > \\sqrt{\\gamma}$ then $\\hat\\lambda \\to \\sigma^2 (1 + \\theta)(1 + \\gamma / \\theta)$, which exceeds the bulk edge, and $|\\langle \\hat u, u \\rangle|^2 \\to \\frac{1 - \\gamma / \\theta^2}{1 + \\gamma / \\theta}$. The limit $\\sigma^2 (1 + \\theta)(1 + \\gamma/\\theta) = \\sigma^2 (1 + \\theta + \\gamma + \\gamma/\\theta)$ is strictly larger than the population eigenvalue $\\sigma^2 (1 + \\theta)$: a detected sample spike always overstates its population value, by $\\sigma^2 \\gamma (1 + 1/\\theta)$. The same statements hold spike by spike for $r$ fixed spikes with distinct $\\theta_k$, each compared with the threshold $\\sqrt{\\gamma}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H real separable Hilbert, W isonormal Gaussian on H","the L^2 space is with respect to the sigma-algebra GENERATED BY W","f_n symmetric, and then unique"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543561+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e77fa0481be857539e984e1e66a556b4287a9c335209411aaef62032c500226b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H be a real separable Hilbert space and let W = { W(h) : h in H } be an ISONORMAL Gaussian process, that is a centred Gaussian family with E[ W(h) W(g) ] = <h, g>_H. For n >= 0 let the n-th WIENER CHAOS H_n be the closed linear span in L^2 of { He_n( W(h) ) : h in H, ||h||_H = 1 }, with H_0 the constants. Then the H_n are mutually ORTHOGONAL and L^2( Omega, sigma(W), P ) is their orthogonal direct sum. Equivalently, every square-integrable functional F of the Gaussian process has a unique expansion F = E[F] + sum_{n >= 1} I_n(f_n) with f_n a symmetric element of the n-fold symmetric tensor power of H, where I_n is the multiple Wiener-Ito integral, and the Ito isometry gives E[F^2] = E[F]^2 + sum_{n >= 1} n! ||f_n||^2. For H = L^2([0,T]) and W Brownian motion, I_n(f_n) is the n-fold iterated Ito integral of f_n and the expansion is the classical chaos expansion. The sigma-algebra must be the one GENERATED BY W: the decomposition describes L^2 of that sigma-algebra and says nothing about functionals involving independent randomness. [Wiener (1938), Ito (1951); see Nualart, The Malliavin Calculus and Related Topics, 2nd ed., Theorem 1.1.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0069-scaling-limit-of-critical-percolation-cluster-sizes-on-the-hypercube","No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:26:45.043212+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e79112836e7be9ac2cb3fff34a4bbaf047ce7bf4d7f7033676f9bfe30b1fdf7b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Compare the exploration process of the hypercube with the Aldous exploration of the Erdos-Renyi graph. Result: Aldous's proof for G(n,p) uses that the exploration process is a random walk with drift theta - t and unit variance, up to depletion; on the hypercube the exploration of a cluster is a random walk whose step distribution depends on the local geometry (the number of unexplored neighbours of the current vertex is d minus the number of explored ones, and explored vertices are geometrically correlated). In the window the explored set has size V^{2/3} = 2^{2d/3}, which is a vanishing fraction of V, but the DEPLETION seen by a single vertex is not uniform: the explored vertices cluster geometrically, so the walk's drift correction is a functional of the geometry, not of the total explored mass as in G(n,p). This is exactly why the hypercube is harder than the Hamming graph (where the geometry is 'mean-field enough' and the scaling limit was obtained by Federico-van der Hofstad-den Hollander-Hulshof for the Hamming cube). A reduction: the scaling limit follows if the exploration's drift satisfies E[step | past] = theta 2^{-d/3} - (explored mass)/V + o(2^{-d/3}) uniformly over the window, i.e. if the local depletion is asymptotically equal to the global depletion; this is a 'non-backtracking randomness' statement about the geometry of critical hypercube clusters (that they are spread out like independent samples), which is the mean-field cluster geometry conjecture and is open. Obstruction: Local versus global depletion in the exploration walk; needs spread-out geometry of critical hypercube clusters.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.499132+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_e7b91c575adbfa0bce4ab714ce4186dd09394e0d520b2b9976c347c96e5089d7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Three hypotheses are load-bearing, and each is routinely dropped. (1) The cycle must be null-homologous in the domain where f is holomorphic (apart from the listed singularities). On the annulus U = {1 < |z| < 3} the function f(z) = 1/z is holomorphic with no singularity in U at all, yet the integral over the circle |z| = 2 equals 2πi, not 0: the circle winds once around 0, a point outside U. 'No singularities inside the contour' is not the hypothesis; 'winding number zero about every point off the domain' is. (2) Winding numbers multiply the residues. For the curve γ(t) = e^{2it}, 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π (the unit circle traversed twice), the integral of 1/z is 4πi = 2πi times n(γ,0) Res, with n(γ,0) = 2. A figure-eight curve can even give cancellation, with winding numbers +1 and -1 about two poles. (3) The singularities must be isolated and f single-valued. f(z) = 1/sin(1/z) has poles at z = 1/(kπ) accumulating at 0, so 0 is not an isolated singularity, no residue is defined there, and the circle |z| = 1/2 encloses infinitely many poles: the residue theorem does not apply as stated (one must exhaust or use a different region). Similarly log z and sqrt(z) are not single-valued holomorphic functions on any punctured disk about 0, so they carry no residue at 0; a branch cut and a keyhole contour are required. Two further habits worth checking: a residue of 0 does not mean the singularity is removable (1/z^2 has residue 0), and when the contour is closed 'in the upper half-plane' the estimate showing the added arc's contribution tends to 0 (Jordan's lemma or an explicit bound) is part of the proof, not a formality.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.378680+00:00","domain":"computability theory","id":"claim_e7c278a5c929afee616c48ad2dda5bb811314d807cba3f15b58d3461e5e114d4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A (deterministic, one-tape) Turing machine consists of: a finite set of states Q with a designated start state and designated halting states (for decision problems, an accept state and a reject state); a finite tape alphabet Gamma containing a blank symbol and an input alphabet Sigma not containing the blank; and a transition function delta mapping (non-halting state, tape symbol) pairs to (state, tape symbol, direction) triples with direction left or right. The machine operates on an infinite tape of cells each holding one symbol of Gamma, with a single head; initially the tape holds the input string from Sigma* followed by blanks, and the head is at the leftmost input cell. A configuration records the state, tape contents, and head position; each step applies delta to the current state and scanned symbol, rewriting the cell, changing state, and moving the head one cell. The machine halts upon entering a halting state; it may also run forever. It computes a partial function from strings to strings (output read off the tape at halting); it decides a language L if it halts on every input, accepting exactly the strings in L, and it recognizes (accepts) L if it accepts exactly the strings in L, possibly failing to halt off L. If a real sequence (a_n)_{n>=1} is subadditive, meaning a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n for all m,n>=1, then lim_{n->infinity} a_n/n exists, possibly equal to -infinity, and equals inf_n a_n/n. This elementary but powerful lemma converts a one-directional combinatorial inequality into existence of a limit, and is the deterministic backbone behind results such as convergence of the free energy per site in statistical mechanics or the growth rate of a combinatorial quantity, for instance existence of the connective constant for self-avoiding walks, or existence of free energy limits in the Ising or Potts models under volume-doubling or concatenation subadditivity. An approximate or almost-subadditive version, a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n + e(m,n) with a controlled error term, such as e(m,n)=o(m+n) or a summable correction, still yields convergence of a_n/n to an infimum-type limit under mild additional conditions, a form often needed when exact subadditivity fails because of boundary effects. It does not give any rate of convergence, only existence of the limit, and it does not apply to sequences that are only superadditive or that fail monotonicity entirely without the appropriate sign flip; Kingman's theorem is the random, ergodic-theoretic generalization for stationary sequences and is not itself implied by Fekete's lemma. Typical failure: Verifying subadditivity only for a convenient special subsequence, such as powers of 2 or specific volume shapes like cubes, and then applying Fekete's lemma as though the inequality had been established for all m, n; the lemma genuinely requires the inequality for all pairs, or at least a cofinal family closed under addition, and skipping intermediate cases silently assumes exactly the regularity, such as shape-independence of the volume limit in statistical mechanics, that itself needs a separate van Hove or Fisher-type argument. Canonical reference: Fekete, 1923, Mathematische Zeitschrift; Steele, Probability Theory and Combinatorial Optimization, 1997, SIAM, Chapter 1.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a centered Gaussian process, almost surely bounded on the index set, for Borell-TIS","for Slepian/Sudakov-Fernique: two Gaussian processes on the same index set with pointwise increment-variance domination E[(X_s-X_t)^2]<=E[(Y_s-Y_t)^2]","for the classical Slepian tail comparison specifically: equal marginal variances (then increment domination is equivalent to E[X_sX_t]>=E[Y_sY_t]); no correlation-sign condition replaces them","measurability and separability of the process so the supremum is well defined"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e8207cb5ab491259a97da1f7e7a1894939cc36b16bef511c7e7ace855947706c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a centered, almost surely bounded Gaussian process (X_t)_{t in T}, let M = sup_t X_t and sigma^2 = sup_t Var(X_t). The Borell-TIS inequality states P(|M - E[M]| >= u) <= 2 exp(-u^2/(2 sigma^2)) for all u >= 0, giving Gaussian concentration of the supremum around its mean at the scale of the process's maximal pointwise variance, regardless of the cardinality or geometry of the index set. Separately, Slepian's inequality compares two centered Gaussian processes on the same index set with equal marginal variances: if E[(X_s-X_t)^2] <= E[(Y_s-Y_t)^2] for all s,t, then E[sup X] <= E[sup Y], and with the equal marginal variances the same condition, equivalently E[X_s X_t] >= E[Y_s Y_t] for all s,t, also gives the tail comparison P(sup X > u) <= P(sup Y > u) for every u; no condition on the sign of the correlations is needed, and none can replace the equal variances. The Sudakov-Fernique inequality removes the equal-variance requirement, needing only the pointwise increment domination, but concludes only the expectation comparison E[sup X] <= E[sup Y], not the stronger distributional comparison. Together these tools reduce bounding E[sup] of a complicated Gaussian field to bounding it for a simpler, dominating comparison field. Borell-TIS does not give the value of E[M] itself, which requires a separate chaining or Dudley-integral bound, and Sudakov-Fernique is strictly weaker in conclusion than the classical Slepian inequality even when both sets of hypotheses happen to hold. Typical failure: Invoking the classical Slepian inequality's tail or distributional comparison after only verifying the weaker Sudakov-Fernique hypotheses, namely increment domination without equal variances; Sudakov-Fernique licenses comparing E[sup X] to E[sup Y] only, and treating the two comparison theorems as interchangeable overstates what has actually been proven. Canonical reference: Borell, 1975, Inventiones Mathematicae; Tsirelson, Ibragimov and Sudakov, 1976, in Proceedings of the School-Seminar on Random Processes; Slepian, 1962, Bell System Technical Journal; Fernique, 1975, Ecole d'Ete de Probabilites de Saint-Flour, Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T is measure-preserving on a probability space; for the one-sided version T need not be invertible","A is measurable with log^+ ||A|| integrable","the splitting version additionally needs T invertible, A(x) invertible a.e., and log^+ ||A^{-1}|| integrable","all statements hold for mu-a.e. x; exponents depend on mu"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, Lyapunov exponents, smooth dynamics","id":"claim_e82eac33ac8c92bb29c9b15bfd94cbfbd85cf0c046e3d5255a98565d37d2934a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system and $A: X \to M_d(\mathbb{R})$ a measurable cocycle with $\log^+ \|A\| \in L^1(\mu)$; write $A^n(x) = A(T^{n-1}x)\cdots A(x)$.

ONE-SIDED (FILTRATION) VERSION - no invertibility of $T$ or of $A$ needed. For $\mu$-a.e. $x$: (a) the limit $\Lambda(x) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \big(A^n(x)^{\mathsf T} A^n(x)\big)^{1/2n}$ exists (a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix); (b) there are an integer $1 \le k(x) \le d$, exponents $\infty > \lambda_1(x) > \lambda_2(x) > \dots > \lambda_{k(x)}(x) \ge -\infty$ (only the smallest may be $-\infty$; this happens at every $x$ whose orbit meets the set where $A$ is singular, hence almost everywhere when $T$ is ergodic and $A$ is singular with positive probability, and can also happen for a.e.-invertible $A$ when $\log^+\|A^{-1}\|$ is not integrable), and a filtration of linear subspaces $\mathbb{R}^d = V_1(x) \supsetneq V_2(x) \supsetneq \dots \supsetneq V_{k(x)}(x) \supsetneq V_{k(x)+1}(x) = \{0\}$, measurable in $x$, such that $A(x) V_i(x) \subset V_i(Tx)$ and
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n \log \|A^n(x) v\| = \lambda_i(x) \quad\text{for every } v \in V_i(x) \setminus V_{i+1}(x);$$
(c) $k$, the $\lambda_i$ and the multiplicities $m_i = \dim V_i - \dim V_{i+1}$ are $T$-invariant functions of $x$ (constants when $T$ is ergodic); (d) $\lim \frac1n \log |\det A^n(x)| = \sum_i m_i \lambda_i(x)$, and more generally $\lim \frac1n \log \|\Lambda^p A^n(x)\|$ (norm on the $p$-th exterior power) equals the sum of the $p$ largest exponents counted with multiplicity; (e) the $\lambda_i$ with multiplicities are exactly the limits $\lim \frac1n \log \sigma_j(A^n(x))$ of the singular values, i.e. the logarithms of the eigenvalues of $\Lambda(x)$.

TWO-SIDED (SPLITTING) VERSION. If moreover $T$ is invertible, $A(x) \in GL_d(\mathbb{R})$ a.e. and $\log^+ \|A^{-1}\| \in L^1(\mu)$, then for a.e. $x$ all exponents are finite and there is a measurable $A$-equivariant splitting $\mathbb{R}^d = E_1(x) \oplus \dots \oplus E_{k(x)}(x)$, $A(x)E_i(x) = E_i(Tx)$, $\dim E_i = m_i$, with $\lim_{n \to \pm\infty} \frac1n \log \|A^n(x) v\| = \lambda_i(x)$ for all $v \in E_i(x) \setminus \{0\}$ (the SAME exponent forwards and backwards), $V_i(x) = \bigoplus_{j \ge i} E_j(x)$, and the angles between the Oseledets subspaces decay subexponentially along orbits: $\lim_{n\to\pm\infty} \frac1n \log \sin\angle\big(E_i(T^n x), \bigoplus_{j\ne i} E_j(T^n x)\big) = 0$.

WHERE IT FAILS. (1) Without $\log^+\|A\| \in L^1$ the limits need not exist: for $d = 1$ the theorem IS Birkhoff's theorem for $\log|a|$, which fails when $\log^+|a| \notin L^1$. (2) Without $\log^+\|A^{-1}\| \in L^1$ (or with $T$ non-invertible) there is in general NO equivariant splitting, only the forward filtration: the subspaces of vectors with exponent exactly $\lambda_i$, $i \ge 2$, are not canonically defined and the 'slow' directions are not invariant under $A$. (3) The exponents depend on the measure $\mu$: different ergodic measures for the same $T$ and $A$ generally have different exponents, and a point outside the full-measure set need not have exponents at all. (4) Convergence is not uniform in $x$, and the Oseledets subspaces are only measurable, in general not continuous, in $x$. (5) The theorem is about $\|A^n(x)v\|$ along ONE orbit; it says nothing about eigenvalues of $A^n(x)$ or about $\|A^n\|$ averaged over $x$.","status":"unverified"}

# Opposite-head balanced two-cycles: exact family and full linear stability

Claim T328-W698-016, v1. Target 1. PROOF, UNAUDITED.
This is a family classification, not a classification of all balanced cycles or a global GD theorem. No novelty claim is made.

## Exact family

Let b,kappa>0. There is a unique T in (1/2,1) with

    cosh(T)^2 = 2 cosh(T/4)^2.

Put a=b(tanh T+tanh(T/4))/2, H=b(tanh T-tanh(T/4))/2,
d=b*kappa*sech(T)^2, V=sqrt(H/(4d)), w=sqrt(T/kappa),
g=(1+exp(-VH))^(-1), eta=2V/(gH).
For logistic loss log(1+exp(-v*h(kq))) and h(s)=a+b*tanh(kappa*s),
simultaneous Euclidean GD has the exact two-cycle

    (V,w,-w) -> (-V,w/2,-w/2) -> (V,w,-w).

Both states have margin -VH and loss log(1+exp(VH))>log 2.
Since 0<a<b this is a legitimate separable two-token link. Repeating the same signed link permits any number of examples and either raw label, but this theorem makes no claim about distinct links.

Indeed, h(-w^2)=-H, h(-w^2/4)=H, and h'(-w^2/4)=2d.
The head increments are -2V and 2V. Writing delta=eta*v*g*h',
the factor multipliers are delta_0=1/2 and delta_1=-1; on k=-q the
k multipliers are 1-delta, namely 1/2 and 2. All cycle identities follow.

## Full spectrum

Set tau=(1-g)VH, R=2T(tanh T+tanh(T/4)),
D0=1/2+2T*tanh T, D1=2-T*tanh(T/4).
On balanced coordinates (v,k), the two Jacobians are

    Jj = [[1-2tau, B], [B/2, Dj-R*tau]],
    B=-w(1+tau)/V,  B^2/2=2R(1+tau)^2.

The full two-step Jacobian has spectrum {0, eigenvalues(J1*J0)}.
The zero multiplier is the normal coordinate k+q. The larger balanced
multiplier is >25/12 throughout the family, so these cycles are never attracting.
Here and below a multiplier is an eigenvalue of the two-step derivative,
not a one-step derivative between the two different points.

Let S=D0+D1, P=D0*D1 and define

    Q(tau) = q0 + q1*tau + q2*tau^2,
    q0 = 2R(2R-S-2),
    q1 = 20R^2-8R-4P+4,
    q2 = 4(P-1)+10RS+24R^2-4R.

There is a unique positive root tau_c of Q. The other balanced multiplier
lambda_minus is positive and is <1, =1, or >1 exactly when tau is <tau_c,
=tau_c, or >tau_c, respectively. Thus the full linear spectrum consists of
one contracting zero multiplier, an always expanding positive multiplier,
and a positive multiplier with this exact threshold. At equality no nonlinear
classification along the unit eigendirection is asserted. Both strict regimes
are realized as b/sqrt(kappa) varies. The cycle always has an unstable direction.

## Root and elementary bounds

The function cosh T/cosh(T/4) has positive logarithmic derivative
tanh T-(1/4)tanh(T/4) for T>0. At T=1/2 its value is <sqrt 2:
cosh(1/2)<=8/7, since (2n)!>=2^n bounds the cosh series geometrically.
At T=1 its value is >sqrt 2, because cosh 1>37/24 and
cosh(1/4)<=32/31, and (1147/768)^2>2.
The intermediate value theorem and strict monotonicity prove uniqueness.

For the cosh series at 1, the terms beginning at 1/24 have consecutive
ratios at most 1/30. Consequently

    cosh 1 <= 3/2 + (1/24)/(1-1/30) = 179/116 < 31/20 < 8/5.

Also 7/3<e<3 (the lower bound follows from 1+1+1/2; the upper follows
from 1/n!<=1/2^(n-1) for n>=2, strictly for n>=3). Hence
tanh(1/2)>2/5 and tanh 1<4/5.

Write A=tanh T, B0=tanh(T/4). The root equation gives

    A^2=(1+B0^2)/2,
    R = 2T*sech(T)^2/(A-B0) = 2T(A+B0).

Since A-B0 is the integral of sech(u)^2 from T/4 to T,

    (8/3)*sech(T)^2 < R < 8/3.

In particular R>3200/2883>11/10, and also R>25/24. Further,

    9/10 < D0 < 21/10,    1 < D1 < 2.

For y=VH>0, tau=y/(1+exp y) satisfies 0<tau<1/3: the Taylor lower bound
exp y>1+y+y^2/2 implies 1+exp y>3y since (y-2)^2/2>=0.
Thus alpha=1-2tau>1/3. Both diagonal terms of the balanced Jacobians
are positive, since

    D0-R*tau > 9/10-8/9 = 1/90,
    D1-R*tau > 2-T*tanh(T/4)-8/9 > 1/9.

Put C=B^2/2=2R(1+tau)^2>25/12. The monodromy trace is

    tr(J1 J0)=alpha^2+2C+(D0-R*tau)(D1-R*tau)>25/6.

Its two off-diagonal entries are B*(alpha+D0-R*tau) and
(B/2)*(alpha+D1-R*tau), both negative. Its eigenvalues are distinct and
real, since their discriminant is the squared diagonal difference plus
four times a strictly positive off-diagonal product. The larger eigenvalue
is therefore greater than half the trace, hence >25/12.

Moreover

    det Jj = (1-2tau)*Dj - R*(2+5tau) < Dj-2R < 0.

For j=0 use Dj<21/10<2R, and for j=1 use Dj<2<2R. Thus
det(J1 J0)>0 and, its trace being positive, both balanced multipliers are
positive. Direct expansion gives

    det(J1 J0-I) = Q(tau).

Since lambda_plus>1, the sign of Q is exactly the sign of lambda_minus-1.
Finally q0<0: using R=2T(A+B0),

    2R-S-2 = 2T*A+5T*B0-9/2
             < 8/5+5/4-9/2 < 0.

Also q1>13/5, since P<21/5 and the function 20R^2-8R is increasing for
R>11/10, with value 77/5 at 11/10. The coefficient q2>0 follows from
P>0, S>0 and 24R^2-4R>4. These signs give the unique positive root and
all the asserted eigenvalue comparisons.

## Both strict regimes occur

For completeness we verify tau_c<1/4 without floating point. The same
geometric tail bound gives, at x=9/10,

    cosh x <= 1+x^2/2 + (x^4/24)/(1-x^2/30).

The square of this rational upper bound is strictly less than
2*(1+(x/4)^2/2)^2. Thus T>9/10. The exponential Taylor bounds
exp(9/5)>17/3 and exp(9/20)>3/2 imply A>7/10 and B0>1/5, so
R>81/50>8/5. These finite rational comparisons are reproduced in
scripts/verify_opposite_cycle_exact.py.

At tau=1/4, expansion yields

    8Q(1/4)=84R^2-11RS-50R-6P+6.

Using S<41/10, P<21/5, R>8/5, and monotonicity of
84R^2-(951/10)R on R>=8/5, the right side exceeds

    84*(8/5)^2-(951/10)*(8/5)-6*(21/5)+6 = 1092/25 > 0.

Hence 0<tau_c<1/4. The quantity y=VH is a positive constant times
b/sqrt(kappa), so it ranges over all positive numbers. Since tau(y)->0
as y->0 or y->infinity, while tau(1)=1/(1+e)>1/4, both strict regimes
occur. This is a full linear stability classification for this family,
including the unit-multiplier threshold, not a proof about other cycles.

## Differentiation and ambient-coordinate check

At a balanced point (v,k,-k), let s=-k^2, h=h(s), d=h'(s), e2=h''(s),
g=(1+exp(vh))^(-1), delta=eta*v*g*d. The balanced Jacobian is

    J11 = 1-eta*g*(1-g)*h^2,
    J12 = -2*eta*k*g*d*(1-(1-g)*v*h),
    J21 = J12/2,
    J22 = 1-delta+2*k^2*eta*v*(g*e2-g*(1-g)*v*d^2).

Substitution gives the displayed J0,J1. In full coordinates U=k+q obeys
U_+=(1+delta)U. Along U=0 its derivative has no dependence on the
balanced perturbations, since the term U*d(delta) vanishes. Its two-step
multiplier is (1+1/2)*(1-1)=0. The derivative is block triangular with
balanced block J1 J0, so this accounts for its complete three-dimensional
spectrum even without assuming an imbalance invariant for GD.

The independent ambient numerical check differentiates the loss as
Lvv=g(1-g)h^2, Lvs=g(1-g)vhd-gd,
Lss=g(1-g)v^2d^2-gv*e2, Ls=-gvd, and uses

    Hessian L = [[Lvv, q Lvs, k Lvs],
                 [q Lvs, q^2 Lss, kq Lss+Ls],
                 [k Lvs, kq Lss+Ls, k^2 Lss]].

This numerical comparison is evidence only. The proof above uses exact
real identities and explicit rational inequalities, with every series tail
bounded geometrically or used as a nonnegative Taylor remainder.

## Scope and unresolved obstruction

The normal multiplier alone would falsely suggest attraction: the balanced
block always has an expanding eigenvalue. This family therefore supplies
no positive-volume attracting third fate. The remaining route is to classify
asymmetric opposite-head cycles (unequal head magnitudes), factor-sign-flip
cycles, longer periods, or nonperiodic bounded orbits. Nothing here proves
almost-everywhere convergence for factored GD or excludes those alternatives.","status":"unverified"}
