Let (X_{m,n})_{0<=m<n} be a doubly indexed family of random variables satisfying subadditivity X_{m,n} <= X_{m,k} + X_{k,n} for m<k<n, stationarity, that the joint law of (X_{m+1,n+1})_{m<n} equals that of (X_{m,n})_{m<n} under a measure-preserving shift, and integrability, E[X_{0,1}^+] < infinity together with a lower bound such as E[X_{0,n}] >= -cn preventing a trivially degenerate -infinity limit. Then X_{0,n}/n converges almost surely and in L^1 to a random variable X, equal to lim_n E[X_{0,n}]/n = inf_n E[X_{0,n}]/n, and X is almost surely constant if the underlying shift is ergodic rather than merely measure-preserving. This is the random, non-i.i.d. generalization of Fekete's lemma, which is its deterministic special case, and of the classical ergodic theorem, which is its additive special case, and it is the fundamental tool establishing existence of limiting growth rates in first-passage percolation (the time constant), longest increasing subsequence problems, and last-passage percolation, with the closely related Furstenberg-Kesten theorem giving Lyapunov exponents for random matrix products via an analogous but distinct subadditive argument. It does not give the value of the limit X, only its existence as an abstract limit or infimum, and does not by itself give a rate of convergence or determine whether X is almost surely constant unless ergodicity, not merely stationarity, of the shift has been separately established. Typical failure: Invoking Kingman's theorem to conclude the limiting growth rate is deterministic without separately verifying ergodicity of the underlying probability-preserving transformation, checking only stationarity; stationarity alone gives convergence to a possibly random limit X that can be a genuine mixture over ergodic components, so asserting a single deterministic time constant or growth rate without checking ergodicity is a common gap, especially in models built from a mixture of environments. Canonical reference: Kingman, 1968, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B; Kingman, 1973, Annals of Probability; Steele, Probability Theory and Combinatorial Optimization, 1997, SIAM.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the pool protocol: members fitted on training data, the test rows split 40/60 into calibration and evaluation with a fixed permutation, metric = mean per-sample relative L2","the small-calibration arms subsample the calibration rows only; evaluation rows are never touched"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T07:07:15.583115+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning / covariance estimation","id":"claim_e9a54df9848e9c966074eb757b8cd899d5745113e3c0dcbfb1a664e5434d1869","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT stacking pool (23 members, 285 outputs, the per-sample relative metric; PLACEHOLDER_CELLS). The error covariance of the members is rank-deficient in practice: $\\lambda_{\\max}/\\lambda_{\\min}$ of $10^{6}$ to $10^{17}$, three to five eigenvalues below $0.05\\,\\sigma^2$ (members that are near-linear combinations of one another). Inside the long-only minimum-variance stack, eight cleaners of that covariance were compared on the same cells, the same split and the same small-calibration draws: the raw sample covariance, the $\\eta$-regularised rotationally invariant estimator with floors $0, 0.05, 0.2, 1.0\\,\\sigma^2$, Ledoit-Wolf 2004 linear shrinkage, Ledoit-Wolf 2020 analytical nonlinear shrinkage and Lam's NERCOME. Result: raw, RIE without floor, LW2020 and NERCOME tie - PLACEHOLDER_TIE - at full calibration ($n = 932$) and in the $n = 60/120/240$ arms; the floor $0.05\\,\\sigma^2$ is marginally negative, floors $0.2$ and $1.0$ lose PLACEHOLDER_FLOORS, linear shrinkage loses PLACEHOLDER_LW2004, and the sum-to-one (unconstrained-sign) forms of the same cleaners lose PLACEHOLDER_S1. Mechanism (seed 101, medians over outputs): the constraint keeps 7-11 of 23 members; the condition number falls from $10^{6}$-$10^{17}$ on the full covariance to $4\\times10^{2}$-$3\\times10^{4}$ on the active principal submatrix; eigenvalues under the floor fall from 3-5 to 0-1; the active sets of raw, RIE and LW2020 overlap at Jaccard 0.86-0.90 (0.80-0.83 at $n = 60$). By the active-set lemma the weights depend on the covariance only through $S_{AA}$, which is well conditioned, and there every consistent cleaner is close to the identity; a floor or a linear shrinkage lifts the small eigenvalues of the full matrix before the constraint acts and distorts $w_A$. The reading of the whole program: random-matrix theory identifies what to clean (the error covariance, in the reported metric, with an intercept) and why the plug-in fails (the near-null directions of a collinear ensemble); the fix that survives the population is the long-only constraint, itself a data-determined covariance shrinkage, and the spectral cleaners are interchangeable inside it. The pre-registered contrary hypothesis - that the floor was a kernel-bandwidth artefact which LW2020's theory-fixed bandwidth would remove - was refuted on its first cell: consistent estimators correctly keep the tiny eigenvalues, because in the population they are tiny.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X and Y are normed spaces over the same field R or C","T: X -> Y is linear"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.571085+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator theory","id":"claim_ea377968f9c0845c7f4fd6c6c2aa4f7c83561cc34ce0b88f7e0503bd67c3c35c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X and Y be normed spaces over R or C. A linear map T: X -> Y is compact if the image T(B_X) of the closed unit ball B_X = {x : ||x|| <= 1} is relatively compact in Y, i.e. its closure in Y is compact. Equivalent forms: (i) for every bounded sequence (x_n) in X the sequence (T x_n) has a subsequence that converges in Y; (ii) when Y is a Banach space, T(B_X) is totally bounded. Every compact operator is bounded, and every bounded operator of finite rank is compact. The set of compact operators X -> Y is written K(X,Y), and K(X) = K(X,X). The identity operator of X is compact if and only if X is finite-dimensional (Riesz's lemma). Terminology warning: older texts say 'completely continuous' for compact; in current usage 'completely continuous' means 'maps weakly convergent sequences to norm convergent sequences', which is implied by compactness but is weaker in general (it is equivalent to compactness when X is reflexive).","status":"unverified"}

# Target 1: joint head, key and query training retains open inferior basins

Version 1. Proof unaudited. Owner own work; global novelty unestablished.

## Statement

Let n>=2, b_i,kappa_i>0 and 0<a_i<b_i. Set
h_i(s)=a_i+b_i tanh(kappa_i s),
L(v,k,q)=mean_i log(1+exp(-v h_i(kq))).
Train all three scalar parameters by simultaneous Euclidean GD, at any fixed eta>0.
Write r_min=min_i atanh(-a_i/b_i)/kappa_i<0.
The following nonempty open subsets of R^3 are forward invariant:

 B_-={v<0,k>0,q<0,kq<r_min},
 B_+={v>0,k>0,q>0}.

The simultaneous sign reversal (k,q)->(-k,-q) supplies two more invariant regions.
On B_-: v->-infinity, k->+infinity, q->-infinity, kq->-infinity,
L->0, and (v,k,q)/sqrt(v^2+k^2+q^2)->(-1,0,0).
On B_+ the three coordinates tend to +infinity and the normalized limit is
(1,0,0). The normalized minimum signed margins, defined here as
min_i v h_i(kq)/sqrt(v^2+k^2+q^2), tend respectively to
Gamma_-=min_i(b_i-a_i) and Gamma_+=min_i(b_i+a_i).
The largest attainable limiting normalized margin is Gamma_+; Gamma_+>Gamma_-.
Consequently the inferior basin has positive three-dimensional Lebesgue measure.
These are invariant-region results, not a classification of all initializations.

The two-token cross-attention and genuine first-token self-attention embeddings
in proofs/004 and 006 remain exact after replacing their attention parameter p
by kq. Thus the claim includes distinct examples and both labels.

## Exact updates and invariance

For s=kq put g_i=1/(1+exp(v h_i(s))),
F=mean g_i h_i(s), G=mean g_i h_i'(s)>0. The exact simultaneous updates are

 v_+=v+eta F, k_+=k+eta vqG, q_+=q+eta vkG.

In B_-, F<0, vq>0 and vk<0. Each sign is therefore preserved and the
product becomes more negative. In B_+ all increments are positive, since
s>0 and h_i(s)>a_i>0. No restriction on eta is needed.

Analyze either branch using positive variables u,w,r. On B_- take
u=-v,w=k,r=-q, x=wr=-s, t_i(x)=b_i tanh(kappa_i x)-a_i.
On B_+ take u=v,w=k,r=q,x=wr=s,t_i(x)=b_i tanh(kappa_i x)+a_i.
Both obey exactly

 Delta u=eta mean g_i t_i, w_+=w+delta r, r_+=r+delta w,
 delta=eta u mean g_i t_i', g_i=(1+exp(u t_i))^-1.

Here x,u,w,r increase, and t_i(x)>=c:=min_i t_i(x_0)>0.
Let H=max_i(a_i+b_i), M=max_i b_i kappa_i, kappa_0=min_i kappa_i.
All t_i<=H and t_i'<=4M exp(-2 kappa_0 x).

## Escape

If u remained bounded, u t_i<=u H would keep every g_i bounded below,
contradicting Delta u>=eta c mean g_i. Hence u->infinity.
If x remained bounded, min_i t_i' would have a positive lower bound d>0.
The exact product update is

 Delta x=delta(w^2+r^2)+delta^2 x.

Using w^2+r^2>=2x_0>0 and
delta/Delta u=u(mean g_i t_i')/(mean g_i t_i)>=u d/H,
we obtain Delta x>=2x_0 d u Delta u/H. The sum of u Delta u diverges
(already u>=u_0>0 and sum Delta u=infinity), contradicting bounded x.
Thus x->infinity, and the loss tends to zero.

## Factor growth is negligible relative to the head

This step is essential: it compares the margin in the actual three parameters,
not the collapsed (v,p) norm. Let D=w-r. The exact relation is
D_+=(1-delta)D. Since g_i<=exp(-c u),
0<delta<=eta M u exp(-c u)->0. Hence eventually delta<=1, and |D| is
bounded by a finite constant D_* (a finite earlier excursion is harmless).
Therefore w^2+r^2=2x+D^2<=2x+D_*^2.
Eventually delta<=1, so

 Delta x<=delta(3x+D_*^2),
 delta<=4 eta M u exp(-c u) exp(-2 kappa_0 x).

The function (3x+D_*^2)exp(-2 kappa_0 x) is bounded for x>=x_0>0.
Consequently Delta x->0, and eventually Delta x<=1. Also

 delta/Delta u<=4M u exp(-2 kappa_0 x)/c.

The mean value theorem now gives

 Delta exp(kappa_0 x)
 <=kappa_0 exp(kappa_0) exp(kappa_0 x) Delta x
 <=C (3x+D_*^2)exp(-kappa_0 x) u Delta u
 <=C' u Delta u.

Summing, using 2u Delta u<=Delta(u^2), yields
exp(kappa_0 x)<=C''(1+u^2). Thus x=O(log u), and
w^2+r^2=O(log u). In particular w/u,r/u->0. Since x->infinity and
|w-r| is bounded, both w,r tend to infinity. This proves every stated
coordinate and normalized limit.

## Margin optimality and positive measure

Endpoint limits give Gamma_+ and Gamma_-. For any parameters, let
N=sqrt(v^2+k^2+q^2). If v>=0, choose an index minimizing a_i+b_i:
min_i v h_i/N<=Gamma_+. If v<0, choose an index minimizing b_i-a_i:
min_i v h_i/N<=Gamma_-. These inequalities remain valid when that
chosen signed prediction is negative. B_+ attains the larger endpoint
asymptotically. Gamma_+>=Gamma_-+2 min_i a_i>Gamma_-.
B_- is nonempty and open; for example take v=-1,k=R,q=-R with
R^2>-r_min. A sufficiently small ball around that point lies in B_-.

## Finite stationary set (flow stability, separate from the GD basin claim)

The only finite stationary points are v=0, kq=p_bar, where
mean_i h_i(p_bar)=0. Indeed v!=0 would force k=q=0 from the factor
gradients, but F(v,0)=mean_i a_i/(1+exp(v a_i))>0.
At v=0 the remaining condition is exactly the displayed mean root.
It is negative, so k,q are nonzero. Put A=mean_i h_i(p_bar)^2/4>=0,
B=mean_i h_i'(p_bar)/2>0. The loss Hessian is

 [[A,-Bq,-Bk],[-Bq,0,0],[-Bk,0,0]].

It has one zero tangent eigenvalue and eigenvalues
(A +/- sqrt(A^2+4B^2(k^2+q^2)))/2 of opposite sign. Thus each point
on this critical curve is a saddle with one attracting and one repelling
normal direction for gradient flow. This does not assert a global
stable-manifold classification or small-step GD stability uniformly along
the noncompact curve.

## Prior work and limits

Tarzanagh et al., arXiv:2308.16898, PDF pp.3-4 defines KQ-ERM with
the explicit phrase 'for a fixed head'; Theorem 2 treats the factored
regularization path and nuclear-norm bias. Sheen et al., arXiv:2403.08699,
source sections/preliminariesAr.tex line 17 likewise fixes the linear
prediction head; its main diagonal/general theorems concern gradient flow
and exponential loss. Neither checked scope is this joint-head logistic
arbitrary-step invariant-region statement. This is a bounded comparison,
not a claim that no such result exists elsewhere. Factor-balance identities
and nuclear-norm bias are prior work, not claimed as discoveries here.
The result does not cover matrices, multiple heads, or the full R^3 basin partition.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a finite, irreducible, reversible Markov chain arising from a weighted graph with conductances c_e","the two states a, b are distinct vertices of the graph","the graph is connected, so hitting and commute times, and R_eff, are all finite","consistent normalization of the total conductance c_G matching the specific convention used for R_eff"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.993395+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ecfa965d432e2bd30d8bada02d7468db0f78ae6ff3009f102b45977594aa17a9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For an irreducible, reversible Markov chain arising from a weighted graph with conductances c_e and total conductance c_G equal to the sum of conductances over all edges, the commute time C(a,b) = E_a[tau_b] + E_b[tau_a] between two vertices a, b satisfies the exact identity C(a,b) = 2 c_G R_eff(a,b), where R_eff(a,b) is the effective resistance in the associated electrical network. The identity is derived by checking that h(x) = P_x(hit a before b) is harmonic away from {a,b} and coincides with the network's voltage function, then relating expected hitting times to the network's energy dissipation. It converts questions about hitting, commute, and cover times of a reversible random walk into purely electrical or combinatorial resistance computations, enabling resistance-based bounds via series-parallel laws, Rayleigh monotonicity, or the Nash-Williams inequality on infinite graphs, on quantities such as cover time and mixing time. It does not directly give the individual one-way hitting time E_a[tau_b] alone, only the symmetrized commute time; and it is specific to reversible chains, since non-reversible walks lack the electrical-network correspondence and require substantially different techniques. Typical failure: Using the commute-time identity to bound a one-directional hitting time E_a[tau_b] alone by simply halving C(a,b), which is valid only under a separate symmetry argument between a and b; in general E_a[tau_b] and E_b[tau_a] can differ substantially even though their sum equals 2 c_G R_eff(a,b), so treating the identity as giving each one-way time individually, without additional justification, is a common overreach. Canonical reference: Chandra, Raghavan, Ruzzo, Smolensky and Tiwari, 1996, Random Structures and Algorithms; Lyons and Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks, 2016, Cambridge University Press, Chapter 2.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:47:41.430489+00:00","domain":"first-order PDE","id":"claim_ed54d7f2f7b7a7d96dbbc8a67228d4b6ca38b4b45884e2cb0b37af76ddb0e0a2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a first-order quasilinear PDE a(x,y,u) partial u/partial x + b(x,y,u) partial u/partial y = c(x,y,u) for unknown u(x,y), the method of characteristics reduces the PDE to a family of ODEs. Parametrize characteristic curves (x(s),y(s)) together with z(s)=u(x(s),y(s)) along them by dx/ds=a(x,y,z), dy/ds=b(x,y,z), dz/ds=c(x,y,z). Along a solution of this system, u is automatically consistent with the PDE, since the chain rule gives dz/ds = (partial u/partial x)(dx/ds) + (partial u/partial y)(dy/ds) = a(partial u/partial x)+b(partial u/partial y), which equals c(x,y,z) exactly when the PDE holds. Solving the PDE with data prescribed on a noncharacteristic initial curve reduces to solving the characteristic ODEs from each point of that curve and assembling the resulting family into the solution surface, then, where the map from characteristic parameters to (x,y) is invertible, reading off u(x,y). The same idea extends to fully nonlinear first-order PDE F(x,u,Du)=0 via characteristic ODEs derived from F, which also propagate Du along the curves.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_i independent and mean zero","each X_i sub-exponential with finite psi_1 norm K_i","no boundedness and no identical distribution required","c is an absolute constant"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627795+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_eda4180819f0b7157752389f126936b1be16f6ab1c12b592bae8cb80e5ad04c2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_N be independent, mean-zero, SUB-EXPONENTIAL random variables, and write K_i for the Orlicz norm ||X_i||_{psi_1} = inf{ s > 0 : E exp(|X_i|/s) <= 2 }. Then there is an absolute constant c > 0 such that for every t >= 0, P( | sum_{i=1}^N X_i | >= t ) <= 2 exp( - c min( t^2 / sum_{i=1}^N K_i^2 , t / max_i K_i ) ). The bound has TWO regimes and that is intrinsic, not an artefact: for small t the tail is Gaussian with variance proxy sum K_i^2, and for large t it is exponential with rate 1/max_i K_i. No almost sure bound on the summands is assumed, which is what distinguishes this from the classical bounded-summand Bernstein inequality; the price is that the sub-Gaussian regime ends at t of order sum K_i^2 / max K_i rather than continuing forever. Squares of sub-Gaussian variables are sub-exponential, which is why this is the inequality behind chi-square tail bounds and the Hanson-Wright inequality. The constant c is absolute and no attempt should be made to read a specific numerical value out of this statement. [standard; e.g. Vershynin, High-Dimensional Probability, Theorem 2.8.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A_n and A are self-adjoint on a common Hilbert space H","the mode of convergence (strong or norm resolvent) is as in the definition of resolvent convergence","in (a) the function f is continuous and vanishes at infinity","in (b) the function f is continuous and bounded on R","f(A) means the bounded functional calculus supplied by the spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.091074+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, spectral theory, functional calculus","id":"claim_edb40d994798192517bbbdee299a16a72daef10511a135ab38712d7a8be01de0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A_n and A be self-adjoint operators on a Hilbert space H, with no assumption relating their domains. (a) If A_n -> A in the NORM resolvent sense, then f(A_n) -> f(A) in operator norm for every continuous f : R -> C vanishing at infinity. (b) If A_n -> A in the STRONG resolvent sense, then f(A_n) -> f(A) strongly for every BOUNDED CONTINUOUS f : R -> C, where f(A) is given by the functional calculus of the spectral theorem. In particular exp(i t A_n) -> exp(i t A) strongly for every real t, and for a fixed vector the convergence is uniform for t in compact sets. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) 'bounded continuous' cannot be relaxed to 'bounded Borel'. On H = C take A_n = multiplication by 1/n and A = 0 (convergence in every sense) and f the indicator of (0, infinity): then f(A_n) = 1 for every n while f(A) = 0. Convergence of spectral projections therefore needs a separate hypothesis - typically that the endpoints of the interval carry no spectral mass for A - and even then it is only strong convergence. (ii) In (b) one gets strong, never norm, convergence, because strong resolvent convergence does not imply norm resolvent convergence: on l^2 let P_n be the orthogonal projection onto the coordinates with index at least n and set A_n = P_n, A = 0; then A_n -> 0 strongly and in the strong resolvent sense, while the resolvent difference has constant operator norm. (iii) Unbounded f is outside the theorem and the natural statement is false: strong resolvent convergence does not give A_n psi -> A psi, even for psi in every domain (rank-one examples with growing coefficients show this). (iv) Nothing is assumed about domains - that is exactly why the hypothesis is phrased through resolvents rather than as pointwise convergence of the operators.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["One FCFS server","Poisson arrival rate lambda>0","Independent exponential service rate mu>lambda","Deterministic nonnegative setup tau and grace g","Setup is never cancelled; setup arrivals queue"],"created_at":"2026-10-10T08:07:30.221932+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ee901e9ab6079a52e8000f515d63eeed51c6cfe36449a529fc20f5c928a510cc","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"PROOF OF THE STATED SCOPED RESULT; independent audit pending. Consider one FCFS server with Poisson arrival rate lambda>0 and independent exponential service rate mu>lambda. After becoming empty it remains on for deterministic grace g in [0,infinity], then switches off. A cold arrival triggers deterministic setup tau>=0, which is never cancelled; arrivals during setup wait. Put p=exp(-lambda g), x=lambda tau, rho=lambda/mu and y=p/(1+xp), with p=0 at g=infinity. The stationary mean queueing wait is lambda/[mu(mu-lambda)] + tau(1+x/2)y. If busy, on-idle, off and setup powers are B,I,O,U, average power is rho B+(1-rho)I+(1-rho)[O+xU-(1+x)I]y. Hence varying the grace period traces an affine waiting-power curve. The formula includes arrivals during setup and the subsequent busy period. It addresses k=1 and does not claim the many-server frontier or optimality among other policies.","status":"unverified"}

# T422 Target 2: a finite-sample-span upper confidence bound

Status: proof (unaudited), C06 v1. The constants below are explicit but the
bound is not asserted to have the sharp epsilon exponent of a typical noise
scale. The fixed-time theorem does not depend on C02 or C03; its final optional
optimal-step corollary inherits their unaudited status.

## Statement

Use the fresh Gaussian online least-squares model: H=diag(h_j),
h_j=j^(-alpha), alpha>1, deterministic initial errors satisfying
h_j e_0,j^2=j^(-gamma), gamma>1. Gaussian L2 predictions are used if the
coefficient vector is not in ordinary l2, as explained in model_conventions.md.
Labels have independent centered noise of finite variance sigma2>=0.
Each of t>=1 deterministic steps uses B>=1 independent fresh samples,
B an integer. A fixed positive step suffices. More generally, the proof
only requires that every update be a finite linear combination of that
step's input vectors, that the Bt inputs remain mutually independent with
law N(0,H), and that expected risk at t is finite.

For ell=1,2 define

    V(e)=sum_j h_j e_j^2,
    W_(ell+1)(e)=sum_j h_j^(ell+1)e_j^2,
    v_t=E V(e_t), Z_r=zeta(r),
    R_ell(e)=1+Z_(ell alpha)(V(e)+sigma2)/W_(ell+1)(e).

These are the single-example instantaneous noise scales: ell=1 is unweighted,
ell=2 is Hessian-weighted. Fix confidence parameter theta in (0,1), and put

    K=Bt, d=K+1,
    A_d=sum_(j=1)^d e_0,j^2/h_j=sum_(j=1)^d j^(2alpha-gamma)>0,
    L_den=h_d^(ell+2) A_d theta^2/(16d)>0.

Then

    P(W_(ell+1)(e_t)>=L_den)>=1-theta/2.                  (S1)

Consequently, with probability at least 1-theta, e_t!=0 and

    1+Z_(ell alpha) <= R_ell(e_t)
      <=1+[16d Z_(ell alpha)/(h_d^(ell+2)A_d theta^2)]
                   [2v_t/theta+sigma2].                  (S2)

The probability of e_t=0 is zero. If t is a finite first EXPECTED-risk
hit v_t<=epsilon Z_gamma, substitute that upper bound for v_t in (S2).
The hitting index is deterministic here; a realized-risk stopping time
requires an additional argument.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["entries of Z i.i.d., mean zero, variance one (finite second moment suffices for the almost-sure convergence in the Bai-Silverstein form)","the spectral distribution of Sigma converges weakly to H; p/n -> c in (0, infinity)","Sigma and Z independent (Sigma may be random)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T07:53:48.737960+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_ef9d87ff35f4c090aed907a91632374e92ff38ec27c2bf7bbb3585b46a41183e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $X = Z\\Sigma^{1/2}$ be $n \\times p$ with $Z$ having i.i.d. entries of mean $0$ and variance $1$, $\\Sigma$ positive semidefinite, and let $S = \\frac{1}{n}X^T X$. {"assumptions":["independent coordinates with finite ranges","f real valued"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T08:50:16.134016+00:00","domain":"Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition on finite product spaces","id":"claim_efbdb008ccb6e350f19afa4b831a7f5eb8be29254ef907e1f0e1aedf7377ba81","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have independent coordinates with finite ranges, f a real function of X, and f = sum over S of f_S its Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition over subsets S of {1, ..., n}: f_S depends only on X_S, f_empty = E f, and E[f_S | X_T] = 0 unless S is inside T. Then M(q) = sum over nonempty S of [1 - (1 - q)^|S|] w_S = Var(f) - J(1 - q), with J the Bernoulli reveal profile, and M(q) = (1/2) E[(f(X) - f(X^(A_q)))^2], where X^(A) redraws X_A independently from its own law. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542735+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f03dd267f4dbe993abe345addd53bd73d98a6535068e27ed077b61bcdaa98a66","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"In BOND percolation on a graph G with parameter p in [0,1], each edge is declared open with probability p and closed otherwise, independently; P_p denotes the resulting product measure on {0,1}^{E(G)}. The open cluster C(x) of a vertex x is the set of vertices reachable from x through open edges. Write theta(p) = P_p( |C(0)| = infinity ) for a fixed origin. Coupling all parameters on a common family of independent uniform variables - edge e open at level p exactly when U_e <= p - shows theta is nondecreasing, so the CRITICAL PROBABILITY p_c(G) = sup{ p : theta(p) = 0 } = inf{ p : theta(p) > 0 } is well defined. SITE percolation is defined analogously with vertices; the two have different critical values on the same graph, and p_c^{bond} <= p_c^{site} on any graph. On Z^d with d >= 2 one has 0 < p_c < 1, with the explicit elementary bounds 1/(2d-1) <= p_c^{bond}(Z^d) < 1. The value is known exactly only in special cases, most famously p_c^{bond}(Z^2) = 1/2. Whether theta(p_c) = 0 in every dimension is a celebrated open problem: it is known for d = 2 (Harris and Kesten) and, by lace-expansion methods, in high dimensions - Hara and Slade for large d, later reduced to d >= 11 by Fitzner and van der Hofstad - and it was still open for the intermediate dimensions 3 <= d <= 10 at the time this node was written. [standard; e.g. Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Chapters 1 and 8]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. nonnegative weights on Z^d, d >= 2","F(0) < p_c(d), so the time constant is a norm and the shape is bounded","E min{t_1^d, ..., t_{2d}^d} < infinity, equivalently E[Y^d] < infinity for Y the minimum of 2d independent copies of tau_e - and this condition is necessary, not just sufficient","no curvature, strict convexity or differentiability of B_nu is asserted; those are open"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f04b0c4ede53c43a4b671c5940e1cf1f891850e48c1cc9a9a34d6b9355fd1e2f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Consider i.i.d. first-passage percolation on Z^d, d >= 2, with edge-weight law nu. Assume the two conditions (i) E min{ t_1^d, ..., t_{2d}^d } < infinity, where the t_i are 2d independent copies of tau_e - equivalently E[Y^d] < infinity where Y is the MINIMUM of 2d copies, the two being the same because x -> x^d is increasing on [0, infinity) - and (ii) F(0) < p_c(d). Let B(t) = {x : T(0, x) <= t}, the random ball. Then there is a DETERMINISTIC, convex, COMPACT set B_nu in R^d with NON-EMPTY INTERIOR, symmetric about the axes, such that for every eps > 0, P( (1-eps) B_nu is contained in B(t)/t which is contained in (1+eps) B_nu for all large t ) = 1. The set B_nu is the unit ball of the time constant. Condition (i) is NOT merely convenient: if it fails then for every C > 0 the sum over x of P(m(x) > C|x|) diverges, where m(x) is the minimum weight over the edges at x, and Borel-Cantelli forces T(0,x)/|x| > C for infinitely many x almost surely, so the shape statement itself fails. Condition (ii) is what keeps the shape bounded: if F(0) >= p_c the time constant vanishes (Kesten) and B_nu is all of R^d; zero-weight edges percolate when F(0) > p_c, but at F(0) = p_c they do not in d = 2 or in high dimensions, so it is the vanishing time constant, not percolation of zero-weight edges, that unbounds the shape. What is NOT known, and is repeatedly imported elsewhere as an unproven hypothesis: whether the boundary of B_nu is STRICTLY CONVEX, whether it is DIFFERENTIABLE, and whether it has uniformly positive CURVATURE. Those are open for every non-degenerate weight distribution in every dimension, which is why the Newman-Piza exponent bounds and the directed-geodesic results carry non-constructive curvature or differentiability hypotheses. B_nu is not computed explicitly for any non-trivial F. [Cox and Durrett (1981), verified against Auffinger, Damron and Hanson, 50 Years of First-Passage Percolation, Section 2.2]","status":"unverified"}

Over the Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms ZF, the axiom of choice is equivalent to Zorn's lemma and to the well-ordering theorem, and also to Tychonoff's theorem for arbitrary compact spaces. {"assumptions":["Abel: sum a_n converges","Tauber: f(x) -> s as x -> 1 from below and n a_n -> 0 (Littlewood: a_n = O(1/n) suffices, with a harder proof)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.476957+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_f1cba3555b43f0874b98c5a0afc289242890ff7c78565e100e36b9d11679d3e9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Abel's theorem (the Abelian direction): if the series sum a_n converges to s, then the power series f(x) = sum a_n x^n converges for |x| < 1 and f(x) -> s as x -> 1 from below. The converse is false in general: f(x) = sum (-1)^n x^n = 1/(1 + x) tends to 1/2 while sum (-1)^n diverges. Tauber's theorem (the Tauberian direction): if f(x) = sum a_n x^n converges for |x| < 1, f(x) -> s as x -> 1 from below, and n a_n -> 0, then sum a_n converges to s. Littlewood strengthened the condition to a_n = O(1/n) (Littlewood's Tauberian theorem, 1911), and Hardy and Littlewood showed that a one-sided bound n a_n >= -C also suffices. 'Abelian' theorems pass from a summability method's convergence to a weaker one; 'Tauberian' theorems go back under an extra growth condition on the terms.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the operator is trace class, or the kernel is continuous and positive semidefinite (Mercer) on a compact space with a finite Borel measure of full support","the kernel is a continuous representative, so that its diagonal values are defined","an L^2 kernel alone determines only a Hilbert-Schmidt operator, whose diagonal is undefined"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.573486+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, integral operators, operator ideals","id":"claim_f1fc0fc20e90cd54d10bec9762389999f830637cbe5b30da36ffa8f104d5b56e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For an integral operator T_k on L^2 with kernel k, the formula tr T_k = integral of k(x,x) dx is not a definition and not automatic. (1) An L^2 kernel is an equivalence class modulo null sets, and on a nonatomic space the diagonal is a null set, so k(x,x) has no meaning at all without choosing a distinguished representative; different representatives give different 'diagonal integrals'. (2) Continuity of the kernel is not enough for trace class. Carleman's example: there are continuous 2pi-periodic functions g whose Fourier coefficients are not absolutely summable. The convolution operator (T f)(x) = (1/(2 pi)) times the integral over the circle of g(x - y) f(y) dy has the continuous kernel k(x,y) = g(x - y)/(2 pi), is normal with eigenvalues the Fourier coefficients of g and eigenfunctions the exponentials, so its singular values are the moduli of those coefficients; hence T is Hilbert-Schmidt but not trace class, while the naive diagonal integral is the finite number g(0). (3) What does hold: if T is trace class on L^2([a,b]) and has a continuous kernel on [a,b] x [a,b], then tr T = integral of k(x,x) dx; and by Mercer's theorem, if k is continuous, symmetric and positive semidefinite on a compact interval (more generally on a compact metric space with a finite Borel measure of full support), then the associated operator is trace class, the eigenfunction series converges absolutely and uniformly, and tr T = integral of k(x,x) dx = sum of the eigenvalues. So the safe routes are positivity plus continuity (Mercer), or an independent proof of trace class plus continuity; 'the kernel is nice' by itself is not a proof.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a well-defined nonnegative counting or indicator-sum random variable X = sum_i X_i","a computable or boundable first moment E[X]","a computable or boundable second moment E[X^2], in particular control of the pairwise correlations E[X_i X_j]","the correlation sum not growing asymptotically faster than (E[X])^2"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.982598+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f22c0577c492845332c3c1bfdcfe54194e3ac9704f0f1fdb3d81ba1f6e0e27d5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a nonnegative random variable X, typically a count of some combinatorial structure written as X = sum_i X_i for indicator random variables X_i, the Paley-Zygmund inequality gives P(X > 0) >= (E[X])^2 / E[X^2]. Expanding E[X^2] = E[X] + sum_{i != j} E[X_i X_j], the method succeeds in proving P(X>0) is bounded away from 0 exactly when the pair-correlation sum sum_{i != j} E[X_i X_j] is of the same order as (E[X])^2, that is, when correlations between the indicators do not overwhelm the square of the mean. This is the standard route to existence results, such as an infinite cluster, a long crossing, or a large clique, once a first-moment computation has already established that E[X] is large or diverging, complementing the first-moment method, which by Markov's inequality only ever gives upper bounds on P(X>0). The method does not give any rate of convergence beyond the crude Paley-Zygmund ratio, gives no lower bound at all if the correlation structure is not controlled, and can produce a vacuous (near-0) bound whenever the variance is dominated by rare, strongly correlated configurations even though the mean itself is large. Typical failure: Computing a large or diverging first moment E[X] and declaring existence of the structure without bounding E[X^2]; if the indicators X_i are strongly positively correlated (a common situation for overlapping structures), the pair-correlation term can dominate (E[X])^2, making the Paley-Zygmund bound vacuous even as E[X] -> infinity, which is exactly the situation where a large first moment gives a false sense of near-certain existence. Canonical reference: Paley and Zygmund, 1932, Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society; Alon and Spencer, The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition, Wiley.","status":"unverified"}

Then: (i) $\\mathbb{E}[V_1^T S_2 V_1 \\mid V_1] = V_1^T \\Sigma V_1$, so each diagonal entry $v_i^T S_2 v_i$ is an unbiased estimate of the population variance in the direction $v_i$ - the Ledoit-Peche oracle $d_i^* = v_i^T\\Sigma v_i$ evaluated on independent data; (ii) as $M, n \\to \\infty$ with $M/n \\to c > 0$ and $m/n \\to r \\in (0,1)$, $\\hat\\Sigma$ is asymptotically optimal in Frobenius loss among estimators of the form $V_1 D V_1^T$ with $D$ diagonal (Lam 2016, Theorem 1); (iii) $\\hat\\Sigma$ is positive semidefinite and carries no bandwidth, floor or shrinkage constant beyond the split fraction (Lam recommends choosing $m$ by minimising $\\|\\hat\\Sigma_m - S\\|_F$ over a grid; $m = n/2$ is the usual default). {"assumptions":["E and C symmetric p x p; the estimator class is restricted to the eigenvectors of E"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:50:37.943255+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_f2c72c8f5c4a1fb5da7d3fb5c8cdf44405907d5be714dd864209131af7efd314","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $E$ be a symmetric $p \\times p$ matrix with eigen-decomposition $E = \\sum_k \\lambda_k u_k u_k^T$ (for instance a sample covariance) and let $C$ be any symmetric $p \\times p$ matrix (the population covariance). Among all estimators of the form $\\Xi = \\sum_k \\xi_k u_k u_k^T$ - the same eigenvectors as $E$, free eigenvalues - the Frobenius loss $\\|\\Xi - C\\|_F^2$ is minimized by the oracle choice $\\xi_k^{\\mathrm{or}} = u_k^T C u_k$, the projection of the population matrix onto the $k$-th sample eigenvector, with minimal loss $\\|C\\|_F^2 - \\sum_k (u_k^T C u_k)^2$. {"assumptions":["(X_n) a martingale with respect to (F_n)","for the optional stopping consequence: tau an almost surely finite stopping time and the martingale uniformly integrable"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627236+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f3381e7ccdd3a3ab4f50fa4aa3f0083f4b6eac81113da66a80d044e9f35491f6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X_n)_{n >= 0} be a martingale for a filtration (F_n) and let F_infinity be the sigma-algebra generated by the union of the F_n. The following are equivalent: (i) the family {X_n} is uniformly integrable; (ii) X_n converges almost surely AND in L^1 to some X_infinity; (iii) there exists Y in L^1 with X_n = E[Y | F_n] almost surely for every n, that is the martingale is CLOSED. When these hold one may take Y = X_infinity, and X_infinity = E[Y | F_infinity]. Consequences: for a UI martingale, E[X_infinity] = E[X_0], and the optional stopping identity E[X_tau] = E[X_0] holds for EVERY almost surely finite stopping time tau, with no boundedness assumption on tau or on the martingale - this is a genuinely stronger conclusion than the standard three sufficient conditions (bounded tau, bounded martingale, or E[tau] finite with bounded increments). An L^1-bounded martingale need not be UI, and then only the almost sure half of (ii) survives. For p > 1, an L^p-bounded martingale is automatically UI by de la Vallee Poussin and converges in L^p as well; p = 1 is the exceptional case. [standard; e.g. Williams, Probability with Martingales, Theorems 13.3 and 14.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["each f_n Riemann integrable on the compact interval [a,b]","uniform bound |f_n| <= M","pointwise convergence to f, AND f Riemann integrable - an independent hypothesis"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752811+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_f36289c5312e1ca03cfca5ba87601f4ac8063f5554a56039a9f33e45b9a5702a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f_n : [a,b] -> R be Riemann integrable, uniformly bounded (|f_n| <= M for all n), and suppose f_n -> f pointwise on [a,b] where f is ALSO Riemann integrable. Then integral_a^b f_n -> integral_a^b f. The Riemann integrability of the limit must be ASSUMED and does not follow: enumerate the rationals of [0,1] as q_1, q_2, ... and let f_n be the indicator of {q_1, ..., q_n}. Each f_n is Riemann integrable with integral 0, the family is bounded by 1, and f_n increases pointwise to the indicator of the rationals, which is not Riemann integrable. This is the essential defect that the Lebesgue integral repairs: the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem needs only measurability of the limit, which is automatic for a pointwise limit of measurable functions. Historically Arzela proved this in 1885 by a direct and rather delicate covering argument, before the Lebesgue theory existed. [Arzela (1885); see e.g. Luxemburg, 'Arzela's dominated convergence theorem for the Riemann integral', Amer. Math. Monthly 78 (1971)]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149599+00:00","domain":"elliptic partial differential equations, maximum principles","id":"claim_f3f681977eb9ae940809b4e58a616eac3c6360d8024519e4cff1f440e2681399","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: an interior ball touching the boundary at the point x0 in question (and, for the strong maximum principle, the fact that such a ball can always be produced inside the open set where the solution is strictly below its maximum). Without it the conclusion 'the inward derivative at a boundary minimum is strictly positive' is false. Counterexample at a convex corner: in the plane let Omega be the sector {0 < theta < beta, 0 < r < 1} with 0 < beta < pi and u(r, theta) = r^{pi/beta} sin(pi theta/beta). Then u is harmonic in Omega, continuous on the closure, u > 0 inside and u = 0 on both straight edges, so 0 is a strict boundary minimum of u; but pi/beta > 1, so for every direction e pointing into Omega the difference quotient (u(te) - u(0))/t = O(t^{pi/beta - 1}) tends to 0: there is no Hopf gain at the vertex. No interior ball touches the vertex, exactly as the hypothesis requires. How far the hypothesis can be relaxed: the interior sphere condition may be replaced by an interior C^{1,Dini} (or interior paraboloid/cone-with-Dini) condition, but not by mere C^1 regularity of the boundary; there are C^1 domains where a positive harmonic function vanishing on the boundary has vanishing gradient at a boundary point - for instance the image of the upper half-plane near 0 under the conformal map z -> z log(1/z), whose boundary is C^1 but not Dini smooth at 0, and for which the inverse map has derivative tending to 0. Practical rule for an auditor: a proof that invokes Hopf's lemma (to get strict inequality, strict monotonicity, a sign of the normal derivative, simplicity of the first eigenvalue, or the strong maximum principle at the boundary) must say why the domain has the interior ball property at the relevant point; convex corners and cusps of the domain are where this silently breaks.","status":"unverified"}

# C019 v1: the averaged central peak is absent from each realized-label curve
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: route-failure. Target: 1. Novelty unestablished.
This is a local-window obstruction, not a global no-double-descent theorem.

## 1. Exact claim and dependencies
Use exactly C018's four stratified inputs, unit-norm single-index ReLU
teacher, fixed nu,kappa>0 (nu<=1), independent Gaussian hidden weights,
iid signed heads, both-layer GD step1/2 and sigma_e=2alpha_e sqrt(rho_e),
rho_e=kappa/sqrt(e). Unlike C018 retain the individual label realization:
 R_(e,m,xi)(k)=(1/4)sum_i(f_(m,xi)(x_i;k)-g_e(x_i))^2.
All sixteen networks share initialization. For any fixed bounded interval
I=[A,B] with A<B, let J_e(I) be the integers k with
 b_s k-(3/2)log(1/e) in I.
Then
 lim_(e downarrow0) liminf_(m to infinity)
 P(each of the sixteen sequences (R_(e,m,xi)(k))_(k in J_e(I))
   is strictly monotone in one direction) = 1.             (1)
The direction may depend on xi and initialization. For small e, J has
many consecutive integers. In particular none of the sixteen individual
curves has decrease/rise/decrease witnesses entirely inside this window,
with probability tending to one in this iterated-limit sense.
C018's sixteen-trajectory average may nevertheless have such witnesses.
No single-realized-label theorem follows from that average. This claim
concerns only a bounded s window around (3/2)log(1/e)/b_s, not other times.

## 2. Exact unaveraged risk derivative
Write c_h=(1/4)sum_i h(i)xi_i for h=0,s,t,st, N_h=2sqrt(rho_e)c_h,
and U_(e,h)=Z_(e,h)/alpha_e-theta_h/alpha_e in the Gaussian width limit.
The frozen residual in mode h divided by alpha_e is
 q_h U_(e,h)+(1-q_h)N_h, q_h=exp(-b_h t).
Thus, with eta_e=(b_t+b_st)/b_s, the derivative normalized by
2alpha_e^2(b_t+b_st) is exactly
 D_(e,xi)(s)=sum_h [b_h/(b_t+b_st)]
       {q_h N_h(N_h-U_(e,h))-q_h^2(U_(e,h)-N_h)^2},       (2)
at t=t_e(s)=((3/2)log(1/e)+s)/b_s.
C016/C017 give a joint Gaussian coupling, locally uniformly in s,
 e U_(e,s)->L_s=sqrt(2)nu G_s,
 U_(e,t)->L_t=sqrt(2)nu G_t-1, U_(e,st)->-1,
 b_t/(b_t+b_st), b_st/(b_t+b_st)->1/2, eta_e~e.
Let a=L_s^2 and B0=(L_t^2+1)/2; B0 is C017's B.
The constant-mode term is negligible faster than any power of e, even
with N_0=O(e^(-1/4)), because b_0 is bounded away from zero and
Z_(e,0)=O(1) in this coupling.

## 3. Exhausting the sixteen sign patterns
The four-dimensional Walsh transform of a sign vector has just two types.
If xi has an odd number of + signs (eight patterns), all four c_h are
+/-1/2. If xi has an even number, xi is one of the eight signed Walsh
characters, so exactly one c_h equals +/-1 and the others vanish.
Consequently there are ten patterns with c_s!=0, four with c_s=0 and
one of c_t,c_st nonzero, and two with only c_0 nonzero.
This finite classification is verified exactly in the accompanying script;
it also follows by direct enumeration of the sixteen vectors.

For c_s!=0, (2) gives the locally uniform limit
 e^(3/4) D_(e,xi)(s) -> -2sqrt(kappa)c_s L_s exp(-s).      (3)
Indeed q_s=e^(3/2)exp(-s), N_s=2sqrt(kappa)e^(-1/4)c_s,
U_s=e^(-1)(L_s+o(1)), and eta_e~e. The cross term
-q_s N_s U_s/eta_e has size e^(-3/4) and gives (3).
The terms q_s N_s^2/eta_e and q_s^2 U_s^2/eta_e are O(1);
all remaining fast terms are smaller. Slow-mode terms are O(e^(-1/4))
and disappear after multiplication by e^(3/4). These estimates are
uniform on each fixed compact s interval.

If c_s=0 and either c_t or c_st is nonzero, the corresponding limit is
 e^(1/4) D_(e,xi)(s) -> sqrt(kappa)(c_t L_t-c_st).         (4)
To check the slow terms without losing cancellations, rewrite their braces
in (2) as
 N_h U_h q_h(2q_h-1)-U_h^2 q_h^2+N_h^2 q_h(1-q_h).
Here q_h=1-O(e log(1/e)). After multiplication by e^(1/4), the
first term converges to 2sqrt(kappa)c_h times its U_h limit;

then gives, locally uniformly,

The constant-label term is again exponentially negligible.

Outside the null events L_s=0 and L_t=0, each of (3)-(5) has a strictly
nonzero, constant sign throughout any fixed compact interval. Uniform
convergence makes each frozen derivative have that sign for all sufficiently
small e. There are finitely many patterns, so this holds for all sixteen

monotone throughout J_e(I). The Gaussian probability of this event tends

## 4. Transfer of the LOCAL obstruction to actual nonlinear GD
For fixed e and finite integer horizon T, C018 Section3 proves joint weak

The event that each of sixteen finite risk sequences is strictly monotone

## 5. Consequence and exact scope
The dominant signed cross term in (3) disappears under noise averaging;

{"assumptions":["X_n => X in distribution","Y_n -> c in probability with c a CONSTANT (not a random variable)","for the quotient: c != 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752684+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f508dc594a18c6b66feda84d09ec4e36e63f895880826437a51899385d203a1c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_n converge in distribution to X and let Y_n converge in probability to a CONSTANT c. Then (X_n, Y_n) converges in distribution to (X, c) jointly, and consequently X_n + Y_n converges in distribution to X + c, X_n Y_n converges in distribution to cX, and if c is not 0 then X_n / Y_n converges in distribution to X / c. The constancy of the limit of Y_n is essential and is not a technical convenience: convergence in distribution alone gives no information about joint behaviour. Take X symmetric with X_n = X for all n and Y_n = -X for all n; then X_n converges in distribution to X and Y_n converges in distribution to X by symmetry, yet X_n + Y_n = 0 does not converge in distribution to X + X = 2X unless X is degenerate. Likewise convergence in probability of Y_n cannot be weakened to convergence in distribution even when the limit is constant, because for a constant limit those two modes coincide, which is precisely why the theorem can be stated with either for a constant target. [standard; e.g. van der Vaart, Asymptotic Statistics, Theorem 2.8]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-20T03:43:30.215430+00:00","domain":"discrete geometry","id":"claim_f528a90663c3e15b8fac1b81c773ee78b7ca979ccfb7ac5f9bc09809c835ec77","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The phrase 'general position' carries two conventions in the theory of hyperplane arrangements, and they are incompatible. For a CENTRAL arrangement, where every hyperplane contains the origin, the useful condition is on the NORMAL vectors: every $d$ or fewer of them are linearly independent. This is the condition under which the central orthant count is exact. For an AFFINE arrangement, a widespread convention instead requires that any $p$ of the hyperplanes with $p$ greater than the ambient dimension have empty intersection. No central arrangement can ever satisfy the affine condition, because all of its hyperplanes share the origin. A central arrangement is therefore never in 'general position' in the affine sense, however generic its normals. Sources using the affine convention will appear to exclude exactly the case a central count is about, and citing one for the other is a live error.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["This is a reduction of candidates, not a classification or a numerical proof for every stable index."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.365116+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f56a0e147e9085ca7af811dce58bae38fe443cd2f2e9f0fb5cdcc82ab3fb1945","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked] This is the remaining-problem reduction in the partial answer to Problem 3.11 of Takahiro Hasebe and Yuki Ueda's Large time unimodality for classical and free Brownian motions with initial distributions, ALEA 15 (2018), 353-374, DOI:10.30757/ALEA.v15-15 (arXiv:1710.08240). A probability measure is unimodal if, for some mode m, it is an atom at m plus an absolutely continuous measure whose density is nondecreasing to the left of m and nonincreasing to the right. Write boxplus for additive free convolution. A law lambda is freely strongly unimodal if lambda boxplus nu is unimodal for every unimodal nu. The source's Theorem 1.4 shows that no nondelta law of finite variance (equivalently, in the free domain of attraction of the semicircle) is freely strongly unimodal. The record's proved Cauchy obstruction excludes every nondelta lambda in the free domain of attraction of a Cauchy law. The same closure argument shows, more generally, that a nondelta lambda is not freely strongly unimodal whenever it lies in the free domain of attraction of a free stable law that is itself not freely strongly unimodal. Problem 3.11 therefore reduces to two questions. (1) Is some free stable law of index alpha in (0,2), alpha != 1, freely strongly unimodal? (The index-1 case is settled by the Cauchy identity, and index 2 by the source's Lemma 3.1.) (2) Is some measure lying in no free domain of attraction freely strongly unimodal? Numerically, for the free stable laws lambda_alpha with K(w)=1/w - i(iw)^{alpha-1}, the unimodal witness nu = (1/10)U[0,0.05] + (9/10)U[0,16] gives lambda_alpha boxplus nu two interior maxima at alpha = 1.95, 1.8, 1.6, 1.4, 1.2, 1.0, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7. This was computed by Belinschi-Bercovici subordination and calibrated against the exact Cauchy case at alpha=1. So those laws, and the laws attracted to them, are excluded numerically; only alpha=1 is a theorem. For alpha = 0.6 down to 0.3 the same nu, and three other one-sided uniform mixtures tried at alpha=0.5, give a single maximum. This is not evidence that those laws are freely strongly unimodal. The case alpha below about 0.65 remains open. This does not answer the existence question. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["alpha is irrational in (0,1) with continued fraction [0; a_1, a_2, ...], a_i >= 1","p_n/q_n are the convergents given by the standard three-term recursions","eta_n = ||q_n alpha|| = |q_n alpha - p_n|, and ||t|| is the distance to the nearest integer","the rotation is R_alpha(x) = x + alpha on the circle R/Z, and 'closest return' refers to the two-sided quantity ||q alpha||"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.732376+00:00","domain":"continued fractions, circle rotations, renormalization","id":"claim_f57732cc5b24796cda6e07d98d78f7bf187cb2277e435a9b21d5d4dfa548e4b2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let alpha in (0,1) be irrational with continued fraction alpha = [0; a_1, a_2, ...], all a_i >= 1, and let p_n / q_n be its convergents, defined by p_n = a_n p_{n-1} + p_{n-2}, q_n = a_n q_{n-1} + q_{n-2} with q_{-1} = 0, q_0 = 1, p_{-1} = 1, p_0 = 0. Put eta_n = |q_n alpha - p_n| and note the signs alternate: q_n alpha - p_n = (-1)^n eta_n. For n >= 1 one has eta_n < 1/q_{n+1} <= 1/2, so eta_n = ||q_n alpha||; at n = 0 this can fail (if a_1 = 1, i.e. alpha > 1/2, then eta_0 = alpha > 1/2 while ||alpha|| = 1 - alpha), so ALL statements below are for n >= 1. Write R_alpha(x) = x + alpha on T = R/Z. Then:

(a) BEST APPROXIMATION / CLOSEST RETURNS. For n >= 1 and every integer q with 1 <= q < q_{n+1} and q not equal to q_n one has ||q alpha|| > ||q_n alpha|| = eta_n. Consequently the denominators q_n are exactly the closest-return times of the orbit of 0 under R_alpha: q_{n+1} is the smallest integer q > q_n with ||q alpha|| < ||q_n alpha||, and the sequence of record-setting return times is precisely q_1 < q_2 < ....

(b) RECURSION AND SIZE. eta_{n-1} = a_{n+1} eta_n + eta_{n+1}; the eta_n strictly decrease to 0; 1/(q_{n+1} + q_n) < eta_n < 1/q_{n+1}; and the exact identity q_n eta_{n-1} + q_{n-1} eta_n = 1 holds for every n >= 1 (and also at n = 0 with the convention eta_{-1} = |q_{-1} alpha - p_{-1}| = 1).

(c) RENORMALIZATION INTO TWO ROKHLIN TOWERS. Let J_n be the arc of T whose endpoints are the two points q_{n-1} alpha - p_{n-1} and q_n alpha - p_n (of opposite signs), so J_n contains 0 and has length eta_{n-1} + eta_n; it is split by 0 into a piece of length eta_{n-1} and a piece of length eta_n. Then the first-return map of R_alpha to J_n is the exchange of these two subintervals: the return time is q_n on the piece of length eta_{n-1} and q_{n-1} on the piece of length eta_n. Equivalently the q_{n-1} + q_n sets R_alpha^i(base) -- i < q_n over the long piece and i < q_{n-1} over the short piece -- are pairwise disjoint and tile T, which is exactly the content of the identity q_n eta_{n-1} + q_{n-1} eta_n = 1 in (b). This is the standard renormalization scheme behind Ostrowski expansions and the three-distance theorem.

SHARP EDGES. (a) is a statement about the TWO-SIDED quantity ||q alpha||. The intermediate (mediant) denominators b q_n + q_{n-1} with 1 <= b < a_{n+1} are best ONE-SIDED approximations but in general do not minimize ||q alpha||, so they are NOT closest-return times -- confusing the two is the classic error here. The hypothesis that alpha is irrational is essential: for rational alpha the algorithm terminates, the orbit is finite and periodic, and the tower picture degenerates. Also note eta_n < 1/q_{n+1} is an inequality, not an asymptotic equality: eta_n and 1/q_{n+1} agree only up to a factor between 1/2 and 1, and a proof that needs the exact value must use eta_n = 1/(q_{n+1} + q_n * [0; a_{n+2}, a_{n+3}, ...]).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["weights nonnegative, not all zero","for the variance interpretation: i.i.d. observations with finite variance"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T09:17:06.630627+00:00","domain":"survey statistics / weighted estimation","id":"claim_f582d2971f91e2d79df8475b7b3a84e28609376a3e46cd4588963e2174f253ba","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For case weights $s_1, \\dots, s_n \\ge 0$ not all zero, the effective sample size is $n_{\\mathrm{eff}} = (\\sum_i s_i)^2 / \\sum_i s_i^2$. It satisfies $1 \\le n_{\\mathrm{eff}} \\le n$, with $n_{\\mathrm{eff}} = n$ if and only if all nonzero weights are equal and $n_{\\mathrm{eff}} = 1$ if and only if a single weight is nonzero. Its meaning: if $X_1, \\dots, X_n$ are i.i.d. with variance $\\sigma^2$, the weighted mean $\\bar X_s = \\sum_i s_i X_i / \\sum_i s_i$ has variance $\\sigma^2 / n_{\\mathrm{eff}}$ - the weighted mean is as noisy as an unweighted mean of $n_{\\mathrm{eff}}$ observations. The same factor governs every entry of a weighted sample covariance $\\sum_i s_i (x_i - \\bar x_s)(x_i - \\bar x_s)^T / \\sum_i s_i$ to leading order, so entrywise concentration bounds for the sample covariance transfer to the weighted one with $n$ replaced by $n_{\\mathrm{eff}}$. For the per-sample relative metric of ensemble stacking, $s_i = 1/\\|y_i\\|^2$, a few small-norm cases can make $n_{\\mathrm{eff}}$ far smaller than $n$ (measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT pool: 150 of 932 rows on one component, 8.7 of 60 in the $n = 60$ arm). (Why: $\\operatorname{Var}(\\bar X_s) = \\sum_i s_i^2 \\sigma^2 / (\\sum_i s_i)^2 = \\sigma^2 / n_{\\mathrm{eff}}$ by independence. The bounds: Cauchy-Schwarz gives $(\\sum_i s_i)^2 \\le n \\sum_i s_i^2$ with equality iff the nonzero weights are equal (restricting to the nonzero ones), and $(\\sum_i s_i)^2 \\ge \\sum_i s_i^2$ since the cross terms are nonnegative, with equality iff at most one weight is nonzero. For the covariance, each entry is a weighted mean of the products $(x_{ik} - \\bar x_{s,k})(x_{il} - \\bar x_{s,l})$ with the same weights, and the centring changes the variance only at second order in $1/n_{\\mathrm{eff}}$.)","status":"unverified"}

## Statement and experiment

Integers d>=1,N>=2d+1,K>=2,1<=r<K. Each of d context pairs has one A
and one S, with VC-d orientation class; N-2d remaining contexts are
known S. S has all K truths; each A has an independent uniform r-subset.
The factual source chooses contexts uniformly, then truths uniformly.
Training consists of actual iid factual context/candidate samples,
without partition tags. An independent verifier may supply ell true
candidates per variable context, uniformly without replacement, also
without orientation labels. Include those identities in the known
truth union C_x. Condition on ANY positive-probability data outcome
with sizes j_x=|C_x|<r in EVERY variable context. Counts and identities
may differ arbitrarily between siblings. Every orientation remains
compatible; compatible A supports contain C_A. The actual posterior
orientation probabilities need not be uniform.

Require exact source Mis_infinity=0 in EVERY compatible world, using
the uniform coarsening within exact g-probability bins. Allow all g.
Set h_i=min(j_left,j_right) for pair i and

 b_h=[1/K+(r-h)/(r(K-h))]/(2N).

The proposed exact CONDITIONAL worst-world false-mass frontier is

 V(0)=sum_{i=1}^d (K-r)*b_{h_i}.                        (1)

An attainer has this risk in every actual compatible world. This is
not an assertion that all other generators have a pointwise lower
bound (C015's varying-count control disproves that). No unconditional
expected minimax value is inferred from (1).

For the same known truths with the partition additionally supplied,
the conditional worst-world oracle value is

 O_worst(0)=sum_i (K-r)*(r-h_i)/(Nr(K-h_i)).              (2)

Thus the exact worst-oracle estimation gap is

 V(0)-O_worst(0)
   =sum_i h_i*(K-r)^2/(2NrK(K-h_i)).                    (3)

The oracle in (2) takes a maximum over supplied orientations; it is
not the average actual-orientation oracle. Formula (3) weights the
conditional 1/N-per-pair classification error of the specified fair
completion of support-consistent ERM. No statistically optimal ERM
rate or general unweighted-error identity is claimed.

## Residual support variability forces one score level

Fix ANY robustly zero-calibrated generator g and its exact score
partition Pi. In every bin B, p_world(B)=g(B) for every compatible
world, hence its source mass is invariant under changing supports or
orientations. For a context x possibly A, let Q_x be its K-j_x
uncertified atoms. Since 1<=r-j_x<K-j_x, any two atoms of Q_x can be
swapped in a compatible A support while all other truth identities
remain fixed. If one were in B and the other outside, this swap would
change p(B) by 1/(Nr), contradicting invariance. Therefore each bin
contains either ALL or NONE of Q_x. Equivalently all Q_x atoms have
one common score; denote their unique bin B_x.

This argument FAILS if j_x=r, since there is then no residual truth
to swap. C016's neutral-bundle counterexample exploits exactly this
boundary, rather than contradicting the present strict hypothesis.

## Classifying each pair's invariant bins

Write s=j_L<=t=j_R<r for one pair; relabel siblings if necessary.
For a bin B let u_x=|B intersect C_x| and epsilon_x=1 if Q_x is in B,
else zero. The difference between its A-context and S-context source
contributions is

 delta_x(B)=(K-r)/(NrK)*(u_x-epsilon_x*j_x).

Independent flipping of this pair's orientation while holding all
other pairs fixed implies delta_L(B)=delta_R(B) for EVERY bin.

If B_L!=B_R, then in B_L the left delta is nonpositive and the right
delta nonnegative. Equality forces u_L=s,u_R=0. Similarly B_R has
u_R=t,u_L=0. Thus each context lies entirely in its own one score bin.

If B_L=B_R=B*, equality gives

 k=s-u_L=t-u_R, 0<=k<=s.

Outside B* every bin contains only known truths from these contexts
and contains the SAME number of known truths from each sibling.
Exactly k known truths from each sibling lie outside B*.

## Reduction to the balanced-count game

For each pair retain the smaller context's complete known set C_L.
In the larger context retain a subset C'_R of size s. If the residual
bins are different, choose any such subset. If they coincide in B*,
retain ALL k larger-context known truths outside B* and choose any
s-k additional known truths inside B*. This is possible since there
are t-k>=s-k such inside truths. The sets may depend on g; this is
a proof comparison, not the algorithm.

Expand the compatible world set by forgetting the t-s surplus truths
in the larger context. In the distinct-bin case both contexts had
one score, so every source bin mass and every false-atom count per
bin are unchanged under this expansion. In the common-bin case all
newly uncertified atoms lie in B*. Every other bin retains the same
known-true counts; in B* the A context always has r-k true atoms and
K-r false atoms, in either orientation and for every expanded support.
Thus again each source bin mass and each actual false-count-per-bin
vector is unchanged.

Do this independently for every pair. For the same fixed g,

* robust zero calibration holds on the EXPANDED balanced-count game;
* the set of possible false masses across its worlds equals the set
  across the original compatible worlds, orientation by orientation.

The expanded game has balanced known counts h_i and arbitrary known
identities. It need not preserve the original sample/verifier labels:
it is an enlarged source-world comparison, not a claimed posterior.
C015's general balanced-count lower bound at c=0 therefore yields
max_original H(g)=max_expanded H(g)>=sum_i(K-r)b_{h_i}.
Dependence of the selected balanced sets on g causes no problem:
the balanced theorem is uniform over all sets of the stated sizes.

## Balanced comparison lower bound, stated here for completeness

For the expanded known sets of balanced sizes h_i, average orientations
fairly and average compatible residual supports uniformly. This is an
artificial lower-bound distribution, not the actual posterior. Its
mean factual law mu gives density a=(1/r+1/K)/(2N) to known truths,
b_h to uncertified atoms in count-h pairs, and 1/(NK) to fixed S.
The false probability of each uncertified atom is tau_h=(K-r)/(2(K-h)).
As h increases b_h decreases and tau_h increases; safe densities are
at least 1/(NK)>=b_h. For E_h the union of uncertified atoms in pairs
with count at least h, every inside density is <=every outside
density. Uniform coarsening in any bin transfers mass INTO E_h, so
mu_Pi(E_h)>=mu(E_h)=T_h with T_h as in (6). Robust feasibility and
TV convexity imply TV(mu_Pi,g)<=c, hence g(E_h)>=(T_h-c)_+.
The artificial average false risk is exactly
tau_0*g(E_0)+sum_{h=1}^{r-1}(tau_h-tau_{h-1})*g(E_h).
It is at least (6), and the maximum original risk equals the maximum
expanded risk and is at least this average. This proves the needed
balanced lower bound directly, for c=0 and throughout (4), without
requiring a prior-card theorem or any actual posterior identity.

## Attainment and oracle comparison

Select h_i known truths from each sibling before constructing g. Put
their two known-true groups at score (1/r+1/K)/(2N); put the remaining
2(K-h_i) pair atoms at b_{h_i}, and fixed S atoms at 1/(NK).
Each pair group has invariant p mass under all original worlds.
Exact-score mergers preserve invariance. This g is robustly calibrated
with zero budget, and each actual world's K-r false atoms per pair
all receive b_{h_i}. This proves the matching upper bound in (1).

If a supplied orientation chooses A at count j, the zero-budget oracle
has risk (K-r)*(r-j)/(Nr(K-j)), by the ordered known-A-group argument
of C009/C015. This quantity decreases with j, so its maximum over
independent orientations picks j=h_i in every pair, proving (2).
Subtracting gives (3) exactly.

## A nonzero calibration-budget interval via discrete TV jumps

The reduction extends to EVERY budget

 0<=c<c_star=(K-r)/(2NrK).                               (4)

Let Pi be the exact score partition of any robustly c-feasible g.
For any two compatible worlds w,w', the triangle inequality gives

 TV(p_w,Pi,p_w',Pi)<=2c.                                (5)

If a context's uncertified atoms occupy two different score bins,
swap one true and one false uncertified atom in its A support. This
is possible since j_x<r<K. The coarsened source laws then differ
by exactly 1/(Nr) in TV. But 2c<(K-r)/(NrK)<1/(Nr), contradicting (5).
Thus all uncertified atoms still occupy one score bin, as before.

Consequently coarsened source masses are independent of residual
supports. On flipping a single pair's orientation their bin-mass
changes are integer multiples of

 eta=(K-r)/(NrK),

by the delta formula above. If any bin changes, the changes sum to
zero, so the sum of their positive parts is at least eta. Uniform
coarsening preserves each bin mass, hence the TV of these two
coarsened laws is at least eta. This contradicts 2c<eta. Therefore
ALL coarsened source laws are identical across every compatible world.
In particular the invariant-bin classification and balanced-set
expansion apply without assuming g equals this common coarsened law.
They preserve both calibration distance to g and false mass, bin by
bin, for each orientation. The earlier reduction is valid throughout (4).

Let D_h count pairs with h_i=h,0<=h<=r-1. Put

 tau_h=(K-r)/(2(K-h)), M_h=D_h*(2-h/r-h/K)/N,
 T_h=sum_{t=h}^{r-1}M_t.

C015's balanced-game formula gives the exact all-generator conditional

context. Actual iid factual samples have no orientation tags. An
optional independent verifier supplies a uniform ell-subset of truths

on ANY positive-probability data outcome with j_x=|C_x|<=r in every
variable context. Thus no orientation is logically excluded. Some
contexts may have j_x=r; sibling counts and sample repetitions may

Write h_i=min(j_left,j_right) and D_h=#{i:h_i=h},0<=h<=r. Put

exact g-probability bins. The same-data partition-supplied WORST-

smaller interval. It does not contradict C016/C018's noncoprime cases.

## Discrete source-bin mass rigidity

Fix any robustly c-feasible generator g and its exact score partition
Pi. For every compatible world and every cell B, p(B) is an integer
multiple of 1/(NrK), since the original atom masses are 0,1/(Nr) or
1/(NK). This is a lattice statement about BIN MASSES; individual
coarsened atom probabilities have the additional bin-size divisor.
For two worlds w,w', uniformity within the SAME cells gives

 TV(p_w,Pi,p_w',Pi)=(1/2)*sum_B |p_w(B)-p_w'(B)|.

If any bin mass differs, the nonzero integer differences sum to zero,
so this TV is at least 1/(NrK). Triangle inequality and feasibility
instead give TV<=2c<1/(NrK). Therefore EVERY source bin mass is

## Coprimality restores rigidity at a saturated sibling

For an unsaturated context j_x<r, swapping a residual true and false
candidate in a compatible A support shows that all uncertified atoms
occupy one score bin, as in C017. Consider an unequal pair with counts

count and epsilon_L indicate inclusion of all K-s uncertified L atoms;

orientation invariance gives

Hence (K-r)|r*v_R. Since gcd(r,K-r)=1, Bezout implies (K-r)|v_R.

saturated context's outside atoms. Thus their score is also constant.

For each unequal pair both outside-known sets now occupy unique bins.
For any cell write u_x for its known-truth count and epsilon_x for
whether it contains the entire outside-known set. The A-minus-S source
contribution is (K-r)*(u_x-epsilon_x*j_x)/(NrK), so equality under the
orientation flip makes these expressions equal for the two siblings.

If the two outside-known bins differ, each contains an ENTIRE context
and none of the other context. If they coincide in B*, the number k
of known truths outside B* is equal in both siblings and at most s,
the smaller count. Retain all smaller-context truths. In the larger
context retain its k known truths outside B* and any s-k of its known
truths inside B*. Forget all other larger-context truths.

Expanding compatible supports by this forgetting preserves every source
bin mass: outside B* known counts are unchanged; in B* the A context
always has r-k truths. It also preserves each bin's false count for
each orientation: all K-r A false atoms remain in the same outside-

from fixed context mass 1/N and fixed false count K-r. Balanced pairs,

robustly c-feasible and has exactly the same possible false masses.

In the balanced comparison game average orientations fairly and
