{"assumptions":["d>=1,N>=2d+1,n>=0,K>=2,1<=r<K,0<=ell<=r integers","Paired A/S VC class; uniform contexts then uniform truths; independent uniform r-subsets in A, all truths in S","Actual iid factual samples without tags; independent uniform ell-subset verifier in every variable context including S","Unresolved sibling pairs have equal distinct observed-plus-certified counts h<=r; identified pairs are logically certified by an S context with >r known truths; each identified A count j is >= maximum unresolved h (vacuous if none)","All generators; robust exact-level source calibration across every compatible orientation and residual support"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T21:03:39.295480+00:00","domain":"statistical learning; calibrated generation; partial truth verification","id":"claim_f75b182c10094807f8f65295a7c116ffcea2d51b7b906b0cc0c6c75d7a006c10","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited); independent review pending. # Pair-balanced factual identities under partial verification

T379-C015 v2, proof (unaudited). Both exact verification suites PASS;
independent mathematical, priority and target-scope review pending.
Targets 1 and 2. This is a conditional data-regime result, not a global
expected minimax claim. The unresolved unequal-sibling-count regime is
the hardest missing piece; C010 shows why its ordering cannot be assumed.

## Model and data region

Use the paired VC-d experiment: d>=1,N>=2d+1,K>=2,1<=r<K integers;
one A and one S per pair, all remaining contexts known S. S has K true
candidates, A has an independent uniform r-subset. The source p chooses
contexts uniformly, then true candidates uniformly. Observe n>=0 iid
factual context/candidate samples without orientation tags. Independently
a perfect verifier supplies a uniform ell-subset of truths in each
variable context, including S, 0<=ell<=r. Let C_x be the union of
distinct observed and verified candidate identities in context x.

Condition on any positive-probability data outcome for which every pair
has |C_left|=|C_right|=h_j<=r. The actual identities may differ. Thus no
orientation is logically excluded, and every one of 2^d orientations
is compatible. Counts and likelihoods of repeated observations can be
unequal: uniform orientation weights below are an ARTIFICIAL proof
distribution, not the actual Bayesian posterior. Under a chosen
orientation, the A support ranges uniformly over r-subsets containing
C_A. Put D_h=#{j:h_j=h}, ell<=h<=r.

Define

 b_h=[1/K+(r-h)/(r(K-h))]/(2N),
 tau_h=(K-r)/(2(K-h)),
 M_h=(D_h/N)*(2-h/r-h/K),
 T_h=sum_{t=h}^r M_t.

Over ALL generators, with source Mis_infinity<=c required in every
compatible world (including every compatible A support), the proposed
exact conditional worst-world false-mass frontier is

 V_D(c)=tau_ell*(T_ell-c)_+
        +sum_{h=ell+1}^r (tau_h-tau_{h-1})*(T_h-c)_+.       (1)

All formulas allow missing D_h and c in [0,1]. Exact score bins define
source Mis_infinity=TV(g,p_Pi), with p uniformly coarsened in each bin.

## Lower bound across arbitrary mixed bins

Average orientations fairly and A supports uniformly conditional on
containing their known identities. Let mu be the resulting mean law.
Every known true atom in a variable context has density

 a=(1/r+1/K)/(2N).

The uncertified atoms of a pair at count h have density b_h and false
probability tau_h under this artificial prior. Their total mu mass is
M_h across the D_h pairs. Known S atoms have density 1/(NK).

As h increases, tau_h increases and b_h decreases: directly,
b_h-b_{h+1}=(K-r)/(2Nr(K-h)(K-h-1)) when h<r. All safe densities
are >=1/(NK)>=b_h. Thus E_h, the union of uncertified atoms in pairs
with count at least h, consists of lower-density atoms than its entire
complement. For ANY partition Pi, uniform coarsening increases its mass:

 mu_Pi(E_h)>=mu(E_h)=T_h.

Indeed in each cell the mean density over E_h is at most the mean over
its complement, so replacing both means by the cell mean transfers
mass into E_h. This proves the assertion per bin, not merely globally.

Robust feasibility and linearity/TV convexity give TV(mu_Pi(g),g)<=c.
Hence g(E_h)>=(T_h-c)_+. Layer-cake decomposition of the artificial
average false risk gives

 max_world H(g)>=tau_ell*g(E_ell)
                   +sum_{h>ell}(tau_h-tau_{h-1})*g(E_h)
                >=V_D(c).

No joint-probability multiplication or actual-posterior identity is used.

## Matching construction

Start from mu. Remove mass min(c,T_ell) from uncertified groups in
decreasing h order, uniformly within each h group, and add it uniformly
to the fixed known S reservoir. All remaining g(E_h)=(T_h-c)_+.
Each pair's known-true group has h atoms from each sibling and invariant
source mass h*(1/r+1/K)/N. Its uncertified group has K-h atoms from
each sibling and invariant source mass (2-h/r-h/K)/N, regardless of
orientation or which residual truths occupy A. The constructed g is
constant on every such group. Exact score bins only merge invariant
groups, so p_Pi=mu_Pi in every compatible world. Since g_Pi=g,
Mis_infinity<=TV(mu,g)<=c. The uncertified false-atom fraction in each
h group equals tau_h in every world. Thus actual H equals V_D(c)
worldwise, proving conditional sharpness of (1).

## Same-data oracle and exact estimation penalty

If the true partition is additionally supplied, let

 A_h=D_h*(r-h)/(Nr), Q_h=sum_{t=h}^r A_t,
 alpha_h=(K-r)/(K-h)=2tau_h.

The same-data known-partition frontier, by the ordered known-A groups,
is

 O_D(c)=alpha_ell*(Q_ell-c)_+
        +sum_{h>ell}(alpha_h-alpha_{h-1})*(Q_h-c)_+.       (2)

Here A_h is the posterior mass of unknown true candidates of the actual
A contexts, and their densities decrease while their false risks rise.
The same mixed-bin tail proof and transfer-to-S construction apply.
Thus V_D(c)=O_D(c)+[V_D(c)-O_D(c)] is an exact matching decomposition,
with nonnegative difference because giving the partition enlarges
feasibility. At c=0 it simplifies to the explicit positive penalty

 V_D(0)-O_D(0)
   =sum_{h=ell}^r D_h*h*(K-r)^2/(2NrK(K-h)).             (3)

The penalty is zero at h=0, and at h=r contributes kappa/(2N) per pair,
recovering C013's unresolved full-verifier value. In general it depends
on the factual-support histogram, not merely VC dimension or a single
unweighted classification-error scalar. A fair completion among the
2^d support-consistent ERM orientations has conditional expected
classification error 1/N per pair; (3) weights that error by
h*(K-r)^2/[2rK(K-h)]. This is a specified ERM, not an optimal posterior
classification claim. The conditional minimax lower bound is not
silently averaged into a global expected lower bound; C014 forbids
that shortcut at positive budgets.

## Scope

This removes supplied tags and retains actual factual identities for
every balanced outcome, all n,K,r,ell and all calibration budgets. It
allows different h across pairs, but does not cover unequal sibling
counts, already identified pairs, or an unconditional exact expected
frontier. Equal h in every pair reduces the conditional formula to the
corresponding earlier C008 experiment with that many known truths;
the histogram, actual untagged-data applicability and explicit oracle
penalty are the proposed extension, not a claim that C008 was unknown.
Primary basis: Kalai--Vempala 2311.14648v3 Definitions 1--2 pp.8--9;
own earlier C008/C009 are unaudited drafts. No novelty or target score
is certified until independent mathematical and priority review.

## Extension: include identified pairs under a coverage ordering

The same theorem extends as follows. Partition the d pairs into resolved
and unresolved pairs. A resolved pair has a context with >r distinct
known truths, logically forcing S and identifying its sibling as A.
Let E_j count these known A contexts with j distinct known truths,
ell<=j<=r. Each unresolved pair still has balanced count h<=r; D_h
now counts just these unresolved pairs. Require

 j>=h_max for every resolved A, where
 h_max=max{h:D_h>0}.                                    (4)

If no unresolved pairs exist, condition (4) is vacuous. Known facts
in identified S and fixed S contexts are all safe and have density
1/(NK), irrespective of their observed identities or counts.

There are two positive-risk group types under the artificial compatible
prior (independent fair unresolved orientations and uniform compatible
A supports):

* Unresolved count h: mass M_h as before, risk tau_h, density b_h.
* Resolved A count j: mass L_j=E_j*(r-j)/(Nr), risk
  alpha_j=(K-r)/(K-j), density a_j=(r-j)/(Nr(K-j)).

Groups at j=r can have zero factual mass and risk one; retain them
without dividing by their mass. All safe groups have density >=1/(NK).
For resolved groups, j increasing makes risk increase and density
decrease. Across the two types condition (4) implies

 alpha_j>=alpha_hmax=2tau_hmax>=tau_h,
 a_j<=a_hmax<=b_hmax<=b_h.

Thus ALL groups are ordered in opposite directions by density and risk.
Let 0<xi_1<...<xi_s<=1 be their distinct risk values; aggregate masses
at equal risk into m_i, and let R_i=sum_{k=i}^s m_k, xi_0=0. The exact
combined conditional robust frontier is

 V(c)=sum_{i=1}^s (xi_i-xi_{i-1})*(R_i-c)_+.             (5)

The same arbitrary-bin tail argument proves the lower bound. Remove
mass in decreasing risk order, uniformly inside each group, and transfer
to fixed S for the upper bound. Resolved A certified and uncertified
groups have world-invariant p masses because all residual supports
have the same size and contain the known truths. Unresolved balanced
groups have the invariance proved earlier. Consequently exact score
mergers remain valid for every compatible support and orientation.
False fractions equal the specified risks in EACH actual world, so
the construction attains (5) worldwise, not just on artificial average.

The same-data partition oracle is formula (2) with A_h replaced by

 (D_h+E_h)*(r-h)/(Nr).

At c=0 its exact difference from (5) is still formula (3), now summed
over unresolved pairs only. The identified-pair terms cancel. At any
c, both explicit formulas match their respective conditional minima.
When ell=r, every resolved A has j=r and condition (4) always holds;
this reduces (5) to C013's conditional frontier for arbitrary mixtures
of resolved and unresolved pairs. For ell<r this is a larger untagged
partial-verifier data regime than the all-unresolved case.

Unequal sibling counts or failure of (4) are NOT covered. No exact
global expected minimax value follows by averaging (5). This extension
has a separate route check, logs/route_014_extension_check.txt, and its
finite exact verification is kept separate from the general derivation.

## Zero-budget pointwise scope and an explicit control

If all pairs are unresolved and share ONE count h, every atom of the
artificial mean law has density at least b_h. Robust zero calibration
implies g=mu_Pi, hence g(atom)>=b_h. Each actual world has exactly
d(K-r) false atoms. Consequently every such generator obeys the
POINTWISE bound H>=d(K-r)b_h=V_D(0), and the construction attains it.
This separate observation applies regardless of actual orientation
likelihoods. It does not extend to varying h by the same argument.

In fact varying h can destroy even a zero-budget pointwise version of
the conditional bound. Take N=5,d=2,K=3,r=2,ell=0 and counts h_0=0,
h_1=1; use C_2=C_3={0}. These are possible actual untagged data, e.g.
the two observations (2,0),(3,0). Form a bin B containing all three
atoms of context 0 and the four uncertified atoms of contexts 2 and 3.
Its source mass is 1/5+7/30=13/30, independent of orientations and
residual A supports; set g=13/210 on its seven atoms. Other bins are
all of context 1 (g=1/15), both certified atoms of contexts 2 and 3
(g=1/12), and all fixed-S context 4 (g=1/15). Merging the equal 1/15
scores preserves invariance. This g is robustly source-calibrated at
zero in every compatible world.

If context 0 is A its actual false mass is 13/105, strictly below
V_D(0)=1/8 by 1/840. If context 1 is A, its false mass is 9/70,
strictly above 1/8. This is a real compatible-world control, not a
violation of (1) or (5): the theorem is conditional WORST-WORLD, and
the latter world meets that lower bound. It forbids silently replacing
the conditional maximum by a per-world bound even at zero budget in
the varying-count family. No claim about the global sampling minimax
value follows from this single outcome.

{"assumptions":["(a_n)_{n >= 0} is a real sequence","the second differences a_n - 2a_{n+1} + a_{n+2} are nonnegative for every n >= 0 (convexity)","a_n -> 0 as n -> infinity","consequences used and derived from these: a_n >= 0, a_n nonincreasing, n(a_n - a_{n+1}) -> 0, sum (n+1)(a_n - 2a_{n+1} + a_{n+2}) = a_0","integrability is with respect to Lebesgue measure on the circle"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.815245+00:00","domain":"Fourier analysis, trigonometric series","id":"claim_f95cf78453cad9016df951c8497b0e8bcbb54049fe66f88a10ab868d7db99aa2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (a_n)_{n >= 0} be real numbers which are CONVEX, meaning the second differences D2 a_n := a_n - 2 a_{n+1} + a_{n+2} are >= 0 for every n >= 0, and which tend to 0. (These two hypotheses already force a_n >= 0 and a_n nonincreasing: the first differences a_{n+1} - a_n are nondecreasing, so if one of them were positive the sequence would tend to +infinity. They also force n(a_n - a_{n+1}) -> 0, since the differences are monotone.) THEOREM (Young; Zygmund, Trigonometric Series, Ch. V). Put S(x) = a_0/2 + sum_{n >= 1} a_n cos(nx). Then: (1) the series converges for every x not in 2 pi Z, uniformly on every compact subset of (0, 2 pi); (2) S(x) >= 0 for all such x; (3) S is Lebesgue integrable on (-pi, pi), with (1/(2 pi)) times the integral of S over (-pi,pi) equal to a_0/2; (4) the series IS the Fourier series of S, that is a_n = (1/pi) times the integral over (-pi,pi) of S(x) cos(nx) dx for every n >= 0. The whole theorem rests on one identity: with K_n(x) = (1/(n+1)) (sin((n+1)x/2) / sin(x/2))^2 >= 0 the Fejer kernel, normalised so that (1/(2 pi)) times the integral of K_n over (-pi,pi) is 1, double summation by parts gives S(x) = sum_{n >= 0} (n+1) (D2 a_n) (1/2) K_n(x), with sum_{n >= 0} (n+1) D2 a_n = a_0 < infinity. Nonnegativity is then read off from D2 a_n >= 0 and K_n >= 0, and integrability from the normalisation. SHARP EDGES. (a) It is CONVEXITY, not monotone decrease, that does the work: monotone decrease to zero gives convergence off the origin by Dirichlet's test, but it does not produce the Fejer representation and therefore gives neither nonnegativity nor integrability of the sum. (b) The SINE analogue is false in this form. If (b_n) is convex and decreases to 0, then sum b_n sin(nx) still converges pointwise off 2 pi Z, but its sum is Lebesgue integrable if and only if sum b_n / n converges. The classical counterexample is b_n = 1/log n for n >= 2, which is convex and decreases to 0 while sum 1/(n log n) diverges: the resulting series converges everywhere but is not the Fourier series of any Lebesgue integrable function. Never transport the cosine statement to the sine case. (c) 'Integrable' cannot be improved to 'bounded': for a_n of order 1/n the sum behaves like log(1/|x|) near 0, which is integrable and unbounded. (d) The conclusion S >= 0 is on (0, 2 pi); nothing is claimed at x in 2 pi Z, where the series may diverge (it diverges precisely when sum a_n = infinity). (e) Convexity is only assumed for n >= 0 on the given sequence; a sequence that is eventually convex gives the same conclusions after subtracting a trigonometric polynomial, but then nonnegativity of the sum is lost.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["G = PSL(2,R) and Gamma < G is discrete with finite covolume (a lattice)","m is the G-invariant probability measure on Gamma\\G","the flow is right translation by the one-parameter unipotent subgroup u_t","no cocompactness, torsion freeness or arithmeticity is assumed for (1)-(3); cocompactness is needed only for minimality and unique ergodicity, which are NOT claimed here","mixing is understood with respect to the normalised invariant probability measure"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090417+00:00","domain":"homogeneous dynamics, unipotent flows, mixing","id":"claim_fa58123752f92f96ece864fcf1e4a8975e90b2041eda5d1899f3190c01222269","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let G = PSL(2,R) and let Gamma be a LATTICE in G: a discrete subgroup such that the quotient M = Gamma\\G carries a G-invariant Borel probability measure m (finite covolume, normalised). Gamma is not assumed torsion free, cocompact, or arithmetic. For real t let u_t denote the image in G of the unipotent matrix with rows (1, t) and (0, 1), and define the horocycle flow on M by h_t(Gamma g) = Gamma g u_t. Then: (1) each h_t preserves m; (2) HEDLUND: the flow is ergodic with respect to m; (3) PARRY: the flow is strongly mixing, that is for all F1, F2 in L^2(M, m) the inner product of F1 composed with h_t against F2 converges, as |t| -> infinity, to the product of the integral of F1 and the conjugate of the integral of F2; equivalently m(A intersect h_{-t}B) -> m(A) m(B) for all Borel A, B. Moreover the flow is mixing of all orders. WHERE THE HYPOTHESES BITE: (i) finite covolume is essential. Mixing as stated is a statement about a probability measure; for a discrete subgroup of infinite covolume the correct statements concern Burger-Roblin and Patterson-Sullivan measures and carry extra hypotheses (for instance on the critical exponent), so (3) must not be quoted there. (ii) Ergodicity and mixing hold for EVERY lattice, but MINIMALITY (every orbit dense), Hedlund's other theorem, needs Gamma cocompact: a noncompact finite-volume quotient has closed horocycle orbits encircling each cusp, so the flow there is mixing yet neither minimal nor uniquely ergodic. Confusing the two Hedlund statements is the usual error. (iii) The result concerns the unipotent direction. The geodesic flow a_s is also mixing but has positive entropy and a huge simplex of invariant measures, whereas the horocycle flow has zero entropy and (in the cocompact case) is uniquely ergodic; rigidity statements do not transfer between them. (iv) Nothing here gives a RATE; quantitative mixing needs a spectral gap input and the rate depends on the lattice.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H_k the Sylvester Hadamard matrix of order 2^k, disc(A) = min over sign vectors x of ||A x||_inf"],"created_at":"2026-09-24T23:46:59.335012+00:00","domain":"combinatorics/Boolean functions","id":"claim_face5f144efa4b4e9a635b179d81577f","kind":"counterexample","schema_version":1,"statement":"Conjecture 13 of the Randomstrasse 2024 problem list asks whether the Sylvester Hadamard matrix H_k of order 2^k has discrepancy disc(H_k) = sqrt(2) sqrt(2^k) for odd k, where disc(A) = min over sign vectors x of the sup-norm of Ax. In plain terms: take the 2^k x 2^k matrix of plus and minus ones whose entry in row a and column u is (-1) to the mod-2 dot product of the k-bit strings a and u, and ask for the smallest possible largest absolute entry of the product Hx over sign vectors x. Indexing H_k by (-1)^{a.u} and reading x as the +-1 truth table of a Boolean function f on k variables, H_k x is the Walsh transform W_f, so disc(H_k) = min_f max_a |W_f(a)| = 2^k - 2 NL_max(k), where NL_max(k) is the largest nonlinearity of a Boolean function on k variables (the covering radius of the Reed-Muller code RM(1, k)). The conjectured value is exactly the bent-concatenation bound NL = 2^{k-1} - 2^{(k-1)/2}, which is beaten for odd k = 15 (Patterson and Wiedemann, 1983) and for every odd k > 7 (Kavut, Maitra and Yucel, 2006), and is optimal for k <= 7. So the conjecture holds exactly for k in {1, 3, 5, 7} and fails for every odd k >= 9. The numbers: for k <= 7 the maximum nonlinearity equals the bent-concatenation value (the covering radius of RM(1,5) is 12, Berlekamp and Welch 1972; of RM(1,7) is 56, Mykkeltveit 1980; k = 1, 3 by hand); for k = 9 functions of nonlinearity 242 exist (Kavut, Maitra and Yucel 2006), so disc(H_9) <= 512 - 484 = 28 < 32; for every odd k = 9 + 2j the direct sum of such a function with a bent function on 2j variables has largest Walsh coefficient 28 * 2^j, below 32 * 2^j, since the Walsh spectrum of a direct sum is the product; and Patterson and Wiedemann's nonlinearity 16276 on 15 variables gives disc(H_15) <= 216 < 256.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the point process is exactly determinantal, or Pfaffian with the analogous but distinct formula, with a well-defined correlation kernel K satisfying the standard positivity and boundedness conditions","the conditioning event is of the specific form covered by the Schur-complement formula, i.e. an exact configuration on a subset, or the corresponding L-ensemble conditioning","invertibility, or a well-defined limiting or pseudo-inverse procedure, for the relevant diagonal block appearing in the formula, e.g. K_AA - I","the block partition A, B is taken with respect to the same index set on which K is originally defined"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.998694+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_faf3e83a28894a41c1931704cf7a671a579f690c334933aa41076761cbab8d22","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a determinantal point process with correlation kernel K, Hermitian and satisfying 0<=K<=I in the discrete finite-space setting, the conditional law of the process restricted to a subset given the exact configuration on the complementary subset is again determinantal, with a kernel given by a Schur-complement formula. Partitioning the index set into A, the observed subset, and B, the remaining subset, and writing K in block form with entries K_AA, K_AB, K_BA, K_BB, the conditional kernel on B given the exact points observed in A is expressed via a Schur-complement expression such as K_BB - K_BA (K_AA - I)^{-1} K_AB, with the precise form depending on the convention used (correlation kernel versus L-ensemble) and on whether one conditions on points being present or absent in A. This identity is the fundamental tool for analyzing conditioning, dynamics, and Gibbs-type properties of determinantal processes, including eigenvalues of random matrices, non-intersecting paths, discrete orthogonal polynomial ensembles, and, via the transfer-current theorem, uniform spanning trees, reducing conditional analysis to linear algebra on the kernel matrix. It does not apply outside the determinantal class of point processes, or its Pfaffian analogue for orthogonal and symplectic ensembles, which has a related but distinct formula, and the exact form of the Schur complement depends sensitively on the specific conditioning event and on invertibility of the relevant block, which can fail or require a pseudo-inverse or limiting argument at special parameter values. Typical failure: Applying a Schur-complement conditional-kernel formula derived under one convention, such as conditioning an L-ensemble on a fixed exact sample, to a different conditioning question, such as conditioning on a sub-event like at least one point in a region, or mixing up the correlation-kernel and L-ensemble conventions, without re-deriving the correct formula; determinantal-process conditioning identities are convention-sensitive, and mixing them up produces a kernel that still looks plausible, expressed via some Schur complement, but does not correctly describe the actual conditional process. Canonical reference: Shirai and Takahashi, 2003, Journal of Functional Analysis; Borodin and Rains, 2005, Journal of Statistical Physics; Lyons, 2003, Annals of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["two-dimensional planar lattice model satisfying the FKG inequality","translation invariance and, in the classical gluing constructions, reflection symmetry of the lattice","an a priori lower bound on square-crossing probabilities, which is a hypothesis to be separately established, not a free consequence of RSW","independence, or at least positive association, of the underlying edge or site variables"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.974286+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fb8fff362c8249e98704b89baabf231efeaf842e818303da3b033c4ea1e6cfba","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). In two-dimensional critical or near-critical percolation, RSW theory states that if crossing probabilities of n x n squares are uniformly bounded away from 0 as n grows, then crossing probabilities of rho n x n rectangles, for any fixed aspect ratio rho, are also uniformly bounded away from 0 (and from 1) by a constant depending on rho but not on n. The classical proof glues together several square-crossing events using the FKG inequality and translation and reflection symmetry of the lattice. RSW estimates are the essential multi-scale input for proving arm-exponent bounds, conformal-invariance-adjacent results, and, via the Duminil-Copin-Tassion approach, for establishing sharpness of the phase transition without relying on exact self-duality. RSW does not by itself prove existence of a scaling limit as n -> infinity, does not give the exact value of any crossing probability, only two-sided bounds; and the classical form required exact self-duality (p=1/2 on the square lattice), so extending the theory to general planar lattices or to p != 1/2 required a genuinely new, duality-free argument (Tassion, 2016). Typical failure: Assuming that RSW-type bounded-away-from-0/1 crossing estimates transfer automatically to a new planar model merely because it is monotone and planar; RSW requires either exact self-duality or the more robust but still nontrivial Tassion-style construction, and models without FKG, or with strong enough long-range dependence, can fail to admit the needed gluing arguments even though they look superficially similar to Bernoulli percolation. Canonical reference: Russo, 1978, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Seymour and Welsh, 1978, Annals of Discrete Mathematics; Tassion, 2016, Probability Theory and Related Fields.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Ω bounded open with Lipschitz boundary, n ≥ 2","1 ≤ p < ∞ for existence, boundedness and kernel; 1 < p < ∞ for the fractional-space range description","Green's identity form: u ∈ H^2(Ω), v ∈ H^1(Ω)"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492614+00:00","domain":"Sobolev spaces, boundary traces, elliptic boundary value problems","id":"claim_fb9c6a675246add69d2d408b990ef27f4904b933fa93e1e739f05b2304fd2786","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Ω ⊂ R^n (n ≥ 2) be a bounded open set with Lipschitz boundary, dS the surface measure and ν the outward unit normal (defined dS-a.e.), and let 1 ≤ p < ∞.

(1) Existence and boundedness. There is a unique bounded linear operator T : W^{1,p}(Ω) → L^p(∂Ω, dS) such that Tu = u|_{∂Ω} for every u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω) ∩ C(Ω̄). Tu is the trace of u, and ||Tu||_{L^p(∂Ω)} ≤ C(Ω, p) ||u||_{W^{1,p}(Ω)}.

(2) Kernel. ker T = W^{1,p}_0(Ω), the closure of C_c^∞(Ω) in W^{1,p}(Ω). A W^{1,p} function vanishes on ∂Ω in the trace sense exactly when it is a W^{1,p}-limit of compactly supported smooth functions.

(3) Range (Gagliardo). For 1 < p < ∞ the range of T is exactly the fractional Sobolev space W^{1−1/p, p}(∂Ω), and T has a bounded linear right inverse W^{1−1/p, p}(∂Ω) → W^{1,p}(Ω). In particular T : H^1(Ω) → H^{1/2}(∂Ω) is bounded and onto, and every g ∈ H^{1/2}(∂Ω) has an extension u ∈ H^1(Ω) with Tu = g and ||u||_{H^1(Ω)} ≤ C ||g||_{H^{1/2}(∂Ω)}. For p = 1 the range is all of L^1(∂Ω). Since H^{1/2}(∂Ω) ↪ L^2(∂Ω) is compact, T : H^1(Ω) → L^2(∂Ω) is a compact operator.

(4) Integration by parts with traces. For u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω), v ∈ W^{1,p'}(Ω) with 1/p + 1/p' = 1 (p' = ∞ for p = 1) and each i,
   ∫_Ω u ∂_i v dx + ∫_Ω v ∂_i u dx = ∫_∂Ω (Tu)(Tv) ν_i dS.
Hence for u ∈ H^2(Ω), v ∈ H^1(Ω) Green's first identity ∫_Ω ∇u·∇v dx + ∫_Ω (Δu) v dx = ∫_∂Ω (∂_ν u)(Tv) dS holds with ∂_ν u := ν · T(∇u) ∈ L^2(∂Ω), and for u ∈ H^1_0(Ω) all boundary terms vanish.

Where it fails. There is no trace operator on L^p(Ω): ∂Ω has Lebesgue measure zero, an L^p class has no boundary values, and an estimate ||Tu||_{L^p(∂Ω)} ≤ C||u||_{L^p(Ω)} is false (the full W^{1,p} norm is needed). For p > 1 the range is NOT L^p(∂Ω): a general g ∈ L^2(∂Ω) has no H^1(Ω) extension. The kernel and range statements use the Lipschitz boundary (a segment / extension property); for domains with cracks, slits or cusps the boundary is not Lipschitz and these statements need modification (a crack has two sides with two different traces). The trace of ∇u exists for u ∈ H^2(Ω), not for a general u ∈ H^1(Ω), so ∂_ν u is not defined in L^2(∂Ω) for arbitrary H^1 functions.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["mu(Omega) < infinity for the global statement; a set of finite measure for the local statement","f_n measurable, f_n -> f mu-almost everywhere, all functions finite a.e."],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752876+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_fc6b659554c68f681ea95004be9535b37b79d34316ba22807d81906efef118ad","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Egorov's theorem states that on a FINITE measure space, almost everywhere convergence of measurable functions implies almost uniform convergence: for every eps > 0 there is a measurable E with mu(E) < eps such that the convergence is uniform on the complement of E. Finiteness cannot be dropped. On R with Lebesgue measure let f_n = 1_{[n, n+1]}; then f_n -> 0 at every point, but for ANY set E of finite measure the complement meets [n, n+1] for infinitely many n, so sup over the complement of E of |f_n| equals 1 for infinitely many n and the convergence is not uniform off any set of small measure. What survives on a sigma-finite space is the LOCAL statement: for every measurable A with mu(A) < infinity and every eps > 0 there is E contained in A with mu(E) < eps and uniform convergence on A minus E; equivalently, almost everywhere convergence implies almost uniform convergence on each set of finite measure. The converse implication holds in general: almost uniform convergence always implies convergence almost everywhere and in measure, on any measure space. [standard; e.g. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.33 and Exercise 2.39]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["γ is a closed piecewise C^1 curve (or a cycle) in C","the point a does not lie on the trace of γ"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.483563+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_fcf7242c6dd1f3172a2cc112bfa1af26bdbbd80032c909e06e994d0138efa1ef","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let γ : [α,β] → C be a closed piecewise C^1 curve and let a be a point not on the trace of γ. The winding number (index) of γ about a is n(γ,a) = (1/2πi) ∫_γ dz/(z - a). It is always an integer; as a function of a it is constant on each connected component of the complement of the trace of γ, and it is 0 on the unbounded component. The definition extends additively to cycles (finite formal integer combinations of closed curves) and, via continuous branches of the argument, to merely continuous closed curves. A cycle γ lying in an open set U is called null-homologous in U (homologous to zero) if n(γ,w) = 0 for every w in C minus U. An open connected U ⊂ C is simply connected if and only if every cycle in U is null-homologous in U, if and only if the complement of U in the Riemann sphere is connected. The homology form of Cauchy's theorem reads: if f is holomorphic on U and γ is a cycle null-homologous in U, then ∫_γ f(z) dz = 0 and n(γ,z) f(z) = (1/2πi) ∫_γ f(ζ)/(ζ - z) dζ for every z in U off the trace of γ.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["proper strictly positive metric for deterministic preservation","iid positive nonatomic finite edge law for the probability reduction"],"created_at":"2026-10-10T08:26:09.577489+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fe5c2644db5e052d48209785b957e13ca9feb79aca265ec63423a884e7f75d3c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Author-proved reduction awaiting independent review. A finite straddling segment decreases by Delta=t_e-s; a simple competitor decreases by either Delta if it uses e or zero if it avoids e. Thus every e-avoiding competitor has new excess cost at least Delta. A subsegment on one side stays minimizing because it sits inside a minimizing straddling segment. In iid nonatomic positive FPP, positive probability of a bigeodesic through e implies positive probability of such a uniformly pinned bigeodesic under the same iid law: choose a<b<c with F(b)>0 and P(A_e,t_e>=c)>0, where a is the essential infimum, then independently resample s with law F. The event has probability F(b)*P(A_e,t_e>=c)>0 and penalty at least c-b. This multiplication uses exactly the fresh independent coordinate. No planar exclusion of these pinned paths is proved.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space","T is closed and symmetric (densely defined)","for (4): a conjugation C commuting with T and preserving D(T)","for (5): T is bounded below"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.770296+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, spectral theory, quantum mechanics","id":"claim_fef73e82220c1605ab1687b464def45e92df0b81dcaad18abcd8ead67320c0b8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let T be a closed symmetric operator on a complex Hilbert space H, with deficiency subspaces K_+ = ker(T* − i), K_- = ker(T* + i) and deficiency indices n_± = dim K_±. Then: (1) D(T*) = D(T) ⊕ K_+ ⊕ K_-, a direct sum which is orthogonal for the graph inner product ⟨x, y⟩ + ⟨T*x, T*y⟩. (2) The closed symmetric extensions of T correspond bijectively to partial isometries from a closed subspace of K_+ into K_-; the self-adjoint extensions correspond bijectively to unitary operators U: K_+ → K_- (onto), via D(T_U) = {x + φ + Uφ : x ∈ D(T), φ ∈ K_+} and T_U(x + φ + Uφ) = Tx + iφ − iUφ. (3) Hence T has a self-adjoint extension iff n_+ = n_-; T is self-adjoint iff n_+ = n_- = 0; if n_+ = n_- = n with 1 ≤ n < ∞, the self-adjoint extensions form a family parametrized by the unitary group U(n); if exactly one of n_± is 0 and the other is not, T is maximal symmetric and has no self-adjoint extension. (4) If there is a conjugation C (antiunitary, C² = I) with C D(T) ⊂ D(T) and TC = CT, then n_+ = n_- (von Neumann's conjugation criterion; e.g. real differential operators with real coefficients). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.627086+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_ff59d2398b1d8908abce8ec01c01a24a737fa38a46423f1defdc0f7bb6f05a02","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a topological space. The Borel sigma-algebra B(X) is the smallest sigma-algebra of subsets of X containing every open set (equivalently, every closed set); its members are the Borel sets. It is the intersection of all sigma-algebras containing the topology, so it exists and is unique. On the real line, B(R) is generated equally by the open intervals, by the closed intervals, by the half-lines (-infinity, a] with a rational, or by any base of the topology; every open, closed, F_sigma (countable union of closed sets) and G_delta (countable intersection of open sets) set is Borel, and the Borel sets are stratified by the Borel hierarchy of countable length omega_1. B(R^n) equals the product sigma-algebra of n copies of B(R). Every continuous map between topological spaces is Borel measurable (preimages of Borel sets are Borel), as is every pointwise limit of a sequence of Borel measurable real functions; but the image of a Borel set under a continuous map need not be Borel - such images are the analytic sets (Suslin, 1917). B(R) has the cardinality of the continuum, 2^{aleph_0}, while the Lebesgue measurable sets number 2^{2^{aleph_0}} (every subset of the null Cantor set is measurable), so there exist Lebesgue measurable sets that are not Borel: Lebesgue measure on B(R) is completed by adjoining all subsets of Borel null sets. Every finite Borel measure on a Polish space is regular (inner regular by compact sets: a Radon measure), which is why Borel sets are the natural domain of measures on metric spaces.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-12T06:09:38.198610+00:00","domain":"general topology","id":"claim_ff61ff48cce572f4f7d51c7a320ea48eadc31611bdd1fdfe4cc31d52318be257","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For A a subset of a topological space (X, tau), the subspace (relative) topology on A is tau_A = { A intersect U : U in tau }: its open sets are the intersections with A of open sets of X, and likewise its closed sets are the intersections with A of closed sets of X. This is a topology - it contains A and empty, and the identities (A intersect U1) intersect (A intersect U2) = A intersect (U1 intersect U2) and union of (A intersect U_i) = A intersect (union U_i) give closure under finite intersections and arbitrary unions. It is the coarsest topology making the inclusion i: A -> X continuous, since i is continuous for a topology sigma on A iff A intersect U is sigma-open for every U in tau, i.e. iff tau_A is contained in sigma. Universal property: for any space Z, a map f: Z -> A is continuous iff the composite Z -> A -> X is continuous - the property that characterizes the subspace topology.","status":"unverified"}

More technically it says that if a sequence of functions is bounded in absolute value by an integrable function and is almost everywhere pointwise convergent to a function then the sequence converges in to its pointwise limit, and in particular the integral of the limit is the limit of the integrals. Its power and utility are two of the primary theoretical advantages of Lebesgue integration over Riemann integration.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Lebesgue measure on R^n","M is the centered or uncentered Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.553467+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, maximal functions","id":"claim_ffa8aee1191447b8b8fa930b110a55716c66233d776634ca4058ba7238a266e6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The Hardy-Littlewood maximal inequality is WEAK type (1,1), never strong type (1,1), and Marcinkiewicz interpolation gives nothing at p = 1 (its constant contains p/(p - p_0) and blows up as p -> 1+). Precisely: if f is in L^1(R^n) and f is not a.e. 0, then Mf is NOT in L^1(R^n). Global counterexample: pick R with c = int_{B(0,R)} |f| > 0; for |x| >= R the ball B(x, 2|x|) contains B(0,R), so Mf(x) >= c / (v_n (2|x|)^n), which is not integrable at infinity. Local counterexample showing the failure is not only at infinity: f(x) = |x|^{-n} (log(1/|x|))^{-2} 1_{{|x| < 1/2}} is in L^1, but averaging over B(x, 2|x|) gives Mf(x) >= c' |x|^{-n} (log(1/|x|))^{-1} near 0, which is not locally integrable. The correct endpoint substitutes are: (i) the weak (1,1) bound |{Mf > t}| <= 3^n ||f||_1 / t; (ii) Stein's L log L theorem: for f supported in a ball B, Mf is integrable over B if and only if int_B |f| log^+ |f| < infinity. So a proof that applies 'M is bounded on L^p' at p = 1, or that interpolates strong (1,1) with strong (infinity, infinity), is wrong; the same warning applies to any operator known only to be weak (1,1), such as the Calderon-Zygmund singular integrals and the Hilbert transform.","status":"unverified"}

The uncentered version is M'f(x) = sup over all open balls B containing x of (1/|B|) int_B |f|; one has Mf <= M'f <= 2^n Mf. {"assumptions":["Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0131-recurrence-transience-dichotomy-for-excited-random-walks-in-dimension","No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:26:45.048267+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ffe45b11bea72f88b0f33db0ab1140dd2a354730db9d40293fa198c173753b6c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Compare with the RWRE 0-1 law in d >= 3 (C0044) and locate the extra difficulty from self-interaction. Result: For Markovian RWRE the dichotomy question is the directional 0-1 law (C0044, open in d >= 3). For excited random walks the process is not Markov, and even the statement 'either recurrent or transient' (return to the origin infinitely often a.s. or finitely often a.s.) is not implied by any Markov-chain dichotomy; the source's Definition 3.1 asks for a 0-1 law for the number of returns. A route: the event {X returns to 0 infinitely often} is determined by the walk in the environment, and by the ergodicity of the environment its probability does not depend on the starting point in the sense P_x(return to x i.o.) is constant in x; but P_0(return to 0 i.o.) in (0,1) is not excluded by that. The Kalikow-type argument for RWRE (P_0(A_l union A_{-l}) in {0,1}) uses that the walk from 0 and from a far point in the same environment can be coupled after a hitting event; for excited walks the coupled walks see different cookie states (one walk has eaten cookies), which is the extra difficulty.
